**T-451 — the Garbled Warning — designed:** T-450 left its warning-fidelity problem named and open: whether a carried warning that arrives garbled, partial, or altered in transit still warns, or whether any infidelity voids the warning and restores the downstream reader to innocence. T-451 answers: fidelity is graded, not binary — a warning that keeps its core still warns however garbled its wording, and a warning that loses its core warns nothing, however faithfully its shell was copied. The core is one sentence: this leg is an echo, and an echo counts nothing as a second seeing. A carried warning that preserves that sentence, in any words, puts the downstream reader on notice under T-450, and he cannot afterwards plead innocence of the echo. A carried warning that drops that sentence, reverses it, or attaches it to the wrong echo is not a degraded warning but no warning at all — and a reversed or misattached warning is worse than silence, because it does not merely leave the reader unwarned, it actively certifies a leg the file has already condemned.

The first reason is that a warning warns by its content, not by its pedigree. T-450 already separated notice from naming: the carrier cannot carry the remedy, but he can carry the doubt. Doubt travels in the sentence that names it, and a sentence survives rewording, abbreviation, and even clumsy copying so long as the doubt it names survives with it. A warning copied with a dropped adjective, a transposed clause, or a carrier's own plain-words paraphrase still says the leg is an echo, and a reader who reads it knows what he is standing on. To void such a warning for infidelity of wording would be to demand that doubt arrive in the file's exact words or not at all — which is to demand the file's naming under another name, and T-450 refused exactly that demand. The test, therefore, is the core, not the copy: does the downstream reader, reading what actually arrived, learn that his leg is an echo? If yes, he is a Warned Reader, and the carrier's garble is a blemish on the road, not a pardon for the reader.

The second reason is that the core test cuts the other way with equal force, and the file must not pretend otherwise. A warning that arrives saying the echo is confirmed, that the second seeing has been supplied, or that the doubt has been cleared reverses the core, and a reversed warning does not warn badly — it un-warns. The reader who trusts it places his date with a confidence the file never gave him, and his confidence is the carrier's work, not his own innocence. Likewise a warning attached to the wrong echo — the right doubt, the wrong leg — warns nobody about the leg it lands on, and leaves the leg it belongs to unwarned; misattachment is not partial fidelity but a filing error with a victim at each end. In both cases the reader is not a Warned Reader at all: he was told the opposite of the truth, or told the truth about something else. The file records him as unwarned, and the blame for his unwarned state is assigned, not absorbed: the carrier bears the garble he introduced, whether by copying error, paraphrase drift, or misattachment, and the file's own correction duty under T-450 stands entirely undischarged until its own naming arrives. A garbled warning never discharges the file, because discharge was never the carrier's to give; it only ever warned, and where it failed to warn, it failed completely.

The third reason is that grading fidelity protects both ends of the road from the two frauds a binary rule would invite. A binary rule that any garble voids the warning would let every Warned Reader plead a dropped comma back into innocence, and no carrier's warning would ever stick — the downstream reader could always find a blemish and claim he never knew. A binary rule that any warning-shaped arrival warns would let a carrier's reversed or misattached copy certify condemned legs wholesale, and the file would have to honour warnings that lie. The graded rule admits neither fraud: the reader cannot plead a blemish against a core he plainly read, and the carrier cannot plead a shell against a core he plainly lost. Between the two poles lies the honest middle the file already keeps for other partial things — T-450's Partial Warning, which is inquiry only, is the sibling here: a warning that keeps the core but loses its date, its source, or its scope still warns, and still owes the reader the file's naming; it does not warn less, it warns without the particulars, and the particulars are the file's to supply, never the carrier's to invent.

**T-452 — the Distrusted Carrier — designed:** T-450 left its warning-source problem named and open: whether a warning from a hand the reader had reason to distrust still warns — whether notice depends on the carrier's credit, or whether a warning warns whoever reads it regardless of who carried it. T-452 answers: the warning warns whoever reads it, regardless of the carrier. Notice is a property of the content read, never of the hand that carried it. A reader who reads the sentence "this leg is an echo" knows the doubt it names whether the sentence arrived from a trusted clerk or a known liar, and he cannot afterwards plead that he never knew what he plainly read. The carrier's credit belongs to the carrier's account, not to the reader's state; it may decide whether the reader believes the warning, but belief is not the test — notice is.

The first reason is that knowledge once read is not unread by distrust. Distrust may make a reader verify, discount, or investigate, but none of those acts un-reads the sentence. A reader who distrusts his carrier and places anyway places with the doubt in front of him; he may doubt the warning's truth, but doubting a warning is itself notice that the leg is contested, and a contested leg placed upon is a placement made with eyes open. To hold otherwise — that a warning from a distrusted hand warns nothing — would let every Warned Reader plead his carrier's bad name back into innocence, the same fraud T-451 refused for garble: the reader could always find a reason to distrust somebody and claim he never knew. The file judges notice by what reached the reader's eyes and what it said, never by whose hand carried it.

The second reason is that distrust cuts the other way with equal force, and the file must not pretend otherwise. A warning from a trusted hand that the reader ignores is still a warning he received; credit neither creates notice nor destroys it. And a warning the reader never read — because distrust made him discard it unread, because it arrived in a tongue he cannot read, because it never reached his desk — warns nothing, not because the carrier lacked credit but because the reader's eyes never met the sentence. The test is the Reader's Eyes: did the reader read a sentence naming echo-ness? If yes, he is a Warned Reader under T-450, whatever he thought of the carrier. If no, he is unwarned, whatever the carrier's standing. Delivery is not reading, and credit is not content.

The third reason is that separating notice from credit protects the file's own naming from becoming a popularity contest. If notice depended on carrier credit, the file would need a register of whom each reader trusts, and every placement would be graded on a reputation the file cannot verify — a second, shadow file of gossip standing beside the file of dates. T-450 already refused the carrier the power to discharge; T-452 refuses him the power to warn or un-warn by reputation either. The carrier's credit matters exactly once: to his own account. A distrusted carrier who carries faithfully has carried faithfully, and the reader he warned is warned. A distrusted carrier who garbles bears his garble under T-451, and the reader he misled is unwarned. In neither case does the carrier's name change what the reader read — only what the reader read changes what the reader knows.

**T-453 — the Disbelieved Warning — designed:** T-452 left its disbelieved-warning problem named and open: whether a warning the reader reads but affirmatively disbelieves after investigation still counts as notice when he places — whether investigation that concludes the warning false restores innocence, or whether only the file's naming can clear a doubt a carrier raised. T-453 answers: the doubt sticks until the file clears it. A reader who reads the warning, investigates, and concludes it false places as a Contested Reliance, not an innocent one: he places knowing a doubt was raised against his leg, and his private conclusion does not erase the notice, because notice is a fact about what reached his eyes under T-452's Reader's Eyes test, and a private investigation is not a fact in the file. Only the file's own naming — echo, date, and third mark together — or a third mark meeting T-444's threshold can clear the doubt. Until then the reader places at his own risk: if the file later confirms the echo, he cannot plead innocence, and if the file clears the leg, his date stands without re-filing.

The first reason is that a private investigation is unverifiable in the file, and clearance must be an act the file can check. The file can verify its own naming: a reader who meets it there can check the echo, the date, and the third mark together. It cannot verify the reader's private inquiry — what he checked, how far he went, whether his sources were independent of the carrier or downstream of the echo itself. To let private investigation clear a public warning would let every Warned Reader manufacture innocence in his own study and present it as fact, and the file would have to take his word for the clearance exactly where the whole echo danger is that a word can travel without its file. Notice is cleared by an act the file can check, never by an act only the reader witnessed.

The second reason is that disbelief is not clearance, and the asymmetry is the whole point. A reader who disbelieves after investigation faces two live possibilities: his investigation was right, and the leg is not an echo, or his investigation was wrong, and his sources were the echo's own downstream wearing the shape of confirmation. He cannot tell which from inside his investigation, because the echo's danger is precisely that it looks like a second seeing. Placing on a disbelieved warning is therefore a gamble the reader takes knowingly, and the file files the gamble, not the innocence. If his investigation was right and the file later clears the leg, the gamble pays and no correction is owed. If it was wrong, the Echo Correction reaches him as a Warned Reader, not as an innocent one: the correction still names the third mark his date actually stands on, but his posture is Contested Reliance, and he cannot claim the file failed to warn him, because the file's warning reached his eyes and his own investigation answered it in private.

The third reason is that the rule keeps the warning challengeable without making it erasable by fiat. The warning is not a verdict — T-450 already refused it discharge power, and T-453 refuses it the opposite power too: it does not become unchallengeable merely because it was carried. The reader may challenge it, but the challenge runs through the file: he brings his investigation to the file, the file checks it against the third mark, and the file's naming settles it. A doubt raised in public is answered in public. A reader who keeps his challenge private keeps his doubt too — and a reader who teaches his private clearance downstream teaches a clearance the file never gave, which files as his act, never as the file's.

**T-454 — the Pending Challenge — designed:** T-453 left its pending-challenge problem named and open: whether a reader's investigation brought to the file but not yet ruled on suspends the Echo Correction or merely queues it, and whether the reader who places while his challenge is pending places as contested or as suspended. T-454 answers: the challenge queues the correction, it does not suspend it — and the reader who places while his challenge is pending places as a Contested Reliance bearing a Pending Challenge, not as a Suspended Reliance. The Echo Correction proceeds on its own schedule, naming the third mark the date actually stands on; the pending challenge does not hold it back, and the placement is not held in abeyance either, because a placement is an act the reader chose to make knowing a ruling was outstanding, and the file files acts, not waits.

The first reason is that suspension would hand every challenger a veto by filing. If bringing a challenge to the file froze the Echo Correction until the file ruled, any reader who wanted his warned date left alone could freeze it indefinitely by lodging a challenge and letting it sit unruled — the correction that T-448 made one-per-placement, direct, and naming would become optional for anyone willing to file paper. A queue preserves the file's motion: the correction arrives, the challenge is heard, and the ruling still has full effect when it lands. If the file clears the leg, the correction is withdrawn and the date stands without re-filing, exactly as T-453 promised for a cleared leg. If the file confirms the echo, the correction stands, and the challenge does not die with the old placement — it survives against the corrected leg, because the challenger disputed the warning, not the date, and the corrected leg is the leg he must now answer.

The second reason is that a placement while pending is a gamble taken with eyes open, and the file must file the gamble, not the wait. A Suspended Reliance would pretend the reader placed nothing until the ruling, and would let him keep the benefit of the date while disowning the act of placing it — the same private-clearance trick T-453 refused, wearing a procedural mask. Contested Reliance with a Pending Challenge flag preserves both facts at once: he placed, and his challenge was live when he placed. If the ruling later clears the leg, the flag lifts and the date stands clean, and no correction is owed. If the ruling confirms the echo, the Echo Correction finds him as a Contested Reliance, not as an innocent one and not as a reader who was waiting — he cannot plead that he placed before the file spoke, because the file had already warned him, his own challenge proves he knew the warning was live, and his placement was made under that knowledge.

The third reason is that only a filed pending counts, and the distinction is what keeps the queue honest. A challenge is pending when it is brought to the file — dated, showing the investigation the reader relies on, and lodged where the file can rule on it against the third mark. A challenge merely announced downstream, told to other readers, or kept in the reader's study is not pending at all: it is T-453's private investigation in another coat, and it buys neither a queue entry nor a flag. The file cannot queue what was never lodged with it, and a reader who teaches his pending challenge downstream teaches a posture the file never gave, which files as his act, never as the file's. Filed pending earns the queue and the flag; announced pending earns nothing, and the correction proceeds as if it had never been spoken.

**T-455 — the Challenge Deadline — designed:** T-454 left its challenge-deadline problem named and open: how long a challenge may sit unruled before it lapses or is deemed abandoned — whether the file owes a ruling deadline, or whether a challenger who lets his challenge age has abandoned it by inaction. T-455 answers: the file owes the deadline, and the deadline is a term of the queue, not a judgment on the challenge — a challenge unruled when its term expires lapses, and a lapsed challenge loses its queue entry and its Pending Challenge flag, but decides nothing about the leg; and a challenger whose challenge lapsed through the file's own delay may re-file on the same investigation, while a challenger who abandoned his challenge may re-file only on new investigation.

The first reason is that a queue without a term is T-454's veto in slow motion. T-454 refused suspension because any reader could freeze the correction by filing and letting it sit; an open-ended queue hands the same reader the same freeze under a slower name — the correction proceeds, but the challenger keeps the flag, the posture of contest, and the threat of a ruling forever, and every later reader must place under a challenge that will never be answered. A term converts the queue from a wait into a tenancy: the challenge holds its place only for the term the file announced when the challenge was lodged, and when the term expires the place reverts. The term is announced at lodging and fixed there — a deadline moved after filing, or extended silently mid-queue, is not a term but a ruling disguised as procedure, and a file that moves its own deadline to kill a challenge it dislikes has ruled without meeting the third mark.

The second reason is that lapse is procedural, never substantive, and that is what keeps the deadline honest. A lapse neither confirms the echo nor clears the leg: the Echo Correction that already arrived stands on its own naming, and the placement keeps whatever posture the correction gave it — a Contested Reliance stays contested, a Warned Reader stays warned — minus only the Pending Challenge flag, which marked a live contest, not a standing one. A deadline that decided the leg would let the file rule by calendar, clearing or confirming without ever meeting the third mark; a deadline that merely ends the tenancy decides nothing, and the challenger who wants a ruling on the merits must earn it by re-filing, not inherit it from the clock. The flag lifts because the contest is no longer live; the placement does not change, because the placement was an act, and acts do not unhappen when a term expires. A ruling delivered after the term is void as a ruling on that challenge — it may still enter as the file's own fresh naming if it meets the Standing Correction form, but not as a ruling on a dead challenge, and whether such a naming binds readers who stood on the lapsed challenge is the stale-challenge problem, sharpened, not solved.

The third reason is that lapse and abandonment are different deaths, and the file must tell them apart, because they carry different re-filing rights. A challenge lapses when the file's own term expires with the challenge still standing and the challenger still answering — the delay is the file's, so the challenger keeps his investigation and may re-file on it; the file's slowness must not eat the challenger's standing. A challenge is abandoned when the challenger withdraws it, or when the file calls for the investigation papers and the challenger does not produce them, or when the challenger's own standing lapses — the death is the challenger's, so re-filing on the same investigation buys nothing; only new investigation earns a new queue entry, because the old one was not lost to the clock but surrendered. The distinction is the whole protection against both abuses at once: the file cannot kill a challenge by dawdling and then plead the deadline, and the challenger cannot kill his own challenge and then revive it unchanged.

**T-456 — the Extended Term — designed:** T-455 left its extension problem named and open: whether the file may extend its own term mid-queue — for instance when the third mark itself is under examination elsewhere — or whether any extension is a new term requiring re-lodging, and whether an extension announced to one challenger extends every pending challenge on the same leg. T-456 answers: the file may not extend a term by fiat mid-queue — an extension is a new term, and a new term requires re-lodging; but when the cause of the delay is the file's own examination, the re-lodging is the file's act, not the challenger's burden, and it preserves the original date; and an extension extends every pending challenge on the same leg only when its cause is leg-common, never when its cause is challenger-specific.

The first reason is that a term announced at lodging is a promise the file made to every reader, not only to the challenger, and a promise the file can quietly move is no promise at all. T-455 fixed the term at lodging precisely so that a file which dislikes a challenge cannot kill it by moving its own deadline — a deadline moved after filing is a ruling disguised as procedure. That protection dies the moment the file may extend by announcement alone: a file that can extend can also extend selectively, holding a favoured challenge alive while letting a disfavoured one lapse, and calling both acts procedure. A new term requiring re-lodging keeps the extension visible: the old term ends on its announced date, the new term begins on a new lodging date, and any reader can see the seam between them. The challenger who must re-lodge bears no penalty for the seam when the delay was the file's — the file re-lodges on his behalf, on his original investigation, with his original date preserved for priority — because the file's slowness must not eat the challenger's standing, the same rule T-455 set for lapse. The challenger who must re-lodge when the delay was his own — papers unproduced, standing lapsed — earns no preservation: his new term files as new, with a new date, because his old term died by his hand, not the file's.

The second reason is that the cause of the delay decides the scope of the extension, and the cause is either in the leg or in the challenger, never in both at once for the same delay. When the third mark itself is under examination elsewhere, the file cannot rule on any challenge against that leg — the ruling standard is the third mark, and a mark under examination cannot be met — so every pending challenge on that leg is delayed by the same cause, and an extension for one is an extension for all, announced once, to the leg, not to the challenger. When the delay is challenger-specific — one challenger's papers outstanding, one challenger's standing in question — the cause touches only that challenger, and an extension announced to him extends nobody else; other challengers on the same leg keep their own terms, lapse on their own dates, and are not held hostage to a stranger's slow papers. A file that extends one challenger's term and lets the extension travel silently to the whole leg has granted every other challenger a tenancy none of them asked for and none of them can be charged with; a file that withholds a leg-common extension from one challenger while granting it to another has ruled against that challenger without meeting the third mark.

The third reason is that a re-lodging the file performs must still be confirmed by the challenger, because a tenancy held for a reader who no longer stands is a tenancy held against the file. The file's automatic re-lodging preserves the date and the investigation, but it does not presume the challenger still stands: the challenger must confirm his standing within the new term's opening, or the re-lodged challenge lapses as abandoned, not as lapsed — the death is his, so re-filing on the same investigation buys nothing, by T-455's rule. This keeps the extension honest in both directions: the file cannot kill a challenge by dawdling, because its own delay triggers its own re-lodging; and a challenger cannot ride a file-caused extension forever, because his failure to confirm ends the tenancy by his own inaction, and the flag lifts with it. A confirmation that arrives after the new term's opening is a fresh filing, not a confirmation, and files as new.

**T-457 — the Late Confirmation — designed:** T-456 left its late-confirmation problem named and open: whether a challenger who confirms his standing late — after the new term's opening but before any ruling — may still be restored to the preserved date, or whether the late confirmation files as new and the preserved date is lost for good. T-457 answers: the late confirmation files as new, and the preserved date is not restored by the challenger's act — but the file may restore it by its own naming, and only while nothing has moved in reliance on the lapse. A late confirmation that arrives before any ruling on the leg, and before any reader has placed in reliance on the lapse, may be met by a Restoration Naming that restores the preserved date for priority; a late confirmation that arrives after a ruling, or after an intervening reliance, files as new and the preserved date is lost for good, not merely withheld.

The first reason is that the opening is a door, not a suggestion, and a door that stays open until the challenger chooses to walk through it is T-455's veto in slow motion. T-456 made confirmation within the new term's opening the act that keeps the file's re-lodging alive, precisely so that a challenger could not ride a file-caused extension forever. If a late confirmation restored the preserved date by the challenger's act alone, the opening would mean nothing: the challenger could confirm at any hour before a ruling and keep his date, and every later reader would place under a date that might spring back to life at any moment. Filing as new keeps the clock honest — the late confirmer stands from the date he actually confirmed, and no reader need guess whether a dead tenancy will revive.

The second reason is that restoration, when it happens, is the file's naming, not the challenger's right, and a naming harms no one only while nothing has moved. A ruling on the leg is a naming that settles standings; a placement made in reliance on the lapse is a reader building on ground the file left empty. To restore a preserved date after either would rewrite another reader's standing by grace — the late confirmer would leapfrog a reader who placed honestly, or stand ahead of a ruling that already spoke. But where neither has happened — no ruling, no intervening reliance — restoration rewrites nothing: the ground is still empty, the date still free, and the file's naming merely records that the challenger who still stands keeps the place he never truly abandoned. That is why restoration is possible at all, and why it is the file's act: only the file can see whether the ground moved, and only the file may name what its own queue still holds.

The third reason is that restoration restores the date for priority only, never the dead term. A restored challenger keeps his original date against readers who placed after the lapse, but his term runs from the restoration, not from the opening he missed — the new term he confirmed into is the term he lives under, and its announced end still binds him. To restore the term as well as the date would resurrect a tenancy that already died, and hand the late confirmer the very open-ended hold T-456 refused. And a challenger who confirms after a ruling, or after an intervening reliance, has not merely been late: his tenancy died and others built on its death, so restoration is impossible, not merely withheld — the file cannot unbuild what readers have built, and the late confirmer answers the ruling as it stands, from his new date.

**T-458 — the Reliance Standard — designed:** T-457 left its restoration-standard problem named and open: whether the intervening reader must have cited the lapse, or whether any placement on the leg after the lapse is enough to block restoration, and whether a placement the file never saw counts at all. T-458 answers: the test is displacement, not citation and not chronology. An intervening reliance is a placement on the leg, filed after the lapse, that would lose its standing — its priority, its date, or its leg — if the preserved date sprang back. A placement after the lapse that would stand regardless of restoration is not a reliance at all, and blocks nothing; a placement the file never saw counts only if it surfaces before the Restoration Naming, and files as new against the restored date if it surfaces after.

The first reason is that displacement, not chronology, is what restoration would injure. A placement filed after the lapse that stands on another leg, or on the third mark alone, or on a date that predates the lapse, loses nothing when the preserved date returns — the restored challenger leaps over no one, and the file's naming rewrites no standing. To let such a placement block restoration would hand every later filer a veto over a date he never stood on, and T-457's restoration would die not by injury but by traffic: any placement anywhere after the lapse, however unrelated, would freeze the ground forever. The file protects standings, not timestamps, and a placement that restoration leaves untouched is no reason to withhold a naming.

The second reason is that citation is evidence of reliance, not the test of it. A reader who cited the lapse in his filing proves his reliance plainly — he read the empty ground and built on it, and his citation is the file's own record of the ground he stood on. But a reader who placed silently on the emptied ground still relied: the file judges the ground, not the paperwork, and a placement that would be displaced by restoration blocks it whether or not its filer wrote the lapse down. The converse holds with equal force: a reader who cited the lapse in words but placed on a leg restoration leaves untouched cited a fact he did not stand on, and his citation blocks nothing — words about the ground are not a standing on it, and the file does not let a footnote veto a naming.

The third reason is that the file can only weigh what it can see, and a naming, once made, settles the ground it names. An unseen placement that surfaces before the Restoration Naming counts in full: the file judges the ground as it stands when it names, and a displaced reader who files in time is a displaced reader, however late his paper arrived. But an unseen placement that surfaces after the Naming files as new against the restored date — it does not unmake the Naming, because a naming unmade by any late paper is no naming at all, and T-457's restoration would become a veto in reverse, hostage to every placement the file never saw. Finality is the price of restoration: the challenger keeps his date because the ground was empty when the file named it, and a reader who arrives after the naming answers the restored date as it stands, from his new filing.

**T-459 — the Demoted Reader — designed:** T-458 left its displacement-cost problem named and open: whether displacement means losing priority only, or losing the date entirely — whether a reader demoted by restoration keeps any claim on his original date.

The first reason is that a date is a fact and a priority is a ranking, and restoration re-ranks; it does not un-file. The demoted reader's placement was filed on a real date, in good faith, on ground that stood open at the time. Restoration moves the restored challenger ahead of him; it cannot rewrite the calendar so that his filing never happened. A file that erases dates erases its own history, and a history-erasing file cannot be audited.

The second reason is that the retained date still does work after demotion. The demoted reader keeps his date against every reader who filed after him, and against any later lapse: if the restored challenger lapses again, the demoted reader is first in line to be restored into the vacated place, by his original date. Demotion is a step down one rung, not an exit from the ladder.

The third reason is that annulment would turn restoration into a weapon. A challenger who restores late could, by erasing the intervening reader's date, strip a good-faith filer of everything he built on his filing — citations, downstream placements, reliance of his own. The file's remedy for reliance is proportionate: the reliance is displaced, so the priority moves; the filing itself was lawful, so the date stays.

Named forms to T-289: the Demoted Reader (FILED), the Priority Loss (FILED), the Retained Date (FILED), the Queue of Dates (FILED), the Good-Faith Filing (FILED), the Demotion-Not-Annulment (FILED).

**What this pairs with.** T-458's Reliance Standard (the displacement this prices — the Displaced Reader loses his priority to the restored challenger and keeps his date against everyone else).

**Admitted-unsolved carried forward.** Whether a demoted reader who later re-files on a new leg recovers his original date or takes the new filing's date — whether the retained date travels with the reader or stays with the placement.

**T-460 — the Travelling Date — designed:** T-459 left its re-filing problem named and open: whether a demoted reader who later re-files on a new leg recovers his original date or takes the new filing's date — whether the retained date travels with the reader or stays with the placement.

T-460 answers: the date travels with the reader, but only as priority, never as record. The demoted reader who re-files on a new leg files as new on that leg's record, and stands on his original date in any priority contest. The record tells the truth about when the new leg was first stood on; the priority tells the truth about who stood first in the queue.

The first reason is that a retention that dies the moment the reader moves is no retention at all. T-459 retained the date precisely so the demoted reader keeps his place in the queue — first in line if the restored challenger lapses again, ahead of every reader who filed after him. A queue position that evaporates on re-filing would make the Retained Date a decoration: it would protect a reader only while he stands still, and punish him the moment he rebuilds elsewhere. Retention must mean the reader carries his standing with him, or it means nothing.

The second reason is that the new leg's record must still tell the truth about when it was first stood on. Filing the re-filed placement under the original date would backdate the new leg's history and mislead every later reader about who stood where, and when. So the placement files as new on the record — its record date is the re-filing date — while its priority date, in any contest, is the original date. Two dates, two offices: the record says when, the priority says who stands first. No reader is misled, because the record date is public and the priority date is claimed openly in the contest, never smuggled into the record.

The third reason is that the carriage is once-only and non-transferable. The carried priority cannot be assigned to another reader, inherited by a downstream placement, or carried on to a third leg after a second demotion; and it dies if the reader abandons the claim. Otherwise a single demoted date becomes a floating priority haunting every leg it touches, and the file's queue becomes a market in old dates rather than a record of standings. A priority that can be traded is a priority that can be bought, and a bought priority is no longer evidence of standing.

**T-461 — the Spent Carriage — designed:** T-460 left its stacked-demotion problem named and open: whether the carried priority survives a second demotion on the new leg — whether a twice-demoted reader carries his original date to a third leg, or whether carriage is spent by the first re-filing.

T-461 answers: the carriage is spent. The twice-demoted reader re-filing on a third leg files entirely fresh — new record date, new priority date, no carried priority of any vintage. The second demotion still costs what T-459 priced it at — priority only, date retained — but the date it retains is retained on the second leg alone. It does not travel again. The retained date stays home.

The first reason is that T-460's carriage was once-only by its own terms, and a once-only carriage that survives a second demotion is not once-only at all. If the original date travels to the second leg and then travels again to a third, the carriage is twice-only; and a twice-only carriage has no principle stopping it at three or four. Once-only means once: the first re-filing spends it.

The second reason is that the third leg's queue must be allowed to be its own queue. A carried date demoted twice arrives at the third leg as a claim about a history the third leg never witnessed, asking readers who filed, placed, and relied in the open to queue behind a date from a leg they never saw. The first carriage was already an exception to the record's honesty; the second would be an exception to the exception, and exceptions to exceptions are how a queue stops being a queue and becomes a pedigree.

The third reason is that spending the carriage does not strip the reader bare. The second demotion retains his date on the second leg: against every reader who filed there after his re-filing date, he still stands first, and if the restored challenger lapses again, he is first in line to return. What he loses is only the travel. The home date is kept; the travelling date is spent.

**T-462 — the Restored Home — designed:** T-461 left its restoration-after-spending problem named and open: whether a twice-demoted reader who is restored (not re-filed) on the second leg recovers his carried priority, or whether restoration returns him to a leg whose carriage is already spent.

T-462 answers: restoration restores the home date, not the carriage. The reader returns to the second leg standing on his retained date — first among every reader who filed on the second leg after his re-filing date, first in line if the restored challenger on that leg lapses again — but the carriage stays spent. Restoration is a return, not a re-filing, and only a re-filing ever spent or earned carriage. A restored reader who later leaves the second leg for a fourth leg files fresh under T-461: new record date, new priority date, nothing carried. The home is restored; the road is not reopened.

The first reason is that restoration undoes the demotion, not the spending. The second demotion displaced him from the second leg; the spending happened earlier, at the first re-filing, by T-460's once-only terms. Undoing a later event does not undo an earlier bargain. The carriage was spent when the reader carried his original date onto the second leg, and no event on the second leg — demotion, restoration, or lapse — reaches back to un-spend it. To hold otherwise would make every standing on the second leg retroactively conditional on a travel right that was already exercised and gone.

The second reason is that the home date is the whole of what restoration needs to restore. What the demoted reader lost on the second leg was standing among that leg's readers, and T-459's retention plus restoration gives it all back: against every reader who filed after his re-filing date he stands first, and if the challenger lapses again he returns first. Travel was never part of the second leg's standing; it was a right to carry a date somewhere it had never been, exercised once and spent. Restoration that also minted fresh travel would give the restored reader more than he had before the demotion — a new road out of a leg he had already arrived on by carriage — and a remedy that enriches is not a restoration.

The third reason is that un-spending by restoration would turn the once-only rule into a revolving door. A reader whose carriage is spent need only arrange a demotion and a restoration on the leg he carried to, and the spent carriage revives, ready to be spent again on a third leg, then a fourth, each revival laundered through a fresh demotion. Spending must be sticky or it is not spending: a carriage that revives whenever its holder is restored is a carriage that was never spent at all, only lent. **T-465 — the Leg-Bound Contest — designed:** T-464 left its dual-home problem named and open: whether a reader holding two home dates may invoke both in a single contest that spans legs, or whether every contest is leg-bound so each home date answers only its own leg's contests.

T-465 answers: every contest is leg-bound, without exception. A contest that spans legs is not heard as one contest with two home dates behind it; it is heard as two contests, one on each leg, each standing on that leg's home date alone. The reader with two homes does not bring both homes into the room. He brings the home that belongs to the leg the contest is heard on — and if his claim touches two legs, he elects a leg, or he is heard twice.

The first reason is that T-464's standing-not-currency rule already decides this, and the dual-home question only tests whether the rule holds under pressure. A home date is the ground a contest stands on, and ground on one leg is not ground on another. A reader who invoked his second-leg date inside a third-leg contest would be doing exactly what T-464 forbids — spending one leg's standing in another leg's queue — only dressed as procedure instead of priority. The contest's leg fixes its ground; the other home date is not in the record for that hearing, however strong it is elsewhere.

The second reason is that a spanning claim is two claims wearing one caption. A claim that a reader was wrongly demoted on the second leg and wrongly demoted on the third is not one wrong with two addresses; it is two demotions, each with its own record, its own lapse history, and its own home date. Hearing them as one contest would let the stronger leg's record rescue the weaker leg's — a reader who lost the third leg's file could borrow the second leg's clean standing to win a contest he would lose on the third leg's own ground. Splitting the hearing keeps each leg's queue honest about its own history, the same discipline T-464 applied to home dates themselves.

The third reason is that the split costs the reader nothing he earned. Election is not forfeiture: electing the second leg for the first hearing defers the third leg's contest, it does not abandon it, and a win on one leg does not decide the other. The reader who wins both hearings wins both standings; the reader who wins one keeps exactly the one he won. What he cannot do is convert two partial standings into one whole victory — a remedy that spans legs requires two wins, not one invocation of two dates. Two homes, two hearings, two verdicts; the file never merges what the legs kept separate.

**T-466 — the Sealed Record — designed:** T-465 left its shared-evidence problem named and open: whether evidence heard on one leg's hearing may be cited on the other leg's hearing without re-filing, or whether each hearing's record is sealed to its own leg.

T-466 answers: each hearing's record is sealed to its own leg. Evidence heard on the second leg's hearing is not evidence on the third leg's hearing until it is re-filed there — offered again, on that leg's record, under that leg's rules. A citation to the other hearing's transcript is notice that the evidence exists; it is not the evidence itself. The reader who wants the same fact heard twice files it twice, once per leg, and each hearing judges only what was filed in its own record.

The first reason is that T-465's split hearing is meaningless if the record is not split with it. Two hearings that share one record are one hearing held in two rooms: the stronger leg's record would rescue the weaker leg's case exactly the way T-465 forbade the stronger leg's home date from rescuing it. A reader who lost the third leg's file could cite the second leg's clean transcript into the third leg's hearing and win a contest he would lose on the third leg's own evidence. Sealing the record is what makes the split real — each leg's queue is judged on its own filings, not on a borrowed transcript.

The second reason is that a record is not a pile of facts but a history of offers, objections, and rulings, and that history belongs to one leg's procedure. Evidence admitted on the second leg was admitted under the second leg's rules, against the second leg's objections, in the second leg's order; the third leg's hearing has its own objections to hear and its own order to keep. Importing the transcript wholesale would import rulings the third leg never made, and would leave the third leg's reader no room to object to evidence he never saw offered. Re-filing gives him that room: the evidence is offered fresh, the objections are heard fresh, and the ruling is the third leg's own.

The third reason is that re-filing costs the reader nothing he earned. The facts do not change when they are re-filed; only their standing changes, from cited to heard. A reader who holds the evidence holds it for both legs, and filing it twice is the same labour the split hearing already asked of him — two hearings, two filings, two records. What he cannot do is convert one filing into two hearings — a hearing that never received the evidence cannot be said to have weighed it, however fully the other hearing did.

The second reason is that hearing speed and queue priority answer different questions, and the file already keeps them apart. A prompt re-filer has shown diligence, and diligence is a reason to hear him soon: the file need not make him wait behind a calendar backlog while intervening readers' filings are considered at leisure. **T-469 — the Added Hearing — designed:** T-468 left its expedition-scope problem named and open: whether expedition of a prompt re-filing displaces intervening readers' hearing order as well — whether hearing a prompt re-filer first delays intervening readers' hearings, or whether expedition means only that his hearing is added, not that theirs move. T-469 answers: added, never displacing. The prompt re-filer's hearing is an added hearing: it takes an open or newly created slot on the calendar, and every intervening reader's hearing keeps its date. Expedition moves the prompt re-filer sooner; it moves nobody else later.

The first reason is that displacement would turn hearing speed back into queue priority in calendar form. T-468's whole distinction was that promptness earns speed, not priority — heard sooner, still ordered behind. If "heard sooner" is achieved by taking another reader's sitting, the intervening reader's hearing is delayed so the prompt re-filer can be considered first, and consideration-first is governance-first in practice: the leg hears his evidence before theirs, on a question where order of consideration shapes what is settled first. That is displacement wearing expedition's name — the same borrowed standing T-467 forbade for dates, now paid in calendar days instead of queue places. An added hearing avoids the cheat: the prompt re-filer is heard soon, and the readers ahead of him are heard on time, both promises kept because the calendar grows by one sitting rather than reordering its existing ones.

The second reason is that the calendar can grow, and the queue cannot be reordered without injury. A queue position is a rival good — one reader's advance is another's retreat. A hearing slot is not: the file can sit an extra day, hear an added matter at the margin of a sitting, or take the next open sitting, without touching any date already promised. Expedition therefore costs the file effort, not the intervening readers' time. If no added slot exists before the intervening hearings — no open sitting, no margin, no extra day the file will sit — then expedition waits: "soon" means the first available added slot, not another reader's slot. A speedy hearing that cannot be added is a hearing at the next open sitting, still ahead of the backlog behind it, still behind the readers already calendared.

The third reason is the vacated-slot boundary, which keeps the rule honest. A sitting vacated by its own reader — withdrawn, adjourned at that reader's instance, abandoned — is an open slot, not a taken one: filling it with the prompt re-filer's hearing displaces nobody, because nobody is waiting for that sitting anymore. What the file may not do is vacate a sitting for the prompt re-filer — adjourning an intervening reader's hearing to make room, or compressing it to half its time, is displacement with a polite name. The test is simple: after expedition, does every intervening reader's hearing still fall on the date it held before? If yes, the hearing was added. If any date moved later, it was displaced, and T-469 forbids it.

**T-470 — the Created Sitting — designed:** T-469 left its no-slot problem named and open: whether expedition fails entirely when no added slot exists before the intervening hearings, or whether the file must create one (an extra sitting) — and who bears the cost of that extra sitting if it is created. T-470 answers: the file creates it, and the file bears it. Expedition is a promise the file made when it granted T-468's prompt re-filing speed; a promise that evaporates the moment it becomes inconvenient was never a grant at all, only a lottery ticket for an open calendar. When no open sitting, no margin, and no vacated slot exists before the intervening hearings, the file sits an extra sitting — an added day, an added margin, a sitting convened for this hearing alone — and the cost of that sitting falls on the file itself: its own time, its own budget, its own effort. It is never charged to the prompt re-filer as a fee for expedition, and never charged to the intervening readers as delay. That is the whole rule: the calendar grows, the bill stays with the promisor.

The first reason is that the promisor pays for its own promises. T-468 granted speed to the prompt re-filer; T-469 forbade paying for that speed with other readers' dates. If the file may instead charge the re-filer — a fee, a cost, a condition — then expedition becomes a purchased priority, and the prompt reader who cannot pay waits while the prompt reader who can is heard, which is queue priority sold back under speed's name. If the file may instead charge the intervening readers — by sitting late into their preparation time, by compressing their hearings to fund the extra one — that is displacement again, T-469's forbidden taking with the cost ledger as its disguise. The only payer left who was party to the grant is the file: it promised speed, it finds the sitting, it absorbs the sitting. A grant that costs its grantee or its neighbours is not a grant; a grant that costs its grantor is simply kept.

The second reason is that "no slot" is a fact about this calendar, not a verdict on the hearing. A calendar with no opening before the intervening hearings is full, not finished: the file can always sit one more day, unless the term itself has ended or the leg has dissolved. So the failure mode is narrow and honest — expedition defers, it does not die, and it defers only to the first sitting of the next term, still added, still undisplacing, still ahead of the backlog behind it. What the file may not do is treat a full calendar as a failed expedition: "we had no room, so your speed is gone" converts a scheduling fact into a forfeiture, and forfeiture for the file's own fullness punishes the reader for the file's calendar. The created sitting is the default; deferral to the next term is the exception, and the file must show the term's end, not merely its fullness, to claim it.

The third reason is the cost-bearing test, which keeps the rule auditable. After a created sitting, ask three questions: did every intervening reader's hearing keep its date (T-469's test)? Did the prompt re-filer pay nothing for the expedition beyond what any reader pays for any hearing? Did the file's own ledger — its sitting days, its budget, its effort — absorb the extra sitting? If all three answer yes, the sitting was created lawfully. If the re-filer paid, expedition was sold. If an intervening date moved, expedition displaced. If the file's ledger shows no cost at all, look harder: a sitting with no cost to anyone is usually a sitting taken from someone uncounted, and the uncounted reader is the one the rule exists to protect.

**T-471 — the Proof of Inability — designed:** T-470 left its impossible-sitting problem named and open: whether a file genuinely unable to sit differs from a file merely unwilling to bear the cost, and what proof of genuine inability the file must show before deferral to the next term is allowed. T-471 answers: inability is a fact about authority, not a feeling about cost, and the file must prove it in public before it may defer. A term ended, a leg dissolved, an authority to convene extinguished — these are showable facts, each with a record outside the file's own say-so. Fullness, expense, inconvenience, fatigue, and a crowded docket are not inability; they are the very costs T-470 already assigned to the file. The burden sits on the file, the showing is made to the readers affected, and doubt resolves against deferral: where the proof is thin, the sitting is created.

The first reason is that unwillingness wears inability's clothes. Every file that would rather not sit an extra sitting can describe its reluctance as impossibility — "we cannot" is cheaper than "we will not pay." If the file's own word sufficed, T-470's exception would swallow its rule: the created sitting would exist only when convenient, which is to say it would not exist at all. A proof standard external to the file's say-so is what keeps the exception an exception. Cost is the test that exposes the disguise: if the only thing standing between the file and the sitting is money, effort, or an unwilling calendar, the file is unwilling, not unable, and T-470 already answered unwillingness with the promisor pays.

The second reason is that the proof has three parts, and all three are required. First, the extinguishing fact named: which term ended, which leg dissolved, which authority lapsed, and on what date — a specific fact, not a general hardship. Second, the record shown: the term's close, the dissolution, the lapsed commission — something a reader can check without taking the file's word for it. Third, the absence of an alternative sitting: no other authority that could convene, no surviving leg that could hear it, no carry-over sitting into which this hearing could be added. Miss any part and deferral fails; the file creates the sitting. A file that names the fact but shows no record is asserting, not proving. A file that shows the record but hides a surviving authority is selecting, not proving.

The third reason is that doubt creates, it does not defer. Where the record is ambiguous — a term arguably extended, a leg arguably surviving, an authority arguably renewable — the file may not spend the reader's expedition on its own uncertainty. The reader's granted speed is not the fund from which the file pays for its unclear authority. So the tie goes to the sitting: an ambiguous record means a created sitting, and the file may revisit deferral only when the record clears, not when its patience thins. This is the same honesty as T-470's cost-bearing test, turned onto the exception itself: a deferral with no cost to anyone is usually a deferral taken from someone uncounted, and the uncounted reader is the one the proof exists to protect.

**T-472 — the Narrower Sitting — designed:** T-471 left its partial-inability problem named and open: whether authority that survives for some matters but not this hearing's kind counts as inability, or whether a narrower sitting — limited to the matters the authority still covers — must be created instead. T-472 answers: partial authority is not inability; it is a narrower sitting. Where the file's authority still covers some of the hearing's matters, the file creates a sitting for those matters and defers only the matters beyond the surviving authority. The hearing is severed by the authority's edge, not abandoned at it. A file that could sit the covered half and instead defers the whole hearing has used a half-extinguishment as a whole excuse, and T-471's unwillingness bar already forbids that trade.

The first reason is that inability is measured matter by matter, not hearing by hearing. T-471 proved inability as an extinguishing fact — a term ended, a leg dissolved, an authority lapsed — and facts of that kind have edges: a commission may lapse for one class of matters while surviving for another, a leg may dissolve for appeals while standing for filings, a term may close for new business while remaining open to matters already begun. The file's showing under T-471 therefore has to name, for each matter in the hearing, whether the authority survives it. A showing that proves extinguishment for the whole hearing is rare; most showings prove it for a part. And a part-proved showing buys a part-deferral, nothing more. The remainder is still sit-able, and what is sit-able must be sat — T-470's created sitting is the default, and a partial proof narrows the exception, it does not widen it.

The second reason is that the narrower sitting protects the reader twice over. First, it preserves expedition for the covered matters: the reader who was granted speed does not lose it on matters the file could still hear, merely because the file could not hear others. Expedition is not an all-or-nothing grant that a single dead matter can forfeit. Second, it keeps the deferred remainder honest: a deferral that names exactly which matters are beyond authority, and why, is checkable in a way a whole-hearing deferral is not. The reader can see the edge — this matter covered, that matter not — and can challenge the edge itself: is the classification right, or has the file drawn the line to push a hard matter into deferral? A whole-hearing deferral hides that question; a severed hearing exposes it. The narrower sitting is therefore not just a smaller sitting; it is the form in which the partial proof becomes auditable.

The third reason is that severance has a limit, and the limit is the hearing's own coherence. Some matters cannot be severed without deciding the others: a matter whose outcome depends on a deferred matter's answer cannot be heard alone, and a hearing whose covered matters are only the preamble to a deferred decision is not a sitting but a rehearsal. Where severance would decide the deferred matter by the back door — hearing the evidence, fixing the facts, leaving only the verdict — the narrower sitting must not be created either; the whole hearing defers, and the reason is coherence, not inability. The file must show this too, matter by matter: not merely that the authority survives for the covered matters, but that those matters can be heard without prejudging the deferred ones. A file that severs to decide is worse than a file that defers whole, because it spends the reader's hearing on a decision it claims not to have made.

**T-473 — the Doubtful Edge — designed:** T-472 left its doubtful-edge problem named and open: whether a matter whose authority is itself doubtful — arguably surviving, arguably lapsed — sits on the covered side of the line or the deferred side, and whether T-471's doubt-creates rule already answers that or only answers whole-hearing doubt. T-473 answers: the doubt-creates rule already answers it, and it answers it on the covered side. A doubtful matter sits. The edge is not a third place between covered and deferred; it is a line the file must draw, and where the file cannot show the line, the matter sits on the side the reader can still reach. A file that defers a doubtful matter has turned its own uncertainty into the reader's loss, and T-471's rule already forbids spending doubt that way.

The first reason is that doubt-creates was never about the size of the doubt. T-471 stated the rule for a whole hearing because the case before it was a whole hearing — a file claiming it could not sit at all. But the rule's reason is not "big doubts create sittings"; it is "doubt is not the file's to spend." Doubt spent to defer is a benefit the file takes from its own failure to prove: it keeps the hearing from happening on the strength of a showing it could not make. That reason bites exactly as hard at the edge as at the whole. A doubtful matter deferred on doubtful authority is the same trade in miniature — the file profits from an unproved lapse — and a rule that forbids the trade at full size cannot permit it at half size. The edge inherits the rule; it does not need a new one.

The second reason is that the errors are asymmetric, and asymmetry decides placement. Sit a matter whose authority later proves lapsed, and the error is reparable: the sitting's work on that matter can be re-heard, re-founded, or struck, and the record of what was heard survives to be heard again on sound authority. Defer a matter whose authority later proves surviving, and the error is not reparable in the same way: the expedition the reader was granted for that matter is spent, the term moves on, the intervening readers T-467 named have already been heard, and no re-hearing restores the place in the queue the matter held. A reparable error on one side and an irreparable loss on the other is not a tie to be split; it is a direction. Doubt breaks toward the side whose mistake can be undone. That is the covered side.

The third reason is that sitting doubtful does not mean sitting blind. The narrower sitting marks the doubtful matter as edge-sitting — named on the record as a matter whose authority is in doubt, heard provisionally, its verdict flagged as riding on authority not yet proved. The mark does three things: it warns the reader which part of the outcome depends on the doubt, it preserves the question for the later proof instead of burying it in a deferral, and it stops the file from later claiming the sitting settled the authority question — an edge-sitting decides the matter, not the edge. A doubtful matter heard in the open, marked, is auditable; a doubtful matter deferred in silence is a decision about authority disguised as a decision about scheduling. The mark is what makes covered-side placement honest rather than merely convenient.

**T-475 — the Election Window — designed:** T-474 left its election-window problem named and open: how long the reader has to elect after the lapse proof is shown, what counts as notice of that proof, and whether silence after notice affirms the verdict by default. T-475 answers: the window opens only on proper notice, runs the remainder of the term in which notice is given plus one full term, and silence at its close affirms — but only because the window is long, the notice is strict, and an act in reliance after notice affirms sooner by conduct. A window that silently took the election away on a short clock would hand T-474's reader's choice back to the file through the calendar; a window with no close would leave every other reader, and the file, under a verdict that might fall at any moment, forever. The window must therefore be generous enough that silence at its end is a choice the reader had time to make, and strict enough about notice that the clock never runs against a reader who was never truly told.

The first reason is that notice must be proof in the record, delivered to the reader, before any clock runs. Publication alone is not notice: a lapse proof filed in the leg's record but never brought to the reader's sitting does not start the window, because the reader who sat under the mark cannot elect against proof he has not seen. A file's assertion alone is not proof either: the file saying the authority lapsed does not start the window, because the file created the doubt and may not spend its resolution — T-474's election belongs to the reader, and a clock started by the file's say-so would let the file manufacture urgency. Proper notice is therefore twofold: the lapse proof entered in the leg's record, where any reader may inspect it, and delivered to the electing reader in the sitting's own channel, so the reader knows both that the proof exists and where to find it. Defective notice never starts the clock, however long ago the defect occurred; the window opens when proper notice is given, not when the lapse happened, and a file that discovers its notice was defective must give proper notice and let the full window run from there. The file bears the cost of its own defective notice, as it bears the re-hearing under T-470.

The second reason is that the window's length must make silence at its close meaningful rather than a trap. The remainder of the term plus one full term is the measure: a reader notified mid-term has the rest of that term and a whole term after it, so even a reader notified on the term's last day has a full term to consider, seek advice, and elect. Shorter measures — a fixed count of days, a single sitting, the next hearing — would punish the reader who needs counsel or who sits on several legs, and would reward a file that times its notice for a thin week. Longer measures — no close at all, or a close only when the reader next appears — would punish everyone else: intervening readers could not tell whether the verdict they rely on will stand, and the file could not close its ledger. Term-plus-one is the honest middle: long enough that the reader's silence is fairly read as contentment with the verdict, short enough that the verdict's future is eventually settled. And the close is announced in the notice itself: proper notice states the window's end, so the reader is never surprised by a close he was not told of.

The third reason is that silence affirms, but election by conduct affirms sooner, and both preserve T-474's reliance carve-out. If the reader, after proper notice, does a fresh act in reliance on the verdict — files on it, settles under it, invokes it before another sitting — that act elects affirm by conduct, and the window closes at once, because a reader cannot both rely anew on a verdict and keep the right to void it. Acts before notice do not count: reliance already made before the lapse proof was shown is exactly what T-474's carve-out protects, and it cannot be retroactively turned into an election the reader never had the chance to make. If the reader does nothing at all, silence at the window's close affirms the verdict in full, with the lapse notwithstanding, and the verdict stands as if sound authority had founded it — not because the file earned that standing, but because the reader, properly told and given a full term and more, chose not to void it. An express election, by contrast, may be made at any point inside the window, and once made it ends the window: affirm closes it as the verdict stands, void closes it as the verdict ceases prospectively under T-474, with reliance already made kept either way.

The reader's own assertion cannot extend the window either: self-granted time would let the reader hold the verdict voidable indefinitely, which is the same evil T-475's close was built to end — a verdict that might fall at any moment, forever. **T-477 — the Pending Request — designed:** T-476 left its late-request problem named and open: whether a request filed inside the window but not decided until after the window's close tolls the close while it pends, or whether the reader who files late in the window bears the risk of the sitting's delay. T-477 answers: it tolls. A request filed inside the window holds the window open until it is decided, and the reader who files in time never bears the sitting's delay. The window closes on the decision, not on the calendar date the sitting failed to meet: a grant closes the old window into the extended end T-476 provides, and a denial closes the window at the delivery of the denial. No reader loses his election because the sitting sat late.

The first reason is that the window is the reader's protection against the file's calendar, and the sitting's delay is calendar, not the reader's act. T-475 built the window so that silence at its close could fairly be read as affirmance, because the reader had a long time and strict notice. That fairness fails if the clock runs while the reader waits on an answer he has already asked for: a reader who filed in time, then watched the window's end pass while his request sat undecided, would lose his election by waiting — and waiting was the only act left to him. A clock that punishes timely filing is not a window but a trap: the reader who files early in the window would keep his election, and the reader who files late in it would lose his, although both filed inside the time the window gave them. The file must not grade timely requests by their filing hour. A request filed inside the window is an act inside the window, and it holds the window open until answered, exactly as an election inside the window would have settled it.

The second reason is that tolling is not revival, and it does not disturb T-468's refusal. A tolled window was never closed: the request arrived before the close, so the window never ended while it pended, and the decision lands inside a window still open. That is the opposite of T-476's late request after silence, which asks for revival of a window already closed, and the opposite of T-468's grace window, which asked a closed queue place to be held after citation. Tolling holds what is open; it reopens nothing and holds no queue place. The distinction is what keeps the rule honest: a reader who never filed at all still loses his election at the window's close, and a reader who filed after the close still asks for revival and gets none. Only the reader who filed in time, and is still waiting, keeps the window — because he did everything the window asked of him, and the delay is not his.

The third reason is that tolling must be bounded, or the window it protects becomes the endless voidability T-475's close was built to end. The toll runs only while the request genuinely pends before the sitting: filed in the window, undecided, neither withdrawn nor mooted. During pendency the reader keeps his election — he may still elect void or affirm, and an election moots the request, because a reader who has chosen needs no more time to choose. A request filed after the window closed files as a revival request under T-476, not as a pending request, and gets none. **T-478 — the Undecided Request — designed:** T-477 left its undecided-request problem named and open: whether a request filed in the window but never decided — the sitting dissolved, the term ended without a sitting — leaves the window tolled until a sitting can be convened, or closes it at some term, the toll being bounded but the bound unplaced. T-478 answers: the toll holds, but it holds to a bound, and the bound is one full term past the original close. A request filed in time and never decided keeps the window open until the first sitting competent to decide it is convened — and if no such sitting is convened within one full term past the original close, the window closes at that bound, by lapse of the bound, not by any decision. The reader never loses his election to a dissolution he did not cause, and no window stays open forever because a sitting never sat.

The first reason is that dissolution is the sitting's failure, not the reader's, and T-477's rule already refuses to punish the reader for the sitting's delay. A sitting that dissolves without deciding has delayed infinitely, not merely late: to close the window at the dissolution would punish the timely filer for the sitting's disappearance, the same wrong T-477 refused in smaller measure. The toll therefore survives the dissolution — the request still pends, because nothing has answered it, and a pending request is exactly what T-477 tolls for. But a toll without a bound is a different wrong: T-475's close exists so that intervening readers can eventually rely on a verdict that will stand, and a window tolled until some hypothetical future sitting would make every verdict voidable forever, whenever a sitting might one day convene. The bound must therefore be set by the same measure that made T-475's window fair in the first place: a term. One full term past the original close gives the system a whole sitting cycle to convene, decide, and deliver, and gives the reader the same measure of time the window itself gave him. If a competent sitting convenes within the bound, the toll holds until its decision, under T-477, and the decision closes the window by grant or by denial at delivery. If none convenes, the window closes at the bound, and the close is a close by lapse, not by decision — the reader's election ends, but it ends by a calendar he could read, not by a dissolution he could not foresee.

The second reason is that the bound must be entered in the record at the moment the toll begins, or the bound is a trap of the same kind T-477's hidden toll was. A reader who files in time and hears nothing cannot tell, from silence alone, whether his window is tolled, dissolved, or closed; an intervening reader who reads the record cannot tell whether his reliance is reliance during an open window or after a close. The file must therefore show three things when a request pends past the original close: the request itself, the dissolution or the absence of a sitting if that is why it pends, and the bound date — one full term past the original close — at which the toll lapses if no sitting decides. With the bound on the record, the reader knows the last day his election can still be made, and an intervening reader knows the last day his reliance is reliance during an open window. A toll whose bound is not entered files as a hidden bound: it may hold between reader and sitting, but it cannot fairly bind a reader who read a record that showed no end to the toll. The third reason is that the reader keeps his election throughout the toll, and the toll's end by lapse must be treated as T-475's silence, not as a decision against him. During the bound the reader may elect void or affirm at any time, and an election moots the request, exactly as T-477 provides during pendency — the reader who chooses needs no more time to choose, and needs no sitting to choose in. If the bound passes with no election and no decision, the window closes as T-475's window closes: silence at the close affirms the verdict in full, with the lapse notwithstanding, because the reader, told of the bound on the record and given a full term past the close, chose not to elect. What the bound's close does not do is decide the request: a request never decided is not a request denied, and the file must not record it as one. The closure record shows the window closed by lapse of the bound with the request undecided, so no later reader mistakes the lapse for a denial, and no later sitting treats the undecided request as a precedent for denying the next one. The request dies with the window, undecided, and the verdict stands — not because the request was weighed and refused, but because the reader, given a full term past the close, did not elect.

What a request files as follows from the three reasons, and the file must show the bound, not merely the toll. A sitting convened within the bound that adjourns without deciding leaves the toll exactly where it was: held open to the bound, and no further. A decision must land within the bound to close the window by decision; a decision after the bound decides a closed window. The first reason is that the bound's condition was a decision, not a meeting. T-478's bound exists because a toll without an end unmakes T-475's close; to let mere convening satisfy the condition would let a sitting convene on the bound's last day, adjourn, and hold the window open until whenever it next chose to decide — the unbounded toll again, wearing a convened face. A clock that a meeting can stop is not a bound but a door the sitting holds ajar. Convening proves a competent sitting exists, and that proof matters — it is why the toll holds to the bound rather than lapsing at a dissolution — but proof of competence is not a decision, and T-477 tolls toward a decision, not toward a meeting. The sitting that convenes and adjourns has done half the work the toll waits on, and half is not the whole: the toll holds, but it holds only to the bound it already had.

The second reason is that adjournment is not one thing. Adjournment to a date certain within the bound keeps the sitting's competence in being: the sitting has named its return, the reader can read when a decision may still land, and an intervening reader can read that reliance before that date is reliance during an open window. Adjournment sine die — without a date — is dissolution in effect: the sitting has vanished as surely as T-478's dissolved sitting, and the same bound governs, because the reader faces the same silence. Adjournment to a date past the bound names a return too late to matter: the bound does not move to meet it, because T-478's bound, once entered, does not move, and a sitting cannot extend its own jurisdiction by adjourning past the calendar the record gave the reader. The record must show the adjournment and its date, or its absence: a convened sitting whose adjournment is not entered files as a hidden adjournment, and an intervening reader who read a record showing a sitting in being cannot fairly be bound by a silence that was really a departure.

The third reason is that the reader keeps his election throughout, and a late decision cannot be smuggled in as the convened sitting's own. A sitting convened within the bound that decides after the bound is a late sitting under T-478: its decision is a decision about a closed window, which asks for revival under T-476 and gets none — the fact that it once convened does not make its late decision timely, any more than a timely filing decided late makes the decision timely. **T-484 — the Unentered Return — designed:** T-483 left its unentered-return problem named and open: whether a sitting that in fact returned in the lag window but whose return is unentered counts as returned for reliance, or whether the record's silence leaves the cutoff standing until the return is entered.
