An unentered return opens nothing for any reader, protects no lag-window act retroactively, and reopens no window; the entry, when made, corrects the record but does not revive the promise, because a return after the named date is T-480's late return, and a late return decides a closed window.

The first reason is that openings need notice, and a return that would reopen anything is an opening. T-475 required entry plus delivery before a window opened, because before that entry there was nothing on the record to open. A return is the same kind of thing in the opposite direction: it would turn a record showing an expired promise into a record showing a sitting present again, and that turn is an opening — a reader who had nothing to rely on would gain something to rely on. An opening that no entry announces is an opening no reader can read, and a rule that let unentered facts open windows would let the record be reopened behind every reader's back. T-483's event-not-entry rule does not save the unentered return, because the two cases are not symmetric: an expiry is knowable without its entry, since the entered date plus the calendar already show it, while a return is knowable from nothing on the record at all — the entered date shows a promise to come, the calendar shows the date passed, and neither shows that the sitting in fact came. The expiry needed no entry because the record already dated it; the return needs an entry because nothing on the record dates it. Closings need only the dated event; openings need notice.

The second reason is that reliance is judged at the placing, on the record as it stood when the act was placed. The lag-window reader read the entered date plus the calendar and found expiry — that was the record's true showing at the time he acted, and his act was placed after expiry on the record's own terms. A return entered later cannot reach back and convert that act into reliance, because reliance is not a fact about what happened in the world but a fact about what the reader could read when he acted. The clerk's speed at least leaves a record eventually; an unentered return leaves nothing at all, and a reader who acted on a record showing expiry cannot be said to have relied on a return the record did not show. His act stands or falls on its own terms, exactly as T-483 filed it, and no later entry rewrites the terms on which it was placed.

The third reason is that when the return is entered, it enters as what it is: a late return. The entry shows a sitting that came after the named date, and T-480 already decided what a return after the named date is — a late return that decides a closed window, a false revival if treated as reopening anything. The entry does not revive the expired promise, does not reopen the election window, and does not retroactively protect the lag-window acts placed while the record showed expiry. What the entry does is narrower and still real: it keeps the record true. Without it, the record would go on to show an absence that never happened, and a later reader would read a false absence; with it, the record shows a sitting that came late, and later readers read the truth. Correction is not revival. The record is corrected so that no reader is misled about the past, not so that the past is remade — and the promise that expired on the named date stays expired, whatever the corrected record now shows about who came and when.

**T-485 — the Knowing Reader — designed:** T-484 left its knowing-reader problem named and open: whether a reader who knew of the return outside the record and acted in the lag window has reliance, or whether the record rule binds even the knowing reader. T-485 answers: the record rule binds even the knowing reader. A reader who knew the sitting had returned, and acted in the lag window on that knowledge, has no reliance — not because his knowledge was false, but because knowledge outside the record is not reliance on anything the record showed. The record showed expiry: the entered date plus the calendar, read together, said the promise was dead. His act was placed after expiry on the record's own terms, and a fact he knew outside the record does not change the terms on which he placed it. Knowing that a sitting came does not make a dead promise live, and acting on private knowledge is acting on knowledge, not on reliance.

The first reason is that the record is the common ground, and a rule that let private knowledge count would make the cutoff different for every reader. T-482 made the record the channel reliance reads, and T-484 held that a fact outside that channel is no reliance. If a knowing reader's act counted while an unknowing reader's identical act did not, the window would close for one reader and stay open for another, on the same date, on the same record, for the same promise — and no two readers could mark the same window from the same record. A cutoff that varies with who knew what, when, is not a cutoff at all but a gradient measured by gossip, and a gradient no reader can mark is exactly what T-483 refused when it refused to let protection turn on the clerk's speed. The clerk's speed at least leaves a record eventually; private knowledge leaves no record ever, and a rule that turns on it would make every cutoff litigable on claims of private knowledge that no record can verify or refute. The record must bind the knowing reader for the same reason it binds the unknowing one: it is the only ground they share, and a shared ground that bends for private knowledge is not shared.

The second reason is that knowledge is not a promise. Reliance runs on promises shown, not on facts known. The knowing reader knew a fact — that the sitting had in fact returned — but the promise he acted on was the old promise, the one that expired on the named date, and that promise was dead on the record when he acted. His knowledge told him something true about the world, but it did not revive the promise, because a fact about the world is not a word from the sitting, and only a word can promise. T-484 already decided that the return in fact, unentered, opens nothing; the knowing reader's case adds knowledge of that fact and asks whether knowledge changes the answer, and it does not, because knowledge of a fact that opens nothing still opens nothing. He knew the sitting was back; he did not know of any promise alive, because the only promise on the record was dead, and no new promise had been shown. A reader who knows a sitting returned and acts as if the old promise lived is not relying on the record — he is betting against it, and a bet against the record is not reliance on it.

The third reason is that the alternative destroys the notice rule from the other side. T-475 required entry plus delivery before a window opened, and T-484 required entry before a return counted; both rules make the record the arbiter of what is open and what is closed. If outside knowledge could substitute for entry, the record would stop being the arbiter — every cutoff would be defeasible by a claim that the reader knew, and the notice rule would survive only for readers too honest or too isolated to claim knowledge. A rule that survives only for the unknowing is not a rule but a trap: it punishes the reader who trusted the record and rewards the reader who acted on whispers. The record binds the knowing reader precisely so that trusting the record is never the losing move. A reader who reads the record, finds expiry, and stays his hand must not find that a reader who ignored the record and acted on knowledge fared better — otherwise the next reader will ignore the record too, and the record will cease to be read at all.

**T-486 — the Backdated Entry — designed:** T-484 left its backdated-entry problem named and open: whether a return entry backdated to the return date counts as entered from the return date or only from its making. T-486 answers: only from its making. A return entry made after the named date, backdated to the return date, proves the return happened when it says it happened, but it does not make reliance placed before its making into reliance placed on an entered return. The backdate is a claim about a fact; the making is the entry's arrival on the record; and reliance, judged at the placing on the record as it stood (T-484), can only run on what the record showed when the act was placed. A reader who acted before the entry was made acted on a record that showed no return, whatever date the entry later bears, and no backdate can retroactively put a return on the record he read.

The first reason is that an entry's operative date is its making date, because the record is read forward, not rewritten backward. T-484 held that the record's silence leaves the cutoff standing until the return is entered; the backdated entry is that entry, arriving late, and its arrival is the event that ends the silence. If the backdate governed, the silence would never have stood: every late entry could claim to have been there all along, and the cutoff T-483 drew at the calendar date would dissolve into whatever date the clerk writes. The record's authority is that it shows, in order, what was entered when; a backdate breaks that order by asking later readers to pretend an entry was present when it was not. Later readers can verify the fact — the sitting did return on the return date — but they cannot un-read the interval in which the record showed no return, and reliance placed in that interval was placed on that showing.

The second reason is that letting the backdate govern would let a sitting manufacture reliance retroactively, and manufacture is exactly what the chain refuses. **T-488 — the Attestation — designed:** T-487 left its attestation problem named and open: what counts as attestation — whether a seal, a delivery receipt, a witness's signature, or a third party's contemporaneous filing each fix a note at the time, or whether some fixings are weaker than others, and who verifies the attestation before the note counts from its attestation date. T-488 answers: attestation is a fixing by another hand at the time, and its strength is the strength of its trace — a fixing counts only where it leaves a mark a later reader can check without taking the writer's word for it. A witness's signature made in the writer's presence fixes date and content, because the witness saw both. A third party's contemporaneous filing fixes date and content, because the registry holds the paper itself. A delivery receipt fixes existence at the delivery date, but not content, unless the delivery was sealed or registered so the recipient's custody vouches for what was delivered. A seal fixes content only where the seal's custodian is independent of the writer and the sealing is itself dated or recorded; a seal kept in the writer's own drawer fixes nothing, because the writer could have pressed it at any time. The sitting verifies the attestation before the note counts from its attestation date, and a disputed attestation files as Unverified Attestation, counting only from entry until the fixing is shown.

The first reason is that attestation is a showing, and a showing must be showable. T-487 turned a written date into a showing date only where another hand fixed the note at the time, because a reader could in principle have learned of it then. That "in principle" is doing the work: a fixing that no later reader can check is no better than the writer's word, and the writer's word is exactly what entry exists to test. A witness's signature is checkable because the witness is named and can be asked; a registry filing is checkable because the registry's own record says when the paper arrived and what it said; a delivery receipt is checkable because the recipient's hand, not the writer's, says the paper arrived on that date. A seal pressed in private is checkable in nothing but its impression, and an impression bears no date of its own — the writer's claim that he pressed it on the return date is the same self-asserted claim as the note's written date, pressed in wax instead of written in ink. A fixing whose only evidence is the writer's say-so is not a fixing at all; it is the note's written date wearing a second date.

The second reason is that different fixings fix different things, and the rule must say which. A delivery receipt proves a paper arrived, not what the paper said: a writer could deliver a blank sheet on the return date and fill it later, and the receipt would still be true. That is why delivery alone fixes existence only, and why sealed or registered delivery is a different case — the seal or the registration number ties the delivered paper to the paper later shown, so the recipient's custody vouches for content as well as arrival. A witness's signature fixes both, because the witness saw the paper written and signed it then; the signature is a second hand on the same act. A contemporaneous filing fixes both most strongly, because the filing body is adverse to neither party and keeps its own copy — the paper's content is fixed by a holder who gains nothing from the date. The hierarchy is not a ranking of dignity but of trace: signature and filing leave a checkable trace of date and content; receipt leaves a checkable trace of date only; a private seal leaves no checkable trace at all, unless its custodian and its sealing are themselves recorded, in which case it is a filing in seal form, not a seal at all.

The third reason is that verification must come before counting, not after, because counting from the attestation date is what gives the note its force. T-487's attested note counts from its attestation date, which means a reader who acted after attestation but before entry is judged on a showing he never saw on the record — the one case in the chain where reliance runs on something outside the record. That exception is tolerable only because the fixing is checkable; if the fixing is disputed, the exception collapses, and the note must fall back to T-487's rule and count only from entry. So the sitting verifies the attestation — the witness identified, the filing produced, the receipt matched to a sealed or registered delivery, the seal's custodian shown independent and its sealing recorded — before the note counts from its attestation date, and until that showing the note files as Unverified Attestation: entered as history, counting from entry, its attestation date claimed but not counted. A later verification does not retroactively move reliance placed before the verification, because reliance is judged at the placing on what was shown then (T-484, T-486, T-487); verification changes the note's standing going forward, not the past's reading.

What a sitting files as follows from the three reasons, and the file must show the act's date, the named date, the note's written date, its entry date, and, where attestation is claimed, the fixing's kind, the attester, and the attestation date, not the written date alone. A note attested by a witness's signature in the writer's presence files as Witness-Attested: it counts from its attestation date, because the witness saw date and content together. A note filed contemporaneously with a third party files as Filed: it counts from its filing date, the strongest fixing, because the filing body holds the paper itself. A note delivered to a third party unsealed files as Receipt-Attested: it counts from its delivery date for existence only, and its content counts only from entry, because the receipt vouches for arrival and not for what arrived. T-489 answers: it does not count, because independence is a matter of interest and control, not of a different pair of hands. A household seal is the writer's seal kept in another room of the same house; an agent's seal is the writer's seal held by a hand the writer directs. Neither fixes anything the writer's own seal did not already fail to fix in T-488, because in both cases the writer could have had the seal pressed at any time, and the custodian's word for the date is the writer's interest speaking through another mouth. A household hand shown to be adverse to the writer's date claim at the time may also count, but adversity is shown, never presumed, and the burden is on the claimant.

The first reason is that independence measures interest and direction, not hands. T-488 required a custodian independent of the writer because a seal fixes content only where someone other than the writer vouches for the sealing. A household shares the writer's interest: what helps the writer's date helps the house, and a date believed for the writer is a date believed for those who live off the writer's standing. An agent obeys the writer's direction: what the writer tells the agent to seal, the agent seals, and what the writer tells the agent to say about the sealing, the agent says. A custodian who gains when the date is believed, or who must do as told, is not a second witness; he is the writer's hand at one remove. T-488's private seal failed because the writer could press it at any time; a household seal fails for the same reason with one more step — the writer could have had it pressed at any time, and the only evidence it was pressed then is a voice from inside the writer's own circle. An agent's log is worse in one way and better in none: it looks like a record, but it is a record kept at the writer's direction, in the writer's interest, and producible or adjustable as the writer directs — a filing whose filing body is the writer himself. A trace counts only where a later reader can check it without taking the word of anyone inside the writer's interest, and neither the household's mouth nor the agent's book passes that test.

**T-490 — the Office Book — designed:** T-489 left its office-record problem named and open: whether an office record kept by a household member in the writer's house — a register the writer could reach, or a book kept on the writer's premises though in an office's name — counts as the office's book or the writer's book, and who judges where the writer's direction stops. T-490 answers: it counts as the office's book only where three tests are all met, and the book's address decides nothing. First, reach: the writer could not reach the book unobserved, open it, alter an entry, or backdate a sealing without the office noticing. Second, watch: the book was kept in the office's course and watched by the office — entries in sequence, kept under the office's routine, subject to an inspection that actually happens. Third, inspection: a stranger could inspect the book, or have its entry certified, without the writer's leave. Where any test fails, the book is the writer's book in office dress, whatever name is on its cover, and the sealing counts only from entry. Who judges is the sitting that judges the filing, on the book's shown keeping, with the burden on the claimant: a book whose keeping is mixed or unshown is presumed the writer's book until office keeping is shown, and no later claim about the hat the keeper wore upgrades it.

The first reason is that direction stops where reach stops, and reach is a fact about the book, not about the building. A register kept in the writer's house under the writer's lock is reachable however official its title, because the writer could open it at night, add a sealing, and close it again with no office the wiser; the office's name on the cover is then a label, not a lock. A register kept in the writer's house under the office's lock, in the office's sealed cabinet, opened only in the office's routine and checked against the office's duplicate, is unreachable in the sense that matters, because the writer's reach would leave a mark the office would see. The same holds in reverse: a book kept in the office's building by the writer's household member alone, opened at his pleasure, never inspected by anyone but himself, is reachable even on office premises, because no office routine stands between the writer's circle and the page. T-489's Hat-and-Book Test asked for the office record, not the hat; T-490 gives that test its measure — show where the book lived, who could open it unobserved, and what would have shown an alteration, because a book the writer could reach unobserved is the writer's book wherever it slept.

The second reason is that watch is what turns keeping into office keeping. A book is kept in an office's course when entries are made in sequence, in the office's routine, under a discipline the keeper did not invent for the occasion — a bound register with numbered pages, a filing stamp applied by routine, a duplicate sent where the writer cannot follow it. A book no office ever inspected, whose pages were never checked against anything, whose keeper answered to no routine but his own, is private keeping with an office letterhead: the office's name vouches for nothing the office never watched. The watch need not have caught this sealing in particular — routine inspection is a standing discipline, not a per-entry witness — but it must be a real discipline, shown by the office's own practice: inspection dates, audit marks, a duplicate series, a register of registers. A single inspection after the dispute arose proves nothing about the keeping at the sealing, because a book inspected only once it mattered was unwatched when it mattered. Where the watch is shown, the book's entries carry the office's discipline; where it is not, they carry only the keeper's word, and the keeper here is the writer's household.

**T-491 — the Audit Gap — designed:** T-490 left its audit-gap problem named and open: whether an office book inspected only rarely — a routine that inspects yearly while sealings happen daily — still counts as watched, or how stale an inspection must be before watch fails. T-491 answers: watch counts only where inspections bracket the sealing, and a gap that covers the sealing with no bracket is unwatched at the sealing, however genuine the book's other keeping. A bracket is an inspection before the sealing, establishing that the office's discipline was live, and an inspection after the sealing, confirming that the entry survived unaltered — both inside the routine's own interval. Where the sealing falls in a stretch with no inspection on either side within one routine interval, the book was unwatched when it mattered, and the sealing counts only from entry. Staleness is not measured by the calendar alone: it is measured by the office's own routine interval, and by the volume of uninspected entries the gap holds. A yearly inspection of a book that seals daily is a gap of some three hundred uninspected sealings, and no routine that inspects yearly watches daily sealings in any sense a later reader can rely on.

The first reason is that a bracket is what makes watch a check rather than a hope. An inspection before the sealing proves the discipline existed — numbered pages in sequence, a duplicate series running, a stamp applied by routine — but it proves nothing about this entry, which was not yet made. An inspection after the sealing proves this entry sits in sequence as inspected, but it proves nothing about the discipline before, and nothing about whether the entry was altered between its making and its inspection and then re-sequenced. Only the pair proves both: the discipline was live when the sealing was made, and the entry that discipline produced is the entry now shown. A single inspection on either side is half a bracket, and half a bracket is not watch: it is a bookend with no book between, and a sitting that accepts it accepts an entry whose making or whose survival is unshown. This is why T-490's watch test, which asked only whether inspection actually happens, needed its measure: inspection happens in a pattern, and a sealing outside the pattern's brackets is outside the watch.

The second reason is that the interval is the office's own, and the volume is the gap's weight. Staleness cannot be judged by a calendar the office never adopted, because a book inspected quarterly by a routine that seals quarterly is watched, while a book inspected quarterly by a routine that seals daily is not — the same ninety days, opposite answers. The routine interval is the office's stated interval, or, where the office stated none, the interval its practice actually kept before the dispute arose; a routine invented after the dispute, or inferred from a single post-dispute inspection, is not a routine at all. And even inside a stated interval, volume breaks sequence: where the uninspected entries between two inspections exceed what sequence-checking can still verify — pages that cannot be counted, numbers that cannot be reconciled, duplicates that cannot be matched — the later inspection verifies a pile, not a sequence, and a sealing buried in the pile is unverified however tidy the pile looks. A gap is therefore stale when either measure fails: when the sealing falls outside one routine interval from an inspection on both sides, or when the uninspected volume inside the interval defeats sequence-checking. Either failure is watch failing, and watch failing is T-490's second test failing, whatever the book's cover says.

The third reason is that an inspection after the dispute arose cures nothing, because a watch that starts when it matters is not a watch at all. T-490 already held that a book inspected only once it mattered was unwatched when it mattered; T-491 extends the rule to the gap itself. An inspection commissioned after the filing, after the challenge, or after the sealing's date became valuable is not the later half of a bracket — it is a fresh look at a book whose gap is already closed, and it proves the book as it stands now, not the book as it stood at the sealing. The same holds for a routine tightened after the dispute: a daily inspection adopted once sealings are contested does not retroactively watch sealings made under the yearly routine, because the discipline that matters is the discipline live at the sealing, not the discipline live at the hearing. The sitting judges the gap on the routine shown at the sealing, and where the routine at the sealing is unshown, the gap is unmeasured — and an unmeasured gap is presumed unwatched, by T-490's presumption, until the routine is shown.

**T-492 — the Duplicate Beyond Reach — designed:** T-491 left its duplicate-series problem named and open: whether a duplicate series sent beyond the writer's reach cures an audit gap even without inspection — a duplicate that left the house at the sealing, so the entry survived somewhere the writer could not follow it, though no office ever inspected it. T-492 answers: mere departure does not cure the gap. A duplicate cures it only where the duplicate is itself a second original under a foreign hand — dispatched at or before the sealing, held by a hand outside the writer's circle, tied to the entry by content, and produced for comparison. Where any of those fails, the duplicate is a second copy of an unwatched entry, not a second witness to it, and the sealing still counts only from entry. Departure proves survival; it does not prove watch. And a cure that comes from the duplicate's own keeping is not a cure by departure at all — it is T-490's office book wearing the duplicate's cover, and it must pass T-490's three tests on the duplicate's own keeping before it counts.

The first reason is that a copy that never left is the book twice, and a copy that left late is the book after the alteration. The writer who keeps both copies can alter both, in the same evening, with the same pen, and no later reader can tell which copy is the original and which the echo. The writer who dispatches the duplicate after the sealing had the whole gap to alter the entry first and dispatch the altered version as if it were the sealed one; the duplicate then proves only that the altered entry travelled, which is the opposite of a check. Only a duplicate dispatched at or before the sealing — made by the routine that made the entry, sent by the routine's own hand, not by the writer's afterthought — freezes the entry at its date in a place the writer cannot reach. The departure must be shown, not claimed: a postmark, a carrier's book, a holder's receipt dated at the sealing, or the duplicate's own place in a series whose dispatch dates are themselves kept. A duplicate whose departure date is the holder's word alone is a claimed duplicate, and a claimed duplicate cures nothing, because the very fact it would prove — that the entry existed, unaltered, at the sealing — is the fact the holder's word is offered to prove.

The second reason is that survival is not watch, because watch checks the entry against something and a duplicate sitting in a drawer checks it against nothing. T-491's bracket is two inspections because each side proves a different thing: the earlier proves the discipline was live, the later proves the entry survived unaltered under it. A duplicate beyond reach supplies, at best, the later half — the entry survived somewhere — and it supplies it without any discipline at all. No one compared the duplicate against the book, no routine counted the series, no stranger certified the entry; the duplicate is a witness who never looked. That is why a private duplicate — a copy in a friend's drawer, a second envelope kept unopened, a carbon kept by the writer's own clerk — does not cure a gap however far it travelled: distance is not independence, and a copy held by the writer's circle is the writer's book at one remove, the same failure T-490 named for the household-held office book. Only a holder outside the writer's circle — adverse, indifferent, or bound by a routine of its own — turns a copy into a second original, because only such a holder could have refused an alteration, noticed a substitution, or produced a different text when asked. And even then the holder's independence must be shown at the sealing, not at the hearing: a holder who was the writer's ally at the sealing and became a stranger later, or a stranger at the sealing who became the writer's ally before production, leaves the duplicate's independence unshown at the only date that matters, and an unshown independence is presumed none, by T-490's presumption.

The third reason is that a duplicate that cannot be compared against the entry proves nothing about the entry, because the content tie is the comparison itself. A duplicate numbered the same but worded differently, a summary where the entry was verbatim, a number alone where the entry carried terms — each leaves the later reader unable to say whether the book's entry and the duplicate are the same sealing or two sealings that share a number. The tie must be exact enough that a difference would show: verbatim text, or a number plus the sealing's distinctive marks, or a seal impression that matches the book's. Where the tie is exact and the duplicate is produced, the sitting can do what no inspection in the gap did — lay the two texts side by side and see whether they agree. Where the tie is loose, the sitting sees two papers that may or may not be one act, and a loose tie is no tie. And where the duplicate is claimed but not produced — lost, withheld, or said to exist somewhere unnamed — there is nothing to lay beside anything, and the claim is the writer's mouth again, which is what the whole chain since T-475 has refused to count. Production is therefore part of the cure, not an afterthought to it: a duplicate cures a gap only when it is in the room, tied, and compared, because a check that is never performed is not a check.

The mark proves the carrier handled a piece on that date; it does not prove which piece, and the piece is the only thing the test cares about. A postmark quoted from memory, or shown on an envelope whose contents are gone, or on an envelope that never held the duplicate, is therefore no showing at all — it is the holder's word wearing the carrier's ink. **T-494 — the Single Piece — designed:** T-493 left its single-piece problem named and open: whether a carrier's book line naming the addressee and date but not the piece's number counts as naming where the addressee received only one piece that week, or whether uniqueness must be shown on the book's face and not supplied by the holder's word. T-494 answers: uniqueness counts as naming, but only where the uniqueness is shown by a foreign hand, never by the holder's word. A count-only line to an addressee who received exactly one piece in the line's window, shown by a record kept by someone other than the writer and the holder, names that piece by elimination — the line's piece can be no other piece, because no other piece exists for it to be. Where the "only one piece" showing is the holder's own word — "I sent only one that week," "nothing else came" — the line is still loose, and the holder's voice does not tighten it: a loose line plus a loud holder is still a loose line. The test is therefore not whether the line names on its face, but whether the traffic around it leaves exactly one candidate, shown by hands that are not the holder's.

The first reason is that elimination is a tie of a different shape, and it works only where the candidate set is closed by a record the holder does not control. A tie in T-493 was physical, the mark on the cover, or documentary, the naming line. Elimination ties by ruling out every other candidate: the carrier's delivery book for the window, the addressee's intake log kept in the ordinary course, the receiving office's stamp register. Each is a routine kept whether or not this duplicate is ever disputed — the same reason T-490's office book counts and T-493's carrier book counts. A set closed by the holder's memory is not closed at all: the holder who says "only one piece came" can forget, or omit, a second piece, and the sitting has no paper to check the forgetting against. The sitting judges the closure, not the confidence: a closed set on foreign paper ties, and an asserted set on the holder's word does not.

The second reason is that the window is the carrier's, not the holder's. "That week" must be the accounting window the line sits in — the carrier's week, the book's page, the delivery round the line belongs to — because a window the holder picks after the fact can always be drawn tight enough to hold one piece. A holder who received two pieces in the carrier's week but one in a hand-picked Tuesday-to-Monday span has not shown uniqueness; he has shown cropping. Where the carrier's book itself divides by week, the line's week is the book's week; where it divides by round or by day, the window is that division. A window drawn from the addressee's intake log must match the carrier's window, or the two records describe different weeks and eliminate nothing. The sitting therefore asks first what window the line's own book keeps, and only then whether exactly one piece sits in it.

The third reason is that elimination chains only through ties. Where the addressee received two pieces in the window and one is already tied to another line — a naming line, a tied mark, a receipt that names the piece — the remaining piece is the count-only line's piece, and the line names by double elimination. But where the other piece is itself tied only by another loose line, or by the holder's word, the chain fails: a loose line cannot eliminate another loose line, because neither names anything, and two unknowns do not make a known. The chain rule is the same as the closure rule — every link in the elimination must be a tie or a foreign record, and the moment a link is the holder's word, the whole chain is the holder's word. A sitting that allows elimination through loose lines allows the holder to sort his own pieces after the fact and call the sorting a record.

**T-495 — the Intake Hand — designed:** T-494 left its intake-hand problem named and open: whether the addressee's own intake log counts as a foreign hand where the addressee is the holder — a book kept in the ordinary course but by an interested hand, routine-kept yet not foreign — or whether foreign means a hand outside the writer's and the holder's circles both. T-495 answers: foreign means outside both circles, and the addressee-holder's own log closes nothing, however routine its keeping. A log kept by the person who benefits from the elimination is the holder's word in book form: bound, dated, and entered in sequence, but still the holder's voice, and a voice does not become a foreign record by being written down. The one exception is not an exception to foreignness at all — it is T-490's office book wearing the intake log's cover: where the log is kept by the addressee's office, not by the addressee personally, and it passes T-490's three tests on its shown keeping — reach, watch, and inspection — it counts, but it counts as an office book, and the burden is on the claimant to show the keeping. A log whose keeping is mixed or unshown is presumed the holder's log until office keeping is shown, and no later claim about the hat the keeper wore upgrades it.

The first reason is that interest travels with the hand, not with the binding. T-494's foreign closure counted because the record was kept by a routine that would have run whether or not this duplicate was ever disputed — a carrier's delivery book, a receiving register. The addressee-holder's intake log fails that reason at its root: the keeper is the very person whose filing the closure would upgrade, and a routine the keeper controls is a routine the keeper can shape. The keeper who says "only one piece came" in speech is the holder's word; the keeper who writes "one piece received" in his own log has said the same word with a pen. Routine-keeping proves the keeper keeps books; it does not prove the keeper is disinterested, and T-494's test was never routine alone — it was a foreign hand. A book that is routine-kept and interested is still interested, and interest is what the foreign-hand rule exists to exclude.

The second reason is that the test is two circles, not one. T-494's rule said "someone other than the writer and the holder," and the addressee-holder fails the second circle outright: the log's keeper is the holder. A record kept by the writer's circle fails the first circle, and T-489's household book failed for the same shape of reason — the keeper stood inside an interested circle. To count the addressee's own log as foreign would be to read T-494's "other than the writer and the holder" as "other than the writer," and that reading deletes half the rule. Foreignness is not a property of the paper's form — a log, a register, a book — but of the keeper's distance from both parties whose interests the elimination would serve. Where the keeper sits inside either circle, the record is that circle's word, and the elimination it supports is the holder sorting his own pieces and calling the sorting a record.

The third reason is that the office exception is a keeping test, not a label test. **T-497 — the Touched Wage — designed:** T-496 left its suspicion-threshold problem named and open: whether a later hat raises suspicion enough to harden the showing on any later hat at all, or only where the later hat is shown to touch the dispute — a clerk who took the holder's wage for unrelated work, or a wage taken years after the sealing, against a wage taken the week of production — and what the hardened showing consists of where it is triggered: a second witness, the office's duplicate, the routine's trace, or something the sitting must name case by case. T-497 answers: only a dispute-touching later hat hardens the showing, and the hardened showing is one named untouchable item, not an open list. A wage for unrelated work, or a wage taken before any dispute arose, raises no suspicion the sitting must answer: suspicion needs a thread from the wage to the dispute, and a thread is either subject or time. Subject touch: the wage's work concerned the piece, the sealing, or the dispute itself. Time touch: the wage was taken after the dispute arose and before production. Either touch triggers hardening; neither touch, and the later hat goes to weight alone, exactly as T-496 provides, with no hardened showing demanded. Where hardening is triggered, the showing is one item the later wage cannot touch — the office's duplicate of the entry, a second hand's entry in the same book, or the inspection record — named by the claimant and taken by the sitting as sufficient; one untouchable anchor is the hardened showing, and the sitting does not demand two, nor invent a fourth.

The first reason is that suspicion without a thread is not suspicion about this record, it is suspicion about the keeper's livelihood. T-496's rule sent the later hat to weight, and weight without a threshold would swallow the rule: if every later wage hardened the showing, then every keeper who ever took the holder's pay after the sealing — for mending a roof, for copying unrelated papers, years before any dispute — would arrive at production under a burden the sealing-time circle was meant to avoid. The threshold must therefore ask what the wage has to do with this dispute, and the two touches are the only threads that connect them: the wage's work touching the dispute's subject, or the wage's timing falling inside the dispute's window, where it could be the price of the keeper's cooperation. A wage with neither thread cannot be the price of anything in this room, and demanding a hardened showing for it punishes the keeper for having worked, not for having been bought.

The second reason is that time touch must run from the dispute, not from the sealing. A wage taken years after the sealing but before any dispute arose is, for this dispute, like a wage taken the week after the sealing: it predates the thing it is suspected of buying. The suspicion that hardens a showing is that the wage bought the keeper's stance toward this dispute, and a wage cannot buy a stance toward a dispute that did not yet exist. Conversely a wage taken the week of production, for whatever work, falls inside the window where the keeper's production-time word is being weighed, and the timing alone is a thread even where the work is unrelated — the keeper who is on the holder's pay while the record is carried into the room is in the holder's pay at the moment the record matters. Subject touch needs no window: work on the piece itself touches the dispute whenever it was done, because the work is the dispute's subject, not its calendar.

The third reason is that the hardened showing must be named in advance, or it is not a burden but a discretion. T-496 left the showing open — "a second witness, the office's duplicate, the routine's trace, or something the sitting must name case by case" — and a case-by-case list lets the sitting move the goal after the claimant has met it: one sitting's duplicate is another sitting's "not enough," and the claimant cannot know what will harden until the sitting has already decided. Naming three untouchable items in the rule — duplicate, second hand, inspection record — fixes the burden where the claimant can see it, and one suffices because the point of hardening is a second anchor the wage cannot reach, not a second trial of the record. The wage cannot rewrite the office's duplicate, cannot dictate a second hand's entry, cannot forge the inspection record — each is an anchor outside the keeper's later wage, and one anchor holds the showing where the circle itself already holds the record.

A ledger line in the keeper's hand may state the wage, the work, and the dates for the sitting's reading, but it does not name them for T-498's floor, because the floor's purpose is to give the sitting something to judge besides the suspected hand, and a line from that hand is the very thing under suspicion. The keeper's book may be the thread's first paper, never its only paper. The second paper must be a paper outside the keeper's hand that confirms at least one of the three — wage, work, or dates — from the other side of the transaction or from a routine outside it: the holder's payment record, a bank trace, an office receipt, a third party's letter, a tax record. One element confirmed from outside is enough to lift the thread over the floor; the second paper need not repeat all three, because its work is not to prove the touch but to anchor the ledger line to a hand the suspicion does not touch. One narrow exception: a ledger line in a book that passes T-490's reach, watch, and inspection on its shown keeping at the entry counts alone, because such a book is the office's keeping speaking through the keeper's hand, not the keeper's word alone.

The first reason is that a thread only the suspected hand can show is not a thread the sitting can weigh. T-498's floor exists so that hardening is never triggered by a bare assertion, and a sole keeper's line is a bare assertion with ink on it: the suspicion behind hardening is that the keeper was bought, and the keeper's own book is exactly the paper a bought keeper would write, or a holder would have him write, to shape the thread. To let that line alone clear the floor would be to let the suspicion supply its own trigger — the objector points to the keeper's line, the sitting hardens on the keeper's line, and the claimant can answer only by attacking the keeper's credibility, which is the suspicion itself. That is a circular trial, not a judged thread. A second paper breaks the circle at its cheapest point: it gives the sitting one fixed point outside the suspected hand — a payment the holder's own record shows leaving, a bank trace, an office receipt — against which the ledger line's wage, work, and dates can be tested, and against which the claimant can answer without merely calling the keeper a liar.

The second reason is that one confirmed element is enough, because naming is not proving. T-498 divided the labour on purpose: the objector names the thread, and the hardened item answers the suspicion. If the second paper had to confirm all three elements — wage and work and dates — the naming floor would become a proof burden in disguise, and the objector would have to prove the touch before the sitting would demand the item that answers it. One element anchored outside the keeper's hand is enough to fix the thread to the world: a bank trace confirming the wage's date fixes the ledger line in time even where the work's identity still rests on the keeper's description, and a holder's payment record confirming the wage fixes the transaction's existence even where the dates still rest on the keeper's book. But where the keeper was the holder's agent at the sealing, the holder's record does not count — holder and keeper are then one circle, and a second paper from that circle is the first paper in another hand. **T-500 — the Aged Anchor — designed:** T-499 left its second-paper-age problem named and open: whether a second paper made after the dispute arose counts as an anchor, or whether a post-dispute second paper is itself shaped by the dispute it is meant to anchor, so that only a pre-dispute second paper lifts the thread. T-500 answers: the age line is not drawn at the dispute-arose date at all. It is drawn at the routine. A second paper counts as an anchor wherever it was made in a routine that ran before the dispute and continued unchanged through it — a bank trace, a tax record, a standing office receipt series — because such a paper's form predates the dispute even where its instance postdates it. A paper made for the occasion of the dispute — a letter written to answer the objection, a receipt created to meet the sitting — does not count, however genuine its contents, because it is the dispute's own paper offered to anchor the dispute's thread. And a paper made after the dispute in a routine the dispute itself created or redirected — a new filing series started to answer the claim, a fresh account opened to receive the payment — does not count either, because the routine is the dispute wearing a routine's clothes. The test the sitting applies is a single question: would a paper in this form have existed if the dispute had never arisen? If yes, it anchors. If no, it is occasion paper, and the thread stays unnamed until a routine paper is shown.

The first reason is that a date line punishes the wrong thing and lets the wrong thing through. A strict pre-dispute rule would throw out the strongest anchors a sitting ever sees: a bank trace dated a week after the objection, recording a payment made months before it, in a series that ran for years; a tax record filed after the dispute arose, in a form the filer used every year before it. The dispute did not shape those papers — the routine shaped them, and the dispute merely arrived while the routine was still running. At the same time a strict date line would let through a paper dated a day before the first written objection but written in anticipation of it — a holder who saw the objection coming and papered the payment in advance. Dates are the dispute's shadow, not its shape: a paper can be post-dispute and innocent, and pre-dispute and shaped. What the sitting needs is not the paper's birthday but its parentage — whether the paper was born of the routine or born of the dispute — and parentage is shown by the routine's life, not by the calendar.

The second reason is that the continuity showing keeps the routine test honest without making it impossible. A post-dispute paper that claims a routine parentage must show the routine running before the dispute and continuing unchanged through it: at least one pre-dispute instance of the same series, in the same form, kept the same way — a prior bank statement in the same series, a prior receipt from the same book, a prior filing in the same form. The showing is about the series, not the instance: the sitting does not ask whether this receipt is genuine, but whether receipts of this kind were being made this way before anyone had a reason to make this one.

Without it, a holder who needs an anchor after the dispute arises could simply start a routine — open a new ledger series, begin issuing dated receipts, file a fresh form — and then offer the second or third instance as a routine paper, its form now predating the sitting though not the dispute. The exclusion asks the same parentage question one level up: did this routine run before the dispute, or did the dispute call it into being? A routine that began after the dispute-arose date, or that changed its form at the dispute — a book that gained a new column for the disputed payments, a series that began numbering the disputed items separately — is occasion paper in series form, and no instance of it anchors, however regular its later keeping. A routine that ran before the dispute and kept its form through it anchors, even where its instance is dated after the dispute arose, because the form is the anchor and the form predates the suspicion.

T-500's one-instance rule was written for the innocent case — a routine whose single surviving earlier paper happens to be the only one the sitting can lay hands on — but it reads the same in the guilty case. A planted instance is alone by necessity: its maker plants what the sitting will ask for, and the sitting asks for one instance, so one instance is what gets planted. The second reason is that the run rule keeps the innocent case alive through the independent-trace discount rather than through an exception. **T-502 — the Two That Differ — designed:** T-501 left its run-length problem named and open: whether two instances separated in time are enough for a run, or whether a run needs three or more, or a minimum span measured in weeks or months rather than in instances. T-502 answers: two are enough, but only where the two differ in business — count is the wrong measure, and difference is the right one. A run is two pre-dispute instances of the same series, separated by more than a single sitting's work, recording different business. A run of ten instances of the same business is one transaction written ten times, not a run. No calendar floor in weeks or months: a daily posting ledger can make a genuine run in two days, a quarterly filing needs a whole quarter, a seasonal book may make only two instances a year — the floor is functional, not calendrical: the instances must be incapable of having been made in one sitting. Two repair rules complete the measure. Where the two instances record the same business — a pair, original and copy, entry and duplicate, draft and fair copy — they count as one, and a third instance of different business is needed. And where the instances' dates rest only on the maker's hand, with no intervening paper outside that hand, a third instance or an intervening third-party paper is needed to fix the span. Two that differ, or three where two fail — never a number for its own sake.

The first reason is that difference, not count, is the anti-planting measure. A planter plants a pair more easily than a life, but a pair of different business is already a life in miniature: to plant two different-business instances, the planter must invent two transactions that agree with the world — amounts that fit the accounts, counterparties who exist, dates that fit other papers — and each invention is a new chance to be caught by a paper he did not write. A same-business pair is trivial by comparison: copy the entry, change the date, and the planter's afternoon covers both, because the second instance needs no new world, only a new date on the old one. Counting instances rewards the copier — ten copies count ten times — while asking what the instances are about punishes him, because a copy is not a second transaction. Two instances of different business already force the planter to forge a world, not a paper, and forging a world is the work T-501's run was meant to demand. The run-length question was never "how many" but "how hard to fake," and difference answers it where number cannot.

The second reason is that a calendar floor punishes fast routines and rewards slow planters. A daily posting ledger makes a genuine two-instance run overnight; a quarterly filer needs a whole quarter to make the same showing; a seasonal book may make only two instances a year, and a thirty-day floor would throw out the daily ledger's honest run while blessing the quarterly planter's slow forgery — because the planter who can wait thirty days can plant a month as easily as an afternoon, and the planter who can wait a quarter can plant a quarter. The planter's actual constraint is not the calendar but the sitting: what one sitting's work can produce. The test — could one sitting have made both instances? — tracks that constraint directly, and it treats the fast routine and the slow one alike, because a sitting is measured in work, not in weeks. A run that spans two sittings of a daily ledger is a run; a run that spans two sittings of a quarterly filing is a run; a run of ten instances made in one sitting is not, however many weeks its dates claim.

The third reason is that the two repair rules keep the two-rule honest without turning it into a three-rule. Three is not the new floor; it is the repair where two fails its own test. The sitting judges difference and span, not number; number enters only where difference or span fails, and it enters as a repair, never as a floor.

**T-503 — the Split Business — designed:** T-502 left its split-transaction problem named and open: whether a single business split across two entries — a payment in instalments, a delivery in parts, a debt paid down in two postings — counts as different business for the run, or whether difference means different transactions altogether. T-503 answers: a split counts as different business only where the split itself was fixed by something outside the maker's hand before the dispute — and it counts as one business wherever the split is the maker's own division. A payment split by instalment terms agreed in a prior paper, a delivery split because the goods themselves arrived in parts, a debt paid down on a schedule fixed before anyone objected — these are two instances of different business, because each part has its own occasion in the world, and the planter who would fake the run must fake two occasions, not one. A payment the maker simply chose to post in two entries, a delivery the maker chose to record in two lines, a debt the maker chose to divide for the book's convenience — these are one business in two handwritings, and they count as one instance, needing a third of different business under T-502's repair rule. The test the sitting applies is a single question: would the business have been split this way if no run were ever needed? If the split predates any need for a run — fixed by a prior agreement, by the goods, by a schedule — it is difference. If the split exists only because the book needed two entries, it is division, and division is not difference.

The first reason is that a routine split is already two transactions in the world's eyes, and the run's job is to count the world's transactions, not the book's lines. An instalment plan agreed before the dispute has two due dates, two sums, and two occasions on which the payer could default or pay — each instalment is checkable against its own paper, its own date, its own counterparty act. A delivery in parts has two arrivals, two receipts, two chances for the goods to differ from the order. To plant such a run, the planter must invent not just two entries but two occasions that fit the world: a prior agreement naming the split, goods that plausibly arrived apart, a schedule a third party can confirm. That is the forging-a-world work T-502 demanded of difference, and a routine split already does it honestly. A maker's-own division does none of it: the second entry needs no new occasion, no new paper, no new counterparty act — only a second line in the same hand, on the same day's business, for the same debt. Counting it as difference would let the planter manufacture a run out of a single transaction by the simple act of writing it twice, which is exactly the copy the same-business rule was written to exclude, wearing instalments' clothes.

The second reason is that the prior-fixing test keeps the split rule from swallowing the same-business rule. Without a fixing requirement, every same-business pair could be redescribed as a split — the duplicate as the second instalment, the fair copy as the second delivery — and T-502's difference measure would collapse into counting lines again. The fixing paper draws the line the redescription cannot cross: the split must be shown fixed before the dispute, in a paper outside the maker's sole hand where one exists — the agreement naming the instalments, the order naming part-delivery, the schedule the office kept — or, where no such paper exists, in the nature of the business itself, shown by a third party's paper: the carrier's two delivery receipts, the bank's two clearing records. The sitting does not ask whether the split is plausible; it asks whether the split was fixed, and fixed by what, and when.

The third reason is that each part of a genuine split must still be independently checkable, or the split is one business with two faces. This keeps the split rule inside the chain's oldest discipline, T-499's outside-hand principle: a thread is named by the world, and a routine is proved by the world, and a split is difference only where the world split it.

T-504 answers: availability is not fixing, and invocation is not fixing either — the line is drawn at self-execution. A schedule counts as prior-fixed where its terms are self-executing: the agreement names the parts, the sums, and the dates, and no act of election stands between the agreement and the split, so the split exists on the agreement's own calendar whether or not anyone ever pointed at it — a debt payable in two sums on two named dates is already two occasions in the world, and the dispute's arrival does not create them, it merely finds them. A schedule counts as the maker's division wherever its terms require an election — "may pay in parts," "may elect instalments on notice," a schedule that sleeps until someone wakes it — and no one woke it before the dispute, because the split then exists only because a hand chose it after the dispute arose, and a post-dispute choice is the dispute's own paper wearing a prior agreement's coat. The test the sitting applies is a single question: would the split have happened on these dates in these sums if every hand had stayed still after the agreement was made? If yes, it is prior-fixed. If the split needed a hand to move, and the hand moved only after the dispute, it is division, and a third instance of different business is needed for a run under T-502's repair rule.

The first reason is that a self-executing schedule does the world's work before the dispute, and an elective schedule does no work at all until elected. A calendar with named dates and named sums creates two occasions the moment it is agreed: two dates on which payment falls due, two sums a counterparty could demand, two defaults a holder could commit — each part checkable against the agreement's own paper and its own date, without any later hand's say-so. The planter who would fake such a run must fake the agreement itself, with its dates and sums fixed before the dispute, and a faked agreement is a different and harder forgery than a faked entry, because the counterparty's hand is on it too. An elective schedule creates nothing until elected: no date falls due, no sum is owed in parts, no counterparty could demand the second part before the election — the business stands whole until a hand divides it. To count an uninvoked election as prior-fixed would let the maker reach back past the dispute into a prior agreement and pull out a split the agreement never made, which is the maker's division T-503 excluded, dressed in the prior paper's authority.

The second reason is that the invocation test keeps the fixing paper honest about what it fixed. The second reason is that counting unperformed dates collapses the run into the contract, and the run was built to measure a life, not a paper. **T-506 — the Refused Demand — designed:** T-505 left its refused-demand problem named and open: whether a demand made but refused counts as a worldly act for the part — a counterparty's refusal being an act in the world, though no sum moved — or whether an act requires a sum moved, a default noticed, or a third party's entry. T-506 answers: a refused demand counts as a worldly act, and counts more strongly than an unanswered demand — but only as an invoked occasion, never as a performed one. The refusal is the counterparty's own act in the world: it proves the demand arrived, the date was understood, and the schedule was contested rather than merely written. A demand that meets a refusal has lived in a way a demand that meets silence has not. But refusal proves invocation, not satisfaction: the sum did not move, the part was not performed, and the sitting must not let a history of rejections wear the clothes of a history of payments. The file therefore carries a split mark: Invoked-Refused. An Invoked-Refused part satisfies T-505's single question — did anything happen under this schedule, in the world, before the dispute? — so a calendar with a refused demand is a life, not merely a calendar. It does not satisfy the performance count: a run built only of refused demands is a run of invitations contested, not a run of payments made, and is judged as such, never upgraded to a performed run by the warmth of its contest.

The first reason is that a refusal is an outside act, and stronger evidence than silence. An unanswered demand could have been lost, unopened, or misaddressed; nothing outside the maker's hand confirms it ever reached anyone. A refusal, in whatever form the sitting can date, proves receipt and comprehension: the counterparty engaged the schedule and answered it, on a date, in words or acts of their own. The planter who would fake a refused demand must fake two hands' acts, not one — the demand and the refusal — and the refusal's hand stands outside the maker's circle, so the forgery surface doubles and the outside hand can be asked whether it refused. T-505's life test asked only whether anything happened; a refusal is the most happened thing a demand can meet short of payment, because it is the one response the maker cannot supply alone.

The second reason is that counting only satisfied demands would punish candour and reward the payer's strategy. The maker who demands each part on its date, openly, and is refused each time has done more in the world than the maker who quietly lets the dates pass and writes nothing; if refusal did not count, the candid maker would stand below the silent one, and the counterparty could kill a run at will by refusing everything demanded of it. The test would then measure not whether the schedule lived, but whether the counterparty cooperated — and cooperation is the one thing a dispute, by definition, no longer supplies. A refusal is the schedule's life meeting resistance, and resistance is still life: the business moved, the parties collided, the date meant enough to someone to be worth refusing.

The third reason is that counting refusal as performance would collapse invocation into satisfaction, and the run was built to measure a life of acts, not a life of arguments. Every instalment agreement refused in full would become a performed run the moment its demands were refused, and a maker could manufacture a performed history out of rejections alone — demanding sums it knew would be refused, collecting refusals as if they were receipts. The split mark prevents both errors at once: Invoked-Refused keeps the refusal inside the life test, where it belongs, and outside the performance count, where it does not. The sitting judges the run on performed parts plus invoked-refused parts marked as such, and a run with no performed part is filed as a run of invitations, honest about what it is.

What a sitting files follows from the three reasons, and the file must show, in addition to T-505's filing, for each refused part: the demand's date and form, the refusal's date and form and hand, whether the refusal was of the sum, of the date, or of the schedule's validity itself — a refusal of a sum on a date invokes the schedule, while a refusal that denies the schedule ever bound anyone is a different act, and the file must say which it was — and the sitting's mark, Invoked-Refused or Performed, never both, never blurred. A refusal dated after the dispute does not retroactively invoke a pre-dispute part: invocation, like any instance, must precede the dispute to count before it. A demand refused in part — part of the sum paid, the rest refused — is filed as two entries, one Performed for the part paid, one Invoked-Refused for the rest, so that no single entry smuggles a mixed history past the sitting.

**T-507 — the Refusal of What — designed:** T-506 left its refusal-of-what problem named and open: whether a refusal of the schedule's validity itself — denying the agreement ever bound anyone — invokes the schedule for the life test, or repudiates it so wholly that nothing under it counts, even as invoked. T-507 answers: a validity refusal repudiates, it does not invoke — but it is not nothing. The sitting must sort refusals by what they refuse, because the three kinds do different work. A refusal of a sum on a date invokes the schedule: the counterparty accepts the agreement's frame and contests only its arithmetic or its calendar, and T-506 files it Invoked-Refused. A refusal of a date's arrival — "not yet due," "the date was moved" — likewise invokes, disputing the schedule's reading, not its being. A refusal of validity itself — "no such agreement," "the signature is not mine," "the schedule was never agreed" — denies the frame, and a denied frame cannot be invoked by the denial: the counterparty's act proves the demand reached a hand and was answered, but what it answers is the dispute, not the schedule. It is filed not as Invoked-Refused but as Repudiated — a worldly act about the agreement's existence, usable as the dispute's own paper, never as a schedule instance.

The first reason is that invocation requires the schedule to be the ground the parties stand on, and a validity refusal removes the ground. The counterparty who refuses a sum says, in effect, "under this agreement, not that much, not on that date" — the agreement survives the refusal as the shared measure, and the sitting can judge the part against it. The counterparty who refuses validity says, "there is no agreement to measure by" — and if the sitting then counted that refusal as a schedule instance, it would be using the counterparty's denial of the schedule as proof the schedule lived, which is the denial wearing the schedule's clothes. The planter who would fake such a run need fake only a demand and a denial — both papers pointing at an agreement whose existence is itself the disputed thing — and the run would then bootstrap itself out of its own contested paper. T-506's outside-touch discipline forbids exactly this: the refusal's hand is outside the maker's circle, but an outside hand denying the paper is not an outside hand confirming it, and confirmation is what an instance requires.

The second reason is that a validity refusal still has a use, and refusing it a schedule instance does not discard it. Writing adds the durable trace: the words survive their speaking, and the sitting reads them rather than reconstructing them. Witnessed writing adds a second hand to the trace: someone besides the maker attests the act happened, so the sitting need not take the maker's word for the making. Sealed writing adds the maker's own standing mark to the trace: the seal says this writing is mine, in a form no second hand can supply and no later denial can shrug off, because the seal was affixed by the maker at the making. Each step removes one way of doubting the act, and a ladder that merged witnessed and sealed writing would merge two different removals — doubt about the act's occurrence, and doubt about the maker's ownership of it — and leave the sitting unable to say which doubt a given re-denial had cleared.

The second reason is that the signed payment under protest settles the lower end of the ladder by the same legibility test. A payment made in silence is conduct: the sitting sees money moved and must infer what the mover meant. A payment signed under protest is conduct plus a written reservation: the signature names the payer, and the protest names the reservation, in words that survive the payment. That written reservation is legible in exactly the way writing is legible, and it outranks a spoken concession for the same reason writing outranks speech anywhere on the ladder — the spoken concession can be denied, the written protest cannot be unmade, because the paper remains. So the signed payment under protest sits on the writing rung, not the conduct rung: it re-denies a spoken withdrawal (it exceeds it), it matches a written withdrawal (it is writing), and it does not reach a witnessed or sealed withdrawal, because a signature alone is neither a witness nor a seal. Conduct, by contrast, always sits below the spoken word: a bare act with no words to quote cannot outrank words spoken, because the sitting can quote the words and can only infer the act.

The third reason is that the five-rung ladder keeps T-510's relative rule honest at the top, where the stakes are highest. Under T-510, a re-denial converts only where it matches or exceeds the withdrawal it retracts, and the withdrawal's weakness lowers the bar to its own rung. With witnessed and sealed writing sharing a rung, a witnessed re-denial would convert a sealed withdrawal, and a sealed re-denial would be needed for nothing a witnessed one could not do — the seal, the strongest mark a maker can affix, would buy no extra standing. With sealed above witnessed, the rule prices each rung: a witnessed withdrawal is re-denied by witnessed writing or by sealed writing; a sealed withdrawal is re-denied only by sealed writing. The maker who sealed a withdrawal paid the highest price for standing, and the counterparty who would retract it must pay the same price. The ladder's top is not decorative: it is where the relative rule does its most consequential work, because the withdrawals that most need protection against cheap retraction are the ones made in the strongest form.

What a sitting files follows from the three reasons, and the file must show, in addition to T-510's filing, for each re-denial: the withdrawal's rung stated as one of the five — conduct, spoken word, writing, witnessed writing, sealed writing — the re-denial's rung stated the same way, and the comparison stated outright — matched, exceeded, or failed. A signed payment under protest is filed on the writing rung, with the protest's words quoted and the signature noted, never filed as conduct with a note attached. A witnessed re-denial of a sealed withdrawal is filed as an attempted re-denial, with the frame's standing stated as continuing, because a witness attests occurrence and cannot supply the maker's seal. A sealed re-denial of a witnessed withdrawal is filed as a conversion, because it exceeds the rung it retracts. Form is measured at the making, per T-510: a seal affixed after the re-denial's making does not retroactively lift its rung, and a witness who arrives after the writing does not lift it either, because the rung is the form the act had when made, not the form its later proof wears.

**Distinguished from the chain it answers.** From T-510's Relative Ladder (the comparison rule — there the question was whether a re-denial counts at all, and the answer was the relative test, at least as strong as the withdrawal it retracts; here the question is what the rungs are, and the answer is five distinct rungs, sealed above witnessed, with a signed payment under protest on the writing rung). From T-509's Re-Denial (the ending rule — there the question was what a re-denial does to the between-acts, and the answer was that it ends the frame's life from its own date, never erasing them; here the ladder decides only whether the ending happened, and a re-denial that fails the ladder's top rung never ends anything). From T-508's Withdrawn Denial (the resumption rule — there the same-or-stronger rule governed a withdrawal retracting a denial; here the same rule is carried to its full ladder, so that a withdrawal's own form, and not just its strength in the abstract, sets the price of retracting it).

**What this pairs with.** T-510's Relative Ladder (the rule this completes — the ladder's rungs are now named and ordered, so a sitting states a rung rather than arguing a strength). T-509's Re-Denial (the rule this guards — the ending now has a five-rung test, so a witnessed whisper at the top cannot silently close a sealed frame).
