**T-526 — the Reconstructed Note — designed:** T-525 left its reconstruction problem named and open: whether a note reconstructed after the act, from memory or from surrounding correspondence, ever counts as a kept paper, and how much weight it carries against a contemporaneous paper that says otherwise. T-526 answers: a reconstructed note never counts as a kept paper on its own, and against a contemporaneous paper that says otherwise it carries no weight at all — it is not weighed against the paper, it is set aside by it. The sitting does not balance memory against paper; it reads the paper, and the reconstruction that contradicts it is memory wearing a paper's clothes, which T-525 already refuses. A reconstruction earns its only credit in two lesser offices: as corroboration of a contemporaneous paper, and as a copy of a proved paper whose original is lost. In neither office does it stand alone.

The first rung is the no-standing rule, and it states the reconstruction's place. A note written after the act, from memory or from the file's surroundings, is not a kept paper under T-525's four-corners rule, because its corners were not kept — they were rebuilt. A rebuilt corner proves what the rebuilder now believes, not what the inquiry was; and a sitting that credited rebuilt corners would credit every inquiry ever claimed, which is exactly the failure T-525's paper rule exists to prevent. The reconstruction's date is its own undoing: a note dated after the act cannot prove a diligence that had to exist before it, and a note that hides its reconstruction date — presented as if contemporaneous — is not a kept paper but a forgery of one, which the sitting treats as T-515's self-blinding in a new coat, not as diligence at all. Honest reconstruction declares itself: "written later, from memory and the file," and the sitting reads it under that label or not at all.

The second rung is the contradiction rule, and it is absolute. Where a contemporaneous paper and a reconstruction disagree — the paper names one person refused, the reconstruction another; the paper records a refusal, the reconstruction a promise — the paper wins outright, with no weighing, no splitting, and no discount for the paper's own thinness. A thin contemporaneous paper still beats a full reconstruction, because thinness is a kept paper's flaw and reconstruction is not a paper's cure. The sitting does not ask which account is likelier true; it asks which account was kept, and the kept account governs even where the reconstruction rings truer, because the sitting's business is proof, not truth-finding by hindsight. The one exception is not a weighing but a replacement: where the contemporaneous paper is itself proved false — a date proved impossible, a person proved absent — the paper falls as a paper, and the reconstruction is then judged as corroboration of whatever else stands, never as a paper in its place.

The third rung is the corroboration rule, and it grades reconstructions by their making. A reconstruction from surrounding correspondence — dates, dispatch records, letters that quote the call — is strong corroboration: it confirms a corner the contemporaneous paper leaves thin, and it can carry a corner the paper states but does not detail, because the correspondence is itself kept paper, and the reconstruction is only its index. A reconstruction from pure memory is the weakest corroboration: it supports a kept paper but never extends it, and it never supplies a corner the paper lacks entirely, because memory supplying a missing corner is memory standing alone under a paper's name. A reconstruction that matches the contemporaneous paper on every corner adds nothing but confidence; a reconstruction that matches on some corners and contradicts on others is severed, not averaged — the matching corners corroborate, the contradicting corners are discarded under the second rung, and the sitting never lets a half-true reconstruction launder its false half through its true one, which is the severability problem left open below.

The fourth rung is the lost-paper cure, and it is the reconstruction's only promotion. Where the contemporaneous paper is lost but its existence and content are proved independently — the counterparty's own file holds a copy, a dispatch record proves the letter went, an admission under T-525's cure proves the inquiry was made — a reconstruction of that proved paper counts as a copy of it, not as a paper of its own. The distinction is the whole cure: the reconstruction is credited because the paper is proved, not because the reconstruction is believed, and it is credited only as far as the independent proof reaches — a dispatch record proves a letter went, not what it asked; a counterparty's file copy proves the whole letter, question and all. Where no independent proof exists, there is no cure: a lost paper with only a reconstruction behind it is an unrecorded inquiry in a new coat, and T-525's rule applies unchanged — for the sitting, it was never made.

The boundary that holds all four rungs together is that a paper is proved by its keeping, and a reconstruction is proved by its sources. A reconstruction with kept sources — correspondence, dispatch records, the other side's file — borrows their keeping and earns corroboration or copy-status accordingly; a reconstruction with only memory behind it borrows nothing and earns nothing against a paper. A fence proved through a lawful crossing binds as terms; a fence proved only through shaping binds as a fact to inquire after; and an inquiry proved only through a reconstruction binds as corroboration of a kept paper, as a copy of a proved paper, or as nothing at all — never as a paper in its own right, because the sitting weighs papers, not memories dressed as papers.

New admitted-unsolved: the second-hand reconstruction problem (whether a reconstruction by a successor or agent who did not make the inquiry — working from the inquirer's file, or from the inquirer's own account — carries even corroboration weight, or whether reconstruction credit requires the rebuilder to have been a party to the inquiry); and the severability problem (whether a reconstruction that matches a contemporaneous paper on some corners and contradicts it on others is severed corner by corner, or whether one contradicting corner discounts the whole reconstruction, including its matching corners); and the admission-cure scope problem (whether the counterparty's admission under T-525's cure admits only that an inquiry was made, or also admits the inquiry's content as the reconstruction states it, and whether an admission of occurrence without content leaves the reconstruction as corroboration only). T-525's waiting-window problem (how long B must wait for an answer before proceeding — a fixed interval, the act's own deadline, or whatever the counterparty's past practice suggests — and whether a counterparty that always answers slowly earns a longer window) remains open, as does T-525's copy-custody problem (whether B must hold the inquiry copy itself, or whether a copy filed with B's agent or counsel, producible on demand, suffices, and whether a lost copy is cured by the counterparty's own file), as does T-524's repeated-inquiry problem and narrowness-measure problem, and all other problems carried in T-525's admitted-unsolved paragraph, all carried forward by reference.

**T-527 — the Second-Hand Note — designed:** T-526 left its second-hand reconstruction problem named and open: whether a reconstruction by a successor or agent who did not make the inquiry — working from the inquirer's file, or from the inquirer's own account — carries even corroboration weight, or whether reconstruction credit requires the rebuilder to have been a party to the inquiry. T-527 answers: the rebuilder's standing is not the test; the sources are. A second-hand reconstruction borrows exactly what its sources lend and nothing more — a successor working from a kept file inherits the file's keeping, while a successor working from the inquirer's memory inherits only memory, one remove further from the act, which is to say nothing at all. Party status never cures a sourceless reconstruction, and non-party status never taints a well-sourced one.

The first rung is the source rule, and it replaces the standing question. T-526 graded first-hand reconstructions by their making — correspondence strong, pure memory weakest — and the second hand changes nothing in that grading except to add distance. A successor who rebuilds from the inquirer's file is doing the same work the inquirer would do from the same file, and the sitting credits it the same way: as corroboration of a kept paper, or as a copy of a proved paper, graded by the file's corners, not by whose hand held the pen. A successor who rebuilds from the inquirer's account of the inquiry — "she told me she asked, and this is what she asked" — is rebuilding from memory at one remove: the inquirer's memory, carried by the successor's report, which the sitting cannot test against the act any better than it could test the inquirer's own memory, and in fact worse, because the successor cannot be asked what the inquirer forgot. Memory of memory is not corroboration; it is a rumour of a reconstruction, and T-526's weakest rung is its ceiling, not its floor.

The second rung is the file-sourced second hand, and it inherits keeping. Where the inquirer's file holds kept paper — dispatch records, correspondence quoting the call, the counterparty's reply — the successor's reconstruction is an index of that paper, and it earns whatever the paper earns: it corroborates a contemporaneous paper's thin corners, and where the original inquiry paper is lost but proved by the file, it counts as a copy of it under T-526's lost-paper cure. The successor's distance is irrelevant here because the paper does the proving, not the successor; the sitting reads the file, and the reconstruction only points. One condition attaches, and it is strict: the successor must show the file, corner by corner, so the sitting can check that each reconstructed corner traces to a kept corner. A file-sourced reconstruction that cites the file generally — "from the file" without corners — is not file-sourced at all; it is an assertion wearing a file's name, and it falls to the third rung.

The third rung is the account-sourced second hand, and it earns nothing on its own. An account is not a paper unless it was kept as one: if the inquirer left a contemporaneous note of the inquiry, that note is a kept paper, and the successor's reconstruction from it is file-sourced under the second rung, not account-sourced at all — the label follows the source, not the story. But an account given later, from the inquirer's memory, whether spoken to the successor or written down by the successor at the telling, is memory with a messenger attached, and the messenger adds no weight: the sitting cannot cross-examine the inquirer's memory through the successor, cannot test what the inquirer misremembered against what the successor misheard, and will not credit a chain whose first link is already T-526's weakest. The only credit an account-sourced reconstruction can earn is derivative: where the account matches a contemporaneous paper, it confirms nothing the paper does not already prove, and where it contradicts a paper, T-526's contradiction rule discards it outright — a second hand cannot overrule a first paper.

The fourth rung is the declaration rule, and it is the second hand's honesty boundary. A successor's reconstruction must declare itself three ways: who rebuilt it, from what sources, and at what distance from the act — "rebuilt by the successor, from the inquirer's file, two hands from the inquiry," or "rebuilt by the successor, from the inquirer's account, memory at one remove." A successor who presents the inquirer's account as their own memory, or who presents a file-sourced index as if they had made the inquiry, commits T-526's hidden-date offence in a new coat: a reconstruction that hides its distance is not a reconstruction but a forgery of standing, and the sitting treats it as self-blinding, not as diligence. Conversely, an honest declaration costs the successor nothing they were entitled to: a declared file-sourced reconstruction keeps its full file credit, because the credit was never the successor's to lose.

New admitted-unsolved: the chain-of-hands problem (whether each further hand — a successor's successor, working from the successor's reconstruction rather than the original file — decays the reconstruction's credit, or whether a faithful copy of a file-sourced reconstruction carries the file's credit undiminished through any number of hands); and the dead-inquirer problem (whether a file-sourced reconstruction gains or loses credit when the inquirer is unavailable to confirm or correct it — the file speaking alone, with no living witness to answer for its gaps); and the adopted-account problem (whether a successor who verifies part of the inquirer's account against the file thereby lifts the unverified remainder, or whether verification is corner by corner and the unverified corners stay at memory's weight). **T-528 — the Chain of Hands — designed:** T-527 left its chain-of-hands problem named and open: whether each further hand — a successor's successor, working from the successor's reconstruction rather than the original file — decays the reconstruction's credit, or whether a faithful copy of a file-sourced reconstruction carries the file's credit undiminished through any number of hands. T-528 answers: the chain decays only where a hand re-derives, never where a hand merely copies. A faithful copy of a file-sourced reconstruction carries the file's credit undiminished through any number of hands, because a copy adds no new claim; a hand that re-derives from the prior reconstruction instead of the file starts a new reconstruction, graded fresh under T-526 and T-527, and its credit is the credit of its own sources — which, where the prior reconstruction is its only source, is nothing at all. The test is never the number of hands; it is whether each hand touched the file or only the last hand's paper.

The first rung is the copy rule, and it states what a faithful copy is. A copy counts as the reconstruction it copies, with the same credit and the same limits, only if it reproduces the reconstruction's corners without alteration, addition, or selection — the same question, date, and refusal, the same declared sources, the same declared distance. A copy that silently corrects a corner, fills a gap from the copier's own knowledge, or drops an inconvenient corner is not a copy but a new reconstruction wearing a copy's name, and it is graded as one under the third rung. The copy must also carry the chain's declarations forward: each hand adds its own line — "copied by the third hand, from the second hand's reconstruction, which was file-sourced" — so the sitting can trace every corner back to the file without taking any hand's word for the trace. A chain whose links are declared is auditable at any length; a chain whose links are merged into one undated "reconstruction" is unauditable at any length, and the sitting treats it as a single undeclared reconstruction, graded at its weakest link.

The second rung is the undiminished-carry rule, and it refuses decay by counting. Where each hand copies faithfully and declares its link, the tenth hand's copy stands exactly where the first hand's reconstruction stood: as corroboration of a kept paper, or as a copy of a proved paper under T-526's lost-paper cure, and no further. Length adds no weight and subtracts none, because the sitting weighs the file, not the hands — and the file has not changed because ten hands pointed at it. This is the same principle that lets a certified copy of a letter prove the letter at any remove: the proof is the original's keeping, transmitted, not the transmitters' number. The rule's limit is strict: undiminished carry transmits the reconstruction's credit, never more. A file-sourced reconstruction that was corroboration only does not become a kept paper by being copied ten times; repetition is not keeping, and ten hands agreeing on a corner the file never stated still prove only that ten hands copied one another.

The third rung is the re-derivation rule, and it is where chains actually decay. A hand that works from the prior reconstruction rather than the file — re-reading the successor's note, re-summarizing it, "tidying" its corners — produces a new reconstruction whose source is a reconstruction, not a paper. Under T-527's source rule, such a reconstruction borrows what its source lends: and a reconstruction lends only its own declared sources, at one further remove. A re-derivation from a file-sourced reconstruction therefore stands as a third-hand account of the file, graded as account-sourced memory at one remove, which T-527 already holds to earn nothing on its own — unless the re-deriving hand checks each corner back against the file, in which case the work is file-sourced again, and the hand has rejoined the chain rather than extending it. The practical test is the file-check: a hand that can show, corner by corner, that it verified its paper against the file is a copier of the file, whatever its place in the chain; a hand that can show only that it verified its paper against the last hand's paper is a re-deriver, and its credit is the last hand's credit minus the distance it added — which, for a paper that was never a kept paper, is zero.

The fourth rung is the break rule, and it states what snaps a chain. A chain breaks at any hand that cannot produce its source: a lost link, an undeclared copy, a hand that copied from a reconstruction it no longer holds. The break does not destroy the earlier links — the file-sourced reconstruction before the break keeps its credit — but nothing after the break inherits it, because inheritance runs through declared links, and a missing link is a missing inheritance. A broken chain can be repaired only by re-anchoring: a later hand that returns to the file and re-derives from it starts a fresh chain at full file credit, and the sitting reads the repaired chain as the new chain, not as a continuation of the old. What never repairs a break is attestation: a later hand's assurance that the missing link was faithful is itself an account-sourced reconstruction, graded under T-527's third rung, and it earns nothing.

The boundary that holds all four rungs together is that credit travels through sources, not through hands. Hands transmit; they do not create. A chain of a hundred faithful copies proves exactly what its file proves, no more and no less; a chain with one re-deriving hand proves what that hand's sources prove, which is the file if it checked, and nothing if it did not. A fence proved through a lawful crossing binds as terms; a fence proved only through shaping binds as a fact to inquire after; and an inquiry proved through a chain of hands binds as far as the chain's links reach back to the file — and not one hand further, because a hand that never touched the file cannot lend the file's keeping.

New admitted-unsolved: the partial-copy problem (whether a copy that reproduces some corners faithfully and drops others carries undiminished credit for the copied corners while losing the dropped ones, or whether a selective copy is a new reconstruction in full); and the digital-copy problem (whether a bit-identical electronic copy, with a hash matching the reconstruction's hash, counts as a faithful copy without a hand's declaration at all, or whether the declaration rule still requires a human link); and the file-loss problem (whether a chain whose file is later lost keeps its credit — the copies now proving a paper no longer producible — or whether the chain's credit dies with the file, leaving only the copies' own declarations). **T-529 — the Partial Copy — designed:** T-528 left its partial-copy problem named and open: whether a copy that reproduces some corners faithfully and drops others carries undiminished credit for the copied corners while losing the dropped ones, or whether a selective copy is a new reconstruction in full. T-529 answers: severance, not wholesale discount. Credit is per-corner, not per-paper. A partial copy carries the file's credit undiminished for every corner it faithfully reproduces, and carries nothing at all for every corner it drops — the dropped corners are simply unproved by this copy, neither proved nor disproved. Selection alone never taints a faithful corner; what taints is only misrepresentation of the selection, or a dropped corner whose absence changes what a kept corner means.

The first rung is the severance rule, and it states the default. A corner's credit travels with the corner, not with the paper's completeness. Where a copy reproduces the inquiry's question and date faithfully but drops its refusal, the sitting credits the question and the date exactly as T-528's undiminished-carry rule credits them, and treats the refusal as unproved by this copy — to be proved, if at all, by another paper, another copy, or not at all. The alternative — discounting the whole copy because it is incomplete — would punish honesty about incompleteness and reward the fuller forgery: a hand that dropped a corner openly would fare worse than a hand that invented one, which is the wrong incentive in every direction. Severance also answers T-526's severability problem from the copy side: matching corners keep their credit even where the copy is silent on the rest, because silence is not contradiction, and a copy contradicts nothing it does not state.

The second rung is the dropped-corner rule, and it refuses to read absence as evidence. A dropped corner proves nothing about itself: not that the inquiry lacked that corner, not that the corner was unfavourable, not that the copier suppressed it. The sitting may draw no adverse inference from a declared omission alone, because a copy's omissions have a hundred innocent causes — a torn page, a redaction, a copier who copied only what was asked for — and an adverse inference would turn every partial copy into a confession. The inference the sitting may draw runs the other way only where the copy was made for a purpose that required the dropped corner: a copy commissioned to prove the refusal that omits the refusal is not merely partial, it is a failed proof, and its failure is the proof's own, not the refusal's. But a copy made to prove the question that omits the refusal proves the question, and the refusal's absence from it is simply a gap the sitting must fill elsewhere or leave open.

The third rung is the material-omission rule, and it is severance's only exception. Where a dropped corner would qualify, limit, or reverse a kept corner — the refusal that was conditional, the date that was later corrected, the question that was withdrawn and re-asked in narrower form — the kept corner's credit is discounted to the extent of the unknown qualification. The discount is measured, not total: a kept question whose dropped condition might have narrowed it is credited as a question, not as the narrowed question, and the sitting reads it at its unqualified weight, which is to say at less than the full paper would have carried. The test is counterfactual and strict: would a sitting that knew the dropped corner read the kept corner differently? If yes, the kept corner is discounted by the difference; if no — the dropped corner is independent, a separate matter, a corner the kept corner never touched — severance holds and the kept corner stands whole. The burden of showing materiality falls on the party who would discount, not on the copier: a challenger must name the dropped corner and say what it would have changed, and a merely speculative "something might have qualified it" discounts nothing.

The fourth rung is the presentation rule, and it is the partial copy's honesty boundary. A partial copy presented as a whole — "the reconstruction," unqualified, with no declaration of what was dropped — is not a partial copy at all but a new reconstruction, graded under T-526 and T-527 as an undeclared reconstruction, because it claims a completeness it does not have. The offence is the same family as T-526's hidden-date offence and T-528's merged-chain offence: a paper that hides its own limits forges its own standing. Conversely, an honestly declared partial copy — "copied corners: question, date; omitted: refusal, dispatch record" — keeps its severed credit in full, because the sitting can see exactly what it is being asked to credit and what it is not. The declaration must name the omission in kind, not merely in general: "some corners omitted" declares nothing the sitting can use, while "the refusal omitted" lets the sitting weigh the question knowing the refusal is unproved. A declared partial copy that is later completed by a second hand copying the dropped corners does not merge into a whole paper by accumulation; each hand's credit stays severed to its own corners, and the sitting reads two partial copies, not one complete one.

New admitted-unsolved: the materiality-measure problem (who decides whether a dropped corner would have changed a kept corner's reading — the sitting's judgment, a stated test, or the counterparty's showing — and whether a corner whose materiality is itself disputed is discounted pending proof or credited pending disproof); and the silent-selection problem (whether a pattern of selection across many copies — always dropping the refusals, always keeping the questions — earns an adverse inference that a single declared omission does not, or whether each copy is still judged alone); and the reassembly problem (whether two partial copies from different hands, covering different corners, combine into full paper credit, or whether credit stays severed per hand even when the corners together cover the whole paper). T-528's digital-copy problem (whether a bit-identical electronic copy counts as a faithful copy without a hand's declaration) remains open, as does T-528's file-loss problem, T-527's dead-inquirer problem, T-527's adopted-account problem, T-526's severability problem and admission-cure scope problem, T-525's waiting-window problem and copy-custody problem, T-524's repeated-inquiry problem and narrowness-measure problem, and all other problems carried in T-528's admitted-unsolved paragraph, all carried forward by reference.

**T-530 — the Reassembly — designed:** T-529 left its reassembly problem named and open: whether two partial copies from different hands, covering different corners, combine into full paper credit, or whether credit stays severed per hand even when the corners together cover the whole paper. T-530 answers: the corners combine; the credit does not. The sitting may read the two partial copies together and know the inquiry's whole content, but it may not upgrade either hand's credit by the other's coverage — the mosaic is a reading, never a paper. A whole paper assembled from severed corners is still severed at every seam, and a seam is not healed by being covered.

The first rung is the mosaic rule, and it separates content from credit. Where one hand's partial copy carries the question and the date, and another hand's carries the refusal, the sitting now holds all three corners and may reason about the inquiry as a whole — the question asked, the date it was asked, the refusal it met. What the sitting may not do is call that whole a kept paper: no single hand copied the whole, no single copy proves the whole, and the whole's credit is exactly the sum of its severed parts — the question at the first hand's credit, the date at the first hand's, the refusal at the second's. Coverage is not keeping: a paper is kept whole or not at all, and two halves kept separately are two kept halves, not one kept paper. The practical consequence is sharp: the mosaic proves the inquiry's content corner by corner, but it never discharges T-525's duty the way a kept paper would, because the duty asks for a paper, and the mosaic is a reading of papers, not a paper itself.

The second rung is the agreement rule, and it governs the corners both hands cover. Where two partial copies agree on a shared corner — both carry the same question, the same date — the agreement adds confidence but not status: two hands pointing at the same corner corroborate each other the way T-526 grades corroboration, and corroboration is not keeping. Agreement never promotes a corner from corroboration to copy, and it never promotes the mosaic to a paper. Where the two copies disagree on a shared corner — one date against another, one refusal against a different refusal — the disagreement discounts the corner in both copies until the file settles it, and the disagreement itself is evidence that at least one hand erred. The sitting may not resolve the disagreement by counting (two hands against one is not truth), by recency (the later copy is not the corrected one), or by preference (the hand the sitting trusts more is not the hand that copied truly); it resolves it only by the file, or it leaves the corner discounted. A disagreement the file cannot settle leaves the mosaic with a hole at that corner, and the hole is declared, not papered over by the hand the sitting likes better.

The third rung is the gap rule, and it refuses to fill holes by shape. A corner covered by neither copy — the dispatch record neither hand copied, the answer neither hand kept — stays unproved, however complete the mosaic looks without it. The sitting may not infer the missing corner from the assembled shape: that the two copies together cover everything except the refusal's condition does not prove the condition, nor its absence, nor that the refusal was unconditional. T-529's dropped-corner rule already forbids reading absence as evidence in a single copy, and the mosaic inherits that forbiddance twice over — a hole in the mosaic is a hole, declared as a hole, and the sitting reasons around it rather than through it. A mosaic that looks whole is the most dangerous partial copy of all, because its completeness is an appearance the sitting did not earn.

The fourth rung is the presentation rule, and it is the mosaic's honesty boundary. A mosaic presented as a single whole paper — "the reconstruction," unqualified, seams hidden — is T-529's presentation offence in a new coat: it claims a completeness no hand achieved, and it forfeits the whole as an undeclared reconstruction, every corner discounted with the presentation. Conversely, an honestly declared mosaic — "question and date from the first hand's copy, refusal from the second's, dispatch record covered by neither, date shared and agreed" — keeps every corner's severed credit in full, because the sitting can see exactly what it is being asked to credit and where the seams run. The declaration must name the seams in kind: which hand supplied which corner, which corners are shared, which are missing. "Assembled from the copies" declares nothing the sitting can use; a seam list does. A mosaic later completed by a third hand copying a missing corner does not merge into a whole paper by accumulation — it becomes a three-hand mosaic, seams intact, credit still severed per corner.

The boundary that holds all four rungs together is that hands transmit and corners carry, and neither operation creates what the other lacks. A mosaic transmits the corners its hands copied, at the credit those hands earned, and nothing further. A fence proved through a lawful crossing binds as terms; a fence proved only through shaping binds as a fact to inquire after; and an inquiry proved through a mosaic of partial copies binds as far as each corner's hand reaches — and not one corner further, because a hand that never copied a corner cannot lend that corner's keeping, and two hands that each copied half a paper cannot together lend a whole one.

New admitted-unsolved: the seam-declaration problem (how precisely seams must be declared — per corner, per hand, or per copy — and whether a mosaic with undeclared seams but traceable sources is repaired by tracing or void as presented); and the disagreement-resolution problem (whether a shared-corner disagreement between two partial copies is resolved by a third copy, by the file, or left unresolved with both discounted, and whether a third copy agreeing with one side counts as resolution or merely as a second disagreement); and the single-hand reassembly problem (whether one hand copying from two partial copies into one fuller copy creates a new reconstruction or a faithful compilation, and whether its compilation credit is the lower of the two sources or each corner's own). **T-531 — the Third Copy — designed:** T-530 left its disagreement-resolution problem named and open: whether a shared-corner disagreement between two partial copies is resolved by a third copy, by the file, or left unresolved with both discounted, and whether a third copy agreeing with one side counts as resolution or merely as a second disagreement. T-531 answers: a third copy never resolves by agreement — agreement is corroboration, and corroboration is not settlement. Only the file settles a disagreement. A third copy can re-frame it, corroborate one side for reasoning, or deepen it, but it cannot close it. Counting hands is not judging them, and two hands against one is a tally, not a truth.

The first rung is the counting rule, and it refuses the tally outright. Where side A reads the date as the 12th and side B reads it as the 14th, and a third hand's copy reads the 12th, the corner does not become the 12th by a vote of two to one. The tally fails for two independent reasons, either of which alone would kill it. First, the third hand may have copied from side A rather than from the file — derivative agreement is an echo, not a witness, and an echo of A counts as A, not as A plus one. Second, even a genuinely independent third hand is still a copy, not the file: three copies agreeing are three copies, and T-530 already holds that agreement adds confidence but not status. What the third copy's agreement does buy is confidence for reasoning: the sitting may lean on the corroborated reading to frame its next question, to seek the file in the right place, to test the counterparty's account against it. Leaning is not keeping. The sitting that leans on the 12th while the corner stays unsettled reasons provisionally; the sitting that records the 12th as kept has mistaken a majority for a witness.

The second rung is the independence test, and it decides what the third copy is worth even as corroboration. A third copy counts as independent evidence only if it shows it touched something the disagreeing copies did not. The marks of independence are difference, not agreement: a corner neither side carries, a distinct slip of its own, a declaration naming the file rather than a prior copy as its source. Conversely, a third copy that reproduces side A's exact error — the same misspelled name, the same dropped qualifier, the same wrong date in the same hand — is presumptively derivative, and adds nothing even as corroboration: it is side A twice, and twice-counted evidence is counted evidence, which the first rung already forbids. The paradox to hold is that the most useful third copy is the one that agrees on the disputed corner and differs elsewhere, because everywhere-agreement smells of copying the copy, while agreement-plus-independent-difference smells of a second hand that actually looked. Independence is never presumed from the mere existence of a third paper; it is proved by marks, or it is not proved at all, and an unproved third copy corroborates nothing.

The third rung is the re-framing rule, and it is the one genuine resolution a third copy can deliver — by dissolving the disagreement rather than deciding it. Sometimes the two readings were never the same corner: side A's date is the inquiry date, side B's is the dispatch date, and the third copy carries both, labelled, showing the two hands each copied a different corner and mistook it for the shared one. Then there was no disagreement at all, only a mislabelled seam, and both sides keep their credit under corrected labels — the seam-declaration problem T-530 left open does part of the work here, because a seam list would have prevented the false disagreement in the first place. But re-framing must be proved, not invited: the third copy must itself carry the distinguishing labels, the two dates side by side with their different offices, not merely suggest that some distinction might exist. A third copy that offers an explanation without the labels is a reconstruction under T-526, graded as one, and its explanation is a claim, not a cure. And where the third copy brings a third reading of the same corner — neither the 12th nor the 14th but the 16th — it deepens the discount rather than resolving anything: all three readings now stand discounted, and the corner is affirmatively doubtful, not merely unsettled, which is a reason to seek the file harder, not to pick the reading the sitting likes best.

The fourth rung is the provisional-reliance rule, and it draws the line the first three rungs imply. While a corner stays unsettled, the sitting may reason on the corroborated side — ask questions framed on it, test accounts against it, direct the search for the file by it — but it may not discharge any duty on it, bind any counterparty by it, or record it as kept. The test is reversibility: an act the sitting can walk back when the file speaks differently is permitted on a corroborated reading; an act that would stand even after the file contradicts it is not. A notice sent on the corroborated date, if the notice can be corrected, is reasoning; a discharge granted on it, if the discharge cannot be recalled, is keeping by another name. The presentation rule enforces the same line: a mosaic that presents its third copy as a "tie-breaker," a "majority reading," or a "deciding copy" commits the counting offence, and forfeits the disputed corner's credit in all three copies as presented — the corner the tally claimed to settle is the corner the tally loses. An honestly declared mosaic — "two readings, one corroborated by an independent third hand, none settled, file sought" — keeps every corner's severed credit in full, because the sitting can see exactly what it is being asked to credit and what it is not.

The boundary that holds all four rungs together is that hands transmit, copies corroborate, and only the file settles. A third hand adds a voice, not a verdict; a third copy adds weight, not standing. The file is the only witness that was present at the paper, and every copy, however numerous, however agreeing, is a report of that witness at one or more removes. A sitting that lets the third copy decide has replaced the witness with the audience, and an audience, however large, cannot swear.

**T-532 — the Two Marks — designed:** T-531 left its independence-proof problem named and open: what marks suffice to prove a third hand touched the file rather than a prior copy — a new corner, a distinct slip, a source declaration — and whether any one mark alone suffices, or independence always needs two. T-532 answers: no one mark alone ever suffices, and two marks suffice only when they are cross-kind — one content mark and one provenance mark, both present. Independence is proved by a pair, never by a single, and never by two of the same kind. A single mark is a hint; a pair of the wrong kinds is still a hint; only the cross-kind pair is corroboration.

The first rung sorts the marks into their two kinds, because the counting rule depends on the sorting. A content mark is something in the copy's matter that the disagreeing copies do not carry: a new corner neither side holds, in the file's idiom; or a distinct slip of the third hand's own, an error traceable to neither side's errors. A provenance mark is something tying the copy to the file's custody rather than to a prior copy: a source declaration naming the file, or a custody chain naming the hands the copy passed through, or a material trace matching a known exemplar of the file's paper, ink, or hand. The sorting matters because each kind fails alone in a way the other kind cures. Content without provenance is explicable by invention: a hand copying side A can invent a new corner and make its own slip while copying, and embellishment is not evidence of sight. Provenance without content is explicable by transmission: a declaration travels with the text it declares, so a copy of a copy inherits its source note verbatim, and the note proves the first hand's sight, not the third hand's. Each kind, alone, has a copying explanation; together, they leave the copying explanation strained on both sides at once — the hand both saw matter the copies lack and ties itself to the file by a route the copies do not share.

The second rung is the specificity test, and it decides whether a claimed mark counts as a mark at all. A generic provenance mark counts for nothing: "from the original," "copied from the file," or "true copy" is the formula every copyist writes, including the copyist of a copy, and a formula proves only that the hand knew the formula. A provenance mark counts only when it names something the disagreeing copies do not name and that the file's known custody can check: a folio, a date of sight, a custodian, a place of keeping. Likewise a content mark counts only when it is checkable in the same way: a new corner in the file's idiom — terms, dating style, and offices matching what the file is known to use — not merely a new corner in any idiom, since a forger's invention can wear any idiom it likes and idiom-matching alone is a weak check. The specificity test is therefore a checkability test, not a length test: a short declaration naming the folio and the custodian beats a long declaration naming nothing checkable, and a single new corner in a checkable idiom beats a page of new matter in none. An uncheckable mark is not a weak mark; it is no mark, and a pair built on one is a pair of one.

The third rung is the tier rule, and it grades what each level of proof buys. Zero proved marks: the third copy weighs nothing, not even as corroboration — T-531's unproved copy, which corroborates nothing, stands. One proved mark of either kind: the copy buys search direction only — the sitting may look where the mark points, ask whether the file's custody matches the declaration, or seek the new corner in the file, but it may not reason on the disputed corner from this copy, because a one-mark copy has a live copying explanation. Two proved marks of the same kind — two new corners, or two declarations — buy no more than one: same-kind doubling repeats the same explanation rather than answering it, and a pair that answers only one side of the copying problem is a hint dressed as a pair. A stopping point is a social fact, not a structural one: the chain ends where dispute ends, and a record everyone accepts needs no further outside record, while a record anyone with standing disputes needs one more, however many already stand behind it.

The first rung is the dispute rule, and it refuses the registry as a stopping point outright. Where the outside record is a public registry entry and a hand with standing disputes that entry's making — a misfiled folio, a backdated stamp, a clerk's error carried into the book — the registry's publicness does not stop the regress, because publicness is a property of access, not of truth: a book anyone may read may still misrecord what it records. The regress stops only when the record's making and keeping stand undisputed by every hand the sitting recognizes as having standing to dispute them. A registry entry no one disputes stops the regress at once; a registry entry one hand disputes stops it nowhere, and the sitting must seek one more record out — not because registries are weak, but because a disputed record is not a stopping point in any coat.

The second rung is the standing test, and it decides whose dispute counts. A dispute stops the regress only when it comes from a hand with standing — a hand the file itself names, a custodian in the chain, or a hand whose interest the sitting has already recognized. A stranger's doubt, a rival's say-so, or a doubt raised for the first time at the sitting without a hand to carry it does not restart the regress, because otherwise any chain could be held hostage by any voice: the regress would never stop, not because the chain is weak but because stopping would be vetoable by anyone at all. Standing is the gate: the sitting names whose disputes count before it asks whether any such dispute stands, and a dispute from outside the gate is noted as a question for inquiry, not as a hole in the chain.

The third rung is the provisional-closure rule, and it grades what an unstopped regress still buys. The fourth rung is the presentation rule, and it punishes the stopping claim, not the chain. A chain does not stop because it has climbed high enough — to a registry, a seal, a public book — but because no hand with standing still pushes against it. The sitting stops asking for one more record when there is no one left with standing to ask for it, and not one record sooner.

**T-542 — the Drift Catch — designed:** T-541 left its deference-drift problem named and open: whether repeated reasonableness review drifts the standard toward whatever appellate sittings prefer — correctness returning in reasonableness's clothes — and what instrument catches the drift. The first rung is the drift mechanism, and it refuses the comforting story that drift is a mistake. Each sitting reviews a line it would or would not have drawn; reasonableness asks whether the line is defensible, but the sitting's own drawing instinct is the nearest yardstick to hand. Over repeated reviews, "defensible" quietly becomes "drawable by us" — not by any sitting's dishonesty, but by the ordinary gravity of preference: a sitting defers easily to a line it likes and searches hard for a reason to vacate a line it dislikes, and after enough cycles the standard's content is whatever the sittings prefer. No single decision announces the drift, because each is defensible on its own record; that is why T-539's reasonableness-on-the-record rule, strong for one decision, is blind to the series. Drift is a property of the series, never of a decision, and only a series-level instrument can see it.

The second rung is the deference receipt, and it disciplines the reviewer, never the line. Every reasonableness decision must carry a receipt naming the record ground it defers to — the specific element of the record that makes the line defensible, not the outcome the sitting tolerates. A decision whose reasons cite only the outcome ("this cut is workable," "this breadth is sensible") carries no receipt and is not deference at all; it is preference wearing the standard's coat, and it is vacatable on that ground alone, without reaching the line's merits. The receipt forces the sitting to point at the record, and a sitting that cannot point has confessed it is not deferring — the confession is the catch, and the catch costs the sitting nothing but its preference.

The third rung is the preference audit, and it is the series-level instrument the first rung demands. A standing audit samples reasonableness decisions — every tenth, or a fixed sample per cycle — and asks only one question: does the decision carry a receipt naming a record ground? It does not re-weigh the line and does not second-guess the outcome; it counts receipts. If the share of receiptless decisions crosses a threshold declared in advance, in the open, the standard is declared drifted. The threshold is declared before the count, because a threshold set after the count is preference counting itself — the audit auditing its own appetite.

The fourth rung is the re-anchoring rule, and it keeps the drift finding from becoming a punishment. Once drift is declared, the next review cycle reverts to correctness — lines judged on their own merits, no deference owed — until a set number of consecutive decisions carry full receipts, at which point deference resumes. The boundary that holds all four rungs together is that a standard that cannot be audited is not a standard but a mood, and deference that cannot show its receipt is not deference but taste. The first rung is the dual trigger, and it refuses to choose between the fraction and the run because each catches a failure the other misses. Drift is declared when either trigger fires on the audit sample — T-542's mechanical sample, every tenth reasonableness decision, no auditor's pick among them. The run trigger fires on three consecutive sampled decisions carrying no receipt: a run means the sittings have stopped pointing at the record altogether, and no share arithmetic is needed to call that drift. The share trigger fires when five or more of the last twenty sampled decisions carry no receipt: a quarter receiptless across a rolling twenty means preference has become the working standard even though receipts still appear often enough to break any run. Either trigger alone suffices, because a standard that has collapsed in a run and a standard that has bled out to a quarter are both drifted, and a rule that waits for both would let each failure hide behind the other's absence.

The second rung is the pinning rule, and it answers the second half of the problem directly: the threshold does not drift, because it is not allowed to move while it measures. The dual trigger — three in a run, five in twenty — is declared in the open before the cycle it governs, and within that cycle it is fixed: no sitting, auditor, or forum may tighten it to catch a disliked series or loosen it to spare a favoured one, and a count taken under it is never re-scored under a later threshold. A threshold that moves mid-count is preference counting itself, which is exactly the failure T-542's advance-declaration rule exists to forbid. The pin holds even when the count is close: a series at four in twenty with no run is not drifted, however uncomfortable, because a threshold that bends at four has already drifted further than the series it measures.

The third rung is the threshold-amendment rule, and it lets the threshold change without letting it drift. Between cycles, the trigger may be amended — three in a run to four, five in twenty to four — but only by an open declaration stating the new numbers and the reason for the change, and only prospectively: the amended trigger governs the next cycle's sample and never reclassifies the last cycle's count. The amendment's stated reason itself joins the audit record, so the next cycle's audit can see whether the threshold was moved to catch drift or to excuse it — a threshold moved after a near-miss, without a reason the record supports, is itself a receiptless decision about the standard, and counts against the forum that moved it. Change in the open, between cycles, with reasons, is amendment; change in silence, mid-count, without reasons, is drift wearing amendment's coat.

The fourth rung is the small-sample rule, and it keeps the dual trigger honest before the sample fills. Until twenty sampled decisions exist, the share trigger is dormant, not extrapolated: four receiptless in the first twelve is not "a third," it is four decisions, and a fraction drawn from a half-filled sample is a guess, not a count. The run trigger, by contrast, is live from the first three sampled decisions, because a run needs no denominator — three consecutive receiptless decisions are drift however short the series. Once the twentieth sampled decision lands, the share trigger wakes with its full rolling window behind it, and from then on both triggers run together, the run catching collapse and the share catching bleed.

**T-544 — the Auditors' Auditor — designed:** T-543 left its audit-forum problem named and open: who audits the auditors — the same drift applies one level up, and a preference audit run by a preference-driven forum is preference counting itself. T-544 answers: the audit is not trusted to a higher forum at all, because a higher forum is only the same problem one storey up. The audit is made recomputable by any hand, audited by lot, and suspended by disagreement — so that no forum's preference ever needs to be trusted, only its arithmetic checked.

The first rung is the recomputation rule, and it dissolves the regress before it climbs. T-542's audit is a computation on a mechanical sample — every tenth reasonableness decision, counted for receipts against T-543's pinned trigger — and a computation with a published input can be redone by anyone who can count. The audit forum therefore publishes, with every drift declaration, the sample itself: the sampled decisions by number, each marked receipt or receiptless, and the count that fired or did not fire the trigger. A drift declaration that withholds its sample is not an audit but an assertion, and is treated as a receiptless decision about the standard — vacatable on that ground alone, under T-543's own logic turned one level up. The regress stops here because the question "who audits the auditors" has a mechanical answer: anyone, from the published sample, with no standing required. A stranger's recount counts exactly as much as a forum's, because both are the same arithmetic on the same numbers.

The second rung is the lot-drawn audit panel, and it keeps the routine audit honest without pretending the panel is above preference. The standing audit panel is drawn by lot, not appointment: each cycle, the panel is the sittings whose numbers fall on a mechanical rule declared in advance — every seventh sitting in the roll, say — with no sitting auditing a series it sat in, and no panel serving two cycles running. Lot-drawn auditors can still prefer, of course; the lot does not purify them. What the lot does is break the chain of appointment: no forum chooses its own auditors, no auditor owes its seat to the forum it audits, and a preference-driven forum cannot staff its own count. Appointment is preference choosing its counters; lot is preference with no hand on the draw. The panel's only office is to publish the sample and the count; it has no power to adjust the trigger, excuse a receiptless decision, or declare drift on an unpublished sample — any of those is outside its office and void on its face.

The third rung is the disagreement rule, and it is what makes the audit self-correcting instead of merely self-asserting. Any hand that recounts the published sample and reaches a different count lodges the recount, with its own marked sample, and the disagreement suspends the drift declaration — not overturns it, suspends it — until a second lot-drawn panel recounts from the same published sample. If the second recount agrees with the first audit, the suspension lifts and the declaration stands; if it agrees with the challenger, the declaration falls and the first panel's count joins the record as a receiptless audit — a mark against the panel, not merely an error, because a forum that miscounts its own audit has shown the drift it was meant to catch. Two recounts that disagree with each other, neither matching the audit, send the sample to a third lot-drawn panel, and the declaration stays suspended until two counts agree. The rule never asks which forum to trust; it asks how many independent counts agree, and lets agreement, not authority, settle the number.

The fourth rung is the forum re-anchoring rule, and it applies T-542's re-anchoring one level up without inventing a new standard for forums. A panel whose count is overturned by recount, or whose declaration is found receiptless for want of a published sample, is itself drifted, and drifts exactly as a standard does: it reverts to no audit authority until it re-anchors — that is, until its next two cycles' samples are published complete and recount-clean, with no disagreement lodged against either. During re-anchoring the panel audits nothing; the mechanical sample is counted instead by any hand that cares to, and the published counts stand on their own arithmetic. A drifted forum is not punished and not disbanded; it is simply set aside until its counting is clean again, because an auditor that cannot count straight is worse than no auditor — it lends preference the shape of a number.

The boundary that holds all four rungs together is that an audit is a receipt about receipts, and it earns trust the same way a receipt does: by pointing at the record where any hand can check it. A forum that publishes its sample needs no trust; a forum that withholds it deserves none; a forum chosen by lot cannot choose its friends; and a count that survives disagreement has earned what no appointment can give it — agreement without authority.

**T-545 — the Agreeing Two — designed:** T-544 left its recount-disagreement problem named and open: whether two recounts that agree with each other but not with the audit settle the count, or whether the audit's own count must be among the agreeing two, and what happens when no two counts ever agree. T-545 answers: the audit's count need not be among the two — two independent recounts agreeing settle the count against the audit itself — but two counts agree only when they are independent, and when no two counts ever agree the declaration is not suspended forever but withdrawn.

The first reason is that the audit's count is a count, not a privilege. T-544 made the audit recomputable by any hand precisely so that no forum's preference needs trusting, only its arithmetic checked. If the audit's own count had to be among every agreeing two, the audit could never be overturned except by its own agreement — preference counting itself, one storey down, the very thing T-544 was built to escape. So the counts stand as votes, the audit's no heavier than any recount's: where a recount agrees with the audit, the declaration stands and the dissenting recount, if any, files as dissent; where two recounts agree against the audit, the declaration falls and the agreed count replaces it, and the audit panel whose count was overturned is a miscounting panel under T-544, losing audit authority until two recount-clean cycles re-anchor it. The audit is not humiliated by this — it is honoured by it, because a count that cannot be overturned is not a count but a decree, and T-544's whole design was to replace decrees with arithmetic.

The second reason is that independence is what makes two counts two. Two recounts by the same panel, by panels sharing a hand, or by a second panel that copied the first panel's working papers instead of recomputing from the published sample, do not agree with each other in any sense that settles anything: they are one count told twice, and a single error in the telling repeats itself faithfully into the agreement. Independence here is independence of hands, not of sample — every recount rightly works from the same published sample, since recomputability is the point — and it requires lot-drawn panels with no hand serving on both, no hand auditing its own series, and each panel recomputing from the sample rather than adopting another panel's arithmetic. A recount that merely checks another panel's addition is a review, not a recount, and its agreement adds no weight. Only when two hands that never met arrive at the same number from the same sample does the agreement carry the force T-544 gives it, because only then has the arithmetic survived two separate chances to go wrong.

The third reason is that a disagreement that never resolves must end in withdrawal, not in eternal suspension. Where the audit's count and two recounts all differ, T-544's suspension holds and a third recount is drawn by lot; where a third recount still leaves no two counts agreeing, the sample itself is the finding. Four counts, no two alike, is not a dispute about the drift declaration any more — it is evidence that the sample cannot be counted stably by the hands given it, whether the sample is thin, the ground is ambiguous, or the counting rule itself is underspecified. To suspend forever would be to leave every line decided under the declaration in limbo and every hand waiting on it in debt to a question that will never answer; to force agreement by further rounds would be to recount until chance produces a pair, which is manufacturing agreement, not finding it. So after three recount rounds with no agreeing two, the drift declaration is withdrawn: not acquitted, not confirmed, but withdrawn as uncountable on this sample. The disagreement is filed in full, the sample is republished with the disagreement attached, and a fresh audit may be drawn later by lot on a repaired sample or a clarified rule. Withdrawal closes the suspension honestly instead of letting it rot into a permanent maybe.

What a count files as follows from the three reasons, and the file must show which counts agreed and which hands made them, not merely the settled number. Two independent recounts agreeing against the audit file as the Agreeing Two: the declaration falls, the agreed count replaces it, the audit panel stands as miscounting until re-anchored. A recount agreeing with the audit against a dissenting recount files as a settled declaration with a Filed Dissent: the dissent is written in full and changes nothing. Two recounts agreeing only because they share hands, a panel, or working papers file as a Dependent Agreement: one count told twice, weighing as one, and settling nothing. Three recount rounds with no two counts agreeing file as an Uncountable Sample: the declaration withdrawn, the disagreement filed, the sample republished with its failure attached. A declaration withdrawn for uncountability files as a Withdrawn Declaration: neither a finding of drift nor a finding of no drift, and never cited later as either. A recount that adopts another panel's arithmetic without recomputing files as a review, not a recount, and its agreement adds no weight to any side.

**The named forms**, all to T-289: the Agreeing Two — two independent recounts agreeing against the audit: FILED to T-289 — the declaration falls, the agreed count stands. The Audit as One Vote — the audit's count weighing no more than any recount's: FILED to T-289 — a count, not a privilege. The Filed Dissent — a recount disagreeing with a settled declaration: FILED to T-289 — written in full, changing nothing. The Dependent Agreement — two recounts agreeing through shared hands, a shared panel, or copied working papers: FILED to T-289 — one count told twice, settling nothing. The Uncountable Sample — three recount rounds with no two counts agreeing: FILED to T-289 — the sample cannot be counted stably by the hands given it. The Withdrawn Declaration — a drift declaration withdrawn for uncountability: FILED to T-289 — neither drift found nor drift cleared, never cited as either.

**The grades.** AGREEMENT-SETTLES-AGAINST-AUDIT — two independent recounts agreeing settle the count even against the audit's own count; the audit's count need not be among the agreeing two. INDEPENDENCE-MAKES-TWO — only lot-drawn panels with no shared hands and no shared working papers count as two; dependence reduces agreement to one count told twice. DISSENT-FILES-NOT-OVERTURNS — a single dissenting recount against a settled declaration is filed in full and changes nothing. **T-546 — the Separate Method — designed:** T-545 left its shared-method problem named and open: whether independence of hands suffices when both panels share a method, a code path, or a counting rule, or whether shared method is itself a dependence that makes agreement one count told twice. T-546 answers: shared method is itself a dependence. Two counts agree, in the settling sense of T-545, only when they differ on at least one of four independence axes — hands, method, code path, counting rule — and a recount that shares all four with the count it agrees with is not a second count at all but a re-performance: it corroborates, it never settles.

The first reason is that T-545's independence requirement was about the count, not the counters. Two panels of different hands running the same code over the same rule will agree wherever the rule is wrong, because the error lives in the shared part, not in either panel. Hands-independence catches a miscounting hand; it cannot catch a miscounting method, and a method error agreed twice is still a method error — only now it wears the Agreeing Two's authority, which is worse than a single error, because the settlement rule has blessed it. So the receipt for every agreeing two must name the axes on which the two counts differ, and a receipt naming hands only, with method, code path, and counting rule all shared, files as single-method settlement: the declaration stands, but it stands flagged, challengeable on method grounds alone, and a successful method challenge reopens the declaration rather than merely narrowing it, because what was settled was never two counts but one count performed twice.

The second reason is that a single method need not doom the settlement. Where only one method exists — one published rule, one counting convention — the second count must re-derive the method from the published sample and the declared rule, not from the first panel's code: an independent re-implementation, built blind to the first implementation's choices, that converges on the same rule by its own route. Re-derivation counts as method-difference even when it converges, because the convergence itself is the evidence — two independent routes arriving at the same rule is what a shared method can never show. Method-difference is graded, not binary: a different rule is the strongest difference; a blind re-derivation is the middle; a shared method run through a different code path is the weakest, counting as a second count for code-path errors only and filing as single-method settlement for everything else. A count that shares method, code, and rule with no re-derivation is not a weak second count — it is no second count, and an Agreeing Two built on it is void on that ground alone.

**T-547 — the Convergent Proof — designed:** T-546 left its convergence problem named and open: how close a re-derivation may come to the original implementation before it is a copy rather than a derivation — whether convergence on identical code proves derivation or betrayal, and who judges the blindness of the re-implementation. T-547 answers: identical code proves neither. The test of a re-derivation is its provenance, not its similarity. A blind re-derivation that lands byte-identical to the original is still a derivation, and a copy that lands different — renamed variables, reordered lines, a paraphrased loop — is still a copy. Similarity is a prompt to look at the provenance; it is never the verdict on it.

The first reason is that a narrow rule forces convergence, and punishing convergence would punish correctness. Where the published rule and the published sample leave only one natural implementation — one counting order, one obvious data shape, one idiomatic way to write it — two honest builders working blind will write near-identical code, and the second will look like a copy of the first precisely because both read the same rule well. Where the rule leaves many choices open, the picture reverses but still does not decide: identical idiosyncratic choices — the same variable order, the same dead branch, the same error no rule forced — are a fingerprint worth investigating, but a fingerprint is not a proof, because shared training, shared idioms, and shared worked examples produce the same quirks independently. So similarity scales the question — the freer the implementation, the harder the question must be asked — and never answers it. A rule that treated convergence as betrayal would forbid the very agreement T-545 needs; a rule that treated convergence as derivation would bless every copy that kept its hands clean.

The second reason is that provenance can be shown, and shown blind. The re-deriver deposits, before any access to the original code, a sealed work trail: the rule as read, intermediate drafts, failed attempts, dead ends abandoned along the way. The judge is a lot-drawn provenance panel drawn the way T-544 draws its panels — excluding both counting panels, judging the trail and the access record, not grading code similarity at all. Its findings are three, and graded. A blind trail with independent dead ends stands as derivation even if the final code is byte-identical, because the dead ends are what a copy never has: a copy arrives, a derivation travels. No trail, or a trail postdating access, files as presumed re-performance under T-546 — a flagged single-method settlement, not a void one — curable only by a fresh blind re-derivation by new hands, never by papers produced after the fact, since a trail made after access proves nothing about blindness. A trail showing access, or no trail plus a shared idiosyncratic error, files as presumed copy, and the Agreeing Two built on it is void on that ground alone, with the copying panel re-anchoring under T-544. The burden shifts on the fingerprint: an ordinary convergence asks nothing, a shared non-forced error asks the re-deriver to produce the blind trail, and silence under that question is the answer.

**T-548 — the Sealer's Seal — designed:** T-547 left its seal-forgery problem named and open: who seals the work trail, and whether a seal can itself be forged or backdated — whether a timestamped deposit is proof of blindness or merely proof of a timestamp, and who audits the sealer. T-548 answers: a seal is trusted not because a sealer says so, but because it was published before it could matter. A seal produced only after the dispute is a claim, not a seal; a seal deposited in public before the dispute is a fact, and the sealer is the least important part of it.

The first reason is that a private seal proves nothing about time. A timestamp written by the sealer's own clock, held in the sealer's own drawer, and produced when the re-deriver needs it, is exactly as forgeable as the trail it claims to protect — the sealer need only write an earlier date, and no one can tell the difference, because the only witness to the sealing is the sealer. So the trail's seal is not a stamp but a deposit: the hash of the sealed work trail is entered, at the moment of sealing, in a public append-only register that anyone may read and no single hand may rewrite, and the deposit receipt — the register's own entry number and the hash it carries — is what the provenance panel judges, not the sealer's word. A re-deriver who cannot produce a register entry predating the dispute has no seal in T-547's sense at all, and files as presumed re-performance; a re-deriver who can, stands on the register, and the sealer's later corruption, recantation, or disappearance changes nothing, because the fact sealed is the public entry, not the sealer's memory of it. The timestamp that matters is the register's, and the register's clock is the public's, not any one hand's.

The second reason is that the register must itself be chained, or the forgery merely moves one step up. A public register held by one keeper can be rewritten by that keeper as easily as a private stamp can be backdated — so each deposit hashes the previous deposit's receipt, and the chain is published whole, entry by entry, so that backdating any one seal requires rewriting every entry after it in public view. Forgery becomes a public act: the forger must alter entries the whole world has already read, and the alteration itself is the evidence. And the sealer is not trusted with the content at all: the sealer seals only the hash, never reads the trail — a sealed envelope, hashed blind — so a corrupt sealer cannot leak, alter, or reconstruct what it never saw, and two sealers, both drawn by lot the way T-544 draws its panels and neither serving on either counting panel nor on the provenance panel, seal the same hash independently, so one corrupt sealer alone forges nothing. The sealing event itself — who sealed, when, which hash — is deposited in the same register, in the same chain, so the sealer's audit trail is the register itself: the auditor of the sealer is anyone who reads the register, and no higher forum is needed, because the chain is the forum. A break in the chain voids every seal after the break until re-deposited under a repaired chain, and a seal whose chain is intact stands even if every hand that touched it has since fallen.

**T-549 — the Outside Anchor — designed:** T-548 left its register-of-registers problem named and open: who holds the public register, and whether a chain ends the forgery or merely moves it to the keepers of the chain — whether a register of registers is needed, and where that recursion stops. T-549 answers: the recursion stops not at a higher register but at a copy the register cannot rewrite. A chain that anchors only to itself proves nothing about its own first entries; a chain whose head hash is copied, at a declared time, into a medium outside its keepers' control can be checked by anyone holding that outside copy, and rewriting the chain then requires rewriting the outside world too.

The first reason is that a register's genesis is its weakest entry. T-548's chain makes backdating any later seal a public act, because every entry after it has already been read — but the first entries predate every reader, and a keeper who writes the whole chain at once, genesis included, leaves no seam for a reader to catch. The chain proves order, not origin: it proves entry N follows entry N-1, never that entry 1 was written when it claims. So the genesis is not trusted on the chain's word at all. A register becomes trustworthy only at the first entry that satisfies two conditions together: it was witnessed at its making by a quorum of independent hands, none of them keepers of the register, who each keep their own dated copy of what they witnessed; and its hash was deposited, at that same declared time, in a medium the register does not control — another register run by other hands, a printed gazette, a dated public artifact that cannot be reissued silently. Entries before that anchored entry are claims, not seals, and a provenance panel judges them as unsealed; entries from the anchored entry onward stand on the chain plus the anchor, and the anchor is what stops the recursion, because the question "who registers the register" now has an answer that is not another register: the outside copy does, and the outside copy is checked by holding it, not by trusting it.

The second reason is that one anchor is not enough, because a single outside copy can itself be forged, lost, or quietly reissued — so the anchor is a cadence, not an event. The register's head hash is copied outward at regular intervals, every fixed number of entries or every cycle, each copy dated and witnessed the same way, so that a break anywhere in the chain voids only the entries since the last good anchor, never the whole register, and a keeper who rewrites the chain must also rewrite every outside copy made since the forgery's point — copies held by hands who have no reason to cooperate and no single throat to choke. And the anchor must never be circular: two registers that anchor each other, each citing the other as its outside medium, are one register wearing two names, and a provenance panel treats a circular anchor as no anchor at all — the outside medium must be one whose keepers gain nothing from this register's seals and lose nothing by exposing a forgery, or it is not outside. A register anchored outward, witnessed at genesis, and re-anchored on cadence needs no register of registers above it, because the recursion stops where the register's control stops: at the first copy it cannot rewrite.

**T-550 — the Three Houses — designed:** T-549 left its witness-quorum problem named and open: how many independent hands make a quorum, and whether a quorum of three witnesses who all work in the same house counts as independent at all — whether independence is counted in hands, in houses, or in interests. T-550 answers: a quorum is counted in interests, not in hands, and not in houses either — three interests, each carried by a different house, with no house supplying a majority of the counted interests at any quorum size.

The first reason is that a hand is not an interest. Three witnesses in one room can be three hands and one interest: the same paymaster, the same liability, the same access grant, the same reason to want the anchor to stand. Counting hands lets one house stage a quorum by sending three employees; counting houses alone is no better, because a house is only a label — a keeper can rent three addresses and call them three houses. So each witness files, with the anchor, a short interest statement naming three things: who pays them, who can end their engagement, and what they personally lose if the anchor proves false. A witness who cannot name a distinct interest counts as zero, however present their hand was. A contractor paid by the register's keeper belongs to the keeper's house whatever their title says; a volunteer with no paymaster belongs to the house that grants their access; a witness paid by nobody and admitted by nobody is not independent, they are unattached, and unattached counts as nothing.

The count itself has three rules. First, the minimum: three counted interests, each from a different house — fewer than three interests is not a quorum, it is a conversation, because two interests can settle a dispute between themselves and call the settlement agreement. Second, the majority bar: no single house may supply a majority of the counted interests at any quorum size, so a five-witness quorum with three witnesses from one house fails even though five hands attended — the extra hands are audience, not quorum, and audience does not cure capture. Third, the cure rule: adding one outside witness to a captured quorum does not cure it. The captured interests are discounted first and the remainder is counted; a quorum that only reaches three by counting captured interests never stood, and no later addition revives it retroactively. An anchor later found to rest on fewer than three true interests voids back to the last good anchor under T-549's voiding rule, not forward-only — and because the interest statements stay filed with the anchor, any later hand can recompute the count from the paper, without trusting the hands that filed it.

The number three is a design choice, stated as one, not a derived constant. Two cannot break a tie without a tiebreaker, and a tiebreaker would itself need a quorum; three is the cheapest count that cannot be staged by a single bargain, since one bargain can buy two interests but must buy a third house to buy the third. A larger anchor, or a disputed one, may need more than three — that scaling question is admitted below, not settled here — but no anchor needs fewer, and no count that includes a captured interest counts at all.
