**T-551 — the Named Interest — designed:** T-550 left its interest-definition problem named and open: where interest ends and affinity begins — whether family ties, shared ideology, former employment, or a long friendship count as a shared interest, and who draws that line without turning the count into a loyalty test. T-551 answers: an interest is not a feeling and not a biography; it is a stake that changes if the anchor proves false. A witness counts as a distinct interest only if they can name, in their filed statement, a loss that is theirs alone — a loss no other counted witness would suffer in the same way if the anchor voided.

The test has three prongs, and a witness must pass at least one with a concrete, dated, checkable loss. First, pay: who pays them, and does the pay stop, shrink, or reverse if the anchor fails — a salary that continues either way is not a stake, it is a seat. Second, power: who can end their engagement, and does that power sit with a party to the anchor — a witness terminable by the register's keeper belongs to the keeper's house whatever their title says, as T-550 already held. Third, loss: what they personally lose if the anchor proves false — a sum, a contract, a license, a bond posted, a reputation staked in a named forum where the loss is recorded. A loss that cannot be stated in those terms — "my standing," "my community's trust," "the cause" — is affinity, and affinity is recorded in the statement but never counted. The statement's job is to make the count recomputable: any later hand must be able to read the three filed losses and reach the same count T-550's rule reaches, without interviewing anyone.

Affinity enters the count only through the three prongs, never beside them. A family tie counts only when the relative is themselves a party to the anchor's stake — a spouse employed by the keeper is the keeper's interest, not a second one; a cousin with no stake is affinity, however warm. Former employment counts only while its money still runs — a pension, a severance schedule, an unvested grant; a job ended cleanly years ago is history, not interest. Shared ideology never counts alone, because an ideology shared by everyone in a field would disqualify every witness in it — but it flags the panel: when two counted interests share an ideological home, the panel must name, in the record, why their losses still differ, and a panel that cannot do so files its quorum as contested rather than clean. Friendship counts only when it moves pay, power, or loss — a friend who can end your engagement is power, whatever you call them at dinner. The line is therefore drawn by the loss, not by the biography, and the loyalty test is avoided because nobody is asked what they believe, only what they stand to lose and who can take it away.

The line-drawer is the lot-drawn panel itself, at filing time, with the statements published alongside the anchor. No separate loyalty board, no background investigation, no private dossier: the panel reads the three losses, counts the distinct ones, and files any interest it discounts with the reason stated in one line. A discounted witness may refile once with a corrected statement before the anchor seals; after sealing, the count is frozen and only a later hand's recomputation can challenge it, under T-549's voiding rule. **T-552 — the Forfeit Bond — designed:** T-551 left its loss-quantification problem named and open: how much loss is enough to count — whether a token stake, a dollar, a reputation point, buys a counted interest, and whether a minimum loss threshold turns the quorum into a purchase. T-552 answers: a loss counts only if it is posted, not promised. A stated future loss is a claim; a counted interest requires a forfeit held outside the witness's control, released while the anchor stands, and forfeited automatically when the anchor voids.

The first rule is that the forfeit must exceed the witness's fee. A witness paid more to witness than they stand to lose profits from the anchor standing either way — their stake points the wrong direction, and no counting rule can fix a witness who is paid to agree. So the panel's floor for any anchor starts at the witness's total compensation for the witnessing, fee plus expenses plus any side payment disclosed in the statement, and any forfeit at or below that figure counts as zero. A token dollar therefore counts as nothing wherever witnessing pays anything at all, and a witness who serves unpaid still needs a forfeit above zero, because a zero forfeit is not a stake, it is attendance. The fee rule is what keeps the threshold from being arbitrary: it is derived from the witness's own paper, not set by taste, and any later hand can recompute it from the filed statement and the forfeit receipt.

The second rule is that the forfeit must come from the witness's own pocket and be posted before the anchor seals. A forfeit funded by the register's keeper, advanced by a party to the anchor, or reimbursed after sealing counts as the keeper's interest, not the witness's — the keeper buying a quorum one forfeit at a time. The forfeit is held in escrow by a holder named in the anchor, outside the keeper's control and outside the witness's reach until the anchor's challenge window closes; a witness who can withdraw their forfeit before the window closes holds no forfeit at all. The floor above the fee minimum is set per anchor by the lot-drawn panel and published with the anchor, so a forfeit below the published floor counts as zero and a floor set high enough to price out small witnesses is itself challengeable — a floor challenged as exclusionary voids the anchor's quorum claim until the panel re-sets it in the open.

The third rule is that the forfeit need not be cash. A license held in escrow, a professional bond posted, a credential surrendered to the escrow holder for the challenge window, or a signed public statement whose retraction publishes automatically on void — each counts, provided forfeiture is automatic and verifiable rather than reputational. A reputation stake that requires a committee to decide whether it was lost is not a forfeit, it is a story about one; the escrow holder must be able to execute the forfeit on the voiding alone, without a second judgment. This is the answer to the purchase objection: a forfeit is a deposit, returned when the anchor stands, so the barrier is willingness to be bound and liquidity for the window, not wealth spent — but the answer is partial, and the partialness is admitted below, because a deposit still excludes a witness who cannot post anything, cash or credential, for the length of the window.

What the forfeit is forfeited to is fixed here, not left open: never to the keeper, never back to the witness, and never to the panel that counted it. It goes to the challenger who proved the void, or, where no challenger stands, it is destroyed — burned, surrendered, or published as voided — so that no party to the anchor profits from its failure. The challenger destination is deliberate: it pays the hand that does the expensive work of recomputation, and it makes a false anchor a bounty rather than a cost. It also creates the bounty-hunting incentive admitted below, and a panel that awards forfeits to its own challengers is a panel paying itself.

**What this pairs with.** T-551's Named Interest (the loss definition this rule makes countable — T-551 says a distinct interest is a loss no other counted witness would suffer in the same way, and T-552 says a loss counts only when posted as a forfeit above the witness's fee, from the witness's own pocket, before sealing). T-550's Three Houses (the counting rule this feeds — a witness whose forfeit falls below the published floor counts as zero, so a quorum that only reaches three by counting unposted losses never stood). T-549's Outside Anchor (the voiding rule that triggers the forfeit — an anchor resting on fewer than three true interests voids back to the last good anchor, and the forfeits on the voided anchor execute on that voiding). T-546's Separate Method (the independence test this completes on the witness side — a recount whose witnesses posted no forfeit is a claim, not a count, however different their methods).

**T-553 — the Self-Executing Forfeit — designed:** T-552 left its forfeit-form problem named and open: which non-cash forfeits are automatic enough to count — whether a license in escrow is executed by the holder alone, or whether every credential forfeiture smuggles in a second judgment. T-553 answers: a non-cash forfeit counts only when the voiding alone executes it, with no second decision by anyone. The test is not whether a human hand moves at voiding — hands move everywhere — but whether that hand has any discretion to refuse on the merits. A ministerial act counts as automatic; a judgment does not, and any forfeit whose execution asks anyone "was this loss real?" or "does this count?" is not a forfeit, it is a hearing wearing a forfeit's name.

The first rule is that the execution instrument must be complete before the anchor seals. A pre-signed surrender held by the escrow holder, a revocation already lodged with the issuing authority and effective on a dated trigger the voiding supplies, or a retraction already written, dated, and held by an outside publisher under standing instruction to publish on voiding — each counts, because at voiding nothing remains to be decided, only delivered. What fails is any forfeit whose execution still needs the witness's cooperation at voiding: a signature still owed, a key still held, a consent still to be given. Cooperation owed at voiding is a veto, and a veto held by the party who stands to lose is no bond at all. The escrow holder's delivery is ministerial for the same reason the sealer's sealing is: the holder is not asked whether the void was just, only whether a void was declared, and a holder who refuses delivery commits a published breach of their own — which is why the holder's own bond, forfeited on refusal, is part of the instrument, not an afterthought.

The second rule is that automaticity must be proved before sealing, not asserted. The panel stages a rehearsal on a parallel dummy instrument of the same form — the same surrender text, the same lodged revocation, the same publisher's standing instruction — and watches it execute end to end without a judgment entering anywhere. The rehearsal proves the mechanism, not the witness's instrument, and that gap is admitted below; but a form that cannot execute even in rehearsal counts as zero without further argument, and a form that executes in rehearsal with a judgment smuggled in — a committee that "confirms" the revocation, an issuer who "reviews" the lodged order — is disqualified on the rehearsal alone, before any witness posts anything. The instrument's text is published with the anchor, redacted only for identifiers that would expose the witness to retaliation, so that any later hand can read the mechanism and judge whether a judgment hides inside it.

The third rule is that a chain of ministerial acts must terminate in an act no one can refuse. Holder delivers to issuer, issuer executes a standing order, publisher publishes a standing text — and if any link refuses, the refusal triggers the next bond, and the chain ends at a destruction or publication act that needs no one's permission: an entry in a public register, a burn, a text already in a publisher's hands. If the chain needs a court at any point — a judge to compel delivery, a tribunal to confirm the loss — it is not automatic, it is a lawsuit wearing a forfeit name, and it counts as zero however impressive the credential at stake. Automaticity is a property of the chain's end, not of its beginning: a forfeit that begins with a signature and ends with a plea was never posted.

**T-554 — the Bonded Holder's Last Link — designed:** T-553 left its holder-bond problem named and open: who bonds the escrow holder, and whether bonding the holder merely moves the trust one link down the chain until some holder stands unbonded. T-554 answers: the regress ends because the last bond is not held by a person at all. A chain of holders, each bonded by the next, is one link short however long it runs — the chain is complete only when its last link is a clock and a page, not a hand.

The first rule is that a holder's bond is a forfeit of the same self-executing form, posted before the anchor seals, and larger than the forfeit it guards. The holder who delivers a witness's surrender on voiding risks nothing; the holder who refuses keeps the forfeit unexecuted, and refusal is profitable whenever the kept forfeit is worth more than the bond lost by refusing. A bond equal to the guarded forfeit is not a bond, it is a wash — the holder trades one loss for an equal gain and keeps whatever side benefit refusal bought. The bond must exceed the guarded forfeit plus the holder's own fee, so that refusal is a loss on every accounting, and the excess is published with the anchor so any later hand can check the arithmetic. A holder whose bond is smaller than the forfeit they hold is a holder holding the anchor hostage at a discount.

The second rule is that the bond's trigger is a clock fact, not a judgment. Delivery is due by a published deadline; non-delivery by that deadline, as recorded on the public clock, executes the bond. No one decides the holder "refused in bad faith" or "had good reason" — the deadline either passed with delivery or it did not, and a holder who delivers late has still missed the deadline, however good the reason. This is what keeps the bond self-executing in T-553's sense: the trigger asks a clock, not a committee, and a holder who wants to dispute the voiding disputes it through the challenge window, not by sitting on the delivery. The deadline is published with the anchor, long enough for a ministerial delivery and short enough that a forger cannot profit by waiting the holder out.

The third rule is that the regress terminates at a mechanism, not a person. The last holder's bond is lodged as a standing instruction in a public register — or any equivalent unrefusable publication — whose execution needs no hand at all: the register publishes the forfeiture on the clock fact, and publication itself is the execution. A holder chain that ends in a person who could refuse is unfinished business; a chain that ends in a page that publishes on a deadline is finished, because there is no hand left to refuse with. The public register is the same outside medium T-549's anchor already trusts for its head hash, so the last link adds no new trusted party — it reuses the one outside copy the system already stands on. If that register is itself one page held by one keeper, the chain has moved the trust rather than ended it, and that gap is admitted below; but a chain ending in a mechanism is shorter by one person than a chain ending in a person, and every person removed is a refusal removed.

**T-555 — the Refusal-Priced Bond — designed:** T-554 left its bond-sizing problem named and open: how much larger than the guarded forfeit the holder's bond must be — whether exceeding the forfeit plus the holder's fee suffices, or whether the bond must also price the holder's temptation to sell the refusal itself. T-555 answers: exceeding forfeit plus fee does not suffice, because the holder's temptation is not priced by the forfeit at all — it is priced by the market for refusal, and a forger who stands to lose more than the forfeit will pay more than the forfeit to buy the refusal. A bond sized against the forfeit alone is a price list the forger can beat.

The first rule is that refusal has a price of its own, and it is set by the buyer, not the bond. A holder who refuses delivery does not merely keep the guarded forfeit unexecuted — the holder sells the forger the one thing the forger cannot buy anywhere else: time, silence, or a missed deadline that lets a voided anchor stand. That value can exceed the forfeit itself, because the forger's loss from a published void — reputation, a chain of dependent anchors, a prosecution — is routinely larger than the single forfeit guarding one witness's surrender. T-554's formula (bond greater than forfeit plus fee) prices the holder's loss from refusing; it never prices the forger's gain from buying the refusal, and wherever gain exceeds loss the refusal sells. A bond that a forger can profitably buy is not a bond, it is a posted price for corruption.

The second rule is that the refusal price is discovered before sealing, not assumed. Before the anchor seals, the holder's bond is set by an open refusal auction: any party may lodge a standing offer to buy the holder's refusal, and the bond must exceed the highest standing offer plus the guarded forfeit plus the holder's fee, checked at sealing. The auction does not need to find the true price of refusal — it needs to find a price no one is willing to beat in public, and a forger who will pay more must say so where the bond can see it. An offer lodged after sealing buys nothing, because the bond is already posted and the deadline already published; post-sealing bribery is still a crime and still a temptation, but it is no longer a price the bond failed to meet — it is a price the forger hid until the market closed, and the bond's answer to a hidden market is the third rule, not a larger number.

The third rule is that where delivery is unique, the bond is auction-priced, and where delivery is duplicated, the refusal price collapses. A holder whose copy is the only copy can sell a refusal worth everything the void would cost; a holder whose copy is one of two independent copies can sell nothing, because the second holder delivers anyway and the buyer pays for a silence that never happens. Duplication is therefore the cheap answer to bond-sizing wherever the instrument allows it: two holders, each bonded at forfeit plus fee, price refusal at zero without any auction, because refusal by one is delivery by the other. Where the instrument cannot be duplicated — a single surrender, a single key — the auction is the price, and a bond no honest holder can post against a high standing offer is itself information: it says the anchor's void is worth more to its enemies than any honest holder can stake, and such an anchor should not seal on a single holder at all.

**T-556 — the Called Bluff — designed:** T-555 left its auction-gaming problem named and open: whether a refusal auction can be gamed by shill offers — a forger lodging a huge standing offer they never intend to pay, purely to inflate the bond beyond any honest holder's means and price honest holders out of holding at all. T-556 answers: a shill offer is only dangerous while it is free, and a single offer, however large, is only one voice — so the auction makes every offer pay for itself, lets any hand call any offer, and prices the bond on the second-highest independent offer rather than the highest. A bluff that must stake its own lie, survive being called, and find a second independent liar stops being cheap.

The first rule is that an offer counts only when it is bonded. A standing refusal offer lodged without a deposit is not an offer at all — it is a wish, and wishes do not move bonds. The deposit equals the offer, lodged in the same public register at the same moment, and it is forfeitable on exactly one fact: the offeror, when called, will not pay the lodged price for a refusal. This changes the shill's arithmetic completely. Under T-555's bare auction, inflating the bond by a million costs the forger nothing but the typing; under the bonded auction, inflating the bond by a million costs the forger a million staked against their own bluff. A forger rich enough to stake a huge shill offer is rich enough to buy the refusal outright, and a forger who buys outright has left the auction and entered the market the bond already prices — the shill has become a genuine buyer, and the bond is right to rise. The deposit does not need to stop rich attackers; it needs to stop free ones, and it does, because a free lie and a million-dollar lie are different acts.

The second rule is that any offer may be called, by any hand, before sealing. Calling an offer means demanding the offeror perform a test purchase: buy a rehearsed refusal on a dummy instrument of the same form, at the lodged price, under T-553's rehearsal rule — the same dummy discipline that proves a forfeit executes without spending the real one. An offeror who performs keeps the offer standing and the deposit intact; an offeror who refuses, stalls past a published call deadline, or performs only in part has the offer struck from the auction and the deposit forfeited to the challenger who called it. The call is therefore not a judgment about sincerity — no committee decides whether the offeror "meant it" — it is a clock fact and a payment fact, the same self-executing discipline T-553 demands of forfeits. A shill offer that survives bonding but will not survive a call is removed before sealing, when removal still matters, rather than discovered after sealing, when the bond has already priced honest holders out. And the call rewards the caller: the forfeited deposit pays the hand that exposed the bluff, so exposing shills is a paid trade, not a public service.

The third rule is that the bond prices the second-highest independent offer, not the highest. A single bonded, uncalled offer — even a genuine one — cannot move the bond alone, because one voice is not a market. The bond exceeds the second-highest independent offer plus the guarded forfeit plus the holder's fee, where "independent" is counted the way T-550 counts interests: offers from one house, or from hands sharing one interest, count once, at their highest. A forger who wants to inflate the bond must therefore corrupt two independent interests, bond both offers, and survive a call on each — and each call is an invitation for any hand to collect the forfeit. The second-price rule also protects the honest holder from the genuine outlier: one enemy willing to pay anything for suppression does not set the price of holding; two independent enemies, both willing and both called, do. Where only one independent offer stands, the bond falls back to T-554's forfeit-plus-fee floor, and the single offer stands recorded but unpriced — a warning, not a tax.

Separate deposits split a ledger only when the suppressions are genuinely separate; where the same suppression is pursued through several purses, the ledger joins the streams by their common thread.

The first rule is that coverage replaces overlap. Streams join as one breadth campaign when the union of their targets covers a market: more than half the live offers of one named market — one issuer class, one sealing window — across the streams together, even where no two streams share a single target. Pairwise overlap was only ever one way for streams to converge; a shared market is the other. The ledger therefore reads the union, not the intersection: ten distinct failures spread across one market's offers in one window count the way ten failures against one offer would, because the harm is to the market's sealing, not to any single offer's standing. The second rule is that deliberate partition is itself the signature. Genuine independent hands overlap by accident: two policers who distrust the same market will sometimes call the same offer, because each chooses from the same shelf without consulting the other. **T-566 — the Derived Horizon — designed:** T-565 left its dormancy-horizon problem named and open: whether the two-window dormancy horizon is principled or arbitrary — two windows mirrors the live union, but nothing in the design proves two is right and one or five is wrong, and a horizon picked for symmetry is still a guess. T-566 answers: it does not have to be picked at all — a horizon can be derived from how genuine returners actually return in that market, published per market, and changed only prospectively. Symmetry was a placeholder; the market's own return gaps are the evidence.

The first rule is that the horizon is a median, not a constant. For each market, the ledger keeps the return gaps of verified-genuine returners only: callers who paused at least one full empty window, then resumed, and were never joined on the resumed burst — either because they never crossed the join, or because they rebutted it with motive receipts that stood. Each such gap is counted in windows from the reset to the first distinct-new-target failure of the resumed burst. The market's horizon is the median of those gaps over the trailing twenty windows, rounded to the nearest whole window, with a floor of one window and a ceiling of four. A market where policers return after one window gets a one-window dormancy; a slow market where genuine hands return after three gets three. Until a market has twenty verified-genuine gaps, the horizon stays at two windows and is labelled provisional in the published register, so nobody mistakes a small sample for a derived rule.

The second rule is that a harasser's own pauses never enter the derivation. Gaps are counted only from callers who were never joined, so a campaign that pauses past the horizon to escape dormancy contributes nothing to the median — its silence is not evidence about genuine return, and a median built from it would be a harasser voting on its own sentence. Equally, a joined campaign's resumed burst is excluded even if it later rebuts: rebuttal severs prospectively under T-565, it does not retroactively certify the gap that led to the join. This keeps the derivation clean at the cost of slowness — the sample grows only from hands the test has already cleared, which is why the twenty-gap threshold and the provisional two-window default exist at all.

The third rule is that a horizon change never reaches back into a sleep already begun. A dormant ledger is born under the horizon published at its reset, and keeps that horizon even if the market's median moves while it sleeps; only ledgers born after a recomputation use the new horizon. Recomputation happens at each window close and is published with the new median, the sample size, and the floor or ceiling if either bound it, so every caller sees the horizon before it sleeps under it. A test that shortens the ground under a sleeping campaign is a trap, not a test, and a test that lengthens it mid-sleep rewrites the bargain the campaign paused under. The join itself is unchanged: warned at a third of the combined union, joined at half, prospectively and rebuttably on T-562's and T-563's terms, with T-559's pattern machinery firing only from the joining failure forward.

**T-567 — the Firm Sample Test — designed:** T-566 left its sample-threshold problem named and open: whether the twenty-gap threshold is itself arbitrary — a sample floor picked for stability is still a guess, and a market may never reach twenty verified-genuine gaps at all, leaving it provisional forever under a rule that calls itself derived. T-567 answers: the threshold does not have to be a count at all — a sample is firm when its median is stable under growth, not when it reaches a number somebody picked. Twenty was a guess about stability; stability itself is the test.

The first rule is that firmness is stability across growth, not size. A market's horizon leaves provisional status when the median of its trailing verified-genuine gaps, rounded to the nearest whole window, is unchanged when the oldest third of the sample is dropped — and the same equality held at the previous window close as well, so firmness survives two successive recomputations while the sample grows. A market with six gaps all reading two windows firms at once: its median is two with or without its oldest third, and it stayed two while two new gaps arrived. A market with forty gaps swinging between one and four never firms: its median moves when the sample moves, and no count rescues it. Size is evidence only through stability — a large unstable sample is less firm than a small steady one, and the register publishes both the sample size and the firmness status, so nobody mistakes a provisional two for a derived horizon or a firm two for a guess.

The second rule is that stability needs at least two points to mean anything, and that minimum is definitional, not picked. A sample of one gap has no spread to test: its median is the gap itself, and dropping its oldest third leaves nothing to compare. So a one-gap sample can never firm, and a two-gap sample firms only when both gaps round to the same window and the equality survives the next recomputation — the smallest sample that can demonstrate stability, not a threshold chosen for comfort. This is the only count in the test, and it is forced by the definition of stability rather than selected for it: one point cannot be stable or unstable, it can only be alone. A market that never grows past one verified-genuine gap stays provisional at two windows forever, honestly — the test would rather admit it does not know a market's rhythm than invent one from a single return.

The third rule is that firmness is reversible, and reversal is prospective only. A firmed market whose median later moves — a burst of genuine returns at a new rhythm, or a slow season changing the market's shape — drops back to provisional at the next recomputation, and the register publishes the demotion with the old median, the new median, and the sample that moved it. Ledgers born under the firm horizon keep it, under T-566's rule that a horizon change never reaches back into a sleep already begun; only ledgers born after the demotion sleep under the provisional two. A test that let a market keep a firm horizon its own data no longer supports would be a stale horizon wearing a derived label, and a test that retroactively shortened sleeping ledgers would be a trap. The join itself is unchanged: warned at a third of the combined union, joined at half, prospectively and rebuttably on T-562's and T-563's terms, with T-559's pattern machinery firing only from the joining failure forward.

**T-568 — the Leave-One-Hand-Out Test — designed:** T-567 left its stability-gaming problem named and open: whether stability can be gamed — fake genuine returners manufactured at a steady rhythm, firming a horizon a real harasser then hides inside, the poisoning problem moved from the median to the firmness test. A steady rhythm is cheap to manufacture when one hand controls the sample: a single manufactured hand returning at three windows, again and again, passes T-567's oldest-third test and both recomputations without a single genuine returner ever agreeing. T-568 answers: stability that rests on one hand is not stability at all — a sample firms only when no single hand is load-bearing for it.

The first rule is that firmness must survive the removal of any single hand. A market's horizon firms only when, for every hand contributing verified-genuine gaps to the sample, the median of the remaining gaps — that hand's gaps removed entirely — rounds to the same whole window as the full-sample median, and that equality holds at both of T-567's successive recomputations, alongside T-567's oldest-third test. A sample of six gaps, four of them from one manufactured hand at three windows and two genuine at two windows, does not firm: remove the manufactured hand and the median falls to two, so the manufactured rhythm was the firmness. A sample firms when two independent hands agree — remove either one and the median still stands, because the other hand's gaps carry the same rhythm on their own. The test does not ask whether any one hand looks genuine; it asks whether the firmness would survive that hand not existing.

The second rule is that the leave-one-out test needs something left to stand on. Removing a hand must leave at least two gaps from at least one other hand, or the test cannot pass — a sample with only one hand in it never firms, however steady, and a sample where one hand's removal leaves a single gap does not firm either, because a single remaining gap is T-567's definitional minimum for nothing at all. This is the rule's honest cost, stated plainly: a genuine market policed by a single hand, or by two hands one of which has barely returned, cannot firm until a second hand's rhythm is actually present in the sample. The register publishes, per market, the number of contributing hands and the largest hand's share as a band — under a third, a third to a half, over a half — without naming any hand, so a reader can see whether firmness rests on breadth or on one voice, without learning whose rhythm the band describes.

The third rule is that striking a manufactured hand demotes prospectively only. If a hand contributing to a firmed sample is later shown manufactured, its gaps are struck, firmness is recomputed over the surviving sample under the first two rules, and a market that no longer passes drops back to provisional at the next recomputation, with the register publishing the demotion, the old median, the new median, and the surviving sample size — but never naming the struck hand. Ledgers born under the firm horizon keep it, under T-566's and T-567's rule that a horizon change never reaches back into a sleep already begun; only ledgers born after the demotion sleep under the provisional two. A rotation that only watches one term at a time cannot see a relay. T-580 answers by judging the rotation as a sequence, so a slow rig counts the same as a fast one.

The first rule is that the sequence is the unit, not the term: a bound move counts as favouring a campaign when it lowers the depth that campaign's reasons must survive, or raises the depth its rivals' reasons must survive, in any market the bound governs. Two consecutive moves favouring the same campaign trigger a full sequence audit at the next recomputation; three consecutive moves favouring the same campaign are presumed captured, whatever each custodian's paperwork says. The presumption is rebuttable only by a showing, under T-574's powers, that no custodian in the sequence could decide, fund, or kill anything the favoured campaign touches — a showing the auditing houses must agree on, not one house alone. A relay that favours a different campaign each term to dodge the count still faces the drift rule below; changing beneficiaries is not the same as changing behaviour.

The second rule is that seating is cross-house, not per-house: a custodian is seated only when neither auditing house objects on T-574 powers grounds, and a person who has held the pen in any house within the last full rotation is ineligible in every house until a full rotation passes without them. **T-581 — the Beneficiary-Attribution Test — designed:** T-580 left its sequence-definition problem named and open: whether a favouring move can be defined when a move helps several campaigns at once — a shallower bound helps every campaign with shallow fakes, so the sequence count names a beneficiary the move never chose, and a controller can hide its campaign inside a crowd it also helps. A sequence rule that counts every helped campaign as favoured fires on tides and misses relays; a rule that counts none fires on nothing. T-581 answers by attributing a move not to everyone it helps, but to the campaign it helps most, measured against the move's own counterfactual — and by treating a crowd as the hiding place it is, not as an excuse.

The first rule is differential benefit, not absolute benefit: at each recomputation the move is replayed against the pre-move bound, and for each campaign the newly surviving reasons are counted — reasons that fail under the old bound and pass under the new one. A campaign is a beneficiary of the move only when its newly surviving share exceeds its share of the sample: a move that lifts every campaign in proportion to its size lifts nobody differentially and counts as neutral, recorded but never counted toward any sequence. A move that lifts one campaign's newly surviving share above its sample share, by any margin, counts as favouring that campaign, and only that campaign, unless the second rule below also fires. A tide that raises all boats equally is weather, not rigging; a tide that raises one boat above the waterline is a hand on the tiller.

The second rule is the crowd test: when two or more campaigns each gain differentially from the same move, the move counts as favouring each of them only when their newly surviving reasons share a control root under T-573's trace, or when one campaign's newly surviving reasons were filed in the same window as another's. Unrelated campaigns that happen to gain together are not a sequence — each gain is recorded, none is counted, and the move is published as shared-benefit with its differential shares. Related campaigns that gain together are a crowd with a conductor: the move counts toward every related beneficiary's sequence, because a controller that helps its own campaign and a friendly one in the same stroke has still favoured its own. A controller cannot hide inside a crowd it also helps when the crowd's roots are traced; it can only hide inside a crowd it does not control, and then the gain is not its favour to claim.

**T-582 — the Sample-Integrity Test — designed:** T-581 left its sample-stuffing problem named and open: whether differential benefit can be gamed by stuffing the sample — a controller flooding the sample with its rivals' weak reasons so its own gain looks proportional, or with its own strong reasons so a rival's gain looks differential, turning the attribution into a denominator game. A share measured against a sample the measurer's subject can inflate is not a measurement, it is a negotiation; a controller that can move the denominator can make any favour look like weather and any tide look like a favour. T-582 answers by freezing the denominator before the stuffing can arrive, and by counting only reasons the sample had already earned — so the attribution measures the move against the sample the move met, not the sample the move's friends manufactured.

The first rule is the frozen denominator: a move's differential shares are computed against the sample exactly as it stood when the move was published, never against the sample at recomputation. Reasons filed after the move's publication enter neither the numerator nor the denominator of that move's attribution; they join the baseline of the next move, not the measurement of this one. A controller that floods the sample after publication therefore changes nothing about the move it is trying to excuse — the flood is visible in the next baseline, where it can be judged as a sample change, but it cannot retroactively dilute a favour into proportionality. The denominator is the sample the move met, frozen at publication, and a share that was differential against that sample stays differential however crowded the sample becomes afterward.

The second rule is firmness before counting: only reasons already in T-567's firm sample at publication count toward either side of the share — the newly surviving count and the sample share itself. A weak reason filed to pad a rival's denominator counts for nothing until it has earned firmness through stability plus breadth plus corroboration, and a strong-looking reason filed to inflate a rival's numerator counts for nothing until it survives the same test. Stuffing with weak reasons is therefore not a denominator game at all: unproven reasons are not in the sample for attribution purposes, however many of them arrive. A controller that wants its padding to count must first make its padding genuine, and genuine reasons are evidence, not stuffing.

The third rule is the growth trip: a sample that grows between publication and recomputation by more than its own prior-cycle growth — judged against the market's own history, never against a fixed number — trips an audit of the attribution before the attribution is published. The audit asks one question only: did the growth arrive as reasons that earned firmness, or as filings timed to the move? Growth that earned firmness is a sample maturing, and the attribution publishes on the frozen denominator as usual. Growth that did not is a stuffing attempt, and the attribution publishes with the growth flagged as contested, the differential shares unchanged, and the stuffed reasons held out of the next baseline until they earn firmness. The trip does not delay the attribution and does not rewrite it: it marks the attempt in public while the measurement stands.

The fourth rule is prospective stuffing, like everything before it: a stuffing attempt discovered after an attribution has published does not rewrite that attribution. **T-583 — the Pre-Freeze Window Test — designed:** T-582 left its pre-freeze-stuffing problem named and open: whether stuffing can arrive before the freeze — a controller padding the sample before a move is published, so the frozen denominator is already stuffed when the move meets it, and the freeze locks in the rig instead of locking it out. A freeze that trusts everything firm at publication trusts the padding that was filed to be firm by publication. T-583 answers by refusing to freeze what the move's friends only just filed: the denominator a move is measured against is not the sample at publication, it is the sample seasoned before the move was ever planned — so padding timed to a move arrives too late to count, however firm it looks by publication day.

The first rule is two-baseline seasoning: a reason enters a move's frozen denominator only if it was already firm at two consecutive scheduled baselines before the move's publication — firm at the baseline before last and firm at the last baseline, with no gap. A reason that became firm only at the last baseline, or only between the last baseline and the move, is unseasoned for this move: it counts toward nothing in the attribution, neither numerator nor denominator. It is not struck and it is not suspect; it simply has not aged into the denominator yet. It joins the seasoning count of the next baseline, and if it is still firm there, it seasons into the denominator of the moves after that. A controller that pads before a move must therefore have padded two full baseline cycles before the move — and padding filed two cycles early, surviving two rounds of firmness testing, is no longer padding timed to a move; it is sample history, judged as a sample change in its own cycle, not as the denominator of a move it predates by two seasons.

The second rule is scheduled baselines, never move-triggered ones: baselines fall on a published calendar fixed before any move in the cycle, and a baseline taken inside a move's approach window — the interval since the last scheduled baseline — is void for that move. A controller cannot force a fresh baseline after stuffing and call the stuffed sample seasoned, because a baseline that follows the stuffing is not a seasoning baseline at all; it is the move's own baseline, and the seasoning count for this move is the two baselines before it. The calendar is published in advance, so a controller that wants its padding seasoned must file it before a baseline it cannot move — and a padding that predates two published baselines has survived two public firmness counts, which is the difference between a stuffed denominator and a sample that changed.

The third rule is the beneficiary-trace penalty: approach reasons — reasons arriving between the last scheduled baseline and a move's publication — that trace to the move's beneficiary under T-573's control-root trace and T-576's distinct-root rule are held out of the next two baselines, not one. Ordinary unseasoned reasons season in one cycle; beneficiary-traced approach reasons season in two, because a controller padding toward its own move has told the auditor exactly whose denominator it was trying to move. The penalty is prospective and mechanical: it does not rewrite the move's attribution, it does not accuse the campaign, and it does not depend on motive — a traced approach reason simply waits two cycles before it can count anywhere, so the next move the same campaign makes meets a denominator its own padding has not yet entered.

The fourth rule is the approach-velocity flag: approach-window arrivals above the market's own prior-cycle arrival rate — judged against the market's own history, never a fixed number — flag the move's attribution as approach-contested before it publishes. The flag changes nothing about the shares, which are computed on the seasoned denominator as usual; it publishes alongside them, naming the approach volume and the beneficiary trace, so a move that met a crowded approach window is read as a move that met a crowded approach window. A quiet approach window publishes unflagged. **T-584 — the Velocity-Tiered Seasoning Test — designed:** T-583 left its seasoning-lag problem named and open: whether seasoning lags fast markets — genuine reasons in a fast-moving market taking two baseline cycles to count, so the attribution measures a move against a denominator two seasons stale and the test fails exactly where samples move fastest. Two baselines in a market that turns over weekly is a fortnight of history; two baselines in a market that turns over hourly is an afternoon. T-583 counted baselines and forgot that baselines are not all the same length. T-584 answers by tiering the calendar to the market's own velocity, so two seasons always mean the same share of a sample's life, never the same number of calendar days — and by showing the fresh reasons it still refuses to count, so a fast market's present is visible even where it is not yet counted.

The first rule is velocity tiers from the market's own history: each market's baseline cadence is set by its own prior-cycle turnover — the share of its firm sample replaced per cycle — never by a fixed number of days and never by another market's pace. A market that replaces half its sample per cycle is a fast tier; a market that replaces a tenth is a slow tier; the tier is published before the cycle it governs, and it moves only at a scheduled re-tiering, never inside a move's approach window. Two baselines still season a reason, exactly as T-583 requires — but in a fast tier the two baselines fall close together in calendar time, because the market's own turnover has already made them two seasons of that market's life. A controller cannot slow a fast market to stale its denominator, because the tier is the market's measured turnover, not a calendar it can lobby; and a slow market is not rushed, because its two baselines still span its own two seasons, however long they take.

The second rule is the staleness cap: a seasoned denominator that covers less than half of the market's currently firm sample is published as stale-denominator-contested, and its shares are provisional. The cap is judged on coverage, never on calendar age — a slow market whose sample barely moved is fresh at two seasons old, and a fast market whose sample turned over twice is stale even if its baselines were yesterday. The provisional shares still publish, computed exactly as T-581 and T-583 require, but they publish with the cap flag attached, naming the coverage share and the tier, so a move measured against a denominator that no longer resembles the market is read as a move measured against a denominator that no longer resembles the market. The flag changes nothing about the shares; it changes what the reader is entitled to conclude from them.

The third rule is the fresh supplement, published alongside and never folded in: reasons firm at the last baseline only — seasoned for nothing yet under T-583 — are listed as a supplement to the attribution, with their own differential shares computed on the same method, clearly marked unseasoned and uncounted. The supplement is visibility, not a second denominator: no move is judged by it, no favouring count is taken from it, and no deference is excused by it. A fast market's genuine new reasons are therefore not invisible while they season; they are present in the publication, in their own column, waiting out their second baseline in public. A controller that pads the supplement gains nothing, because the supplement counts toward nothing — and a reader who suspects the seasoned denominator is stale can see, in the supplement, exactly what the next baseline will add.

The fourth rule is tier-boundary discipline: a market re-tiers only at its scheduled re-tiering, on its own prior-cycle turnover, and a re-tiering never applies to a move already in its approach window. A controller cannot push a market into a faster tier to season its padding early, because the tier that seasons its padding is the tier published before the approach window opened; and it cannot push a market into a slower tier to stale a rival's denominator, because the slower cadence governs only moves published after the re-tiering. The tier is a published band, like every band before it: the market's tier and its coverage share publish, never the authors, chains, or reasons behind them.

The fifth rule is prospective staleness, like everything before it: a denominator discovered stale after an attribution has published does not rewrite that attribution. The attribution gains its stale flag retrospectively as a published correction, the shares stand, and the next move in that market is measured against a denominator re-tiered at the next scheduled re-tiering. **T-585 — the Tier-Shopping Test — designed:** T-584 left its tier-shopping problem named and open: whether tiers can be shopped — a controller choosing the market whose turnover tier seasons its padding fastest, or splitting a list across a fast-tier market and a slow-tier market, so the velocity rule becomes a choice of calendars. T-584 tiered the calendar to each market's own turnover and forgot that a controller who can choose the market can choose the calendar. A fast tier is only a fast clock if the controller is stuck with it; a controller free to file anywhere files where the clock runs fastest, and a list split across two markets seasons at the faster market's pace wherever the controller wants it counted. T-585 answers by nailing the tier to the market the move governs, refusing seasoning any passport between markets, and making a split list season at its slowest fragment's pace — so shopping for a tier buys nothing, and splitting a list buys only delay.

The first rule is home-market anchoring: the tier follows the market the bound governs, never the market the filer chose to file in. A move published under a bound is measured in that bound's market, at that market's tier, whatever market the reasons supporting it were filed in. Filing the same reasons in a faster market creates a second sample in a second market; it does not lend the first market a faster clock, and it does not move the attribution. A controller that wants the fast tier must govern a bound in the fast market and publish the move there, in public, under that market's own houses — which is not shopping, it is moving house, and the move is then judged by the fast market's own sample, its own auditors, and its own staleness cap under T-584.

The second rule is no cross-tier seasoning credit: seasoning is per-market, and it does not travel. A reason seasoned across two baselines in a fast market counts in a slow market only after it seasons across that slow market's own two baselines, at the slow market's own cadence. Seasoning is a fact about a reason's standing in a market, not a stamp the reason carries between markets; a fast market's afternoon of history is not a slow market's two seasons, and counting it as such would let a controller season padding in the fastest market on the board and spend it everywhere. The supplement rule from T-584 applies in each market separately: a reason waiting out its seasoning in one market may appear in that market's supplement, and in no other market's share.

The third rule is split-list aggregation at the slowest tier: fragments of one campaign, split across markets, are one campaign, and the campaign seasons at the slowest tier among its markets. Fragments share a campaign when they share a control root under T-573 or a filing window under T-581's shared-benefit rule — the same tests that already join shared-benefit moves. Once joined, the campaign's favouring counts aggregate across markets toward T-580's sequence — favour in two markets is two favouring moves, not one move seen twice — and the campaign's padding seasons only when its slowest fragment seasons. Splitting a list across a fast market and a slow market therefore buys the slow market's calendar, not the fast market's: the controller that splits to go faster goes slower, in public, by its own choice of fragments.

The fourth rule is the migration flag: a campaign whose filings migrate toward faster tiers after a move is published is published as market-migration-contested, and its migrated filings are excluded from the shares until they season in the new market under the second rule. Migration is judged on filing volume by market before and after publication, against the market's own prior-cycle rate, the same comparison T-582 uses for growth; a migration that merely follows the market's own growth is not flagged. The flag changes nothing about the shares already published — the migrated filings were never in them, because seasoning does not travel — it changes what the reader is entitled to conclude about the campaign's next move, which will be measured against a denominator the campaign has not yet learned to shop.

The fifth rule is prospective shopping, like everything before it: a tier shopped before this trick publishes does not rewrite the attributions it already bought. The first rule is joint-home publication: a move published under a bound that governs two markets is published in both markets' shares, under each market's own houses and auditors, with the dual-home fact printed on the attribution. Governing is judged by the bound's text and effect, not by where the filer filed: if the bound's text runs in a market, or the move's effect lands there, that market is home, whatever the filing header says. A flag that holds counts forever is not a flag, it is a second pen, and a second pen in the hands of one house is capture by another name. T-587 answers by giving every contest a clock, every house a standing record, and every unresolved split a third reader — so disagreement stays visible, but it can no longer stop the count by itself.

The first rule is the contest clock: a contest against a dual-home attribution must be adjudicated within one slower-tier cycle — one full baseline-to-baseline turn in the slower home, on T-584's tiered cadence — or it lapses. The clock runs from the contest's publication, never from the attribution's, so a house cannot bank a contest filed early and spend it late; and the clock is measured in the slower home's time, so a fast home's house cannot run out a slow home's audit by filing at the fast cadence.

The second rule is contest standing: a house that contests three consecutive dual-home attributions and loses all three — three failed contests in a row, each adjudicated against it on the frozen denominator — loses contest standing for one full rotation, on T-579's rotation terms. Standing returns automatically at the next rotation, clean, with no carryover — the rule is a circuit breaker, not a punishment, and it counts losses only, never contests filed, so a house that contests rarely and wins keeps its standing whatever the volume of moves. Two houses alternating contests to dodge the three-loss run is itself a sequence: where two houses' contests alternate on the same attribution class, the alternating pair is counted as one house's run for standing purposes, and the third house audits the alternation.

**T-588 — the Staged-Lapse Test — designed:** T-587 left its lapse-exploit problem named and open: whether the lapse can be exploited in reverse — a house slow-walking adjudication so its own contest lapses and the attribution counts, where the controller wanted it counted all along and the contest was theatre. T-587 made a lapsed contest count the attribution, and that rule is exactly what theatre wants: file a contest nobody intends to prosecute, wait out the slower-tier clock, and collect a counted attribution that arrives wearing the costume of a contested one — opposed in form, unopposed in fact, and credited to the controller as though it had survived a fight it never had. A count that survives a contest is worth more than a count that was never contested, and theatre manufactures the dearer kind for free. T-588 answers by forcing the choice theatre refuses to make: prosecute the contest and risk losing it, or let it lapse and accept a count that is flagged, sterile, and on the record — never both the fight and the prize.

The first rule is prosecute-or-lapse: a contesting house must file its evidence within the first half of T-587's slower-tier contest clock — the reason plus the record it rests on, published, against the same frozen denominator T-582 fixes. A contest with no evidence filed by mid-clock is downgraded to a note at mid-clock: visible and reasoned, but holding nothing from that moment, so a house cannot both hold the attribution out of both shares and stage its lapse. The clock is never paused for house-side silence — silence is the house's own time, spent, not banked — and only adjudicator-side delay, published as such by the adjudicator, pauses the clock. T-590 fixed the pen at filing, and that fix is exactly what calendar shopping walks around: a house that cannot pick its pen can still pick its filing date, and a filing date is a pen choice made slowly. Hold the contest through the strict rotations, file it in the rotation your own house holds the pen, and the rotation rule that was meant to stop shopping delivers the shopped pen on schedule — assigned, not chosen, in form, and chosen in fact, because the filer chose the calendar that produced the assignment. A rule that fixes the pen at filing without fixing the filing has fixed nothing; it has only moved the choice from the forum to the calendar, where it is harder to see and easier to deny. T-591 answers by taking the filing date out of the pen assignment entirely: the pen follows the ground, not the filing, and a contest filed late arrives marked, seconded, and counted double, so delay buys scrutiny instead of a friendly pen.

The first rule is ground-date anchoring: the adjudicator for a contest is the house holding the pen in the rotation in which the contest's ground first published — the record, decision, or attribution the contest rests on — not the rotation in which the contest is filed. A house files when it files, and the pen is the ground rotation's pen, whenever the ruling lands. Holding a contest through strict rotations buys nothing, because the pen was fixed the day the ground published, before the holding began; filing in your own pen's rotation buys nothing either, because the filing rotation does not assign the pen. The only way to reach a different pen is a different ground — a fresh record published in a later rotation, contested on its own terms, with the prior ruling attached, so the new pen rules on the new ground with the old ruling in view rather than in ignorance of it. A contest that names no ground publishes as groundless and is not assigned a pen at all: it waits, on the record, until its ground is named and dated, and the waiting time counts against its promptness, not for it.

The second rule is the self-pen bar: where the filing house holds the ground rotation's pen, that pen does not rule its own contest. The pen passes to the next pen in the rotation sequence, published as passed, and the passed pen's ruling counts toward the passed pen's pattern record, not the holder's — so holding the pen in the ground rotation is a disqualification, not an advantage, and a house that publishes a ground while holding the pen has published its own contest into another house's hands. The bar is automatic: no recusal motion, no holding published, no discretion. A house that files a contest grounded on its own pen rotation's record and expects its own pen to rule it has misread the rule in public, and the public reading is the correction.

The third rule is the promptness window and the deferred mark: a contest must be filed within one rotation of its ground's publication. A contest filed later publishes as "deferred-filed," with the reason for the delay stated on the filing, and its ruling is automatically seconded — dissent not required, as with T-590's boundary filings — with a deferred-filed padding-pass counting double toward the adjudicator's three-ruling pattern count. The window is not a forfeiture: a genuine contest discovered late files late honestly, states why, and is simply checked. But the check is automatic precisely because delay is where calendar shopping hides: a contest held for a friendly pen arrives wearing its delay on its face, and the face of the filing is published. A house that files promptly and a house that files deferred are not treated the same, because they have not done the same thing — one prosecuted its contest, the other timed it — and the rule marks the difference instead of pretending promptness and delay are the same act.

The fourth rule is disputed ground dates: where the ground's first-publication date is itself contested — a private record later published, a backdated publication, a ground that reached different houses at different times — the earliest publication on the record governs, rebuttably. A house claiming a later ground date must publish the first-publication record it rests on; until it does, the pen is the earliest date's pen, ruling provisionally, with the counts it produces flagged until the date is settled. The burden sits on the house that wants the later date, because the later date is the date shopping wants: every ground-date dispute that moves the pen later is a calendar-shopping claim wearing a dating dispute's clothes, and it is heard as one. The ruling stands; the shopper does not walk away clean, and the assigner does not deal again next cycle.

**T-603 — the Open-Reveal Test — designed:** T-602 left its challenge-window-theatre problem named and open: whether a challenge window published as one full window after the sealed order-hash reveal can be theatre — a window published as one full window while in practice the reveal is delayed, buried, or published where no rival looks, so the window runs out before any house can frame a challenge. T-602 gave the challenged house one full window after the reveal, but it never asked what counts as a reveal: a timestamp on a private channel, a hash dumped in an unindexed annex, or a notice whose deadline is omitted or misstated all wear the date of a reveal while giving no rival anything to challenge from, and a claimant that can run the clock out on a buried reveal keeps the ruling exactly as a claimant that ran it out on a shopped assignment did. T-603 answers by making the window run from notice, not from posting: a reveal counts only when it is retrievable, indexed, and deadline-stated in the place every house already reads, and a ruling becomes final by expiry only under a reveal that passes that test.

The first rule is that notice, not posting, starts the clock: a reveal is effective only when it is published to the standing common channel every house already reads, indexed under the window's own identifier, and stated in plain terms naming the window, the assignment, the sealed order hash, and the challenge deadline. A posting to a private channel, a side annex, an unindexed dump, or a channel no rival house reads is not a reveal, however precisely it is timestamped, and the challenge window does not run from it. The revealer bears the burden as before: the location, the index entry, and the stated deadline are published so any house can re-perform the retrieval, check that the notice names the window it claims to open, and check whether the deadline it states matches the one full window T-602 grants. A date that cannot survive a retrieval check, an index check, and a deadline check is a date that was never revealed, however early its posting claims to be.

The second rule is that the clock starts at first provable retrievability: where the claimed reveal time and the first proven retrieval differ, the window is measured from the first proven retrieval, not from the claimed posting. Proof is a retrieval receipt, a hash anchor in the common channel, or any record a rival house can independently re-perform — not the revealer's assertion that the notice was there all along. A house that says it looked in the right place at the claimed time and found nothing rebuts the claimed start, and the window restarts from the first time the notice can be shown to have been there to find. This closes the delayed-reveal half of the theatre: a reveal held back and then backdated buys no window, because the window follows the evidence of retrievability, not the date written on the notice.

The third rule is the burial cure: a reveal later shown buried — wrong index, misleading title, truncated hash, deadline omitted or misstated, or any defect that kept a diligent rival from framing a challenge — is void as a reveal, and a corrected re-reveal restarts a full challenge window. A ruling that became final by expiry under the buried reveal is reopened as if that window never closed, because T-602's finality attaches only to a valid reveal's window, not to any window-shaped interval a revealer declares. The distinction matters and is stated honestly: this cure does not reopen a ruling whose reveal was valid and whose window genuinely ran — that ruling stands under T-602's second rule, shopping counted but finality intact — it reopens only a ruling whose expiry was manufactured by burial, where no valid window ever ran to protect it.

The fourth rule is that no expiry is silent: a ruling becomes final by expiry only when the revealer files a closing certificate naming the reveal's common-channel location, its retrieval proof, and the fact that no challenge was filed inside the window it opened. A certificate that omits the location, leans on a private posting, or states a deadline the original notice never stated proves nothing, and expiry claimed without a certificate counts as no expiry at all — the window stays open until a valid certificate is filed or a challenge lands. A rival that shows it searched the stated location and index during the window and found no matching notice rebuts the certificate outright, and the burden returns to the revealer to re-reveal under the third rule. A window that closes only on a certificate any house can check is a window no house can close by burying the notice and waiting.

The first rule is independent retrieval, not shared address: a channel passes only when a rival house, searching by the window's own identifier and without assistance from the revealer or the keeper, retrieves the identical notice — same window, same assignment, same sealed order hash, same stated deadline — that the revealer claims to have posted. A channel every house names but only some houses can read, a channel whose retrieval requires a keeper's key, password, approval, or private pointer, or a channel whose copy differs by reader is not common, however public its address sounds. The test is performed by retrieval, not by description: a keeper's claim that the channel is open proves nothing, and a rival's failed independent retrieval rebuts it outright, whatever the keeper's access policy says on paper.

The second rule is that flood is burial in another form: a notice that can be retrieved only by sifting through decoys is buried, even when its index entry is technically correct. Where the keeper floods the channel with lookalike notices — same window shape, near-identical titles, truncated or shifted hashes — so that a diligent rival searching by the window identifier must wade through unrelated material to reach the true notice, the channel fails for that window and the reveal on it is void under T-603's burial cure. The distinction is directness, not volume alone: a busy channel with many unrelated windows still passes if the window identifier reaches the notice directly, while a quiet channel fails if its few notices are arranged so the true one hides among them. A revealer that benefits from the flood counts the benefit as shopping by delay under T-590's discipline, exactly as a revealer that benefited from a buried reveal did.

The third rule is that a gate pauses the clock: where the keeper gates, throttles, or interrupts retrieval — a hold placed on the notice, a rate limit that bites only rivals, a window of unavailability during the challenge period — the challenge window pauses for the duration of the gate and resumes only when independent retrieval is restored. **T-608 — the Withdrawn-Pointer Test — designed:** T-607 left its withdrawn-pointer problem named and open: whether a pointer published in time yet withdrawn before the window ends counts as public — findable on the retrieval day, deleted or rotated out before the window closes, so the window opened on a public path and closed on a vanished one, and no rule says which moment counts. T-607 dated the beginning of a pointer's public life — a pointer counts only if public before the retrieval it supports — but it never dated the end: a pointer that was public when the rivals walked it and gone when the window closed leaves the window's record pointing at an empty address, and a verifier arriving late finds nothing where the certificate says a public path stood. The choice is between judging the pointer by the window's open, which lets a keeper publish, wait for the retrieval, and quietly delete, and judging it by the window's close, which lets a routine cleanup void a retrieval that was honestly public when made. T-608 answers that neither window edge counts — the retrieval moment does — and that a pointer whose retrieval moment was public carries a preservation duty after it, because a public path that vanishes without a trace is a private path with a delayed alibi.

The first rule is the moment-of-retrieval rule: a pointer counts as public for a retrieval if and only if it was independently timestamped and cold-findable at the moment of that retrieval, whatever the window's open and close say. A pointer withdrawn after the retrieval it supports does not retroactively privatize that retrieval — the rivals walked a public path on the day, and the path's later vanishing changes the archive, not the walk. A pointer withdrawn before any retrieval relying on it never supported that retrieval at all, and a window that opened on a public path and closed on a vanished one still holds every retrieval made while the path stood. The window's edges are not the pointer's life; the retrieval is the moment the pointer earns or loses its standing, and a keeper that deletes after the retrieval has deleted evidence, not the walk itself.

The second rule is the preservation duty that follows a supported retrieval: once a pointer supports a retrieval, the keeper must preserve a dated snapshot of what the pointer pointed at — content hash plus retrieval record — through the window and through T-602's challenge window, because a pointer that vanishes must leave its content behind for the houses that arrive late. A deletion that preserves the snapshot costs the retrieval nothing: late verifiers check the snapshot, not the vanished address. A deletion without preservation does not void the retrieval outright, but it forfeits the keeper's benefit of it — any house may demand re-performance from a surviving pointer, and if re-performance fails, the retrieval falls, because a keeper cannot both delete the evidence and keep the ruling the evidence supported. The duty runs to the keeper, not the rivals: a rival that deletes its own copy deletes nothing the window relied on, and a keeper that preserves badly — a snapshot whose hash does not match the retrieved content — has preserved nothing.

The third rule separates rotation from deletion: a rotation that carries a forwarding record preserves continuity — the same pointer under a new address, its original timestamp intact, because a reader following the forward arrives where the old address pointed. A silent rotation without forwarding is a fresh publication at the new address under T-607, and retrievals after the silent rotation count only if the new address was itself public in time; a keeper that moves a pointer without leaving a forward has not preserved the path, it has replaced it, and the replacement dates from its own publication, not the original's. A forwarding record posted after the retrieval it is claimed to bridge is a retroactive publication in T-607's sense, and counts for nothing — the forward must be findable before the retrieval that relies on it, exactly as the pointer itself must be.

The fourth rule is pointer rebuttal, mirroring T-607: any house may rebut a withdrawn-pointer ruling by showing, from the record alone, that the pointer was not public at the retrieval moment — a retrieval timestamp against a withdrawal or silent-rotation timestamp — or that the keeper's preservation snapshot does not match the retrieved content, and a rebuttal that, if proven, voids the pointer's support does not need to disprove the finding itself. A pointer that survives both rebuttals stands twice over: public at the retrieval, and preserved or re-performed after it. A pointer that fails either never stood for that retrieval — it stood for a window edge, or for a vanished address, and neither is a public path.

**T-609 — the Withdrawal-Theatre Test — designed:** T-608 left its withdrawn-pointer-theatre problem named and open: whether a withdrawal can be theatre — a targeted deletion staged as routine rotation or cleanup, the forwarding record posted, the old address retired on a plausible schedule, so the vanishing looks like housekeeping and no rule yet separates honest maintenance from a pointer deleted because a rival was about to follow it. T-608 dated the pointer's life by the retrieval moment and imposed a preservation duty, but it never asked why the pointer died: a keeper that deletes after the retrieval, posts a forward, and calls it rotation passes every T-608 check while still stranding exactly the rival it wanted to strand, because a forward to a new address is no help to a rival whose certificate, tooling, or sealed order names the old one, and a plausible schedule is easy to write after the fact. The choice is between judging the withdrawal by its paperwork, which any keeper can forge in form, and judging it by its timing and its class, which a keeper cannot forge after the rival has already approached. T-609 answers that a withdrawal counts as routine only when it was pre-committed, class-uniform, and forward-complete — and that a deletion failing any of the three is presumed theatre, with the burden on the keeper, not the stranded rival.

The first rule is the pre-commitment rule: a withdrawal counts as routine only if its schedule and class were sealed before the retrieval it follows — the rotation cadence, retention policy, or address lifecycle announced in the sealed order under T-598 before any rival walked the pointer, naming the class of pointers and the retirement rule, not the individual address. A justification that appears only after the rival's approach, or after the retrieval, is not a schedule; it is an alibi. A keeper with no pre-sealed schedule cannot claim routine maintenance at all, and the withdrawal is judged as targeted unless the keeper proves, from the record alone, that the same retirement would have happened on the same day without the rival — a proof that requires a dated policy, not a plausible story.

The second rule is the approach-then-delete rule: a withdrawal executed after a rival's recorded approach to that pointer — a follow attempt, a retrieval request, a certificate naming the old address — and before that rival's completion is presumed theatre, whatever the paperwork says. The presumption is rebuttable only by the pre-sealed schedule: if the sealed schedule independently required retirement on that exact date, the timing is coincidence and the withdrawal stands as routine; if the schedule is silent, flexible, or dated after the approach, the timing is the finding. A keeper that deletes the one pointer a rival is about to follow, on the day the rival approaches it, has not performed maintenance; it has performed an interception, and the burden of proving otherwise sits with the keeper because the keeper holds the schedule and the rival holds only the vanishing.

The third rule is the class-uniformity rule: routine maintenance touches a class, not a singleton. A retirement applied uniformly to the whole sealed class on the sealed schedule passes even if a rival loses a path — honest maintenance strands rivals sometimes, and T-608's preservation snapshot is what keeps that stranding honest. A retirement that singles out the one pointer a rival is following, while sibling pointers under the same policy stand untouched, fails the class test outright, and no forwarding record cures a singleton deletion, because the forward is posted by the same hand that chose the singleton. Uniformity is checked from the record: the class as sealed, the members retired, the members left standing — a class of one, sealed after the approach, is not a class.

The fourth rule is the forward-completeness rule: a forwarding record cures a routine retirement only if it was posted in the same common channel as the original pointer under T-604, before the retirement, carrying the original timestamp — findable by the same cold search that found the pointer. A forward posted only after the rival complains, posted in a different or obscure channel, or carrying a fresh timestamp is theatre evidence, not a cure: it proves the keeper knew the old address still mattered and chose where the rival would not look. Forward-completeness does not excuse a targeted deletion — a perfect forward after a singleton, approach-timed deletion is still theatre — but a missing or late forward turns even a scheduled retirement into a presumed targeting, because the keeper withheld the bridge its own schedule promised.

The fifth rule is theatre rebuttal and remedy, mirroring T-608: any house may rebut a routine-maintenance claim by showing, from the record alone, any one of the four failures — no pre-sealed schedule, approach-then-delete timing, singleton targeting, or late or obscure forwarding — and a rebuttal that, if proven, voids the keeper's benefit of the withdrawal does not need to disprove the finding itself. A proven theatre withdrawal counts as shopping by vanishing on the keeper's record under T-590, forfeits the keeper's benefit of the supported retrieval on demand for re-performance under T-608, and reopens the window under T-604's cure if a rival was stranded. The keeper's staff being unknowing changes nothing: housekeeping performed by the keeper's own hands is the keeper's act, and a house that cannot show its schedule cannot claim its maintenance was routine.
