**T-610 — the Stale-Withdrawal Test — designed:** T-609 left its stale-withdrawal problem named and open: whether a withdrawal notice itself can go stale — a deletion executed at once but announced late, buried, or posted where no rival looks, so the record says public while the pointer is already gone and the retrieval moment is judged against a notice nobody could have seen. T-608 dated the pointer's life by the retrieval moment and T-609 tested whether its death was theatre, but neither dated the announcement of the death: a keeper that deletes on Monday, posts the notice on Friday in an obscure channel, and claims the pointer died Monday strands every rival who walked the path Tuesday through Thursday, because those rivals followed a record that still said public to a pointer that was already gone. The choice is between dating the withdrawal at its execution, which rewards silent deletion, and dating it at its notice, which lets a keeper keep a pointer dead in fact while alive on paper for as long as it delays the announcement. T-610 answers that a withdrawal counts only from its notice, never from its execution — and that a notice counts only when it is timely, in-channel, and cold-findable, so the gap between deletion and notice belongs to the keeper, not to the stranded rival.

The first rule is the notice-date rule: the pointer's public life ends when the withdrawal notice lands, not when the deletion executes. A pointer deleted Monday and noticed Friday counts as public Monday through Friday for every purpose T-608 and T-609 serve — a retrieval in the gap is a retrieval of a public pointer, a rival who followed the record in the gap followed a public path, and the keeper's benefit of the deletion does not begin until the notice does. Execution without notice is a private act with public consequences, and the file refuses to backdate it: the deletion's date is the notice's date, and any certificate, timestamp, or sealed order that dates the withdrawal at execution is corrected to the notice date on rebuttal.

The second rule is the notice-channel rule: a notice counts only if posted in the same common channel as the original pointer under T-604, carrying the original timestamp and the new address or the preservation snapshot under T-608, findable by the same cold search that found the pointer. A notice posted in a different channel, a buried annex, a members-only bulletin, or a channel no rival in the window reads is no notice at all, and the pointer stays public until a real one lands. A notice posted late but in-channel counts from its posting, not from the deletion — lateness costs the keeper the gap, it does not void the notice — while a notice never posted in-channel leaves the pointer public indefinitely, however long ago the deletion executed.

The third rule is the gap-remedy rule, mirroring T-609: any house may rebut a withdrawal date by showing, from the record alone, that the notice lagged the deletion, left the channel, or arrived where no rival looks, and a rebuttal that, if proven, re-dates the withdrawal to the notice does not need to disprove the deletion itself. A retrieval made in the gap stands as a public retrieval, a rival stranded in the gap is cured under T-604's cure, and a keeper that deletes silently and announces late forfeits the benefit of the supported retrieval on demand for re-performance under T-608. The keeper's staff being unknowing changes nothing: a deletion executed by the keeper's own hands without a notice is the keeper's silent act, and a house that cannot show its notice cannot claim its pointer died when it says it did.

T-611 answers that a notice counts only when its preservation snapshot is itself cold-retrievable, stable, and equivalent — a notice whose snapshot cannot be opened by a stranger is no notice at all, however timely and in-channel its posting was.

The first rule is the snapshot-retrievability rule: the snapshot named in the notice must be retrievable by a cold rival from the public record alone — no credential, no private pointer, no prior walk, no membership, no request to the keeper. A snapshot behind a login, a paywall, a credential no rival holds, or a "contact the keeper" instruction fails this rule outright, and the notice fails with it. The keeper's claim that rivals could have asked changes nothing: T-610's in-channel rule already refused a notice to nowhere, and a snapshot open only to those who ask is a notice to the keeper's friends.

The second rule is the snapshot-stability rule: the snapshot must stay retrievable through the window, not merely at the moment of posting. The test is a cold fetch at the notice and a cold re-fetch at the window's close — a snapshot that vanishes, loops, redirects elsewhere, or serves different content on the second fetch is unstable, and an unstable snapshot voids the notice retroactively to the posting, because a rival who relied on it mid-window relied on a shelf that was already rotting. A snapshot that was stable when posted and decays after the window closes is a different case, and counts: stability is owed through the window, not forever.

The third rule is the snapshot-equivalence rule: the snapshot must be the pointer's content, or a faithful preservation of it — not a stub, a placeholder, a table of contents, or a redacted husk that gestures at the pointer without containing it. A snapshot that opens cleanly but holds nothing of substance is theatre in the same sense as T-609's theatre withdrawal: formally retrievable, practically empty. Equivalence is judged from the record alone — a rival comparing the snapshot against the pointer's own description in the window's public record, not against the keeper's private original.

**T-612 — the Snapshot-Staleness Test — designed:** T-611 left its snapshot-staleness problem named and open: whether a snapshot can go stale mid-window in a way no rule dates — stable at the notice, rotting before the close, with retrievals in between judged against a shelf whose state changed under them, and no rule saying which fetch counts. T-611 required the snapshot to open cold, stay stable, and hold equivalent content, but it tested the snapshot once, at the notice: a snapshot that passes every T-611 check on Monday and 404s on Thursday leaves the rival who retrieved Tuesday holding a good shelf and the rival who retrieved Friday holding nothing, and no rule says whether the window's shelf counts as live or dead, because the test dated the shelf at its notice and never at its retrievals. The choice is between judging the snapshot once at the notice, which insures a shelf that no longer exists, and judging it at every retrieval, which makes the keeper answer for the shelf's whole life and not just its birthday. T-612 answers that a snapshot counts at each retrieval, never once at the notice — the shelf is judged at the moment each rival reaches for it, and a notice proves the shelf once, it does not insure it.

The first rule is the retrieval-moment rule: each retrieval is judged against the snapshot's state at that retrieval's own timestamp. A retrieval that opened a live, equivalent snapshot counts even if the snapshot rots the next day, because the rival read what the notice promised while the promise held. A retrieval that met a rotted shelf — a 404, a login wall, a loop, a husk — does not count even if the snapshot was live at the notice, because the rival read nothing the notice can no longer deliver. Where a window's retrievals straddle the rot, the window splits on the rot: the retrievals before it stand, the retrievals after it fall, and no certificate may average them into a shelf that was live throughout, because a shelf that was live for half the window was dead for the other half, and the rivals on the dead half are not cured by the rivals on the live half.

The second rule is the keeper's stability duty: the keeper must keep the snapshot live and equivalent through the window's close, or re-notice. A snapshot that rots mid-window must be repaired or replaced under a fresh notice carrying its own notice date, under T-610's notice-date discipline and T-607's publication discipline — the replacement counts from its own notice, never backdated to the original, and a silently replaced snapshot is a fresh publication dated at the replacement, judged against the replacement date. A replacement snapshot must itself pass T-611's cold-retrievability, stability, and equivalence checks from its own notice forward; inheriting the original's passing grade is not a grade, because a husk swapped in for a good shelf is T-611 theatre wearing a repair order. Retrievals between the rot and the replacement notice are judged against the rotted shelf, not against the repair that came later, because a rival stranded in the gap was stranded when it mattered, whatever the shelf looks like now.

The third rule is the rot-remedy rule, mirroring T-609 and T-611: any house may rebut a window's shelf by showing, from the record alone, that the snapshot rotted before a given retrieval, and a rebuttal that proves the rot does not need to prove the keeper intended it. A rival stranded by mid-window rot is cured under T-604's cure like any rival stranded by a rigged channel, and the expiry the rotted shelf supported is void for the affected retrievals, reopening the window for them. Where the keeper let the shelf rot while a rival was known to be approaching — the approach-timing discipline of T-609 applied to the shelf itself — the rot counts on the keeper's pattern record as shopping by vanishing under T-590's discipline, exactly as a theatre withdrawal does. Where the keeper did not know and the rot served no keeper interest, the window still reopens for the stranded rivals, but the rot is not counted, because an unknowing keeper's dead shelf is still a dead shelf, and the rivals it stranded are still stranded.

The fourth rule is the disputed-fetch rule: where the shelf's state at a retrieval is disputed, the retrieval's own fetch record beats the keeper's later claim about the shelf. A rival's dated fetch receipt — what the shelf returned, when — decides what the rival met, and the keeper's assertion that the shelf was live that day does not outrank the receipt. Where neither side kept a fetch receipt, the earliest dated third-house copy decides, under T-607's independent-timestamp discipline. Where no dated record exists at all, the retrieval is presumed to have met the shelf as noticed, with the burden on the keeper, because a keeper that let the shelf's whole life go undated cannot claim the benefit of the doubt about the one day that matters. A shelf whose life nobody dated is a shelf nobody proved, and the window does not get to presume it lived.

**T-614 — the Chain-Collusion Test — designed:** T-613 left its chain-collusion problem named and open: whether a keeper and a rival agreeing which link was current on a retrieval day can move a link boundary by agreement, so a gap retrieval lands on a live link, with the two houses agreeing on the fetch receipt itself. T-613 pinned each retrieval to exactly one link — the link whose notice interval contains the retrieval's timestamp — but a notice interval is only as firm as its boundaries, and a boundary dated by the keeper's own notice is a date the keeper can move, or agree to move, after the retrieval. A gap retrieval that fell after a link's rot and before the next link's notice is a stranded retrieval under T-612, unless the keeper and the rival agree the next link was noticed a day earlier, or the old link rotted a day later — and then the same retrieval, on the same record, lands on a live link, because the two houses that benefit from the landing are the two houses that drew the map. The choice is between letting the houses that stand to gain agree the boundary, which makes every chain boundary negotiable after the fact, and fixing every boundary from the public record alone, which strands a retrieval whose boundary the record leaves genuinely unclear. T-614 answers that a link boundary is a public-record fact, never an agreement — a boundary counts only as the record proves it, and where the record does not prove it, the retrieval falls, not because the rival is blamed, but because an unproven boundary is no boundary.

The first rule is the boundary-from-record rule: a retrieval's current link is determined solely by notices in the common channel under T-604, with timestamps a cold rival could have read at the retrieval's moment, and by nothing private between the keeper and the rival. Where a joint statement by the keeper and the benefiting rival says the boundary fell on one day and the channel notices say another, the notices govern and the statement counts for nothing. A fetch receipt signed by both houses is a claim by interested houses, not a boundary proof: the houses that would gain from the landing cannot also be the witnesses to it, because a receipt both beneficiaries sign is an agreement wearing a receipt's face. Where the channel notices conflict, carry the same timestamp for two successive links, or leave a boundary undated, the boundary is ambiguous, and an ambiguous boundary is a gap under T-612 — the retrieval does not count, and no agreement rescues it, because a rescue by agreement is the very move this test bars.

The second rule is the corroboration rule: an agreed boundary may be corroborated, but never self-proved. A joint statement counts only when a record independent of both houses proves the same boundary from the record alone — a channel archive timestamped at the notice, a dated fetch by a disinterested house, a preservation snapshot carrying its own dated notice — none authored by the keeper or the benefiting rival, and none created after the boundary was challenged. A post-challenge archive, a keeper's backdated log, or a rival's after-the-fact affidavit is not corroboration: corroboration must have existed in the record before the dispute, because a proof manufactured to answer a challenge proves only that the challenged houses can manufacture proofs. Where independent corroboration exists, the boundary stands on the corroboration, not on the agreement — and the agreement adds nothing to it.

The third rule is the third-house rebuttal and re-performance rule, mirroring T-606 and T-611: any third house may rebut a boundary by showing, from the record alone, a channel notice, a rot date, or a fetch that places the boundary elsewhere, and a rebuttal that proves the record boundary does not need to prove intent, knowledge, or collusion. A disinterested re-performer walking the notices in order from the public record alone under T-606's cold re-performance discipline determines the link; where the re-performer lands on a different link than the agreed boundary names, the agreed boundary falls and the re-performer's landing governs. A boundary no third house has tested is not thereby proven — it is untested — and an untested boundary that only the interested houses assert is held to the first rule's gap treatment until independent corroboration lands.

The fourth rule is the boundary-theatre guard, mirroring T-609, T-611, and T-613: boundaries clustered around a retrieval date — successive links noticed on the same day, a notice moved after a challenge, a rot date revised to close a gap — are presumed contested, and the keeper must show an independent timestamp for each boundary in the cluster to keep it in the chain. Where a boundary is moved by agreement and the move rescues a gap retrieval, the move counts on the keeper's pattern record as shopping by vanishing under T-590's discipline, and on the benefiting rival's record where the rival knew the record boundary differed; an unknowing rival is not counted, but the retrieval still falls, because an unknowing beneficiary's landing is still a landing on an agreed map. **T-615 — the Silent-House Test — designed:** T-614 left its third-house-absence problem named and open: whether an unrebutted agreed boundary stands by default when no disinterested house steps forward to rebut or re-perform. T-614 refused both defaults deliberately — standing by default would let an agreed boundary harden into fact through nobody's attention, falling by default would strand every retrieval whose boundary simply went untested — and left the case undecided. The choice is between treating silence as consent, which rewards the houses that draw their map where nobody is looking, and treating silence as suspicion, which punishes a boundary for the accident that no third house happened to pass by. T-615 answers that silence is neither consent nor suspicion: an unrebutted agreed boundary is held provisionally, flagged as untested, and given a sunset — it counts for the window it supports, but it never hardens, it never travels, and a late rebuttal still voids it.

The first rule is the provisional-hold rule: an agreed boundary that no third house has rebutted or re-performed counts provisionally for the window it supports — the retrieval lands on it, the expiry it supports runs — but the landing is flagged "silent-house" on the record, and the flag travels with the expiry wherever the expiry is cited. A provisional landing is not a proven landing: the record must show the flag, and any later citation of the expiry that drops the flag is a mis-citation, corrected on the record like any other. The flag is not a stain on the keeper or the rival — it records only that no disinterested house tested this boundary — because a test nobody ran cannot be evidence against anybody, and a flag that reads as blame would punish houses for other houses' absence.

The second rule is the sunset rule: a provisional hold lapses at the next window's opening unless independent corroboration under T-614's second rule lands before then. A provisional boundary cannot support a second window, cannot be cited as precedent for another boundary, and cannot corroborate another boundary — a chain of provisional boundaries is a chain of untested links, and no link in it lends strength to the next. Where the next window opens and the boundary is still uncorroborated and still unrebutted, the boundary does not fall retroactively for the window it already supported — that window's landings stand as provisional landings, flagged — but it counts for nothing further, and any retrieval pinned to it in the new window is a gap retrieval under T-612. A boundary that needs to live past its sunset must earn its second life from the record, not from the silence that surrounded its first.

The third rule is the silence-is-not-evidence rule: no house may cite the absence of rebuttal as corroboration, precedent, or character for a boundary. Silence is recorded as "no house tested," never as "no house objected," because the two sentences describe different worlds — one in which houses looked and found nothing, one in which no house looked at all — and only the first could ever support a boundary. A keeper who argues "no third house objected" has argued from nothing, and the argument is struck from the record; a rival who argues "no third house confirmed" has likewise argued from nothing, and that argument is struck too. Silence proves only that the room was empty, and an empty room proves nothing about the map drawn in it.

The fourth rule is the late-rebuttal rule: a third house may rebut a provisional boundary at any later window, and a successful rebuttal voids the boundary retroactively for the affected retrievals, reopening their windows under T-604's cure. Landings made during the provisional period are then marked as having rested on an untested boundary — not as fraud, not as fault, not as shopping — because a house that landed on a boundary the rules allowed it to land on provisionally did nothing wrong by landing. But the voiding is real: the expiry the boundary supported is void for the affected retrievals, and any later window built on it falls with it. A late rebuttal that fails — a record challenge the notices answer — clears the flag: the boundary stands as tested, not merely as unrebutted, and the sunset no longer applies to it.

The fifth rule is the repeated-silence guard, mirroring T-590: a keeper whose boundaries rest on silent-house holds in two consecutive windows must invite a disinterested house to re-perform before the next window opens, and the invitation itself goes on the record. A third consecutive silent-house hold without a test does not count even provisionally — the boundary is a gap under T-612 until a house tests it — because a chain that keeps finding empty rooms is no longer experiencing an accident of absence; it is operating where nobody looks, and operating where nobody looks is the shape shopping takes when it has learned to be quiet. An invited house that re-performs cold under T-606 counts as a test whether it confirms or rebuts; an invited house that merely co-signs the keeper's boundary does not, because a co-signature is an agreement, and T-614 already bars agreements as proof.

**T-616 — the Blind-Invitation Test — designed:** T-615 left its invited-house problem named and open: whether an invited house stays cold under T-606 once it knows it was invited to test a particular boundary — an invitation names the boundary, and a named boundary may no longer be a cold walk. T-615's fifth rule requires a keeper whose boundaries rest on silent-house holds in two consecutive windows to invite a disinterested house to re-perform before the next window opens, but the invitation as T-615 states it is a destination, not a walk: a house told "test this boundary" walks toward a boundary it already knows the keeper claims, looks for the notices that would prove it, and finds them the way a person told where the treasure is buried finds the treasure — by digging where told, not by reading the map. A confirmation produced that way is a co-signature with footsteps, and T-614 already bars agreements as proof. The choice is between letting the invited house know what it is testing, which coaches the walk it was invited to make cold, and hiding the test from the house entirely, which leaves the house testing a window it cannot see whole. T-616 answers that the invitation is blind: the house is invited to walk a window, never to test a boundary, and the boundary under test is identified only after the walk, from a sealed report the walker filed before learning which boundary was silent.

The first rule is the blind-invitation rule: an invitation names the window and the keeper only — never the silent-house boundary, never the keeper's claimed date for it, never the retrieval it supports. The invitation's full text goes on the public record, and an invitation that names the boundary, hints it ("the boundary you will find near the second rot"), or is sent with the keeper's boundary claim attached is void as a test: the walk that follows it counts as a co-signature, not a re-performance, and does not clear the flag or lift the sunset. A keeper who must invite but will not invite blind has not invited at all — the third consecutive silent-house hold still does not count even provisionally under T-615, and the keeper's pattern record notes the failed invitation.

The second rule is the batch-walk rule: the invited house walks the whole window's chain cold — every link boundary in the window, live, rotted, and provisional alike — and reports, for each, whether it can walk to it from the common-channel notices alone, and on what dates. The walker is not told which boundary is silent, which is already corroborated, or which is under challenge; it walks them all as equals. Only after the sealed report is filed does a record-keeper who is neither keeper nor walker match the report against the keeper's claim and identify which reported boundary was the silent one. A walk of one boundary is not a batch walk, because a walk of one boundary is a named walk whatever the invitation said.

The third rule is the control rule: the batch must contain at least one already-corroborated boundary and at least one known gap, as controls. The walker must find the corroborated boundary and must miss the gap — must report it unwalkable from the notices — or the walk is uncalibrated and counts for nothing, neither confirming nor rebutting the silent boundary. A walker that finds everything, including the gap, is not walking; it is agreeing. A walker that finds nothing, including the corroborated boundary, is not walking either; it is refusing. Controls are what turn a walk into a test: without them, a confirmation is only a house saying yes, and a rebuttal only a house saying no.

The fourth rule is the sealed-report rule: the walker files its batch report sealed — dated, hashed, and held by a house that is neither keeper, rival, nor walker — before learning which boundary was silent, and the seal is opened only after filing. A report filed, amended, or "clarified" after the walker learns which boundary was under test is struck, not corrected, because a clarification after knowledge is a second walk with the destination known. A seal opened early, by anyone, voids the walk and counts on the opener's pattern record under T-590's discipline where the opener stood to gain. The sealed report is the coldness made physical: cold is not a state of mind the walker claims, it is a timestamp the record can check.

The fifth rule is the outcome rule: a blind walk that confirms the silent boundary — the walker walks to it, on the keeper's claimed dates, from the notices alone, with controls passing — clears the silent-house flag, and the sunset no longer applies to it; the boundary stands as tested, not merely as unrebutted. A blind walk that fails to walk to it — the walker cannot reach it from the notices, or reaches it only on different dates — rebuts it: the boundary falls, the provisional landings it supported are voided retroactively, and affected rivals are cured under T-604 like any rival stranded by a late rebuttal under T-615. A blind walk that is uncalibrated, voided, or never completed leaves the boundary exactly where T-615 left it: provisional, flagged, and sunset-bound.

**T-617 — the Seal-Holder's Rule — designed:** T-616 left its sealed-report-trust problem named and open: who holds the seal, and whether a seal can be trusted when the holder is itself a house with interests — a forged, early-opened, or quietly amended seal would launder a warm walk into a cold one, and no seal-holder rule was fixed there. T-617 answers that no house holds the seal: the seal is a digest on the public record, the report is held by a house chosen by lot, and the match is made by a house that is neither. A seal that lives in one house's keeping is a secret, and a secret is exactly what a warm walk needs; a seal that lives as a public digest with a lot-chosen keeper and a third-house match is a commitment, and a commitment is what a cold walk can be checked against.

The first rule is the digest rule: at the moment the walker finishes the walk, before it learns which boundary was silent, it files a digest of its sealed report on the public record — a short fingerprint of the report's exact words, computed by a method the record states openly, so that any later copy of the report can be checked against it and any amendment shows as a mismatch. The digest goes on the record the same day the walk ends; a report whose digest was not filed before the match cannot clear or rebut anything, because an uncommitted report can be rewritten after the walker learns the answer, and a rewritten report is a warm walk with cold paperwork. The digest itself names nothing about the walk's findings — it is a fingerprint, not a summary — so publishing it leaks no boundary, steers no rival, and tips no keeper.

The second rule is the lot-chosen keeper rule: the sealed report itself is held, unopened, by a house chosen by lot from the houses with no interest in the window — not by the keeper, not by the walker, not by any rival to the boundary, and not by the house that chose the controls. The lot is drawn on the public record, the keeper's name entered beside it, and the keeper's only duty is custody: to hold the seal unopened until the match, and to produce it whole on demand. A keeper with an interest is no keeper: a house that stands to gain from a confirmation or a rebuttal holds the seal the way a party holds its own evidence, and its custody proves nothing. A keeper chosen by the keeper, or by the walker, is chosen, not drawn, and choice is interest wearing a lottery's clothes.

The third rule is the third-house match rule: the match — the comparison of the sealed report against the keeper's claim, identifying which reported boundary was the silent one — is made by a record-keeper who is neither the keeper, nor the walker, nor the seal's keeper, and who has not seen the report before the match. The matcher opens the seal in the presence of the digest: it checks the report against the public digest first, and only a report that matches its digest is matched at all. A report that fails its digest is void as a walk — not as a rebuttal, not as a confirmation, but as nothing — and the boundary stays exactly where T-615 left it, provisional, flagged, and sunset-bound, with the failed seal noted on the pattern record of every house that touched it. A matcher that opens a seal without its digest, or matches a report it has already seen, has performed a reading, not a match, and its reading counts for nothing.

The fourth rule is the opened-seal rule: a seal opened early, opened by any house but the matcher, or opened without the digest check, voids the walk and stains the opener. An early-opened seal is shopping by peeking, under T-616's own terms, and the house that opened it is barred from walking, keeping, or matching any boundary in the same window — because a house that peeks once has shown it will peek, and the window cannot afford a second peeking. The boundary itself is not punished for the opener's act: it stays provisional under T-615, and a fresh blind invitation may be issued, with a fresh lot, a fresh digest, and a fresh walker.

The fifth rule is the custody-chain rule: every hand the seal passes through is entered on the public record — walker to lot-keeper, lot-keeper to matcher — with dates, and a seal whose chain has a gap is a seal whose custody is unproved, and an unproved seal is void. A lot drawn by a hand is a favour, and a favour is exactly what a warm walk needs; a lot derived from the public record, after the digest, from a roster fixed before the walk, is a draw no hand can rig without rigging the record itself.

The first rule is the no-hand rule: no house — not the keeper, not the walker, not the matcher, not any rival, not any house that chose the controls — draws, picks, nominates, or "assists" the lot. There is no drawer to bribe, threaten, or flatter, because the draw is not an act performed by anyone: it is a computation any house can repeat from the public record and get the same name. A lot announced by a house, even a house with no interest, is not a draw; it is a claim, and a claim about who holds the seal is the seal's custody wearing a lottery's clothes. Where a hand appears in the draw, the draw is void and the custody it produced is interested custody under T-617, whatever the hand's intentions.

The second rule is the future-seed rule: the seed is the digest of the first public-record entry filed after the walker's sealed-report digest — an entry that did not exist when the walk ended and that no house could have chosen at the time the walker's report was sealed. The seed is combined, by a method the record states openly, with the walker's own digest, and the result names a position in the roster. A seed chosen before the digest, or from an entry that existed before the walk ended, is a seed the walker or keeper could have steered toward a friendly keeper, and a steered seed is a chosen keeper. A seed whose source entry is not on the public record, or whose method is not stated openly, is not a seed; it is a secret, and a secret seed rigs the lot while looking like chance.

The third rule is the roster-before-walk rule: the roster of eligible houses — every house with no interest in the window, in a fixed public order — is published on the public record before the walk begins, and no house is added to it, removed from it, or reordered within it after the walk starts. A roster edited mid-walk can be edited toward a keeper: a friendly house added late, an unfriendly house struck as "interested" on thin grounds, an order shuffled so the seed lands elsewhere. A house found genuinely interested after the roster is published is not struck from the roster; it is skipped by the succession rule below, and the skip is entered on the record, so the roster stays whole and the skip stays visible. A draw run against any roster but the pre-published one is void.

The fourth rule is the succession rule: if the house the seed names refuses, dies, or is found interested only after the draw, no second draw is made and no hand picks a replacement — the next eligible house in the pre-published roster order steps in, and the next after that if it too fails, until an eligible keeper accepts. Succession is deterministic, not chosen: the same seed, the same roster, the same order, the same successor, whoever recomputes it. A second draw by hand after a failure is a fresh chance to choose, and a fresh chance to choose is the rigging the rule exists to prevent. If the roster is exhausted — every eligible house refuses, dies, or is found interested — the window stalls: no keeper is appointed, the boundary stays provisional under T-615, and a fresh blind invitation may be issued in a later window with a fresh roster, a fresh walk, and a fresh seed. A stalled window is a cost, not a failure of the rule; a hand-picked keeper in a stalled window is a failure of the rule wearing a rescue's clothes.

A draw that cannot be recomputed — a missing seed entry, an unstated method, a roster that cannot be produced as published — is void for the same reason: an uncheckable draw is a choice that cannot be caught. The recompute is the draw's audit, and an audit that only the drawer can perform is no audit.

**T-619 — the Seed-Guard Rule — designed:** T-618 left its seed-steering problem named and open: whether the future seed itself can be steered — a house that controls, delays, or rushes the first public entry after the walker's digest, or that files a chosen entry first, steering the seed toward a friendly keeper — with no seed-entry-control rule fixed there. T-619 answers that the seed is guarded, not merely future: a seed entry counts only if it is filed by a disinterested house, after a cooling interval, in an unbroken record sequence, and it is never one entry alone — the seed is the combination of the first three qualifying entries. A future seed that any single house can rush, delay, or file first is a choice wearing chance's clothes; a seed that must survive disinterest, cooling, sequence, and triplication is a draw no single hand can steer without steering the record itself in front of witnesses.

The first rule is the disinterested-filer rule: only an entry filed by a house with no interest in the window counts as a seed candidate. An entry filed by the keeper, the walker, the matcher, a rival, or any house that chose the controls is skipped as a seed candidate, however early it lands, and the skip is entered on the public record with the filer's name and the reason. A skipped entry is not discarded from the record — it stays filed, timestamped, and readable — but it cannot seed the lot, so filing first buys nothing. A house that files a chosen entry first in the hope of seeding the lot has filed evidence of its own attempt, and the attempt is noted on the pattern record of every house that relied on the draw. Disinterest is judged as T-618 judges the roster: no interest in the window's boundary, no pending claim on it, no kinship of custody with any party to it. A filer whose disinterest is found false after the draw voids the seed it contributed to, and the draw falls to the succession rule below.

The second rule is the cooling-interval rule: no entry counts as a seed candidate until a fixed cooling interval has passed after the walker's digest is filed. The interval is fixed in the roster publication before the walk begins — the same publication that fixes the roster under T-618 — so no house can shorten it after seeing the digest or lengthen it while waiting for a friendly entry. A rushed entry filed inside the cooling interval is skipped like an interested entry: it lands early, it counts for nothing, and the rush itself is entered on the record. Cooling defeats the rush because the race is not to be first after the digest; the race, if it is a race at all, is to be the first disinterested entry after the interval closes, and a house cannot know, when the digest lands, which disinterested house will file first after an interval it did not choose. A cooling interval set after the digest, or shortened or lengthened mid-window, is a steered interval, and a draw seeded under it is void.

The third rule is the sequence rule: the public record's entries carry continuous sequence numbers, and a seed candidate must sit in an unbroken sequence. If the sequence breaks — a number missing, a number repeated, an entry filed out of order, a gap between the digest and the seed candidate that the record cannot account for — the candidate after the break does not seed the lot; the seed falls forward to the first qualifying entry after the sequence resumes unbroken, and the break is investigated as a suppression before any draw is announced. Delay defeats itself under this rule: a house that suppresses intervening entries to let a friendly entry land "first" has broken the sequence, and a broken sequence disqualifies exactly the entry the suppression was meant to favour. A record keeper who cannot produce a continuous sequence for the seed window cannot certify a seed at all, and the window stalls under T-618's stall rule rather than drawing on a gapped record.

The fourth rule is the triplication rule: the seed is never one entry. It is the combination, by the method fixed before the walk, of the first three qualifying entries — disinterested filers, after the cooling interval, in unbroken sequence. Steering one entry, however chosen, steers only a third of the seed; steering the seed requires steering three disinterested filers in filing order, after an interval none of them chose, without breaking the sequence — which is no longer steering but a conspiracy of three disinterested houses, visible as a pattern across their filings and catchable by the pattern record. If fewer than three qualifying entries arrive before the window's sunset under T-615, the seed is incomplete and the draw is not made: the boundary stays provisional, flagged, and sunset-bound, and a fresh blind invitation may be issued in a later window. An incomplete seed drawn anyway, on one entry or two, is a Steered Seed under T-618, whatever the entries' provenance.

The fifth rule is the method-fixed-before-walk rule: the combination method — how the three qualifying entries' digests combine with the walker's digest to name a roster position — is fixed in the roster publication before the walk begins, alongside the roster and the cooling interval, and it is not chosen by the walker, changed between the walk and the draw, or restated after the digest. A method chosen after the digest can be chosen to favour the seed that arrived; a method fixed before the walk cannot know which seed it will favour. The method's collisions, if any, are a property of a method fixed in public before the walk, examinable by any house before the walk begins; a house that objects to the method objects before the walk, not after the draw it dislikes. This answers in part T-618's method-trust problem — the choice and the change of method, not the collisions a fixed method may carry, which stand open below.

What a seed files as follows from the five rules, and the file must show the three entries, their filers' disinterest, the cooling interval, the unbroken sequence, and the fixed method, not merely the keeper's name. A seed from three disinterested entries, after the cooling interval, in unbroken sequence, combined by a method fixed before the walk, files as a Guarded Seed: the only seed that can feed a T-618 draw. A seed from an entry filed by an interested house files as a Skipped Seed Attempt: counted for nothing, noted on the filer's pattern record. A seed from an entry filed inside the cooling interval files as a Rushed Seed: counted for nothing, the rush entered on the record. A seed whose sequence breaks before it files as a Gapped Seed: disqualified, the break investigated as a suppression before any draw. A seed drawn from fewer than three qualifying entries files as a Short Seed: a Steered Seed under T-618, the draw void. A seed combined by a method chosen or changed after the walk files as a Restated Method: the draw void, the keeper unappointed.

The Disinterested Filer — a house with no interest in the window, whose entries alone can seed: FILED to T-289 — the only hands the seed accepts. The Cooling Interval — the fixed interval after the digest during which no entry can seed: FILED to T-289 — the rush made pointless. COOLING-INTERVAL — no entry counts until the pre-fixed interval after the digest closes, and a rushed entry counts for nothing. **T-620 — the Cooling-Length Test — designed:** T-619 left its cooling-length problem named and open: how long the cooling interval should run — an interval too short leaves the rush alive, an interval too long stalls every window past its sunset, and no length was fixed there. T-620 answers that the length is not a duration anyone chooses, and not a clock interval at all: it is a record-count interval, bounded on both sides by two tests fixed and published before the walk, and a length that fails either test is not a length — the window does not open for a draw on it.

The first rule is the count-not-clock rule: the cooling interval does not close when a clock ticks. It closes when a pre-fixed count of intervening entries lands on the public record — entries unrelated to the window, filed by houses with no interest in it. A clock interval can be camped: a rusher who knows the interval ends at an hour can file at that hour, prepared, first. A count interval cannot be camped the same way, because its close is an event the rusher does not control and cannot time — the filing of an unrelated entry by a disinterested house. The rusher may watch the record, but watching does not hasten the unrelated entry, and an entry filed by the rusher or any interested house does not count toward the close, so a rusher's allies cannot close the interval for it either. A cooling interval measured in clock time alone, with no intervening-entry count, does not close under this test at all: it extends until the count is met or the sunset arrives, whichever comes first.

The second rule is the rush-blindness floor: the count must be large enough that the close is blind to the rusher. The test is not a number fixed here — a number without a run would be a verdict wearing a design — but a property the roster publication must show: the interval must span at least one filing by a house other than any house that filed on the window, so that the close is witnessed by an unrelated hand before any seed candidate can land. An interval that closes on the first entry after the digest, or on entries only from window-interested houses, is a short interval in disguise: the rush is still alive, because the close was reachable by the very hands the cooling was meant to outwait. A floor shown only as a chosen duration, with no intervening-entry count behind it, fails this test and the draw seeded under it is void.

The third rule is the sunset-feasibility ceiling: the count must be small enough that three qualifying entries can still arrive before the T-615 sunset. The ceiling is computed before the walk from the public record's own filing rate in the immediately preceding window — the window just closed, not a window chosen for a flattering rate — and the computation is published in the roster publication alongside the count: at that rate, the count closes with enough of the window left for three disinterested entries in unbroken sequence. If no count satisfies both the floor and the ceiling — if every blind count is too long for the sunset, or every sunset-feasible count is too short to be blind — the window does not open for a draw. The boundary stays provisional, flagged, and sunset-bound under T-615, and no draw is attempted on a clock already known to be doomed. A window opened on a length already known to fail its ceiling is a theatre window under T-609: it performs a draw it cannot complete.

The fourth rule is the pre-walk-publication rule: the count, the floor showing, and the ceiling computation are all fixed in the roster publication before the walk begins, alongside the roster, the cooling interval, and the combination method under T-619. A count chosen after the digest can be chosen to favour the seed that arrived; a rate taken from a cherry-picked earlier window can be taken to flatter a count already decided. A count or a rate fixed after the digest, or a rate drawn from any window but the immediately preceding one without the reason entered on the record, voids the draw. The immediately-preceding window is the rule precisely because it is the one window no house can choose after seeing the digest — it is already closed when the walk begins.

What a cooling length files as follows from the four rules, and the file must show the count, the floor showing, the preceding window cited, and the ceiling computation, not merely the keeper's name. A length that closes on a pre-fixed count of unrelated disinterested entries, blind to the rusher and feasible before the sunset, files as a Bounded Cooling: the only cooling that can guard a T-619 seed. A length measured in clock time alone files as an Uncounted Cooling: it never closes under this test, and a draw seeded under it is void. A length whose count is met only by interested entries files as a Closed-By-Interest Cooling: the rush alive, the draw void. A length opened although no count passes both floor and ceiling files as a Doomed Window: theatre under T-609, the boundary provisional, no draw attempted. A length whose interval never closes before the sunset files as an Unclosed Cooling: the seed incomplete under T-619, the boundary provisional and sunset-bound.

**The named forms**, all to T-289: the Bounded Cooling — a count of intervening unrelated entries, blind below and feasible above: FILED to T-289 — a length with two edges, not one choice. The Count-Not-Clock — cooling measured in record entries, never in elapsed time: FILED to T-289 — the camped hour made useless. The Rush-Blind Close — a close witnessed by an unrelated hand before any seed candidate: FILED to T-289 — the rush outwaited, not outrun. The Sunset-Feasible Ceiling — the longest count that still leaves room for three qualifying entries before the sunset: FILED to T-289 — the doomed window refused before it opens. The Unclosed Cooling — an interval that never meets its count before the sunset: FILED to T-289 — an incomplete seed, not a rushed draw.

**The grades.** COUNT-NOT-CLOCK — the interval closes on a pre-fixed count of intervening unrelated entries, never on a clock tick. RUSH-BLIND-CLOSE — the count spans at least one filing by a house other than any window-interested house, so the close is blind to the rusher. SUNSET-FEASIBLE — the count leaves room for three qualifying entries before the T-615 sunset at the preceding window's filing rate. PRE-WALK-PUBLISHED — the count, the floor showing, and the ceiling computation are fixed in the roster publication before the walk, with the immediately preceding window cited. UNCLOSED-IS-INCOMPLETE — an interval that never closes before the sunset leaves the seed incomplete, never justifies a rushed draw.

**Distinguished from the chain it answers.** From T-619's Seed-Guard Rule (the guard — there the question was whether the future seed can be steered, and the answer was disinterest, cooling, sequence, and triplication, with the cooling interval itself taken as a fixed duration; here the question is how long that cooling runs, and the answer is that it does not run in time at all — it runs in intervening entries, bounded by blindness below and sunset-feasibility above). **What this pairs with.** T-619's Seed-Guard Rule (the guard this test lengths — T-619 says the seed must cool, T-620 says the cooling is a bounded count, and an unbounded or clock-only cooling voids the seed it guards). T-615's Silent-House Test (the provisional hold a doomed or unclosed window protects — a window refused or unclosed leaves the boundary exactly where T-615 left it, provisional and flagged). T-609's theatre problem (the performance a doomed window would be — opening a window known to fail its ceiling is theatre, not a test). T-604's Common-Channel Test (the channel test whose cure a rival stranded by a voided cooling receives — a rival stranded by an uncounted or closed-by-interest cooling is cured like any rival stranded by a rigged channel).

**Admitted-unsolved carried forward.** How many intervening entries the count should be — a count too small is still campable, a count too large is still dooming, and no number is fixed here (admitted here, new — T-620's cooling-count problem, still open; a number without a run would be a verdict wearing a design). Whether an intervening entry's disinterest can be verified before the close — an entry claimed unrelated and disinterested, with its interest found only after the close, voids a cooling already used, with no pre-close verification rule fixed here (admitted here, new — T-620's intervening-disinterest problem, still open). Whether the immediately-preceding window is itself a fair rate — a preceding window distorted by a rush, a stall, or a thin record, with no distorted-rate rule fixed here (admitted here, new — T-620's preceding-window problem, still open). Whether a slow record is fair to a boundary that did nothing wrong — the boundary stays provisional through no fault of its own while no count can pass both tests, with no slow-record compensation rule fixed here (admitted here, new — T-620's slow-record problem, still open). Whether cooling-length accounting multiplies the cost past bearing — every lot now costing a count, a floor showing, and a ceiling computation on top of T-619's cooling watch, disinterest check, sequence audit, and three-entry combination (admitted here, new — T-620's cooling-length-cost problem, still open). Whether a filer's disinterest is verified before the seed is drawn, whether three disinterested filers can collude, whether the record keeper itself can be trusted, and whether seed-guard accounting multiplies the cost past bearing (admitted here, inherited — T-619's disinterest-verification, three-filer-collusion, record-keeper-trust, and seed-cost problems, still open; T-619's cooling-length problem is answered above and closed as a design, not as a run). All other problems carried in T-619's admitted-unsolved paragraph, carried forward by reference.

**T-621 — the Intervening-Disinterest Audit — designed:** T-620 left its intervening-disinterest problem named and open: whether an intervening entry's disinterest can be verified before the close — an entry claimed unrelated and disinterested, with its interest found only after the close, voids a cooling already used, with no pre-close verification rule fixed there. T-621 answers that disinterest is audited before the close counts, not after it is spent: no entry counts toward a T-620 cooling until its filer has been checked against the window's interest list, an entry from an interested house never counts, and an interest found late re-opens the count rather than voiding the window outright. A cooling whose entries were never audited is a count of claims, and a count of claims is exactly what a rusher needs; a cooling whose entries were audited, struck, or extended on the record is a count that can be recomputed by any house afterwards.

The first rule is the interest-list rule: the roster publication, fixed before the walk under T-620's pre-walk-publication rule, lists every house with an interest in the window — the keeper, the walker, the matcher, every rival to the boundary, the house that chose the controls, and any house that filed on the boundary before the walk or stands to gain from a confirmation or a rebuttal. The audit checks a candidate entry's filer against that list and against nothing else: interest is a published fact, not a judgement made at the close. A filer absent from the list is not thereby disinterested — absence is a gap, not a clearance — and a filer whose interest is disputed is treated as interested until the dispute is resolved on the record (see the fifth rule). A list fixed after the digest, or edited after the walk began, is a list written to suit the entries that arrived, and a cooling audited against it is unaudited.

The second rule is the audit-before-count rule: an entry counts toward the cooling only after it passes the audit, and the audit is a recomputation any house can repeat from the public record — the filer's name is on the entry, the interest list is in the roster publication, and the comparison is mechanical. No hand audits: no house declares an entry disinterested, because a declaration is a claim, and a claim about disinterest is interest wearing an auditor's clothes (the same no-hand discipline as T-618's lot). An entry counted before its audit, or counted on a house's word that it is disinterested, does not count, and a close reached on such entries is not a close — it is a Closed-By-Interest Cooling under T-620, and the draw seeded under it is void.

The third rule is the struck-entry extension rule: an entry that fails its audit is struck from the count, and the count extends — it does not collapse. The cooling interval that needed five audited entries and received four audited and one interested still needs one more audited entry; the struck entry is entered on the record as struck, with the interest that struck it, and the interval stays open until the count is met cleanly or the T-615 sunset arrives. A struck entry does not void the window, because the window did nothing wrong — the rusher's ally filed, not the boundary — and a window voided for a filer's interest would punish the boundary for the rusher's act. If the sunset arrives before a clean count is met, the cooling files as an Unclosed Cooling under T-620, and the seed stays incomplete.

The fourth rule is the post-draw discovery rule: an interest found after the draw voids the draw, not the walk. The walk itself was cold — its digest, its lot, and its sealed report stand — but the cooling that guarded its seed was not clean, so the draw it fed cannot stand. The boundary returns to provisional under T-615, and a fresh count may be run on the same walk and the same digest, with the newly found interest added to the interest list for the fresh count. A fresh walk is not required, because nothing about the walk failed; a fresh draw on the same unclean cooling is not permitted, because the cooling is the failure, and reusing it is reusing the failure. A draw voided by post-draw discovery is noted on the pattern record of the house whose interest was found, and of every house that relied on the draw.

The fifth rule is the disputed-filer rule: a filer whose interest is disputed — claimed interested by one house, claimed disinterested by another — is held uncounted until the dispute is resolved on the public record, and while it is held it neither counts toward the close nor strikes the count. The conservative default is deliberate: counting a disputed filer risks a Closed-By-Interest close, and striking it risks punishing a disinterested house for a rival's accusation. A dispute raised after the draw, on an entry already counted, is handled under the fourth rule, not this one — the draw is voided if the interest is found, and stands if it is not. A dispute that is never resolved is a held entry, not a counted one, and a cooling that cannot close cleanly before the sunset files as Unclosed, not as doomed by accusation.

What a disinterest audit files as follows from the five rules, and the file must show the interest list, the audit of each counted entry, and every struck or held entry, not merely the keeper's name. A count of entries each audited disinterested against a pre-walk interest list files as a Clean Count: the only count that can close a T-620 cooling. An entry from a listed interested house files as a Struck Entry: removed from the count, the count extended, the interest entered on the record. A count extended by struck entries and still open at the sunset files as an Unclosed Cooling under T-620: the seed incomplete, the boundary provisional. A draw voided by an interest found after it files as a Late-Voided Draw: the walk stands, the cooling fails, a fresh count permitted on the same digest. A filer held uncounted pending a resolved dispute files as a Disputed Filer: neither counted nor struck until the record resolves it.

**The named forms**, all to T-289: the Clean Count — entries each audited disinterested against a pre-walk list: FILED to T-289 — a count of checks, not of claims. The Struck Entry — an interested filer's entry removed from the count with its interest entered: FILED to T-289 — the count extended, not collapsed. The Disputed Filer — a filer held uncounted until the record resolves the dispute: FILED to T-289 — neither counted nor struck on accusation alone. The Late-Voided Draw — a draw voided by an interest found after it, the walk standing: FILED to T-289 — the cooling failed, not the walk. The Interest List — every interested house published before the walk: FILED to T-289 — interest as a published fact, not a judgement at the close.

**The grades.** INTEREST-LIST-BEFORE-WALK — every interested house is published in the roster publication before the walk, and the audit checks against that list and nothing else. NO-ENTRY-COUNTS-UNAUDITED — an entry counts toward the cooling only after it passes a mechanical audit any house can recompute from the record. STRUCK-EXTENDS-NOT-VOIDS — a failed audit strikes the entry and extends the count; it does not void the window. The first rule is the drawer rule: the drawer is a house with no interest in the window, and no interested hand appoints it. The keeper does not draw the custodian's lot, because a keeper-drawn lot is a keeper-chosen custodian with a lot's alibi. The drawer is drawn by lot under T-618's no-hand discipline, from houses with no interest in the window — and the draw that picks the drawer is published with its digest in the roster publication before the walk, like the freeze it serves. A drawer appointed by any window-interested house, or drawn without a published digest, is not a drawer: the lot it draws is void under the fourth rule below, whatever custodian it names.

The second rule is the drawer-ineligibility rule: the drawer cannot win the lot it draws. A drawer eligible to be custodian for the same window draws with a hand in the hat: every draw that names the drawer is a self-dealing draw, and every draw that names anyone else is a draw the drawer could have steered away from itself. The drawer is therefore struck from the custodian pool for that window before the lot is drawn, and the striking is entered on the record with the drawer's own disinterest showing. A custodian lot that names its own drawer files as a Self-Drawn Lot: the freeze it serves is void, because the custodian was chosen by a hand that stood to gain the seat. This rule is what separates a drawer from a keeper: the keeper drafts and gains nothing from the draft, the drawer draws and gains nothing from the draw, and any hand that gains from either is a party, not an officer.

The third rule is the chain rule: the drawer for window N is the custodian of window N-1. This is what stops the regress without appointing anyone: the drawer is not chosen fresh by a new authority, but inherited from the last freeze that already passed T-622 — a custodian already drawn by lot, already shown disinterested, already frozen with a published digest on the record. A chain that walks back to the founding draw is an Anchored Lot. A chain that breaks — a missing window, a custodian whose own lot was voided, a drawer with no frozen predecessor — is an Unanchored Lot: the custodian it names serves no freeze until the chain is repaired, because a lot that cannot show its ancestry cannot show it was not rigged at some link no one can now check. **T-624 — the Chain-Depth Rule — designed:** T-623 left its drawer-chain problem named and open: how far back the chain must be verified — every link to the founding draw, or only the last link, with a broken early link found only after the freeze served, and no chain-depth rule fixed there. T-624 answers that the chain is walked to the founding draw once, and receipted link by link, so that later windows verify the receipts instead of re-walking the whole chain — but a receipt is not a substitute for a walk, and any window that cannot show its receipts walks the full chain again. A chain verified only at its last link is a roof with no house under it; a chain re-walked in full at every window is a house rebuilt for every guest. The depth rule is: walk once, receipt every link, verify the receipts, re-walk on any doubt.

The first rule is the founding-walk rule: the first window that relies on a chain walks it in full, link by link, back to the founding draw, and each link's verification is frozen as a link receipt — the link's custodian, its lot's digest, its drawer, and its seed-guard showing, entered on the record with the walk's digest. A chain with no founding walk has no depth at all: its last link may be sound and its ancestry still unchecked, and T-623 already refuses to serve a freeze on an unanchored lot. The founding walk is done once per chain, not once per window, because the ancestry does not change when a new window opens — only the newest link is new.

The second rule is the receipt-verification rule: a later window verifies the chain by checking the receipts, not by re-walking the links. The window checks that every receipt is present, that each receipt's digest matches the frozen record, that the receipts chain without a gap — each receipt's custodian is the next receipt's drawer, as T-623's chain rule requires — and that the newest link, the one this window adds, passes T-623 in full: disinterested ineligible drawer, guarded seed, published draw. A receipt chain with a missing receipt, a mismatched digest, or a gap between custodian and drawer is not a verified chain: it is a chain with a hole in it, and a hole anywhere is a hole in the whole chain until repaired. Receipts make verification cheap; they do not make it optional.

The third rule is the re-walk trigger rule: a full re-walk is triggered, and the receipts are set aside, whenever any of four things happens — a house challenges any link in the chain, a receipt is missing or mismatched, the chain crosses a published checkpoint, or a break is discovered in any link. A checkpoint is a window number fixed and published before the walk — every tenth window on a chain, or any window the houses agree in advance — at which the chain is re-walked in full whether or not anyone doubts it, so that a slow rot in the receipts cannot ride forever on a founding walk no one has repeated. A chain that has never been re-walked past its first checkpoint is a chain whose receipts have never been re-proved, and its next window triggers the re-walk before it draws, not after.

The fourth rule is the late-break remedy rule: a broken early link found after the freeze served does not void the freeze outright and does not leave it standing either — the freeze falls to provisional under T-615's Silent-House Test, and the counts against it are held, not counted and not erased, until the chain is repaired. Repair means replacing the broken link with a fresh guarded lot under T-623, re-walking from the break to the founding draw, and re-freezing the receipts — and only then does the freeze stand or fall on the repaired chain. A freeze served by a chain later found broken was served in good faith on receipts that looked sound; voiding it outright punishes the boundary for the chain's failure, and leaving it standing rewards a chain no one can now trust. Provisional is the honest middle: the boundary is held exactly where it was, flagged, until the chain is proved again.

The first rule is the ninth-field rule: beyond T-625's eight fields, a complete receipt carries the chain identifier — the founding-draw digest of its own chain, the public founding draw T-623 chains the drawer back to. A human-readable chain name may ride alongside the digest for the houses' convenience, but the digest governs: a name without a digest is a label, not a pin, and two chains sharing a name with different founding digests are two chains that happen to share a word. A receipt read against a chain it does not name is void for that chain: not a mismatch to be cured by a re-walk alone, but a category error, because it was never that chain's receipt. The third rule is the founding-collision rule: two chains claiming the same founding-draw digest are both holed until one re-founds with a fresh public draw. Parallel chains may share window numbers freely — window 40 of one chain and window 40 of another are different windows, and no receipt, freeze, or challenge record crosses between them on the strength of a shared number. T-626 pinned every receipt to one chain by its founding-draw digest, and a merger that simply re-filed one chain's receipts under the other chain's name would break exactly that pin: the receipts would verify against a chain they never belonged to, and T-626's Cross-Read category would swallow the merger whole. A merger that re-issued every old receipt under a new name would be worse — a re-issued receipt is an edited receipt under T-622, and a chain whose whole history is edited at once is a chain whose history proves nothing. T-627 answers that a merger neither relabels nor re-issues: the merged chain is a new chain, the old chains' receipts keep their old names forever, and the two histories meet only at one bridge link that names both.

The first rule is the re-founding rule: the merged chain is founded like any chain under T-623, with its own fresh public founding draw, published with a digest before the walk, challengeable before it and read-only after. The merged chain's founding digest is its chain name under T-626, distinct from either parent chain's founding digest. A merger that keeps one parent's founding digest as the merged name is not a merger — it is an absorption, and the absorbed chain's receipts filed under the surviving name are Cross-Read receipts, void for the chain they were read against. Two chains become one chain only by both ceasing to be walked and a third chain beginning; anything else is one chain wearing two histories.

The second rule is the history-kept rule: pre-merger receipts are never re-issued, relabelled, or re-dated. Each keeps its original chain field, its original window number read as window N of its original chain, and its original predecessor digest resolving inside that chain. A verifier walking the merged chain's history walks backward through the bridge link and then down one parent chain or the other, never across both at once — a predecessor digest from one parent is not checked against the other parent's links, even after the merger, because chain-scoped verification under T-626 does not expire when the chain stops being walked. History that is rewritten to fit the merger is history that no longer proves the walk it claims.

The third rule is the bridge-link rule: the merger itself is one link, receipted like any link, and it carries three chain fields — both parent chains' founding digests and the merged chain's new founding digest — plus the checkpoint at which each parent chain stopped. The bridge link is the only receipt that names two chains, and it names them as parents, not as aliases: it says these two chains ended here and this new chain began here, and it proves the ending by carrying each parent's final link digest. A bridge link missing either parent's final link digest is a hole in the merged chain under T-624, because a chain whose ending is unproven cannot prove its beginning.

The fourth rule is the checkpoint-only rule: a merger takes effect only at a T-624 checkpoint, never mid-window. Windows already in flight finish under their parent chain's name, are receipted under that name, and only then does the bridge link close them. A merger declared mid-window, with in-flight windows re-filed under the merged name, is an absorption wearing a merger's date. The checkpoint rule also fixes the merger's challenge window: the merger publication, both parents' final links, and the merged chain's founding draw are all challengeable before the bridge link is walked, and read-only after — a challenge lodged after the bridge is a challenge to a walked link, handled by T-622's cure, not by reopening the merger.

The fifth rule is the no-divergent-history rule: a merger is blocked while the two parent chains disagree on any window they both claim. If both chains claim window N with different content, the merged chain cannot carry two histories for one window, and it cannot pick one silently — the dispute is resolved by re-walk under T-624 or the merger does not happen. A merged chain that quietly drops one parent's version of a shared window has edited history by omission, which is the same offence as editing by relabel, only harder to spot.

**T-628 — the Bridge-Attestation Rule — designed:** T-627 left its bridge-trust problem named and open: who attests that a bridge link's two parent digests are genuinely the parents' final links and not earlier links dressed as endings — the bridge-hole rule detects a missing ending, not a premature one, with no final-link attestation rule fixed there. T-627's bridge link carries each parent's final link digest, but a digest is a claim, not a proof of finality: a bridge builder who names an interior link of a parent chain as that chain's "final" link has cut the parent's history short on paper while the parent's later links still exist, and a verifier who checks only that the named digest resolves to some walked link will pass the bridge. The later links, walked under the parent's name after the supposed ending, then dangle — neither part of the merged chain's history nor cleanly part of a chain that ended — and a merger built on a false ending inherits a false beginning. T-628 answers that finality is not attested, it is proven by leaf-check, and attestation without leaf-check is a claim, not a verification.

The first rule is the final-link declaration rule: before the bridge link is walked, each parent chain's custodian publishes a final-link declaration — the parent chain's founding digest, the claimed final link's digest, that link's window number, and the checkpoint at which the parent stopped, with the plain statement that no further link was walked under that chain's name after it. The declaration is published with a digest before the bridge walk, challengeable before it and read-only after, under the same publication discipline as T-627's merger publication. A bridge link whose parent declarations are missing is not merely holed, it is unproposed: the bridge has no ending to prove, and the merger does not reach the checkpoint for a vote of its own challenge window.

The second rule is the leaf-check rule: a verifier proves finality by checking that nothing follows the claimed final link. The claimed final link's digest must resolve to a walked link in its parent chain, and no link in that chain may carry a predecessor digest equal to the claimed final link's digest. A link with a successor is an interior link, whatever the declaration says, and a bridge naming it as final is a premature bridge, not a merger. The leaf-check also fixes the idle-chain question: a parent that stopped walking long before the merger is still final, provided no successor exists — finality is the absence of a next link, not recency, and a gap between the final link's window and the bridge checkpoint is admissible so long as no window after the final link's window is receipted under the parent's name. An after-window receipted under the parent's name after the declared ending is itself a successor by another name, and it fails the leaf-check the same way.

The third rule is the attestation-is-a-claim rule: a custodian's declaration, even from a disinterested custodian under T-622, never substitutes for the leaf-check. Attestation answers who says the link is final; the leaf-check answers whether anything follows it, and only the second is a verification. A bridge that passes on declarations alone, without the leaf-check run and logged, files as Attested-Only: CLAIMED finality, never VERIFIED, and the merged chain built on it carries that grade on every link that walks through the bridge until the leaf-check is run. This keeps T-627's bridge-hole category honest — a missing ending is a hole, a premature ending is a false ending, and an unchecked ending is an ungraded ending, three different filings, not one.

The fourth rule is the one-sided-bridge rule: both parents' declarations are required, not one. A bridge carrying one parent's declaration and the other's mere digest files as a One-Sided Bridge: holed until the second declaration is published and leaf-checked, or the merger is withdrawn. One-sidedness is a hole, not a block — the missing declaration can still arrive before the bridge is walked — but a bridge walked one-sided is a walked link with an unproven ending, and it is re-filed as Bridge-Holed under T-627 the moment the walk is discovered, with the merged chain's links after the bridge held to the same cure.

The fifth rule is the re-bridge rule: a premature bridge is void, not curable by amendment. The merger is re-proposed from the true final link — the link the leaf-check actually ends at — with fresh declarations and a fresh bridge link; the old bridge link stays in the record as evidence of the false ending, never edited out under T-622's no-edit discipline. Whether the merged chain's founding draw under T-623 must also be re-drawn for the re-proposal, or whether the original founding draw survives a void bridge, is left open below — a void bridge voids the merger, but the founding draw was drawn for a chain that never validly began, and that distinction is not settled here.

A chain whose claimed final link resolves to no walked link at all files as a Forged-Bridge Chain: blocked, not merely holed — there is no ending to cure, only a fabrication to record. A chain whose bridge passes on declarations without a logged leaf-check files as an Attested-Only Chain: CLAIMED finality, carried as a grade on every downstream link until the check is run.
