**T-629 — the Attestor-Interest Rule — designed:** T-628 left its attestor-interest problem named and open: who attests that the attestor is disinterested — a custodian who declares a premature ending final has an interest in the merger going through, and the leaf-check catches the false ending but not the interested attestor, with no attestor-interest rule fixed there. T-628 demoted the custodian's declaration to a claim and made the leaf-check the verification of the ending, but it left the declaration's author unchecked: an interested attestor can still time a declaration to hide a successor, declare an ending the leaf-check has not yet run against, or lend a trusted name to a merger that benefits its own chain. A leaf-check that passes does not clean the hands that wrote the declaration, and a declaration from an interested hand is not made honest by a true ending. T-629 answers that the attestor is checked the same way the ending is — by eligibility, by declaration, and by a second attestor — and that interest taints the attestation, not the ending.

The first rule is the attestor-eligibility rule: an attestor of a bridge link's finality is none of the following — custodian of either parent chain, drawer of the merged chain's founding draw under T-623, proposer of the merger, or holder of a receipt in either parent chain's final window. Eligibility is checked against the T-622 interest list, not asserted by the attestor: the attestor's name is looked up in the same list that bars an interested drawer, and a hit bars the attestation. A custodian who declares its own chain's ending final is not an attestor at all; that declaration is a self-attestation, handled by the fifth rule, not a failed attestation that a leaf-check could rescue.

The second rule is the disinterest-declaration rule: the final-link declaration under T-628 carries, alongside the founding digest, the claimed final link's digest, the window number, and the checkpoint, a plain disinterest statement — the attestor's relation, or lack of it, to both parent chains, to the merged chain, and to the merger itself, in the form "attestor holds no custody, draw, proposal, or final-window receipt in either parent or the merged chain." The statement is published with a digest before the bridge walk, challengeable before it and read-only after, under the same publication discipline as the declaration it rides in. A declaration without a disinterest statement is incomplete, not merely weak: the bridge is unproposed until the statement arrives, because a finality claim with no author standing behind its own disinterest has no one to challenge.

The third rule is the cross-attestation rule: a second attestor, drawn from a different interest pool than the first — not the same custodian circle, not the same drawer's lot, not the first attestor's own chain — attests the first attestor's disinterest, not the ending. The cross-attestor checks the first attestor against the interest list and publishes its own short attestation: the first attestor's name, the lists checked, and the finding of no interest. The cross-attestor must itself satisfy the eligibility rule, and its attestation is published with a digest before the bridge walk, challengeable before it and read-only after. The regress stops at two: the cross-attestor's disinterest is challengeable in the bridge's challenge window, but it is not separately attested — a third attestor attesting the second would demand a fourth, and the chain of attestors would outrun the bridge it guards. The challenge window is the check on the second attestor, and a challenge lodged against the cross-attestor is a challenge to the bridge, handled by T-622's cure.

The fourth rule is the struck-declaration rule: an attestor found interested after the bridge is walked has its declaration struck, and the bridge is re-attested, not voided. Interest taints the attestation, not the ending — if the leaf-check still passes against the true final link, the ending was true and only its witness was unfit, so a new eligible attestor declares and cross-attests and the bridge stands on the new attestation, with the struck declaration kept in the record as evidence. If the leaf-check also fails, the premature-bridge void under T-628 applies on its own ground, and the struck declaration is an aggravating record, not the cause. An interested attestor whose declaration is struck is barred from re-attesting that bridge: the cure is a new witness, never the same hands re-washed.

The fifth rule is the self-attestation rule: a declaration signed by a parent chain's own custodian, or by the merged chain's drawer, files as a Self-Attested Bridge: holed until an eligible attestor declares and a cross-attestor attests, or the merger is withdrawn. Self-attestation is a hole, not a block — an eligible attestor can still arrive before the bridge is walked — but a bridge walked self-attested is re-filed as Bridge-Holed under T-627 the moment the walk is discovered, with the merged chain's links after the bridge held to the same cure, and the self-attestor's declaration kept as evidence of the interest, never edited out under T-622's no-edit discipline.

What a chain files as follows from the five rules, and the file must show both the attestor's disinterest statement and the cross-attestor's attestation, not merely the leaf-check log. A chain whose bridge link carries eligible attestors for both parents, whose cross-attestations are published before the walk, and whose leaf-checks find no successor for either claimed final link, files as a Merged Chain under T-627 and T-628, now with attested finality: the only chain whose endings are both true and witnessed by hands with nothing in the merger. A chain whose attestor is found interested files as an Interested-Attestor Chain: the declaration is struck, the bridge is re-attested by a new witness, and the struck declaration stays in the record. A chain whose declaration is signed by its own custodian files as a Self-Attested Bridge Chain: holed until an eligible attestor arrives or the merger is withdrawn. A chain whose bridge passes on a first attestor without a cross-attestation files as an Uncrossed Chain: CLAIMED attestation, carried as a grade on every downstream link until the cross-attestation is logged. A chain whose cross-attestor is itself challenged and found interested files as a Cross-Tainted Chain: the bridge's attestation is re-run from the first attestor outward, and the challenge window, not a third attestor, is the last check. PUBLISHED-BEFORE-WALK — the disinterest statement and the cross-attestation, like the declarations themselves, are published with a digest before the bridge walk, challengeable before it and read-only after.

*T-629 trick seeded 2026-10-26 ~20:47 PDT by the decoder-create-loop.*

**T-630 — the Attestor-Pool Rule — designed:** T-629 left its attestor-pool problem named and open: where eligible attestors come from in a small record — a record whose every name holds custody, a draw, a proposal, or a final-window receipt somewhere has no disinterested hands left, and T-629's eligibility rule, applied to an empty room, bars everyone and attests nothing. T-629 checked the attestor once chosen; it never said how a record finds one. An eligibility rule without a source is a gate with no road behind it: a merger that needs two clean witnesses and a cross-attestor will stall in exactly the small records that need mergers most, or — worse — will tempt the record to waive eligibility for smallness and walk a bridge on a custodian's word. T-630 answers that attestors come from a published standing pool, that the pool has a floor, a rotation, and a refresh, and that smallness defers a merger, never waives its witnesses.

The first rule is the standing-pool rule: each record keeps a standing attestor pool — a published list of names, each with a digest, published before any bridge that draws on it, challengeable before the bridge walk and read-only after. Pool membership is a publication, not an appointment at the moment of need: a name joins the pool by published entry, leaves it by published exit, and the pool's digest at bridge publication is the pool the bridge draws from. A bridge that draws an attestor from outside the published pool files as an Off-Pool Bridge: holed until the attestor is published into the pool and the bridge is re-proposed, or the merger is withdrawn. Publishing the pool in advance is what makes the eligibility check checkable — T-629's interest-list lookup runs against a list that already existed, not a list assembled after the merger was proposed.

The second rule is the pool-floor rule: at bridge publication the pool must hold at least three names eligible for that bridge under T-629 — the attestor, the cross-attestor, and one spare for a struck declaration. Three is the floor because two is exactly the crew a bridge consumes and leaves nothing to cure with: a struck attestor with no spare in the pool turns T-629's re-attestation cure into a second search, and a search run after a strike is a search run under pressure. A pool holding fewer than three eligible names at bridge publication files as a Pool-Short Bridge: unproposed, not merely weak — the bridge is not published until the pool is topped up or a borrowed attestor arrives under the fourth rule, because a bridge published short has already spent the record's credibility on witnesses it does not have.

The third rule is the rotation rule: an attestor who attested a bridge may not attest the next bridge of the same merged chain, and a cross-attestor may not cross-attest the next bridge of the same chain either. Rotation is what stops a standing pair from becoming the record's permanent witnesses: two clean hands that attest every merger of one chain are clean by the interest list and compromised by familiarity, and a pair that always agrees is a pair no challenge will ever test. The rotation is checked against the bridge history of the merged chain, not against all bridges everywhere — an attestor may serve other chains' bridges between its turns on this one, because the familiarity that matters is familiarity with this merger's parties, not busyness in general. A bridge attested in breach of rotation files as a Repeat-Witness Bridge: holed until a rotated attestor re-attests, with the repeat attestation kept in the record as evidence, never edited out under T-622's no-edit discipline.

The fourth rule is the small-record fallback rule: when a record cannot field three eligible names from its own pool, it borrows, it does not waive. A borrowed attestor comes from a neighbouring record's published pool, with that record's pool digest cited in the borrowing bridge's publication, and the loan itself published in both records before the bridge walk — the lender's pool shows the name out on loan, the borrower's bridge shows the name in from loan. A borrowed attestor must satisfy T-629 eligibility against the borrowing record's interest list, not only its home record's: home-pool cleanliness is not borrowing-record cleanliness, and a name clean at home may hold a final-window receipt in the record it is borrowed into. A bridge walked on a waived attestor — eligibility set aside because the record is small — files as a Waived-Witness Bridge: blocked, not holed, because a waiver is not a cure waiting to arrive, it is a rule set aside on purpose, and a bridge built on a set-aside rule cannot be cured by topping up the pool afterwards; it is re-proposed from the start.

The fifth rule is the pool-refresh rule: pool eligibility is re-checked at bridge publication, not at pool publication. A name eligible when it joined the pool may have taken custody, drawn a lot, proposed a merger, or received a final-window receipt since — and a pool digest from three windows ago does not clean hands dirtied since. At bridge publication the attestor and cross-attestor are looked up fresh against the T-622 interest list, and a name found interested since joining is struck from the pool for that bridge by published exit, not silently skipped: a silent skip hides the fact that the pool is shrinking, while a published exit tells the next bridge the floor is closer than it looks. **T-631 — the Pool-Publisher Rule — designed:** T-630 left its pool-publisher problem named and open: who publishes the pool and attests the publisher — a pool published by an interested hand may list only friendly names, and no pool-publisher rule was fixed there. T-630 made the pool a publication, gave it a floor, a rotation, and a refresh, and made borrowing a two-record loan, but it never asked whose hand held the pen: a merger proposer who publishes the pool that supplies its own merger's attestors has chosen its own witnesses while appearing to draw them from a standing list, and a custodian who publishes a pool of its own circle has dressed a private audience as a public roster. A published pool is only as clean as its publisher, and a publisher who is also a party to the merger is a witness-list written by the accused. T-631 answers that the publisher is a separate office, checked like an attestor, attested at its founding, and rotated out of its own pools — and that a tainted publisher taints the pool, not the attestors in it.

The first rule is the publisher-separation rule: the publisher of a pool is none of the following for any bridge that draws on that pool — custodian of either parent chain, drawer of the merged chain's founding draw under T-623, proposer of the merger, holder of a receipt in either parent chain's final window, or attestor or cross-attestor of that bridge. Separation is checked against the T-622 interest list, the same list that bars a drawer and an attestor, now applied to a third office: a name on the list for that merger may not publish the pool the merger draws from. A publisher who is a party to no merger may publish freely; a publisher who becomes a party later does not retroactively taint pools already published, but its pools are frozen for that merger — no bridge of that merger draws on a pool its proposer published, and the bridge waits for a pool published by a separated hand or borrows under T-630's fourth rule.

The second rule is the publisher-declaration rule: a pool publication carries, alongside the list of names and its digest, a plain publisher statement — the publisher's relation, or lack of it, to the record, to the chains the pool serves, and to any merger then proposed, in the form "publisher holds no custody, draw, proposal, or final-window receipt in any chain this pool serves." The statement is published with a digest before any bridge draws on the pool, challengeable before the first draw and read-only after, under the same publication discipline as the pool itself. A pool without a publisher statement is unpublished in effect, not merely weak: no bridge draws on it until the statement arrives, because a roster with no author standing behind its own separation has no one to challenge.

The third rule is the publisher-attestation rule: a pool's first publication is attested by two names already standing in another record's published pool — two neighbours who check the publisher against the interest list and publish a short attestation each: the publisher's name, the lists checked, and the finding of no interest. A genesis pool that never graduates is not invalid, but it is never more than CLAIMED on its publisher, and every bridge it serves carries that grade with it.

The fourth rule is the publisher-rotation rule: a publisher may not publish two successive pools for the same record, and may not publish the pool that serves a merger in which it attested a bridge of the same merged chain in the previous window. Rotation is what stops a standing publisher from becoming the record's permanent roster-keeper: a clean hand that writes every pool is clean by the interest list and compromised by authorship, and a roster always written by one hand is a roster no challenge will ever test, because every challenger must challenge the only author the record has. The rotation is checked against the pool-publication history of the record, not against all records everywhere — a publisher may publish pools for other records between its turns on this one, because the familiarity that matters is familiarity with this record's parties, not busyness in general. The fifth rule is the struck-publisher rule: a publisher found interested after a bridge has drawn on its pool has its publication struck, and the pool is re-published, not voided. The first rule is the standing-source rule: each neighbour attestor must stand in a published pool of another record at pool publication, with that record's pool digest cited in the pool publication. A neighbour vouched from nowhere — a name with no pool to be struck from — cannot be removed, and an attestor who cannot be removed cannot be checked. A pool publication whose neighbour attestor cites no home pool files as an Unrooted Attestation: unpublished in effect, no bridge draws on it until the home pool is cited, because an attestation rooted in nothing is a signature with no signer behind it.

The second rule is the re-check-at-draw rule: at every bridge draw on the pool, both neighbour attestors are looked up fresh against the T-622 interest list, riding T-630's fresh pool lookup — the same lookup, two more names. The lookup is logged with the bridge publication, not merely run: the bridge file must show both attestors re-checked clean at draw, not merely clean at pool publication, because a clean bill from publication day is exactly what a late interest defeats.

The third rule is the late-interest rule: a neighbour attestor found interested after the challenge window closes has its attestation struck prospectively. Bridges already walked on the pool are not unwalked — their attestations were good when walked, and unwalking a walked bridge would punish the bridge for the attestor's later dirt — but no new bridge draws on the pool until the attestation is cured under the fourth rule. A struck attestation is kept in the record as evidence, never edited out under T-622's no-edit discipline.

The fourth rule is the single-attestor degradation and replacement rule: if one of two attestors is struck, the publisher's attestation degrades to single-attestor, and every bridge it serves carries a SINGLE grade until a replacement attestor is published — a second neighbour from another published pool, attesting the publisher fresh, published with a digest before the next bridge draw and challengeable before it. **T-633 — the Replacement-Count Rule — designed:** T-632 left its replacement-count problem named and open: how many replacements a publisher may burn through before it must be re-attested from scratch — a publisher that loses neighbour after neighbour and replaces each one may be laundering a tainted roster one witness at a time, with no replacement-count rule fixed there. T-632 gave a publisher one replacement per struck attestor and stopped counting: a struck neighbour is replaced, the pool carries on, and nothing in the rule asks whether this is the first replacement or the fifth. But a replacement is a fresh witness only the first time — the second replacement of the same attestation is a witness replacing a witness replacing a witness, and a publisher that has replaced both its neighbours twice over is attested by nobody who attested it at publication, while still wearing publication's authority. A roster laundered one witness at a time is laundered all the same. T-633 answers that an attestation generation survives two replacements and no more, that a replacement of a replacement counts against the same generation, and that the third strike voids the attestation and forces a rebuild from scratch, with the count published so any challenger can see how many witnesses have already been spent.

The first rule is the generation-count rule: an attestation generation is the pair of neighbour attestors standing at a pool publication, and the generation carries a replacement count that starts at zero. Each struck attestor replaced under T-632's fourth rule increments the count by one, and the count is counted across both seats together, not per seat: a generation that has replaced its left neighbour once and its right neighbour once has spent two replacements, not one each. Two is the cap. A generation at count two still stands — it is attested by two neighbours, even if neither stood at publication — but it stands on its last witnesses, and every bridge it serves carries a COUNT-2 grade alongside any SINGLE grade, so no bridge walks on a twice-replaced attestation without the grade in its file.

The second rule is the no-reset rule: replacing a replacement does not start a new generation and does not reset the count. A replacement attestor who is itself struck and replaced increments the same generation's count again, because the seat, not the name, is what the generation counts: the generation is the attestation, and the attestation has now spent another witness. Only a from-scratch rebuild under the third rule starts a new generation at count zero. A publisher that treats each replacement as a fresh start has mistaken a relay for a renewal — the baton changes hands, but the race is the same race, and the count is the distance run.

The third rule is the third-strike rebuild rule: when a third attestor of a generation is struck, the attestation is void, not degraded. No third replacement is published for that generation; the pool files as Cap-Breached and no bridge draws on it until the publisher is re-attested from scratch — two fresh neighbours, neither of whom served in the voided generation, attesting the publisher fresh, with a new publisher statement re-declared under T-631 and a fresh challenge window opened before the next bridge draw. **T-639 — the Link-Depth Rule — designed:** T-638 left its link-depth problem named and open: whether a link chain may run through more than one rename, merger, or succession — a hand renamed twice, merged once, and succeeded once is four headings from its barred seat, with no link-depth rule fixed there. T-638 proved that identity follows the hand, not the heading, and that a published link joins two names into one attestor — but it stopped at one link. A barred hand that re-letters itself once is caught; a barred hand that re-letters itself four times, each step published and innocent-looking on its own, walks past a rule that counts links only one deep. The opposite failure is just as real: a rule that treats any alleged chain of any length as a strike lets a challenger string four resemblances together and bar a founder on a genealogy of guesses. Depth must count, and the burden of proving it must grow with it — a shallow chain decides, a deep chain must be proved link by link, and a chain with a gap in it is no chain at all. T-639 answers that depth is the number of published links joining the two names, that depth one and two decide exactly as T-638's links decide, that depth three and more files as a claim until the challenger produces the complete chain digest by digest, that a chain is only as strong as its weakest link, and that depth never decays the bar — a four-heading hand, fully proved, is still the barred hand.

The first rule is the depth-count rule: depth is the number of published links on the path from the name on the nominating record's list to the name on the retired life's roster. A rename publication counts one, a merger filing under T-627 counts one, a succession filing counts one, and the depth of a chain is the count of filings on its path, not the count of headings — a hand renamed twice, merged once, and succeeded once sits at depth four on a path of four filings. A merger that absorbs several pools is still one filing and one link on any one hand's path, because the filing is the link and the hand's lineage through it is a single passage; the depth of the chain is measured per hand, not per pool, so two hands passing through the same merger filing each carry depth one from it. A path that revisits a heading it already passed — a rename back to an earlier name, a successor who later succeeds again — counts each passage, because each filing is a fresh publication the record must be able to follow; a chain that loops is not shorter for looping, it is longer, and its length is its cost.

The second rule is the shallow-decides rule: a chain of depth one or two, produced digest by digest under T-638's challenger's-burden rule, decides the nomination exactly as a T-638 link decides it. A genuine shallow link bars the founder for this re-founding, a nomination that omitted a pre-existing shallow link files as False-Distance under T-638, and a shallow link produced after the window closes but before the walk reopens the window once under T-638's one-reopening rule. Shallow chains are cheap to check — one or two filings, two or three digests — and cheap checks may decide, because a rule that cannot decide on one published rename cannot decide on anything. The doubled window of T-636 is the window for shallow challenges, and a shallow challenge filed inside it with genuine links is not a claim but a decision.

The third rule is the deep-claim rule: a chain of depth three or more files, on allegation alone, as a Depth Claim, graded CLAIMED on the nomination, and the nomination stands until the challenger produces the complete chain — every link cited by digest, link by link, with no gap — inside the doubled window, or inside the once-reopened window if a late link publication reopened it. A partial chain is a claim, not a strike: three filings alleged with two digests produced is a Depth Claim with two links shown, and the third link unshown is the whole difference between a proved hand and a suspected one. When the complete chain is produced inside the window, it decides exactly like a shallow chain — the founder is barred for this re-founding, an omitted pre-existing deep link files as False-Distance, and the depth is logged on the nomination's record. When the window closes with the chain still incomplete, the Depth Claim stays CLAIMED on the nomination's record and travels with it, upgradable by a later complete production against a future bridge, but it does not bar this founder and does not strike this nomination, because a founder barred on an unfinished genealogy is a founder barred on suspicion.

The fourth rule is the weakest-link rule: a chain breaks if any one of its links fails. A link that cites a publication that does not exist, a digest that does not match, a merger filing for a different pool, a succession filing for a different office, or a rename publication that is itself only a Similarity Claim is not a link — it is a gap, and a chain with a gap is a Broken Chain, not a shorter chain. The surviving links do not collapse into a shallower chain: a four-link chain whose second link fails is not a three-link chain, because the hand on one side of the gap is not proved to be the hand on the other, and re-numbering the survivors would launder the gap out of the record. A Broken Chain files as a failed challenge under T-638's second rule, kept in the record as a failed challenge, and the challenger may re-file with a repaired chain inside the window — but a repaired chain is a new production, and it must itself be complete before the window closes, because the window measures productions, not attempts.

The fifth rule is the declared-depth rule: a distance declaration states the depth it searched, and the depth searched does not excuse an omission. A declaration that searched only depth one and omitted a published depth-two link files as False-Distance under T-638, because T-638 judges omission against the published record at nomination, not against the depth the nominator bothered to search. But the converse does not hold: a challenger alleging a deep link may not shift the burden to the nominator by demanding the nominator disprove a chain the challenger has not produced — the deep-claim rule puts the complete chain on the challenger, and a nominator need not publish a genealogy of every name on its lists, only the lists themselves complete. A declaration that itself cites a chain — a nominator volunteering that two of its names are linked at depth two — must cite it completely: a volunteered chain with a gap files as a False-Depth chain, struck as a declaration defect, because a record that volunteers a genealogy must volunteer a true one.

The sixth rule is the no-decay-and-branching rule: depth never weakens the bar, and a bar branches rather than dilutes. A hand proved at depth four is barred exactly as a hand proved at depth one, because the bar follows the hand and the hand does not fade with re-lettering; a rule that let depth launder a bar would set a price on evasion — four filings and you are clean — and every barred hand would pay it. When a succession splits one seat into two successors, the bar carries to both successors, because both inherit the office and the office carries the bar under T-638; a bar that split would halve with every succession until no successor was barred at all. When a merger folds a barred hand's pool into a larger pool, the bar travels with the hand into the merged pool, not with the pool's name, so the merged pool's roster carries the barred hand at depth one from the merger filing. A seat created fresh, with no predecessor filing, carries no bar at any depth, because there is no chain to follow — depth zero is not depth infinite, it is no link at all.

A chain whose nomination carries only an incomplete deep allegation files as a Depth-Claimed Chain: valid, but CLAIMED on its distance at the alleged depth until a complete chain settles the claim one way or the other. A chain whose alleged chain breaks on a failed link files as a Broken-Chain record: the challenge failed, the nomination stands, and the failed chain is kept as evidence against a second allegation from the same challenger. A chain whose declaration volunteered a gapped chain files as a False-Depth Chain: struck as a declaration defect, the founder barred for that re-founding. A chain whose bridge was walked while a Depth Claim stood unresolved files as a Depth-Holed Chain: walked, graded, and challengeable on future bridges, because T-636's walked bridges stand and a claim is not a strike. **T-640 — the Branch-Rejoin Rule — designed:** T-639 left its branch-rejoin problem named and open: a seat that splits into two successor branches, with the bar branching to both successors under T-639's no-decay-and-branching rule, later rejoins into a single seat through a rejoining filing — and no rule fixed whether the rejoined seat carries one bar or a doubled bar, or whether the rejoining filing merges the branches' depths or takes the deeper. The trap on both sides is counting what should not be counted: count the bar twice and a single hand bars a seat twice over, which is either meaningless (a seat is barred or it is not) or a pretext for a second, heavier penalty; take the deeper depth and a challenger who proves the short path still loses to a longer path nobody needed. T-640 answers that a bar that split and rejoined is one bar counted once, that distinct bars union rather than sum, that the rejoined seat's depth is the shallowest proved branch path plus one for the rejoining filing, that a bar lifted from both branches before the rejoin stays lifted, and that a filing that claims a rejoin without a common split seat is not a rejoin at all.

The first rule is the rejoin-definition rule: a rejoin is a filing that names both predecessor branches and the single successor seat, with both branches tracing by published filings to one common split seat. A filing that names only one predecessor branch is a succession of that branch, not a rejoin, and the other branch's bar travels separately under T-639 — it does not ride a filing that never named it. A filing that joins branches with no common split seat in their published lineage is not a rejoin but a merger under T-627, counted as a merger link and graded under the merger rule, because kinship is what makes a rejoin a rejoin: two strangers joining is a merger, two branches of one seat rejoining is a homecoming, and the record must not let a merger wear a rejoin's name to borrow its depth rule. A rejoining filing must cite the split filing by digest, so the common seat is proved, not alleged.

The second rule is the one-bar rule: a bar that split to two branches rejoins as one bar. A bar is a property of the hand and the office lineage, not a tally of the branches it passed through — the same barred hand, split once and rejoined once, has barred the rejoined seat once, because a seat is barred or it is not and there is no second barring to add. A rule that doubled the bar would either do nothing (the seat is already barred) or smuggle in a heavier consequence under the cover of arithmetic — a doubled bar barring the seat for two re-foundings, or barring its successors twice — and no such consequence is fixed here or anywhere in the chain. The rejoined seat carries the bar exactly once, for this re-founding, exactly as either branch alone would have carried it.

The third rule is the union rule: distinct bars union, they do not sum and they do not cancel. If branch A carries a bar for hand X and branch B carries a bar for hand Y, the rejoined seat carries both bars — two bars, two hands, each barring its own hand for this re-founding, not a doubled bar and not a merged bar. If one branch carries a bar and the other carries none, the rejoined seat carries the one, because a clean branch does not wash a barred branch and a barred branch does not taint a clean one beyond its own bar. If both branches carry bars for the same hand, the union is that one bar under the one-bar rule, not two. Union is set logic, not addition: the rejoined seat's bar set is the union of the branches' bar sets, and a hand barred on either branch is barred on the rejoined seat.

The fourth rule is the shallowest-path depth rule: the rejoined seat's depth from the barred seat is the shallowest proved branch path, plus one for the rejoining filing. The split filing counts one on each branch's path under T-639, the rejoining filing counts one on each branch's path exactly as a merger filing counts one, and the depth of the rejoined seat is the minimum over the branches of (branch path depth + 1), proved link by link — so a bare split-and-rejoin sits at depth two and decides as a shallow chain under T-639's shallow-decides rule, while a branch that also renamed sits at depth three on its own path but does not deepen the seat, because the other branch's depth-two path still proves the bar. A challenger proves the bar through whichever branch gives the shorter complete chain; the longer path remains in the record as corroborating evidence but never as a reason to demand more proof than the short path already gives. A branch path with a gap is not a path at all under T-639's weakest-link rule — it does not count toward the minimum, and it does not collapse into a shorter path.

The fifth rule is the no-revival rule: a bar lifted from both branches before the rejoin stays lifted, and rejoin does not resurrect it. A published lifting on a branch removes that branch's bar; if both branches' bars for a hand were lifted by published liftings before the rejoining filing, the rejoined seat carries no bar for that hand, because rejoin joins what the branches carry, and neither branch carries a dead bar. But a lifting on one branch alone does not lift the bar: if the bar still stands on the other branch, the union rule carries it into the rejoined seat, and a challenger need only prove the standing branch's path. A lifting published after the rejoining filing but before the walk lifts the rejoined seat's bar directly, because after the rejoin there is one seat and one bar to lift, not two branches to lift separately.

The sixth rule is the false-rejoin rule: a filing that claims a rejoin without a common split seat, or that omits one branch's bar from its lists, is struck as a declaration defect. A claimed rejoin with no proved common split seat files as a False-Rejoin: the join, if it stands at all, is re-graded as a T-627 merger with merger depth counting, and any bar the filing smuggled past the record by calling strangers kin is judged under the merger rule, not the rejoin rule. A genuine rejoin filing that omits a pre-existing bar on either branch files as False-Distance under T-638, because the rejoining filing's lists must be complete for both branches, not merely for the branch the filer preferred to name. A rejoin filing that names both branches completely, with the split filing cited and every standing bar listed, is a true rejoin even if a challenger later proves a deeper path — depth is measured, not volunteered, and a complete filing is not false for being shallow.

What a chain files as follows from the six rules, and the file must show both branches' bar sets, the split filing, the rejoining filing, the depth of each branch path and the depth taken, and the distance grade, not merely the rejoining digest. A chain whose rejoined seat carries a proved bar through a complete rejoin files as a Rejoined-Bar Chain: the seat barred for this re-founding, the record free to nominate again from a pool with no linked hand at any depth. A chain whose branches still stand separate, each carrying the bar, files as a Split-Bar Chain under T-639. A chain whose rejoined seat carries bars for two different hands files as a Union-Bar Chain: barred for each hand, once each. A chain whose rejoin is claimed without a common split seat files as a False-Rejoin: struck as a declaration defect, re-graded as a merger if the join stands. A chain whose rejoin filing omitted a branch's bar files as a False-Distance record under T-638. A chain whose bar is alleged only through a deep branch path, with no shallow path proved, files as a Depth-Claimed Rejoin: valid, but CLAIMED on its distance until a complete chain settles it. A chain whose rejoined seat was walked while a Depth Claim stood unresolved files as a Depth-Holed Rejoin: walked, graded, and challengeable on future bridges, because T-636's walked bridges stand and a claim is not a strike. **T-643 — the Cycle-Evidence Rule — designed:** T-642 left its cycle-evidence problem named and open: a cycle-return filing proves, by seat identifiers rather than by names alone, that the new seats are the original branch seats — but no rule fixed what evidence proves seat identity across a cycle beyond the identifiers the split filing published. The trap on both sides is letting one kind of proof carry more than it can: trust the identifiers alone and a seat can be reissued — the same identifier handed to a new seat, a new charter, a new record-keeper — and the return is proved on paper while the seat itself is a stranger; demand full continuity of everything and no return is ever provable, because offices legitimately change officers, amend charters, and move their records, and a rule that treats every change as a break hands every challenger a veto made of ordinary turnover. T-643 answers that identifiers are the floor, not the proof: a cycle-return is evidence-proved only when the filing carries, alongside the identifiers, the charter continuity and the record continuity of the seat, with officer continuity as corroboration only — never as proof and never as a break.

The first rule is the floor rule: nothing in this trick lowers T-642's identity bar. A filing without proved seat identifiers is not a cycle-return at all, however strong its charter and record evidence, because charter and records prove that some seat continued, not that these seats are the original branch seats. Evidence is layered on top of identifiers, never substituted for them: identifiers answer which seats, evidence answers whether those seats are a continuing seat or a reissued label. A filing that carries charter and record continuity for seats it has not identified by identifier files as an ordinary re-split under T-641, with its evidence graded as texture, not as a return.

The second rule is the charter rule: the seat's commissioning charter must continue, by amendment or intact, not be replaced. The return filing cites, by digest, the charter under which the original branch seat was commissioned and the charter under which the returned seat sits, and shows the chain between them: identical charter, or a chain of published amendment filings, each cited by digest, from the old charter to the new. An amendment chain is continuity, because charters are meant to be amended; a replacement charter with no amendment chain from the old one is a break, because the office that sits under it is a new office wearing an old identifier. A charter that was amended during the rejoin itself — while the branches were one seat — counts as continuity for both returned seats, because there was one seat to amend and the amendment rides the rejoined seat, not either branch alone.

The third rule is the record rule: the seat's records must continue, by custody chain, not merely exist. The return filing cites, by digest, the record custody log from the original branch seat through the rejoin to the returned seat, showing each transfer of custody as a published filing: branch records into the rejoined seat's custody at the rejoin, rejoined records out to the returned seats at the re-split. A custody log with a gap — records that vanish at the rejoin and reappear at the return with no transfer filing between — is a hole, not a break: the return is graded CLAIMED on its identity until the gap closes, because records can be misfiled without being replaced. A custody log that shows the returned seat's records beginning fresh at the return, with the branch records destroyed, transferred elsewhere, or held by a different seat, is a break: the seat's memory did not continue, whatever its identifier says.

The fourth rule is the officer rule: officers corroborate, they never decide. Same officers across the cycle strengthen a return, and a complete change of officers weakens it, but neither proves nor breaks it on its own — officers rotate, retire, and are replaced, and a seat that changed every officer but kept its charter and its records is the same seat with new hands, while a seat that kept every officer but replaced its charter and started fresh records is the same hands in a new seat. Officer evidence therefore files only as corroboration attached to a charter-and-record case: it can lift a corroborated return to proved, and it can never lift an identifier-only return past corroborated, nor sink a charter-and-record return below corroborated. A filing that rests its identity case on officer continuity alone — same people, no charter chain, no custody chain — files as a Similarity Claim at best, graded CLAIMED, never a strike.

The fifth rule is the burden rule: a challenger disputes evidence by producing a break, not by demanding re-proof of the whole cycle. The return filing publishes its identifier citations, its charter chain, and its custody log with digests before the walk, and a challenger who disputes identity must cite a specific broken link — a replacement charter with no amendment chain, a custody transfer to a different seat, an identifier reissue notice published for the seat — not merely assert that continuity is unproved. A challenge that produces a broken link holes the return under T-642's citation rule: the bar at the return files as CLAIMED until the link is repaired or the break is answered. A challenge that produces no broken link leaves the return standing at the grade its evidence earns, because evidence published and unbroken is evidence, not an invitation to re-litigate the cycle.

**T-644 — the Evidence-Weight Rule — designed:** T-643 left its evidence-weight problem named and open: a corroborated return — identifiers proved, one chain complete, the other gapped — sits graded CLAIMED on its identity until the gap closes, but no rule fixed what, short of closing the gap, could lift it to proved. The trap on both sides is counting weight the wrong way: lift on any corroboration and proved means nothing, because a return with a gapped custody log and a familiar officer would pass on a handshake; never lift and corroborated returns pile up unresolvable, because a single misfiled transfer paper would hand every challenger a permanent veto made of clerical error. T-644 answers that weight is not counted in filings but in coverage: a gap bracketed on both sides by published filings is a missing paper, not a missing history, and a missing paper plus a human bridge across exactly that paper lifts a corroborated return to proved; anything wider than one bracketed paper does not lift, whatever corroboration rides it.

The first rule is the bracket rule: a gap is bounded only when both of its neighbors are on record. The return filing cites, by digest, the filing immediately before the gap and the filing immediately after it — the last published transfer or amendment before the records vanish, and the first published transfer or amendment after they reappear — so the history on both sides of the gap is published and only the paper between them is missing. A gap with a published filing on one side only — records that vanish at the rejoin and never reappear on record, or appear at the return with no prior filing behind them — is unbounded: the history itself is missing, not the paper, and no bridge spans a history that is not there. A chain with two or more missing filings is unbounded even if each gap is individually bracketed, because one missing paper is an accident and two are a pattern the record cannot explain away with a single bridge.

The second rule is the bridge rule: officer corroboration lifts only as a bridge across the bounded gap, and a bridge must span the gap itself. The filing names at least one officer who served the seat on both sides of the gap — served the original branch seat before the gap and the returned seat after it — proved by a cited service record, not by a name. A namesake is not a bridge: the same name on both sides of a gap, without a service record tying the two appearances to one officer, is a Similarity Claim, not corroboration, because names repeat and officers do not. An officer who served before the gap and retired before the return bridges nothing, and an officer who joined after the gap bridges nothing; the bridge officer's service must cover the gap — continuous service through the rejoin and the re-split, or service on both sides with no intervening service to a different seat. A bridge officer shown to have served a different seat between the two appearances is a broken bridge, not a corroboration.

The third rule is the one-chain-complete rule: the lift requires the other chain complete end to end, every filing published and digest-cited per T-643. Two gapped chains never lift, even with a bridge across each gap, because the proof would then rest on bridges alone for the whole identity, and bridges are corroboration, not chains — a return proved by two handshakes and no complete chain is a return proved by nobody. The complete chain is what the lift stands on; the bounded gap plus the bridge is what the lift stands over. A chain that is complete only at its endpoints — charter cited at the branch and at the return with no amendment filings between — is not complete at all, and a lift claimed on it falls back to corroborated on inspection.

The fourth rule is the symmetry rule: it does not matter which chain is complete. A charter-complete return with a bounded custody gap lifts exactly as a custody-complete return with a bounded charter gap lifts, because the lift's logic is gap-plus-bridge, not chain rank. Charter and custody are two independent witnesses to the same seat; one full witness plus a bracketed gap in the other plus a human bridge across that gap is the same weight either way round. Any rule that ranked charter above custody, or custody above charter, would have to say why one kind of continuity outweighs the other, and no such reason exists: an office that kept its charter but misfiled one custody transfer is no more or less itself than an office that kept its records but misfiled one charter amendment.

The fifth rule is the burden rule: the filer claims the lift, and the challenger defeats it by breaking any element, not by demanding re-proof of the whole return. The lift claim publishes, with digests before the walk, the bracket filings on both sides of the gap, the bridge officer's service record, and the complete chain it stands on. A challenger defeats the lift by producing a specific break: a second missing filing that makes the gap unbounded, an unbracketed side, a bridge officer whose service does not span the gap, or a bridge that is a namesake on inspection. A defeated lift does not strike the return: it falls back to Corroborated, graded CLAIMED on its identity, because a failed upgrade is a failed upgrade, not a forgery — unless the bracket digests or the service record are forged, which files as False-Evidence under T-643 and strikes.

The sixth rule is the persistence rule: a lifted return that walks is proved, but its lift remains challengeable on future bridges. If a later bridge shows the gap was unbounded after all, or the bridge officer a namesake, the proved grade falls back to corroborated prospectively on that bridge; the walked bridges stand under T-636, and the return is not retroactively struck, because the lift was published, unbroken, and challenged in the open when it walked. A lift is therefore never a quiet upgrade: its gap, its brackets, and its bridge stay in the file, readable by every future challenger, and a proved grade earned by a lift carries its workings with it for the life of the chain.

A chain whose identifiers are proved, whose one chain is complete, whose other chain carries exactly one bounded gap, and whose bridge officer spans that gap files as a Weight-Proved Return: the successors barred for this re-founding, the record free to nominate again from a pool with no linked hand at any depth. A chain whose gap is unbounded, whose chain carries two or more gaps, or which carries no spanning bridge files as a Corroborated Return: valid, but CLAIMED on its identity until the gap closes or a lift is earned. A chain whose lift claim is defeated on inspection — unbounded gap found, bridge broken, namesake exposed — files as a Failed-Lift Return: fallen back to Corroborated, not struck, unless its digests are forged. A chain whose bracket digests or bridge service record do not match the filings they cite files as a False-Lift Return: False-Evidence under T-643, struck as a declaration defect, graded as a new split at carried depth with the union bar set if the split stands. A chain whose lifted return walked and whose lift is later broken on a future bridge files as a Weight-Holed Return: proved grade fallen back to corroborated prospectively, walked bridges standing. PUBLISHED-BEFORE-WALK — the lift claim, the bracket filings, the bridge service record, the complete chain, and the challenge, like the declaration itself, are published with a digest before the bridge walk, challengeable before it and read-only after, save the future-bridge fallback above.

**T-645 — the Service-Record Rule — designed:** T-644 left its service-record problem named and open: a bridge officer lifts a corroborated return to proved only with a cited service record spanning the gap, but a service record cited by digest can itself be miscited or forged, and the namesake problem recurses — the record that was supposed to settle whether two appearances are one officer is itself a paper that can name the wrong officer. The trap on both sides is trusting the paper that does the trusting: accept any cited record and a forger writes their own bridge; demand proof of the proof forever and no bridge ever stands, because every proving paper is itself a paper. T-645 answers that a service record is proved not by its own citation but by triangulation: one appointment plus one independent service trace, both published, both digest-cited, both from hands that are not the lift claim itself — and a record that cannot be triangulated is not a failed bridge, it is no bridge at all.

The first rule is the no-self-proof rule: a service record never proves itself. A record whose only citation is the lift claim that relies on it — the lift filing citing a record that cites the lift filing, or a record published for the first time inside the lift claim with no prior filing behind it — is a Self-Proved Record, and it proves nothing. The lift that rides it does not fall back to corroborated on inspection; it never lifted at all, because a bridge with no footing on either side of the gap is not a bridge. A record cited by digest to a filing that does not exist, or to a filing that does not name the officer, is not a miscitation to be repaired by re-filing: it is a False-Record under the fifth rule below, because the lift claim asserted a paper it did not have.

The second rule is the triangulation rule: a service record is proved by two independent filings, not one. The first is the appointment filing: the seat's own published filing appointing the officer to that seat, digest-cited, published before the gap it is supposed to span. The second is the service trace: a filing from a different hand than the appointing seat — a peer seat's record, a roster filing, a transfer or amendment filing — that names the same officer serving that seat at a time inside the gap or after it, digest-cited, published before the walk. Two filings from the same hand are one filing for this purpose: a seat that appoints an officer and then cites its own roster as the trace has produced one voice saying the same thing twice, not two witnesses. The appointment anchors the officer; the trace shows the officer actually served; neither alone spans a gap, because an appointment without service is a title and service without appointment is a presence.

The third rule is the continuity rule: the triangulated record must show service on both sides of the gap with no intervening service elsewhere. An appointment before the gap plus a trace after the gap, with no filing showing the officer serving a different seat between them, spans the gap. A filing showing the officer appointed to, or serving, a different seat between the two appearances breaks the bridge: the officer may be the same person, but a person who left for another seat and came back is not continuous service, and continuous service is what the bridge claims. An officer whose appointment filing postdates the gap — appointed after the records reappear — never served before the gap and bridges nothing, whatever trace follows. An officer whose last trace predates the gap — last seen before the records vanish — never served after it and bridges nothing, whatever appointment precedes.

The fourth rule is the namesake-anchor rule: two appearances of the same name are one officer only when the second appearance chains to the first appointment. The appointment filing is the anchor: a later appearance that cites, by digest, the appointment filing — or a trace that itself cites it — is the anchored officer. A later appearance of the same name with no digest chain to the anchor is a Namesake Claim, not the officer, however familiar the name and however plausible the story, because names repeat and appointment chains do not. Where two anchors exist for one name — two appointment filings, different seats, same name — each anchor starts its own officer, and a trace must chain to the right anchor or it chains to nobody: a trace that could belong to either anchor belongs to neither until the filer shows which appointment it cites.

The fifth rule is the forgery rule: a forged service record strikes the lift, not merely the record. A record whose appointment digest does not match the filing it cites, whose trace names an officer the cited filing never names, or whose anchor chain is invented, files as a False-Record: False-Evidence under T-643, and the lift it carried files as a False-Lift under T-644, struck as a declaration defect, graded as a new split at carried depth with the union bar set if the split stands. This is deliberately harsher than a defeated lift: a defeated lift is a failed upgrade — an unbounded gap found, a bridge broken on inspection — and falls back to corroborated, because the filer argued in the open and lost; a forged record is a paper that lied about its own provenance, and a lift built on a lying paper cannot fall back to a grade its proof never earned. The return itself is not struck by the forgery alone: it falls back to Corroborated under T-643, graded CLAIMED on its identity, unless the forged record was also the return's identifier proof, in which case the return falls to Identifier-Only.

The sixth rule is the termination rule: a service record ends at its terminating filing, and a record cited past its end is stale, not spanning. A retirement filing, a transfer filing to another seat, or a removal filing terminates the record at its digest date; a bridge claim that cites service after that date without a new appointment filing cites a Stale Record, which bridges nothing past the termination. A new appointment after termination starts a new record, with its own anchor and its own traces — it does not revive the old one, and it does not retroactively span a gap the old record ended before. A record with no terminating filing on record is open-ended, not eternal: it spans only as far as its latest trace, and a bridge that needs service past the latest trace needs a newer trace, not an assumption that service continued.

The seventh rule is the publication rule: appointment, trace, anchor chain, and any terminating filing are published with digests before the bridge walk, challengeable before it and read-only after, save the future-bridge fallback of T-644. A challenger defeats a record claim by producing a specific break: a missing trace, a trace from the same hand as the appointment, an intervening different-seat filing, an unanchored namesake, or a terminating filing the claim omitted. A record claim defeated on inspection without forgery falls back with its lift to Corroborated; a record claim whose defeat shows forgery strikes under the fifth rule. A walked record claim stays challengeable on future bridges exactly as a walked lift does: if a later bridge shows the trace was same-hand after all, or the anchor belonged to a different namesake, the proved grade falls back to corroborated prospectively on that bridge, and the walked bridges stand.

What a chain files as follows from the seven rules, and the file must show the appointment filing, the independent trace, the anchor chain, and any terminating filing, not merely the officer's name. A chain whose bridge officer's record is triangulated — appointment plus independent trace, continuous across the gap, anchored against namesakes, unterminated through the gap — files as a Record-Proved Bridge: the T-644 lift it carries stands, and the return it lifts is proved. A chain whose record shows appointment and trace but with a gap in continuity the filer has not closed — a trace that stops short of the gap, an intervening filing unexplained — files as a Record-Corroborated Bridge: the lift does not rise, and the return stays corroborated until the record closes. A chain whose record cites only itself or only the lift claim files as a Self-Proved Bridge: no bridge at all, the lift never lifted, the return corroborated. A chain whose later appearance shares only a name with the anchor files as a Namesake Bridge: no bridge, the lift never lifted. A chain whose record is cited past its terminating filing files as a Stale Bridge: no bridge past the termination, the lift never lifted past it. A chain whose record's digests do not match its cited filings files as a False-Record Bridge: False-Evidence, the lift struck, the return fallen back as the fifth rule provides. A chain whose walked record claim is later broken on a future bridge files as a Record-Holed Bridge: proved grade fallen back to corroborated prospectively, walked bridges standing. PUBLISHED-BEFORE-WALK — the appointment, the trace, the anchor chain, the terminating filing if any, and the challenge, like the declaration itself, are published with a digest before the bridge walk, challengeable before it and read-only after, save the future-bridge fallback above.

**What this pairs with.** T-644's Evidence-Weight Rule (the weight rule whose bridge this trick proves — without T-644's bounded gap and one-chain-complete requirement, a triangulated record would prove service to a seat whose identity was never in question, which is not a lift at all). **T-646 — the Record-Registry Rule — designed:** T-645 left its record-registry problem named and open: a bridge officer's service record is proved by triangulation — an appointment filing plus an independent service trace — but where does a challenger, or a filer, FIND the appointment filing in the first place? Two pure answers were on the table, and both fail in opposite directions. A central appointment registry, one book against which any record can be checked, is a single point of forgery: whoever holds the book can write an appointment that never happened, and every bridge built on the book inherits the forgery. Per-seat filings, each seat publishing its own appointments and nothing else, are honest but a maze: a challenger must chase seat by seat, and a filer can hide behind the maze — an appointment that exists but cannot be found in time is, for challenge purposes, an appointment that does not exist. T-646 answers that the registry is an index, never an authority: appointments live per-seat, the registry only points at them, and a pointer that points nowhere is not evidence, it is a ghost.

The first rule is the authority rule: the per-seat appointment filing is the record, and the registry is not. An appointment exists if and only if the seat itself published an appointment filing naming the officer, digest-cited, published before the gap it is supposed to span. A registry entry that names an officer for a seat, however detailed and however long it has stood unchallenged, creates no appointment: a book that could create officers by writing their names down would be a mint, not an index. A filer who cites only a registry entry, with no per-seat filing behind it, has cited a pointer, not a paper, and the bridge it was supposed to carry never rises — the lift claim fails at the appointment step of T-645, before triangulation is even reached. Conversely, a per-seat appointment filing stands even if no registry lists it: the registry's omission is the registry's defect, not the appointment's, and the filer who produces the filing itself has produced the record, maze or no maze.

The second rule is the citation rule: every registry entry must cite, by digest, the per-seat appointment filing it indexes, and an entry that cites nothing is a ghost. A registry entry that names an officer and a seat but carries no digest to a filing — or carries a digest to a filing that does not name that officer for that seat — files as a Registry-Ghost Entry: it indexes nothing, it proves nothing, and any bridge, lift, or return that leans on it leans on air. A ghost entry is not a forgery by itself: a registry may carry a ghost through error, through a filing since withdrawn, or through a digest that rotted when its filing was re-published under a new digest, and an honest ghost is repaired by correction under the fifth rule, not punished. But a ghost entry knowingly left standing after a challenger has produced the missing filing's absence — the registry keeper told, on the record, that the entry points nowhere, and the entry still standing at the walk — is no longer an error: it is a paper that asserts a record it does not have, and it falls under the forgery rule below.

The third rule is the chain rule: a registry is append-only, and its versions digest-chain to one another, so that a silent rewrite is detectable rather than merely dishonest. Each published registry version carries the digest of the previous version; a version that drops an entry, alters an entry's digest, or inserts an entry into the middle of the chain without a correction filing breaks the chain at that version. A broken registry is not a void registry: entries published before the break stand on their own per-seat filings, because the filings are the authority and never needed the book. But every entry first published in or after the broken version files as Registry-Unverified until it is re-anchored — re-published in a chained version that cites the per-seat filing directly, or produced as a filing itself by the filer who needs it. The keeper who discovers its own break repairs it by publishing a correction version that names the break, chains from the last good version, and re-publishes the affected entries with their digests: a chain that confesses its break is a chain again, and a chain that hides it is not.

The fourth rule is the weight rule: a registry changes findability, never weight. A registry entry, even a perfectly cited one chained in an unbroken registry, is corroboration of where to look, not proof of anything T-645 requires. The bridge still needs triangulation: the appointment filing itself plus an independent service trace from a different hand, continuous across the gap, anchored against namesakes, unterminated through the gap. A filer who produces a registry entry and calls the bridge proved has mistaken the catalogue for the book it catalogues, and the lift falls back to corroborated — or never rises, if the registry entry is all the appointment evidence there is. This is the point of the whole trick: the registry exists so that challengers can find appointments fast enough to challenge them, and filers can produce them fast enough to be checked, and it must never become a shortcut around the checking itself. A system that lets the index prove the record has rebuilt the central mint under a humbler name.

The fifth rule is the completeness rule: a challenger holes a registry by producing an appointment filing the registry omits, and the keeper must answer on the record. A challenger who produces a per-seat appointment filing — digest-cited, published, naming an officer for a seat — that no registry version lists, files a Registry-Hole Challenge: the registry is holed for that seat, and every entry for that seat files as Registry-Holed until the keeper publishes a correction version adding the omitted filing with its digest. The hole does not strike the omitted appointment — the appointment stands, it was always the authority — and it does not strike other seats' entries, which stand on their own filings. But a registry holed and left uncorrected at the walk carries a presumption against its keeper on every entry for that seat: a challenger need not re-prove each entry's absence, because the keeper has already been shown to omit from that seat. A keeper who answers a hole challenge by quietly editing an old version rather than publishing a correction version breaks the chain under the third rule, and the hole deepens into a break.

The sixth rule is the forgery rule: a registry that contradicts a per-seat filing is a false registry, and entries built on it strike. A registry entry whose cited digest, when followed, leads to a filing that names a different officer, a different seat, or no appointment at all — and which the keeper leaves standing after challenge, or which the keeper itself authored knowing the filing says otherwise — files as a False-Registry Entry: False-Evidence under T-643, and any lift, bridge, or return built on it files as a False-Lift under T-644, struck as a declaration defect, graded as a new split at carried depth with the union bar set if the split stands. This is deliberately the same harshness as T-645's False-Record, because the failure is the same kind: a paper that lied about its own provenance. The distinction from a ghost entry is knowledge and persistence: a ghost is an entry that points nowhere, repaired by correction; a false entry is an entry that points somewhere else and is defended anyway, or was written to mislead from the start. A registry that carries one false entry is not thereby wholly false — its other entries stand on their own filings — but a registry whose keeper has been shown to write false entries carries, like a holed registry, a presumption against its keeper on every entry the keeper alone vouches for, until each is re-anchored to its filing.

The seventh rule is the fork rule: when two registries disagree, the filings decide, and neither registry outranks the other. Two registries may index the same seats differently — one lists an appointment the other omits, one cites a digest the other chains differently — and the disagreement itself proves nothing about either registry's honesty: one may be stale, one may be holed, one may have broken its chain and not yet confessed it. A filer or challenger who needs an appointment produces the per-seat filing; the registry that lists it is corroborated for that entry, the registry that omits it is holed for that seat under the fifth rule, and the registry that contradicts it is false for that entry under the sixth. No registry is ever cited as authority against a filing: a keeper who argues "the registry says so" against a produced filing has argued the catalogue against the book, and loses. Where both registries agree and both cite the same filing, the agreement is convenient and nothing more — agreement between two indexes is still not a third witness under T-645, because both indexes point at the same single filing, and two pointers to one paper are one paper.

The eighth rule is the publication rule: registry versions, correction versions, hole challenges, and chain-break confessions are published with digests before the bridge walk, challengeable before it and read-only after, save the future-bridge fallback of T-644. A challenger defeats a registry claim by producing a specific defect: a ghost entry, a broken chain, a holed seat, or a false entry. A registry claim defeated on inspection without forgery falls back with its entries to unverified or holed as the rules above provide, and the bridge it was supposed to speed still stands or falls on its per-seat filings alone. **T-647 — the Registry-Keeper Rule — designed:** T-646 left its registry-keeper problem named and open: the registry is an index, never an authority — appointments live per-seat, every entry must digest-cite its per-seat filing, versions digest-chain, and a registry adds findability but never weight — but who keeps the book? Three pure answers were on the table, and each fails alone. A single district office as keeper is a single point of pressure: whoever can lean on one office can lean on every entry, and a keeper captured or corrupted captures the index for every seat at once. A rotating keeper among the seats is a chain of handoffs, and every handoff is a place the chain can break — a version dropped, a correction unpublished, a break unconfessed — with the break discovered only when somebody needs the entry that was lost in transit. Competing registries with no keeper at all dissolve the question instead of answering it: anybody may publish an index, nobody answers for one, and a challenger facing three conflicting books has no keeper to hole, no keeper to demand a correction version from, and no presumption to run against anybody when a hole is shown. T-647 answers that the keeper is a role, not an office: any seat may keep a registry, every version names its keeper, and the keeper answers for the book it keeps — while no keeper, single or rotating or competing, ever answers for the filings, which remain per-seat and remain the authority.

The first rule is the role rule: a keeper is whoever publishes a registry version, and the version names the keeper. A registry has a keeper only in the sense that each published version carries the publishing seat's identifier, digest-cited, published before the bridge walk it is supposed to serve. There is no appointment of a keeper, no district office chartered to keep the one true book, and no registry that keeps itself: a version with no named keeper files as an orphan version, citable as a finder by whoever produces it but carrying no keeper to hole, no keeper to correct, and no presumption either way — a book with no author is a rumour with pagination. A seat that publishes versions regularly is a keeper in fact, and a seat that publishes once is a keeper for that version; the role attaches to the act, not to a title, and it lapses when the publishing stops. A keeper who stops publishing does not thereby withdraw its versions: published versions stand on their filings, and the keeper's silence is a vacancy under the sixth rule, not a retraction.

The second rule is the plurality rule: there may be many keepers, and no keeper's registry outranks another's. A district office, a rotating seat, and a volunteer third seat may each keep a registry indexing the same appointments, and T-646's fork rule already decides disagreements between them: the filings decide, neither registry outranks the other, agreement between two indexes is still not a third witness. Plurality is not a defect to be cured by crowning one keeper; it is the answer to the single-point-of-pressure failure. A challenger who finds an appointment in one registry need not ask which registry is official, because none is official, and a filer who produces a per-seat filing need not ask which registry lists it, because the filing stands whether listed or not. The cost of plurality is duplication — three books to check instead of one — and that cost is paid in findability, which is exactly what a registry sells, not in weight, which no registry may sell. A system that crowns one keeper to save the challenger a second look has traded away the only protection the index had against capture.

The third rule is the self-interest rule: a keeper's entries for its own seat carry no presumption, and a keeper never vouches alone for its own appointments. A seat that keeps a registry indexing its own officers' appointments is keeping a book about itself, and a book about itself is the one book most worth forging: the keeper could write an appointment for its own officer that no per-seat filing supports, and then cite its own registry as the finder for its own bridge. T-646 already forbids the registry from proving anything, but T-647 adds the keeper-side bar: an entry in a registry kept by the very seat the entry is about files as a Self-Kept Entry, and a Self-Kept Entry, even perfectly cited, is corroboration of where to look and nothing more — it never counts as the independent service trace under T-645, never counts as a second witness under T-644, and never answers a hole challenge for its own seat, because the keeper answering for its own book about itself is the filer answering for itself under a second name. A bridge whose appointment evidence is a self-kept registry entry plus the per-seat filing it cites has one paper, not two, and triangulation still needs its independent trace from a different hand. A keeper that wants its own appointments found fast should publish its per-seat filings promptly and let another seat's registry index them; the fastest honest index of your own appointments is somebody else's book.

The fourth rule is the handoff rule: when a keeper passes the book to another seat, the handoff is itself a published, digest-chained filing, and a handoff that is not published is not a handoff. A rotating keeper does not hand the book over by stopping and the next seat starting: the outgoing keeper publishes a closing version that names the incoming keeper and digests the last version it vouches for, and the incoming keeper publishes an opening version that chains from the closing version's digest and names the outgoing keeper it succeeds. A gap between closing and opening versions — weeks in which no version appears, during which appointments are published per-seat but indexed nowhere — is a vacancy in coverage, not a break in the chain: the chain resumes when the opening version chains correctly, and entries for appointments published during the gap are indexed late, not lost. The fifth rule is the liability rule: the keeper answers for the book, on the record, by correction or by presumption. The sixth rule is the vacancy rule: a keeper's silence freezes its book, it does not void it and it does not transfer it. A registry whose keeper stops publishing — office dissolved, seat withdrawn, keeper simply silent — files as a Vacant Registry: its published versions stand on their filings, its entries remain findable, and no new entries, corrections, or chain confessions appear in it until some keeper resumes it by a published resumption version chaining from the last version. A vacant registry is not a broken registry: a break is a version that mis-chains, a vacancy is the absence of versions, and the absence of new versions accuses nobody. The seventh rule is the pressure rule: a keeper under pressure is a keeper to be routed around, not a keeper to be obeyed or deposed. The single-point-of-pressure failure that damned the district-office model is not cured by forbidding district offices — any keeper, single or rotating, can be leaned on — but it is cured by plurality plus the authority rule: because the filings are per-seat and remain the authority, a captured keeper can at worst corrupt its own index, and a corrupted index is routed around the moment a filer or challenger produces the filing. A keeper that publishes entries contradicting their cited filings under pressure files as a False-Registry keeper under T-646's sixth rule, and its entries strike; a keeper that omits entries under pressure files as a Holed keeper under T-646's fifth rule, and its seat's entries are presumed against it; a keeper that stops publishing under pressure files as vacant under the sixth rule here, and a new registry rises beside it. In no case does pressure on a keeper touch the appointments themselves, because appointments live per-seat and no keeper holds them. The system does not need an incorruptible keeper; it needs a keeper whose corruption is detectable, attributable, and survivable, and a named keeper publishing digest-chained versions over per-seat filings is exactly that.

The eighth rule is the succession rule: a registry's keeper may be succeeded, but a registry's authority may not be inherited, because it never had any. When a keeper is succeeded — by handoff under the fourth rule, by resumption after vacancy under the sixth, or by supersession when filers and challengers simply start using a new keeper's book — the successor inherits the chain, the correction history, and the presumptions attached to the versions it chains from, but inherits no authority over the filings, which remain per-seat, and no weight for its entries, which remain finders.
