A keeper that claims succession without chaining — "we are the new keepers of the old book" with no closing version, no opening version, no digest link — claims a title without a paper, and the claim files as an orphan assertion: the old book stands vacant, the new book stands new, and nobody's chain connects them.

**T-648 — the Keeper-Concentration Rule — designed:** T-647 left its keeper-concentration problem named and open: a keeper that keeps registries for many seats at once becomes a district office in fact whatever it is called, with plurality in name and capture in practice. T-647's plurality rule was supposed to be the answer to the single-point-of-pressure failure — many keepers, no keeper official, no keeper's registry outranking another's — but plurality is a property of the system, not a property of any one walk, and a system can be plural in its books while every walk that matters consults the same book. A district office that keeps every registry, a rotating keeper that never actually rotates because nobody else volunteers, a volunteer third seat whose book is simply the best-kept and therefore the only one anybody opens: each is plurality on paper and a single point of pressure in practice. The keeper is named, the versions digest-chain, the filings remain per-seat and remain the authority — and still, whoever can lean on that one keeper can lean on every appointment anybody can find. T-648 answers that concentration is a fact about reliance, not a title, and it is measured, disclosed, and priced at the walk — never crowned, never ignored, and never cured by renaming the keeper.

The first rule is the dependency rule: concentration is measured by reliance, not by headcount. A keeper indexing a hundred seats that nobody consults is not concentrated; a keeper indexing three seats that every walk cites is. Three measures, taken together, decide whether a keeper is concentrated for a given walk: sole-index share — how many of the seats in the keeper's book are indexed by no other keeper, so that this book is the only finder for them; walk share — how many recent walks actually cited this keeper's book rather than merely having it available; and dwell — how long the reliance has run unbroken, because a book consulted once in an emergency is a convenience and a book consulted for a year is an institution. No single measure decides alone: a high sole-index share with low walk share is a quiet monopoly waiting for a customer, a high walk share with low sole-index share is a popular book with competitors standing by, and either one grown over a long dwell is a habit, and habits are where pressure goes to hide. A challenger need not prove all three to raise concentration; raising any one puts the concentration question on the record, and the walk prices it under the fourth and fifth rules rather than pretending the book is one among equals.

The second rule is the disclosure rule: a concentrated keeper's versions declare their coverage, because hidden concentration is the failure and disclosed concentration is a fact. Each published version names, alongside its keeper under T-647's role rule, the seats it indexes and marks which of those seats it alone indexes — the sole-indexed seats by identifier, digest-cited like every other entry. A version that omits its sole-indexed seats, or that lists a seat another keeper also indexes as though it alone held it, files as a mis-declared version: its entries stand on their filings, but the keeper's declaration is struck, and the walk treats the book as undisclosed-concentrated until a corrected version publishes. The disclosure costs the keeper one list per version and buys the system the one thing plurality was supposed to guarantee but did not: the ability to see, before the walk, whether the book about to be consulted is one book among many or the only book anybody uses. A keeper that declines to declare — "the book speaks for itself" — has declined the price of concentration, and its book files as undisclosed for every walk that cites it, which is a heavier price than the list would have been.

The third rule is the no-crown rule: heavy use confers no authority, no presumption, and no shortcut. A keeper consulted by every walk for a year is still, under T-646, an index and never an authority; under T-647, a named role and never a chartered office; and under this trick, a concentrated keeper and never a crowned one. Its entries remain finders, its reputation adds no weight under T-644's evidence-weight rule, and a walk that cites the concentrated book plus the per-seat filing has exactly what a walk citing any other book plus the filing has — one paper and one finder, not one paper and a guarantee. The temptation to crown by usage is the concentration failure wearing a merit badge: "everybody uses this book, so this book must be right" is the district-office argument with the office's name filed off, and it fails for the same reason the office failed — the book's popularity is evidence about the book's convenience, not about the appointments, and convenience is not a witness. A system that lets usage crown a keeper has re-created the single point of pressure and called it a reward for good service.

The fourth rule is the sole-index bar: a walk whose appointment is found only in one keeper's book is a weaker walk, and it must say so and cure it. When the seat's appointment appears in no registry but the cited keeper's — sole-indexed under the second rule's declaration, or discovered sole-indexed when a challenger checks and finds no second book — the walk files as a Sole-Indexed Bridge, not a Kept Registry Bridge, and it stands only when the per-seat filing itself is produced in the walk record, not merely cited by the registry entry. The reason is the capture geometry: sole-index is exactly where a forged or omitted entry hides, because there is no second book to disagree with it, and a registry entry citing a filing the walk never sees is a pointer to a paper nobody has read. Producing the filing cures the walk, not the book: the bridge stands on T-645's triangulation with the filing in hand, and the keeper's book returns to being a finder that happened to point at a real paper. A walk that refuses the production — "the book is reliable, the filing is on file somewhere" — files as a Sole-Indexed Bridge unproduced, and it does not stand, because somewhere is not a place a challenger can check.

The fifth rule is the bounded-contagion rule: a concentrated keeper shown false or holed on one seat does not poison its whole book, but it does trigger a batch re-anchor. T-647 already runs a presumption against a keeper that leaves a hole uncorrected or writes false entries, and that presumption follows the keeper across rebranded registries; T-648 bounds its blast radius for the concentrated book. When a concentrated keeper's entry is struck as false under T-646's sixth rule, or holed and left uncorrected at the walk under T-646's fifth rule, every other entry the keeper published in the same version batch — the same version, or versions chained without an intervening correction version — must be re-anchored to its per-seat filing at the next walk that cites it, and a walk citing a batch entry without producing its filing files as a Batch-Holed Bridge until the re-anchor lands. Entries in other batches, published before or after with clean correction history between, stand until challenged: contagion that runs to the whole book would punish the seats for the keeper's sin and strand every appointment the keeper ever indexed, while contagion that runs nowhere would let a keeper who forged once keep forging quietly in the same batch. The batch is the honest middle: the unit in which the keeper actually worked, and therefore the unit in which its work is suspect.

The sixth rule is the vacancy-grace rule: when a concentrated keeper goes vacant, its dependent seats are not stranded and not penalized. T-647's vacancy rule already freezes a silent keeper's book rather than voiding it, with published versions standing on their filings and holes noted without a keeper to answer them; for a concentrated keeper that freeze could strand every seat that relied on the book, because no second book exists to consult and no keeper remains to correct. T-648 adds the grace: a walk for a seat whose only keeper has gone vacant proceeds on the per-seat filing produced directly, the omission in the vacant book is noted as a hole without a keeper, and no presumption runs against the seat for the keeper's silence — the seat did not choose to be sole-indexed, and the keeper's vacancy is the keeper's fact, not the seat's fault. The grace is per-seat and per-walk, not a general amnesty: a seat that could have produced its filing and did not still files as unproduced, and a seat whose filing is itself missing still files as holed, because grace excuses the keeper's absence, not the paper's. The seventh rule is the cure rule: concentration is cured per-seat, not per-book, and the cure is a second finder or a produced filing. A concentrated keeper's book is not broken up by decree — there is no office to order the breakup from, and a forced fragmentation would trade one single point of pressure for several smaller ones while destroying the best-kept book in the system — but any walk can cure its own concentration: a second keeper indexes the seat, and the walk cites both books; or the filer produces the per-seat filing in the walk record, and the walk stands on the filing rather than on the finder; or the seat's appointments are published per-seat promptly enough that challengers stop needing any book at all. A walk so cured files as a Deconcentrated Bridge: the appointment was findable under a concentrated keeper, and the walk refused to rest on that fact alone. A book that many walks cure, seat by seat, deconcentrates in fact as second finders accumulate and filings get produced; a book that no walk cures stays concentrated, disclosed, and priced — which is the system working as designed, not the system failing, because a disclosed concentration that every walk prices is a risk the system has chosen with its eyes open.

The eighth rule is the pressure-amplification rule: pressure on a concentrated keeper is system pressure, and it is routed around, not obeyed, not negotiated, and not treated as an excuse. T-647's pressure rule already routes around a captured keeper through the per-seat filings; for a concentrated keeper the routing is the same but the stakes are the system's, because the keeper under pressure holds the only finder for many seats at once. A concentrated keeper that publishes entries contradicting their cited filings under pressure files as a False-Registry keeper and triggers the fifth rule's batch re-anchor; a concentrated keeper that omits entries under pressure files as a Holed keeper and carries T-647's presumption on the affected seats; a concentrated keeper that stops publishing under pressure files as vacant and triggers the sixth rule's grace for its dependent seats. In no case does pressure on the keeper touch the appointments, because appointments live per-seat, and in no case does the system's dependence on the keeper convert dependence into deference: the moment a walk defers to a concentrated keeper because no alternative exists, the walk has crowned the keeper under the third rule's ban, and the crown is void whatever the pressure.

What a chain files as follows from the eight rules, and the file must show the registry version with its named keeper and its coverage declaration, the per-seat appointment filing itself, any second keeper's index or produced filing, and any hole challenge, correction version, or batch re-anchor, not merely the concentrated book's word. A chain whose appointment is indexed by more than one keeper, with no keeper carrying the walk alone, files as a Distributed Bridge: plurality in fact, not merely in name, and the walk stands or falls on T-645's triangulation. **T-649 — the Concentration-Threshold Rule — designed:** T-648 left its concentration-threshold problem named and open: concentration is measured by reliance — sole-index share, walk share, dwell — but no number says when a keeper counts as concentrated without argument, so every walk re-litigates the three-measure judgement from scratch, and a judgement re-litigated from scratch is a judgement a pressured keeper can win by exhaustion. A challenger who must argue all three measures, against a keeper who need only dispute one, walks uphill every time; a keeper who must defend all three measures, against a challenger who need only gesture at popularity, is presumed guilty by busyness. T-648's three measures were a ruler without markings: they told the walk what to measure and not what the measurement means. T-649 answers that concentration gets numbers, but numbers are presumptions, never verdicts — a threshold crossed shifts the burden, it does not decide the case, and no number ever crowns a keeper, adds weight to an entry, or excuses a missing filing.

The first rule is the presumption rule: a threshold crossed creates a presumption, and a presumption is a burden, not a finding. When a keeper's measures cross a threshold under the second rule, the walk treats the keeper as concentrated unless the keeper shows otherwise — by a second finder for the cited seats, by a recount under the sixth rule, or by a produced filing that cures the walk under T-648's seventh rule — and the challenger need not re-argue the three measures. When the measures sit below every threshold, the walk treats the keeper as unconcentrated unless the challenger shows otherwise — by the three-measure judgement T-648 already provides, which survives below the thresholds as the argument of last resort. The threshold does not replace judgement; it prices it. Above the line, the keeper pays the argument; below the line, the challenger pays it; on the line, the walk judges. A system with no threshold makes the challenger pay every time, and a system where the threshold decides makes the number the judge — both failures, one by attrition and one by arithmetic.

The second rule is the three-numbers rule: sole-index share at one half, walk share at two thirds, dwell at one hundred and eighty days, and two of three makes the presumption. Sole-index share is the fraction of the keeper's indexed seats that no other keeper indexes: at one half or more, the book is the only finder for at least half its seats, and a book that is the only finder for half its world is not one book among many for that half. Walk share is the fraction of walks in the measurement window that cited this keeper's book: at two thirds or more, the book is not merely available but actually consulted by a supermajority of walks, and availability is not reliance but citation is. Dwell is the length of unbroken reliance: at one hundred and eighty days, the reliance has survived a season, outlasted an emergency, and become a habit, and habits are where pressure goes to hide. Meeting any two of the three raises the presumption of concentration; meeting all three raises it strongly, meaning the keeper's rebuttal must produce a second finder or a filing, not merely a counter-argument about the measures; meeting only one raises the concentration question on the record under T-648's first rule but presumes nothing. The numbers are deliberately asymmetric: sole-index share needs only a half because sole-index is the sharpest edge of capture, while walk share needs two thirds because popularity without sole-index still leaves competitors standing by.

The third rule is the window rule: the measures are computed over a stated window, published with the version, and stale numbers count for nothing. The window is the last ninety days or the last thirty walks, whichever covers more walks — ninety days so that a quiet quarter cannot hide behind a busy week, thirty walks so that a busy week cannot drown a quiet quarter — and the version that declares coverage under T-648's second rule states the window its numbers were computed over, digest-cited like every other declaration. A threshold finding older than its window is a rumour with arithmetic: a keeper concentrated last year and deconcentrated since does not carry last year's presumption into this year's walk, and a keeper unconcentrated last year does not carry last year's innocence into this year's capture. A version that publishes numbers without stating its window files as mis-declared under T-648's second rule, and its book files as undisclosed-concentrated until a corrected version publishes, because a number without its window is a claim without its conditions.

The fourth rule is the small-book floor: below a floor, numbers presume nothing, because a threshold built for districts misfires on hamlets. T-650 answers that calibration is a published, counted, bounded, and never-retroactive process — the numbers move only on counted walks, only by small steps, only forward, and only under a calibrator who decides no live walk.

The first rule is the counted-walks rule: only filed walks calibrate, because a citation is not a walk and a walk without its paper is not evidence. A walk counts toward calibration only when its bridge record is filed complete — the registry version published before the walk, the per-seat filing produced or its absence filed as holed, any threshold contest or batch re-anchor noted on the record — so the calibration dataset is built from walks a later challenger can re-read, not from a keeper's claimed popularity. The second rule is the separation rule: the calibrator proposes, the walk disposes, and no calibration version ever decides a live walk. Each answer alone fails in a different direction. A standing calibrator office recreates the district office T-648 was built to prevent, now wearing a statistician's coat and holding the ruler itself. A rotating seat hands the ruler to whoever's turn it is, qualified or not, and a rotation schedule is itself an appointment power someone must keep. An open publisher with no selection rule at all lets the loudest arithmetic win, and a keeper with a printing press for calibration versions can out-publish every honest counter. T-651 answers that the calibrator is none of these alone: a named publisher per calibration version, eligible only by separation, earning authority only by adoption walk by walk, and barred from consecutive adoption — selection by eligibility plus adoption, never by appointment, rotation, or volume.

The first rule is the eligibility rule: a calibrator must be separated from every interest the numbers price. A publisher is eligible to calibrate only while it is not a keeper of any registry version, not a walk judge on any live walk, and not a party to any live threshold contest — the same separation T-650's second rule demands of the calibration version itself, now demanded of the hand that writes it. A keeper that publishes a calibration version while keeper files as Self-Calibrated, and walks citing it file as Self-Calibrated Bridges: priced under the numbers in force before it, because a keeper pricing its own concentration is a keeper grading its own examination. Eligibility is declared, not assumed: the calibration version carries a separation declaration naming the publisher and stating, version by version, that it holds no keeper seat, judges no live walk, and stands in no live contest — and a declaration later shown false voids the version under T-650's sixth rule as a gamed calibration, not merely a mistaken one.

The second rule is the candidacy rule: calibration versions are published openly, and any eligible publisher may publish one — there is no gate before publication, only judgement after it. A publisher becomes a calibrator candidate the moment its calibration version publishes with its separation declaration, its stated windows, and its counted walks under T-650's first rule; no authority appoints it, no registry lists it, no rotation seats it. Open candidacy is what keeps calibration from becoming an office: the moment a publisher needs permission to propose numbers, the permission-granter holds the ruler. But open candidacy without adoption is only proposal — a version with no adopting walk is a pamphlet, not a calibration, and it moves no number for any walk that does not cite it.

The third rule is the adoption rule: a calibration version earns authority only when walks cite it, and its authority extends only to the walks that cite it. A walk adopts a calibration version by citing its digest in the walk's published-before-walk record, under T-650's second rule; a walk that cites no calibration version is priced under the numbers in force before it, and a walk that cites a version still in candidacy — published but adopted by no walk yet — prices itself under that version at its own risk, filing as a First-Adopter Bridge, because the first adopter is the walk that tests whether the numbers survive contact with a real bridge. There is no election, no quorum, and no adoption threshold fixed here: the version adopted by the most walks is the most-used calibration, not the official one, and a minority version cited by one honest walk still prices that walk, because calibration authority that required a majority would let the largest keeper bloc outvote the arithmetic.

The fourth rule is the rotation-by-adoption rule: no publisher's calibration version may be the adopted version for two consecutive calibration adoptions, because consecutive adoption is how a publisher becomes an office without ever being appointed. When a calibration version is adopted — cited by a walk after publication — the next calibration version adopted by a later walk must come from a different publisher; a version from the same publisher, published while its predecessor still stands as the last adopted version, files as a Calibrator-Repeated version, disregarded for walks after it until a different publisher's version is adopted. The rule bars consecutive adoption, not consecutive publication: the same publisher may publish as many candidate versions as it likes, and walks may read them all — but no walk may adopt a second consecutive version from the same hand, because a ruler held by one hand through two revisions is a ruler owned, not a ruler kept. The exception is scarcity, not convenience: if no other eligible publisher has published a candidate version within one full measurement window after the last adoption, a walk may adopt a same-publisher version, filing as a Scarcity-Adopted Bridge, with the scarcity on the record — because a threshold with no fresh calibration at all is worse than a second version from a known hand, and the scarcity filing is the signal that the field needs new publishers.

The fifth rule is the void-bar rule: a publisher whose calibration version was voided for gamed walks under T-650's sixth rule is barred from calibration for four full measurement windows after the voiding, and a publisher whose separation declaration was shown false is barred for twice that. The bar runs from the voiding version's publication, not from the gaming, because the voiding is the public finding; during the bar, any version the publisher publishes files as a Calibrator-Barred version, disregarded like a repeated version, and walks citing it file as Calibrator-Barred Bridges, priced under the numbers in force before it. A bar is not a ban for life: after four windows (or eight, for a false declaration) the publisher may publish again, because a calibration field that permanently exiles every publisher it catches will eventually have no publishers left — but the voiding stays on the publisher's record, cited on every later version, so that a returning publisher returns watched, not washed.

The sixth rule is the keeper-cooling rule: a publisher that steps down from a keeper seat may not calibrate until one full measurement window has passed since its last keeper version, because a keeper's knowledge of its own book does not evaporate the day it resigns the seat. A version published inside the cooling window by a former keeper files as a Cooling-Violated version, disregarded, and walks citing it file as Cooling-Violated Bridges. Cooling is what keeps resignation from becoming a costume change: without it, a keeper could resign on Monday, calibrate its own book's thresholds on Tuesday, and resume the seat on Wednesday, having laundered self-calibration through a week's absence.

The seventh rule is the divergence rule: competing calibration versions may coexist, and their coexistence is information, not failure. When two eligible publishers' versions are both adopted by different walks in the same window, the field files as Calibration-Diverged: each walk is priced under the version it cited, neither version is declared wrong by the other's existence, and the divergence itself is noted on both versions' records, triggering a T-650 review at the next cadence whether or not the contested-threshold rate crosses one quarter. Divergence is not resolved by authority — there is no authority to resolve it — but by the next window's walks, which adopt the version whose numbers survived their bridges, and by the review, which publishes counted walks for both. A field that forbade competing versions would need an official version, and an official version needs an office, and an office is what this trick exists to prevent.

What a chain files as follows from the seven rules, and the file must show the calibration version with its publisher, its separation declaration, its stated windows and counted walks, and any adoption, repetition, bar, cooling, or divergence note, not merely the threshold's verdict. A chain whose walk cites a version from an eligible, non-consecutive publisher, unbarred and past cooling, files as a Calibrator-Adopted Bridge: priced under adopted numbers, standing on its filing like any other bridge. A chain whose walk is the first to adopt a published-but-unadopted version files as a First-Adopter Bridge: priced under the version it tested, flagged as the test. A chain whose walk cites a same-publisher consecutive version files as a Calibrator-Repeated Bridge: priced under the numbers in force before it, the repetition on the record. A chain whose walk cites a barred publisher's version files as a Calibrator-Barred Bridge: priced under the numbers in force before it, the bar on the record. A chain whose walk cites a keeper's own calibration files as a Self-Calibrated Bridge: priced under the numbers in force before it, the self-dealing on the record. A chain whose walk adopts a same-publisher version for want of any other candidate files as a Scarcity-Adopted Bridge: priced under the version, the scarcity on the record, the field warned. PUBLISHED-BEFORE-WALK — the calibration version with its publisher and separation declaration, the adoption citation, the bar or cooling note, and the divergence note, like the declaration itself, are published with a digest before the bridge walk, challengeable before it and read-only after, save the future-bridge fallback of T-644.

**T-652 — the Calibrator-Adoption Rule — designed:** T-651 left its calibrator-adoption problem named and open: what adoption count, if any, turns a much-cited version into the field's working calibration rather than merely the most-used proposal — whether a version cited by a hundred walks carries any standing beyond those hundred walks. The temptation is to crown the count: a version cited by a hundred walks feels like the field's calibration, and a field that has counted that far feels entitled to stop counting. T-652 answers that no count crowns anything. Adoption is per-walk, never field-wide: a version cited by a hundred walks prices those hundred walks and nothing else, and walk one hundred and one is priced under whatever it cites, or under the numbers in force before it if it cites nothing. What a count does is narrower and still real: it seasons the version, it evidences survival at review, and it puts dormancy on the record — but it never makes a version mandatory, never retires a rival, and never prices a walk that did not cite it.

The first rule is the per-walk rule: a calibration version's authority extends exactly to the walks that cite it, and no further. A walk adopts a version by citing its digest in the walk's published-before-walk record, under T-650's second rule and T-651's third rule; a walk that cites no version is priced under the numbers in force before it, even if every walk before it cited the same version, because silence is not adoption and ubiquity is not consent. A publisher that describes its version as "the field's calibration," "the working calibration," or "adopted by the field" — rather than "cited by N walks" — files as an Adoption-Crown claim: the claim is struck, the version itself is untouched, and any walk that priced itself under the version only because "everyone uses it," without citing its digest, files as a Crowned Bridge, priced under the numbers in force before it, because a walk that follows the crowd instead of citing a digest has adopted nothing it can be held to.

The second rule is the seasoning rule: a version becomes Seasoned once twenty-five counted walks cite it. Twenty-five is a design number, not a discovered constant — fixed here so the field has a line to argue against, and itself reviewable under T-650's cadence — and "counted" carries T-650's first rule: only filed walks count, and a walk whose adoption filing is holed does not count. A Calibrator-Adopted Bridge counts; a First-Adopter Bridge counts, because the first adopter is still a walk that priced itself under the version; a Scarcity-Adopted Bridge counts, because scarcity does not make the bridge less real. A Calibrator-Repeated Bridge does not count, a Calibrator-Barred Bridge does not count, a Self-Calibrated Bridge does not count, a Cooling-Violated Bridge does not count, and a Crowned Bridge does not count — a version cannot season itself on walks that were priced under the numbers in force before it. Seasoning changes nothing about what the version prices: a Seasoned version still prices only the walks that cite it. What seasoning changes is the record: a Seasoned version earns a published counted-walk table at the next T-650 review, its windows and counted walks stated rather than merely asserted, and a walk citing a Seasoned version files as a Seasoned-Cited Bridge, which is a Calibrator-Adopted Bridge with its seasoning noted — same pricing, fuller record.

The third rule is the survival-evidence rule: a count is evidence at review, not authority over any walk. At a T-650 review, a version's counted-walk table is read as survival evidence — its numbers survived contact with that many real bridges, and a version whose counted walks number in the hundreds has survived more contact than a version cited once — but the review may recommend, never mandate. A review that finds a Seasoned version's numbers held across its counted walks publishes that finding as a recommendation walks may cite; it does not retire rival versions, does not oblige the next walk to cite the Seasoned version, and does not convert the most-cited version into the default for walks that cite nothing. The moment a review could mandate a version, the review would be the office T-651 exists to prevent, wearing a statistician's coat one size larger. A minority version cited by one honest walk in the current window still prices that walk, however Seasoned its rival, because a field that let count retire versions would let the largest keeper bloc outvote the arithmetic by walking often.

The fourth rule is the dormancy rule: a version with no counted citation in two consecutive full measurement windows files as Dormant. Dormancy is not voiding, not barring, and not disgrace: a Dormant version remains citable, and a walk that cites it after dormancy files as a Revived Bridge, priced under the version, with the revival noted — because a version abandoned for two windows may have been abandoned for fashion rather than failure, and a field that voided unfashionable arithmetic would lose numbers it may need again. What dormancy changes is the review list: a Dormant version drops from the review's live-versions table to its dormant appendix, so the review counts the field's live arithmetic rather than its archive, and a publisher claiming a Dormant version as "widely adopted" files as an Adoption-Crown claim under the first rule, because a count earned in an earlier era is not a count in this one. A version that revives and re-seasons — twenty-five new counted walks after revival — files as Re-Seasoned, its old table archived beside its new one, so that a revival cannot launder an old count into a new reputation.

The fifth rule is the subtraction rule: gamed citations subtract, and a version that seasons on gamed walks unseasons. When a walk's adoption filing is voided for gamed calibration under T-650's sixth rule, its citation is struck from the version's counted-walk table, and if the subtraction drops the version below twenty-five, the version files as Unseasoned, its Seasoned note struck and its review table corrected — not voided, because the version's numbers may still be sound, but no longer seasoned, because seasoning earned on false walks is not seasoning. A publisher that re-adds struck citations to a published table files as a False-Evidence version under T-643's evidence rule, and the version is voided rather than merely unseasoned, because re-adding struck evidence is forgery, not error. Subtraction is what keeps seasoning honest: without it, a publisher could season a version by walking it itself a hundred times through holed filings and arrive Seasoned on paper.

The sixth rule is the no-retirement rule: no count, however large, retires a rival version, and no review, however unanimous, declares a version dead. Versions end only by voiding under T-650's sixth rule (gamed calibration), by barring under T-651's fifth rule (barred publisher), or by dormancy under the fourth rule here — and dormancy is a change of list, not of standing. A Seasoned version and a once-cited version coexist exactly as T-651's seventh rule provides for competing versions: each prices the walks that cite it, the coexistence is filed as Calibration-Diverged where both are adopted in the same window, and the next window's walks decide by citing, not by voting. A field that retired versions by count would need a counter with the power to kill, and a counter with the power to kill is an office with a different name.

A chain whose publisher claims field-wide standing for a version files as an Adoption-Crown claim: the claim struck, the version untouched, the walks priced as they cited. **T-653 — the Seasoning-Count Rule — designed:** T-652 left its seasoning-count problem named and open: whether twenty-five is the right seasoning line, or whether the line itself should be calibrated from walk volume — whether a field that walks rarely should season at fewer walks and a field that walks constantly should demand more. The temptation is to defend twenty-five as if it were discovered: a round number that has already seasoned one version feels earned, and a field that has already counted to it feels entitled to keep counting to it. T-653 answers that twenty-five was a placeholder with a review date, not a constant, and that a fixed line misprices both quiet fields and busy ones — in a quiet field it seasons nothing, because no version ever reaches twenty-five, and in a busy field it seasons everything, because every version that survives a week reaches twenty-five. A seasoning line that cannot tell a rare achievement from a common one is not a line; it is a habit.

The first rule is the banded line: the seasoning line for a measurement window is set from the counted-walk volume of the previous full window, in three bands. Fewer than fifty counted walks in the previous window sets the line at ten; fifty to one hundred and ninety-nine sets it at twenty-five, the T-652 baseline; two hundred or more sets it at fifty. Ten, twenty-five, and fifty are design numbers, not discovered constants — fixed here so the field has bands to argue against, and themselves reviewable under T-650's cadence — and "counted" carries T-652's discipline: only filed walks count, struck citations excluded, holed adoption filings excluded. The bands are deliberately coarse: a line that moved walk by walk would let a publisher season a version by timing its citations to a dip, and a line with only three steps can be published, checked, and contested without a statistician in the room. A field that walks rarely seasons at ten, which is still a real count — ten filed walks that priced themselves under a version — and a field that walks constantly seasons at fifty, which is still reachable — fifty filed walks, not five hundred — so the line stays a seasoning test in both directions rather than a wall in one and a turnstile in the other.

The second rule is the window lock: the line is fixed for a whole window, published before the window, and never moves mid-window. The line for the coming window is published with the previous window's counted-walk table, challengeable before the window opens and read-only during it, like the calibration version itself under T-652's published-before-walk rule. A version that seasons mid-window seasons under the line in force for that window, even if the next window's band would have set a different line, because a version that earned seasoning under the published line earned it. A version that sits at twenty-four when its window closes does not season because the next window's line drops to ten; it seasons only when a twenty-fifth counted walk — or a tenth, under the new line — is filed inside a window whose line it meets, because seasoning is earned inside a window, never by retroactive re-banding. The lock is what keeps the bands honest: without it, every publisher would argue its version should be judged under whichever band seasons it soonest.

The third rule is the grandfather rule: a version seasoned under an old line keeps its seasoning when the line rises, noted as Grandfathered-Seasoned. A version seasoned at ten in a quiet window does not unseason when the field grows busy and the line rises to twenty-five or fifty, because unseasoning it would punish a version for the field's success rather than for any failure of its own. What the rise changes is the record, not the standing: the version's review table states the line it seasoned under and the window in which it seasoned, so a reader can tell a ten-walk seasoning from a fifty-walk seasoning without either being hidden, and a walk citing a Grandfathered-Seasoned version files as a Grandfathered-Cited Bridge — priced under the version, the grandfathering noted, same pricing, fuller record. A version that has never seasoned seasons only under the line in force when its seasoning walk is filed; grandfathering protects earned seasoning, never promised seasoning, because a version that merely approached an old line earned nothing the new line must honour.

The fourth rule is the re-seasoning rule: a Dormant version that revives under T-652's fourth rule re-seasons under the current window's line, not under the line it seasoned under before dormancy. Its old table is archived beside its new one, as T-652 already provides, and its new count starts from the revival walk — old counted walks do not carry over, because a revival is a new test of numbers that were abandoned, not a resumption of an old reputation. A version that seasoned at ten, went Dormant for two windows, and revives in a busy window must reach fifty new counted walks to file as Re-Seasoned; a version that revives in a quiet window must reach ten. A publisher that claims a revived version is "already seasoned" on the strength of its archived table files as an Adoption-Crown claim under T-652's first rule, because an old count in an earlier era is not a count in this one, and the archive exists so the old count can be read, not so it can be spent twice.

The fifth rule is the volume-honesty rule: the band is set from counted walks only, and a walk manufactured to move the band is a gamed walk. A publisher, keeper, or bloc that files walks whose purpose is to push total volume across a band boundary — upward, to raise the line and strand a rival below fifty, or downward, by withholding walks, to drop the line and season a favourite at ten — files those walks as Band-Gamed walks, and each such walk's citation is struck from every table it touched, under T-652's subtraction rule. The band moves only on walks that priced real bridges, because a line set by manufactured volume would season nothing but the manufacture. Whether a walk was filed to move the band is judged the way T-643 judges evidence: by its filing pattern, not by its author's stated motive — a cluster of walks filed in the last days of a window, all citing one version or none, that tips the total across a boundary, is evidence enough to open the contest, and the contest, not the accusation, decides.

**T-654 — the Band-Boundary Rule — designed:** T-653 left its band-boundary problem named and open: whether the band boundaries themselves — fifty and two hundred — are the right steps, or whether a field whose volume hovers at a boundary should hold its band across windows rather than flicker between lines. The failure is easy to picture and hard to argue away once seen: a field that walks forty-nine times in one window and fifty-one in the next, then forty-nine again, seasons its versions at ten, then twenty-five, then ten, then twenty-five — and a version that seasons at ten in a quiet window and would have needed twenty-five in the next is not a version whose achievement changed, it is a version whose field breathed. The temptation is to defend the flicker as responsiveness: the line follows the volume, and a line that follows the volume is honest. But a line that changes on a single walk is not following the volume; it is following the noise, and a seasoning test that a publisher can move by filing one more walk — or withholding one — is a test the publisher writes, not a test the publisher passes. T-654 answers that a boundary is a threshold with a door, not a line on the floor: a field crosses a boundary only when it crosses it by enough, and stays crossed only while it stays across, and a field that hovers at a boundary holds the band it already holds until the crossing is unmistakable.

The first rule is the dead-zone rule: each boundary carries a dead zone ten walks wide on either side, and volume inside the dead zone holds the previous band. The fifty boundary's dead zone runs forty to sixty; the two hundred boundary's runs one hundred and ninety to two hundred and ten. A field in the ten band whose volume rises to fifty-five stays in the ten band, because fifty-five is inside the dead zone and a rise of six walks over a boundary is a breath, not a migration. A field in the ten band whose volume rises to sixty-one moves to the twenty-five band, because sixty-one clears the dead zone and the crossing is no longer deniable. A field in the twenty-five band whose volume falls to forty-five stays in the twenty-five band, because forty-five is inside the dead zone; it moves down to the ten band only at thirty-nine or below. The dead zone is symmetric by design: the same ten walks that keep a rising field from jumping too early keep a falling field from dropping too early, and a publisher that wants the line moved must move the field's volume by more than a rounding error in either direction. Ten is a design number, not a discovered constant — fixed here so the field has a width to argue against, itself reviewable under T-650's cadence — and the dead zone is measured in counted walks only, under T-653's discipline: struck citations excluded, holed adoption filings excluded, Band-Gamed walks excluded before the total is ever compared to a boundary.

The second rule is the confirmation rule: a crossing that clears the dead zone takes effect only when the next window confirms it, and a single window beyond the dead zone is a touch, not a move. A field in the ten band that walks sixty-one times in one window and forty-eight in the next never leaves the ten band: the sixty-one was a touch, the forty-eight was the retreat, and the line that moved on the touch would have seasoned versions at twenty-five for a window in which the field, by its own second measure, was still a ten-band field. A field that walks sixty-one and then sixty-three moves to the twenty-five band for the third window, because two consecutive windows beyond the dead zone are a migration and not a breath. The confirmation window's line is the old band's line — the field seasons under the band it holds until the move is confirmed, never under the band it merely touched — because a version that seasons during an unconfirmed touch seasons under a line the field had not yet earned. A touch is not hidden: the published line table notes it as a Boundary-Touched window, with the volume and the band held, so a reader can see the field pressing against its boundary without the line pretending the pressure was a decision.

The third rule is the hold rule: a field that sits inside a dead zone for four consecutive windows holds its band and files as Boundary-Locked, and the lock is a flag for review, not a verdict on the boundaries. A field walking fifty-two, forty-eight, fifty-five, and forty-nine across four windows is a field living on its boundary, and its line — ten or twenty-five, whichever band it held when it entered the dead zone — stays put for all four windows, because four windows of hovering are four windows of evidence that the field's true volume is the boundary itself. The lock does not move the line, and it does not move the boundary: it publishes the fact that the field has been boundary-locked for four windows, and a T-650 review reading that flag may recommend re-centring the boundary — moving fifty to fifty-five, say, or widening the dead zone for this field — but the recommendation, like every T-650 recommendation, never mandates, and the line stays where the hold rule holds it until a calibration version adopting the new boundary is itself walked in. A Boundary-Locked flag that persists for eight windows is a standing invitation to the review, not a failure: some fields genuinely live on a boundary, and a rule that forced them to pick a side would be manufacturing a decision the field itself refuses to make.

The fourth rule is the re-entry rule: a field that leaves its dead zone and re-enters it later re-enters under the same discipline, and no crossing is ever grandfathered. A field that moved to the twenty-five band on two confirmed windows above sixty, then falls to fifty-five, holds the twenty-five band inside the dead zone; a field that falls to thirty-nine moves down, and if it later rises to sixty-one and sixty-three again, it moves up again by the same two-window confirmation, not by memory of its earlier stay. Bands are states a field occupies, not titles a field earns: a field that has once been a twenty-five-band field carries no presumption that it still is one, and a version seasoned under the twenty-five line during the field's earlier stay keeps its seasoning under T-653's grandfather rule, because the version's achievement is its own even when the field's band moves on. The re-entry rule is what keeps the dead zone honest in both directions: without it, a field that once crossed would never have to cross again, and the boundary would be a door that locks behind the first crosser.

The fifth rule is the gaming rule: a walk cluster filed to push volume across a dead-zone edge, or to manufacture a confirmation window, is judged under T-653's volume-honesty rule, and the judgement is stricter at a boundary than anywhere else. A cluster of walks filed in the last days of a window, all citing one version or none, that carries a total from fifty-eight to sixty-one — just past the dead-zone edge — is evidence enough to open the contest, and a cluster that repeats the trick in the next window to manufacture confirmation is evidence enough to open it twice. Walks struck as Band-Gamed are subtracted from the totals of both windows they touched before any boundary comparison is made, so a manufactured crossing uncrosses itself and a manufactured confirmation unconfirms itself, and the field's band is recomputed on the honest totals. A publisher that games a boundary does not merely lose the walks: the gaming is noted on the field's line table, so a reader weighing a later genuine crossing can see that this boundary has been pushed before, and a boundary pushed twice by the same hand is a boundary the review reads with suspicion.

**T-655 — the Dead-Zone-Width Rule — designed:** T-654 left its dead-zone-width problem named and open: whether the dead-zone width itself — ten walks — should scale with field size, so that a field walking thousands treats ten as noise while a field walking dozens treats ten as a migration. The failure is the mirror image of the flicker T-654 fixed. A ten-walk zone around the two hundred boundary is a ±5% neighbourhood: a field walking two hundred and five times in a window is five walks over a boundary whose zone swallows it, and a field walking two hundred and fifteen is fifteen over — still inside a zone drawn for a boundary four times smaller. Meanwhile the same ten walks around the fifty boundary are a ±20% neighbourhood, wide enough to hold a field whose whole volume is forty walks. One width cannot serve both boundaries, because the boundaries do not live at the same scale — and a zone that is generous at fifty and stingy at two hundred misprices exactly the large fields whose seasoning line matters most. T-655 answers that the dead zone scales with the boundary it guards, with a floor that protects small fields from a proportion that would shrink their zone to nothing.

The first rule is the proportional-width rule: each boundary's dead-zone half-width is the greater of ten walks and one-tenth of the boundary value. The fifty boundary's zone stays forty to sixty, because one-tenth of fifty is five and the floor of ten governs. The two hundred boundary's zone widens to one hundred and eighty to two hundred and twenty, because one-tenth of two hundred is twenty and the proportion governs. The width is computed from the boundary, never from the field's current volume: a zone sized from the volume it measures would move as the field moves, and a measuring stick that stretches with the thing measured measures nothing. A field walking two hundred and eight times holds its band inside the widened zone; a field walking two hundred and twenty-one clears it and begins its two-window confirmation under T-654's second rule, unchanged. The proportion itself — one-tenth — is a design number, not a discovered constant, fixed here so the field has a ratio to argue against, itself reviewable under T-650's cadence.

The second rule is the floor rule: no boundary's dead zone ever narrows below ten walks on either side, whatever the proportion says. The floor exists because the proportion, left alone, would give the fifty boundary a five-walk zone — a neighbourhood so narrow that a field walking fifty-four and forty-six across two windows would flicker between bands on weather, which is the failure T-654 was written to kill. The floor is absolute across boundaries and across windows: a future boundary drawn below fifty — a twenty-five boundary, say — would still carry a ten-walk zone, fifteen to thirty-five, because a zone narrower than ten is noise for every field size, and the rule that protects the smallest field is the rule that keeps the system honest at every scale.

The third rule is the window-lock rule: a boundary's zone width is fixed for the window and published with the band table before the window, challengeable before it and read-only during it, and a width change never re-bands a closed window. If a T-650 review recommends moving the proportion from one-tenth to one-eighth, the new widths take effect for the next window's table, not for the window already walked — because a version that seasoned under a published zone seasoned under that zone, and re-banding history on a new width would unseason versions whose achievement was real when it was earned. The fourth rule is the neighbourhood rule: a dead zone governs only the field volumes near its boundary, and a field far from every boundary holds its band without reference to any zone. A field walking two thousand times does not live "inside" the two hundred boundary's widened zone — it lives above it, in the top band, and no width calculation touches it. The zones are doorways, not climates: they matter only where a field might cross, and a field that has crossed by an order of magnitude is not hovering. This is what keeps the proportional width from becoming a general volume tax: the width scales the doorway, and only the doorway, and a field that walks thousands is taxed nothing by a twenty-walk zone it never enters.

The fifth rule is the hover-gaming rule: a field that parks its volume inside a widened zone to avoid confirmation is judged under T-654's fifth rule, and the wider zone does not widen the excuse. A cluster of walks filed in the last days of a window, all citing one version or none, that holds a total at two hundred and ten — inside the widened zone, short of confirmation — is evidence enough to open the contest, and walks struck as Band-Gamed are subtracted from the totals of both windows they touched before any zone comparison is made, exactly as T-654 provides. A one-tenth zone around a two thousand boundary is two hundred walks wide on either side — a four-hundred-walk neighbourhood in which a field can wander for windows without ever confirming a crossing, and in which a version can season, unseason, and re-season without the field ever deciding anything. The proportion was drawn to fix a small-boundary problem — ten walks is a wide neighbourhood at fifty — and then applied, unexamined, to boundaries where ten walks is a rounding error and two hundred walks is a season. A scale that grows as fast as the thing it measures does not absorb noise; it absorbs signal, and a zone that absorbs signal is a hiding place, not a doorway. T-656 answers that the dead zone scales with the square root of the boundary it guards, because counted walks are counts, and the noise in a count grows as the square root of the count — and a zone matched to the noise absorbs the noise and nothing else.

The first rule is the noise-scale rule: each boundary's dead-zone half-width is the greater of ten walks and the square root of the boundary value, rounded to the nearest walk. The fifty boundary's zone stays forty to sixty, because the square root of fifty is about seven and the floor of ten governs. The two hundred boundary's zone narrows to one hundred and eighty-six to two hundred and fourteen, because the square root of two hundred is about fourteen and the root governs — narrower than T-655's one hundred and eighty to two hundred and twenty, and narrower in exactly the direction the evidence points: at two hundred, the proportion was already absorbing fourteen walks of genuine movement on either side. A two thousand boundary's zone is one thousand nine hundred and fifty-five to two thousand and forty-five, because the square root of two thousand is about forty-five — a ninety-walk neighbourhood where the proportion would have drawn a four-hundred-walk one. The square root is computed from the boundary, never from the field's current volume, under T-655's discipline: a measuring stick that stretches with the thing measured measures nothing. The root itself — not a multiple of it, not a logarithm of it — is a design number's shape, not a discovered constant, fixed here so the field has a scale to argue against, itself reviewable under T-650's cadence.

The second rule is the logarithm-set-aside rule: a logarithmic scale was considered and is not adopted, and the reason is recorded so it is not re-proposed as though unexamined. A log zone would carry the floor almost everywhere: log base two of two hundred is about eight, below the floor, so the two hundred boundary would keep its forty-to-sixty shape by another name, and a boundary would have to pass one thousand before its log zone exceeded ten walks at all. A scale that is indistinguishable from the floor across the whole range the system actually uses adds a formula without adding a decision, and a formula that adds no decision is decoration. The logarithm is set aside, not refuted for all time: if a future boundary is drawn at one hundred thousand, where the square root is three hundred and sixteen and the log is seventeen, the review may reopen the question — but it reopens it as a new proposal with its own calibration version, not as a correction to this rule.

The third rule is the floor-at-one-hundred rule: the floor of ten governs every boundary below one hundred, because the square root of one hundred is ten and the two rules meet there. **T-657 — the Root-Multiplier Rule — designed:** T-656 left its root-multiplier problem named and open: whether the half-width should be one times the square root or two, for fields whose walks arrive in clusters rather than singly. The failure is what a cluster does to the noise T-656 measured. The square root is the noise of independent draws: a hundred walks, each filed on its own day by its own keeper citing its own version, scatter around their mean by about ten, and a ten-walk zone absorbs that scatter and nothing else. But a field whose walks arrive in bursts — twelve walks filed on one day by one keeper citing one version, then silence for a week, then twelve more — does not scatter by ten. Its scatter is the scatter of bursts, and a burst counts once however many walks it wears: twelve walks that arrive together are one decision in twelve coats, and a zone sized for twelve independent walks is sized for a field that never existed. The temptation is to double the root everywhere and call it safety: two times the square root at every boundary, because clusters might exist. But a doubled zone at a boundary that walks singly is a zone that absorbs signal, which is the failure T-656 was written to kill, now wearing a safety excuse — and a rule that doubles the zone wherever it might be needed doubles it precisely where it is not. T-657 answers that the multiplier is one by default and two only where clustering is shown, per boundary, published before the window, and earned again each time it is claimed — a multiplier is evidence, not insurance.

The first rule is the default-one rule: every boundary's dead-zone half-width is the greater of ten walks and one times the square root of the boundary value, unless a multiplier of two is in force for that boundary for that window. The default is not a presumption that walks arrive singly; it is the burden rule. The field that wants a wider zone shows its clusters, and the field that shows nothing walks under the root. A boundary that has never shown a cluster carries multiplier one in every window without a hearing, because the absence of cluster evidence is itself the evidence that the root fits — and a reader who wants the zone doubled at a quiet boundary must produce a cluster, not a worry. The default-one rule is what keeps the multiplier honest in the direction that matters: it is easy to widen a zone on suspicion and hard to narrow it again, so the widening must be the thing that is earned, and the narrowing must be the thing that happens on its own.

The second rule is the cluster-evidence rule: a multiplier of two is in force for a boundary in a window when the previous window's counted walks for that boundary's field show clustered arrival. A cluster is three or more counted walks sharing a filing day, a keeper seat, and a cited version — or no cited version, which counts as a shared citation of none. The clustered share is the fraction of the window's counted walks that fall in such clusters, computed on counted walks only under T-653's discipline: struck citations excluded, holed adoption filings excluded, Band-Gamed walks excluded before the share is ever computed. When the clustered share is one half or more, the multiplier for the next window is two; below one half, it is one. One half is a design number, not a discovered constant — fixed here so the field has a threshold to argue against, itself reviewable under T-650's cadence — and the cluster definition is deliberately coarse: three walks sharing a day, a keeper, and a citation are a burst by any honest reading, and a definition finer than that would let a publisher split a burst across two days, or two keepers, or two citations, and call the pieces independent.

The third rule is the per-boundary publication rule: the multiplier is published per boundary with the band table before the window, under T-656's fourth-rule machinery, and a multiplier granted for one boundary widens no other. **T-660 — the Strike-Threshold Rule — designed:** T-659 left its strike-threshold problem named and open: whether a single manufactured walk suffices to strike a two, or whether the strike requires a pattern — whether one dressed walk collapses a coefficient that a hundred genuine walks support. The failure is what an unthresholded strike does to a genuine coefficient. Under T-659 a two struck as manufactured collapses straight to one, and under T-657's fifth rule manufactured walks are subtracted before any zone comparison is made — but neither rule says how much manufacture earns the strike. The temptation is a hair trigger: any manufactured walk, however small, collapses the two, because manufacture is manufacture and a coefficient touched by fraud is a coefficient untrusted. But a hair trigger hands every rival a one-walk veto: plant a single dressed walk in a neighbour's hundred-walk burst and watch its doubled zone collapse, which is the collapse-gaming T-659's fifth rule was written to kill, now wearing a purity excuse — and a coefficient that a single walk can kill is a coefficient no field can hold. The opposite temptation is a pattern requirement: no strike without a pattern, so a lone dressed walk is always forgiven, which lets a field manufacture one walk per window forever and never face a strike. T-660 answers that the strike is but-for, not hair-trigger and not pattern-gated: subtract the manufactured walks, re-test the two on the genuine walks alone, and strike only if the two falls without them.

The first rule is the but-for rule: the manufactured walks are subtracted from the window total and the cluster share first, under T-657's fifth rule, and the two is then re-tested against T-657's second rule on the genuine walks alone — clustered share at or above one half on counted walks. If the two still clears on genuine walks, the two stands: the struck walks are noted as Struck Walks on the field's line table, subtracted from every later count, and nothing else follows — no collapse, no taper loss, no flag beyond the note. If the two no longer clears without the manufactured walks, the two falls under T-659's collapse rule: straight to one, no taper window, and the fall is a strike, not a lapse, so no echo follows it. The re-test is the threshold: manufacture earns a strike only when it is load-bearing for the coefficient, because a coefficient that stands on its own genuine walks was never the manufacture's creature.

The second rule is the single-walk rule: a single manufactured walk never strikes a two unless it is but-for — unless the two's margin is exactly that walk, the clustered share sitting exactly at the threshold with the walk carrying it over, or the walk being the only clustered walk in the window. A lone dressed walk inside a genuine burst is subtracted and noted, and the coefficient survives with the note travelling on the field's line table, so a reader weighing a later strike can see the field has been pushed once. A single walk is evidence, not a verdict: it proves the field can be dressed, not that its coefficient is dressed.

The third rule is the aggregate re-test rule: where several walks are shown manufactured, the re-test subtracts all of them at once and tests once, never walk by walk — a sequential re-test would let a pattern survive by margins, each walk's removal tested against a total that still contains the next manufactured walk. And a pattern finding — three or more manufactured walks in one window, or manufactured walks from two or more keeper seats, or the same citation dressed twice — is flagged Pattern Manufacture on the field's line table even when the two survives the re-test. The flag is not a strike and collapses nothing, but three Pattern-Manufacture flags in eight windows invite T-650 review to ask whether the threshold is being gamed one walk at a time, because a field that manufactures just below the but-for line every window is manufacturing a strategy, not a walk.

The fourth rule is the challenger-showing rule: the challenger must show manufacture walk by walk, or the pattern showing of the third rule — walks shown to be manufactured, split, or dressed, under T-657's fifth rule — not walks merely suspected, and not a burst merely quieter than the challenger expected. A challenge that shows only suspicion, or only that the field is quieter than the threshold, is struck as a Frivolous Challenge under T-659's third rule, noted on the challenger's line table, and the two stands. The re-test uses only the window's own counted walks: no importing walks from other windows to save a two, and no borrowing a neighbouring boundary's walks, because a coefficient saved by another window's walks is a coefficient that never stood in its own.

The fifth rule is the re-test timing rule: the re-test is decided before the window the coefficient would govern, under T-658's publication discipline — the published band table is corrected before the window, challengeable before it, read-only during it. A strike decided during a window governs the next window, not the current one: the current window completes under the published coefficient flagged Struck-Lineage, parallel to T-659's taper-in-flight rule, save the future-bridge fallback of T-644 — the field that walked through a published doorway does not find the doorway narrowed under its feet. A strike decided before the window governs that window, and the table corrected before it opens is the correction the field walks under.

**T-661 — the Pattern-Count Rule — designed:** T-660 left its pattern-count problem named and open: whether three is the right count for a pattern, or whether the count should scale with window size — whether a thousand-walk window needs more than three dressed walks to flag a pattern. The failure is what a fixed three does at both ends of the scale. In a ten-walk window, three dressed walks are nearly a third of the field: a takeover wearing a pattern's name, and a flag that says pattern is barely saying enough. In a thousand-walk window, three dressed walks are three tenths of one percent: noise wearing a pattern's name, and a flag that says pattern is saying far too much — because at that size three walks can be planted by a rival as cheaply as they can be manufactured by the field itself, and the Pattern-Manufacture flag, which under T-660 invites T-650 review after three flags in eight windows, becomes a flag a rival can farm against any large field at the price of nine walks. The temptation is to keep three fixed because a fixed number is publishable, arguable, and the same for every field — but a number that means a takeover in a small window and noise in a large one is not one rule, it is two accidents sharing a numeral. The opposite temptation is a pure share — a pattern is one percent of the window, say — but a share threshold lets a large field manufacture just below the share forever, and it makes the pattern count a fraction of a walk at small sizes, which is no count at all. T-661 answers that the pattern count scales by the hundred, with a floor of three: one dressed walk per hundred counted walks, rounded up, and never fewer than three.

The first rule is the scaled-count rule: the pattern count P for a window is the greater of three and the ceiling of the window's counted walks divided by one hundred — P = max(3, ceil(N/100)), where N is the window's counted-walk total. A window of ten walks has P = 3, because the ceiling of a tenth is one and the floor holds; a window of a hundred walks has P = 3, because the ceiling of one is one and the floor holds; a window of three hundred and one walks has P = 4, because the ceiling of 3.01 is four; a window of a thousand walks has P = 10. The floor of three is not a concession to the old rule but the recognition that below three there is no pattern to count: one walk is an incident, two walks are a coincidence or a pair, and a pattern begins where a pair ends. The per-hundred step is a design number's companion, not a discovered constant: fixed here so the field has a scale to argue against, itself reviewable under T-650's cadence. A field whose manufactured walks in a window reach P files as Pattern Manufacture under T-660's third rule, with everything that follows from it — the flag on the line table, the three-flags-in-eight-windows invitation to T-650 review — unchanged, because what scales here is the count that earns the flag, not the flag itself.

The second rule is the prong-preservation rule: only the raw-count prong scales, because only the raw count measures volume. T-660's third rule names three prongs for a pattern finding: three or more manufactured walks in one window, manufactured walks from two or more keeper seats, or the same citation dressed twice. The seat prong and the citation prong do not scale with window size, because they measure coordination, not volume: a second keeper seat manufacturing a walk is a second actor whatever the window's size, and a citation dressed twice is one citation worn twice whatever the window's size. A thousand-walk window with manufactured walks from two seats still flags Pattern Manufacture on the seat prong even if the count prong's P = 10 is nowhere near met, because two actors dressing walks is a pattern of actors, and a pattern of actors does not need ten walks to be a pattern. Likewise a single citation dressed twice still flags, because the re-dressing is the pattern, not the number of walks that carry it. What scales is the anonymous bulk: walks from one seat, under distinct citations, with no coordination showing — there the count must clear P, because bulk without coordination is only a pattern when it is large enough, relative to the window it sits in, to stop being noise.

The third rule is the denominator rule: N is the window's counted-walk total as published before the window, not the genuine total after subtraction, because a pattern is judged against the field as presented, and manufacture must not shrink its own denominator. Under T-660 the but-for re-test subtracts the manufactured walks and tests the two on the genuine walks alone — that subtraction is the re-test's machinery, and it stays there. But the pattern count is computed before that subtraction, on the published total, for the same reason T-657 subtracts before comparison only inside the re-test: if the pattern count used the post-subtraction total, a field that manufactured heavily would lower its own P by the manufacture, and a challenger who showed ten manufactured walks in a thousand-walk window would watch P fall from ten to nine as the showing succeeded. The published total is also the total the field itself put forward, challengeable before the window under the published-before-window discipline, so no field can complain that its P was computed on a number it did not publish. A window whose published total is itself challenged and corrected before the window uses the corrected total, because the correction is the publication the window walks under.

The fourth rule is the grandfather rule: the scaled count governs windows opening after its publication, and flags issued under the fixed three stand, noted as Fixed-Three flags on the field's line table. A field flagged Pattern Manufacture under T-660's fixed three in a window that opened before this rule's publication does not get its flag retroactively unflagged because its window's P under the new scale would have been higher: the flag was earned under the rule in force when the window opened, and a rule that rewrites old flags rewrites the record the review reads. But the review reads the flag with its scale noted — a Fixed-Three flag from a thousand-walk window weighs less at T-650 review than a Scaled-Pattern flag from the same size window, because the review knows the first was earned under a count the field has since outgrown, and the second was earned under the scale that fits the window. A field may not re-litigate an old flag under the new scale as a challenge, because a challenge contests a showing, not a scale, and the scale is the review's business, not the challenger's. The grandfather rule is what keeps the scale change honest: it changes the future without laundering the past.

The fifth rule is the below-threshold accumulation rule: manufacture below P in a window is not a flag, but it is a note, and notes accumulate where flags cannot. A window in which manufactured walks are shown but do not reach P files a Below-Scaled Note on the field's line table, showing the manufactured count, P, and the shortfall, and the note travels like a flag for reading purposes without carrying a flag's weight. Three windows in eight carrying Below-Scaled Notes invite T-650 review to ask whether the threshold is being gamed one walk at a time — parallel to T-660's three-flags-in-eight-windows invitation, but weaker by design, because a note is a showing that fell short, not a pattern found. The review that reads three notes asks a different question than the review that reads three flags: not whether the field manufactured a pattern, but whether the field manufactures just below the pattern count every window, which is the strategy T-660's flag logic was written to catch wearing a smaller number. A field that manufactures below P once is unlucky or careless; a field that manufactures below P three times in eight windows is budgeting, and a budget is a pattern even when no single window's count is one.
