**T-662 — the Root-Scaled Count Rule — designed:** T-661 left its scaling-form problem named and open: whether one per hundred is the right scaling, or whether the count should grow by the root of the window or the log of it — whether a ten-thousand-walk window's pattern count of one hundred is too lenient to ever flag, or whether a root-grown count would flag noise again. The failure is what the linear per-hundred scale does at the top end. At a thousand walks it is exacting but reachable: ten manufactured walks are a showing a challenger can assemble and a field cannot shrug off. At ten thousand walks it demands one hundred: a count so large that a field can manufacture ninety-nine walks in every window forever and never once earn a flag, which is not a threshold but a licence, priced at ninety-nine. At a hundred thousand walks it demands one thousand, which no challenger will ever assemble walk by walk, so the pattern rule quietly repeals itself exactly where the windows are largest and the manufacture cheapest to hide. The opposite temptation, a log scale, fails the other way: a count that crawls from three to ten while the window grows a hundredfold is a count that stops measuring the window at all, and a rival can farm flags against a large field at the price of ten walks, which is the flag-farming T-661 was written to kill wearing a slower number. The linear scale asks too much of the challenger; the log scale asks too little of the flag. T-662 answers that the pattern count grows by the root: three times the square root of the window measured in hundreds, with a floor of three.

The first rule is the root-scale formula: the pattern count P for a window is the greater of three and the ceiling of three times the square root of the window's counted walks divided by one hundred — P = max(3, ceil(3·√(N/100))), where N is the window's counted-walk total under T-661's denominator rule. A window of ten walks has P = 3, because the floor holds; a window of a hundred walks has P = 3, because three times the root of one is three and the floor holds with it; a window of three hundred and one walks has P = 6, because three times the root of 3.01 is 5.2 and the ceiling is six, where the linear scale would have said four; a window of a thousand walks has P = 10, because three times the root of ten is 9.49 and the ceiling is ten, the same number the linear scale gives, which is why the linear scale felt right at a thousand and only betrayed itself above it; a window of ten thousand walks has P = 30, because three times the root of one hundred is thirty, where the linear scale demanded one hundred; a window of a hundred thousand walks has P = 95, because three times the root of one thousand is 94.9 and the ceiling is ninety-five, where the linear scale demanded one thousand. The formula is calibrated to agree with the old scale at the sizes where the old scale was trusted — three at a hundred, ten at a thousand — and to part from it only where the old scale stopped being a threshold and became an exemption.

The second rule is the noise rationale, and it is why the root is the form rather than a compromise picked for its table: random counts fluctuate by their root, not by their volume. A field's manufactured walks, if they were mere noise, would scatter around their mean with a spread that grows as the square root of the window, so a threshold meant to separate a pattern from noise must itself grow as the root, or it will either drown in noise at large sizes (the log scale, which grows slower than the noise it must clear) or rise so far above the noise that no pattern can reach it (the linear scale, which grows faster than the noise and leaves a widening band of manufacture that is neither noise nor flag). The root scale tracks the noise it separates from: at every size it sits the same distance, in fluctuation units, above what chance alone would produce. This is counting statistics applied by analogy, not a measured property of walk fields — no field's walk counts have been measured for their fluctuation scale, and if a field's measured overdispersion (T-656's open problem) turns out wider than the root, the root scale will need widening with it. The formula is fixed here so the field has a scale to argue against, itself reviewable under T-650's cadence, not because the root is discovered law.

The third rule is the prospective-grandfather rule: the root scale governs windows opening after its publication, and flags issued under the linear per-hundred scale stand, noted as Linear-Pattern flags on the field's line table. A field flagged Pattern Manufacture under T-661's linear scale in a window that opened before this rule's publication does not get its flag retroactively unflagged because its window's P under the root scale would have been lower: the flag was earned under the rule in force when the window opened, and a harder-earned flag is not undone by an easier scale. But the review reads the flag with its scale noted, and the direction of the weight reverses against T-661's grandfather rule: a Linear-Pattern flag from a ten-thousand-walk window weighs more at T-650 review than a Root-Pattern flag from the same size window, because the first was earned under a count of one hundred and the second under a count of thirty, and a flag earned against a harder count is stronger evidence. Fixed-Three flags from before T-661 still stand below both, weighed as T-661 directed. A field may not re-litigate an old flag under the new scale as a challenge, because a challenge contests a showing, not a scale, and the scale is the review's business, not the challenger's.

The fourth rule is the prong-and-denominator carry: nothing else in T-661 moves. The seat prong and the citation prong still do not scale, because they measure coordination, not volume, and a root scale for the count prong does not make a second seat or a twice-dressed citation any less a pattern. N is still the window's counted-walk total as published before the window, not the genuine total after subtraction, because manufacture must not shrink its own denominator, and a window whose published total is challenged and corrected before the window still uses the corrected total. **T-663 — the Window-Size Definition Rule — designed:** T-662 left its window-size-definition problem named and open: whether N, the window's counted-walk total that the root formula turns into a pattern count, should count all counted walks or only clustered walks — whether a window of a thousand walks with only a hundred clustered ones measures its pattern against the thousand or the hundred. The failure is what the clustered-only reading does to the denominator. A field that wants a small P buys it by flooding its window with single, unclustered walks: a hundred clustered walks inside a thousand-walk window would measure P against the hundred and demand only three, while the same hundred clustered walks standing alone would also demand three, so the flood costs the field nothing and the pattern rule learns nothing from the nine hundred singles that surround the cluster. Worse, the clustered-only reading lets the field choose its own denominator after the fact: clusters are a finding, not a filing, and a field that disputes which walks cluster can dispute N itself, so every pattern challenge becomes a fight about what counts before it becomes a fight about what was manufactured. The opposite reading, counting everything filed in the window whether or not it counts toward anything, fails the other way: a window's N would swell with walks filed to other fields, walks filed twice, and walks filed late to a window already closed, and a challenger would face a P inflated by walks that never belonged to the window at all. T-663 answers that N counts all counted walks published for the window, and nothing else, with counted, published, and window each defined so the number cannot be re-argued after the window opens.

The first rule is the counted-walk definition: a counted walk is a walk filed to the field's line in the window that counts toward the field's band, zone, or seasoning — a walk the line table counts, not merely a walk that exists. A walk filed to a different field's line is not counted here, however genuine, because N measures this window, not the walker's activity. A walk filed twice is counted once, because a duplicate filing is one walk wearing two filings, and the second filing is struck as Duplicate before any count, the only subtraction that shrinks N, since a duplicate never was a second walk. A walk filed for no reason but to earn the coefficient — manufacture under T-657 — is still counted in N, because T-661's denominator discipline is absolute: manufacture must not shrink its own denominator, and a manufactured walk that left N when struck would let a field manufacture its way to a smaller P. A genuine burst split into its walks under T-657 still counts as its walks, because the burst was filed as walks and the split is a showing about manufacture, not a re-filing. Single walks count exactly as clustered walks do: a single is a counted walk that happens not to cluster, and the denominator does not discount it for being lonely.

The second rule is the full-window count: N is the whole published counted-walk total for the window, clustered and single together, and the clustered subset is reported alongside N but never replaces it. A window of a thousand counted walks with a hundred clustered ones has N = 1,000 and P = 10 under the root formula, not N = 100 and P = 3, because the pattern the rule guards against is manufacture inside a window of a thousand, and a threshold set by the hundred would let ninety-nine manufactured walks hide inside a window that only ever had to answer for a hundred. A window of a hundred counted walks, all clustered, has N = 100 and P = 3, the same number the clustered reading would give, which is why the clustered reading felt right in small windows and only betrayed itself when singles could dilute it. **T-664 — the Late-Filing Grace Rule — designed:** T-663 left its late-filing-grace problem named and open: whether a late-filed walk's filing window ever reopens a closed window's N on a showing of good cause — whether a misfiled walk corrected after the digest but before the next window counts in its claimed window or only in its filing window. The question looks like mercy and behaves like a rewrite. A window's digest is the point other parties rely on: N is published, P is derived from it under T-662's root formula, flags are judged against that P, and challengers decide whether to spend their challenge on the window as published. If a good-cause showing could reopen that number, every published window would be provisional until nobody could say when, and the party with the most to gain from a different N would be the party best placed to manufacture the good cause. The opposite answer, that a late walk simply counts wherever it lands and the claimed window never hears of it again, fails the other way: the claimed window's record would show a clean N that everyone involved knows is wrong, a field that systematically misfiles would leave no trace on the windows it distorted, and review of the claimed window would judge a number whose known error is recorded nowhere. T-664 answers that a closed window never reopens, a correction counts only in its filing window, and the claimed window still hears of it — as an annotation that changes no count.

The first rule is the closed-window rule: once a window's digest is published, the window is closed, and its N, its P, and its flags are frozen. No showing reopens them — not good cause, not an admitted error, not new evidence, not a walk that everyone agrees belongs to the window. The freeze is what makes the digest worth relying on: a challenger who reads N = 1,000 and P = 10 knows that no later filing will turn that window into N = 1,001 and P = 11 after the challenge is spent, and a field that wants a different P must earn it in a window still open, not buy it by correcting an old one. A window that was never digested is not closed: walks filed to an undigested window count in it under T-663, because there is nothing yet to rely on. Closure happens at publication, not at the window's end, so the gap between a window's last filing day and its digest is still open season for ordinary filings and corrections, and a walk filed in that gap counts in the window it was filed to, not in grace.

The second rule is the filing-window rule: a correction counts in the window in which the correction is filed, and nowhere else. A walk misfiled to the wrong field's line and refiled to the right one counts in the refiling window, under T-663's counted-walk definition, because the refiling is the filing the right line's table counts. A walk first filed late — never filed anywhere before, claiming an earlier window — counts in the window of its first filing, because a claim about which window a walk belongs to is not a filing to that window, and T-663 already fixed the filing window as the window of record. The filing window's N therefore absorbs every correction filed inside it, which is honest: the walks are in the line's table for that window, and the denominator must not pretend otherwise. But the absorption is published as a subtotal, under the sixth rule, so the filing window's review can see how much of its N arrived as corrections rather than as first filings.

The third rule is the grace-attachment rule: a correction filed after the claimed window's digest but before the NEXT window's digest is published as a Grace Correction attached to the claimed window's record. **T-665 — the Grace-Note Weight Rule — designed:** T-664 left its grace-note-weight problem named and open: whether a Grace Correction attached to a claimed window's record weighs at review of that window, or is annotation only — whether a window carrying ten grace attachments is judged as a window whose number was ten walks wrong. The two pure answers both fail, and they fail in opposite directions. Treat the attachments as annotation only and review goes blind: a window published at N = 1,000, later shown to have missed sixty walks, is judged exactly like a window whose number was never questioned, and a field that systematically files late learns that the cost of late filing is a note nobody reads. Treat the attachments as a recount and the closed-window rule dies by the back door: judging the window as if its N were N + A reopens the number T-664 froze, lets a challenger or a defender re-derive P after the challenge is spent, and turns every grace attachment into a second, unappealable digest. T-665 answers that grace attachments weigh at review without ever moving a count: the frozen N and P stand exactly as published, and the attachment ledger is read as a disclosed error band that grades how much trust the frozen number deserves.

The first rule is the error-band rule: the claimed window's review reads its published N together with its attachment count A, the number of Grace Corrections attached to its record under T-664, and treats the window's true count as disclosed to lie in the band the attachments describe, not as corrected to any point in it. Every T-664 attachment asserts a walk that belongs to the claimed window but was counted in its filing window, so the disclosed direction is undercount: the window's published N missed at least the attached walks, and the band runs upward from N toward N + A. The band is disclosed, not decided: attachments are assertions published with stated reasons, not findings, and a reason later struck as false under T-664's fifth rule removes that attachment from A, with the weight recomputed and the note amended, never silently left standing. A window whose attachments were all struck therefore returns to annotation-only weight, and the strike, not the original attachment, is what review remembers.

The second rule is the weight-band rule: the ratio r = A / N, attachments against published count, sets the weight in three bands. Below one percent, attachments are annotation only: the window is reviewed exactly as published, and the attachments are read as the ordinary friction of filing, not as evidence about the window. From one percent up to but not including five percent, the window carries a Grace-Weight Note: review must answer, in writing, the sensitivity question — whether each flag judged against the frozen P would survive if the window's true count were N + A — and the flag stands as judged, with the answer attached to it. At five percent and above, the window carries a Heavy Grace Note: its flags stand as judged, but they stand as provisional, marked so that any later proceeding citing the window as precedent reads the note first, and three Heavy Grace Notes in eight windows invite T-650 review, on the same pattern as T-664's Grace-Flood Notes, wrong-line strikes, and Dilution Notes. The bands are deliberately coarse: one and five percent are round thresholds a reviewer can apply without a calculator, and a band edge crossed by a single attachment is still a band edge crossed, because a rule that softens at its own boundary invites exactly the attachment-counting games it exists to stop.

The third rule is the no-recount rule: weight never changes N, P, or any flag. The sensitivity question in the middle band is a question, not a recomputation: the reviewer asks whether the flag would survive at N + A, answers it, and the flag's published outcome is untouched by the answer either way. A flag that would not survive at N + A is not overturned, because overturning it would be the recount T-664 forbids, and a flag that would survive is not strengthened, because the attachments disclose error in the window's own number, and error disclosed does not become evidence for the flag. What the answer buys is transparency for the next proceeding: a later window citing this flag as precedent cites it with the sensitivity answer attached, so precedent built on a number known to be wrong carries its own warning label. The Heavy Grace Note works the same way at larger scale: provisional means cited-with-warning, never vacated.

The fourth rule is the window-separation rule: grace weight lives on the claimed window, grace flood lives on the filing window, and the same correction batch can trigger both without double-counting anything. A batch of sixty grace corrections filed into window W2 and attached to window W1 gives W1 a Heavy Grace Note if sixty reaches five percent of W1's N, and gives W2 a Grace-Flood Note if sixty reaches one quarter of W2's N, and neither note moves either window's count. The two notes answer different questions: the weight note asks how much W1's published number can be trusted, the flood note asks whether W2's denominator was diluted by corrections, and a reviewer who confuses them will either excuse a flooded filing window because the claimed window looks clean, or condemn a claimed window because its corrections happened to land in a small filing window. A correction attached to a Reopened-N window under T-664's grandfather weighs one band higher than its ratio alone would place it: a Reopened-N window whose attachments would otherwise be annotation-only carries a Grace-Weight Note, and one that would carry a Grace-Weight Note carries a Heavy Grace Note, because a window whose number has already been reopened once and then shown wrong again has twice demonstrated instability, and review reads the two marks together, exactly as T-664's grandfather requires.

The fifth rule is the citation rule: a window's grace weight travels with every citation of that window. A later design, report card, or proceeding that cites a flagged window's outcome as precedent must cite the window's Grace-Weight or Heavy Grace Note alongside it, and a citation that omits the note is itself a misstatement of the record, noted as such where the citation is published. This is the teeth the annotation-only answer lacked: a field can file late and accept the note, but it cannot file late, accept the note, and then cite the window as clean precedent elsewhere, because the note follows the citation. A window that earns a Heavy Grace Note and is then cited three times without its note earns a Citation-Strike on the citing record, and three Citation-Strikes in eight windows invite T-650 review of the citing field, not of the cited window — the abuse being punished is the laundering of a warned precedent into a clean one.

Worked cases fix the rules. A window W1 published at N = 1,000, later carrying A = 5 grace attachments: r = 0.5 percent, annotation only, reviewed exactly as published. A window W2 published at N = 1,000, carrying A = 10: r = 1 percent, Grace-Weight Note, and review answers in writing whether each W2 flag would survive at N + A = 1,010, with every flag standing as judged whatever the answer. A window W5 carrying A = 10, of which 6 attachments are later struck as false reasons: A recomputed to 4, r = 0.4 percent, the Grace-Weight Note amended to annotation only, and the strikes published on W5's record as the reason the weight fell.

What counts as surviving the sensitivity question — whether a flag survives if its margin exceeds the band width, or only if its reasoning holds at every point in the band, with no sensitivity-standard rule fixed here (admitted here — T-665's sensitivity-standard problem, newly open). A Grace-Weighted bridge is a claimed window reviewed with its attachment band read alongside its frozen number. A Sensitivity-Answered bridge is a middle-band flag carrying its written sensitivity answer. A Provisional-Flagged bridge is a heavy-band flag standing with its warning attached. A Citation-Struck bridge is a precedent cited without its note, struck on the citing record — the cited window's flags still stand, and the strike is the record.

**T-666 — the Weight-Band Calibration Rule — designed:** T-665 left its weight-band-calibration problem named and open: whether one and five percent are the right band edges, or whether the bands should scale with window size — a small window's single attachment crosses one percent at N = 100, a large window's hundred attachments barely reach it at N = 10,000. The fixed-ratio answer misfires at exactly one end, and the misfire is not symmetric. At the small end it is a real failure: one late walk on a window of a hundred is ordinary filing friction, not evidence about the window, yet the fixed one-percent edge promotes it to a Grace-Weight Note, and five late walks promote a hundred-window to Heavy, which is a warning label earned by a handful. At the large end the complaint dissolves on inspection: ninety-nine missing walks on a window of ten thousand are 0.99 percent of the number, and a number wrong by under one percent is not a number review should distrust more because the absolute count looks large — the ratio already is the measure of trust, and an absolute-count alarm at large scale would punish large windows for being large. T-666 therefore calibrates one-sidedly: absolute floors lift the edges for small windows, and the ratio edges stand unmodified for large ones.

The first rule is the calibrated-edge rule: the low edge is the larger of one percent and five divided by N, and the high edge is the larger of five percent and twenty-five divided by N. In symbols, e_low = max(1%, 5/N) and e_high = max(5%, 25/N), and the band is read from r = A/N against those edges exactly as T-665 read it against the fixed edges: below e_low, annotation only; from e_low up to but not including e_high, Grace-Weight Note; at e_high and above, Heavy Grace Note. The floors are attachment counts, not percentages: five attachments are the smallest error worth a written sensitivity answer, twenty-five the smallest worth a provisional warning, whatever the window size. A window too small for five attachments to be a small share therefore keeps its bands honest: its edges rise to meet the floors instead of its bands falling to meet a single walk.

The second rule is the continuity rule: every T-665 worked case at N = 1,000 stands unchanged, because at N = 1,000 the floors do not bind. Five divided by 1,000 is 0.5 percent, below the one-percent edge, and twenty-five divided by 1,000 is 2.5 percent, below the five-percent edge, so the calibrated edges are exactly one and five percent and the three T-665 cases — A = 5 annotation only, A = 10 Grace-Weight, A = 60 Heavy — come out identically. Calibration is a correction to the small end, not a revision of the middle: any design that changed the outcome for the ordinary thousand-window would be a new rule wearing calibration's name, and T-666 refuses it. The same arithmetic fixes the small end transparently. At N = 100, the calibrated edges are five percent and twenty-five percent: A = 1 gives r = 1 percent, below the low edge, annotation only where the fixed rule would have written a Grace-Weight Note; A = 5 gives r = 5 percent, Grace-Weight Note; A = 25 gives r = 25 percent, Heavy Grace Note. At N = 10,000, the floors do not bind either — 5/10,000 and 25/10,000 are far below the ratio edges — so A = 99 stays annotation only and A = 100 earns its Grace-Weight Note at exactly one percent, and the large window is judged by the same ratio as every other window, neither excused nor punished for its size.

The third rule is the order-of-operations rule: calibrate first, then apply T-665's Reopened-N lift. A Reopened-N window's one-band-higher treatment applies to the band the calibrated edges produce, never to the band the fixed edges would have produced, and never before calibration. Lifting first and calibrating second would double-count the correction: a small Reopened-N window with A = 1 at N = 100 would lift from annotation to Grace-Weight under the fixed edge and then calibrate nowhere, keeping a note the calibrated rule says it never earned. Calibrating first gives it annotation only, and the Reopened-N lift then carries it one band higher to a Grace-Weight Note — the lift is the window's own history speaking, not the edge misfiring, and the two marks stay distinguishable on the record. The same order governs struck attachments: when a strike recomputes A under T-665, the band is recomputed under the calibrated edges from the new A, never patched from the old band.

The fourth rule is the prospective-application rule: calibration applies to windows reviewed after T-666, and windows already banded under the fixed edges keep their bands. A published Grace-Weight or Heavy Grace Note is not re-banded because the edges moved, for the same reason T-665's weight never moves a count: re-banding a published note would rewrite the review record after the challenge is spent, and a field that accepted a note under the rule in force has no grievance that a later, kinder edge exists. The one exception is recomputation on a changed A: when a new attachment arrives or a strike removes one, the window's band is recomputed under the calibrated edges, because the review is already reopening the weight for a new fact, and it reopens under the current rule. A note that falls on such a recomputation is amended on the record with the reason stated — the new A and the calibrated edge that produced the fall — never silently lowered.

The fifth rule is the floor-hugging rule: the floors must not become a target. A field that repeatedly files just under a floor — A = 4 on window after window, each time with r above the uncalibrated one-percent edge — is not filing cleanly, it is aiming at the floor. Worked cases fix the rules. A window W1 published at N = 100, carrying A = 1: calibrated edges 5% and 25%, r = 1%, annotation only — the fixed rule's Grace-Weight Note corrected. **T-669 — the Anchor-Weight Rule — designed:** T-668 left its anchor-weight problem named and open: whether a count anchor should ever change the weight a note carries at review. A "Grace-Weight, 1 of 10" note and a "Grace-Weight, 10 of 100" note wear the same band under T-665's edges, capped under T-667 and fixed under T-668, yet they rest on very different evidence — one walk against nine, ten walks against ninety — and no rule fixed whether the review treats them alike. The tempting answers both fail. Treating them alike lets a single walk carry the same consequences as a pattern, so one stray attachment can invite a T-650 review or hold a provisional flag. Treating them by re-banding — demoting the thin note to an annotation — breaks T-668's coarse-grid settlement, which said one walk in ten honestly earns its note. T-669 splits the difference the only way that keeps both settlements: the band is the grade, the anchor is the weight, and consequences follow weight, not band alone.

The first rule is the weight-class rule. Every Grace-Weight Note and Heavy Grace Note carries a weight class read from its anchored count A, not from its ratio r and not from its band. A note with A = 1 is Thin: it stands as a true record of one walk, but it is advisory only. A note with A >= 2 is Standing: it carries the full consequences its band names. The line is deliberately at one, not at a ratio: at any window size, a single attachment is one observation, and one observation is a report, not a pattern. A note with A = 0 is not a note at all — it is the annotation-or-nothing T-665 already gives below the edge — so weight classes apply only where a note exists. The class is written with the anchor, never instead of it: "Grace-Weight, 1 of 10 (Thin)" and "Grace-Weight, 10 of 100 (Standing)" are the full forms, and a citation that drops the class while keeping the band is a partial citation, corrected by re-anchoring, not by re-banding.

The second rule is the consequences-follow-weight rule, and it is where the split does its work. A Thin note cannot alone invite a T-650 review, cannot alone hold a provisional flag, and cannot alone count toward any pattern threshold — the three-in-eight Grace-Flood Note threshold from T-664, the cap-hugging pattern from T-667, and the coarse-grid pattern from T-668 all count Standing notes only. A Thin Heavy Grace Note still reads Heavy — half the walks missed at N = 10 is half the walks missed, and T-668's band stands — but its provisional flags stay advisory until corroborated: the warning is recorded, the hold is not imposed. A Standing note carries everything its band names, including provisional flags for Heavy and pattern-threshold counting. Nothing here demotes a band and nothing here promotes a count: a Thin note that later gains a second attachment is recomputed under T-665's strike-and-recompute rule, and only then, with A = 2, becomes Standing.

The third rule is the corroboration rule, because a Thin note that can never gain weight is a dead record, and a Thin note that gains weight by repetition alone is a loophole. Two Thin notes on the same field within eight windows corroborate each other for pattern purposes: together they count as one Standing observation toward a pattern threshold, though each note stays Thin on its own record and neither alone holds a provisional flag. Three Thin notes within eight windows corroborate to a full Standing pattern observation — the third walk is the pattern, not the repetition — and a Thin Heavy note corroborated by any second Thin note on the same field gains its provisional flags, the hold imposed by the pair, not by either walk alone. Corroboration requires the same field: Thin notes from different fields do not combine, and a Thin note corroborated once does not corroborate again — the same two walks cannot be spent twice toward two thresholds. A Standing note needs no corroboration and gives none; it already carries its own weight.

Weighing sits between anchoring and lifting because the weight is read from the anchored count, and the lift then carries the weighed band one higher without changing its weight — a Thin note lifted by Reopened-N history reads "Heavy, 1 of 10 (lifted, Thin)", its flags advisory, its warning earned by the reopening and its thinness earned by the window, each marked with its own source. **T-670 — the Corroboration-Window Rule — designed:** T-669 left its corroboration-window problem named and open: how far apart corroborating windows may sit. T-669 borrowed eight windows from T-664's Grace-Flood threshold — three Grace corrections in eight windows invite a T-650 review — and used it as the span inside which two or three Thin notes on the same field corroborate each other. The borrowing was never justified, and the justification matters, because the two spans measure different things. T-664's eight windows measure accumulation: how many corrections pile up before the pile itself is worth a review. Corroboration measures persistence: whether a second thin observation is still evidence about the same condition the first observation reported, or merely a coincidence wearing the same field name across a season. A span built for accumulation will over-credit coincidence; a span built for persistence must be short enough that the condition it spans is plausibly one condition, and long enough that a genuine repeat has a chance to arrive. T-670 fixes the corroboration span on its own ground, and retires the borrowed eight.

The first rule is the span rule. Two or three Thin notes on the same field corroborate only if every corroborating note falls within three windows of the first note in the chain: a chain opened at window W may be completed by notes at W, W+1, W+2, or W+3, and no later window completes it. Three is chosen because it is the smallest span that survives an ordinary review rhythm — a note filed, a window in which the taker looks and finds nothing new, a window in which the repeat arrives — while still being short enough that the field's condition cannot plausibly have turned over twice inside it. Eight windows, by contrast, spans a quarter of a review year under the loop's own cadence, long enough for a field to fail, be repaired, and fail again for an unrelated reason, and a pair spanning that distance proves nothing except that the field has failed twice in a season. The corroboration span is therefore three, not eight, and the eight-window flood span keeps its own job untouched: T-664's flood threshold still counts Standing notes across eight windows, and a corroborated pair becomes one Standing observation dated at the completing note, which the flood count then measures from that date forward, in its own eight.

The second rule is the gap rule. Inside the three-window span, no single gap between consecutive notes in a chain may exceed two windows: a note at W followed by a note at W+3 completes a chain only if a note at W+1 or W+2 also stands between them, and a note at W followed by nothing until W+3 does not complete it — the chain has a hole in it wider than the silence a persisting condition leaves. The gap rule is what keeps the span rule honest: without it, a chain could claim persistence across a silence that is itself evidence the condition lapsed. A gap of three windows or more breaks the chain outright, and the broken chain's notes do not linger as half-corroboration for a later chain: the note after the gap opens a new chain, and the notes before the gap stand alone, each still Thin, each still on the record, each still advisory.

The third rule is the distinct-window rule. Corroboration requires distinct windows: two Thin notes filed in the same window on the same field count as one Thin observation, not as a corroborated pair, however the filings are dated inside the window. Two notes from one window are one walk seen twice, or one walk filed twice — and T-663's duplicate-identity problem is exactly the warning against letting a filing count as a second observation. A chain therefore needs at least two windows for a pair and at least three windows for a trio, with the span rule capping how far those windows may spread. A same-window second note is not discarded: it is recorded as a duplicate filing on the first note, it strengthens the record's confidence that the first note was filed carefully, and it adds nothing to any threshold, any flag, or any pattern count.

The fourth rule is the expiry rule. A Thin note that has not been corroborated within its span expires as corroborable, and expiry is a change in power, not a change in the record. The expired note stays on the record exactly as filed, still Thin, still advisory, still citable as history — a reader may cite it to show the field failed before, and the citation carries its date and its expired state — but it can no longer complete a chain, and a later Thin note on the same field does not revive it. Expiry is judged at each digest: a chain opened at W is open through the digest of W+3 and expired at the digest of W+4, and a corroborating note filed after expiry opens a new chain dated at its own window. Nothing here is retroactive in either direction: an expired note does not retroactively lose the advisory warning it carried while open, and a completed chain does not retroactively promote the first note's window — the pair counts toward thresholds only from the completing digest forward, exactly as T-669's prospective-application rule requires for weight changes.

The fifth rule is the recomputation rule, which ties the span to T-665's strike-and-recompute and T-669's weigh-and-lift order. When a strike removes a note from a chain, the chain is recomputed from the surviving notes under the span and gap rules as they stand at recomputation: a pair that loses one member falls back to a single Thin note, a trio that loses its middle member may fail the gap rule and fall back to two unlinked Thin notes, and a trio that loses an end member may survive as a pair if the survivors still satisfy span and gap. The recomputation is recorded with the reason stated, the surviving notes named, and the new weight class — a note that was Standing by corroboration and falls back to Thin loses its pattern counting and its provisional flags at recomputation, and the record says so in plain words rather than silently unholding a flag. A chain broken by a strike cannot be repaired by a later note claiming the struck walk: the struck walk is gone, and the later note opens its own chain. The order of operations extends by one harmless step at the end: calibrate, cap, anchor, weigh, lift, then chain — chaining last, because a chain's weight is read only after each member's own weight is fixed.

The sixth rule is the flood-span separation rule, stated once so the two spans are never borrowed from each other again. The corroboration span is three windows and answers whether observations combine. The flood span is eight windows and answers whether Standing observations accumulate to a review. A writer who cites one span for the other's job has made a citation error, corrected by re-anchoring the citation to the right rule, not by re-banding either span. The separation is also the reason T-670 does not disturb T-664: no flood threshold moves, no flood count is recomputed, and a pair corroborated under T-670 inside three windows still needs two more Standing observations inside eight windows, dated from the completing note, before any flood note issues.

Admitted here, still open: whether the corroboration span should be measured in windows at all, or in walks — a field reviewed rarely may see three windows pass with only a handful of walks between them, while a field reviewed often may see dozens of walks inside three windows, and no walk-count span is fixed here (admitted here — T-670's span-measure problem, newly open). Whether expiry may ever be waived for documented cause — a corroborating walk delayed by a closure, a sealed record, or a taker's own postponement may arrive at W+4 through no fault of the field, and no expiry-waiver rule is fixed here (admitted here — T-670's expiry-waiver problem, newly open). **T-671 — the Expiry-Waiver Rule — designed:** T-670 left its expiry-waiver problem named and open: a corroborating walk delayed by a closure, a sealed record, or a taker's own postponement may arrive at W+4 through no fault of the field, and no rule fixed whether expiry may ever be waived for documented cause. The hard case is real — a chain opened at W, open through the digest of W+3 and expired at the digest of W+4, can be killed by a closure that had nothing to do with the field's condition — but the easy answer is a trap. A waiver that can be claimed after the fact, for any reason, or twice over, is not an exception to expiry; it is expiry abolished by petition, and every chain that ever missed its span would return wearing a waiver. T-671 therefore grants the waiver narrowly, on three causes only, claimed before expiry, extended by one window only, and marked forever on anything it completes.

The first rule is the cause rule. Only three causes qualify, and each must be documented, not merely asserted. A closure qualifies: the field, the window, or the walk itself was closed for the window in which the corroborating note would otherwise have been filed, and the closure is on a record the reviewer can check. A sealed record qualifies: the record the corroborating walk needed was sealed or otherwise unavailable to the taker for that window, and the seal is named. A taker's postponement qualifies: the taker itself deferred the corroborating walk to a later window, and the deferral is on the taker's own record. Nothing else qualifies. The field's own inaction does not qualify — a field that simply produced no repeat has not been delayed, it has not repeated. A taker's oversight without a record does not qualify — an undocumented deferral is indistinguishable from a walk that never happened. The mere absence of a repeat does not qualify — absence is what expiry already prices in. A cause asserted without a checkable record is treated as no cause, and the petition is denied on that ground alone, without reaching anything else.

The second rule is the before-expiry rule. A waiver extends an open chain; it never resurrects an expired one. The petition must be filed before the digest of W+4 at which the chain would expire, naming the cause, the window or windows the cause covered, and the record that documents it. A petition filed at or after that digest is denied as untimely however good its cause, because a chain that has already expired has already changed the record's expectations — later notes on that field already open their own chains dated at their own windows, and reviving the old chain would strand those new chains mid-flight. The one mercy in the rule is its timing: a petition filed while the chain is open tolls nothing and promises nothing, but it preserves the question for decision at the expiry digest, so a taker who files early is not punished for the digest's own schedule. A chain whose petition is still undecided at the expiry digest is held open until the decision, for that digest only, and no longer.

The third rule is the one-window rule. A granted waiver extends the chain by exactly one window: a chain opened at W, otherwise open through the digest of W+3, is open through the digest of W+4 if waived, and expires at the digest of W+5. No second waiver issues on the same chain, for the same cause or any other — a chain that needs two waivers has not been delayed, it has not corroborated — and no waiver stacks a further window onto a waived window. A completing note filed at W+4 under waiver completes the chain exactly as a note at W+3 would have, dated at the completing note, counting forward from that digest under T-670's prospective rule. The span and gap rules otherwise stand unchanged, with one narrow exception stated in the fourth rule: the extension moves expiry, it does not widen the span for any other purpose, and a chain that still has not completed by the waived digest expires then, finally, with no further petition.

The fourth rule is the cause-covered-gap rule. Under T-670, a gap of three windows or more between consecutive notes breaks the chain, because silence is itself evidence the condition lapsed. A silence fully covered by a documented qualifying cause is not that evidence: a field closed for a window cannot be said to have lapsed during the closure, and a record sealed for a window cannot be said to have gone quiet. A gap window fully covered by the granted waiver's cause therefore does not break the chain, and the notes on either side of it may still combine if the span and the waived expiry allow. The exception is narrow in both directions: it covers at most one gap window per chain, it covers only the window or windows the documented cause actually covered, and a gap that extends even one window beyond the covered window breaks the chain as T-670 already provides. A waiver that covers the gap but not the expiry, or the expiry but not the gap, is granted only for the part it covers, and the record says which.

The fifth rule is the decision-and-mark rule. A waiver is granted or denied in writing at the expiry digest, with the cause named, the record cited, the extended expiry date stated, and the decision attached to the chain's record where any later reader will see it before the chain's notes. A denied waiver leaves the chain on its ordinary expiry, and the denial itself extends nothing — a denied petition is not a partial waiver, and a chain is not held open by the fact that someone asked. A granted waiver marks everything it touches: a pair or trio completed only by waiver — one that would have expired without it — counts as Standing exactly as any corroborated pair counts, but it carries a Waived-Completion mark into every later use. The flood count includes it, the citation of it names the waiver and its cause, and a citation that omits the mark is a misstatement of the record on the same pattern as T-670's grace-weight citation rule. The mark is transparency, not discount: the completion counts fully, and counts honestly.

The sixth rule is the abuse guard. Three waivers granted on the same field in eight windows invite a T-650 review, on the same pattern as T-664's flood threshold and T-670's flood separation: a field that needs waivers that often is either chronically closed, chronically sealed, or chronically deferred, and any of the three is itself worth a review. A waiver granted on a cause later shown false is struck, and the chain is recomputed under T-670's recomputation rule from the surviving notes: a Standing observation that depended on the waived completion falls back to Thin, its pattern counting and provisional flags fall with it, and the record states the strike and the cause's failure in plain words. A waived completion may never itself be cited as precedent for another waiver: each waiver stands on its own documented cause, and a field that cites its last waiver as the reason for its next one has cited a mark, not a cause, and the petition is denied on that ground.

Admitted here, still open: whether the corroboration span should be measured in windows at all, or in walks — T-670's span-measure problem, carried forward unsolved, since a waived chain on a rarely reviewed field still spans three windows that may hold only a handful of walks. Whether a Thin Heavy note whose chain expires should keep any trace of its near-corroboration — T-670's near-miss problem, carried forward, since a chain denied a waiver at W+4 is, on the record, indistinguishable from one that never came close. Whether a closure covering two windows should ever justify a two-window extension — the one-window rule denies it here by declaration, and no multi-window-closure rule is fixed (admitted here — T-671's multi-window-closure problem, newly open). What documentation standard a taker's postponement must meet before it counts as a record rather than an assertion — a dated deferral order, a logged reschedule, or something thinner is not fixed here (admitted here — T-671's postponement-proof problem, newly open). T-669's thin-flag problem (whether a Thin Heavy note should ever impose a provisional flag on its own) and weight-decay problem (whether weight decays as windows age), T-668's tiny-window problem (whether a window below ten walks is reviewable at all), T-667's cap-holding problem, T-666's absolute-trigger problem, T-665's attachment-netting and sensitivity-standard problems, T-664's correction-cap and grace-window-length problems, T-663's duplicate-identity problem, T-661's pattern-cap problem, T-660's tie and challenger-cost problems, and all other problems carried in T-670's admitted-unsolved paragraph, carried forward by reference.

A Waiver-Granted bridge is a written grant at the expiry digest, stating the extended expiry at W+4 and any cause-covered gap window. **T-672 — the Multi-Window-Closure Rule — designed:** T-671 left its multi-window-closure problem named and open: a closure covering two windows, and the one-window rule denying a two-window extension by declaration. The denial was honest as a stopgap — a waiver that stretches to fit any closure is expiry abolished by petition — but it is too blunt as a settlement, because not all causes are alike. A closure is not a delay in the ordinary sense; it is an absence of opportunity. A field closed for two windows could not have been walked in either of them, so the silence of those windows is not evidence about the field's condition at all, and T-670's persistence rationale — a chain spans windows only while the condition is plausibly one condition — is not offended by spanning windows in which nothing could have been observed. T-672 therefore grants the two-window extension, narrowly: closures only, one continuous event only, fully covered windows only, capped at two, claimed in the original petition, and marked twice over on anything it completes.

The first rule is the closure-only rule. Only closures earn a multi-window extension. A sealed record does not: a seal is partial by nature — it can be lifted in part, worked around through another record, or narrowed by petition — and a record sealed for two windows is two windows of a taker not trying hard enough, not two windows of nobody able to walk. A taker's postponement does not: the taker controls its own deferral, and a longer deferral earning a longer extension would reward the taker for deferring longer, paying the petitioner in patience for its own delay. A cause the petitioner controls cannot extend the petitioner's own chain twice over, and a cause the petitioner could have mitigated cannot earn the mitigation's absence as a second window. The closure must meet T-671's cause definition unchanged: the field, the window, or the walk itself was closed, and the closure is on a record the reviewer can check. A closure asserted without a checkable record is treated as no cause, exactly as in T-671, and the petition is denied on that ground alone.

The second rule is the single-event rule. The two windows must be covered by one continuous closure event, on one record: a single closure order spanning both windows, a single shutdown log covering the interval, a single seal on the field's own door. Two separate closures, even back-to-back with no open window between them, are two causes, and T-671's no-second-waiver rule bars stacking them — a chain that needs two closures has needed two waivers, and the second is denied however tidy the seam. The petition names the single event and its span, and the record must show continuity, not merely adjacency: a closure order reissued daily is daily closures wearing one event's name, and the reviewer treats it as what it is. A gap between two closure events, even a window in which the field was merely unobserved rather than closed, breaks the singleness, and the petition falls back to a single-window waiver for the covered window if one window qualifies on its own.

The third rule is the full-coverage rule. Each extended window must be fully covered. A window half-closed — a closure lifted mid-window, or imposed mid-window — earns no extension for that window, because the taker had part of the window to walk, and part of a window is a chance, not a closure. Partial coverage counts toward nothing: it neither extends expiry nor excuses a gap window, and it is noted on the petition's record as partial rather than silently rounded up or down. One fully covered window plus one partial window therefore earns a one-window extension only, under T-671's ordinary rule, with the partial window named and unextended. Two fully covered windows earn two. The reviewer judges coverage window by window against the closure record, and a window whose coverage the record leaves doubtful is treated as partial — doubt resolves against extension, because extension is the exception and expiry is the rule.

The fourth rule is the two-window cap and its expiry arithmetic. The extension equals the number of fully covered consecutive windows, capped at two. A chain opened at W, otherwise open through the digest of W+3 and expired at the digest of W+4, is open through the digest of W+4 if waived for one window and expires at the digest of W+5, exactly as T-671 provides; if waived for two windows it is open through the digest of W+5 and expires at the digest of W+6, and a completing note filed at W+4 or W+5 completes the chain exactly as a note at W+3 would have, dated at the completing note, counting forward from that digest under T-670's prospective rule. Three or more fully covered windows still earn two and no more: beyond two windows the persistence rationale fails — a condition unobserved for three windows is not plausibly one condition, it is a condition that may have lapsed and returned wearing the same field name — and the chain expires at W+6, with later notes opening new chains dated at their own windows. The double extension must be claimed in the original petition, filed before the digest of W+4 under T-671's before-expiry rule: a granted single-window waiver cannot later be upgraded to a double, because the upgrade would be a second waiver, and a petition amended before the W+4 digest to claim double is one petition amended, not two petitions filed.

The fifth rule is the gap, mark, and abuse-guard rule. T-671's cause-covered-gap exception extends to at most two gap windows, and only when both are fully covered by the same single closure, contiguously: a silence fully covered by the closure is not evidence the condition lapsed, but a gap window beyond the covered pair breaks the chain as T-670 already provides, and a gap window only partially covered breaks it too. **T-673 — the Effective-Closure Rule — designed:** T-672 left its partial-closure problem named and open: a window half-closed, but the walk itself impossible in the open half — a closure lifted mid-window while the walk's subject was gone, or the record destroyed in the open half — leaves a window that was open in name and closed in fact, and T-672's full-coverage rule gives that window nothing, because the taker had part of the window in calendar time. Calendar time is the wrong measure. A window is not an opportunity because its door stood open; it is an opportunity only while a walk could actually have been taken in it. T-673 therefore earns a partial window an extension, narrowly: not because the window was mostly closed, but because the open half contained no walkable opportunity at all — and the petitioner proves that, on a checkable record, or the window stays unextended.

The first rule is the walkable-opportunity test. A window is walkable only while three conditions hold together: the walk's subject is present and reachable, the record the walk would read is intact and accessible, and the route to the field is open. Lose any one of the three for the whole of the open half, and the open half is not an opportunity: a subject removed before the closure lifted and not returned within the window, a record destroyed or sealed in the open half with no surviving copy the taker could read, a route washed out or barred for the open half's duration. Lose one of the three for only part of the open half, and the window stays partial and unextended — a single walkable hour is a chance, and T-672's "part of a window is a chance" stands for every part that was genuinely walkable. The test is about the walk this chain would have taken, not walks in general: a field open to other takers for other purposes is still closed in fact to a walk whose subject is gone, and a record intact for other readers is still destroyed for a walk that needed the one destroyed page.

The second rule is the proof standard, and it is deliberately the strictest in the waiver chain. The petitioner proves impossibility the way T-671 proves a cause and T-672 proves a closure: on a record the reviewer can check — a removal log, a destruction certificate, a route-closure notice, a witness statement tied to a dated record — naming the missing condition, the interval it was missing for, and why no substitute walk existed. An assertion without a checkable record is treated as no proof, exactly as an uncheckable closure is treated as no cause, and the petition is denied on that ground alone. Doubt resolves against extension twice over here, because the claim is stronger than T-672's: the petitioner asks the reviewer to treat a window the calendar says was open as a window that was closed, and a rule that grants that on a shrug would let every half-closed window dress itself as effective closure. A window whose walkability the record leaves doubtful is treated as walkable, and therefore partial and unextended.

The third rule is the one-effective-window cap and its place in the extension arithmetic. At most one effective-closure window may be counted on any one petition, and it counts as one window toward T-672's two-window cap: a double extension may consist of two fully covered windows, or of one fully covered window plus one effective-closure window, but never of two effective-closure windows — a chain that needs two windows of proved impossibility has needed two exercises of the reviewer's hardest judgment, and the second is denied however clean its proof. An effective-closure window claimed alone, with no fully covered window beside it, earns a one-window extension under T-671's ordinary arithmetic: a chain opened at W, otherwise expired at the digest of W+4, is open through the digest of W+4 and expires at the digest of W+5, with a completing note at W+4 completing exactly as a note at W+3 would have, dated at the completing note under T-670's prospective rule. An effective-closure window paired with a fully covered window earns the double: open through the digest of W+5, expires at the digest of W+6, on T-672's arithmetic unchanged. The effective-closure window must be claimed in the original petition before the W+4 digest, on the same no-upgrade rule as a double: a granted single-window waiver cannot later be recharacterised as effective-closure, and a petition amended before the W+4 digest to claim it is one petition amended, not two petitions filed.

The fourth rule is the gap, mark, and abuse-guard rule. An effective-closure window may excuse a cause-covered gap window under T-671/T-672 only when the gap window's silence is itself covered by the same proved impossibility — the same missing subject, the same destroyed record, the same barred route, for the whole gap window — and at most one such gap window per petition, because the effective-closure judgment is already spent once on the extension itself. A completion only by effective closure carries three marks into every later use where applicable: the Waived-Completion mark from T-671, the Double-Extension mark from T-672 where the extension was a double, and the Effective-Closure mark from this rule, naming the missing condition and its interval. The flood count includes it, the citation of it names every mark it carries, and a citation omitting any is a misstatement of the record on the T-671 pattern. For the abuse guard, an effective-closure window counts as one waiver toward the three-waivers-in-eight-windows T-650 invitation and carries window-weight two on the field's tally, on the T-672 pattern for doubles: a field whose windows keep proving unwalkable is either chronically emptied or chronically mismanaged, and either is itself worth a review, and two effective-closure windows on the same field in eight windows — across different petitions, since one petition allows only one — invite a T-650 review on their own. An effective-closure grant on a condition later shown present, intact, or passable is struck exactly as in T-671, and the chain is recomputed under T-670 from the surviving notes, with all its marks falling together.

The fifth rule is the subject-refusal boundary. A subject that could have been walked but would not be — a witness refusing to speak, a holder refusing access, a taker declining the open half's chance — is not an absent subject, and a record withheld by its holder is not a destroyed record. Impossibility here means the walk could not have been taken, not that it would have been unpleasant, unproductive, or refused. A petitioner who had a walkable hour and chose not to walk it has a partial window and no extension, and a petition that dresses a refusal as an impossibility is denied on that ground, with the denial noting the distinction so the next petition on that field does not repeat it. The sixth rule is the prospective-application and order rule. T-673 applies to petitions filed after T-673, and to petitions still pending at an expiry digest, which may be amended to claim effective closure before the W+4 digest. Chains already expired under T-671 or T-672 stay expired: a chain that expired at W+5 under a one-window grant, or at W+6 under a double, is not revived by the effective-closure rule, for the same reason T-671 never resurrects an expired chain — later notes on that field already opened their own chains, and reviving the old one would strand them mid-flight. **T-674 — the Taker-Specific-Walkability Rule — designed:** T-673 left its taker-specific-walkability problem named and open: a route open to others, barred to this taker, leaves a window walkable in general and unwalkable in particular, with no rule fixed for which of the two the walkability test judges. The answer is particular. Walkability is judged for the walk this chain would have taken, and that walk has a taker. T-673 already says the test is about the walk this chain would have taken, not walks in general — a field open to other takers for other purposes is still closed in fact to a walk whose subject is gone. T-674 makes that sentence operational across all three of T-673's conditions, and draws the line that keeps it from swallowing the rule: a bar counts only when it is specific to this taker, imposed from outside the taker's control, total for the open half, and proved on a checkable record.

The first rule is the taker-specific test. Each of T-673's three conditions is judged for this taker, not for takers in general: the subject must be present and reachable by this taker, the record must be intact and accessible to this taker, the route must be open and open to this taker. A condition satisfied in general but failed for this taker fails the walkability test for this chain: a subject present on the field but under an order barring this taker from approaching it is not reachable; a record intact in its vault but with this taker's reading credential suspended is not accessible; a route open to every other taker but closed to this one by a revoked pass is not open. The converse also holds, and it matters: a condition failed in general but satisfied for this taker does not fail the test — a route barred to most takers but held open to this one by a standing permit is open for this walk, and a record sealed to the public but readable by this taker's credential is accessible. General walkability is evidence, never the test; the test is always this taker, this walk, this window.

The second rule is the exogenous-versus-self-created line, and it is the rule that keeps T-674 honest. A taker-specific bar counts as impossibility only when it was imposed by a third party or by circumstance outside the taker's control: a credential suspended by its issuer, access revoked by the record's holder, an order barring this taker from the field, a physical incapacity striking inside the window, a permit applied for in time and denied. A bar the taker created or allowed does not count, and is treated as a refusal under T-673's fifth rule: a credential left to lapse when renewal was available before the window, a refusal to meet a neutral requirement every taker meets, a declined offer of the access that would have opened the route. The test for the line is diligence before the window: could the taker, acting diligently before the window opened, have avoided the bar? If yes, the bar is self-created however it arrived; if no — the issuer suspended without cause, the holder revoked without notice, the permit was denied despite a timely application — the bar is exogenous. A petitioner who pleads a self-created bar as impossibility is denied on that ground, with the denial noting the distinction so the next petition on that field does not repeat it.

The third rule is the alternative-route rule. If an alternative route was open to this taker in the window and would have reached the same subject and the same record, the window was walkable, and the bar on the first route is irrelevant. Longer, harder, or costlier still counts as a route: a walk that takes the whole open half is still a walk, and a petitioner who declined a passable detour had a chance and did not take it. An alternative fails as a route only when it was itself barred to this taker, impassable in the window, or would not have reached the subject or the record the walk needed — a road to the wrong field is not an alternative route. The petitioner must show, on the checkable record, that no alternative existed or that every alternative was equally barred; silence about alternatives is treated as an unproved petition, on T-673's proof standard.

The fourth rule is the substitute-taker rule, and it cuts both ways. A walk by another taker does not complete this taker's chain: chains are taker-specific, and the note must be the taker's own observation — a colleague's note on the same field is a note on the field, not a note on this chain, and it completes nothing here. But if the petitioner could have delegated the walk to an available, willing, qualified taker and did not, the window counts as walkable, because delegation available defeats impossibility exactly as an alternative route does: the walk could have been taken, by a hand the petitioner could have engaged. The exception is where delegation is forbidden by the chain's own rules — a sealed field, a single-taker designation, a credential that cannot be lent — or where no qualified taker was available in the window: willing, qualified, and reachable in time are all three required, and a taker who exists somewhere is not a taker available here. A petitioner claiming no delegation existed must name why: forbidden, or none available, on the record.

The fifth rule is the proof standard, and it is T-673's strictest standard applied to the bar itself. The petitioner proves the bar the way T-673 proves impossibility: on a record the reviewer can check — a suspension notice, a revocation order, a permit denial, a medical record, a delegation refusal — naming the barred condition, the source of the bar, the interval it held for, and why no alternative route and no delegation existed. An assertion without a checkable record is treated as no proof, and a bar the record shows to be self-created is struck rather than weighed. Doubt resolves against extension twice over here as in T-673, because the claim is the same strong one with a narrower ground: the petitioner asks the reviewer to treat a window the calendar says was open, and the field says was open to others, as a window closed to this taker. A window whose taker-specific bar the record leaves doubtful is treated as walkable, and therefore partial and unextended.

The sixth rule is the cap, mark, and abuse-guard rule, and it deliberately creates no new window category. A taker-specific bar is a finding inside T-673's walkability test, not a fourth cause beside closure, sealed record, and postponement: it counts exactly as an effective-closure window under T-673 — at most one per petition, counting as one window toward T-672's two-window cap, one cause-covered gap window excused at most, and a completion only by taker-specific bar carrying the Waived-Completion mark, the Double-Extension mark where applicable, the Effective-Closure mark, and the Taker-Specific-Bar mark naming the barred condition and its source. The flood count includes it, the citation of it names every mark it carries, and a citation omitting any is a misstatement of the record on the T-671 pattern. For the abuse guard it follows the T-673 pattern exactly: one waiver toward the three-waivers-in-eight-windows T-650 invitation, window-weight two on the field's tally, and two taker-specific bars on the same field in eight windows — across different petitions, since one petition allows only one — inviting a T-650 review on their own. A field whose windows keep proving barred to one taker after another is either chronically gated or chronically mismanaged, and either is itself worth a review. A taker-specific grant on a bar later shown absent, self-created, or bypassed by an available route or delegation is struck exactly as in T-671, and the chain is recomputed under T-670 from the surviving notes, with all its marks falling together.

The seventh rule is the prospective-application and order rule. T-674 applies to petitions filed after T-674, and to petitions still pending at an expiry digest, which may be amended to claim a taker-specific bar before the W+4 digest. Chains already expired under T-671, T-672, or T-673 stay expired, for the same reason T-671 never resurrects an expired chain — later notes on that field already opened their own chains, and reviving the old one would strand them mid-flight. The order of operations does not gain a step: calibrate, cap, anchor, weigh, lift, chain, waive, then test walkability — taker-specificity is judged inside the walkability step, not after it, because it recharacterises conditions the walkability step already judges, and a separate step would let a general-walkability finding harden before the particular question is asked. A petition that pleads a taker-specific bar without pleading effective closure pleads nothing: the bar is a ground inside T-673, and it must be claimed as one.

Whether a bar lifted mid-open-half, restoring a walkable hour the taker could have used, defeats the claim or merely shortens it — a partial bar inside a partial window — is not decided here (admitted here — T-674's bar-lapse problem, newly open). How much renewal lead time makes a lapsed credential self-created rather than exogenous — a renewal window longer than the window itself, a renewal refused despite timely application — has no lead-time rule fixed here (admitted here — T-674's renewal-lead problem, newly open). Whether the window-weight of a taker-specific bar falls on the field's tally, the taker's tally, or both, when a field carries several takers and only one is barred, is not fixed here (admitted here — T-674's multi-taker-field problem, newly open). T-673's partial-copy problem (whether a destroyed record with a surviving partial copy counts as destroyed for a walk that needed the whole record) and unknown-return problem (whether a surprise return with no notice defeats an impossibility claim, or whether notice is part of walkability itself), T-672's closure-continuity problem (what proves one continuous closure event against two back-to-back events with a paper seam) and triple-closure problem (whether a closure covering three or more windows with a documented reopening plan should ever break the two-window cap), T-671's postponement-proof problem (what documentation standard a taker's postponement must meet), T-670's span-measure problem (windows or walks) and near-miss problem (trace of a near-corroboration), T-669's thin-flag problem (whether a Thin Heavy note should ever impose a provisional flag on its own) and weight-decay problem (whether weight decays as windows age), T-668's tiny-window problem (whether a window below ten walks is reviewable at all), T-667's cap-holding problem, T-666's absolute-trigger problem, T-665's attachment-netting and sensitivity-standard problems, T-664's correction-cap and grace-window-length problems, T-663's duplicate-identity problem, T-661's pattern-cap problem, T-660's tie and challenger-cost problems, and all other problems carried in T-673's admitted-unsolved paragraph, carried forward by reference.
