**T-675 — the Delegation-Availability Rule — designed:** T-674 left its delegation-availability problem named and open: its substitute-taker rule defeats impossibility where delegation to an available, willing, qualified taker existed, but never fixed whether a taker on standby who was never asked counts as available, or whether willingness must be proved or merely not disproved. Both answers are strict, because both cut against extension: a delegation never sought is not a delegation that was available, and a willingness never shown is not a willingness the reviewer can count. Availability is not a property of takers in the world; it is a property of the delegation this petitioner could have engaged, in this window, for this walk.

The first rule is the three-limb test, and every limb is judged for this window, not for takers in general. Willing means the taker would have accepted this walk, on this field, in this window — not that the taker is generally willing, or was willing last season. Qualified means the taker holds, for the whole open half, the credential, clearance, or standing the walk itself requires — the same standing the barred taker lacked or lost, not general competence in the field's work. Reachable in time means notice, travel, and the walk itself all fit inside the open half, counted from when the petitioner knew, or diligently should have known, that the bar held. All three limbs are required, as T-674 already says; a taker who fails any one of them is not an available delegation, and a taker who satisfies all three defeats the impossibility claim exactly as an alternative route does.

The second rule is the asked rule, and it answers the standby question directly. A taker who was never asked does not count as available, however willing that taker might have been. A standby list is a list of names, not a delegation: the petitioner who never sought a substitute cannot plead, after the fact, that a substitute existed somewhere, because the window's walkability is judged on the delegation the petitioner could have engaged, and an unasked taker was never engaged. The single exception is a standing delegation channel: a pre-committed on-call roster with a duty to accept, a pre-authorised delegation naming this field, a standing instruction under which the substitute would have walked without being asked in the window. A channel counts as asked, because the asking happened before the window opened. A standby list with no duty to accept, no pre-authorisation, and no prior engagement is not a channel, and a taker on it who was never asked is not available.

The third rule is the willingness-proof rule, and it answers the proof question directly. Willingness must be proved affirmatively, not merely not disproved. Proof is an acceptance for this walk, or a standing duty to accept under a channel within the second rule; a pattern of past acceptances is evidence, not proof for this window, because a taker who accepted last season may decline this one, and a taker who accepted other walks may decline this field. Mere absence of a refusal proves nothing: a taker never asked has neither accepted nor refused, and silence is not willingness. The petitioner who claims no delegation existed must show, for each taker considered, which limb failed — and a taker whose willingness the record leaves unproved is not counted as willing, on T-674's rule that doubt resolves against extension.

The fourth rule is the qualification rule, and it draws the line general competence cannot cross. Qualified is judged against the walk's own requirement, not the field's general work: a skilled taker without the field's credential is not qualified for this walk, and a credentialed taker whose credential lapsed mid-open-half, or arrived only after the open half closed, was not qualified in the window. Qualification must hold for the whole open half, because a substitute who could have walked only the closed half of a window is no substitute at all; the walk needed the open half, and the qualification had to be there for it. A petitioner who names a taker as available must name the credential that qualifies that taker, and a taker named without a credential is named, not proved.

The fifth rule is the reachability rule, and it counts the clock honestly. Reachable in time is judged from the moment diligent notice would have gone out, not from the moment the petitioner finally sent it: a petitioner who knew of the bar early in the window and sat on it until the open half was nearly gone cannot plead the substitute's lateness as unavailability, because the lateness is the petitioner's own delay wearing the substitute's name. Conversely, a taker reachable only after the open half closed, or reachable only by a route itself barred to that taker, is not reachable, and the petitioner who asked promptly and still could not be answered in time has proved that limb's failure. Reachability never resurrects a taker the second rule already excluded: a taker never asked and outside any channel is not made reachable by the fact that, had the petitioner asked, the taker might have arrived in time — the question the second rule answers first is whether there was a delegation to reach for at all.

The sixth rule is the cap, mark, and abuse-guard rule, and it deliberately creates no new window category. Availability is a finding inside T-674's substitute-taker rule, inside T-673's walkability test, not a new cause and not a new mark: a Delegation-Available finding is recorded as a ground of a Taker-Specific-Bar-Denied bridge — "available delegation" — and it extends nothing, waives nothing, and marks nothing on its own. A grant on a "no delegation" claim later shown wrong — a taker available under these rules, asked or channel-bound, willing on the record, qualified for the whole open half, reachable in time — is struck exactly as in T-674's sixth rule, and the chain is recomputed under T-670 from the surviving notes, with all its marks falling together. A petition claiming no delegation existed must name every taker considered and the limb each failed, on the record; a petition naming none is unproved, not merely thin, and is denied on that ground so the next petition on that field names its takers.

The seventh rule is the prospective-application and order rule. T-675 applies to petitions filed after T-675, and to petitions still pending at an expiry digest, which may be amended to claim or to answer a delegation-availability finding before the W+4 digest. Chains already expired under T-671, T-672, T-673, or T-674 stay expired, for the same reason T-671 never resurrects an expired chain — later notes on that field already opened their own chains, and reviving the old one would strand them mid-flight. A petition that pleads a taker-specific bar without pleading effective closure still pleads nothing, on T-674's seventh rule unchanged.

**T-676 — the Bar-Lapse Rule — designed:** T-675 left its bar-lapse problem named and open: a bar lifted mid-open-half, restoring a walkable hour the taker could have used, and the question whether that restoration defeats the impossibility claim or merely shortens it — a partial bar inside a partial window. Both outcomes are real, and the line between them is the walkable interval the lapse actually restored. A lapse is not a date on a calendar; it is an interval of walkability returned to the window, and the claim stands or falls on what that interval contained. T-676 therefore judges the lapse the way T-673 judges the open half itself: by the three conditions together, for a continuous walk-length interval, inside the open half — and a lapse that restores less than that shortens nothing and defeats nothing, while a lapse that restores that much defeats the claim for that window entirely, because the window was not, in fact, unwalkable.

The first rule is the defeat rule, and it is total for the window. A bar lifted mid-open-half defeats the impossibility claim for that window when the lapse restored a walkable opportunity: all three of T-673's conditions together — subject present and reachable by this taker, record intact and accessible to this taker, route open and open to this taker — for one continuous interval at least as long as the walk itself, inside the open half. The interval is measured in walk time, not clock time: a lapse restoring three scattered hours to a walk needing four continuous hours restores nothing walkable, and a lapse restoring a single hour to a walk needing an hour restores a walk. Where the defeat rule is met, the window is walkable and therefore partial and unextended — not shortened, not discounted, not carried at half weight. Windows are indivisible in the T-671/T-672 arithmetic: a window either earns its extension or it does not, and a window that held a walkable hour earns none. The petitioner who had a walkable hour and did not walk it has, under T-673's fifth rule, a refusal-shaped failure, not an impossibility; the denial names the restored interval and the three conditions it satisfied, so the next petition on that field does not re-plead the same bar for the same window.

The second rule is the shorten rule, and it shortens the excused span, never the window count. A lapse that restores only part of walkability — two conditions together but the third still barred, or all three together for an interval shorter than the walk, or all three together only in fragments that never form one continuous walk-length interval — does not defeat the claim, and the window may still earn its effective-closure extension. What it shortens is the cause-covered gap the extension excuses: the pre-lapse portion of the open half is excused as bar-covered, and the post-lapse remainder is treated as ordinary open time, not as bar time. That matters downstream, not in the window's own arithmetic: a later petition on the same field cannot re-plead the same bar for the post-lapse remainder, a failure to walk in a restored-but-insufficient interval is not held against the petitioner (an insufficient interval is no opportunity), and a chain that later breaks in the post-lapse remainder breaks on ordinary delay, not on a fresh bar — so no second effective-closure window can be claimed on the same bar for the same window. The extension itself stays one window: the shorten rule never halves a window, never grants half an extension, and never converts a lapse-mitigated grant into a double.

The third rule is the knowability rule, and it decides whether a lapse counts at all. A lapse defeats a claim only if the taker knew, or diligently should have known, of the lift in time to use the restored interval. Knowability is judged through the bar's own channel: a bar imposed by registry, roster, credential record, or order is lifted through that same channel, and a petitioner who checked the channel on the cadence the channel itself sets — the roster's publication day, the credential's renewal check, the order's docket — is charged with knowledge of the lift from its publication. A bar lifted only by the taker's private word, never entered in any channel the petitioner could check, is not knowable, and does not defeat: a credential quietly restored by its issuer with no notice to the field is, for walkability purposes, still suspended until notice arrives. The petitioner proves diligence by the check record — dates checked, channel checked, result recorded — and a petitioner with no check record is charged with knowledge only where the channel published the lift openly enough that any diligent check would have found it. This rule is the bar-side twin of T-673's unknown-return problem, and it differs from it deliberately: a subject's surprise return is an event in the world, while a bar's lift is an act recorded by the very authority that imposed the bar, so the channel that imposed it is the channel that must publish its end.

The fourth rule is the flicker rule, and it refuses to sum scraps. A bar lifted and reimposed inside the same open half — lifted Monday, reimposed Wednesday, lifted again Friday — creates intervals, not one interval, and intervals do not aggregate into a walkable opportunity unless one of them alone is walk-length and satisfies all three conditions. Fragmented scraps summing to a walk are not a walk, because a walk cannot be taken in instalments across days the bar closed between them. Each flicker interval is judged on its own under the first rule; if none qualifies, the claim survives the flicker, and the flicker itself is recorded as a lapse-mitigated grant under the second rule, with each interval named. A petitioner who pleads flicker as defeat must name the single qualifying interval; a reviewer who finds only scraps denies the defeat and grants, if the rest of T-673 is met, on the mitigated footing. Flicker also does not reset the bar: a bar reimposed after a qualifying lapse is a new bar for the next window, not a continuation of the old one, and a petition for the next window pleads it fresh, with its own proof.

The fifth rule is the delegation-and-alternative interplay rule, and it keeps T-674 and T-675 inside the lapse. A lapse restoring the original taker moots the delegation question for the post-lapse interval: where the barred taker could walk again, the petitioner need not show no delegation existed for that interval, because the walk itself was available. Conversely, a lapse restoring only the delegation channel — a substitute taker freed while the original taker stayed barred — is judged under T-675's three limbs for the substitute, not under the first rule for the original: the substitute must be willing, qualified for the whole restored interval, and reachable in time from diligent notice of the lift. And a lapse that restores an alternative route, while the first route stayed barred, is judged under T-674's alternative-route rule: a passable detour reaching the same subject and record, for a walk-length interval, defeats exactly as a lapse of the bar itself does. No lapse is judged in isolation from the walk it would have enabled; a lift that returns nothing the walk needed returns nothing at all.

The sixth rule is the mark, cap, and abuse-guard rule, and it creates no new window category. A lapse-defeated window takes the Bar-Lapse mark on its denial bridge — naming the restored interval, the channel that published the lift, and the check record that charged the petitioner with knowledge — and consumes no effective-closure count, because it earned no extension. A lapse-mitigated grant takes the Lapse-Mitigated mark alongside T-673's Effective-Closure mark and, where applicable, T-674's Taker-Specific-Bar mark, and consumes exactly one effective-closure window toward T-672's two-window cap: a mitigated grant plus a full grant may make a double, never two mitigated grants a double on their own, because mitigation is a narrowing, not a second closure. A grant obtained by concealing a qualifying lapse — a petition that omits a lift the check record shows, or a check record falsified to hide one — is struck exactly as in T-675's sixth rule, and the chain is recomputed under T-670 from the surviving notes, with all its marks falling together. A petition that pleads a bar without pleading its lift history — lifts checked, lifts found, lifts missed — is unproved on the lapse question, and the reviewer decides it on the record the channel itself holds.

The seventh rule is the prospective-application and order rule. T-676 applies to petitions filed after T-676, and to petitions still pending at an expiry digest, which may be amended to plead or to answer a bar-lapse finding before the W+4 digest. Chains already expired under T-671, T-672, T-673, T-674, or T-675 stay expired, for the same reason T-671 never resurrects an expired chain — later notes on that field already opened their own chains, and reviving the old one would strand them mid-flight. The order of operations does not gain a step: calibrate, cap, anchor, weigh, lift, chain, waive, then test walkability — the lapse is judged inside the walkability step, as part of the impossibility finding, not after it, because a lapse recharacterises the very walkability the step judges, and a separate step would let an impossibility finding harden before the lift that undoes it is asked about. A petition that pleads a taker-specific bar without pleading effective closure still pleads nothing, on T-674's seventh rule unchanged, and a petition that pleads effective closure without pleading the bar's lift history pleads it incompletely.

Admitted here, still open: how often a petitioner must check the bar's channel before a missed lift counts as the petitioner's own delay rather than an unknowable lapse — a daily check, a check on the channel's publication cadence, a check only when the window's work requires it — has no check-cadence rule fixed here (admitted here — T-676's lapse-notice-cadence problem, newly open). **T-677 — the Lapse-Notice-Cadence Rule — designed:** T-676 left its lapse-notice-cadence problem named and open: its knowability rule charges a petitioner with knowledge of a lift published through the bar's own channel, proved by a check record — but it fixed no cadence, so no one could say how often the petitioner must check before a missed lift stops being an unknowable lapse and becomes the petitioner's own delay. A daily check, a check on the channel's publication cadence, a check only when the window's work requires it — all three were on the table, and T-676 chose none of them. The answer is that the channel, not the petitioner and not the reviewer, sets the cadence — bounded by a floor the channel cannot go below and a ceiling the petitioner cannot be pushed above — because the channel is the authority that imposed the bar, and the rhythm at which it speaks is the rhythm at which a diligent petitioner can be expected to listen.

The first rule is the channel-sets-cadence rule, and it is the whole doctrine in one line. The required checks fall on the channel's own publication schedule: the roster's publication day, the credential record's renewal checkpoint, the order's docket update, the register's gazette day. A lift published between two required checks is charged from the next required check, not from its publication date — the petitioner is charged with what the cadence would have shown, when the cadence would have shown it, and no earlier. A petitioner who checked on cadence and found nothing is protected for the whole interval until the next required check, even if the lift published the day after the check: the gap between publications is the channel's silence, not the petitioner's delay, and a reviewer who charges a mid-interval publication charges the petitioner for listening at the wrong hour to a channel that only speaks on its own days. The check record must therefore name, for each check, the publication it answers — the roster issue, the docket entry, the checkpoint — so the reviewer can see the cadence being followed rather than a list of dates that merely look diligent.

The second rule is the floor, and it stops a slow channel from swallowing the window. No channel cadence may run longer than the open half: if the channel publishes less often than once per open half, one check per open half is still required, timed so that a walk could still be taken after it — before the walkable deadline, not after the window has already closed around the petitioner. If the channel publishes nothing at all during the open half, the floor check is the only required check, and a lift published nowhere during the half is unknowable for that window no matter when the issuer claims it was lifted internally, because T-676's third rule already requires publication through a checkable channel, and a channel that never speaks in the half cannot be said to have spoken. The floor is a minimum, not a target: a petitioner who checks more often than the floor is not penalised for it, and a check made early in the half does not excuse the floor check later in the half, because a lift published after the early check and before the floor check belongs to the floor check's answer.

The third rule is the ceiling, and it stops a fast channel from turning diligence into surveillance. No petitioner is required to check more often than once a day, even for a continuously updated channel — a docket that updates hourly, a register that refreshes in real time, a credential system that never sleeps. For such channels the required cadence is one check per day during the open half, and a check made within the last day before the window's walkable deadline satisfies the cadence for that window, so a petitioner who checked yesterday morning is not charged for a lift published yesterday afternoon that no daily check could have caught before the deadline. The ceiling also caps the work-triggered rule below: a channel that updates continuously does not convert every hour of the open half into a required check, and a reviewer who demands hourly checks demands what no petitioner can give and what T-676 never asked for.

The fourth rule is the cadence-after-expiry rule, and it protects the petitioner the cadence itself strands. If the next required check falls after the window's end, or after the walkable deadline inside the window, the lift is unknowable for that window: the petitioner is not charged for a check the cadence never offered in time. A roster published monthly, a window expiring mid-month, a lift published in the issue that falls after expiry — the petitioner did everything the cadence asked, and the cadence asked for nothing in time. This is not a loophole for the petitioner who never checked at all: a petitioner with no check record is judged under T-676's third rule, charged where the channel published openly enough that any diligent check would have found the lift, and the cadence-after-expiry rule excuses only the petitioner whose check record shows the cadence followed to the window's end. A channel that publishes after expiry has spoken too late for that window, and its late speech belongs to the next window's petition, not to this window's denial.

The fifth rule is the work-triggered check, and it is the one check no cadence excuses. When the window's work itself is attempted or prepared — the walk begun, the route travelled, the subject sought, the record requested — a check at the attempt is required regardless of cadence. An attempted walk without a check at the attempt is not diligence, and a lift that check would have found defeats the impossibility claim even if no cadence check was due that day, because the petitioner stood at the walk itself and chose not to ask whether the bar still stood. Conversely, a work-triggered check that finds nothing protects the attempt that follows it for the whole of that attempt: a petitioner who checked at the walk's start and walked into a bar reimposed mid-walk is not charged for a lift or a reimposition that happened while the walk was already underway. The work-triggered check is the cadence's conscience — the cadence governs the waiting, but the attempt governs itself.

The sixth rule is the flicker-between-checks rule, and it keeps T-676's flicker rule honest about what a petitioner could see. A flicker interval falling entirely between two required checks, found by neither, is unknowable unless a work-triggered check caught it: T-676 judges intervals by whether one alone is walk-length and satisfies all three conditions, and T-677 judges whether the petitioner had any occasion to see the interval at all. Flicker does not change the cadence, and the cadence does not change flicker: each interval is still judged on its own under T-676's fourth rule, and T-677 decides only whether the petitioner is charged with seeing it.

The seventh rule is the cadence-evidence rule, and it decides what proves a cadence at all. The check record must name the cadence source: the channel's published schedule, its docket rule, its credential policy, its gazette calendar. A cadence asserted without a source is unproved, and the reviewer falls back to the default cadence: one check per open half, plus one at any attempted walk. Where the channel changed its cadence mid-window, the cadence in force at each publication governs that publication — a petitioner is never charged under a cadence published after the check date, and a channel that accelerates its publications mid-window cannot retroactively make a petitioner late. Where the channel publishes no schedule and no rule anywhere, the default cadence governs and the petitioner proves diligence by the default alone; the channel's silence about its own rhythm is not held against the petitioner, because a channel that will not say when it speaks cannot complain that no one listened on its days.

The eighth rule is the mark, cap, and abuse-guard rule, and it creates no new window category. A missed-check defeat takes the Missed-Check mark on its denial bridge — naming the missed check date, the publication that predated it, and the cadence source that made that date required — and consumes no effective-closure count, because it earned no extension, exactly as T-676's Bar-Lapse mark consumes none. The ninth rule is the prospective-application and order rule. T-677 applies to petitions filed after T-677, and to petitions still pending at an expiry digest, which may be amended to plead or to answer a cadence finding before the W+4 digest. Chains already expired under T-671, T-672, T-673, T-674, T-675, or T-676 stay expired, for the same reason T-671 never resurrects an expired chain — later notes on that field already opened their own chains, and reviving the old one would strand them mid-flight. **T-678 — the Multi-Channel Cadence Rule — designed:** T-677 left its multi-channel problem named and open: it fixed the cadence for a lift published through the bar's own channel, but said nothing about a bar imposed through one channel and lifted through another — a roster that bars, a docket that lifts; a credential record that bars, a gazette that lifts; an order that bars, a register that lifts. The three candidate answers were the imposing channel's rhythm, the lifting channel's rhythm, or the stricter of the two, and T-677 chose none of them. The answer is that the lifting channel governs the lift, the imposing channel governs the bar, and neither rhythm substitutes for the other — because a lift is knowable only where it was published, and a bar's standing is knowable only where the bar itself speaks, and a petitioner who listened faithfully to one channel has not thereby listened to the other.

The first rule is the lifting-channel-governs rule, and it is the whole doctrine in one line. A lift published through a channel other than the bar's own channel is charged under that lifting channel's cadence, judged exactly as T-677 judges a cadence: the lift is charged from the next required check on the lifting channel's schedule, not from its publication date, and a petitioner who checked the lifting channel on cadence and found nothing is protected for the whole interval until the next required lifting-channel check. The imposing channel's cadence is irrelevant to the lift's knowability — a petitioner who checked the imposing channel daily gains nothing about a lift published in a gazette she never opened, and a reviewer who charges her under the imposing channel's rhythm charges her for listening at the wrong hour to the wrong speaker. Conversely, the lifting channel's cadence is irrelevant to the bar's standing: a lift is not a reimposition, and a petitioner who checked the lifting channel and found the lift cannot be charged with knowledge that the bar was reimposed through the imposing channel, which is judged under the imposing channel's own cadence. Each publication is judged under the cadence of the channel that published it, and no channel's rhythm ever answers for another channel's speech.

The second rule is the direction rule, and it stops a lifting channel the petitioner was never told to watch from becoming a trap. A lift published through a channel the petitioner was never directed to — at imposition, at the bar's renewal, or at any point before the lift — is unknowable for that window unless it was cross-posted to the imposing channel, because T-676's third rule requires publication through a checkable channel, and a channel no one told the petitioner to check is not checkable for her, however public it is in the abstract. Direction need not name the channel by name: a direction to "the register," "the docket for this field," or "the channel that publishes lifts for this bar" directs well enough, but a direction to the imposing channel alone does not direct to a different lifting channel, and a lift published in a channel the issuer chose unilaterally, after imposition, without telling the petitioner, is an internal lift until it is cross-posted. The direction is proved by the imposition record or by a later direction record, not by the petitioner's say-so and not by the issuer's after-the-fact claim that the channel was "obvious" — obviousness is not direction, and a channel obvious to the issuer is not thereby obvious to the petitioner.

The third rule is the cross-post rule, and it is how a lift in a foreign channel becomes knowable at home. A lift cross-posted to the imposing channel is charged under the imposing channel's cadence from the cross-post, not from the original lift publication: the petitioner is charged with what the imposing channel's cadence would have shown, when it would have shown it, exactly as T-677 provides for a publication through the bar's own channel. The cross-post does not retroactively charge the original publication — a petitioner who missed the gazette but checked the roster on cadence is charged from the roster's next required check after the cross-post, and a cross-post that arrives after the window's end leaves the lift unknowable for that window under T-677's cadence-after-expiry rule, applied to the imposing channel's cadence. A cross-post that misstates the lift — wrong field, wrong taker, wrong scope — is no cross-post at all, and the lift stays unknowable until a correct cross-post or a directed check of the lifting channel finds it. A petitioner who actually found the lift in the lifting channel before any cross-post is charged from the finding, because actual knowledge is not unknowability, but the finding must be proved by a check record naming the lifting channel, not asserted.

The fourth rule is the no-substitution rule, and it rejects the stricter-of-the-two answer outright. The required checks are not the union of both channels' cadences collapsed into the stricter rhythm, and they are not the stricter cadence applied to both channels: a check on the imposing channel does not satisfy a required check on the lifting channel, and a check on the lifting channel does not satisfy a required check on the imposing channel, because the two checks answer different publications. A single sitting that checks both channels satisfies one required check on each, and a check record that names both channels with the publication each answered proves both at once — diligence is not doubled by sitting once and looking twice. But the floor and ceiling of T-677 apply per channel, not across the pair: a petitioner is never required to check either channel more often than once a day, and never less often than once per open half on a channel that bears a required check, so a two-channel bar demands at most two checks a day and at least one check per open half per channel. A reviewer who demands the daily rhythm of a fast lifting channel on a slow imposing channel, or who counts a missed imposing-channel check as a missed lifting-channel check, has collapsed two speeches into one and defeated a petitioner for a confusion the reviewer created.

The fifth rule is the conflict rule, and it protects the petitioner when the channels disagree. Where the imposing channel says the bar stands and the lifting channel says it is lifted, the bar stands until the conflict is reconciled by a cross-post, a correction, or a direction naming which channel prevails — because a lift contradicted by the bar's own channel is not a knowable lift, it is a contradiction, and a petitioner who walks on a contradicted lift walks on a guess. The conflict itself is not charged as knowledge of a lift, and a walk attempted during a conflict is judged as a walk against a standing bar, not as a walk that should have known the bar was lifted. Where the channels agree, there is no conflict to judge. Where the imposing channel is silent and the lifting channel speaks a lift, the lift stands on the lifting channel's cadence alone, because silence is not contradiction — but where the imposing channel affirmatively reimposes after the lift, the reimposition is charged under the imposing channel's cadence from its next required check, and the lift's window closes at that charge date, not at the reimposition's publication date.

The sixth rule is the work-triggered multi-channel check, and it extends T-677's fifth rule to both speakers. A check at an attempted walk must cover both channels: the imposing channel, for whether the bar still stands, and any directed lifting channel, for whether it has been lifted. An attempted walk checked on one channel only is not a work-triggered check at all, and a lift that a two-channel attempt check would have found defeats the impossibility claim even if no cadence check was due that day on either channel, because the petitioner stood at the walk itself and asked only half the question. An undirected lifting channel is not part of the work-triggered check — the petitioner cannot be required to ask a channel she was never told exists — unless the lift was cross-posted to the imposing channel, in which case the imposing-channel half of the check finds it.

The seventh rule is the cadence-after-expiry rule applied per channel, and it keeps T-677's fourth rule honest about two clocks. If the next required check on the imposing channel falls after expiry, a reimposition published through the imposing channel is likewise unknowable for that window, and the lift's window does not close on an unknowable reimposition. A missed-check defeat on a multi-channel bar takes the Missed-Check mark on its denial bridge — naming the missed check date, the channel the check belonged to, the publication that predated it on that channel, and the cadence source that made that date required on that channel — and consumes no effective-closure count, exactly as T-677 provides. The ninth rule is the prospective-application and order rule. T-678 applies to petitions filed after T-678, and to petitions still pending at an expiry digest, which may be amended to plead or to answer a multi-channel finding before the W+4 digest. **T-679 — the Cross-Post Lag Rule — designed:** T-678 left its cross-post-lag problem named and open: a cross-post a year later cannot fairly pretend the lift was published yesterday, but no lag limit was fixed. The answer is that a stale cross-post does not retroactively charge the petitioner — the direction rule of T-678 stands — but the issuer's delay beyond tolerance is repaid to the petitioner as time, not taken from her as knowledge. Lag is measured, tolerance is fixed, and excess is credited.

The first rule is the lag measure, and it starts from publication, not from intention. Lag is the cross-post's publication date on the imposing channel minus the lift's original publication date on the lifting channel. The cross-post date is the date the imposing channel published it, not the date the issuer drafted it, approved it, or filed it internally — an internal memo is not a cross-post, and a cross-post dated by memo while published weeks later lags from its publication. The original publication date is the lifting channel's publication date, not the lift's effective date where the two differ: a lift effective Monday but published Friday lags from Friday, because Friday is the earliest any checker could have found it. Where either date is unproved, the lag is unproved, and the cross-post is judged timely — the issuer who cannot date its own publications does not earn a stale-cross-post finding against itself, but neither does it earn one against the petitioner; an undated cross-post is treated as timely and charged under T-678 exactly.

The second rule is the lag limit, and it is the longer of two measures, so that neither a fast channel nor a slow window makes the limit absurd. The limit is two required-check intervals on the lifting channel's cadence, or one open half of the window in which the lift was published, whichever is longer. Two intervals is the tolerance a diligent lifting-channel checker needs: one interval to find the lift, one more for publication lag and for the check itself to be recorded. One open half is the floor: a lift published just before a half boundary must not go stale before the petitioner has had half a window to meet it through the imposing channel. Where the lifting channel publishes continuously, T-677's ceiling of one check per day makes the interval one day, so the limit is two days or one open half, whichever is longer. Where the lifting channel publishes no schedule and no rule, T-677's default cadence governs and the interval is one open half, so the limit is two open halves or one open half — that is, two open halves.

The third rule is the timely cross-post, and it changes nothing. A cross-post whose lag is within the limit is charged exactly as T-678 provides: under the imposing channel's cadence from the cross-post, not from the original publication. Tolerance exists precisely so that ordinary administrative delay — the days between a gazette entry and a roster update — does not punish either side: the petitioner is charged when her own channel would have shown her the lift, and the issuer is not penalised for a delay shorter than the rhythm of its own publication.

The fourth rule is the stale cross-post, and it repays excess as time. A cross-post whose lag exceeds the limit is still charged from the cross-post — never retroactively from the original publication, because T-678's direction rule is not undone by delay — but the walkable deadline inside the window extends by the excess lag, the lag minus the limit, capped at one open half. The petitioner gets back exactly the time the issuer's delay stole beyond tolerance, and no more: a cross-post three intervals late on a channel whose limit is two intervals earns one interval of extension, not three, because the first two intervals were the issuer's tolerated delay, not stolen time. The extension runs from the walkable deadline, not from the cross-post date: a petitioner who learns of the lift late gets late time to walk, not a new window measured from her learning. Where the window has no walkable deadline distinct from its end, the extension runs from the window's end.

The fifth rule is the expired-window reopening, and it is the fourth rule applied where the cross-post arrived too late to matter. Where a stale cross-post arrives after the window's end, and the lift's original publication predated the window's end, the window reopens for the extension period — the excess lag capped at one open half — measured from the cross-post's imposing-channel charge date under T-678's cadence. The reopened window is a continuation of the expired window, not a new window: it carries the expired window's marks, its T-672 cap consumption, and its chain position, and it closes at the end of the extension whether or not the petitioner walks. Where the original publication postdated the window's end, there is nothing to reopen — the lift never belonged to that window, and a stale cross-post about a later lift opens no door to an earlier one. Where the cross-post is timely but arrives after the window's end, T-678's cadence-after-expiry rule stands and the lift stays unknowable for that window: timeliness forgives delay within tolerance, not arrival after death.

The sixth rule is the fault rule, and it denies the extension to the petitioner who could have found the lift herself. No extension, and no reopening, where the petitioner was directed to the lifting channel and failed to check it on cadence during the lag period — a petitioner who could have found the lift in the gazette within one interval gains nothing from the roster's slow cross-post, because her own missed check, not the issuer's delay, is what kept her ignorant. The extension belongs only to the petitioner who checked the imposing channel on cadence, or who was never directed to the lifting channel at all: the petitioner who listened where she was told to listen is repaid for the delay; the petitioner who listened nowhere is not. Fault is proved by the check records on each channel, not by assertion on either side, and where neither side's check record survives, the extension is granted — the issuer's delay is the proved fact, the petitioner's diligence the unproved one, and the tie goes to the petitioner who was kept waiting.

The seventh rule is the successive-cross-post rule, and it stops a bad cross-post from laundering its own lag. The first correct cross-post governs: lag is measured to it, and a later corrected cross-post does not restart the clock, because the petitioner was already told truly once. But a cross-post that misstates the lift — wrong field, wrong taker, wrong scope — is no cross-post at all under T-678's third rule, so lag is measured to the first correct cross-post, and the incorrect one's delay counts in full against the issuer. A cross-post corrected before any petitioner relied on the incorrect version still counts its full lag: the correction cures the misstatement, it does not forgive the time the misstatement consumed. A cross-post withdrawn and re-posted identically restarts nothing; the original publication date governs, and the withdrawal interval counts as lag unless the withdrawal itself was published as a correction through the imposing channel.

The eighth rule is the mark, cap, and abuse-guard rule, and it creates no new window category. A stale-cross-post extension consumes no additional effective-closure count and creates no new window for T-672's two-window cap: the extension lengthens a window the petitioner already holds, it does not grant her another one, and a grant on an extended or reopened window consumes exactly one effective-closure window, as T-676 and T-677 already provide. A falsified cross-post date, a falsified original publication date, a cadence source invented after the fact to inflate the lag limit, or a check record that omits a required check on a directed channel, is struck exactly as in T-675's sixth rule and T-676's sixth rule, and the chain is recomputed under T-670 from the surviving notes, with all its marks falling together. A petition claiming a stale-cross-post extension without pleading, per channel, the original publication date, the cross-post date, the cadence source, the lag, the limit, and the excess, pleads the extension incompletely, and the reviewer decides it on the record the channels themselves hold.

The ninth rule is the prospective-application and order rule. T-679 applies to petitions filed after T-679, and to petitions still pending at an expiry digest, which may be amended to plead or to answer a stale-cross-post finding before the W+4 digest. Chains already expired under T-671 through T-678 stay expired, for the same reason T-671 never resurrects an expired chain — except that a chain expired solely because a stale cross-post arrived after its window's end, where the original publication predated the window's end, may be reopened under the fifth rule on amendment before the W+4 digest, because that expiry was the issuer's delay wearing the petitioner's deadline, and the reopening restores only the excess time, not the whole window. The order of operations does not gain a step: calibrate, cap, anchor, weigh, lift, chain, waive, then test walkability — the cross-post lag is judged inside the walkability step, as part of the knowability finding T-676 placed there and T-677's cadence and T-678's multi-channel findings refine, not after it.

Admitted here, still open: whether extensions stack across multiple stale cross-posts on the same lift — a second stale cross-post after a first extension, or successive lifts each cross-posted late — or whether one extension per lift is the cap (admitted here — T-679's stacking problem, newly open). What counts as a required-check interval when the lifting channel's cadence is irregular — publications clustered, then silent for months — and whether the interval is the mean, the maximum, or the interval in force at the original publication (admitted here — T-679's irregular-cadence problem, newly open). T-678's channel-succession problem (whether checks on a successor channel satisfy a predecessor's cadence, or the petitioner must be re-directed), T-677's cadence-source problem and delegation-cadence problem, T-676's flicker-aggregation problem and lapse-evidence problem, T-675's renewal-lead problem and multi-taker-field problem, T-673's partial-copy problem and unknown-return problem, T-672's closure-continuity problem and triple-closure problem, T-671's postponement-proof problem, T-670's span-measure problem and near-miss problem, T-669's thin-flag problem and weight-decay problem, T-668's tiny-window problem, T-667's cap-holding problem, T-666's absolute-trigger problem, T-665's attachment-netting and sensitivity-standard problems, T-664's correction-cap and grace-window-length problems, T-663's duplicate-identity problem, T-661's pattern-cap problem, T-660's tie and challenger-cost problems, and all other problems carried in T-678's admitted-unsolved paragraph, carried forward by reference.

Filings: Taker-Specific-Bar-Petition / Taker-Specific-Bar-Denied bridges, unchanged in form. A Taker-Specific-Bar-Petition bridge claiming a stale-cross-post extension names, per channel, the original publication date, the cross-post date, the cadence source, the lag, the lag limit, the excess, the extension claimed, and the check records proving cadence compliance on the imposing channel, with the publication records attached. A Taker-Specific-Bar-Denied bridge on the ground that no extension is due names the fault — the missed lifting-channel check, the direction record that required it, and the cadence source that made that date required — so the next petition on that field does not re-plead the same lag for the same lift. A grant on an extended or reopened window rides on T-676's lapse-mitigated bridge with the lag, limit, and excess stated, unchanged in all else.

**T-680 — the Stacking-Cap Rule — designed:** T-679 left its stacking problem named and open: whether extensions stack across multiple stale cross-posts on the same lift — a second stale cross-post after a first extension, or successive lifts each cross-posted late — or whether one extension per lift is the cap. The answer is both halves of that question, kept apart: one extension per lift, and stacking across distinct lifts, but stacking is measured as a union of credited intervals, not as a sum of excesses, and it is capped per window, because an uncapped stack would quietly grant the new window T-679's eighth rule refuses to create. A petitioner repaid once for a lift is repaid; a petitioner repaid for two lifts is repaid twice, but never repaid for the same stolen time twice, and never repaid so much time that the window she holds becomes a different window.

The first rule is the per-lift rule. One lift earns one extension, however many cross-posts it suffers. T-679's seventh rule already fixes the measurement: the first correct cross-post governs, and lag is measured to it. T-680 draws the consequence the seventh rule left unstated: a second cross-post of the same lift, stale or timely, correct or corrected, adds no second extension, because it adds no second delay. The petitioner was already told truly once, and the excess already credited is the whole of what that lift's delay stole. An incorrect cross-post followed by a correct one is still one lift and one extension, measured to the first correct cross-post, with the incorrect one's delay counted in full under T-679 — counted once, not once per version. A cross-post withdrawn and re-posted identically is the same lift told twice, not two lifts, and earns nothing new. Pleading the same lift twice — under two cross-post dates, two channel names, or two descriptions of one publication — is a duplicate pleading: the duplicate is denied, and only the first correct pleading's credit stands. A duplicate pleading built on a falsified cross-post date is struck under T-679's eighth rule, and the chain is recomputed under T-670 from the surviving notes.

The second rule is the distinct-lift rule. Successive lifts, each cross-posted late, each earn their own credit, computed independently. Each lift has its own original publication date, its own lag limit under T-679's second rule, its own first correct cross-post, its own excess, and its own fault finding under T-679's sixth rule. Fault is per lift: a petitioner at fault on lift A — directed to lift A's lifting channel and missing its cadence checks during A's lag — earns no credit for A, but that fault does not taint lift B, whose lifting channel she checked or was never directed to. Conversely, diligence on B does not cure fault on A. Independence is the point: the issuer's delay on one lift is not the issuer's delay on another, and the petitioner's diligence on one channel is not diligence on another. A lift whose cross-post was timely earns no credit at all, and a timely lift in a stack contributes nothing to the stack's total — timeliness is not a negative credit, and it does not consume cap room.

The third rule is the union rule. Stacked credits are intervals on the window's timeline, and overlapping intervals count once. Each lift's credit is an interval of credited time, running from the walkable deadline as T-679's fourth rule provides, or from the reopened window's charge date where T-679's fifth rule applies. Where two lifts' credited intervals overlap — two lifts published in the same window, cross-posted late by the same slow roster, stealing the same weeks — the stack credits the union, not the sum: the petitioner lost those weeks once, and being told twice about two lifts in the same lost weeks does not lose them twice. Where the intervals are disjoint, both count, in full, up to the cap. The reviewer lays the intervals on the window's timeline in original-publication order, earliest lift first, and measures the union before applying the cap, so that order cannot manufacture credit by double-counting an overlap the union would have removed.

The fourth rule is the per-window cap. Total stacked credit on a single window is capped at one open half — the same cap T-679 places on a single extension, now applied to the stack as a whole. The cap is per window, not per chain and not per lift: a chain spanning two windows may hold up to one open half of stacked credit in each, because each window is lengthened on its own terms, but no single window may be lengthened by more than half itself, for the same reason T-679 caps one extension there — beyond half a window, the lengthened window is a new window wearing the old window's name, and T-679's eighth rule creates no new window category. Credits are applied in original-publication order, earliest first, and later credits are truncated to the cap remainder: a first lift crediting three quarters of an open half leaves one quarter for every later lift combined, and the remainder is lost, not carried to the next window, because credited time belongs to the window whose deadline it extends. A stack that reaches the cap is complete: further stale cross-posts on that window's lifts are noted and earn nothing, however stale.

The fifth rule is the supersession rule. A lift superseded before its first correct cross-post arrives earns no credit, unless the petitioner acted on it in reliance before the supersession. Supersession is the case T-679 never had to reach: lift B replaces lift A, and A's cross-post arrives after B has already replaced it, so the petitioner never needed A's knowledge at all — the delay in telling her about a lift that no longer stands stole no walkable time, because there was no walk under A left to take. The exception is reliance: where the chain's walk, or a petition filed on it, was made under A before B's publication, A's credit survives for that walk, because the petitioner acted on the lift as it stood, and supersession does not retroactively un-act her. Reliance is proved on the record — a walk note, a petition, a check record dated under A and before B — not by assertion after the fact. Where B supersedes A after A's first correct cross-post, there is no supersession question at all: A was told truly while it stood, its credit stands, and B's credit is computed on its own, subject to the union and the cap.

The sixth rule is the reopening rule. A window reopened under T-679's fifth rule reopens once, and its reopening period is the stack's credit, not each lift's. Where a second lift's original publication also predated the window's end, its credit may extend the reopened period, up to the same one-open-half total cap, if pleaded before the reopened window closes — the reopening is a continuation of the expired window, and a continuation lengthened twice is still one continuation, not two reopenings. Where the reopened window has already closed, a later lift's credit opens nothing: the petitioner had the reopened period and the cap, and a lift discovered after that period is a lift for the next window's chain, not a key to the last one. A chain already expired for reasons other than a stale cross-post — fault on every lift, or expiry under T-671 with no stale-cross-post cause — is not reopened by stacking, for the same reason T-679 reopens only chains expired solely on a stale cross-post.

The seventh rule is the pleading, mark, and order rule. A stacked petition pleads, per lift, every particular T-679's eighth rule requires — original publication date, cross-post date, cadence source, lag, limit, excess, and check records — plus a stacking table: each lift's credited interval, the union measured, the cap, the cap remainder after each lift in original-publication order, and the total claimed. A petition without the stacking table pleads the stack incompletely, and the reviewer decides it on the records the channels themselves hold, measuring the union and the cap from those records. A completion by stacked credit carries a Stacked-Credit mark naming each lift whose credit contributed and its interval; a citation omitting a contributing lift, or naming a lift whose credit was truncated to nothing by the cap, is a misstatement of the record on the T-671 pattern. The order of operations gains no step: calibrate, cap, anchor, weigh, lift, chain, waive, then test walkability — stacking is judged inside the walkability step, as part of the knowability finding, with the union and the cap applied there before any expiry digest is computed.

Admitted here, still open: whether the per-window one-open-half stacking cap should instead be a per-chain cap — a chain holding a half in each of two windows holds a full window of credit in total, and no rule here says whether that total itself offends persistence (admitted here — T-680's chain-cap problem, newly open). What record proves reliance on a superseded lift where the walk was prepared but never filed under it — a draft, a check record, or a note never submitted is not distinguished here (admitted here — T-680's reliance-proof problem, newly open). Whether credits for lifts in different windows on the same chain should pool toward one cap when the windows are contiguous and the chain is one chain, rather than capping window by window, is not fixed here (admitted here — T-680's pooling problem, newly open). **T-681 — the Chain-Cap Rule — designed:** T-680 left its chain-cap problem named and open: a chain holding one open half of stacked credit in each of two windows holds a full window of credit in total, and no rule there said whether that total itself offends persistence. The answer is that it does, but only at twice the per-window cap: the per-window cap stands, and a second, chain-level cap stands above it. One window may never be lengthened by more than half itself, and one chain may never be lengthened by more than one full window in total, however many windows it spans. The chain cap is a second cap, not a replacement for the first: a stack that offends neither cap is granted in full, a stack that offends either is truncated to the offended cap, and a stack that offends both is truncated to the tighter of the two remainders at each step.

The first rule is the chain-cap measure. The chain cap is one full window of stacked credit, counted as credited time across every window on the chain, where a "full window" means the sum of the windows' own lengths measured in the same units the per-window cap uses — an open half of a short window and an open half of a long window are not equal credits, and the chain cap counts time, not halves. A chain with two windows of equal length reaches its chain cap exactly when both windows are capped at their per-window halves; a chain with windows of unequal length reaches it sooner or later than that, by the arithmetic of the lengths, not by counting windows. Credits that were truncated by a per-window cap never count toward the chain cap — only credited time counts, so a lift whose credit was truncated to nothing by its window's cap contributes nothing to the chain total, and a lift truncated in part contributes only the part that survived. Timely lifts contribute nothing, as in T-680: timeliness is not a negative credit and does not buy chain-cap room back.

The second rule is the chain-cap order. Chain-cap truncation applies in chain order, earliest window first, and within a window in T-680's original-publication order. The reviewer first applies T-680 window by window — union, then per-window cap — and then lays the surviving credited intervals across the chain in order, accumulating credited time until the chain cap is reached; every later credit is truncated to the chain-cap remainder, and the remainder, once exhausted, is lost, not carried to a later window and not returned to an earlier one. A chain whose first window already consumed the whole chain cap — possible where one window is long and its credited half exceeds the chain's total in time, though not where windows are equal — leaves nothing for later windows, however stale their cross-posts. The order matters for the same reason T-680's order matters: a reviewer who applied the chain cap window by window in reverse order would grant the latest window's credit and starve the earliest, rewarding the most recent delay over the oldest, and the chain's earliest petitioner is the one the delay stole from first.

The third rule is the inheritance rule. A successor chain inherits its predecessor's consumed chain cap. Where a chain is succeeded — a new chain pleaded on the same field, the same lifts, the same stale cross-posts, under a successor name or a refiled petition — the consumed chain cap travels with the field, not with the name. A petitioner may not evade a exhausted chain cap by re-pleading the same stack under a new chain number, any more than she may evade a per-window cap by re-pleading the same lift under a new cross-post date. The inheritance is measured in credited time: the successor chain's cap remainder is the predecessor's chain cap minus the predecessor's credited time, and the successor's own per-window caps apply fresh to its own windows, because the windows are new even when the chain's history is not. A genuinely new chain — new lifts, new original publications, new stale cross-posts, no overlap with the predecessor's stack — starts with a fresh chain cap, and the reviewer decides genuineness on the lift dates and the cross-post records, not on the petitioner's description of the chain.

The fourth rule is the reopening rule. Credit that reopens a window counts toward the chain cap exactly as credit that lengthens a live window does. A reopened window's period is credited time, and the chain that reopens it has spent that time from its cap. Where a second lift's credit extends a reopened period under T-680's sixth rule, the extension counts too, up to the same chain-cap remainder. A chain that has already spent its chain cap on live windows cannot reopen an expired window on stacked credit, however stale the cross-post that expired it — the reopening is a continuation, and a continuation that would push the chain past its total is a new window wearing the chain's name, the same offence T-680's per-window cap guards against, measured at the chain's scale. A chain expired for reasons other than a stale cross-post is not reopened by chain-cap arithmetic at all, under T-680's sixth rule, unchanged.

The fifth rule is the pleading, mark, and order rule. A stacked petition pleads, per window, every particular T-680 requires — the stacking table for that window — plus a chain table: each window's credited time after its per-window cap, the running chain total in chain order, the chain cap, the chain-cap remainder after each window, and the total claimed. A petition without the chain table pleads the chain incompletely, and the reviewer decides it on the records the chains themselves hold, measuring the chain total and the remainder from those records. A completion by stacked credit across a chain carries a Chain-Credit mark naming each window whose credit contributed and its credited time, alongside T-680's Stacked-Credit mark naming the lifts; a citation omitting a contributing window, or naming a window whose credit was truncated to nothing by the chain cap, is a misstatement of the record on the T-671 pattern. The order of operations gains no step: calibrate, cap, anchor, weigh, lift, chain, waive, then test walkability — chain-cap truncation is judged inside the walkability step, after T-680's per-window union and cap, with the chain total applied there before any expiry digest is computed.

Admitted here, still open: whether the chain cap should be one full window, or whether a long chain — ten windows, each honestly delayed — earns a larger total by the number of windows, with the per-window cap alone doing the persistence work (admitted here — T-681's long-chain problem, newly open). Whether a successor chain that inherits a partially consumed cap should inherit it in full, or only the portion attributable to lifts it actually re-pleads, where the successor drops some of the predecessor's lifts (admitted here — T-681's partial-inheritance problem, newly open). Whether credits for lifts in different windows on the same chain should pool toward one cap when the windows are contiguous and the chain is one chain, rather than capping window by window, is not fixed here (carried — T-680's pooling problem, still open). **T-682 — the Lift-Ledger Rule — designed:** T-681 left its partial-inheritance problem named and open: whether a successor chain that inherits a partially consumed cap should inherit it in full, or only the portion attributable to lifts it actually re-pleads, where the successor drops some of the predecessor's lifts. The answer is attribution by lift: the cap travels with the lift, not with the chain name. A successor inherits exactly the credited time of the lifts it re-pleads, and nothing for the lifts it drops. A dropped lift's credit stays on the field's ledger, binding any future chain that re-pleads it, but it does not bind a successor that never touches it — because a successor that never touches a lift cannot be repaid for it twice, and cannot be charged for a repayment it never received. The ledger is the record; chain names are labels.

The first rule is the lift-ledger rule. Every granted stacked credit is entered on the field's lift ledger, keyed by lift — original publication plus first correct cross-post — with its credited time after T-680's per-window cap and T-681's chain cap. The ledger is kept per field, not per chain: two chains on the same field read the same ledger, and a lift's entry survives its chain's closure, its successor's renaming, and its petitioner's re-description. A chain's chain-cap consumption is exactly the sum of the ledger entries of the lifts on its stack; there is no chain-level consumption apart from the lifts. A petitioner who re-pleads a lift under a new cross-post date, a new channel name, or a new description of one publication pleads the same lift, and the ledger answers with the same entry, because the key is the publication, not the pleading.

The second rule is the re-pleading rule. A successor chain that re-pleads a lift inherits that lift's ledger entry in full: the entry's credited time counts against the successor's chain cap from the successor's first window, before any new credit is measured. Re-pleading cannot enlarge the entry. The ledger entry is fixed once granted — a second pleading of the same lift claims the same credited time, not a new one, and a claim for more than the entry is a claim for the same stolen time twice, denied on the T-680 duplicate-pleading pattern. Where the successor re-pleads a lift and also pleads new lifts, the new lifts' credit is measured against the chain-cap remainder after the inherited entries, in chain order, earliest window first, as T-681 provides.

The third rule is the dropped-lift rule. A lift the successor drops contributes nothing to the successor's chain total, and the successor's chain cap is not reduced by it. Dropping is neither evasion nor forgiveness: the predecessor's grant stands on the predecessor's record, and the successor simply never claims that lift's time, so there is nothing to inherit. A dropped lift may still be re-pleaded by a third chain, and that chain inherits its entry in full under the second rule — dropping a lift from one successor does not launder it for the next. What dropping does buy is only this: a successor that genuinely abandons a lift is not charged cap room for a repayment it does not seek, and a petitioner is not punished for narrowing her claim.

The fourth rule is the overlap-attribution rule. Where T-680's union counted an overlap once, the overlap is attributed to the earliest lift in original-publication order, and later lifts' ledger entries carry only their non-overlapping credited time. This keeps the ledger additive: summing a chain's ledger entries reproduces its chain total exactly, with no double-counted week and no unattributed gap. A reviewer who attributed the overlap to the later lift, or split it, would let a successor that re-pleads only the later lift inherit time the union had already paid to the earlier one — the same stolen time repaid twice under a new name, which the first rule forbids.

The fifth rule is the zero-entry rule. A lift whose credit was truncated to nothing by a per-window cap or a chain cap carries a zero ledger entry. A zero entry binds nothing: a later chain re-pleading that lift starts from zero for it, and may earn fresh credit for it up to the later chain's own caps, because nothing was ever granted for it. But the zero is itself recorded, so a re-pleading cannot claim the pre-truncation excess as fresh credit — the excess was measured, truncated, and spent to nothing, and the ledger remembers the truncation, not just the grant. A lift with no entry at all — never pleaded, never granted — is not a zero entry; it is simply unpleaded, and its first grant is measured fresh.

The sixth rule is the pleading, mark, and order rule. A successor petition pleads, per window, every particular T-681 requires — the stacking table and the chain table for that window — plus a ledger table: each re-pleaded lift, its ledger entry, the inherited total, the chain cap, the chain-cap remainder for new lifts, and each dropped lift named as dropped, so the reviewer can see what was abandoned and what was carried. A petition without the ledger table pleads the succession incompletely, and the reviewer decides it on the records the fields themselves hold, measuring the inherited total from the ledger. A completion by stacked credit on a successor chain carries a Ledger mark naming each re-pleaded lift and its inherited credited time, alongside T-681's Chain-Credit mark and T-680's Stacked-Credit mark; a citation omitting a re-pleaded lift, or naming a dropped lift as contributing, is a misstatement of the record on the T-671 pattern. The order of operations gains no step: calibrate, cap, anchor, weigh, lift, chain, waive, then test walkability — ledger inheritance is judged inside the walkability step, after T-681's chain-cap truncation, with the inherited total applied there before any expiry digest is computed.

The successor inherits the recomputed entry, never more than the original entry, and the difference — the falsified excess — is forfeited, not banked, not carried, not spendable by any later chain.

Strike the falsified date, substitute the corrected date, and re-run the whole measurement for that lift: T-680's union in original-publication order, the per-window cap, then T-681's chain cap in chain order. A corrected date that would yield more credit than the original entry yields nothing extra: the excess was never pleaded, because the date pleaded was the falsified one, and new credit needs a new pleading, not a correction. A corrected date that yields less leaves the successor with the less, and the gap between the original entry and the inherited entry is the falsified excess, struck from the ledger.

Where the corrected date shows the lift was timely — no stale period at all — or where the recomputation truncates to nothing, the successor inherits a corrected-zero entry for that lift. **T-684 — the Admission Rule — designed:** T-683 left its admission problem named and open: whether a correction that comes from the petitioner's own admission should be treated more leniently than one the reviewer discovers — a shorter proof burden, or a preserved remainder — or whether the source of the correction changes nothing, because the ledger records dates, not motives. The answer splits the question in two, and the split is the rule: the source of the correction changes nothing about the entry, and everything about the sanction. The ledger records dates, not motives, so an admitted correction earns exactly the same recomputed entry as a discovered one — no preserved remainder, no extra credit, no softened cap. But the ledger also records conduct, and an admission is conduct the reviewer can trust, so an admitted correction carries a lighter proof burden and no misstatement sanction, where a discovered correction carries the full burden and the full sanction. Motive does not buy time; candour buys standing.

The first rule is the same-entry rule. An admitted correction is recomputed through T-683 exactly as a discovered one is: strike the falsified date, substitute the corrected date, re-run T-680's union and caps and T-681's chain cap, inherit the lesser of the original and recomputed entries, forfeit the falsified excess. Admission preserves no remainder of the excess — the petitioner who admits a falsified date does not keep a slice of the time the lie bought, because a remainder would pay for the falsification, once as granted and once as kept. Admission frees no chain-cap room, restates the predecessor's grant the same way, and moves no publication under T-682's overlap attribution. A petitioner who pleads admission expecting a bonus has misunderstood the bargain: the bargain is not more time, it is a clean record.

The second rule is the lighter-proof rule. An admission is itself a checkable source for T-683's proof rule — the petitioner's own signed statement naming the falsified date, the corrected date, and the lift — but it is not sufficient alone. It needs one corroborating record: the channel's own log, the cross-post's own timestamp, or a record the field itself holds, confirming the corrected date. One corroboration, not a chain of custody: the admission supplies the motive evidence the reviewer would otherwise have to build, so the reviewer checks the date, not the story. A discovered correction, by contrast, needs the full proof T-683 requires, built without the petitioner's help, and the reviewer may demand the channel's log and the cross-post's timestamp both. An admission pleaded without any corroboration is not an admission at all, it is an assertion, judged as a new pleading; an admission whose corroboration contradicts the corrected date pleaded is a misstatement on the T-671 pattern, and the admission credit in the third rule is lost with it.

The third rule is the no-sanction rule. An admitted correction is never a T-671 misstatement, and it never draws the T-683 struck-date sanction. The petitioner who admits before the reviewer finds the falsification keeps standing to re-plead the lift under the corrected date, and a completion on that corrected chain carries an Admission mark naming each admitted lift, its corrected date, and its corroborating record, alongside T-683's Corrected-Ledger mark, T-682's Ledger mark, T-681's Chain-Credit mark, and T-680's Stacked-Credit mark. The mark is the protection: a later petition that cites the admitted lift's corrected entry, and pleads it correctly, is not re-opening the falsification, it is relying on the corrected record. A discovered correction earns no Admission mark, and a petitioner who re-pleads a discovered falsification under the falsified date anyway draws the struck-date sanction in full — the lift's entry struck to zero for that chain, the pleading denied, not corrected by the reviewer.

The fourth rule is the timing rule. Admission counts only before discovery. An admission made after the reviewer has already found the falsification — after a finding, a struck date, or a denied bridge on that lift — is a concession, not an admission: it earns the same entry as a discovered correction, and no Admission mark, no lighter proof, no no-sanction protection. The line is the reviewer's finding, not the petitioner's knowledge: a petitioner who admits the day before the finding is candid, a petitioner who admits the day after is cornered, and the ledger marks the difference because the next petitioner on the field needs to know which one she is dealing with. Admission after a grant but before any walk under it is still before discovery if the reviewer has made no finding — but it reopens the grant for restatement under T-683, and the restated grant, not the grant as made, is the one the walk is judged under.

The fifth rule is the completeness rule. An admission must be complete for the petition it rides on: every falsified date the petitioner knows, on every lift pleaded in that petition, admitted together. A partial admission — admitting one falsified date while omitting another the petitioner knows — is concealment, and concealment is worse than silence. The omitted lift's entry is struck to zero for that chain on the T-679 eighth-rule pattern, the Admission mark is withheld from every lift in that petition including the ones admitted, and the petition is decided on the records the fields hold, with the omitted date treated as discovered. The reviewer does not grade admissions lift by lift; a petitioner who picks which lies to confess has not confessed, she has negotiated, and the ledger does not negotiate.
