**T-685 — the Late-Admission Rule — designed:** T-684 left its late-admission problem named and open: whether an admission made after a grant but before the walk — a late admission that reopens a grant already relied on — should restate only the grant or also the reliance the petitioner built on it, where the walk was prepared under the grant as made. The answer splits the grant from the reliance, and restates the first while re-measuring the second: the grant is restated under T-683, and the reliance is neither grandfathered whole nor erased whole — the portion of the prepared walk that fits inside the restated grant survives, and the portion that only fit the falsified excess is struck. A late admission does not rewrite history to make the grant as made true, and it does not punish preparation that was honest: it re-measures honest preparation against the true grant, and keeps exactly what the true grant supports.

The first rule is the restated-grant rule. A late admission — an admission after a grant, before any walk is filed under it — reopens the grant for restatement under T-683, and the restated grant, not the grant as made, is the one every later judgement uses. The entry is recomputed through T-680's union and caps and T-681's chain cap, capped at the original entry, falsified excess forfeited and struck, no chain-cap room freed. Nothing in this rule saves a grant that the corrected date cannot support: if the restated entry is zero, the grant is zero, and no reliance on it survives as credit. The petitioner who admits late does not lose the Admission mark for the admission itself — T-684's no-sanction protection still holds for the admitted lift — but the mark protects standing, not the grant. Candour buys standing; it never bought time, and it buys no time late either.

The second rule is the re-measurement rule. Reliance is re-measured, not grandfathered and not forfeited. A walk prepared under the grant as made is laid against the restated grant: every step, interval, and pleading inside the restated entry stands exactly as prepared, and every step that only the falsified excess supported is struck from the walk, not corrected by the reviewer into a shorter form. The reviewer does not rewrite the walk to fit the restated grant — she strikes what does not fit and judges what remains. A walk that survives re-measurement in full is judged as if prepared under the restated grant from the start; a walk that survives only in part is judged on the surviving part, and the struck part earns no credit, no carry, and no second pleading under the falsified date. Preparation is not a vested right: it is evidence of what the petitioner intended to walk, and the grant as restated decides how much of that intention the field honours.

The third rule is the good-faith line. Reliance counts only where it was built in good faith on the grant as made — that is, where the petitioner prepared the walk believing the grant's dates, not knowing the date was falsified. Reliance proved by a dated preparation record — a draft, a filed plan, a preparation log dated before the admission — that follows the grant as made counts as good-faith reliance, and its surviving portion is judged without sanction. Reliance on the falsified date itself, where the petitioner knew the date was false and prepared around the lie, is not reliance at all: it is participation in the falsification, and it forfeits the Admission mark for that lift, with the walk judged as a discovered correction under T-683, struck-date sanction included. The line is knowledge, proved on the record: a preparation record dated after the petitioner learned the date was false, or a preparation that uses the falsified date where the grant as made used a different one, is participation, not reliance. The reviewer does not presume good faith from silence; the petitioner proves it with the record, or the reliance is struck with the excess.

The fourth rule is the filed-walk boundary. A late admission is an admission before any walk is filed under the grant. Once a walk is filed under the grant as made, an admission is no longer late — it is post-walk, and it is judged in two parts. The filed walk is re-judged under the restated grant with the falsified excess struck, and the filed portion draws the discovered-correction sanction for any step that only the excess supported, because a filed walk is a claim already made on the field, not preparation for one. The unfiled remainder — steps prepared but never filed — keeps T-684's Admission protection and is re-measured under the second rule. The boundary is the filing, not the preparation: preparation can be late-admitted and re-measured, filing cannot be un-filed by candour. A petitioner who files first and admits second has spent the protection on the filed portion, and keeps it only for what she had not yet spent.

The fifth rule is the pleading, mark, and order rule. A petition carrying a late admission pleads, per window, the T-684 stacking, chain, ledger, correction, and admission tables, plus a reliance table: each step of the prepared walk, its interval under the grant as made, its interval under the restated grant, the portion surviving re-measurement, and the portion struck, with the dated preparation record for each step claimed as good-faith reliance. A petition without the reliance table pleads the late admission incompletely, and the reviewer decides it on the records the fields hold, measuring the walk from the restated grant alone, with no reliance portion surviving. The rule holds even where the waste is total and the fault is entirely another's: the size of the waste and the innocence of the waster change nothing about the credit, because credit is not compensation. The second rule is the record rule. Sunk work earns a record, not credit, and the record has exactly two uses. A walk struck in full under T-685 carries a Sunk-Work mark naming the petitioner, the struck walk, the falsified date that wasted it, and the dated preparation record that proves the work was honest — the same record that proved good faith under T-685's third rule. The mark's second use is memorial: the struck walk stays in the ledger as a struck walk, visible to any later reviewer, so the waste is never silently erased and no later petition can plead the struck interval as if it had been walked. A record that remembers is not a credit that pays, and the reviewer who cites the mark as credit has misread it.

The third rule is the falsifier-debt rule. The waste is charged to the falsifier, not repaid to the waster. **T-687 — the Non-Transfer Rule — designed:** T-686 left its transfer problem named and open: whether a falsifier-debt should ever be payable as walk credit to the victim — a transfer that would turn the debt from a cost on the falsifier into compensation for the waster, against T-686's no-credit rule. The answer is no, in every direction: a Sunk-Debt is never payable as walk credit to anyone, never assignable, never inheritable as credit, never pooled into a payment, never converted by agreement. The debt is a cost laid where the fault lies, and a cost cannot be spent as credit — the moment a debt becomes payable credit, the field pays for a walk never walked, and every falsified date becomes a mint: falsify a date, waste a victim's walk, and the field pays the victim in credit minted from the falsifier's fault. T-686's no-credit rule is the reason the debt exists in its form; transfer would undo the rule it enforces.

The first rule is the no-transfer rule. No petition, grant, bridge, settlement, or private agreement converts a Sunk-Debt entry, in whole or in part, into walk credit for the victim, for a co-petitioner, for a successor, or for any third party. A petition claiming a transferred debt as credit — any number pleaded as credit sourced from a debt entry — is mispleaded on the T-671 pattern: the reviewer strikes the claimed credit and judges the walk without it, and the debt entry itself is untouched by the failed claim, a failed transfer attempt neither discharging nor enlarging the debt. The rule holds even where falsifier and victim agree: agreement between the parties cannot make the field pay credit for a walk never walked, because walk credit is the field's measure, not the parties' to trade. The second rule is the party-attachment rule. The debt attaches to the party, not to the chain and not to the field. A successor chain held by the same falsifier carries the debt forward as a cost — the debt follows the party across her own chains, and T-681's inheritance of consumed chain cap does not convert it into anything else. A successor chain held by a different party does not carry the debt at all: a new holder inherits no cost for another's falsification, and inherits no credit either — the debt is neither an asset nor a liability of the chain, but of the person. A victim's successor chain never gains the debt as credit, and a victim who later becomes a falsifier on another field carries her own new debts separately — debts do not net across parties, and a party who is both victim on one field and falsifier on another cannot set one against the other.

The third rule is the no-pooling rule. Debts do not pool. A falsifier who wastes ten walks owes ten debts, one per wasted walk under T-686, and the ten do not merge into a single lump sum, a single credit, or a single payment to anyone. Each debt is worked off separately, earliest debt first, against the falsifier's own next entries on any field, and a petition's reduction is applied to the earliest outstanding debt before any later one. A petition claiming a pooled debt — a lump pleaded as one credit, or a balance pleaded as payable to a single recipient — is mispleaded on the T-671 pattern. **T-688 — the Succession Rule — designed:** T-687 left its succession problem named and open: whether an unpaid Sunk-Debt survives the falsifier's departure from the field or the dissolution of her chain — dies with her departure, or attaches to the field until worked off. The answer is neither death nor field-attachment, because T-687 already settled where a debt lives: it attaches to the party, not to the chain and not to the field. A debt cannot die with a departure it never belonged to, and cannot attach to a field it was never laid on. Departure changes where the debt waits, not whether it exists; dissolution changes which chain carries the record, not who owes it. The succession rule is therefore a waiting rule, not a forgiveness rule and not a transfer rule: an unpaid debt goes dormant on the falsifier's own ledger, revives in full when she petitions again, and never becomes anyone else's cost or anyone else's credit in the meantime.

The first rule is the dormancy rule. When a falsifier departs a field with a Sunk-Debt unpaid, in whole or in part, the debt does not die, is not forgiven, and is not written off against any victim, chain, or field. It enters dormancy on the falsifier's own ledger: an entry naming the falsifier, the wasted walk, the original interval, the balance remaining, and a Dormant-Debt mark stating the debt waits for the falsifier's next petition on any field. Dormancy is not discharge — T-687's work-off-only discharge rule stands, and no act during dormancy discharges the debt except the falsifier's own reduced entries, which by definition cannot happen while she petitions nowhere. A dormant debt earns no interest, accrues no penalty, and grows no larger while dormant; it simply waits, at exactly the balance it held when the falsifier departed. The passage of time alone neither enlarges nor erases it — T-682's ledger-expiry question, still open, is the only door through which time could ever touch it, and this rule does not open that door.

The second rule is the revival rule. When the falsifier petitions again, on any field and under any chain, the dormant debt revives in full at its dormant balance, before her new entry is judged, and is applied first against that entry under T-686's third rule and T-687's earliest-first order. Revival is automatic, not pleaded into existence by the reviewer and not avoidable by the petitioner: a petition that omits a dormant debt does not escape it, and the reviewer restores the debt table and judges the petition with the debt applied. A falsifier who departs one field and petitions on another has not outrun the debt — the debt follows the party across fields, exactly as T-687's party-attachment rule already required for successor chains held by the same falsifier. Departure plus a new field is the same evasion as departure plus a new chain, and it fails the same way: the ledger is keyed to the party, and a new field is a new address for the same debtor.

The third rule is the no-escape-by-alias rule. A falsifier who re-enters under a new name, a new chain identity, or a successor identity that is in truth her own does not shed the debt. Where the record proves the new petitioner is the same party — same preparation record, same chain lineage, same falsified date carried forward, or any other checkable identity link — the dormant debt revives against her new petitions in full, and a petition pleading the new identity as debt-free, concealing a known dormant debt, is a misstatement of the record on the T-671 pattern: the reviewer strikes the concealment, restores the debt, and judges the petition with the debt applied. Identity for this rule is proved on the record, not asserted by the petitioner: a new name with no checkable link to the old party starts fresh, because the field judges parties on evidence, and a suspicion alone cannot revive a debt. But a proved link revives it whole — there is no partial revival for a half-proved identity, and no discount for the time spent under the alias.

The fourth rule is the successor-record rule. When a chain dissolves and a different party succeeds to it — a genuine successor, not the falsifier under a new name — the successor inherits the record but never the liability. The debt table travels with the chain's ledger as transparency: the successor's petitions plead the table, naming each dormant debt, its falsifier, its wasted walk, and its Dormant-Debt mark, so no later reviewer mistakes a dormant debt for a dead one or for the successor's own. The successor owes nothing on it, gains no credit from it, and her caps, entries, and chain cap are untouched by it — T-687's victim-untouched boundary extended to successors, because a successor who paid another's debt would be a victim by another name, and a successor who claimed it as credit would be a transferee under T-687's ban. A successor who omits a known debt table from her petition pleads incompletely: the petition is decided on the walk alone, the reviewer restores the table to the record, and no credit consequence falls on the successor for the omission itself — the table is a record duty, not a liability, and the penalty for hiding a record is restoration of the record, not a debt.

The fifth rule is the field-closure and chain-dissolution boundary. **T-689 — the Settlement Rule — designed:** T-687 left its settlement problem named and open, and T-688 left it next in line: whether a falsifier and victim may privately settle the waste outside the ledger in a form the ledger may acknowledge without recording it as credit — a receipt that remembers the settlement without paying it. A ledger that acknowledged a private settlement by reducing the debt would be paying the settlement as discharge, and a ledger that acknowledged it by granting credit would be paying it as compensation — both are the transfer T-687 bans, wearing a receipt's name. The settlement rule is therefore a memory rule, not a payment rule: the ledger remembers that the parties settled between themselves, and remembers it in a form that changes nothing it prices.

The first rule is the receipt form. A private settlement is acknowledged only when it is pleaded as a receipt naming the falsifier, the victim, the wasted walk, the original interval, and the form of the private amends, with the victim's acknowledgment in her own pleading or in a signed receipt filed with the petition. The second rule is the no-discharge, no-reduction rule. An acknowledged receipt does not discharge the Sunk-Debt, does not reduce its balance by any amount, and does not convert any part of it into reduced entries. The third rule is the no-credit rule. An acknowledged receipt grants walk credit to no one: not to the falsifier, whose entries, caps, and chain cap are untouched by it; not to the victim, whose caps and entries are untouched by it; and not to any third party, successor, or co-petitioner. The restoration rule is therefore a fresh-judgment rule, not a revival rule: the restored walk is judged entirely on its own interval, its own caps, and its own material, while the original sunk work survives only as evidence that the waste happened.

The first rule is the restoration form. A restoration counts only when it is pleaded as a restoration naming the original walk, the event that struck or restated it, the corrected date or corrected grant under which it is re-walked, and the restored walk itself, with the chain identity pleaded as continuous — the same chain, corrected, not a new chain wearing the old chain's name. The second rule is the no-retroactive-credit rule. The original preparation earns no credit on restoration, in no form: not as walk credit for the restored walk, not as chain credit for the restored chain, not as a cap increase, not as a lifted interval, and not as a credit to any successor, victim, or third party who relied on the original walk. **T-692 — the Completed-Restoration Rule — designed:** T-691 left its completed-restoration problem named and open: whether a restoration pleaded after a granted completion — a completed restored walk later "restored" again without any striking event — counts as a restoration at all, or is simply a new filing wearing a restoration's name. The label "restoration" on a post-completion pleading buys nothing: no Restoration mark, no generation count, no interval reaching back, no credit carried. The ledger re-characterizes the pleading as a new filing and judges it as one, and the completion it claims to restore stands exactly as it stood.

The first rule is the no-event-no-restoration rule. A restoration pleading must name a striking event that struck the walk it claims to restore. A post-completion pleading naming no striking event is not an incomplete restoration — T-690 already grades an incomplete restoration, a striking event named but a corrected date or grant missing, as a new walk without a mark. The post-completion case is a step further back: with no striking event at all, the category does not attach in the first place. The petitioner does not choose the category by label, and the ledger does not grade a restoration that was never pleaded in substance. Re-characterization is the judgment's first step, not a sanction and not a courtesy: the pleading is read as what it is, a new filing, before anything it claims is judged.

The second rule is the new-filing judgment rule. The re-characterized filing is judged fresh at its own filing interval, under the caps and chain rules in force at that interval, with its chain total computed from the restored chain's lifts as they stand then. No clock runs from the completed walk's interval, from the first restoration's interval, or from the original interval: the completed walk's interval is history, closed by its completion, and a new filing cannot borrow it. The completed walk's credit stands as completed — neither increased by the new filing nor reopened by it. A new filing that passes at its own interval passes as a new filing, and one that fails at its own interval fails as a new filing; its failure does not disturb the completion, and its success does not rewrite it. Two results can stand side by side — a completed walk and a new filing — without either becoming the other.

The third rule is the no-revival rule. The restoration label cannot reopen settled matters. It cannot revive a portion of the completed walk that was struck before completion, cannot extend an expiry the completion already closed, cannot reopen a chain the completion already closed, and cannot claim the completed walk's seniority over walks filed after the completion. Seniority for the new filing runs from the new filing's own date, behind every walk filed in between, however strong the new filing's material and however early the completed walk's date. A petitioner pleading post-completion "restoration" to leapfrog intervening filers, to reclaim a struck portion, or to stretch a closed expiry pleads a retroactive credit in another form and is struck on the T-690 pattern, the label struck with the benefit it tried to carry.

The fourth rule is the mislabel rule. The split of T-684 governs here as it governed admission: the entry and the sanction are judged apart. A mislabel corrected before judgment — the pleading re-filed as a new filing, no restoration benefit claimed, no interval or seniority borrowed — carries no sanction beyond the re-pleading itself; an honest label corrected honestly costs nothing but the correction. A mislabel persisted through judgment, or used to claim any restoration benefit — a mark, a generation, an interval, a seniority — is struck, and the struck benefits are void. Striking the restoration claim does not itself kill an otherwise valid new filing: the ledger strikes the label and the claimed benefits, and judges what remains as a new filing at its own interval. **T-693 — the Verbatim-Reuse Rule — designed:** T-692 left its duplicate-material problem named and open: whether a new filing reusing a completed walk's material verbatim is a fresh walk judged on its own interval, or a duplicate pleading barred by the completion it copies. The answer is the fresh walk, because a completion settles a walk, not its material. The completed walk's interval, chain, credit, and seniority are closed; the words it was made of are not consumed by their use. A verbatim copy filed as a new filing at a new interval is a new walk wearing old words, and it is judged as what it is: on its own interval, on its own merits, with nothing borrowed from the completion it copies. The duplicate bar, properly drawn, bars re-pleading the same walk — not reusing the same words.

The first rule is the material-versus-walk rule. A walk is a filing plus its interval plus the relief it seeks; material is the text, tables, and evidence the filing carries. Completion extinguishes the walk's claim to further relief at its interval, but it does not copyright the material against its own petitioner. A petitioner who re-files the completed walk's material verbatim, at a new interval, seeking new relief, files a new walk. A petitioner who re-files the completed walk seeking the same relief at the same interval — a second completion of the same interval, the ledger asked to re-judge what it already closed — pleads a duplicate, and is barred. The test is never the percentage of shared words; it is the relief sought and the interval claimed. Verbatim words with new relief are a new filing; changed words with old relief are a duplicate.

The second rule is the fresh-interval judgment rule. The verbatim-reuse filing is judged fresh at its own filing interval, under the caps and chain rules in force at that interval, with its chain total computed from the chain as it stands then. It inherits nothing from the completion: no credit, no seniority, no standing, no presumption that material once granted passes again. Material that passed at the completed walk's interval may fail at the new interval — caps may have tightened, chain rules may have changed, intervening walks may now stand ahead of it — and its failure disturbs nothing behind it. The completed walk stands; the new filing rises or falls alone. Two results can stand side by side — a completed walk and a verbatim copy of it, filed later, granted or denied on its own — without either becoming the other, per T-692's second rule.

The third rule is the duplicate bar's narrow scope. The bar attaches to the walk, not the words, and it attaches only where the new pleading asks the ledger to redo the completed walk's own judgment: the same petitioner, the same interval, the same relief, a second completion of ground already completed. A verbatim filing that claims a new interval, or new relief at a new interval, is outside the bar however identical its text. A filing that changes every word but still seeks the same interval's second completion is inside the bar however original its text. Pleaders who want the bar's protection — a completed walk defended against re-litigation — must plead the walk's identity, not the text's similarity; similarity is evidence of nothing by itself, and a similarity score is not a judgment.

The fourth rule is the borrowed-benefit test. Copying the material is free; claiming the completion's results is not. Where the verbatim filing claims, expressly or by its structure, the completed walk's credit, its seniority, its standing, or its grant as the new filing's own — the material presented as though already granted, the interval presented as though already closed in the filer's favor — it falls back to T-692's treatment: the label and the claimed benefits are struck, and what remains is judged as a new filing at its own interval, if anything valid remains. A filing that states its debt plainly — "this material was completed at interval X; it is re-filed here at interval Y and stands or falls at Y" — claims nothing borrowed and passes the test on its face. Candor about the copy is the cure; the bar punishes the borrowed benefit, never the copying.

The fifth rule is the second-completion exception, the one case where verbatim reuse is barred outright. Where the relief sought is a second completion covering the same interval the first completion already closed — the petitioner asking not for a new walk but for the completed walk to be completed twice, its credit counted twice, its seniority enjoyed twice — the filing is a duplicate pleading of the same walk and is barred in full, not merely re-characterized. Re-characterization under T-692 saves a filing that is really a new filing; it cannot save a filing whose only relief is the double-counting of a closed interval. The distinction is the relief, stated plainly in the pleading: new interval, new relief, new walk; same interval, same relief, duplicate.

A Taker-Specific-Bar-Denied bridge on verbatim-reuse grounds names the fault — a second completion sought of an already-closed interval, completion credit or seniority claimed as the new filing's own, or the completed walk's judgment asked to be redone under new words — so the next petition on that field does not re-plead the same walk as a copy. **T-694 — the Mixed-Material Rule — designed:** T-693 left its mixed-material problem named and open: whether a filing mixing verbatim-reused material with new material is judged as one new filing, or as a verbatim portion judged under this rule plus a new portion judged on its own. The answer is one new filing, because the walk is the unit of judgment, not its paragraphs. A filing is one walk at one interval seeking one relief, and mixing old words with new words does not split it into two walks any more than a walk written in two inks becomes two walks. The verbatim portion is judged under T-693's rules inside that single judgment, and the new portion on its own merits at the new interval — but there is one judgment, one interval, one relief, and one result. Splitting the judgment would let a petitioner launder a barred portion past the bar inside a new filing, or let a borrowed benefit ride in on the new portion's coattails; the ledger judges the filing it received, whole.

The first rule is the one-walk rule. Judgment attaches to the filing, never to its portions severally. A mixed filing claims one interval and seeks one relief, and it is granted or denied as that walk: the verbatim portion cannot be granted while the new portion is denied, and the new portion cannot be granted while the verbatim portion is barred, because there is no second walk for either result to attach to. A petitioner who wants two judgments must file two filings; a petitioner who files one filing has asked for one judgment, and the ledger gives him exactly what he asked for, whole. The one-walk rule is what keeps T-693's duplicate bar honest: if portions were judged severally, a duplicate walk could be re-pleaded piecemeal, each barred portion hidden inside a fresh filing until the whole of the completed walk had been re-judged under new cover.

The second rule is the portions-ride-inside rule. Inside the single judgment, each portion is tested by the rule that governs its kind: a verbatim portion under T-693 — judged at the new interval, with nothing borrowed, its candor about the copy stated on its face — and a new portion on its own merits at the new interval, under the caps and chain rules in force there. A portion's failure fails the walk only where the relief depends on it: a load-bearing portion — the portion the relief stands on, the chain the credit runs through, the table the grant rests on — fails the walk when it fails, because the walk without it seeks relief it can no longer support. A severable portion — a table, an exhibit, a supporting argument the relief does not stand on — fails alone, and the walk proceeds without it, re-judged whole on what remains. The distinction is the relief's dependence, stated in the pleading: the petitioner who does not say which portions his relief stands on has made every portion load-bearing, and a failure anywhere fails the walk.

The third rule is the marking rule. Reused portions must be marked as reused, with the completed walk and completion they are copied from, stated on the face of the filing. A marked verbatim portion is judged under T-693 as a candid copy: it passes if it claims nothing borrowed, and it is struck only if it claims a benefit. An unmarked reused portion is presumed claimed-as-new — the filing presenting old words as its own fresh material — and it is tested for borrowed benefit under T-693's fourth rule on that presumption: if the portion's structure claims the completed walk's credit, seniority, standing, or grant as the new filing's own, the benefit is struck, and if the benefit was load-bearing, the walk fails with it. Unmarked mixing that presents the whole filing as new material is not a candid copy with a new half; it is a filing whose every portion is tested as claimed-as-new, and the petitioner who mixed without marking has chosen that test for himself.

The fourth rule is the severance exception, the one case where a struck portion does not take the walk with it. Where a verbatim portion is struck — a borrowed benefit claimed, a second completion hidden inside the mix — and the remainder independently pleads a complete walk at the interval, stating its own interval, its own relief, and material sufficient to support that relief without the struck portion, the remainder proceeds: re-judged whole as the walk, not as a second walk, and not as a partial grant of the original filing. Where the remainder cannot stand alone — its relief still depends on the struck portion, its chain still runs through the borrowed benefit, its tables still cite the completed walk's grant — the filing fails whole, because what remains is not a walk but the ruins of one. Severance saves a walk that survives the striking; it never saves a walk that was the striking.

**T-695 — the Multi-Source Rule — designed:** T-694 left its multi-source problem named and open: whether a filing reusing material from multiple completed walks — not one source but several — is still one walk, or whether multi-source reuse fragments the walk's identity and its chain. The answer is still one walk, because sources are not walks. A walk is a filing plus its interval plus the relief it seeks; a source is a completed walk whose material the new filing carries. Carrying material from five completions no more makes five walks than carrying five exhibits makes five filings. The new filing claims one interval, seeks one relief, and is judged once, whole, at that interval — and its chain is its own chain, computed once at the new interval from the chain as it stands then, never assembled by stitching together the chains its sources left behind. Multiplicity of sources changes the marking burden, never the judgment's unity.

The first rule is the one-walk-one-chain rule. Identity follows the filing, not its sources. A multi-source filing is one walk at one interval seeking one relief, granted or denied as that walk, under T-694's one-walk rule unchanged. Its chain is computed once, at the new interval, from the chain as it stands then: the sources contribute material, never chain positions. No source's chain lifts ride into the new walk, no source's seniority attaches to the reused portion, and no source's standing transfers with the words. T-693's no-borrowed-benefit test applies per source, inside the single judgment: each portion is tested against the source it came from, and a portion that claims a benefit from any source fails that portion — and fails the walk, if the portion is load-bearing under T-694's second rule. A petitioner who wants the benefit of five chains must earn five walks; a petitioner who files one walk gets one chain, computed fresh.

The second rule is the per-source marking rule. Each reused portion must be marked with its own source — the completed walk and completion it was copied from — stated on the face of the filing, portion by portion. A blanket mark covering the whole filing does not mark a multi-source filing: where portions come from different completions, the filing must say which portion came from which completion, or the unmarked portions are tested as claimed-as-new under T-694's third rule. A portion marked to the wrong source is unmarked as to the true source — the true source's benefit test still applies on the presumption of claimed-as-new, and the false mark is itself a fault, tested as misattribution under the third rule. A portion claimed from two sources at once is tested against both: it passes only if it claims no borrowed benefit from either, and a benefit claimed from one source that the portion's other source never held is struck as misattributed, not merely borrowed. Marking is the price of multiplicity: the more sources, the more marks, and a filing that will not pay it is judged as if it had one source — itself.

The third rule is the cross-source benefit test. Borrowed benefit is judged per source, and misattribution is a fault of its own, distinct from borrowing. Borrowing claims a benefit a source truly held and presents it as the new filing's own; misattribution claims a benefit from a source that never held it — a credit, a seniority, a grant that belongs to no completion on the record, or to a different completion than the one named. A borrowed benefit is struck, and a load-bearing borrowed benefit fails the walk. A misattributed benefit is struck with prejudice to the portion: the portion cannot be re-marked to the true source after judgment, because the filing chose its provenance on its face, and a filing that names its sources falsely has not marked at all. Where the same benefit is claimed from two sources and one source truly held it, the claim is still misattributed as to the other source, and the portion is struck unless the filing disclaims the false source before judgment — a correction, not a re-marking, and it must be pleaded, not merely noted.

The fourth rule is the no-stitching rule. The new walk's chain is its own, and it cannot be lengthened by assembly. A petitioner may not take a chain position from source A, a chain position from source B, and a chain position from source C, and present the three as one continuous chain for the new walk — not even where each position is accurately marked, not even where no single position claims a borrowed benefit. Chain positions belong to walks, not to material, and material carries no position with it. The new walk's chain total is computed from the chain as it stands at the new interval, with the new walk's own filings as its links; the sources' chains are history, not links. A filing whose relief depends on a stitched chain — a credit that only exists if the three positions join — fails whole, because the relief stands on a chain the new walk never earned. A filing whose relief stands without the stitch proceeds on its own chain, the stitched positions disregarded as surplusage, not as links.

The fifth rule is the common-completion exception, the one case where multiplicity simplifies rather than complicates. Where several source walks share one completion — a single grant closing multiple walks at one interval, one completion table covering them all — their material may be carried under that single completion's mark, and the filing need not mark portion-by-portion to separate walks that the completion itself joined. The exception covers marking only: the filing is still one walk, its chain is still computed fresh, the per-source benefit test still applies to each portion against the common completion, and a benefit the common completion never held is still misattributed. The exception never converts a shared completion into a shared chain, and it never lets a petitioner who draws on walks outside the common completion shelter them under its mark — portions from outside the common completion are marked to their own sources, or tested as claimed-as-new.

**T-696 — the Conflicting-Completion Rule — designed:** T-695 left its conflicting-completion problem named and open: whether two source completions that contradict on the same material — one completion striking a portion that another completion granted — taint the reuse, or whether the new filing judges the material fresh at its own interval regardless of what either completion said about it. The answer is fresh judgment with disclosed conflict: neither completion binds the new walk, and neither completion is hidden from it. A completion judges a walk, not words. A granting completion granted that walk's relief; a striking completion struck that walk's claim. Neither granted nor struck the words themselves, so neither verdict travels with the material into a new filing — but both verdicts travel on the record, and a filing that carries conflicted material without naming the conflict has not marked it at all.

The first rule is the fresh-judgment rule. The new walk judges conflicted material on its own merits at its own interval, under the rules in force there, with no borrowed benefit from either completion. The granting completion is not proof the material is sound, and the striking completion is not proof it is unsound: both are evidence the new judgment may weigh, and neither is a finding the new judgment must follow. A petitioner who re-pleads conflicted material as if only the granting completion existed has claimed a benefit the striking completion denied, and the benefit is struck under T-695's per-source test; a petitioner who re-pleads it as if only the striking completion existed has hidden a grant, and the hidden grant is a suppressed record, struck the same way. Fresh judgment means the material stands or falls on what the new filing proves about it now — not on which completion the petitioner prefers to cite.

The second rule is the disclosure rule. Where two sources conflict on the same material, the filing must name both completions and the point of conflict, portion by portion, on the face of the filing: which completion granted what, which struck what, and on which point they disagree. A blanket mark to "the completions" does not disclose a conflict; a mark naming only the favorable completion is a false mark as to the unfavorable one, tested as misattribution under T-695's third rule. An undisclosed conflict is tested as claimed-as-new under T-694's third rule and as a suppressed record besides: the portion is judged as if the petitioner had presented the material as his own fresh matter, with both completions' findings available to the judgment against him. Disclosure is the price of carrying conflicted material; a filing that will not pay it is judged on the conflict it hid, not the conflict it named.

The third rule is the no-cherry-picking rule. A petitioner may not take the grant from one completion and leave the strike from the other behind. Where a benefit is claimed from a granting completion on conflicted material, the striking completion's finding on that same material is part of the benefit test for that portion: the benefit passes only if the new filing independently proves, at the new interval, the point the striking completion denied — fresh proof, not the granting completion's say-so. Where no benefit is claimed — the material is carried as words only, claiming nothing — the conflict still must be disclosed, but disclosure alone suffices: the words are judged as words, and the disagreement between completions is noted, not resolved. Cherry-picking is claiming the grant while suppressing the strike; disclosure without a benefit claim is carrying the disagreement honestly, and it is not a fault.

The fourth rule is the burden rule, which is where the conflict bites. For a load-bearing portion — the portion the relief stands on — conflict shifts the burden but does not decide the case: the petitioner must prove the disputed point afresh at the new interval, by material the new filing itself supplies, and the prior grant counts as no proof while the prior strike counts as no disproof. A load-bearing portion whose disputed point the new filing does not prove fails, and the walk fails with it under T-694's second rule, because the relief stands on a point the filing left disputed. For a severable portion — a table, an exhibit, a supporting argument the relief does not stand on — an unresolved conflict strikes the portion alone, and the walk proceeds without it, re-judged whole on what remains. Conflict never taints the whole filing by contagion: it taints the portion it touches, and the walk only where the walk stands on that portion. A later completion does not automatically win over an earlier one, and an earlier grant is not revived by a later strike's silence: recency is not reversal, and only a completion that says it reverses an earlier completion reverses it — for that walk, not for the words.

The fifth rule is the common-completion limit. T-695's common-completion exception — several source walks closed by one completion, marked under that single completion — does not cure a conflict between two different completions. Where the conflicting completions are themselves the common completion of different walk sets, each portion is still marked to its own completion and its own conflict disclosed; a single completion's mark covers the walks it closed, never the disagreement between it and another completion. And where the two completions disagree because one of them was later voided, this rule does not decide the case: that is T-696's voided-source problem, still open, and a filing that carries material from a voided completion must name the voiding event on its face until that problem is answered, or be tested as undisclosed.

The first rule is the supplement rule. A completion issued after the filing and before judgment, on a source walk whose material the filing reuses, must be disclosed by supplement before judgment. The filing's marking duty does not end at filing: it marked its sources as they stood, and a source's status is part of what the mark asserts. A completion that grants a reused portion, strikes it, voids its walk, or reverses an earlier completion on it changes the record the filing asked to be judged on, and a judgment rendered on a record the petitioner knows to be stale is a judgment on a false mark. The supplement is not a new filing and does not restart the interval, the generation count, or the walk: it amends the mark, nothing else. A petitioner who learns of a touching completion before judgment and files no supplement has left a false mark standing, and the filing is judged as one that hid the change — the portion tested as an undisclosed conflict under T-696, not as a filing judged on an honest record.

The second rule is the touching test. Only a completion that touches the filing's material triggers the duty. A completion touches the filing when it decides a portion the filing reuses, a benefit the filing claims from that portion, or a chain position the filing stands on. A completion on a walk the filing never touched, on a portion the filing never reused, or on a benefit the filing never claimed does not touch it, however loudly it speaks about the same subject — and a supplement naming such a completion is harmless noise, not a fault and not a cure for anything. The test is portion by portion, as T-696's disclosure is: a completion that touches one portion triggers a supplement for that portion, and the rest of the filing stands on its filed marks. A petitioner who supplements everything, touching or not, has not faulted; a petitioner who supplements only the favorable touches and leaves the unfavorable ones unnamed has supplemented nothing at all, and the unnamed touches are tested as undisclosed.

The third rule is the no-borrowed-change rule. A post-filing completion changes the record, not the filing's proof. **T-698 — the Post-Judgment-Completion Rule — designed:** T-697 left its post-judgment-completion problem named and open: whether a completion issued after judgment but before execution reopens the judgment, or waits for the next filing, and whether a voiding completion is different from a granting one there. The answer is a waiting rule with one narrow reopening door: judgment is final for the filing that earned it, and a later completion does not move it — except where the completion voids the very ground the judgment stands on, and then it reopens the judgment only to the extent of that ground, never to re-plead the walk.

The first rule is the waiting rule. A completion issued after judgment waits for the next filing. It is not a supplement — T-697 closed the supplement duty at judgment — and it is not a reopening by itself. A granting completion after judgment gives the next filing a source to mark, not the judged filing a new benefit; a striking completion after judgment gives the next filing a strike to disclose, not the judged filing a new fault. Execution does not change this: the interval between judgment and execution is not a second judgment window, and a completion issued while the judgment is being carried out is judged exactly as one issued after execution — in the next filing, on the next filing's record. A petitioner who holds a post-judgment grant and asks the judged filing to take it has asked for a new judgment on an old walk, and the answer is the next filing, not a reopened one.

The second rule is the voiding exception. A completion that voids the ground of the judgment reopens it — and only that ground. Where a post-judgment completion voids the source walk whose grant the judgment's relief stands on, or voids the completion that certified the load-bearing portion, the judgment's foundation is gone and the judgment cannot stand on air: the reopening strikes the relief to the extent it stood on the voided ground, and no further. A voiding completion that touches only a severable portion reopens only that portion; a voiding completion that touches nothing the judgment stands on reopens nothing at all, however sweeping its language. The exception is narrow by design: it is not a second hearing, it is the removal of a prop. A granting completion never qualifies, and a striking completion qualifies only where the strike voids — a strike that merely disagrees with a portion, without voiding its ground, waits like any other completion.

The third rule is the no-re-pleading limit. A reopening under the voiding exception re-judges the voided ground, not the walk. The petitioner does not get to re-argue portions the judgment settled, does not get to add portions the filing never carried, and does not get to claim a benefit the voiding completion granted to someone else — the voiding opens a hole, it does not open the filing. Where the voided ground was load-bearing and no fresh proof survives it, the relief falls with the ground; where fresh proof survives it, the relief stands on the fresh proof, and the reopening closes with the judgment restated on that proof, not re-earned. A petitioner who uses the voiding exception to smuggle in a new walk has filed a new filing inside a reopening, and it is judged as a new filing, without the reopening's shelter.

The fourth rule is the execution-stay limit. A post-judgment completion does not stay execution by itself. Execution proceeds on the judgment as rendered unless a reopening under the second rule has actually been opened — and the opening, not the completion, is what stays the portion it touches. A petitioner who learns of a voiding completion after judgment and before execution must plead the reopening before execution of the affected portion, or execute and reopen after: the completion does not pause the clock, and a portion executed before the reopening was pleaded is executed, not un-executed. The stay, where granted, reaches only the portion the voiding touches; the rest of the judgment executes on schedule. A completion pleaded as a stay without a voiding ground is a delay paper, judged as one.

The fifth rule is the next-filing marking duty. Whatever the judged filing does with a post-judgment completion, the next filing marks it. A petitioner who carries post-judgment material into a new filing names the completion, its date relative to the judgment, and whether it was pleaded as a reopening, granted or denied — because a denied reopening is itself part of the record the next filing stands on, and a next filing that hides a denied reopening has hidden a strike. A post-judgment completion that was never pleaded anywhere is still marked in the next filing: silence in the judged filing does not erase the completion from the record, and the next filing's marking duty does not depend on the judged filing having used it. The freeze of T-697 protects the judged filing from being faulted for what it could not supplement; it never protects a later filing from being faulted for what it chose not to mark.

**T-699 — the Severable-Execution Rule — designed:** T-698 left its severable-execution problem named and open: whether a completion issued after judgment but during execution that voids only a severable portion stays that portion's execution, or whether severable portions execute regardless. The answer is a stay that follows the voiding, not the judgment: a voiding completion on a severable portion stays that portion's execution once a reopening is opened — and it stays nothing else, and it un-executes nothing already done.

The first rule is that severability is tested, not declared. A portion is severable only where the judgment's relief can stand without it — the load-bearing/severable split T-698 drew in its second rule, applied at execution rather than at judgment. A portion the judgment called severable but whose removal collapses the relief is not severable in fact, and a portion the judgment called load-bearing but whose removal leaves the relief intact is severable in fact. The completion does not decide severability, and neither does the label in the judgment: the test is whether the relief stands when the portion is lifted out. A petitioner who pleads a stay on a portion the relief stands on has pleaded a stay on the relief, and it is judged as one under T-698's voiding exception, not as a severable stay.

The second rule is the stay itself. A post-judgment completion that voids a severable portion stays that portion's execution — but only once a reopening under T-698's second rule has actually been opened. T-698's fourth rule already said the opening, not the completion, is what stays; T-699 fixes the reach of that stay at the portion. The stay reaches the voided severable portion and the execution steps that depend on it, and no further: the rest of the judgment executes on schedule, the unaffected portions are not paused by sympathy, and a petitioner who asks the stay to cover the whole judgment on a severable voiding has asked for a general stay, judged as one. A completion pleaded as a stay without an opened reopening is still a delay paper under T-698, and a stay pleaded on a portion the completion merely disagrees with — without voiding its ground — waits like any other completion.

The third rule is the executed-portion limit. A portion executed before the reopening was pleaded is executed, not un-executed. T-698's fourth rule said a portion executed before the reopening was pleaded is executed; T-699 extends that limit to severable portions expressly, because severable portions are the ones most likely to be executed early, while the petitioner is still deciding whether to plead. The reopening's remedy for an executed severable portion is not reversal of the execution: it is restitution in the next filing — the value of the portion, or its replacement, claimed there — and a petitioner who asks the reopening to unwind an executed severable portion has asked for a remedy the reopening does not carry. What the reopening can do is stop what has not yet been executed; what it cannot do is reach back past the execution line.

The fourth rule is the mis-severed correction. Where a portion was treated as severable but the relief in fact stands on it, the stay reaches the relief to the extent it stands on it — and no further than that extent. The correction runs one way only: a load-bearing portion wrongly called severable pulls its share of the relief into the stay, but a severable portion wrongly called load-bearing does not expand the stay beyond the portion, because the voiding touches only the portion and the relief stands without it. The petitioner who discovers the mis-severing must plead it with the proof that the relief stands on the portion; a bare claim that the portion "matters" does not move the stay's reach. The correction is measured at the reopening, not re-litigated at every execution step: once the stay's reach is fixed, execution proceeds on everything outside it without re-arguing severability at each step.

The fifth rule is the resumption rule. A stay on a severable portion ends when the reopening ends, and the portion's execution resumes where it stopped — unless the reopening struck the portion, in which case there is nothing left to execute, or restated it on fresh proof, in which case it executes as restated. A denied reopening does not retroactively fault the stay: the stay was proper while the reopening was open, and the execution clock for the stayed portion resumes, not restarts, from the point the stay lifted. A petitioner who treats a denied reopening as a reason to re-plead the same voiding ground at the next execution step has filed a second reopening, judged as one — and T-698's denied-reopening problem, whether the next filing may re-plead a denied ground with fresh proof, is the door that question must go through, not this rule.

**T-700 — the Severable-Stay Tolling Rule — designed:** T-699 left its severable-stay tolling problem named and open: whether a stay granted on a severable portion tolls the execution clock for the remaining portions, or whether only the stayed portion's clock pauses while the rest run on. The answer is a clock per portion: the stay tolls the stayed portion's clock and the clocks of the steps that depend on it, and nothing else — the remaining portions' clocks run on, and a petitioner who idles them while the stay is open bears the lapse.

The first rule is the clock-per-portion rule. Every portion carries its own execution clock, and a stay tolls only the clock it names. The judgment's execution is not one clock with many hands; it is many clocks running side by side, and T-699's stay reached the portion, not the judgment — so the tolling follows the stay's reach exactly. An unaffected portion's clock does not pause because its sibling is stayed, does not slow because the petitioner is busy with the reopening, and does not reset because the stay lifted: it runs from its own start through its own deadline, and a portion whose deadline passes during another portion's stay is lapsed, not stayed. A petitioner who asks the stay to toll the whole judgment's clock on a severable voiding has asked for a general stay, judged as one under T-699's second rule.

The second rule is the dependent-steps rule. A step that depends on the stayed portion tolls with it — but only the dependency slice. Where an execution step cannot proceed without the stayed portion's output, its clock pauses for exactly the steps it cannot take, and resumes the moment the portion's output is available or the stay lifts; where a step can proceed in part without the stayed portion, the part that can proceed runs on, and only the blocked part tolls. Dependency is proved, not asserted: the petitioner names the step, the output it needs, and why no substitute output serves, and a step whose dependency is merely convenient — faster with the stayed portion, possible without it — does not toll at all. The stay's tolling never reaches a step that depends on the stayed portion only through a chain of choices the petitioner could have ordered differently.

The third rule is the no-sympathy-tolling rule. The petitioner's attention is not a clock. That the reopening consumed the petitioner's time, that counsel was engaged on the stayed portion, or that executing the remaining portions during the stay felt imprudent does not toll their clocks. Prudence is not a stay, and a petitioner who holds the remaining portions in reserve while the stay is open, hoping the reopening will change them, has made a strategic choice with a clock attached: if the reopening fails, the remaining portions execute from where their clocks stand, not from where they would have stood had the petitioner executed them promptly. A stay pleaded as a reason for delay on unaffected portions is a delay paper, judged as one.

The fourth rule is the lapse interaction. Tolling pauses a clock; it never revives one. A portion whose clock had already run out before the stay opened is lapsed, and the stay does not resurrect it; a portion whose clock runs out during the stay because it was never stayed is lapsed, and the reopening's outcome does not restore it. Conversely, a stayed portion whose clock was tolled for the whole stay resumes with exactly the time it had left when the stay opened — no bonus for the stay, no penalty for it — and T-699's resumption rule governs the step it resumes at. Tolling and resumption are companions, not substitutes: tolling fixes the time, resumption fixes the step, and neither reaches the other portion's ledger.

The fifth rule is the clock-record rule. The party claiming a toll proves it with the clock record: the stay's opening and lifting dates, the portions named in the stay, the steps claimed dependent with their dependency proof, and the time each clock had left when the stay opened. A clock without a record runs: where the record does not show a portion was stayed or a step was dependent, that clock is treated as having run on, and a petitioner who kept no clock record cannot reconstruct one from the reopening's outcome. The record is made at the stay, not after it lifts — a tolling claim first raised when a lapse is pleaded is a late paper, judged as one.

**T-701 — the Partial-Dependency Rule — designed:** T-700 left its partial-dependency problem named and open: whether a step that depends only partly on the stayed portion tolls in proportion to its blocked part, or tolls wholly once any dependency is shown, or not at all unless wholly blocked. The answer is proportional tolling: the blocked slice tolls, the runnable slice runs, and a step is never tolled whole on a partial dependency — the toll follows the block, not the step.

The first rule is the slice rule. A step is tolled slice by slice, never step by step. Where a step can be taken in part without the stayed portion's output — its runnable sub-steps performed, its blocked sub-steps waiting — the clock on the runnable part runs on exactly as if there were no stay, and only the clock on the blocked part pauses. A petitioner who idles the runnable part while the stay is open, then pleads the stay for the whole step, has pleaded a general stay on a severable step, judged as one under T-699's second rule. The toll is measured on the step's own work, not on its calendar: a step that is half blocked tolls half its work, and the half that could have been done during the stay is done late at the petitioner's cost, not tolled at the court's.

The second rule is the decomposition rule. The petitioner decomposes the step before the toll is claimed — at the stay's opening where the dependency is known, or at discovery where it is not — naming each sub-step, which ones the stayed portion blocks, and why no substitute output serves for those. An undecomposed step tolls nothing: a step pleaded as one indivisible whole, without a decomposition showing which slice is blocked, is treated as runnable, and its clock runs on. The burden of decomposition sits on the claimant, not on the court: the court does not carve a petitioner's step into slices for her, and a decomposition first offered when a lapse is pleaded is a late paper, judged as one. Decomposition is a record made in advance, not a reconstruction made after the clock ran out.

The third rule is the no-whole-toll rule. Any dependency, however real, never tolls the whole step. A step that needs the stayed portion for one sub-step out of ten tolls that one sub-step, and the other nine run on; a step that needs it for nine out of ten tolls nine, and the one runs on. Whole-step tolling is reserved for a step proved indivisible — a step whose sub-steps cannot be taken apart without destroying the step itself, where performing the runnable part first would corrupt the blocked part's result or render it meaningless. Indivisibility is proved, not asserted: the petitioner shows the corruption or the meaninglessness concretely, and a step that is merely inconvenient to split, slower split, or customarily taken whole is divisible. Custom is not indivisibility, and inconvenience is not corruption.

The fourth rule is the substitution rule. A blocked slice shrinks whenever a substitute serves. Where a provisional output, a prior version, a parallel source, or a workaround lets a sub-step proceed, that sub-step is runnable, and its clock runs on — the petitioner who refuses a serving substitute to preserve a larger toll has chosen delay, not suffered blockage. Where the substitute is partial — good enough to proceed but requiring rework once the stayed portion's true output arrives — the toll covers the rework slice only, not the whole sub-step: the work done on the substitute stands, and only the correction attributable to the difference between substitute and true output tolls. A substitute that would itself have to be discarded whole is no substitute at all, and the sub-step stays blocked; a substitute that merely needs checking against the true output is a serving substitute, and the checking time is the petitioner's ordinary diligence, not a toll.

The fifth rule is the partial-record rule. Partial-dependency tolling rides on T-700's clock record with one addition: the decomposition table, stating per step the sub-steps, the blocked slice, the dependency proof for each blocked sub-step, the substitute considered and why it did or did not serve, and the time each slice had left when the stay opened. A toll claimed without a decomposition table is a toll claimed without a record, and under T-700's fifth rule a clock without a record runs. The decomposition table and the clock record are made together, at the stay; a decomposition table assembled after the stay lifts is evidence of what the petitioner now wishes the slices had been, not of what they were.

**T-702 — the Discovered-Dependency Rule — designed:** T-701 left its discovered-dependency problem named and open: whether a dependency discovered only after the stay opened — a blocked slice nobody named at the stay — tolls from its discovery, from the stay's opening, or not at all. The answer is from discovery, and only from discovery: the toll starts when the dependency is discovered and noticed, never backdated to the stay's opening, and never denied outright for the sin of late naming — but the time before discovery is the petitioner's, not the court's.

The first rule is the discovery-date rule. A dependency first discovered after the stay opened tolls its blocked slice from the date of discovery, not from the stay's opening and not from the lifting. The slice was blocked all along, but a toll is a record, and a record cannot reach back before the fact it records existed on it: the stay's opening tolls only the slices named at the stay (T-700, T-701), and a slice named later tolls from its naming. The clock on the discovered slice therefore runs from the stay's opening until discovery, then pauses from discovery until the stay lifts. A petitioner who discovers a blocked slice on day forty of a fifty-day stay gets ten days of toll, not fifty — the forty days she ran a step she believed runnable are days she chose, in ignorance, to run, and ignorance is not a stay.

The second rule is the diligence rule. Discovery tolls only where the petitioner was diligent. At the stay's opening the petitioner owes the dependency audit T-701's decomposition rule already demands: she names what she knows is blocked, and she looks, with ordinary care, for what else might be. A dependency she would have found by that audit — named in the stayed portion's own papers, visible in the step's ordinary inputs, or already known to her own team — is not discovered late; it is omitted, and an omitted dependency tolls nothing, whenever it is finally pleaded. Discovery means a dependency no diligent audit at the stay's opening would have surfaced: a hidden input, a changed output format, a third party's quiet reliance. Diligence is judged at the stay, not at the discovery: the question is never "did she look hard once she suspected," but "would she have found it had she looked when the stay opened."

The third rule is the notice rule. Discovery alone tolls nothing; discovery noticed tolls. The petitioner records the discovered dependency on the clock record promptly upon discovery — the slice, the proof of the block, the reason no diligent audit at the stay's opening would have found it — and the toll runs from that notice, not from the private moment of realization. A dependency discovered and sat upon, then pleaded when a lapse is raised, is T-700's late paper wearing a discovery's face, judged as one: the toll runs only from the notice, and the gap between discovery and notice runs at the petitioner's cost. Where the discovery date itself is disputed, the notice date governs — the record is the only discovery the court can date, and an undated discovery is an undiscovered dependency until it is noticed.

The fourth rule is the no-revival rule. A discovered dependency never revives a clock that already lapsed before discovery. If the slice's clock ran out between the stay's opening and the discovery — because the petitioner, believing the step runnable, let it run — the discovery does not rewind it: tolling pauses a clock, never revives one (T-699's fourth rule), and a pause that starts after the clock stopped is no pause at all. The petitioner who discovers a dependency after the lapse has discovered the reason she lost the step, not a ground to reclaim it. The only relief a post-lapse discovery offers is prospective: it tolls what time remains, if any, and it bars the next filing from re-pleading the same slice as runnable.

The fifth rule is the amended-record rule. A discovered dependency amends, never rewrites, the clock record and the decomposition table. The amendment states the original decomposition, the discovered slice with its dependency proof, the diligence showing (why no audit at the stay's opening would have found it), the discovery date, the notice date, and the time the slice had left at discovery. The original entries stand unaltered — a record that is rewritten to make the slice look named at the stay is a falsified record, and a filing built on it is judged as one. The amendment is itself dated and filed before the stay lifts where the stay is still open; where the stay has already lifted, the amendment is a late paper, and its toll is measured from notice to lifting only if time remains, and to nothing if the clock has already run.

**T-703 — the Suspicion Rule — designed:** T-702 left its suspicion problem named and open: whether suspicion counts as discovery — a petitioner who suspects a dependency but has not proved the block tolls from suspicion, from proof, or from neither until the block is shown. The answer is from proof, and only from proof: suspicion tolls nothing, but suspicion is not nothing either — it starts a duty, and the way the petitioner answers that duty decides whether the later proof is treated as a discovery at all.

The first rule is the no-toll-from-suspicion rule. A suspected dependency is not a discovered dependency. A petitioner who suspects a step is blocked — a hunch from a changed output, a warning from a third party, a resemblance to a slice already stayed — has no toll until the block is proved: the dependency shown, the slice identified, the proof recorded and noticed under T-702. The toll, when it comes, runs from proof-as-noticed, never from the suspicion date. A suspicion nursed for thirty days and then proved tolls from the proof, not from the first unease — to toll from suspicion would be to toll from a feeling, and a record cannot pause a clock on a feeling. The suspicion window runs at the petitioner's cost in every case; what suspicion can buy is not toll, but the preservation of discovery treatment, and only where the second rule is met.

The second rule is the inquiry-duty rule. Suspicion imposes a duty to inquire, promptly and proportionately. The petitioner who suspects a dependency must look, with ordinary care, into the suspected block — check the step's inputs, ask the party whose output changed, test the slice the suspicion points to — and must record the suspicion when it arises: the date, the slice suspected, the ground of the suspicion, and the inquiry undertaken. The inquiry need not be exhaustive; it must be proportionate to the suspicion's ground, pursued without delay, and pursued until it either proves the block or clears the slice. A suspicion recorded and diligently pursued is a suspicion honored; a suspicion sat upon, noted nowhere, or pursued only when a lapse is raised, is a suspicion abandoned, and an abandoned suspicion earns no treatment at all.

The third rule is the diligent-inquiry preservation rule. Where the inquiry was prompt, proportionate, and continuous, the later proof is treated as a T-702 discovery in full: the toll runs from proof-as-noticed, the diligence showing is the inquiry record itself, and the suspicion window — the days between suspicion and proof — is simply time the petitioner spent proving, not time tolled and not time forfeited. The petitioner loses nothing for having suspected early and proved late, provided the proving was diligent: the gap is not tolled, but it does not defeat the toll that starts at proof. This is the only reward suspicion offers, and it is enough — it is the difference between a discovery and an omission, and it is earned by the inquiry, not by the suspicion.

The fourth rule is the neglected-suspicion rule. Where the inquiry was delayed, desultory, or absent, the later proof is treated as an omitted dependency to the extent a prompt inquiry would have proved it earlier. The test is the would-have-proved date: the date a prompt, proportionate inquiry, begun at the suspicion date, would have proved the block. Time before the would-have-proved date is the petitioner's, as under T-702's diligence rule; time from the would-have-proved date to actual proof is likewise the petitioner's, because the block was provable and unproved through her own delay. The toll therefore runs only from actual proof-as-noticed, and — decisively — if the slice's clock lapsed between the would-have-proved date and actual proof, the lapse stands: a neglected suspicion never revives a lapsed clock (T-702's no-revival rule, T-699's fourth rule), and a petitioner who suspected, dawdled, and then proved after the lapse has discovered the reason she lost the step, not a ground to reclaim it. A suspicion pleaded as a discovery, without an inquiry record, is judged as an omission, not as a discovery delayed.

The fifth rule is the unfounded-suspicion rule. A suspicion that inquiry clears — the step proves runnable, the changed output proves unrelated, the warning proves mistaken — tolls nothing, and the inquiry time is the petitioner's own cost for proceeding carefully. That cost buys no toll credit against any later, genuine discovery on another slice, and it buys no prejudice either: a recorded suspicion that proved unfounded does not taint a later genuine discovery, and does not count as a prior omission. What it does buy is a cleared slice on the record: the slice, once cleared by inquiry, may not later be pleaded as suspected-blocked on the same ground without fresh proof, and a petitioner who re-pleads a cleared suspicion as if still open is pleading a closed question, not a new discovery.

The sixth rule is the unrecorded-suspicion rule. A suspicion counts only as recorded. A petitioner who claims she suspected a dependency weeks before she proved it, but recorded nothing — no suspicion entry, no inquiry note, no letter, no test — bears the proof of the earlier suspicion date, and without it the suspicion is dated at its first record, which is the proof itself. An unrecorded suspicion pleaded only when a lapse is raised is T-700's late paper wearing a suspicion's face, judged as one: it neither tolls, nor preserves discovery treatment, nor moves the would-have-proved date earlier. The record is the only suspicion the court can date, just as under T-702 the notice is the only discovery the court can date — and a suspicion the record never saw is, for tolling purposes, a suspicion that never existed.

The seventh rule is the suspicion-record rule. The suspicion table amends, never rewrites, the clock record, the decomposition table, and the discovered-dependency table. The suspicion entry states the suspicion date, the slice suspected, the ground, the inquiry steps with their dates, the outcome (proved, cleared, or still open), and, where proved, the proof date and notice date; the discovered-dependency amendment under T-702 then cross-references the suspicion entry rather than absorbing it. The original entries stand unaltered — a record rewritten to make a suspicion look recorded at the stay, or an inquiry look prompt that was in fact late, is a falsified record, and a filing built on it is judged as one.
