**T-704 — the Suspicion-Threshold Rule — designed:** T-703 left its suspicion-threshold problem named and open, and left it next in line: whether every suspicion triggers the inquiry duty, or only a suspicion with an articulable ground — a named input, a changed output, a warning from a party — so that mere unease, the background possibility that any step might be blocked, imposes no duty at all. The answer is the articulable ground, and only the articulable ground: a suspicion triggers T-703's inquiry duty only when it can name its ground, and a suspicion that cannot name one triggers nothing — no duty, no record, no later penalty for the silence.

The first rule is the articulable-ground rule. A suspicion crosses the threshold when it states a ground a second reader can test: a named input whose value changed, an output that differs from the output the step last produced, a warning from a party or a record that points at this slice, a resemblance to a slice already stayed with the point of resemblance identified. "Something feels off about this step" states no ground; "the step's input file changed on Tuesday and its output no longer matches the last run" states one. The ground need not prove the block — T-703 already settles that proof comes later — but it must point at the block: at this slice, for this reason, on this fact. A suspicion that points nowhere imposes no inquiry duty, because there is nothing to inquire into; a duty to investigate a feeling would be a duty to investigate everything, and a duty to investigate everything is no duty at all.

The second rule is the ground-specificity rule. The inquiry duty follows the ground, not the suspicion's mood. Where the ground names a changed input, the inquiry is into that input and the slice it feeds; where the ground names a changed output, the inquiry is into that output and the slice that produced it. The petitioner owes the inquiry the ground describes, pursued promptly and proportionately under T-703 — not a general audit of the whole walk, and not an inquiry into slices the ground never touched. A ground that names three slices imposes a duty on three slices; a ground that names one imposes a duty on one. A petitioner who inquires beyond her ground is diligent beyond duty, and the extra diligence earns her nothing extra — but a petitioner who inquires into a different slice than the ground names, and leaves the named slice unexamined, has not answered the duty at all.

The third rule is the background-possibility rule. The bare possibility that any step might be blocked — the fact that blocks happen, that stays exist, that dependencies are sometimes discovered late — is not a suspicion at all, and it triggers nothing. Every filing in a stayed district carries that background possibility; if it counted as suspicion, every petitioner would owe an inquiry into every step of every walk, and T-703's duty would collapse into a duty to prove a negative before filing. The threshold exists precisely to stop that collapse: the background possibility is the weather, not a warning, and a petitioner who files without inquiring into every conceivable block has neglected nothing. What she owes is an inquiry into the warnings she actually has, not into the warnings the world might someday give her.

The fourth rule is the hindsight rule. The threshold is judged at the suspicion date, on the facts then known, never on what the later proof showed. A suspicion that later proved right — the block was real, the slice was stayed — but that named no ground at the time was still below threshold when it arose: no duty attached, no inquiry was owed, and the later proof is judged as a T-702 discovery on its own terms, not as a neglected suspicion, because there was no duty to neglect. Conversely, a suspicion that named a ground at the time but later proved unfounded was still above threshold when it arose: the inquiry was owed, and a petitioner who sat on it and then proved nothing has still neglected a duty, even though the slice turned out runnable. The threshold tests the suspicion's ground, not its fortune; hindsight may not promote a feeling into a duty, nor demote a grounded warning into mere unease.

The fifth rule is the threshold-crossing rule. A below-threshold unease that later gains a ground crosses the threshold at the gaining date, not at the first unease. A petitioner who felt vaguely that a step might be blocked in March, and in April learned the step's input file had changed, owes her inquiry from April: the suspicion date for T-703's purposes is the crossing date, the would-have-proved date runs from a prompt inquiry begun at the crossing, and the March unease counts for nothing — neither as an earlier duty nor as an earlier suspicion to be penalized. The record must show the crossing: the unease's first date, the ground's arrival date, and the fact that the ground, not the unease, started the duty. A petitioner who backdates the ground to the unease is backdating a duty, and a filing built on it is judged as one.

The sixth rule is the mistaken-ground rule. A ground's articulability, not its truth, decides the threshold. A warning from a party that later proves mistaken, a changed output that later proves unrelated, a resemblance that later proves superficial — each still crossed the threshold when stated, because each named a testable reason to look. The petitioner who inquired diligently into a mistaken ground has honored the duty and, under T-703's fifth rule, holds a cleared slice; the petitioner who sat on a mistaken ground has neglected a duty even though the slice was runnable, because the duty was to inquire, not to be right. What a mistaken ground never does is toll: an inquiry into a ground that proves empty ends, under T-703, as an unfounded suspicion, and its cost is the petitioner's own.

The seventh rule is the threshold-record rule. The suspicion table carries, for every suspected dependency, a threshold entry: the suspicion date, the ground as stated (or the words "below threshold, no ground stated"), the crossing date where an unease later gained a ground, and the inquiry duty's answer — triggered or not, and on what ground. A below-threshold unease is recorded as below threshold, not omitted and not upgraded: omission invites a later claim that the unease was a grounded suspicion all along, and upgrading invites a duty the petitioner never owed. The threshold entry amends, never rewrites, the suspicion table, the decomposition table, and the discovered-dependency table; the original entries stand unaltered, and a record rewritten to give an unease a ground it never had is a falsified record, and a filing built on it is judged as one.

**T-705 — the Private-Ground Rule — designed:** T-704 left its private-ground problem named and open, and left it next in line: whether a ground stated only to the petitioner herself — a private note, an unshared test result — counts as articulable, or whether articulability requires a ground a second reader could have tested at the time. The answer is testability, not sharing: a private ground counts when a second reader could have tested it at the time, whether or not any second reader actually did — and a private ground no second reader could have tested counts for nothing, however vividly the petitioner felt it.

The first rule is the second-reader testability rule. Articulability under T-704 never required an audience; it required a test. A ground is articulable when a second reader, given the ground as stated, could check it: a named input whose value the reader could compare, a test the reader could re-run, a fact the reader could verify against a record. A petitioner who kept such a ground to herself still held an articulable ground, because the ground was testable from the moment it was stated — to herself, in the first instance, and to any reader to whom she later shows it. What fails the test is not privacy but untestability: a ground stated only as "I knew something was wrong" names no input, no test, no fact, and no second reader could have tested it then or can test it now. Privacy does not demote a ground; untestability does.

The second rule is the recorded-private rule. A private ground counts from its recording date when it was preserved in a form a second reader can later inspect: a dated notebook entry, a test log, a file with an unaltered timestamp, a message sent to herself and kept. The recording is what makes the private ground testable after the fact — it fixes the ground's words, its date, and its content against later improvement. A petitioner who wrote "input file changed Tuesday, output no longer matches last run" in a dated note on Tuesday held an above-threshold suspicion on Tuesday, even if she showed the note to no one until the filing. The threshold date is the recording date, not the disclosure date, because the duty under T-703 attached when the ground became articulable, and articulability attached when the ground was stated in testable form.

The third rule is the unrecorded-private rule. A ground never recorded anywhere — held in memory only, felt but never written, never tested, never logged — counts for nothing. A petitioner who claims, months later, that she privately suspected on a ground she can now articulate has not shown an above-threshold suspicion at the claimed date; she has shown a present articulation of a past feeling, and T-704's hindsight rule already bars promoting a feeling into a duty after the fact. Memory improves grounds the way it improves stories: the ground as remembered is not the ground as stated, and a threshold that turned on remembered grounds would be unfalsifiable — every neglected inquiry could be re-described, after the fact, as a private ground diligently held. The line is therefore bright: no record, no ground, no threshold crossed.

The fourth rule is the delayed-disclosure rule. A recorded private ground need not have been shared at the time, and late disclosure does not demote it — but the petitioner bears the burden of producing the record intact and explaining the delay. She must produce the record itself, not a summary of it, in a form that shows its date and its unaltered content; a summary invites the suspicion that the ground was improved in the retelling, and a record produced without its date proves a ground but not a threshold date. An unexplained gap between recording and disclosure does not demote a genuinely recorded ground, but it invites scrutiny: the longer the gap, the more the record must speak for itself, because the petitioner's present account of her past ground is the weakest evidence of it. A recorded ground disclosed late is still a ground; a ground first articulated at disclosure is not a recorded ground at all.

The fifth rule is the altered-or-lost-record rule. A private record altered after the fact, or lost and reconstructed from memory, loses its original recording date. An altered note proves only the ground as altered, and its threshold date is the alteration date at the earliest — and only if the alteration itself is dated and disclosed, so the record shows both versions. A reconstructed record — a note rewritten from memory after the original was lost — is a new statement, not a revival of the old one: it crosses the threshold, if it articulates a testable ground, at the reconstruction date, judged on the reconstructed ground's testability then, and it proves nothing about the lost original's date. A petitioner who presents a reconstruction as the original has falsified the threshold record, and a filing built on it is judged as one.

The sixth rule is the withheld-ground rule. A ground the petitioner lawfully withheld — privileged, sealed, under a protective order — still counts when its existence and testability were logged at the time: a sealed entry, a docket note, a privilege log naming the ground's subject and date without disclosing its content. The log, not the content, proves the threshold: it shows a second reader could have tested the ground had the seal lifted, and it fixes the date. A ground withheld with no log at all — no sealed entry, no docket note, nothing a second reader could later point to — is unrecorded under the third rule, whatever privilege covered it. Privilege may excuse nondisclosure; it does not excuse non-recording, because the threshold needs a date and a test, and a wholly unlogged ground supplies neither.

The seventh rule is the private-ground record rule. The threshold table carries, for every ground claimed as private, a private-ground entry: the ground as stated, the recording form and date, the disclosure date, the testability showing (what a second reader could check, and when), and any alteration, loss, reconstruction, or seal affecting the record. A private ground claimed without a record is entered as unrecorded, not omitted and not credited: omission invites a later claim that the ground was recorded all along, and crediting invites a duty — or an excuse — built on nothing testable. The private-ground entry amends, never rewrites, the threshold table, the suspicion table, the decomposition table, and the discovered-dependency table; the original entries stand unaltered, and a record rewritten to give a private ground a date it never had is a falsified record, and a filing built on it is judged as one.

**T-706 — the Sealed-Content Rule — designed:** T-705 left its sealed-content problem named and open, and left it next in line: whether a sealed log that names no content at all — a date and a seal, nothing more — still proves a ground existed, or whether a log must name the ground's subject to count as a record. The answer is that a bare date-and-seal proves a seal, not a ground: it proves something was sealed on that date, and nothing about what was sealed, whether it was a testable ground, or which ground a later filing pleads. A log counts as a record of a ground only when it names the ground's subject in terms a second reader can later match to the ground itself. A seal preserves a date; only a subject preserves an identity.

The first rule is the bare-seal rule. A log entry carrying only a date and a seal — no subject, no descriptor, no identifier of any kind — proves the existence of a sealed item on that date and nothing further. It does not prove a ground existed, because a sealed item need not be a ground at all: it could be a letter, a draft, a document unrelated to any dependency, or an empty envelope. It does not prove testability, because testability attaches to a stated ground, and a bare seal states none. It does not fix a threshold date for any particular ground pleaded later, because there is nothing to tie the later ground to the earlier seal except the petitioner's present assertion that the sealed item was that ground — and T-705's unrecorded-private rule already bars promoting a present assertion into a past record. A bare seal is therefore entered as a seal, not as a ground: it stands on the record as proof that sealing happened, and it carries no ground, no threshold date, and no tolling consequence of its own.

The second rule is the subject-minimum rule. A sealed log counts as a record of a ground when it names the ground's subject specifically enough that a second reader, when the seal lifts, can tell whether the ground then produced is the ground the log recorded. The subject need not be the content: the log need not disclose the test result, the input value, or the fact itself. But it must name what the ground is about in identifying terms — the input file and the test it failed, the dependency and the step it blocks, the output and the run it no longer matches — rather than a category so broad it fits any ground. "Matter concerning the filing" names nothing; "output of run 14 no longer matches run 13 on input file K" names a subject a second reader can match. The minimum is matchability, not disclosure: a log that lets a later reader say "this ground is that log's ground, and no other ground is" satisfies it, and a log that would fit half the filing's grounds does not, however detailed its seal.

The third rule is the match-on-unsealing rule. When the seal lifts, the ground produced must match the subject the log named, or the log proves nothing for that ground. A ground whose subject differs from the logged subject is a new ground at the unsealing date, not a recorded ground backdated to the seal date — the seal preserved the logged subject's date, and a different subject has no date preserved at all. A ground that matches the logged subject in part — the same input file but a different test, the same dependency but a different blocked step — matches only to the extent of the match: the matched portion carries the seal date, and the unmatched portion is judged as a ground first stated at unsealing. A petitioner who produces, at unsealing, a ground broader than the logged subject cannot stretch the log to cover the excess; the log's subject is the ceiling of what it records, and the excess stands or falls on its own recording.

The fourth rule is the content-withheld rule. Privilege and protective orders excuse withholding content, not withholding subject. A ground whose content is privileged can still be logged by subject — the dependency, the step, the file, the test — without disclosing the privileged fact, and T-705's withheld-ground rule already required exactly that logging for the ground to count. A petitioner who withholds both content and subject, and logs only a date and a seal, has not used privilege as a shield for content; she has used sealing as a substitute for recording, and the bare-seal rule governs: a seal, not a ground. Where a subject itself would disclose the privileged content — where naming the test names the secret — the log must say so, and must name the subject at the finest granularity that does not disclose it, so a second reader can still test the match when the seal lifts. A claim that even the finest subject discloses the secret must itself be logged and testable, not merely asserted at unsealing.

The fifth rule is the coded-subject rule. A subject named only by a code, an abbreviation, or a reference — "item 7," "the K matter," a file number with no key — counts as named only when the code was decodable by a second reader at the seal date: a codebook logged with the seal, a key held by the court, a reference whose referent was itself on the record. A code whose key existed only in the petitioner's memory, or in a notebook produced for the first time at unsealing, is a bare seal in coded dress: at the seal date no second reader could have matched the code to any ground, so the log recorded a placeholder, not a subject. A code decoded only at unsealing dates the subject at unsealing, not at sealing, because the matchability that the subject-minimum rule requires did not exist until the key appeared. The codebook, like the record itself, amends never rewrites: a codebook produced at unsealing is a new record, and a filing built on it as if it had been logged at sealing is judged as one.

The sixth rule is the bare-log cure rule. A bare seal is never cured by later annotation. A petitioner who annotates a bare seal at unsealing — adding a subject the seal never named, or a note explaining what the sealed item "really was" — creates a new statement at the annotation date, not a completion of the old record. The annotation may prove a ground at its own date, if the ground it states is testable then, but it proves nothing about the seal date, because the seal date's record, as it stood, named nothing to match. The one cure that works is not a cure of the bare seal at all: an independent contemporaneous record — a dated private-ground record under T-705, a threshold-table entry, a docket note — that names the subject at the seal date proves the ground from that record's own date, and the bare seal adds nothing to it. The bare seal is then surplus, not foundation: the filing rides on the independent record, and if that record fails, the seal does not save it.

The seventh rule is the sealed-content record rule. The sealed-content table carries, for every sealed ground claimed, a sealed-content entry: the seal date, the subject as logged (verbatim, not paraphrased at unsealing), the content status (disclosed, withheld by privilege or order, or never stated), the unsealing date, the ground as produced at unsealing, and the match determination (full, partial with the matched portion identified, or no match). A bare seal is entered as a seal with no subject and no match, not omitted and not credited: omission invites a later claim that the seal recorded a ground all along, and crediting invites a threshold date built on nothing identifiable. The sealed-content entry amends, never rewrites, the sealed-content table, the private-ground table, the threshold table, the suspicion table, the discovered-dependency table, and the decomposition table; the original entries stand unaltered, and a log rewritten at unsealing to give a bare seal a subject it never had is a falsified record, and a filing built on it is judged as one.

**T-707 — the Sealed-Codebook Rule — designed:** T-706 left its sealed-codebook problem named and open, and left it next in line: whether a subject named only by a code whose key is itself sealed — a codebook under the same seal as the ground it decodes — counts as named at the seal date, or whether a code counts only when its key was available to a second reader while the seal stood. The answer is availability, not enclosure: a code counts as named only when its key was available to a second reader while the seal stood. A codebook sealed with the code it decodes is a sealed package, not a named subject: at the seal date no second reader could have decoded the code, so the subject was not named until the day code and key became jointly available — and that day is the unsealing, not the sealing. A seal preserves a date; only joint availability preserves a naming.

The first rule is the joint-availability rule. A coded subject is named at the earliest date on which both the code and its key were available to a second reader. Availability is conjunctive: a code without its key is a placeholder, and a key without its code is a dictionary for a book nobody holds. The naming date is therefore the later of the two availabilities — the code's unsealing or the key's availability, whichever comes last. A petitioner who sealed code and codebook together on March 1 and unsealed them together on June 1 named the subject on June 1, whatever the seal's date says: between March and June no reader, second or otherwise, could have matched the code to any ground, and T-706's subject-minimum rule was never satisfied in that interval. The seal date proves a package was sealed; it proves no naming.

The second rule is the sealed-package rule. A code and its codebook under one seal are one sealed item, not two records. The package is entered as a seal with no subject, per T-706's bare-seal rule, until the seal lifts; at unsealing the package yields a subject dated at unsealing, and the ground produced at unsealing is matched against the decoded subject under T-706's match-on-unsealing rule. The package's contents do not leak their date backwards: a subject decoded at unsealing was not "really" named at sealing in any sense the record recognizes, because at sealing the code was, to every reader but the petitioner, indistinguishable from a bare seal. A petitioner who pleads the seal date for a package-decoded ground pleads a bare seal as a recorded ground, and the filing is judged as one.

The third rule is the split-custody rule. The answer flips when the key was held outside the seal while the code was sealed. A codebook held by the court, lodged in escrow, or already on the public record while the code sat sealed counts as available to a second reader throughout the seal: the seal withheld the code, not the naming, because any reader who held the key could have decoded the code the moment the seal lifted — and the naming was complete at sealing, subject only to the code's own unsealing. The key's custodian must be a second reader in fact, not in title: a codebook held by the petitioner herself, in her own drawer, under her own control, is not second-reader availability, however she labels the drawer. A codebook held by the petitioner's counsel under the same order that sealed the code is under the same seal in everything but name, and the sealed-package rule governs.

The fourth rule is the partial-key rule. Availability is per entry, not per book. A codebook whose general entries were public at the seal date, with only the entry for this ground sealed, names the subject to the extent the public entries decode it: a code decodable from the public portion counts at the seal date, and only the sealed-entry portion dates at unsealing. Conversely a codebook public in bulk but sealed in the single entry that decodes this code is, for this ground, a sealed package: the subject counts only when that entry becomes available. The test is always the same — could a second reader, with the key as it stood at the seal date, have decoded this code to this subject? — applied entry by entry, never to the book as a whole.

The fifth rule is the staggered-seals rule. A code under one seal and its codebook under another name the subject at the later unsealing, when both are jointly available. A code unsealed while its key remains sealed is a bare seal in coded dress: readers can see the code and cannot read it, and the subject remains unnamed until the key's seal lifts. A key unsealed while the code remains sealed leaves a readable dictionary for an unreadable book, and the subject remains unnamed until the code's seal lifts. Neither unsealing alone names anything; the naming happens at the second unsealing, and the sealed-codebook entry records both unsealing dates and the joint-availability date as the naming date. A filing that pleads the earlier unsealing as the naming date pleads half a naming.

The sixth rule is the amended-codebook rule. A codebook amended after sealing — entries added, entries changed, a new edition substituted — dates the amended entries at amendment. A code decoded only by an entry added after the seal date was not named at the seal date, even if the codebook itself was available then: the subject the amended entry decodes did not exist in readable form until the amendment. The codebook, like every table in this chain, amends and never rewrites: the original entries stand unaltered, the amendment is entered with its own date, and a filing that reads the code through the amended entry as if the entry had stood at sealing is judged as a filing built on a rewritten record. Where the amendment corrects an error in an original entry, the corrected reading dates at the correction, and the original reading's date is preserved for whatever the original entry decoded.

The seventh rule is the sealed-codebook record rule. The sealed-codebook table carries, for every coded ground claimed, a sealed-codebook entry: the code as logged (verbatim), the codebook's identity and edition, the key's custody (sealed-with the code, court-held, escrowed, or public), the key's availability date, the code's unsealing date, the key's unsealing date where separately sealed, the joint-availability date claimed as the naming date, the ground as decoded at joint availability, and the match determination (full, partial with the matched portion identified, or no match). A sealed package is entered as a seal with no subject and no match, not omitted and not credited, per T-706. The sealed-codebook entry amends, never rewrites, the sealed-codebook table, the sealed-content table, the private-ground table, the threshold table, the suspicion table, the discovered-dependency table, and the decomposition table; the original entries stand unaltered, and a codebook produced or amended at unsealing and pleaded as if logged at sealing is a falsified record, and a filing built on it is judged as one.

**T-708 — the Lost-Key Rule — designed:** T-707 left its lost-key problem named and open, and left it next in line: whether a codebook that was available to a second reader at the seal date but was lost or destroyed before unsealing still counts as having named the subject, or whether the loss un-names it retroactively — so that a ground whose key perished before the seal lifted was never named at all. The answer is that naming survives the loss but proof does not travel with it: the naming date stands where joint availability fixed it, and the loss is an evidentiary event, not a temporal one. A subject named at sealing is not un-named by a fire, a flood, or a misplaced file; it is left named-but-unmatched, and a filing that pleads it as a proved ground pleads a name as a match.

The first rule is the naming-date rule. Joint availability at the seal date fixes the naming date under T-707, and nothing that happens afterwards moves it. Loss destroys the key, not the date: the second reader who could have decoded the code at sealing did have that power, and the record of that power does not perish with the paper. A petitioner who pleads a later date because the key is gone pleads the loss as a re-naming, and a petitioner who pleads the seal date for a code whose key was never available pleads T-707's sealed package, not this rule — the two cases differ on availability at sealing, and availability at sealing is the whole test.

The second rule is the proof-versus-naming split. Named is not proved. To carry a ground forward, a filing must produce the decoded subject and match it under T-706; a key lost before unsealing means the decoded subject can no longer be produced from the code, so the ground cannot be matched, however firmly it was named. The entry is therefore recorded as named-but-unmatched: the naming date stands, the match column reads no match, and the ground earns nothing a matched ground earns. A named-but-unmatched ground tolls nothing, voids nothing, and bars nothing — it is a name on the record, not a weapon in the filing.

The third rule is the recorded-decoding exception. Loss after a second reader actually decoded the code and logged the subject changes nothing, because the ground no longer lives in the key. A decoded subject entered in a transcript, a second copy, or a reader's log before the loss is the ground's record, dated at decoding, and the key's later fate is irrelevant to it. The log must be a record of the decoding, not a recollection of it: a note that says "the code meant X" written after the loss from memory is a reconstruction under the fifth rule, not a recorded decoding, however confident its author.

The fourth rule is the per-entry rule. Loss, like availability under T-707, is per entry, not per book. Entries that survive — a surviving volume, a surviving page, a surviving copy — keep their matched status; only the lost entries fall to named-but-unmatched. A codebook half-lost is half-usable, and a filing that pleads the lost half as if the surviving half decoded it pleads a surviving entry as a lost one.

The fifth rule is the fault rule. How the key was lost decides what the loss costs beyond the match. Loss by a neutral event — fire, flood, a court's own misfiling — leaves the ground named-but-unmatched with no fault attached. Loss by the petitioner after a duty to preserve arose, or loss the petitioner caused and cannot explain, leaves the ground fault-unmatched: the petitioner bears the burden of the missing key, the ground is presumed unmatched against her, and she may not plead the loss itself as a reason the ground should be taken on her word. Neutral loss excuses; faulty loss condemns; neither restores the match.

The sixth rule is the reconstruction rule. A key rebuilt after loss — from memory, from fragments, from another edition — does not restore the original naming unless it is proved identical, entry by entry, to the lost key. A reconstruction proved identical is entered as a reconstruction with its own date, and the decoded subject it yields dates at reconstruction, not at sealing: the subject was named at sealing, but this proof of it is new, and the filing is judged on the new proof. A reconstruction not proved identical is a new codebook, not the old one, and a ground decoded through it is a new ground dated at reconstruction, amending the record, never rewriting it.

The seventh rule is the lost-key record rule. The lost-key table carries, for every coded ground whose key was lost: the code as logged, the codebook's identity and edition, the joint-availability date claimed as the naming date, the loss date and manner, whether any second reader decoded and logged the subject before the loss, the match determination (matched pre-loss, named-but-unmatched, or fault-unmatched), and any reconstruction with its date and identity proof. The lost-key entry amends, never rewrites, the sealed-codebook table, the sealed-content table, the private-ground table, the threshold table, the suspicion table, the discovered-dependency table, and the decomposition table; the original entries stand unaltered, and a reconstruction pleaded as the original key is a falsified record, and a filing built on it is judged as one.

**T-709 — the Discovered-Loss Rule — designed:** T-708 left its discovered-loss problem named and open, and left it next in line: whether a loss discovered only after unsealing — a key thought available throughout the seal but in fact already gone — dates the loss at discovery or at actual loss, and whether a ground unsealed in reliance on a key already lost tolls from unsealing or from discovery. The answer splits the date in two: the loss dates at actual loss on the record, and the petitioner's obligations run from discovery. A loss happened when it happened, and learning of it later does not move it; but a petitioner cannot be judged for a loss she could not have known of, so every duty, deadline, and fault assessment that turns on the loss runs from the day she discovered it, or was noticed of it. The record keeps the true date; the petitioner is judged from the known date.

The first rule is the actual-loss date rule. The loss column reads the actual loss date whenever the actual loss date can be proved — a fire's date, a flood's date, a misfiling's log entry, a destruction certificate. Discovery does not re-date the loss: a key lost in March and discovered in June was lost in March, and a record that writes June as the loss date falsifies the record. Where the actual loss date cannot yet be proved, the entry reads provisional: "loss discovered [discovery date], actual loss date unknown," and the entry is corrected, never rewritten, when proof of the actual date arrives. A provisional entry is not a claim that the loss happened at discovery; it is a claim that discovery is all the record yet knows.

The second rule is the reliance-protection rule. A ground unsealed in reliance on a key already lost is not fault for the reliance itself. Between unsealing and discovery, the petitioner relied on a record that showed the key available — the sealed-codebook table, the seal's own inventory, a custodian's assurance — and reliance on the record as it stood is diligence, not negligence. Acts taken in that window on the strength of the key — a filing pleading the ground as matchable, a deadline computed from unsealing, a bridge built on the ground — are not falsified by the later discovery. They are re-judged at discovery, not condemned at discovery: the matched claim falls to named-but-unmatched under T-708, because the key is gone and the match cannot be produced, but the filing that pleaded it in good reliance stands as a filing made in reliance, and its author bears no fault for the reliance alone.

The third rule is the tolling-from-discovery rule. For the petitioner who could not have known, the ground's operative clock runs from discovery, not from unsealing. A deadline that ran from unsealing on the assumption the key was available — a deadline to produce the decoded subject, to match the ground, to plead the ground's proof — is re-run from discovery for the affected slice only: the time between unsealing and discovery is tolled, because the petitioner was waiting on a key that did not exist and could not have cured the wait by diligence. The toll covers only the slice the lost key blocked; slices with surviving keys, surviving copies, or pre-loss recorded decodings run on their own clocks, and a petitioner who pleads a whole filing tolled on one lost key pleads a slice as a walk.

The fourth rule is the backdated-proof bar. A decoding claimed to have been produced between unsealing and discovery, from a key already lost before unsealing, is not a recorded decoding under T-708's third rule. If the key was gone, no decoding from it could have happened in that window; what the petitioner holds is a reconstruction, judged under T-708's sixth rule, and it dates at reconstruction, never at unsealing. A decoding log dated inside the reliance window, purporting to come from the lost key, is either a log of a different key's work or a falsified record, and a filing built on it is judged as one. The reliance window protects acts taken on the record; it does not manufacture proof the record could not have produced.

The fifth rule is the search-and-notice rule. Discovery starts duties it does not excuse: the petitioner owes prompt notice to the record that the key is lost, and a diligent search for what survives — other copies, other readers, surviving volumes, a pre-loss recorded decoding. Promptness is judged from discovery, not from actual loss: a petitioner who discovered the loss in June and noticed it in June has noticed promptly, however long the key had been gone. A petitioner who discovers the loss and sits on it — who files on as if the key lived, who lets the search slide, who notices only when challenged — converts the loss from neutral to fault-unmatched, and the conversion dates at the sitting, not at the loss: from the date diligence lapsed, the ground is presumed unmatched against her, and she may not plead the earlier reliance as a continuing excuse.

The sixth rule is the third-party discovery rule. Discovery by the court, or by the other side, counts as discovery for the petitioner when it is noticed to her, and not before. A court that learned the key was lost in May and told the petitioner in June has given her a June discovery date: her duties, her tolling, and her fault assessment all run from June, because June is when she could have acted. Until noticed, her operative date does not run, however widely the loss was known elsewhere. The record's actual-loss date is untouched by who discovered it: the loss column reads the actual loss, and the discoverer column reads who found it and when, and the two columns answer different questions.

The seventh rule is the discovered-loss record rule. The discovered-loss table carries, for every coded ground whose key's loss was discovered after unsealing: the code as logged, the codebook's identity and edition, the joint-availability date claimed as the naming date, the unsealing date, the actual loss date or its provisional unknown, the discovery date, the discoverer and the notice date if the discoverer was not the petitioner, the reliance-window acts taken between unsealing and discovery, the notice date, the search record and its result, the match determination (matched pre-loss, named-but-unmatched, or fault-unmatched, with the conversion date if fault attached after discovery), and any reconstruction with its date and identity proof. The discovered-loss entry amends, never rewrites, the lost-key table, the sealed-codebook table, the sealed-content table, the private-ground table, the threshold table, the suspicion table, the discovered-dependency table, and the decomposition table; the original entries stand unaltered, and a discovered loss pleaded as a loss at discovery, or a reliance-window decoding pleaded as a recorded decoding, is a falsified record, and a filing built on it is judged as one.

**T-710 — the Unprovable-Date Rule — designed:** T-709 left its unprovable-date problem named and open, and left it next in line: whether a loss whose actual date can never be proved — no fire record, no log entry, no witness to when the key perished — stays permanently provisional on the record, or whether the record must eventually default the loss date to the discovery date, and what a filing built on a permanently provisional entry may claim. The answer is neither permanent provisionality nor a silent default: the entry stays provisional but bounded, and it proves the loss without proving any date.

The first rule is the no-default rule. An unprovable loss date never defaults to the discovery date by mere passage of time. Defaulting would rewrite history: the loss certainly happened before discovery, and writing the discovery date into the loss column would assert a fact no record holds. A date the record cannot prove stays unproved, however long the entry stands.

The second rule is the bounded-range rule. The entry does not stay an open blank; it hardens into a range. The loss column reads "lost on or before [discovery date], exact date unproved" — discovery caps the range, because the key was certainly gone by the day it was found gone, and no earlier bound is claimed than the record can support. The range is the entry's permanent form until proof arrives; it is not a placeholder awaiting a default.

The third rule is the claim-cap rule. A filing built on a provisional entry may claim only what the range proves. It may claim the loss itself — the key is gone, the ground's loss stands, the T-707 lost-key consequences follow. It may not claim any date-dependent benefit that needs an exact date: no priority from an earlier loss, no tolling start from a chosen date, no first-in-time ordering against a rival entry. Date-dependent claims wait for date proof; the range proves loss, not date.

The fourth rule is the proof-revival rule. Later proof of the actual date reopens the entry and collapses the range to the proved date, and every filing built on the range is re-read against the proved date. Claims that survive the collapse stand as they stood; claims that depended on the range's breadth — a claim that needed the loss to predate a rival filing, for instance — fall with the breadth that carried them. Revival corrects the record; it does not punish the filing that used the range honestly.

The fifth rule is the no-adverse-inference rule. Neither side draws an adverse inference from unprovability alone. The petitioner is not faulted for failing to prove a date no record holds, and the other side may not treat the gap as proof the loss is recent, convenient, or fabricated. Unprovability is a property of the record's survival, not of either party's honesty, and it is charged to neither.

The sixth rule is the burden-stays rule. The burden of proving any date-dependent benefit stays on the party claiming it, and the provisional entry shifts nothing. The entry proves the loss for both sides equally; whoever wants a date attached to that loss — earlier, later, before a deadline, after a filing — proves it or goes without it. Provisionality is not a burden-shifting device.

The seventh rule is the provisional-entry record rule. The provisional table carries, for every coded ground whose key's loss date cannot be proved: the code as logged, the discovery date as the range's cap, the earliest bound the record can support if any, the proof searched and found wanting, and the claims already built on the range. The entry amends without rewriting: when proof arrives, the range collapses in place and the amendment is noted, never backdated over the provisional history.

**T-711 — the Judgment-Freeze Rule — designed:** T-710 left its revival problem named and open, and left it next in line: whether a later-proved date that contradicts a filing already judged on the provisional range reopens the judgment, or whether the judgment's freeze protects filings built in good faith on the range. The answer is the freeze, with one exception: a judgment rendered on a filing built in good faith on the range stands when the proved date arrives, and the collapse of the range re-reads the record, not the judgment — unless the proved date shows the ground itself could never have existed as pleaded, in which case the judgment reopens on that ground alone.

The first rule is the freeze rule. A judgment rendered on a filing built in good faith on the provisional range stands when the proved date arrives. T-710's fourth rule reopens the entry and re-reads filings built on the range; it does not reopen judgments already rendered on them. The range was what the record proved when the court decided, and a decision made on what the record then proved is not undone by what the record later proves. Finality protects reliance: the parties ordered their affairs on the judgment, and the judgment's authority does not flicker with every later proof.

The second rule is the pending-filing rule. The freeze draws its line at judgment, not at filing. A filing still pending when the proved date arrives is re-read in full under T-710's fourth rule: claims that survive the collapse stand, claims that depended on the range's breadth fall. Only a filing already judged is frozen; everything undecided is still corrected by the collapse.

The third rule is the never-available-ground exception. If the proved date shows the ground itself could never have existed as pleaded — the filing leaned on a loss that provably postdated its reliance, so the key still existed when the filing claimed it gone — the judgment reopens on that ground alone. This is not a collapse of breadth but a failure of the ground: the range never contained a date on which the ground existed, so the judgment rested on a ground that was never there. The reopening reaches only that ground; every other ground of the judgment stands frozen.

The fourth rule is the no-upgrade rule. A judged filing gains no date-dependent benefit from the proved date it could not claim from the range. If the proved date would have given the filing a priority, a tolling start, or an ordering it was denied under T-710's third rule, that benefit is not awarded retroactively to the judged filing. The benefit may be pleaded fresh in a new filing, judged on the proved date as its own date, but the old judgment is not rewritten into a better one.

The fifth rule is the executed-reliance rule. Where the exception reopens a ground, execution already performed under the judgment stands; only the unexecuted remainder is re-decided. A walk already walked, a payment already made, a step already taken in reliance on the judgment is not unwound by the reopening. Revival unwinds the ground, not the work done in reliance on it.

The sixth rule is the annotation rule. The proved date is annotated on the judgment's record — the range the judgment was decided on, the date later proved, and whether the judgment stands or a ground reopened — so later readers see both the decision's basis and its correction. The annotation never rewrites the judgment's original reasoning; the judgment stands as decided, with its correction attached, not substituted.

Whoever holds the proved date — the taker who proved it, the reader who found it, the court that received it — discloses it to the court and to every side that stood on the judged filing, promptly on proof, without waiting for a new filing to plead it. The disclosure states the range the judgment was decided on, the date now proved, and whether the judgment stands under T-711 or a ground reopens under its exception. The second rule is the no-reopening-by-disclosure rule. Disclosure alone reopens nothing. The other side's receipt of the proved date is not a motion, not a plea, and not a ground: a judged filing that stands under T-711 keeps standing after disclosure exactly as before, and only a pleading on the never-available ground under T-711's third rule can reopen it. A party that treats mere disclosure as an opening has confused being told with being granted, and the court answers that confusion by noting the disclosure and leaving the judgment untouched.

The third rule is the pending-filing carve-out. Where a filing is still pending when the proved date arrives, disclosure is not merely a courtesy to the record but a duty to the pending decision itself: the pending filing is re-read under T-710's fourth rule, and a re-reading conducted without the proved date would repeat the very error the range was meant to contain. For pending filings, then, disclosure goes first and the re-reading follows it, in that order, so the decision-maker never decides a second time on a range already collapsed. The carve-out changes the timing, not the content — the same fact, disclosed to the same sides, but before the pending decision rather than after the judged one.

The fourth rule is the third-party reader rule. The fifth rule is the concealment rule. Concealment is the one act that converts a standing judgment into a tainted one, not because the proved date changes the judgment — T-711 still decides that — but because the concealer has used the freeze as a shield for silence, and a shield used that way stops being a shield. A halt that preserves is ministerial — the same family as refusing to execute a facially void writ — and a ministerial halt is not contempt, not disobedience, and not an act of his own against the judgment. The third rule is the prompt-report rule. A halt unreported is a halt half-taken. **T-715 — the Pause-Cost Rule — designed:** T-714 left its pause-cost problem named and open, and left it next in line: whether the costs of a vindicated halt's pause — the delay itself, borne by the party who sought execution or shared among the parties — fall on the execution-seeker alone, or whether a proper halt's pause is a cost of the freeze that all parties bear. T-715 answers: the pause is the freeze's cost, and the freeze belongs to no party. A vindicated halt was a duty performed, not a favor granted and not a wrong committed; the delay it caused is the price of the judgment protecting itself from deciding on a falsehood, and a price the judgment exacts is borne by the proceeding, not by the party who happened to seek execution. To load it on the execution-seeker alone would punish the party for the court's own protection — and would teach every future seeker to resist the halt, which is exactly the resistance T-714's duty rule forbids. The seeker sought execution under a judgment the freeze then stayed; the freeze, not the seeker, made the pause.

The first rule is the shared-cost rule. The delay of a proper, promptly reported, vindicated halt is shared among the parties as a cost of the freeze: no party recovers delay damages for the pause itself, no fee-shift follows from the pause alone, and no adverse inference is drawn from the fact that execution waited. Each party bears its own waiting cost — its own time, its own idled preparation — and none bills another for the interval the freeze owned. This is the direct corollary of T-714's fourth rule: an officer who answers for nothing for having halted cannot leave behind a bill for the halt that someone else must pay, and a seeker who was owed execution cannot be charged for the judgment's decision to pause it.

The second rule is the improper-halt exception. Shared cost covers a proper halt only. Where the halt was an over-halt — steps the proved date did not touch, frozen past the next severable step — or a late-reported halt, the excess delay falls where T-714's fifth rule already puts it: on the halting officer or party as his own act. The excess is measured against the proper halt, not against no halt at all: the delay a proper halt would have caused anyway stays shared, and only the delay the excess added is charged to the one who added it. A party who pleads the whole pause as excess has confused the freeze's cost with the officer's fault, and the court answers by splitting the pause at the proper halt point.

The third rule is the no-double-counting rule. The pause cannot be pleaded twice. A party that has already had the pause counted in its favor — as time excused, as a deadline extended, as a step re-read under the proved date — cannot also recover it as damages, and a party that recovers the excess under the second rule cannot also plead the same excess as a ground to reopen under T-711: disclosure alone reopens nothing, and a paid excess is not a new ground. The pause is one interval with one accounting, and the accounting is entered on the same record as the halt, so the next reader sees the whole ledger at once.

The fourth rule is the clock rule. A proper halt suspends the execution's own clock. Time spent inside a proper halt does not count against execution deadlines, limitation periods, or any clock the proceeding sets for itself, because a clock that ran through a freeze would punish the parties for obeying it. The clock resumes from the exact halt point on the court's word, in step with T-714's resumption rule, and the resumed clock is marked resumed-from-halt-point so no later reader mistakes the pause for laches. An improper halt's excess, by contrast, suspends nothing: the excess interval counts against the clock of the party who caused it, which is the clock-rule form of the second rule's charge.

**T-717 — the Notice-Form Rule — designed:** T-716 left its notice-form problem named and open, and left it next in line: what counts as notice to a third party — record notice on the proceeding's own file, or actual notice reaching the party, or the record the party's dealing required him to search — and whether a stranger who never dealt with the proceeding at all can be charged with its record. T-717 answers: notice is three forms, not one, and each binds a different party from a different date — actual notice binds whoever receives it, record notice on the proceeding's own file binds whoever deals with the proceeding, and search-required record notice binds whoever deals in the record's subject whether or not he searched it. A pure stranger is bound by none of the record forms, and is bound only by actual notice when it reaches him.

The first rule is the actual-notice rule. Actual notice binds from receipt. A halt, a proved date, or an affected step is actually noticed when it is delivered to the party, or to the party's agent or address of record, in a form that names the element it notices. Sending is not receipt: a letter posted but never delivered, a message sent to an address the party never held, a filing the party never opened because it was never served on him, none of these is actual notice. Delivery to the address of record counts as receipt on the delivery date even if the party never opens it — the party who holds an address of record holds the duty to read what arrives there. Actual notice is the only form that binds a stranger, and it binds him only from the receipt date, never back to the filing date.

The second rule is the proceeding-file rule. Record notice on the proceeding's own file binds a party who deals with the proceeding, from the filing date of the entry that names the element. A purchaser of the halted step's fruit, a lienholder perfecting against it, a party who acts on the proceeding's steps, each deals with the proceeding and is charged with its file as it stood when he dealt. But the charge runs element by element: an entry binds as notice of the elements it names — the halt point, the proved date, the affected step — and of nothing else. An entry that records that something was filed, without naming the halt or the step it halts, is notice that a paper exists, not notice of the freeze; a party charged with the file is charged with what the file says, not with what the file implies. The notice date for each element is the date of the first entry naming that element, and a later entry naming it more plainly does not move the date earlier.

The third rule is the search-required-record rule. A party whose dealing required him to search a record class is charged with what that search would have found in that class, whether or not he searched it. A dealer in the step's subject who was required to search the subject's register, the lien index, or the proceeding's public file is charged with the freeze entry in that class from the date the search would have found it — the filing date, if the entry was searchable then, or the date it became searchable, if the record lagged behind the filing. He is not charged with records outside the class his dealing required: a party required to search the lien index is not charged with the proceeding's private file, and a party required to search the proceeding's file is not charged with a stranger's ledger. The charge follows the dealing's own search duty, not the world's whole record — and a party who dealt without searching a record his dealing required him to search is not without notice under T-716's fourth rule; he is without diligence, and the search-required rule charges him as if he had searched.

The fourth rule is the stranger rule. A party who never dealt with the proceeding, and whose dealing required no search of its records, is not charged with record notice at all. The proceeding's file is not the world's file, and a stranger's bargain is not judged by a record he had no dealing that required him to read. Until actual notice reaches him, his reliance is judged as T-716's notice-gap reliance — reasonable and in good faith on the record as it stood to him, which for a stranger is no record at all. A stranger who later deals with the proceeding becomes a dealer from that dealing forward, and is charged with the file from that dealing's date; the later dealing does not re-date reliance he formed while a stranger, and does not turn gap reliance into post-notice reliance retroactively.

The fifth rule is the per-element notice-date rule. Every notice claim under T-716 pleads, element by element, the form of notice and its date: the actual-notice receipt date, the proceeding-file entry date, or the search-required date the search would have found it. A reliance claim that pleads "notice" without a form or a date pleads nothing — the same discipline T-716 put on reliance formation dates, applied to notice itself. Where two forms give two dates for the same element, the earliest binding form governs: a dealer who received actual notice after the filing date is bound from the filing date, and a stranger who received actual notice is bound from receipt, because no record form bound him earlier.

**T-718 — the Notice-Language Rule — designed:** T-717 left its notice-language problem named and open, and left it next in line: whether a record entry written in the proceeding's internal jargon or step codes alone counts as notice to a lay dealer who deals in the subject but not in the code, or whether notice must be intelligible to the party it binds. T-718 answers: notice must be intelligible to the class it binds, not merely present on the file — a code-only entry is notice to a code reader and a signpost, not notice, to a lay dealer; but intelligibility is judged by the bound party's dealing class, not by his personal reading ability, and a lay dealer who was told where the key is kept cannot plead the code as ignorance.

The first rule is the intelligibility-by-class rule. Notice binds when a reader of the bound party's dealing class, exercising that class's ordinary diligence, would understand the entry to name the element — the halt point, the proved date, the affected step. A step-code entry binds a code-fluent dealer, a party whose dealing is in the proceeding's own steps, from its entry date. It does not bind a lay subject dealer — a purchaser of the halted step's fruit, a lienholder on the subject — until a plain-language entry, a code key filed in the same record class, or actual notice in plain terms reaches him. The entry's presence on the file is not its intelligibility: a file that speaks only in code has spoken only to code readers, and T-717's proceeding-file rule charges a dealer with what the file says, which for a lay dealer a code entry does not yet say.

The second rule is the key-on-file rule. Where the code key — the glossary mapping codes to elements — is filed in the same record class the dealing required the party to search, the code entry counts as notice from the date the key became searchable in that class. The party charged with the class is charged with its key, and a code entry plus a filed key in the searched class is plain notice in two parts. A key filed only in the proceeding's private file does not make a code entry intelligible to a subject dealer charged only with the public register: the key must live where the search duty lives, or the lay dealer was never given the means to read what he was charged with reading. A key filed after the code entry moves the notice date to the key's searchable date, not back to the entry date — the entry waited, unintelligible, until its key arrived.

The third rule is the signpost rule. A code-only entry is never nothing: it is a signpost that something affecting the subject was filed, and it starts a duty to inquire for a party who saw it or whose search would have found it. The inquiring party who asks the record-keeper, the proceeding, or the dealing counterparty for the plain meaning and is refused or misled is not charged with notice of the element — the refusal breaks the chain — but is charged with notice that the subject is encumbered in some way, which defeats a claim of clean-title reliance while preserving gap reliance on the element itself. A party who saw the signpost and never inquired is charged as if the inquiry would have answered plainly, from the date the inquiry would have answered: the signpost gave him the question, and his silence answers it against him.

The fourth rule is the personal-ability rule. Intelligibility is class-level, not personal. A dealer who cannot read the proceeding's language, or who hired no reader when his class ordinarily does, cannot plead personal inability: the class standard binds him, and his class's ordinary diligence includes engaging the reader his class engages. Conversely, a party whose class is lay is not held to a code reader's standard merely because he happens to be personally code-fluent: personal fluency without a dealing duty is knowledge, and knowledge unaccompanied by a duty is T-717's informal-knowledge problem, not notice. The test is always what the party's dealing required him to understand, never what he privately could.

The fifth rule is the translation-duty rule. Where the proceeding files only in code and deals with lay parties, the proceeding bears the translation duty for every element it wants to bind lay dealers: a plain-language entry, a filed key in the searched class, or plain actual notice. Until one of the three exists, lay reliance on the subject is gap reliance under T-717, not post-notice reliance — but the proceeding's failure to translate does not erase the signpost. The lay dealer who saw the code entry cannot claim he saw nothing at all: he saw that something was filed, and the signpost rule, not clean ignorance, governs what follows.

**T-719 — the Key-Regress Rule — designed:** T-718 left its key-regress problem named and open, and left it next in line: whether a code key that is itself written in jargon — a key needing a key — counts as a key at all, or whether the regress stops only at a plain-language key. T-719 answers: the regress stops only at a plain-language key, and a key that needs a key is not yet a key — it is one more signpost in the chain, and notice runs from the date the chain first reaches plain language in the searched class, never back to the first coded link.

The first rule is the terminal-plain rule. A key counts as a key, for T-718's key-on-file rule, only when a reader of the bound party's dealing class, exercising that class's ordinary diligence, can read it without a further key. A glossary that defines step codes in further step codes, a key filed in the proceeding's internal jargon, or a key whose definitions point to a second key still on file elsewhere has not terminated the regress: it has extended it. The chain is the entry, the first key, the second key, and so on until the first layer written in the class's plain language — and only that terminal plain layer turns the code entry into notice. A chain that never reaches plain language never becomes notice at all, however many coded layers it stacks: a cipher with a coded index is still a cipher.

The second rule is the chain-date rule. Where the chain does terminate in plain language, the notice date is the date the terminal plain layer became searchable in the class the dealing required the party to search — not the entry date, not the first key's date, and not the date of any intermediate coded layer. Each layer's filing is credited only for what it did: an intermediate coded layer signposted that a further layer existed, and the terminal layer made the entry intelligible. A party who dealt after the first key but before the terminal plain layer dealt under signpost rules, not under notice: gap reliance under T-718's translation-duty rule, with the signpost's duty to inquire running through every layer he could have followed. Retroactivity would reward the proceeding for filing a puzzle instead of a key, and T-719 forbids it.

The third rule is the same-class rule. Every layer of the chain must be judged in the searched class, not merely somewhere on file. A terminal plain layer filed only in the proceeding's private file does not terminate the regress for a subject dealer charged only with the public register, just as T-718's private-file key did not make a code entry intelligible to him. The chain terminates where the search duty lives: a plain layer in the wrong class is a plain layer nobody charged with that class was required to find, and the regress, for that dealer, is still open. Conversely, a plain layer filed in the searched class terminates the chain even if a coded layer elsewhere on file is still untranslated — the dealer was given the means to read, and the proceeding's extra puzzles elsewhere do not un-give them.

The fourth rule is the diligent-follower rule. A party who follows the chain diligently — who reads each layer, asks for the next key where the layer points to one, and reaches the terminal plain layer — is charged with notice from the terminal layer's searchable date, and no earlier, even if he in fact understood the code sooner by private fluency: T-718's class rule, not his private ability, sets the date. A party who stops mid-chain — who reads a coded key, sees it points onward, and never asks — is charged as T-718's signpost rule charges him: as if the inquiry would have answered plainly, from the date the diligent following would have reached the terminal layer. A party who asks for the next key and is refused or misled is not charged with notice of the element at all, on T-718's refusal rule, but is charged with notice that the subject is encumbered in some way, which defeats clean-title reliance while preserving gap reliance on the element itself.

The fifth rule is the proceeding's terminal duty. Where the proceeding files in code and wants to bind lay dealers, its translation duty under T-718 is not discharged by filing a key — it is discharged by filing a terminal plain key in the searched class. A proceeding that files a coded key and stops has filed a longer code entry, not a translation, and lay reliance remains gap reliance until the terminal layer arrives. The proceeding may file intermediate layers for its own readers, but it cannot charge a lay dealer with the time spent climbing them: the climb is the proceeding's cost of having written in code, and T-715's shared-cost logic applies — the freeze's pause was the proceeding's, and so is the key-chain's climb.

**T-720 — the Machine-Reading Rule — designed:** T-718 left its machine-reading problem named and open, and left it next in line: whether a machine-readable entry with no human-readable rendering counts as plain to a dealer class that ordinarily reads by machine, or whether plainness always means human-readable. T-720 answers: plainness is class-relative to reading method as well as to language — a machine-readable entry counts as plain to a class that ordinarily reads by machine, and counts as code, a signpost only, to a class that ordinarily reads by eye, until a human rendering is filed in the searched class. Plainness never means human-readable in the abstract; it means readable by the bound class's ordinary method, without a further key.

The first rule is the reading-method-by-class rule. Notice binds a class when a reader of that class, exercising that class's ordinary diligence and ordinary method, would understand the entry to name the element. A structured entry with a published schema binds a machine-reading class — a title plant that parses the register, an automated lien index, a registry that reads by API — from the entry's searchable date, even with no human rendering on file. The same entry does not bind a human-reading class — a purchaser who reads the register by eye, a lienholder whose search is a human search — until a human-readable rendering is filed in the searched class or plain actual notice reaches him. Until then the machine entry is, to him, what T-718's code entry was to a lay dealer: a signpost that something was filed, triggering the duty to inquire, not notice of what it says. A class that ordinarily reads both ways is bound from the earlier of its two plain dates, because either method gives it the means to read.

The second rule is the deterministic-rendering rule. A machine entry counts as plain to a machine class only when its rendering is deterministic: the entry plus its published schema yields the element's meaning without a further key, without a proprietary decoder, and without discretionary interpretation. A data blob readable only through a vendor tool, a format whose schema is unpublished or paywalled, or an encoding whose parser must guess at ambiguous fields is not plain to anybody — it is a coded layer under T-719, and the regress runs until a deterministic layer arrives. Determinism is judged at the entry's searchable date: a schema published later does not retroactively make an earlier opaque entry plain, just as T-719's terminal plain layer never backdates notice to the first coded link. A schema change after filing does not un-plain an entry already rendered under the schema then published, but a dealer who must read under the new schema reads under the new schema's date — that is T-720's schema-change problem, admitted below, not answered here.

The third rule is the fidelity rule. A machine rendering counts as plain only when it is verifiably faithful: the rendering must be checkable against the filed entry, by checksum, by round-trip, or by audit sample, so that a silent parse failure — a dropped field, a mis-mapped code, a truncated value — is detectable rather than silently binding. A machine class that parses without any fidelity check reads at its own risk for parse errors it could have caught, but it is not charged with notice of an element its parser silently dropped where no check would have caught the drop: that is a filing defect, and the proceeding bears it under T-718's translation duty. Where the parse fails for only part of the class — some parsers current, some stale — the entry is plain only to the parsers that render it faithfully, and the stale-parser readers stand as the human class stands before a human rendering: signposted, not noticed. That partial-plainness boundary is T-720's render-failure problem, admitted below.

The fourth rule is the mixed-dealing rule. Where a single dealing spans classes — a machine-reading registry that certifies to a human-reading purchaser, a human searcher who relies on a machine index's summary — the entry must be plain in each bound class's method before notice runs to that class, and the notice date for each class is its own plain date. The machine class cannot lend its plainness to the human class by certifying what the human never read, any more than T-718's code-fluent dealer could lend his fluency to a lay dealer; and the human class cannot borrow the machine's date by pointing at a machine it never ran. A machine summary shown to a human reader is a third-party translation for T-718's third-party-translation problem, not a rendering: it binds only if it is itself filed in the searched class as the proceeding's own rendering, not merely displayed.

The fifth rule is the proceeding's rendering duty. Where the proceeding files machine-only and wants to bind human dealers, its translation duty under T-718 is discharged only by filing a human-readable rendering in the searched class, in the same way its key duty under T-719 was discharged only by a terminal plain key. The cost of rendering is the proceeding's, on T-715's shared-cost logic and T-719's terminal-duty rule: the proceeding chose the machine format, and it cannot charge a human dealer with the time spent waiting for a rendering, nor charge a machine dealer with the time spent waiting for a human rendering it never needed. A machine dealer is bound from the machine entry's searchable date; a human dealer is bound from the human rendering's searchable date; neither date borrows from the other.

**T-721 — the Third-Party Translation Rule — designed:** T-718 left its third-party-translation problem named and open, and T-720 left it newly next in line: whether a translation supplied by a third party, not the proceeding, binds the proceeding to the translation's errors, or whether only the proceeding's own translation counts as its notice. T-721 answers: only the proceeding's own translation counts as its notice — a third-party translation is a private reading aid, never the proceeding's word, and its errors are the translator's, not the proceeding's; but a proceeding that adopts a third-party translation makes it its own, errors and all, from the adoption date.

The first rule is the own-translation rule. A proceeding is bound only by a translation it filed, cited, or acted on as its own in the searched class. A translation supplied by a stranger to the proceeding — a fellow dealer, a commercial index, a volunteer reader, a machine summary displayed but never filed — does not become the proceeding's notice merely because a dealer read it, relied on it, or could not have read the original without it. The dealer's notice is measured against the proceeding's own rendering, in the proceeding's own language class, under T-718 and T-719: if the proceeding filed in code with a terminal plain key, notice runs from the terminal layer's searchable date; if it filed machine-only, notice runs per class under T-720. A third-party translation neither accelerates nor delays that date, and it never supplies a notice the proceeding's own file does not contain.

The second rule is the reliance-at-own-risk rule. A dealer who relies on a third-party translation relies at his own risk for the translation's errors: he is charged with notice of what the proceeding's own rendering actually says, not of what the third party said it says, and a translation error that understates an element does not shrink the element, while one that overstates it does not enlarge it. But reliance on a third-party translation is not willful blindness. Where the proceeding filed no translation of its own and the dealer diligently sought one — where the third-party translation was the only reading available to his class by ordinary diligence — his reliance remains gap reliance, not clean-title defeat, for the element the translation misstated: he inquired, he read what inquiry produced, and the proceeding's failure to file its own translation is what left him to a stranger's reading. A dealer who had the proceeding's own translation in hand and chose the stranger's instead has no such shelter: he passed the proceeding's word for another's, and his reliance is his own.

The third rule is the adoption rule. A proceeding adopts a third-party translation when it files it in the searched class, cites it as the rendering of its entry, or acts on it as its own — certifying a dealing on its basis, answering an inquiry by pointing to it, or pleading from it. Adoption is by passage, not by document: the proceeding adopts the passages it files, cites, or acts on, and no more, so a translation adopted for one element does not become the proceeding's rendering of every element the document touches. From the adoption date the adopted passages are the proceeding's own translation, errors included, and dealers are charged with notice of the adopted text from its searchable date in the searched class — never retroactively to the third party's original publication, which bound nobody as the proceeding's word. A proceeding that later disowns an adopted translation must file a correction under the fourth rule; it cannot un-adopt by silence.

The fourth rule is the correction rule. When a third-party translation error is proved — by the proceeding, by a dealer, or by a reader's ordinary-path disclosure under T-712 — the proceeding's duty depends on whether it adopted the translation. An adopting proceeding must file a correction in the searched class, and notice of the true element runs, for dealers who relied on the adopted error, from the correction's searchable date, with gap reliance preserved for the interval between adoption and correction. A non-adopting proceeding owes no correction of a stranger's work, but it owes its own translation where T-718's translation duty already required one: the proved error is evidence that its own file left its dealers to strangers, and a proceeding that knows its dealers are reading a wrong stranger's version and still files nothing of its own has breached its translation duty from the date it learned of the error. In either case the correction, when filed, is judged as the proceeding's own translation, and the stranger's version remains what it always was: a private aid, not notice.

The fifth rule is the disclosure boundary. A third-party reader who discloses a proved date or a proved translation error under T-712's ordinary-path disclosure does not thereby become the proceeding's translator, and his disclosure does not become the proceeding's translation. His disclosure binds nobody to his wording: it binds the proceeding to answer it, under T-712's duty, and it binds dealers who receive it only to the proved date or error it discloses, not to any rendering he wrapped around them. The reader's privacy problem — whether his disclosure must name the judged filing it corrects — stays open under T-712, and T-721 does not answer it: naming the filing would make his disclosure look like the proceeding's citation, and T-721's adoption rule would then have to ask whether the proceeding, by acting on a named disclosure, adopted the reader's rendering along with his date. That adoption-by-action question is T-721's own newly open problem, admitted below.
