**T-722 — the Answer-Adoption Rule — designed:** T-721 left its adoption-by-action problem named and open: whether a proceeding that acts on a third-party reader's named disclosure thereby adopts the reader's rendering along with his proved date, or whether adoption requires a filing, citation, or certification distinct from merely answering. T-722 answers: answering is not adopting. A proceeding that answers a named disclosure adopts the proved date or error disclosed, and nothing more; the reader's rendering stays the reader's, unless the proceeding performs a distinct adopting act — filing the rendering in the searched class, citing it as the rendering of its entry, or certifying a dealing on its basis.

The first rule is the answer rule. An answer discharges the proceeding's duty to answer under T-712, and it adopts exactly what the disclosure proved: the date, or the translation error. A proceeding that answers "the proved date is accepted" has made the date its own from the answer's date; it has not made the reader's words its own, even when the disclosure named the judged filing it corrects. Naming the filing does not convert an answer into a citation: the reader's naming is the reader's act, and the proceeding's answer is an answer to a fact, not an endorsement of the wrapper the fact arrived in. Dealers who receive the answer are charged with notice of the proved date, not of the reader's rendering of the entry the date corrects.

The second rule is the distinct-act rule. Adoption of a rendering requires an act distinct from answering, aimed at the rendering itself: filing the rendering in the searched class, citing it as the rendering of the proceeding's entry, or certifying a dealing on the rendering's basis. Each act must be identifiable as an act about the rendering, not merely an act that follows from the disclosed fact. A proceeding that reopens a dealing because the proved date moved the interval has acted on the date; a proceeding that certifies the dealing because the reader's rendering says the element reads a certain way has acted on the rendering. The line is the object of the act: the date, or the words.

The third rule is the quotation boundary. Quoting a reader's rendering does not by itself adopt it. A proceeding that quotes the rendering in order to dispute it, to correct it, or to show what it is answering has cited the rendering as an object, not as its own word — the quotation is evidence of the answer's occasion, not of the proceeding's translation. A proceeding that quotes the rendering as its own statement of the element — pleading from the quoted words, answering an inquiry with the quoted words and no words of its own — has cited it as its rendering, and adoption follows under T-721's third rule from the quotation's date. The test is not whether the words appear in the proceeding's filing, but whether the proceeding speaks them as its own.

The fourth rule is the date-action rule. Acting on a proved date never, by itself, adopts the rendering that carried the date. Reopening a filing, re-pleading an interval, or recalculating a freeze on the proved date's basis are all acts on the fact, and they leave the rendering unadopted even when the rendering was the proceeding's only route to the fact: the proceeding learned the date from the reader, and it acts on what it learned, not on how the reader phrased the entry. But a proceeding that cannot state the act's basis without the rendering — that pleads the element's meaning, not merely the date's consequence — has crossed from date-action to rendering-action, and adoption follows for the passages pleaded.

The fifth rule is the correction consequence. Where a proceeding answered a disclosure but did not adopt the rendering, T-721's correction duty attaches only as T-721 already provides: an adopting proceeding must correct its adopted error, while a non-adopting proceeding owes no correction of a stranger's work, but owes its own translation where T-718's translation duty already required one. The answer does not change that allocation, and it does not make the proceeding the guarantor of the reader's wording: a dealer who relied on the reader's rendering after the proceeding's answer still relies on a stranger's reading, and his reliance is judged under T-721's second rule — gap reliance where the proceeding filed no translation of its own, own-risk reliance where the proceeding's own translation was in hand. The answer's only new notice is the proved date itself.

**T-724 — the Unknowing-Working Rule — designed:** T-723 asked whether a proceeding that quotes a rendering to dispute it, then works from it unknowingly, has adopted by working or merely by accident. T-724 answers: unknowing working counts. Adoption by working is judged objectively, from the dealing's reasoning, not from the proceeding's intent. A proceeding that reasons from the quoted words has adopted them whether it meant to or not; accident explains how the adoption happened, it does not undo it.

The first rule is the objective-tracking rule. Working counts as adoption when the dealing's reasoning tracks the quoted words in a way it would not track under any other reading: distinctive phrasing carried into the dealing's own words, an element mapped the way only the quoted rendering maps it, an inference available only on the quoted reading. Mere consistency is not tracking — a dealing whose outcome stands on either reading has not been shown to track the quotation, and that is T-723's implicit-reliance problem, left open here.

The second rule is the adoption-date rule. Unknowing adoption dates from the first dealing that tracks the quotation, never from the quotation itself and never from the later discovery of the tracking. Discovery changes nothing retroactively: learning, a year later, that a dealing tracked a rendering meant to be disputed does not un-adopt the year's dealings; it reveals the date the adoption already took effect.

The third rule is the prospective-correction rule. A proceeding that discovers its unknowing working may correct prospectively by filing its own rendering and naming the passages it displaces. Correction governs dealings after the correction date only; it does not reopen dealings already closed on the quoted reading. A correction that silently substitutes new words without naming the displaced passages does not correct at all — it borrows the reader's phrasing under a new cover, and that is T-723's borrowed-phrasing problem, still open here.

**T-726 — the Independent-Source Rule — designed:** T-725 left its independent-source problem named and open: what counts as an independent pre-quotation source — whether working papers must be dated before the quotation itself or merely before the tracking dealing, and whether a source the proceeding never filed counts at all. T-726 answers: an independent source must predate the quotation itself, and an unfiled source counts only when its date is proved by custody outside the proceeding's own hands — a private draft dated by its author alone counts for nothing.

The first rule is the pre-quotation dating rule. A source created after the quotation but before the tracking dealing is presumed contaminated: it may have absorbed the quoted reading, knowingly or not, and absorption after the quotation is exactly the unknowing working T-724 describes, only one step removed. The presumption is rebuttable, not conclusive: the proceeding may show the post-quotation source was sealed from the quotation — kept in a closed file, written by a dealer who never saw the quotation, or produced under a procedure that barred the quotation from the room — and a sealed source defeats tracking for the passages it covers as fully as a pre-quotation one. But the burden of the seal is on the proceeding claiming independence, and the seal must be shown by the procedure's own record, not by the dealer's later assurance that he did not look. A source dated before the quotation needs no seal: it cannot have absorbed what did not yet exist, and its independence is presumed rather than proved.

The second rule is the custody rule for unfiled sources. A source the proceeding never filed counts only when its date and content are fixed by custody outside the proceeding's own hands: a dated entry in a third party's archive, a timestamped version-control record, a filed copy in another proceeding, a contemporaneous publication. A private draft, a notebook page, or a memo whose only date is the author's own word counts for nothing — not because it is necessarily false, but because a proceeding that could backdate its independence could defeat any tracking claim at will, and T-725's text-first standard would collapse into a contest of undated paper. An unfiled source with independent custody counts exactly as a filed one: filing is evidence of date, not the date itself, and custody elsewhere is filing's equal. An unfiled source without it is inadmissible to defeat tracking, though it remains admissible to corroborate tracking the dealing's text already shows — a private draft that echoes the quotation corroborates absorption, it does not prove independence.

The third rule is the same-reasoning rule. A qualifying independent source defeats tracking only for the passages where it already carries the same reasoning: the same element mapped the way the dealing maps it, the same inference drawn from the same premises, the distinctive phrasing already present in the source's own words. A source that reaches the same outcome by a different path defeats nothing — the dealing's tracking is a matter of its reasoning, per T-724, and an outcome that stands on either reading is T-723's tie, not a defeat. A source that carries the same reasoning for some passages defeats only those passages; adoption follows passage by passage under T-725, and so does defeat. A source that predates the quotation and carries the whole reasoning defeats the whole adoption claim; a source that carries half of it leaves the other half adopted, and the notice must say which half stands.

**T-727 — the Sealed-Provenance Rule — designed:** T-726 left its sealed-provenance problem named and open: what proof rebuts the contamination presumption for a post-quotation source — whether a closed-file procedure's own record suffices, or whether the dealer who wrote it must also be shown never to have seen the quotation. T-727 answers: the procedure's record is necessary and, when complete and contemporaneous, sufficient for the seal — but it never covers a dealer who had an access path outside the seal, and a record made after the claim is worth nothing on its own.

The first rule is the procedure-record rule. A closed-file procedure's own contemporaneous record rebuts the presumption when it shows two things: that the quotation was barred from the drafting room and file for the whole drafting window, and that the bar was in force before the source was written — a seal order dated inside the window, an access log showing no quotation entry, a quarantine instruction filed at the time. The dealer's later assurance that he did not look never rebuts alone: T-726 already bars a proceeding's own word as proof of date, and the same bar applies to proof of non-looking. A record created after the tracking claim counts only when a contemporaneous artifact anchors it — a dated seal order, log entries from the time, a filing that mentions the seal before the claim. A seal reconstructed from memory after the claim is inadmissible to defeat tracking, though it remains admissible to corroborate a seal the contemporaneous record already shows.

The second rule is the dealer-exposure proviso. The procedure's record seals the room, not the dealer. Where the dealer who wrote the source had any access path to the quotation outside the sealed procedure — he saw it in another proceeding, received it before the seal closed, or worked from notes that may have carried it — the record does not suffice, and the proceeding must also show the dealer's non-exposure: no access path at all, or a documented gap (leave, reassignment, a transfer that removed him before the quotation circulated) covering the quotation's circulation. A dealer with an unclosed access path leaves the presumption standing no matter how tight the room's seal, because contamination travels with the dealer, not the file. Conversely, a dealer with no access path needs no further showing: the room's record plus a clean dealer is a complete seal.

The third rule is the lapse rule. A seal that lapsed briefly and was restored rebuts only for drafting done while the seal held: passages written during the lapse are presumed contaminated like any unsealed post-quotation source, and passages written before or after stand on the seal. A lapse the record does not date defeats the whole seal — an undated gap is a gap everywhere, since the proceeding claiming the seal bears the burden of its dates. A restored seal with a dated lapse is a partial seal, and the notice must say which passages it covers.

**T-728 — the Seal-Completeness Rule — designed:** T-727 left its seal-completeness problem named and open: what counts as a complete seal record — whether the barred-room order alone suffices, or whether the record must list every person with access to the room and file. T-728 answers: the order alone never suffices. A complete seal record has three elements, all contemporaneous, and a seal missing any one of them is an incomplete seal, which rebuts nothing.

The first element is the bar itself: the seal order with its window — the date the bar closed, the date it lifted (or that it still holds), and what it barred (the quotation, by identifying description, from the drafting room and the file). An order without a window proves a bar existed, not that it covered the drafting: a seal dated after the source was written, or lifted before the drafting finished, covers only the overlap, and the passages outside the overlap stand unsealed. An order that names the room but not the file, or the file but not the room, is a half-bar: the quotation barred from the room but left in the file the drafters drew on is not barred at all, and vice versa. The bar must name both doors, because contamination walks through either.

The second element is the access roster: every person who held access to the room or the file during the window, each with a dealer-exposure status — clean (no access path to the quotation, per T-727's dealer-exposure proviso) or exposed-and-gapped (an access path, but a documented gap covering the quotation's circulation). A roster that names only the drafters is incomplete: a clerk who carried the file, a custodian who shelved it, a reader who sat in the room all held access, and an unlisted person is an unexamined dealer. The roster need not be long to be complete: a contemporaneous custodian's signed negative statement — "no other person held access to the room or file during the window" — closes the roster, provided the custodian is himself rostered and his own exposure status is shown. A negative statement signed after the tracking claim counts only when a contemporaneous artifact anchors it, under T-727's reconstruction rule: a duty roster from the time, a key log, a staffing record that already names the same closed set.

The third element is the entry log: a record showing no quotation entry during the window — an access log with no quotation admission, a file inventory taken at seal and at lift showing the quotation absent at both, or a quarantine receipt showing the quotation held outside the room for the whole window. The bar says the quotation was forbidden; the log says it stayed out. An order plus a roster without a log proves the room was guarded, not that the guard held: a barred room into which the quotation nevertheless walked is an unsealed room. Where no log was kept, the seal fails for want of the third element — the proceeding that kept no log kept no proof, and the presumption stands. A log with a gap in its own dates fails like T-727's undated lapse: an entry log that does not cover the whole window proves nothing about the uncovered days, and passages written on uncovered days stand unsealed.

The incompleteness rule is passage-graded, not all-or-nothing — except where attribution fails. A seal missing the roster defeats only the passages whose authors are unrostered: a passage written by a rostered clean dealer, under a complete bar and a complete log, stands sealed even though another passage's author is unlisted. But where a passage cannot be attributed to a rostered person — an unsigned draft, a composite passage with no author line, a passage the roster does not account for — the incompleteness defeats the whole seal for that passage, since the proceeding claiming the seal bears the burden of its attribution. A seal missing the bar's window, or missing the entry log, defeats the whole seal outright: without a window there is no drafting the seal is shown to cover, and without a log there is no showing the bar held. Partial completeness is not completeness with a discount; it is completeness for the passages it actually covers, and nothing for the rest.

**T-729 — the Roster-Cure Rule — designed:** T-728 left its roster-cure problem named and open: whether a roster omission can be cured after the claim by showing the omitted person had no access path, or whether a roster closed after the claim is a reconstruction under T-727 and inadmissible to defeat tracking. T-729 answers: a roster omission is curable, but only as a cure — never as a rewrite. A post-claim addition to the roster defeats tracking only when it passes three gates; anything that fails a gate is a reconstruction, and a reconstruction defeats nothing.

The first gate is the contemporaneous anchor. A cure must rest on an artifact from the window itself — a duty roster from the time, a key log, a leave or staffing record, an access-control export — that already puts the omitted person in a no-access position, or already names the same closed set the cure now asserts. A post-claim affidavit alone, a fresh negative statement alone, a custodian's present recollection alone, is not a cure: it is a reconstruction under T-727, admissible to explain but inadmissible to defeat tracking. The anchor need not name the omitted person by name if it names the closed set by role and the person falls outside every role — a key log showing only three keys issued, all three rostered, anchors a cure for a fourth person who held no key — but an anchor that merely repeats the proceeding's present claim, in a document created after the claim, anchors nothing. The proceeding claiming the seal bears the burden of the anchor: a cure with no anchor is a sentence, not a showing.

The second gate is promptness before judgment. A cure must be filed promptly after the omission is discovered, and in any event before the tracking judgment on the affected passage. A cure filed after judgment on a passage does not reopen that passage: the judgment stands on the incomplete seal as it stood when judged, and the cure governs only passages still unjudged. Promptness is judged from discovery, not from the claim: a proceeding that sat on a known omission until the tracking judgment went against it has not cured, it has waited, and a waited cure fails the gate even with an anchor. A proceeding that discovers the omission through the tracking claimant's own showing must still file promptly from that discovery — the claimant's showing is notice, not an excuse to delay.

The third gate is completeness of the cure itself. A cure must show no access path for that omitted person specifically — not merely re-assert that the roster is closed. A cure that names a new closed set which itself omits another person cures nothing: it trades one omission for another, and the seal stays incomplete for every passage the new omission touches. A cure that shows the person had access to the room but not the file, or the file but not the room, shows half of T-728's bar and cures neither door: access to either door is access, unless a documented gap covers the quotation's circulation through that door, per T-727's dealer-exposure proviso.

A cure can backfire, and a backfired cure cannot be withdrawn. Where the anchor the proceeding files shows the omitted person did hold access — a key log with his key, a duty roster with his shift — the cure fails and converts: the person joins the roster as exposed, or exposed-and-gapped if a gap is documented, and passages by that person stand unsealed unless the gap covers the quotation's circulation. The proceeding that files a cure files the anchor with it, and the anchor stays in the record even when it hurts: a cure is a showing, not an offer that can be pulled back when the showing goes the wrong way. A proceeding that suspects its anchor may backfire and files only the affidavit instead has filed no cure at all — it has filed a reconstruction.

The cure rule is passage-graded like T-728's incompleteness rule. A cure for one omitted person does not cure other omissions, and a cure that restores the roster does not restore a missing bar window or a missing entry log: T-728's three elements stand separately, and curing one element leaves the other two exactly where they were.

**T-730 — the Cure-Notice Rule — designed:** T-729 left its cure-notice problem named and open: whether a cure must be served on the tracking claimant with time to answer, or whether filing the cure alone suffices and the claimant answers only by challenging the anchor. T-730 answers: filing alone never perfects a cure. A cure is perfected by service — served on the tracking claimant, with the anchor attached, and with time to answer before any judgment rests on it. An unserved cure is a paper on the file, not a defeat of tracking; a served cure whose answer window has run unanswered is decided on its anchor alone; a served cure answered by a counter-anchor is contested, and decided on the papers.

The first rule is that service is part of the cure, not an accessory to it. A cure must be served on the tracking claimant and on every dealer whose passage the cure touches, with the anchor itself attached — not a summary of the anchor, not a description of it, not a promise that it exists on the file. Service on the proceeding's own file, on a clerk, or on a dealer who is not the claimant is not service. A cure filed but never served does not fail T-729's promptness gate — the filing date still counts for promptness — but it defeats nothing until served, and a judgment rendered before service stands on the incomplete seal as it stood, under T-729's too-late rule applied at service rather than at filing. Filing starts the cure; only service can finish it.

The second rule is the answer window, measured from service and never from filing. The claimant gets an answer interval running from proper service, and judgment on the affected passage is stayed until the window runs or the answer is filed, whichever comes first. A judgment that rests on a cure before the window runs is premature: it falls with the cure's papers, not with the seal — the passage returns to the incomplete seal, not to a granted cure, and the cure must be re-perfected by a fresh window before any judgment rests on it again. The window is the claimant's, not the proceeding's: a proceeding that files on the eve of judgment and serves the same day has not shortened the window, it has postponed the judgment.

The third rule is what an answer can do, and what it cannot. An answer may challenge the anchor's contemporaneity (a document created after the claim), its identity (the wrong person, the wrong role), or its coverage (an anchor naming a closed set the person falls inside, or a gap that does not cover the quotation's circulation). Mere denial — "the person had access" without a counter-anchor — is a note, not a defeat: the cure is then decided on its anchor, and an unanchored denial cannot hold a passage unsealed. A counter-anchor — a key log with his key, a duty roster with his shift — defeats like a T-729 backfire: the person joins the roster as exposed, or exposed-and-gapped if a gap is documented, and the cure converts against the proceeding that filed it.

The fourth rule grades service defects, and no defect is cured by insistence. Service on the wrong person is no service: the window never starts, and no judgment can rest on the cure. Service without the anchor is service of a reconstruction, not a cure: the claimant cannot answer what he was not shown, so the cure counts as unserved until the anchor itself is served, and the answer window runs only from that service. Service after judgment on the passage is too-late service: it governs unjudged passages only, per T-729. A defective service cured by re-service before judgment perfects the cure from the re-service date; the original filing date still counts for T-729 promptness, but nothing else runs from it — the window, the stay, and the judgment all wait on proper service.

The fifth rule is waiver and silence, and they are not the same thing. A claimant who answers on the merits — challenging anchor, identity, or coverage — without objecting to service waives the service defect but never the anchor challenge: waiver is of the form of service, never of the anchor itself. Silence after proper service is not consent and not a concession: it is default on the cure's papers, and the cure is decided on its anchor alone — a sound anchor cures, a thin one does not, and the claimant's silence adds nothing to either side. But silence after defective service is nothing at all: no window ran, no default can be taken, and a judgment resting on that silence rests on nothing.

The cure-notice rule is passage-graded like T-728's incompleteness rule and T-729's cure rule. A cure served on one tracking claimant perfects only the passages that claimant's tracking touches; a second claimant tracking the same seal must be served separately, and an unserved second claimant's passages stand unsealed until he is served. Service on one claimant never perfects against another, and an answer by one claimant binds no other claimant's passages. A seal with three claimants and one service is two-thirds unsealed.

**T-731 — the Absent-Claimant Service Rule — designed:** T-730 left its cure-service-on-absent-claimant problem named and open: whether a cure can be perfected against a tracking claimant who has no address of record, has departed, or cannot be found — whether filing plus a public posting perfects it, or whether an unservable claimant's passages can never be cured. T-731 answers: an absent claimant freezes nothing forever, and a posting perfects nothing silently. Perfection against an absent claimant runs through proved absence, then substitute service, then an extended window — and a claimant who later appears gets his window back, on terms that depend on when he appears.

The first rule is that absence must be proved, not asserted. A proceeding claiming an absent claimant must show a diligent search on the record: the claimant's address of record if one exists, the last channel the claimant used in the proceeding, and the proceeding's own claimant list checked for a newer address. A proceeding that never looked has no absent claimant; it has an unserved claimant, and the cure stands exactly where T-730 leaves an unserved cure — a paper on the file, defeating nothing. A search that finds a live address ends the absence at once: the cure is then served personally under T-730, and no substitute service is needed or allowed. The search papers are filed with the cure, not held back: a substitute service whose search is not on the record is defective service, and its window never starts.

The second rule is substitute service itself, and it has three parts, all required. The cure, with the anchor attached, is filed; a notice of the cure, naming the passage and the omitted person and stating where the full cure and anchor may be read, is posted in the place the claimant would look — the record where the tracking claim itself was filed, or, if the claim was filed elsewhere, the proceeding's public notice record; and the same notice is sent to the claimant's last known channel if one exists, even if delivery is doubtful. Posting alone, without the search and without the last-channel attempt, is a notice to nobody and perfects nothing. A posting in a place the claimant never had reason to look — a new board, a private file, a record from another proceeding — is not a posting at all. Substitute service starts an extended window, double the ordinary answer window under T-730, running from the posting date.

The third rule is what the extended window does, and it is T-730's stay with one addition. While the extended window runs, judgment on the affected passage is stayed, as under T-730 — and a judgment that merely notes the cure without resting on it is not a judgment on the cure. When the extended window runs unanswered, the cure is decided on its anchor alone, exactly as T-730 decides silence after proper service: a sound anchor cures, a thin one does not, and the claimant's absence adds nothing to either side. The difference from personal service is only the length of the wait and the proof that preceded it; the decision itself is the same decision, on the same papers.

The fourth rule is the late appearance, and it turns on when the claimant appears. A claimant who appears before judgment on the passage gets a fresh ordinary window from his appearance, and any extended-window default is vacated without a showing: his answer is heard on the merits, counter-anchor included, as if substitute service had never run. A claimant who appears after judgment must do more than appear: he must defeat the search or the posting — show a live address the search missed, a last channel never tried, or a posting in the wrong place. If he defeats either, the cure falls back to unserved under T-730, the judgment resting on it falls with the cure's papers, and the passage returns to the incomplete seal. If he defeats neither, the judgment stands, and his appearance is noted for unjudged passages only. Mere appearance after judgment reopens nothing.

The fifth rule grades the kinds of absence, because not every absence is the same absence. A claimant with no address of record is searched from the claim itself — the claim's own filing channel, its signatory, its stated provenance. A departed claimant is searched through forwarding: the last channel, plus any forwarding address the record holds. A deceased or incapacitated claimant is not served by substitute at all while a successor or representative is known: service on the successor or representative is personal service under T-730, with the ordinary window. Only when no successor is known does substitute service run for a deceased claimant, and then the extended window runs longer — double again — and a successor who later appears takes the late-appearance rule with its search-defeating burden. And absence manufactured by the proceeding itself is no absence: where the proceeding withheld the claimant's address, refused a known channel, or drove the claimant from the record, substitute service is barred outright — the proceeding cannot perfect a cure against a claimant it made unservable, and the cure waits until personal service is possible.

The absent-claimant service rule is passage-graded like T-728's incompleteness rule, T-729's cure rule, and T-730's cure-notice rule. Substitute service against one absent claimant perfects only the passages that claimant's tracking touches; a second claimant, present or absent, must be served in his own way, and a posting for one claimant is not a posting for another. A seal with one served claimant, one absent claimant under substitute service, and one unserved claimant is cured for the first, provisionally cured for the second, and unsealed for the third.

**T-732 — the Diligent-Search Rule — designed:** T-731 left its diligent-search problem named and open: what counts as a diligent search for an absent claimant — how many channels must be tried, whether a single failed delivery to the last channel suffices, and whether the proceeding must wait any interval between attempts. T-732 answers: a search is diligent only when it is attempted, recorded, and repeated — a check of a list is not an attempt, a single failure is not diligence where another channel exists, and two attempts made at once are one attempt, not two.

The first rule is that every known source is checked, and every live channel found is attempted. T-731 names three sources: the claimant's address of record, the last channel the claimant used in the proceeding, and the proceeding's own claimant list checked for a newer address. Diligence requires all three checked, and an attempt sent to every channel any of them yields. A search that tries the address of record while the claimant list holds a newer address is not diligent; it is a search that stopped before the answer. A search that tries the last channel while an address of record sits unattempted is the same failure in the other direction. The proceeding need not invent channels — an unknown channel cannot be attempted — but it must attempt every channel it knows, and it must say, in the search papers, which sources it checked and what each one yielded, including the ones that yielded nothing. A source checked but not reported is treated as unchecked.

The second rule is that a single failed delivery suffices only where it is the only attempt there is to make. Where the claimant has exactly one known channel — one address, one last channel, no newer address on the list — a single failed delivery to that channel, properly recorded, completes the search. Where more than one channel is known, a failure on one channel proves nothing about the others, and the search is incomplete until every known channel has been attempted. A bounced message, a returned letter, and an unanswered message are all failures for this purpose, but they are failures of one channel only: diligence is measured channel by channel, never by the loudest failure. A proceeding that attempts one channel, fails, and files substitute service while a second known channel sits untried has no absent claimant under T-731; it has an unserved claimant, and the cure stands where T-730 leaves an unserved cure.

The third rule is the repeat attempt and its interval. Where the only known channel fails, the proceeding must try it a second time before substitute service runs — and the second attempt must be separated from the first by an interval, not fired in the same sitting. A same-day double attempt counts as one attempt: it tests the channel once, twice over, and proves nothing about a claimant who was merely away, a mailbox merely full, or a server merely down. The interval is judged by the channel: long enough for the channel's ordinary cycle to turn — a postal cycle for mail, a delivery cycle for an electronic channel — and never less than one full ordinary cycle of that channel. The proceeding need not wait out a claimant who has plainly departed — a returned letter marked moved, a channel closed by its provider — but a mere silence, with no return and no closure, always earns the second attempt after the interval. The second attempt's result, like the first's, is recorded with its date; an undated second attempt counts for nothing, under the same discipline T-727 applies to undated evidence.

The fourth rule is the search papers themselves. A diligent search is proved by its papers, filed with the cure under T-731, and the papers must show, for each channel: the channel attempted, the date of each attempt, and the result — delivered, returned, bounced, or silent after the interval. A bare statement that a search was made and the claimant was not found is no search paper; it asserts the conclusion the papers exist to prove. A paper that records attempts but omits a known channel is a defective search, and a substitute service resting on it is defective service: its extended window never starts, and a judgment resting on it falls with the cure's papers under T-731's late-appearance rule. Conversely, a complete paper cures a thin result: a search that attempted everything known, waited the interval, and found nothing is diligent even though it found nothing — diligence is about the trying, not the finding.

The fifth rule is freshness. A search ages. A search conducted more than one ordinary answer window before the cure is filed must be refreshed on the last channel before substitute service runs: one fresh attempt, recorded, after the interval from the last prior attempt if that attempt was silent. A claimant who moved last month is not proved absent by a search from last year, and a channel that was live when last tried is not proved dead by an old failure. Freshness does not require the whole search redone — the address of record and the claimant list, once checked, stand until something suggests they changed — but the last channel, the channel most likely to reach a living claimant, is always re-tried fresh. A proceeding that files on a stale search, without refresh, files on no search.

The diligent-search rule is passage-graded like T-731's substitute-service rule: a search proved for one claimant proves nothing for another, and a channel attempted for one claim is not attempted for a second claim by the same claimant unless the attempt itself named that claim. A search that is diligent for the cure's passage may still be thin for a passage the cure never named, and the cure's papers must say which passages the search serves.

**T-733 — the Self-Search Check Rule — designed:** T-732 left its self-search problem named and open: whether a search conducted by the proceeding itself — the party that benefits from the claimant's absence — needs an independent check, or whether the filed search papers alone suffice even when the searcher gains from failure. T-733 answers: the papers alone never suffice where the searcher gains from failure — a self-search needs an independent check before substitute service perfects, and a substitute service resting on an unchecked search is defective service whose extended window never starts.

The first rule is that gain disqualifies self-certification. T-731's substitute service lets the proceeding move forward without the claimant: the cure rests, judgment may follow, and the claimant's window to answer is replaced by an extended window that runs from a posting the claimant may never see. The proceeding that files the search is therefore the party that profits if the search finds nothing — every unattempted channel, every unreported source, every stale result left unrefreshed moves the cure closer to resting. A search paper signed only by the searcher asks the record to take the beneficiary's word that he tried hard enough to fail. T-732's papers discipline — channel, date, and result per attempt — makes the search checkable, but checkable is not checked. Where the searcher gains from failure, the record requires a second pair of eyes before it treats absence as proved.

The second rule is the checker's independence. The checker must not be the searcher, must not be the dealer whose roster omission the cure serves, and must not share in the cure's benefit — no fee, share, or outcome interest that grows if the claimant stays absent. A second member of the same proceeding may check only with separation shown in the papers: no shared reporting line on the cure, no hand in drafting the search papers, and no benefit from the cure's resting. Separation stated but not shown — a bare line that the checker is independent — counts for nothing; the papers must name the checker's role, the line that separates him from the cure, and the absence of benefit. A checker who is merely the searcher's colleague on other matters, with no stake in this cure and no hand in this search, qualifies. A checker who reviewed the search papers before they were filed, and suggested which channels to try, does not: he is a co-author of the search, not its check.

The third rule is what the check covers. A check is verification plus one fresh touch, never a rubber stamp on the papers. The checker re-checks each of T-732's three sources against the record — the address of record, the last channel the claimant used, and the claimant list for a newer address — and confirms that each source's yield in the papers matches what the record actually holds. Where a source's yield is disputed or the record is ambiguous, the checker resolves it from the record, not from the searcher's account of it. And the checker makes one independent attempt of his own: an attempt on the last channel, sent by the checker himself, recorded with its date and result. A check that never touches a channel is a reading of the papers, not a check of the search; it verifies that the papers are internally consistent, which a careful searcher could fabricate. The independent attempt need not repeat the whole search — the sources are re-checked, the last channel is re-tried — but it must be real: a message actually sent, a letter actually posted, a result actually recorded, not a notation that the checker agrees.

The fourth rule is the check papers and their timing. The checker files his own statement with the cure, before substitute service runs: the sources re-checked and what each yielded, the independent attempt with its date and result, and the separation showing. The check must precede the substitute service, not follow it — a check filed after the posting has run is a post-mortem, and it cannot retroactively start a window that already ran on an unchecked search. Where the checker's independent attempt reaches the claimant, the search ends: the claimant is found, substitute service does not run, and service proceeds on the found channel. Where the checker's attempt fails like the searcher's, the check is complete and substitute service may run on the checked search. Where the checker finds an unattempted channel or a live channel the search called dead, the search fails outright: the proceeding must attempt the found channel, file fresh search papers, and obtain a fresh check. A failed check cannot be cured by amending the old papers; the search that failed is spent, and only a new search, newly checked, supports substitute service.

The fifth rule is the single-person proceeding. A proceeding with no second person cannot check itself, and it cannot waive the check by pleading smallness — the gain-from-failure problem is sharpest exactly where one person both searches and benefits. A single-person proceeding must use an outside checker: an officer of another proceeding, the record-keeper, or any disinterested person with no stake in the cure, who performs the same re-check and independent attempt and files the same statement. Where no outside checker can be had, substitute service does not run on the ordinary extended window; it runs only on a doubled extended window with posting in two venues — the claim's record and the last channel's public place — so that the missing check is answered, imperfectly, by more time and more surface for the claimant to find. Smallness earns a heavier substitute service, never an unchecked one.

The sixth rule is benefit arising after the check. A check made while the checker was disinterested stands even if the checker later gains an interest in the cure's resting — a later appointment, a later share, a later dealing on the passage. Retroactive voiding would punish a good check for a future the checker did not hold when he made it, and would let a claimant unravel a perfected service by pointing at a benefit that postdates it. But the later benefit must be disclosed when it arises, and a checker who knew, when he checked, that benefit was coming — an appointment already promised, a share already agreed — was never disinterested, and his check was never a check. The line is knowledge at the time of checking, not benefit at any time after.

The self-search check rule is passage-graded like T-731's substitute-service rule and T-732's search rule: a check proved for one claimant proves nothing for another, and a checker who verified one claim's search has verified nothing for a second claim by the same claimant unless the check itself named that claim. A check that is complete for the cure's passage may still be thin for a passage the cure never named, and the check papers must say which passages the check serves.

**T-734 — the Checker-Qualification Rule — designed:** T-733 left its checker-qualification problem named and open: whether the checker's separation must be structural — a different office, a different proceeding — or whether a stated absence of benefit and reporting line inside one proceeding ever suffices, and who judges the showing when the proceeding itself files it. T-734 answers: separation is proved, not proclaimed — a checker qualifies by a showing the record-keeper can judge from the papers, structural separation is sufficient but never required, and a same-proceeding checker qualifies only when all three disinterest tests are met and shown. A check filed by an unqualified checker is no check at all, and a substitute service resting on it is defective service whose extended window never starts.

The first rule is that qualification is a showing, judged by the record-keeper, never by the proceeding. T-733 requires a disinterested checker but leaves the judge unnamed, and the proceeding that files the check cannot be its own judge — the party that gains from the claimant's absence would then certify the very independence that stands between it and a resting cure. The judge is the record-keeper: the officer who holds the claim's record, takes the checker's statement, and marks the substitute service as checked or unchecked. The proceeding files the showing; the record-keeper accepts or rejects it on the papers. A showing the record-keeper has not accepted supports no substitute service, and a service that ran on an unaccepted showing is defective even if the checker was in fact disinterested — qualification must be proved on the record before service runs, not demonstrated after the fact when the service is challenged. Where no record-keeper exists for the claim, the checker's statement goes to the next disinterested officer the record names, and if the record names none, the proceeding must use an outside checker whose qualification needs no judging because his office is outside the proceeding altogether.

The second rule is the three disinterest tests. A checker qualifies only if all three hold at the time of checking, and the papers must show all three, not merely assert them. First, no benefit: the checker holds no fee, share, appointment, or outcome interest that grows if the claimant stays absent, and no benefit promised or agreed even if not yet paid — T-733's knowledge-at-check line governs, so a promised benefit disqualifies exactly as a paid one does. Second, no hand in the search: the checker did not draft the search papers, did not choose which channels to try, and did not advise the searcher on the search before it was filed; a checker who shaped the search is its co-author, and co-authors do not check their own work. Third, no reporting line on the cure: the checker does not report, on this cure, to the searcher or to anyone who benefits from the cure's resting, and no one who benefits from the cure directs the checker's work on it. A bare line that the checker is independent satisfies none of the three; the papers must name the checker's role, his benefit position (including promised benefits), his distance from the search's drafting, and the line that separates his reporting from the cure. A showing that answers only one or two tests is an incomplete showing, and an incomplete showing is an unaccepted check.

The third rule is that structural separation is sufficient, never required. A checker from a different office or a different proceeding — an officer of another proceeding, the record-keeper himself, or any person whose office sits outside the proceeding that benefits — qualifies on separation alone, provided the no-benefit and no-hand tests still hold: outside office is no cure for a promised share or a hand in drafting. But separation inside one proceeding can also qualify, and small proceedings are not priced out of checking by a structural rule they cannot meet. A second member of the same proceeding qualifies when the three tests are shown: no benefit from the cure's resting, no hand in the search, and no shared reporting line on the cure — a reporting line on other matters, on other cures, or on the proceeding's ordinary work does not disqualify, because the disinterest that matters is disinterest in this cure. What never qualifies is a checker whose only separation is a sentence: a colleague who shares the cure's benefit, who reviewed the search papers before filing, or who reports to the searcher on the cure, fails the tests whatever the papers call him. Structure answers the question easily; shown disinterest answers it adequately; assertion answers it not at all.

The fourth rule is the consequence of an unqualified checker. A check by an unqualified checker is void, not voidable and not curable by re-papering: the search it purported to check returns to unchecked, the substitute service resting on it is defective, and the extended window never started. The proceeding cannot save the service by filing a better showing for the same checker after the fact — a checker who was disqualified at checking cannot become qualified retroactively by fuller papers, because the defect is in the checker, not in the description of him. The cure for a void check is a fresh check by a qualified checker: a new re-check of the sources, a new independent attempt, a new statement filed before substitute service runs. Where substitute service already ran on the void check, the service must be re-run on the fresh check, with a fresh extended window from the fresh posting; the old window, never validly started, counts for nothing. A claimant who appears and proves the checker unqualified defeats the service under T-731's late-appearance rule, and the proceeding that knowingly filed an unqualified checker — a benefit hidden, a hand in drafting concealed — forfeits the substitute-service route for that claimant altogether: it must serve personally or not at all.

The fifth rule is the checker's competence and the limits of qualification. Qualification is disinterest, not expertise, and the rule does not require the checker to be a search professional — but a checker who cannot read the record he re-checks, or cannot attempt the last channel he must try, cannot perform the check T-733 requires, and a check he cannot perform is no check even if he is perfectly disinterested. The showing must therefore name, alongside the three tests, the checker's access: that he holds the record, or was given it, and that he can attempt the last channel — a checker with no access to the channel is not a checker for that search. Competence beyond access is not judged: the record-keeper does not grade the checker's skill, only his disinterest and his access, because the re-check is verified by its own papers — sources re-checked with yields, attempt with date and result — and a thin check fails on its papers, not on the checker's résumé. A checker who is disinterested, unhanded, unlined, and given access qualifies even if he has never checked a search before; a checker who is expert but interested never qualifies, whatever his record.

The sixth rule is disqualification discovered late. A checker accepted by the record-keeper, later shown to have been disqualified at checking — a promised benefit unearthed, a drafting hand revealed, a reporting line exposed — voids the check from the start, exactly as if the showing had been rejected when filed. The substitute service resting on it falls, the window falls with it, and any judgment resting on the cure falls with the service's papers under T-731. But a checker who was qualified at checking and only later gains a benefit stands under T-733's sixth rule: later benefit, disclosed when it arises, does not void a good check. The line is the same knowledge-at-check line, applied to qualification as a whole: disqualification is judged at the time of checking, on what the checker held and knew then, and later facts matter only as evidence of what he held and knew then. A promised benefit discovered later proves disqualification then; a benefit first arising later proves nothing about then.

The checker-qualification rule is passage-graded like T-733's check rule: a checker qualified for one claimant's search is qualified for another's only if the showing names that claimant and that search — qualification is not a general license, and a checker who is disinterested in one cure may hold a benefit in the next. A single statement may carry several claimants only if it shows the three tests for each, and a benefit in any one disqualifies the checker for that one alone, leaving the others checked.

**T-735 — the Judge-Checker Separation Rule — designed:** T-734 left its judge-checker problem named and open: whether the record-keeper who judges a checker's qualification may himself be the checker, or whether judging and checking must sit in different hands even where the record-keeper is the only disinterested officer available. T-735 answers: judging and checking must sit in different hands for the same search — a record-keeper who checks a search does not judge his own check, and a check judged by its own checker is no check at all. The one narrow exception is not self-judgment but deferred judgment: where the record-keeper is the only disinterested officer available, his check may stand provisionally, unjudged, until a disinterested officer ratifies it — and no judgment may rest on the cure until that ratification lands.

The first rule is that judge and checker are different hands for the same search. T-734 makes qualification a showing judged by the record-keeper from the papers, precisely so the proceeding that gains from the claimant's absence cannot certify the independence standing between it and a resting cure. That protection collapses if the judge and the checker are one person: a checker who accepts his own showing has proved nothing to anyone but himself, and the papers show a signature twice, not a judgment once. The separation is per search, not per proceeding and not per cure: one record-keeper may judge claimant A's check and check claimant B's search in the same cure, because the hands differ on each search judged. But where two searches share sources and the check under judgment re-uses the judge's own earlier yields — his re-checked sources, his attempt's result — the hands have merged on that search too, and the judge must step aside for it even though the searches are nominally distinct. What matters is not the org chart but the act: no person judges a check whose work is his own.

The second rule is the substitute judge. Where the record-keeper is himself the checker for a search, judgment passes before substitute service runs, never after, to the next disinterested officer the record names — the record-keeper of a neighbouring claim, an officer of another proceeding, any office outside the proceeding that benefits. The substitute judge qualifies on structural separation plus the no-benefit test: he holds no fee, share, appointment, or outcome interest, present or promised, that grows if the claimant stays absent. He need not pass T-734's no-hand and no-reporting tests in full, because he does not check — but a substitute judge who drafted the search papers, or who reports on this cure to someone who benefits from its resting, fails for the same reason the checker would: he would be judging work he shaped or an outcome he serves. The showing must name the substitute judge, his office, and his benefit position, and the substitute judge must accept the checker's showing on the papers before service runs, exactly as the record-keeper would have. A substitute judge needs no judge of his own, because judging is not checking: the regress stops at the first hand that does no search work of its own, and a judge who neither searched nor checked has nothing of his own to certify. A proceeding that cannot name a substitute judge from the record must find one outside the proceeding before service runs; it may not proceed on the record-keeper's check unjudged except through the sole-officer route below.

The third rule is the sole-officer exception, and it is deferred judgment, not self-judgment. Where the record-keeper is the only disinterested officer available — one office, one officer, no neighbouring record, no outside checker to be had — his check may be filed provisionally, marked provisional on its face, with its showing complete under T-734 but accepted by no one. Provisional service may then run, but on T-733's doubled extended window and two-venue posting, and with a hard limit the doubled window does not itself supply: no judgment may rest on the cure until a disinterested officer ratifies the provisional check on its papers. Ratification is judgment deferred, not judgment waived: the ratifier reads the same papers the record-keeper would have judged — the three disinterest tests, the re-checked sources with yields, the independent attempt with date and result — and accepts or rejects them. If no ratifier appears by the end of the doubled window, the provisional service lapses: the window closes unperfected, the service must be re-run on a judged check, and the cure cannot rest in the meantime. A provisional check is therefore a bridge, not a resting place — it keeps the proceeding moving while a judge is sought, and it never, by the mere passage of the doubled window, matures into a judged check on its own.

The fourth rule is the consequence of merged hands. A check judged by its own checker — the record-keeper accepting his own showing, a checker countersigning his own qualification, a substitute judge who turns out to have checked the same search under another hat — is void, exactly as a check by an unqualified checker is void under T-734: the search returns to unchecked, the substitute service resting on it is defective, and the extended window never started. The cure for a merged check is a fresh check by a different checker judged by a different judge, with a fresh extended window from the fresh posting; the old window counts for nothing. Merged hands cannot be cured by after-the-fact ratification of the same check, because the defect is that no independent judgment ever attached to that check's papers — a later officer's blessing on papers already acted on is a new judgment on a spent check, not the judgment the service required before it ran. The sole-officer provisional route is not an exception to this rule but its confirmation: the provisional check was never self-judged, only unjudged, and its ratification is the first judgment it ever receives, arriving before any judgment rests on the cure. A proceeding that knowingly filed a self-judged check — a record-keeper who accepted his own showing while a substitute judge was available and unnamed — stands where T-734 puts a proceeding that knowingly filed an unqualified checker, subject to T-734's forfeiture-scope problem, still open: whether forfeiture runs to that claimant alone or to every claimant in the cure.

The fifth rule is the judge's own papers and the limits of the separation. The showing for a checked search must now name judge and checker separately, as two hands: the checker's name, office, and three-test showing; the judge's name, office, and basis for judging — record-keeper, substitute judge by office, or provisional with no judge yet. A showing that names one person in both roles, without a substitute judge or a provisional marking, is an incomplete showing, and an incomplete showing is an unaccepted check under T-734. Separation does not require the judge to be expert in the search's channels: like T-734's checker, the judge is judged on disinterest and on the papers, not on skill — the re-check is verified by its own papers, and a thin check fails on its papers, not on its judge's résumé. And separation does not disqualify a record-keeper from all work in a cure because he checked one search: he may still judge other searches, still hold the record, still mark service — he simply may not judge the search he checked, and may not check a search he has already judged, because the second act would retroactively merge the hands on the first.

The judge-checker separation rule is passage-graded like T-734's qualification rule: separation is judged per claimant and per search, so a merged check for one claimant voids the service for that claimant alone, leaving other claimants' judged checks standing — subject, again, to the open forfeiture-scope question where the merger was knowing. A single statement may carry several claimants only if it names a separate judge and checker for each, or a single judge-checker pair shown to hold for each; a merger in any one voids that one alone.

**T-736 — the Ratification Standard — designed:** T-735 left its ratification-standard problem named and open: whether ratification of a provisional check is papers-only like ordinary judgment, or whether the ratifier must make his own fresh attempt on a live channel before the cure may rest. T-736 answers: ratification is papers-only, and a ratifier who makes a fresh attempt has stopped ratifying and started checking. The ratifier reads the same papers the record-keeper would have judged — the three disinterest tests, the re-checked sources with yields, the independent attempt with date and result — and accepts or rejects them on their face. He makes no attempt of his own, searches no channel, and adds no yield to the file. A ratification bought by a fresh attempt is no ratification at all: it is a second check, unjudged, standing where the first check stood.

The first reason is that a fresh attempt merges the very hands T-735 separated. The ratifier exists because the record-keeper could not judge his own check; the ratifier's office is judgment, and judgment is done by hands that did no search work of their own. A ratifier who attempts a live channel has done search work on that search, and his attempt now needs a judge of its own — the same regress T-735 stopped at the first hand that does no search work, restarted one step later. The proceeding would then need a ratifier for the ratifier, and a ratifier for that ratifier, until it runs out of officers or patience; and if it stops anywhere, it stops by accepting a check judged by its own checker, which T-735 voids. The papers-only rule is not a shortcut taken for convenience. It is the only form ratification can take without destroying the separation it exists to complete. A judge who searches is a checker wearing a judge's coat, and the coat does not change the hands.

The second reason is that the papers are the check, by T-734's own design. T-734 made qualification a showing judged from the papers precisely so that a proceeding that gains from the claimant's absence cannot certify its own independence, and so that a later reader can see, from the file alone, whether the search was diligent. The independent attempt is filed with its date and result; the re-checked sources are filed with their yields; the three tests are filed as showings, not as assurances. A ratifier who finds those papers thin, inconsistent, or undated does not repair them by going out and searching better — he rejects the provisional check, and the service lapses under T-735, to be re-run on a judged check. Repair by the judge would hide the thinness it was his office to expose: a file whose check was thin and whose ratifier searched well would read, to every later auditor, as a file whose check was sound, and the auditor could never tell which hands did which work. Rejection keeps the record honest. The ratifier's verdict is on the papers as filed, and a rejected provisional check files as rejected, with the reasons stated, so the re-run knows what it must do better.

The third reason draws the line the ratifier may still walk, because papers-only does not mean eyes-closed. The ratifier may verify what the papers themselves show: that the dates run in order, that the yields match the sources named, that the attempt's result is stated and not merely asserted, that the three tests are each addressed and not merely recited. He may consult the record already filed — the roster, the earlier postings, the service papers — to test whether the check's papers contradict the file they sit in. What he may not do is go outside the filed record for a new fact about the search: no live channel, no fresh attempt, no quiet inquiry to a source the checker never named. A question put to the checker is not a fresh search, but it is also not a repair: the checker may explain a paper already filed, and may correct a clerical error in it, but any new yield, any new source, any new attempt date supplied in answer is a new check, and a new check needs a new judgment before service runs on it — not a ratification of the old one. The line is the file's edge. Inside it, the ratifier reads; outside it, he would be searching, and searching is the checker's office, not his.

What a ratification files as follows from the three reasons, and the file must show the ratifier's office and his standard, not merely his signature. A ratification on the papers as filed, accepting the three tests, the re-checked sources with yields, and the independent attempt with date and result, files as a Papers-Only Ratification: the provisional check becomes a judged check, and judgment may rest on the cure from the ratification date only, never backdated to the provisional service. A ratification supported by a fresh attempt of the ratifier's own files as an Attempting Ratification: the ratifier has become a second checker, his attempt is unjudged, and the provisional check remains unratified until a disinterested officer judges the papers without attempting — the attempt itself is filed as the ratifier's own account, never as part of the check. A ratification that rejects thin, inconsistent, or undated papers files as a Rejected Provisional: the service lapses under T-735, the cure cannot rest, and the re-run starts from a fresh check, not from the rejected papers patched. A ratification that accepts papers on a showing the ratifier never read — a signature without a reading — files as an unread ratification, void like an unread check under T-734's own logic: judgment that never engaged the papers is not judgment at all.

**The named forms**, all to T-289: the Papers-Only Ratification — a ratification on the filed papers alone, accepting the three tests, the re-checked sources with yields, and the independent attempt with date and result: FILED to T-289 — judgment completed, from the ratification date only. The Attempting Ratifier — a ratifier who makes his own fresh attempt on a live channel before the cure may rest: FILED to T-289 — a second checker, unjudged, his attempt filed as his own account and never as part of the check. The Clarified Check — a checker's explanation or clerical correction of a paper already filed, offered at the ratifier's question: FILED to T-289 — reading aid, not new search, and any new yield it smuggles in files as a new check needing a new judgment. The Rejected Provisional — a provisional check rejected on its papers as thin, inconsistent, or undated: FILED to T-289 — service lapsed, cure unresting, re-run from a fresh check. The Unread Ratification — a ratification signed without a reading of the papers: FILED to T-289 — void, judgment never engaged, the provisional check still unratified.

**The grades.** PAPERS-ONLY-RATIFICATION — ratification reads the same papers ordinary judgment would have read, and adds no yield, attempt, or channel to the file. ATTEMPT-CONVERTS-JUDGE-TO-CHECKER — a ratifier who attempts a live channel becomes a checker on that search, and his attempt needs a judge of its own, which is the regress T-735 stopped. REJECTION-NOT-REPAIR — thin, inconsistent, or undated papers are rejected, never repaired by the judge's own search, and rejection files with reasons stated. RATIFICATION-DATES-JUDGMENT — judgment rests on the cure from the ratification date only, never backdated to the provisional service or the doubled window. FILE-EDGE-RULE — the ratifier may verify the papers against the record already filed, but may not go outside the filed record for a new fact about the search.

**T-737 — the False-Paper Rule — designed:** T-736 left its false-paper problem named and open: whether a ratifier who discovers, from the filed record alone, that a paper is false — a yield contradicted by a roster already in the file — must reject only, or must also report the false paper as a filing defect beyond the claimant's service. T-737 answers: reject and notice, both, and neither alone suffices. The ratifier rejects the check, because a check resting on a false paper is no check at all; and he files a False-Paper Notice on the record, because a false paper left unmarked will be re-filed, re-judged, and rested on by the next hand that finds it. Rejection protects this cure. Notice protects the next one.

The first rule is that a contradiction inside the record is papers-only knowledge, and papers-only knowledge is enough to reject. T-736 kept ratification to the papers so the ratifier would not become a second checker, and a ratifier who finds a yield contradicted by a roster already in the file has found it exactly where he was told to look: on the papers, against the record already filed. He needs no fresh attempt, no outside fact, and no new channel to know the paper is false — the file contradicts itself, and a file that contradicts itself cannot be accepted on its face. This is not repair and not rescue: T-736's rule that thin papers are rejected, never repaired by the judge, holds with full force for false papers, and holds harder. A thin paper fails to prove; a false paper proves against itself. The ratifier therefore rejects, and the rejection is passage-graded in the first instance: a false yield defeats only the passages that rest on it, and a check whose other passages stand on true papers may be re-filed for those passages without re-proving the whole search. But where the false paper is the check's foundation — the qualification showing itself false, a benefit denied in the showing but recorded in the roster, a no-reporting line contradicted by the filing's own cover — the whole check fails, not merely a passage. A foundation cannot be passage-graded, because every passage was judged through it.

The second rule is that rejection without notice is a defective rejection. A rejected check leaves the search standing and the cure unrested, which is the right outcome for this cure; but the false paper, unmarked, stays in the file as if it were merely unaccepted, and nothing stops the same checker — or a successor checker who never saw the rejection — from filing it again under a fresh check, where a fresh judge reads it cold. The ratifier therefore files a False-Paper Notice on the record at the moment of rejection, naming three things and no more: the paper (by filing, date, and passage), the contradicting record item (by filing, date, and passage, already in the file — never a new fact brought in from outside), and the passages the falsehood infects. The notice is filed in the claim's record, where the claimant will find it on appearance and where any later judge will find it before judging a re-filed check. It is not service on the claimant, because the claimant is absent and substitute service is the very machinery under judgment; it is not a new claim, because it asserts nothing the record does not already show; and it is not a verdict on the checker, because it decides nothing about knowledge or intent. A paper can be false because its author misread a roster, copied a stale yield, or filed the wrong attachment, and the notice records the contradiction, not the motive. Whether a knowingly filed false paper converts the notice into forfeiture is a separate filing, by a separate hand, on a separate showing — not the ratifier's office, and not decided by the notice.

The third rule is what the notice does and does not do to the rest of the machinery. It does not restart the doubled window, because the window measures the provisional service's life, not the check's drafts; a checker who re-files corrected papers does so inside the window the provisional service already runs, or not at all. It does not void the search itself: the search papers stand or fall on T-732, and a false check paper is the checker's failure, not the searcher's — the search may be checked again, by a qualified checker, on its own papers. It does not taint a corrected re-filing: a checker who re-files with the false yield corrected, or the false passage withdrawn, and who addresses the notice on the face of the new filing — naming the notice, the correction, and the record item that now supports the corrected yield — is judged on the new papers, fresh, and the notice stays on the record as history, not as a bar. What the notice does bar is silent re-filing: a new check that re-files the noticed paper unchanged, without addressing the notice, is rejected on the notice alone, without re-reading the contradiction, because the file already contains the judgment that the paper is false. And it does not, by itself, rest anything: a notice filed and a cure rested anyway is the NOTICED-AND-RESTED grade below, void, because notice was never a substitute for rejection.

The fourth rule is the boundary the ratifier may not cross while noticing. He may verify the papers against the record already filed — that is T-736's permitted line — and a contradiction found there is his to notice. He may not go outside the filed record for a contradicting fact, because that would be a fresh attempt wearing a notice's name: a roster from another proceeding's archive, a channel result the search never filed, a witness the ratifier consulted on his own motion, are all outside facts, and a notice built on one is no notice at all. If the suspected falsehood can only be shown from outside the record, the ratifier's office is rejection for thinness, not notice for falsehood — the papers fail to prove, and the proof, if it exists, must be filed by a hand entitled to file it and judged by a hand entitled to judge it. The same boundary governs the notice's wording: it quotes the paper and the contradicting item, and states the infection, and stops. A notice that argues the checker's motive, recommends forfeiture, or invites the claimant to a remedy has exceeded the ratifier's office and is struck to its quoted core, the argument disregarded, the notice surviving only as the contradiction it names.

**The named forms**, all to T-289: the False-Paper Notice — a record filing naming the false paper, the contradicting record item already in the file, and the infected passages, filed at rejection, addressed by any corrected re-filing. The Passage-Scoped Rejection — a rejection defeating only the passages resting on the false paper, the remaining passages re-filed without re-proving the search. The Foundation-False Rejection — a rejection defeating the whole check where the false paper is the qualification showing itself, because every passage was judged through it.

**The grades.** REJECTED-AND-NOTICED — the ratifier rejects the check and files the notice naming paper, contradicting item, and infected passages; the only proper grade for a false paper found on the record. REJECTED-UNNOTICED — the check is rejected but the false paper is left unmarked to be re-filed cold; defective, and the next judge who rests on it inherits the defect. NOTICED-AND-RESTED — the notice is filed but the cure rests anyway; void, because notice never substitutes for rejection. REPAIRED-BY-JUDGE — the ratifier corrects the paper himself instead of rejecting it; void under T-736, because a judge who repairs has become a checker. NOTICED-FROM-OUTSIDE — the notice rests on a fact outside the filed record; void, and the proper grade was rejection for thinness.

**Distinguished from the chain it answers.** From T-736's Ratification Standard (the office — there the question was whether ratification is papers-only or requires a fresh attempt, and the answer was papers-only; here the question is what a papers-only reader must do with a falsehood the papers themselves show, and the answer is reject and notice, because reading that finds falsehood and files nothing has read for nothing). From T-734's Checker Qualification (the showing — there the question was what showing qualifies a checker, and the answer was three disinterest tests judged from the papers; here the question is what happens when the showing itself is false, and the answer is that a false showing fails the whole check, not merely a passage). From T-732's Diligent Search (the search — there the question was what the search itself must contain, and the answer was attempted, recorded, and repeated channels; here the question is the check's papers, not the search's, and a false check paper leaves the search standing to be checked again).

**What this pairs with.** T-736's Ratification Standard (the standard this rule completes — papers-only reading, and the line between verifying against the filed record and going outside it). T-735's Judge-Checker Separation Rule (the separation this rule serves — the ratifier as the first hand that does no search work, now with a filing duty of his own).
