**T-738 — the Correction Window Rule — designed:** T-737 left its correction-window problem named and open: whether a checker who must correct a noticed paper has any window of his own inside the doubled window, or whether correction rides the provisional window and dies with it. T-738 answers: correction rides the provisional window and dies with it. There is no correction window. There is one span — the doubled window opened by the provisional service under T-735 — and a corrected re-filing must be filed inside it, or not at all. The notice does not toll it, extend it, restart it, or double it again.

The first rule is that the notice is not a clock. T-737 held that a False-Paper Notice does not restart the doubled window, because the window measures the provisional service's life, not the check's drafts; T-738 extends that holding to its full consequence. A notice filed on the first day of the window and a notice filed on the last day give the checker exactly the same correction span: whatever remains of the provisional window. A checker who receives a late notice and finds three days left has three days; a checker who receives a notice after the window has closed has no days, and no complaint lies in the lateness of the notice, because the notice never promised time — it promised only a mark on the record. The ratifier owes no promptness the doctrine has not yet imposed (see the diligence problem below, still open); the checker owes a correction inside a window he never owned.

The second rule is that the window measures filing, not judgment. A corrected re-filing filed inside the window is a live filing even if its judgment lands after the window closes; the window's close bars new filings, not pending judgments. This is a filing rule only, and it deliberately stops short of T-736's open ratification-deadline problem: whether the RATIFICATION of a provisional check may land after the window is a question about judgment, and it stays open. What T-738 settles is narrower — that a corrected check filed in time does not die merely because the judge reads it late. A filing that dies on the judge's calendar instead of the filer's would punish diligence and reward delay in the same stroke, and no window in this chain has ever measured anything but the act it names.

The third rule is that expiry kills the check, not the search, and not the notice. A notice filed after the window closed — a ratifier who reads late papers and finds a falsehood in a check whose window has already run — is still filed, and still names paper, contradicting item, and infected passages, because the record's history does not expire with the window. But it opens no correction path under that service: the check is dead, the cure unrested, and the only road back is a fresh provisional service opening a fresh doubled window, under which a new check must address the notice on its face, per T-737's bar on silent re-filing. The notice survives as history across the expiry; what dies is only the correction it would have invited. And the doubling is spent once: a corrected re-filing earns no second doubling, because the doubling belongs to the provisional service, not to each draft of the check. A checker who treats correction as a fresh service has doubled a window the doctrine doubled already.

The fourth rule confines what counts as a correction. A corrected re-filing may correct the noticed papers and the passages they infect, and nothing else under correction's name. A re-filing that corrects the noticed yield and smuggles in a new yield, a new channel, or a new source has not corrected a check; it has filed a new check, unqualified, and it is rejected as one — its new matter judged under T-734's qualification showing, not grandfathered by the old check's papers. Correction is repair of named falsehood, not a second search wearing the first check's filing date. A re-filing that corrects some noticed papers and leaves others unaddressed is rejected on the notice alone for the remainder, per T-737, and that rejection extends nothing: the window that was running keeps running, and a second correction filed inside it is still a correction, judged on the same terms.

**The named forms**, all to T-289: the Ridden Window — the single doubled span, opened by the provisional service, inside which every correction must be filed. The Expired-Window Notice — a notice filed after the window closed: history on the record, opening no correction path under that service. The Inside-Filing — a corrected re-filing filed inside the window, live for judgment even if judgment lands after the close.

**The grades.** CORRECTED-IN-WINDOW — a corrected re-filing filed inside the window, addressing the notice on its face; judged fresh on the new papers, the notice staying as history. CORRECTED-OUT-OF-WINDOW — a corrected re-filing filed after the close; dead on arrival, no judgment, the only road a fresh provisional service. NOTICED-TOO-LATE — a notice filed after expiry; valid as history, void as an invitation to correct under that service. CORRECTED-BEYOND-NOTICE — a re-filing that smuggles new yields, channels, or sources under correction's name; rejected as a new, unqualified check. UNADDRESSED-REMAINDER — a partial correction leaving noticed papers unaddressed; rejected on the notice alone, the window unextended.

**T-739 — the Prompt-Notice Rule — designed:** T-738 left its diligence problem named and open: whether a ratifier who discovers a false paper early and files the notice late — leaving the checker days instead of weeks — owes any duty of prompt notice, or whether the checker bears the whole risk of a late notice inside a window he never owned. T-739 answers: the ratifier owes prompt notice, and the price of lateness falls on the notice, never on the window. T-738's holding stands untouched — the notice never promised time, and no lateness tolls, extends, or re-doubles the provisional window — but a notice filed late loses the summary bar that made it more than history. The checker still bears the window; the ratifier bears his own delay.

The first rule is that promptness is measured from the papers, and the papers date both ends. Discovery is dated by the ratifier's own reading record: the date his ratification papers land, showing the contradiction found, is the discovery date, and the notice's filing date is the other end. A notice that hides its discovery date — that names the paper and the contradicting item but never says when the contradiction was found — is defective on its face, because no promptness can be judged from it, and a promptness that cannot be judged is treated as lateness. This is T-736's papers-only discipline turned on the ratifier himself: the office that judged from the papers alone must now be judged from the papers alone, and a ratifier who will not date his own discovery has filed a notice no later hand can trust for timing. The ordinary window — the undoubled span, not the doubled provisional span — is the measure: a notice filed within one ordinary window of discovery is prompt; a notice filed after it is late. The doubled window belongs to the provisional service and is never the promptness measure, because measuring the ratifier's duty by the checker's doubled span would let the ratifier spend the checker's time and call it his own.

The second rule is that lateness suspends the bar, not the notice. A late notice still stands on the record as history — it still names paper, contradicting item, and infected passages, and any later judge still reads it before judging a re-filed check — but it no longer carries T-737's summary bar: a re-filing that re-files the noticed paper unchanged, without addressing a late notice, is judged on its papers fresh, not rejected on the notice alone. The reasoning is the chain's oldest equity, stated plainly: a ratifier who slept on the mark cannot demand the checker heed it summarily. The summary bar was the reward for a notice filed in time to be answered; a notice filed too late to be answered in the window it rode has earned history, not obedience. This sanction is deliberately narrow. It does not revive a dead check, it does not reopen a closed window, and it does not forgive the false paper — a re-filing judged fresh on papers that are still false still fails, on the contradiction, not on the notice. What it removes is only the shortcut: the next judge must read the contradiction again, because the ratifier who filed late forfeited the right to have it taken on his word.

The third rule is that an excuse, to count, must be filed with the notice and judged from the papers. A ratifier who could not file in time — the record withheld, the file incomplete when he read, the contradicting item itself filed late by another hand — may file the notice late with the reason on its face, naming the impediment and the papers that show it. A reason so filed and so shown excuses the lateness, and the bar stands: an excused-delay notice is judged as prompt, because the delay was the record's, not the ratifier's. But a reason filed after challenge — raised only when a checker complains of lateness, or offered from outside the papers — is no reason at all, and the notice is late without excuse. This is the same boundary T-737 drew for contradiction sources, applied to delay: what is not on the papers at filing does not exist for judgment. A ratifier who discovers a false paper, waits, and then explains the wait with a story no paper shows has told the record nothing, and the record answers with the bar suspended.

The fourth rule is that lateness is paper-graded, and the window's close does not change the grade. Where a notice names several papers, promptness is judged per paper, not per notice: a notice prompt for the papers discovered this week and late for a paper discovered last month is prompt where it is prompt and late where it is late, and the bar stands for the former and falls for the latter. A single notice is not one delay; it is as many delays as it has discovery dates. And where the window has already closed by the time a late notice lands, the notice is still graded — late, excused, or undated — because the grade governs the next service, not the dead one: a checker who files a fresh provisional service after expiry must address a prompt notice on the face of the new check, per T-737, but need only answer a late notice on the papers, judged fresh, because the ratifier's delay already spent the summary bar once and cannot spend it again on a new service. The expired-window notice of T-738 thus splits by grade: prompt history binds the next service's face; late history merely warns its judge.

**The named forms**, all to T-289: the Prompt Notice — a notice filed within one ordinary window of a discovery dated on the ratifier's reading papers, carrying the full summary bar. The Late Notice — a notice filed after that measure, standing as history with the summary bar suspended. The Excused Delay — a late filing with its reason on its face, shown from the papers, judged as prompt. The Undated Notice — a notice hiding its discovery date, defective on its face, treated as late.

**The grades.** PROMPTLY-NOTICED — the notice lands within one ordinary window of a dated discovery; the T-737 bar stands in full. LATE-NOTICED — the notice lands after that measure without excuse; history stands, bar suspended, the next re-filing judged on its papers. EXCUSED-DELAY — the reason filed with the notice and shown from the papers; judged as prompt, bar intact. UNDATED-NOTICE — the discovery date hidden; defective, treated as late, bar suspended until a dated notice replaces it. BAR-SPENT-ACROSS-SERVICE — a late notice carried into a fresh provisional service; it warns the new judge, it does not bind the new check's face.

From T-737's False-Paper Rule (the notice — there the question was what a ratifier must do with a falsehood the papers show, and the answer was reject and notice; here the question is when he must do it, and the answer is within one ordinary window of discovery, because a notice that arrives too late to be answered has earned history, not obedience). **T-740 — the Discovery-Date Rule — designed:** T-739 left its discovery-date problem named and open: whether a ratifier who reads over several days — finding one contradiction on the first reading and another on a re-reading — dates discovery per paper from its own reading, or whether the whole reading counts as one discovery dated at its close. T-740 answers: discovery is dated per paper, from the reading in which that paper's contradiction was first found. A multi-day reading is not one discovery; it is as many discoveries as it has findings. T-739's promptness measure cannot run any other way — lateness there is paper-graded, and a paper-graded lateness needs a paper-dated discovery. The close-date theory would let the ratifier bank an early finding, spend the checker's window in silence, and then date the whole reading at its close as if the first contradiction had only just been found. The papers date the finding; the reading's close dates nothing.

The first rule is the per-paper date. Each paper's discovery date is the date of the reading entry that first shows its contradiction — the entry in the ratifier's own reading papers where the paper and its contradicting item first appear together. A notice that names several papers found across several readings therefore carries several discovery dates, one per paper, and T-739 grades each paper against its own date: prompt where the notice lands within one ordinary window of that paper's finding, late where it does not. The notice is not one delay with one date; it is a bundle of delays, and the bundle is graded paper by paper. This is the direct consequence of T-739's fourth rule, made explicit: a rule that grades lateness per paper must date discovery per paper, or the grade has nothing to measure against.

The second rule is first-finding: a re-reading never re-dates a contradiction already found. Where the first reading found the contradiction and a later re-reading finds it again, the discovery date stays at the first reading, and the notice clock runs from there. A ratifier who found a false paper on Monday, re-read it on Friday, and filed on the strength of Friday's reading has still discovered on Monday, and a notice filed more than one ordinary window after Monday is late for that paper whatever Friday showed. The reason is the same anti-banking reason that defeats the close-date theory: a second look at a known falsehood is confirmation, not discovery, and confirmation does not restart a clock that discovery started. Only a contradiction never before found gets a new date on re-reading. A re-reading that finds a genuinely new contradiction — a second paper false in a way the first reading never showed — dates that paper at the re-reading, and the notice clock for the new paper runs from the re-reading alone. The reading is thus segmented by finding, not by sitting: one sitting can hold several discoveries with several dates, and several sittings can hold one discovery with one date.

The third rule is that discovery means actual finding, not findability. The date is when the ratifier's papers first show the contradiction, not when a more diligent reader would have found it. T-739 imposed a duty of prompt notice after discovery, never a duty of diligent reading before it, and a rule that backdated discovery to the earliest a hypothetical reader could have found the falsehood would turn every promptness judgment into an audit of reading quality — a question no paper can answer, because the papers show what was found, not what could have been. The one exception proves the boundary: where the first reading's papers state the contradiction in the ratifier's own hand — he wrote the paper and its contradicting item down together, in his own notation — the finding is dated at that first reading even if he later claims he only noticed it on re-reading. His own notation is a paper, and a paper that states the contradiction dates the discovery against its author. What he wrote, he found; what he merely could have written, he did not.

The fourth rule is the lump-date penalty for an undifferentiated reading record. Where a reading record lumps findings without dating them — a single entry naming several contradictions, or a record filed as one paper with one filing date and no per-finding dates — every finding in the lump is dated at the record's filing date, the latest date the papers support, and the promptness clock for each paper runs from that filing. The ratifier who controls the record and will not date its findings dates them late: the lump gives him no earlier date than the paper that carries it, because no earlier date appears on any paper. This is T-739's undated-notice treatment applied one level down, from the notice to the reading behind it. A lumped record is not defective the way an undated notice is — it still shows the contradictions, and the notice built on it still stands — but it forfeits every early date it fails to show, and a notice prompt only from an early date the record never stated is late for every paper in the lump. A ratifier who wants the benefit of a Monday finding must write Monday on it; a record that says only "found" says it on the day it was filed.

**The named forms**, all to T-289: the Per-Paper Discovery — a discovery dated per paper from the reading entry that first shows that paper's contradiction. The First Finding — the first reading that shows a contradiction, fixing its date against any later re-reading. The Self-Dated Finding — a contradiction stated in the ratifier's own hand on an earlier reading, dated at that reading whatever he later claims. The Lump Date — the filing date of an undifferentiated reading record, imposed as the discovery date for every finding it lumps.

**The grades.** PER-PAPER-DATED — each paper's discovery dated from its own first-finding entry; T-739 promptness graded per paper against its own date. T-741 answers: the lump date stands against a bare amendment, and yields only to an evidenced one. An amendment is a claim about a date, not a date. A ratifier who files a lump on Friday and then amends it to say "found Monday" has added a sentence, not a paper, and a sentence written after filing cannot prove what happened before it. If it could, T-740's lump-date penalty would be a dead letter: every ratifier whose notice came late on the lump date would simply amend the record to the earlier date and erase the lateness, and the rule that a record saying only "found" says it on the day it was filed would never bite. The amendment must therefore bring something the lump never had — a paper that predates the filing and itself dates the finding — or it changes nothing.

The first rule is the bare-amendment bar. An amendment that asserts an earlier date without attaching a pre-filing paper showing it leaves the lump date exactly where T-740 put it: the record's filing date, for every finding in the lump. The ratifier's say-so is not a paper, however sworn, however detailed, however filed with the amendment itself. Detail does not cure timing: a long affidavit written Friday about Monday is still written Friday, and a record that could have dated its findings when filed but did not cannot buy the earlier date with a later paragraph. The bar is not a judgment on the ratifier's honesty — the finding may truly date from Monday — it is a judgment on what the papers prove, and papers written after the date they assert prove nothing about that date. T-740's discipline was papers-only from the start, and an amendment that is only words is the one paper the discipline cannot count.

The second rule is the evidenced amendment. An amendment re-dates a finding earlier only when it attaches a paper that itself predates the lump's filing and itself dates the finding: the ratifier's own notation dated Monday naming the paper and its contradiction, a dated reading entry filed elsewhere before Friday, a channel receipt or filing stamp from Monday showing the reading took place. The attached paper, not the amendment, does the dating — the amendment is only the hand that brings the paper into the claim's record. The re-date runs to the attached paper's date, never earlier than the earliest paper attached, and only for the papers that paper names: an amendment attaching Monday's notation for one paper re-dates that paper alone, and the rest of the lump stays dated at filing. Where several papers attach with several dates, the re-date is per paper again, exactly as T-740 dated discovery per paper in the first place. An evidenced amendment thus splits the lump the way a well-kept record would have split it at filing — it does not rewrite the lump, it replaces the lump's silence with a paper for each finding the paper covers.

The third rule is the amendment's timing against the notice. An evidenced amendment filed before the notice it supports carries its earlier date into that notice, and T-739 grades the notice's promptness from the amended date. An evidenced amendment filed after the notice — or after judgment has already rested on the lump date — does not retroactively cure lateness already accrued. A notice graded late on the lump date stays late, even if a later amendment proves the finding was early; the cure for a late notice is a fresh notice filed after the amendment, graded from the amended date, not a rewriting of the old notice's grade. The reason is reliance: a checker, a claimant, and a record-keeper who all read the lump date and acted on it cannot have their actions unmade by a paper that arrived after they acted. Where the amendment attaches a pre-filing paper that contradicts the lump's stated date, the attached paper controls for the papers it names, because a paper that predates the lump and dates the finding is a better witness to the finding than the lump that lumped it. But the amendment never controls by assertion against a dated record: the louder the contradiction, the more paper it needs, and a contradiction with no paper behind it is not a contradiction at all, it is a second lump. A failed amendment — bare, contradicted, or late — spends nothing but time: it does not poison a later evidenced amendment, and it does not forfeit the finding. **T-742 — the Self-Dated Paper Rule — designed:** T-741 left its amendment-evidence problem named and open: whether a notation dated Monday but filed Friday — a private note the ratifier dates himself, with no outside stamp — counts as a pre-filing paper at all, or whether a self-dated paper filed late is a bare amendment in paper form, and what outside mark, if any, makes a self-dated notation contemporaneous rather than backdated. T-742 answers: a self-dated notation is a claim about a date wearing a paper's clothes, and it counts as a pre-filing paper only when an outside mark fixes its date independently of the hand that wrote it. The date written on a paper by its own author proves the author's say-so, not the day; a rule that accepted a self-written date at face value would let every bare amendment pass T-741's bar by the cheap trick of writing the earlier date on a fresh sheet and calling the sheet a paper. T-741's evidenced amendment required a paper that predates the filing and itself dates the finding — and a paper whose only date is the amender's own handwriting does not predate anything, because the handwriting could have been laid down yesterday. The question is therefore never "does the notation say Monday" but "does anything besides the ratifier say Monday."

The first rule is the outside-mark requirement. A self-dated notation counts as a pre-filing paper only when it carries, or is carried by, a mark made by a hand or a system other than the ratifier's: a filing stamp or receipt stamp from the record, a channel receipt showing the notation was sent or received on the dated day, a dated entry in another hand's log naming the notation, an archive accession stamp predating the lump's filing, a second paper filed before the lump that quotes or names the notation. The outside mark need not be elaborate — a stamp is enough — but it must be independent: it must be a mark the ratifier could not have produced alone after the fact, or could not have produced without leaving a trace in another hand's keeping. A notation on the ratifier's own letterhead, in the ratifier's own hand, dated by the ratifier's own pen, with nothing else on it, is not a pre-filing paper; it is T-741's bare amendment with better stationery, and it leaves the lump date standing exactly as a bare amendment does. The bar is not suspicion of the ratifier — the notation may be honest, and Monday may be the true day — it is the same papers-only discipline that ran through T-740 and T-741: what the record proves is what the record holds, and a date proved only by the interested hand is proved by nothing.

The second rule is the corroboration ladder. Not every outside mark is equal, and T-742 grades them by how hard they are to forge after the fact. At the top stands a system mark: a filing stamp, a channel receipt, a transmission log kept by a system the ratifier does not control — a mark whose date is fixed by a mechanism, not by a person, and which the ratifier cannot rewrite without rewriting the system's own record. Next stands a third-hand mark: a dated entry by a disinterested hand — a record-keeper's log, a checker's receipt, a successor's inventory — naming the notation and dated before the lump's filing; weaker than a system mark because a hand can be persuaded, but still independent, because it lives in another hand's keeping. At the bottom stands a same-hand corroboration: a second notation by the ratifier himself, or a paper in the ratifier's own archive, dated Monday and naming the first notation — this corroborates nothing, because it is the same hand vouching for itself twice, and two self-dated sheets are no more a paper than one. The ladder decides close cases: where a system mark and a third-hand mark disagree, the system mark controls; where only a third-hand mark exists, it suffices; where only same-hand corroboration exists, the notation fails and the lump date stands. A mark dated after the lump's filing proves nothing about the finding's date either, however independent — a checker's receipt dated Saturday cannot prove a Monday finding — so the mark must predate the lump's filing as well as stand outside the ratifier's hand.

The third rule is the backdating presumption and its burden. A self-dated notation first produced after the lump's filing is presumed written at production, not on the date it bears, and the presumption is rebutted only by an outside mark of the kind the first two rules describe. The burden sits on the amender throughout: he who asks the record to move an earlier date must bring the mark, and a checker, claimant, or record-keeper need not disprove the notation's date. Silence in the record is not evidence against the notation — a notation may be genuine and simply unmarked — but silence is also not evidence for it, and a genuine but unmarked notation earns no re-date. This is the hard edge of the rule and it is deliberate: T-740's lump-date penalty exists precisely because records that could have dated their findings at filing did not, and a regime that let the ratifier cure that silence with his own pen would repeal the penalty for anyone willing to write an earlier date. The presumption is rebuttable, not conclusive — a system mark or a third-hand mark defeats it outright — but until rebutted, the notation is treated as written when produced, and an amendment attaching only such a notation is graded as bare.

The fourth rule is partial corroboration and failed claims. Corroboration runs per paper, as T-741's re-date did: a notation naming three papers, corroborated by an outside mark for one of them, re-dates that one paper alone, and the other two stay at the lump date. A notation whose outside mark dates it later than the date it bears — a channel receipt from Wednesday for a notation dated Monday — re-dates its papers to Wednesday, the mark's date, never to Monday, because the mark, not the handwriting, is the witness. And a failed self-date claim spends nothing but time, as T-741's failed amendments did: it does not poison a later amendment attaching a genuine outside mark, it does not forfeit the finding, and it does not bar the ratifier from filing a fresh notice from the lump date. Only a showing that the notation was knowingly backdated — an outside mark proving the notation was written after the date it bears, offered as if contemporaneous — converts the claim from a failed amendment into a false paper, and that conversion is judged under T-737's False-Paper Rule, not here. Honest failure is cheap; only knowing falsity is dear.

**The named forms**, all to T-289: the Self-Dated Notation — a paper whose only date is its author's own hand, first produced after the lump's filing; presumed written at production until an outside mark rebuts it. The Outside Mark — a date fixed by a system or a disinterested hand independent of the ratifier, predating the lump's filing; the only witness that makes a self-dated notation a pre-filing paper. The Corroboration Ladder — system mark above third-hand mark above same-hand corroboration, which corroborates nothing. The Partial Re-Date — a notation corroborated for some papers it names re-dates those alone, at the mark's date, leaving the rest at the lump date.

**The grades.** OUTSIDE-MARKED — a self-dated notation carried by a system or third-hand mark predating the lump's filing counts as a pre-filing paper and re-dates the papers it names to the mark's date. SELF-DATED-ONLY — a notation with no outside mark is a bare amendment in paper form; the lump date stands. LADDER-RESOLVED — where marks conflict, the system mark controls over the third-hand mark, and same-hand corroboration never counts. PRESUMED-AT-PRODUCTION — a notation first produced after filing is presumed written at production until an outside mark rebuts it; the burden stays on the amender, and honest failure costs nothing but time.

**T-743 — the Controlled-System Mark Rule — designed:** T-742 left its controlled-system problem named and open: whether a system mark the ratifier himself controls — his own channel log, his own archive's accession stamp, a system he administers — counts as an outside mark at all, or whether control defeats independence however mechanical the mark. T-743 answers: a machine is not a witness merely because it is a machine. A system mark counts as an outside mark only when the system stands outside the ratifier's power to rewrite it; a log the ratifier can edit after the fact is the ratifier's own handwriting with a printer attached, and it corroborates nothing. T-742 graded a system mark at the top of its ladder because a system mark's date is fixed by a mechanism, not by a person, and cannot be rewritten without rewriting the system's own record — but that reasoning assumed a system the ratifier does not control. Where the ratifier is the system's keeper, the mechanism's date is his date, and the ladder's top rung collapses into its bottom rung: same-hand corroboration in machine form. The question is therefore never "did a system stamp it" but "could the ratifier have stamped it himself, after the fact, and left no trace."

The first rule is the control test. Control means the ratifier, alone or with hands that answer to him, can create, alter, or delete the mark or its log without leaving a trace in another hand's keeping: sole administrator of the channel, sole keeper of the archive, holder of the only copy of the log, power to re-run the accession sequence and re-number the stamps. Where that power exists and was unexercised in any provable sense — no mirror, no export, no audit — the mark is not an outside mark at all, and the notation it carries is graded exactly as T-742 graded a self-dated-only notation: a bare amendment in paper form, the lump date standing. The burden, as in T-742, sits on the amender: he who offers a mark from his own system must show the system stood outside his rewrite power in the respect that matters, and a bare assertion that "the system stamped it" proves nothing, because his system stamps whatever he tells it to stamp. A system mark offered without a showing about control is not a weak outside mark; it is no outside mark.

The second rule is the anchor that rescues a controlled system. A controlled-system mark counts as an outside mark when its date is anchored somewhere the ratifier cannot reach: a log mirrored in real time, or at regular intervals predating the lump's filing, to a keeper who does not answer to the ratifier; an append-only log whose entries are hash-chained and whose chain head was published or filed before the lump's filing, so that rewriting one entry breaks every entry after it in a way the record can detect; an audit trail examined and signed by a disinterested hand before the lump's filing, naming the entry and its date. The anchor need not be elaborate — a single exported copy filed in the record before the lump is enough — but it must predate the lump's filing and must live outside the ratifier's reach, because an anchor the ratifier can still move is no anchor. Where such an anchor exists, the controlled-system mark counts as a system mark in full: the mechanism's date is fixed by something beyond the ratifier, and T-742's ladder applies as written. Where the anchor postdates the lump's filing — a mirror exported after the notation was produced, a chain head published after the dispute arose — it proves the log's contents at export, not the notation's date at filing, and the notation fails as self-dated-only. An anchor is a date fixed by another keeping; a late anchor is a late witness, and late witnesses do not re-date.

The third rule is shared control and partial control. Control is rarely all-or-nothing, and T-743 grades it by who else holds a key. A system administered jointly, where no single hand — ratifier included — can rewrite the log without another administrator's key, counts as outside the ratifier's control, because rewriting requires a second hand's complicity, and complicity by a second hand is a fact the record can examine rather than a power the ratifier holds alone. A system where the ratifier holds one key among several disinterested administrators counts the same way, provided no administrator answers to him and the log shows whose key authorized each entry. But a system where the other administrators are the ratifier's own hands — his clerks, his successors, hands that answer to him — is sole control with extra steps, and the mark fails as controlled. The test is not the number of keys but the independence of the hands holding them: a second key held by a hand the ratifier directs is the ratifier's own second hand, and two hands answering to one will are one hand for the purposes of this rule. Where the record does not show who held the other keys, the mark is treated as controlled, because the amender has not carried his burden of showing independence.

The fourth rule is downgrade, not disgrace. A controlled-system mark that fails as an outside mark does not poison the notation, and it does not convert the claim into a false paper. It is graded as T-742 graded a failed self-date claim: the notation stays self-dated-only, the lump date stands, honest failure costs nothing but time, and a later amendment attaching a genuine outside mark — a true system mark, a disinterested third-hand mark, or a controlled-system mark with a predating anchor — may still re-date. Only a showing that the log was in fact rewritten — an entry altered after the date it bears, offered as if contemporaneous — crosses from failed amendment into false paper, judged under T-737, not here. And a controlled-system mark that succeeds through an anchor re-dates exactly as T-742's system mark did: per paper, at the anchor's date where the anchor dates the entry later than the notation bears, never at the notation's own written date where the anchor disagrees. Control defeated by an anchor is control defeated; control merely asserted away is control intact.

**The named forms**, all to T-289: the Controlled-System Mark — a system mark from a system the ratifier administers or solely keeps; not an outside mark unless anchored outside his reach. The Anchor — a mirror, export, hash-chain publication, or disinterested audit predating the lump's filing, living outside the ratifier's power to rewrite. The Shared-Key System — a system no single hand can rewrite alone, whose other key-holders do not answer to the ratifier; outside control. The Downgraded Mark — a controlled-system mark without an anchor, graded as same-hand corroboration: it proves nothing, costs nothing, and bars nothing later.

**The grades.** ANCHORED — a controlled-system mark with a predating anchor outside the ratifier's reach counts as a system mark in full and re-dates as T-742's system mark did. CONTROLLED-ONLY — a mark from a system the ratifier can rewrite unobserved, with no anchor, is no outside mark; the notation stays self-dated-only and the lump date stands. SHARED-KEY — a system no single hand can rewrite alone, with independent key-holders, counts as outside control. DOWNGRADED-NOT-POISONED — a failed controlled-system claim costs nothing but time and does not bar a later genuinely anchored amendment; only a shown rewrite crosses into false paper under T-737.

**T-744 — the Mirror-Lag Rule — designed:** T-743 left its mirror-lag problem named and open: whether a mirror that lags — copied weekly, so that an entry stamped Monday is mirrored only the following Monday — anchors the entry at its stamp date or only at its mirror date, and whether a lagging mirror can ever prove a date earlier than the mirror itself. T-744 answers: a mirror anchors at its own date, never at the stamp date it copies. A mirror is a copy, and a copy proves its contents at copy time. The entry's internal stamp date is still the ratifier's own claim until an outside keeping fixes it; mirroring does not adopt the stamp's date, it replaces it with the mirror's. A lagging mirror therefore never re-dates a notation to its stamped Monday. At best it re-dates it to the Monday it was mirrored — and only if that mirror predates the lump's filing, as T-743 already required. Lag is not a defect in the mirror; it is a delay in the proof, and the proof dates from when it exists, not from when the thing proved claims to have existed.

The first rule is copy-time, not stamp-time. The anchor date of a mirrored entry is the date the mirror was made and placed outside the ratifier's reach — the export date, the mirror run's date, the filing date of the exported copy — never the date written inside the entry. The reasoning is T-743's control test applied to time: the stamp inside the entry is a date the ratifier's system wrote, and a system the ratifier controls writes whatever date he tells it to write. Copying that stamp into an outside keeping copies the claim, not the fact; what the outside keeping fixes is that the entry, with that stamp on it, existed by the mirror's date. A notation claiming Monday, first mirrored the following Monday, is therefore evidenced as existing by the following Monday, and by no earlier date. Where the following Monday still predates the lump's filing, the notation re-dates as T-742's system mark did, but at the mirror's date where the mirror dates the entry later than the notation bears — never at the notation's own written date where the mirror disagrees. Where the mirror postdates the lump's filing, it proves the log's contents at export, not the notation's date at filing, and the notation fails as self-dated-only, exactly as T-743's late anchor failed. A late mirror is a late witness, and lag does not make a late witness early.

The second rule is the interval bound, and its limit. A pair of consecutive mirrors can bound an entry's creation, but the bound is an interval, not a date, and the interval never moves the anchor earlier than its far end. Where the prior mirror is shown gapless and complete — sequence numbers continuous, no entries missing, the mirror's own completeness provable from the papers — and it lacks the entry, and the next mirror contains it, the entry is bounded between the two mirrors: created after the prior mirror and by the next. That bound rules out one kind of fabrication — an entry invented after the second mirror and back-stamped into the interval cannot be in the second mirror — but it does not date the entry to any day inside the interval, and it does not date it to its stamp. The anchor for re-dating remains the first containing mirror, because re-dating needs a dated paper, and the only dated paper that names the entry is that mirror; the prior mirror's silence is negative evidence, not a paper dating the entry. A ratifier who claims a Monday stamp inside a Monday-to-Monday interval has shown, at most, that the entry could have been stamped Monday; a claim that could have been true is not a paper showing it was. Where the prior mirror is missing, gapped, or its completeness merely asserted, there is no interval at all: the single mirror still anchors at its own date if it predates the lump, but it bounds nothing, and any claim about what the missing mirror would have shown is the ratifier's word, not a keeping.

The third rule is that cadence must be shown, and delay is measured by the actual mirror, not the scheduled one. A mirror described as "weekly" anchors as a weekly mirror only where the papers show the cadence — dated mirror runs at regular intervals, each filed outside the ratifier's reach — and a cadence claimed but not shown is treated as a single mirror: anchor at its date, no interval, no bound. A batch delayed beyond its interval — the weekly run that in fact ran a fortnight late — anchors at its actual export date, not its scheduled date, because a scheduled date is an intention, not a keeping; the record that fixes a date is the mirror that exists, dated when it was made. Lag length therefore matters only to usefulness, never to principle: a longer lag means a later anchor, a later anchor means a re-date further from the notation's claim, and a lag long enough to push the first containing mirror past the lump's filing means no re-date at all. Lag never excuses a late anchor, and no showing that the mirror "would have" run earlier, had the schedule held, re-dates anything. The mirror that exists is the witness; the mirror that should have existed is not.

The fourth rule is that lag does not cure control. Everything in this rule assumes a mirror that already satisfies T-743: a copy living outside the ratifier's rewrite power, kept by a hand that does not answer to him, or hash-chained and published, or audited by a disinterested hand. A lagging mirror inside the ratifier's own keeping — his own backup, his own archive's second copy, a mirror he can rewrite as easily as the original — is a controlled-system mark with a delay attached, and it anchors nothing at any date, because there is no outside date to anchor to. Lag plus control is control; the interval bound of the second rule requires two outside mirrors, not two copies in the ratifier's own drawer. And where the mirror keeper is shown independent but the mirror's own date is disputed — export stamp against receipt stamp, mirror-run date against filing date — the anchor date is the earliest date the papers prove the copy outside the ratifier's reach, because a copy still in his hands on Monday and filed Wednesday was still rewritable Monday night. The anchor is fixed when the copy leaves his power, not when his system made it.

**The named forms**, all to T-289: the Lagging Mirror — a periodic mirror whose copy date trails the entry's stamp date; anchors at copy date, never at stamp date. The Mirror Date — the date the mirror was made and placed outside the ratifier's reach; the only date a mirror proves. The Interval Bound — the span between a gapless prior mirror lacking the entry and the first containing mirror; it bounds creation but dates nothing inside itself. The Delayed Batch — a mirror run later than its scheduled cadence; anchors at its actual export date, never its scheduled date. The Unshown Cadence — a regularity claimed but not proved from the papers; treated as a single mirror, anchor at its date only.

**The grades.** MIRROR-DATED — a lagging mirror predating the lump's filing re-dates the notation at the first containing mirror's date, never at the entry's stamp date. INTERVAL-BOUNDED — consecutive gapless mirrors bound creation between them but date the entry only at the far end; the interval is a limit on fabrication, not a date. SINGLE-MIRROR — a mirror without a shown gapless predecessor anchors at its own date and bounds nothing. **T-745 — the Mirror-Receipt Rule — designed:** T-744 left its mirror-receipt problem named and open: whether the anchor date is the mirror's export date or the record's receipt stamp when the two differ — a copy exported Monday but filed Wednesday, still in transit between. T-745 answers: the receipt controls. A mirror anchors at the date an outside keeping receives it, not the date its maker sent it. Export is a claim by the sender that a copy left his hands; receipt is a keeping's own record that a copy arrived in hands that are not his. T-744 already fixed the principle — the anchor is fixed when the copy leaves the ratifier's power, not when his system made it — and T-745 applies it to the gap between leaving and arriving: a copy in transit has left the sender's desk but has not yet entered any keeping, and a thing in no keeping is in no one's dated record. Monday's export therefore proves nothing until Wednesday's receipt, and where the lump's filing falls between them, the mirror is a witness who had not yet arrived.

The first rule is receipt over export. The anchor date is the date the receiving keeping's own record shows the copy arriving — the keeper's file stamp, docket entry, intake log, or accession record — never the date the sender's system stamped on export. The reasoning is T-742's self-dated rule applied to the sender: an export stamp is a date the ratifier's own system wrote, and a system the ratifier controls writes whatever date he tells it to write. A receipt stamp, by contrast, is a date a hand that does not answer to him wrote in a keeping he does not control, and that is exactly T-743's outside anchor. Where export and receipt differ, the receipt date governs, even when the receipt is later: a copy exported Monday and receipted Wednesday anchors Wednesday, and a notation it carries re-dates, if at all, at Wednesday. Where the receipt stamp is itself the sender's own notation — a "received" mark written by the sender on his own copy, a self-stamped intake sheet — it is not a receipt at all; it is a self-dated notation under T-742, and the mirror waits for a genuine keeper's record. The test for a receipt is whose record it is, not what word it bears.

The second rule is the transit gap. Between export and receipt the copy proves nothing, because during that interval it is in no keeping: not yet in the keeper's, no longer evidenced in the sender's. A lump filed during the gap gets no re-date from that mirror, even when export predates the lump. This is the hard case, and the rule is deliberately hard: a sender who exported before the lump but whose copy arrived after it has shown, at most, his own pre-lump intention to mirror, and intention is not a keeping. During transit the sender, or a carrier who answers to him, could still rewrite the copy; the copy that arrives Wednesday may not be the copy exported Monday, and no paper in the interval proves it is the same. The mirror is therefore a late mirror under T-744 — proving contents at receipt, not the notation's date at filing — and the notation stays self-dated-only. Transit is not a defect in the mirror; it is a period in which the mirror does not yet exist as evidence.

The third rule is the handover exception, and its sealed-chain form. Where export IS handover — the sender hands the copy directly to an independent keeper, and the keeper dates the handover in the keeper's own record — export and receipt coincide, and there is no gap to rule on: the handover date is the receipt date, and the mirror anchors there. A mere carrier is not a keeper for this rule: a carrier moves the copy, a keeper keeps it, and a waybill dates movement, not keeping. But a sealed, dated, unbroken carrier chain from handover to filing preserves the handover anchor: where the copy was sealed at handover, each transfer dated in a record outside the ratifier's reach, and the seal arrives unbroken, the chain is continuous keeping from handover, and the anchor stays at handover. A break in the chain — an undated transfer, a broken seal, a carrier who answers to the ratifier — reopens the gap, and the anchor falls to the next independent receipt after the break. The chain must be shown, not asserted: a claim of sealing without the seal's papers is an unshown cadence under T-744, a single mirror at receipt.

The fourth rule is the publication exception. Where export is publication — a hash published, a ledger entry made, a filing in a public record open to any reader — publication is receipt by the public at large, and the anchor is the publication date, with no transit gap at all. Publication differs from posting because publication itself is the outside keeping: the copy is not travelling toward a keeping, it is already in one that the ratifier cannot rewrite, namely the public record. A hash published Monday anchors Monday even though no keeper receipted it, because any reader could have captured it Monday and the ratifier could not have recalled it Tuesday. Private posting to a single addressee is not publication; it is export toward a receipt, and the receipt rule governs. The line is whether the export itself placed the copy beyond recall, not whether many people saw it.

The fifth rule is that a carrier's stamp is not a receipt. A stamp by a carrier who answers to the ratifier — his employee, his contractor, his own mailroom — is the ratifier's own mark, not an outside anchor, and the mirror waits for the independent keeper's stamp. A stamp by a carrier independent of the ratifier but who merely transports is evidence of movement, not of keeping: it dates the copy's transit, and transit proves nothing under the second rule. The carrier's stamp becomes evidence only where it is part of a sealed chain under the third rule, or where the carrier is itself the keeper because it holds the copy in its own dated keeping rather than passing it on. In every case the question is T-743's control test, asked of the stamper: does this hand answer to the ratifier, and does this keeping live outside his rewrite power? A stamp that fails that test is a controlled-system mark with a date attached, and it anchors nothing at any date.

The sixth rule is the disputed date. Where the stamps conflict — a receipt stamp predating the export stamp, an export stamp later than the receipt it supposedly precedes, clocks disagreeing between sender and keeper — the mirror's date is disputed, and a disputed mirror anchors nothing until a third paper resolves it: the keeper's intake log, a hash chain over the mirror's contents, a publication record. If the third paper dates the receipt, that date anchors; if it dates only the export, the receipt rule still governs and the mirror waits for a receipt. If no third paper resolves the conflict, the mirror anchors nothing, and the notation it carries stays self-dated-only. A disputed date is not a false paper: falsity needs a showing the stamp was forged, judged under T-737, while dispute needs only contradiction on the papers. The burden stays on the amender throughout: a mirror whose date the papers contradict is the amender's problem, not the checker's, and honest failure costs nothing but time.

The Transit Gap — the interval between export and receipt, in which the copy is in no keeping and proves nothing. **T-746 — the Receipt-Authenticity Rule — designed:** T-745 left its receipt-forgery problem named and open: whether a receipt stamp is proved genuine at all — what distinguishes a keeper's genuine receipt from a forged stamp, or a keeper's rubber stamp kept in the ratifier's pocket, short of a T-737 falsity showing. T-746 answers: a receipt is proved by its keeping, not by its face. A stamp proves nothing about itself; what proves a receipt is that the keeper's own books, the keeper's custody of the instrument, or a second independent paper says so. The face of a stamp is ink, and ink can be bought, borrowed, or pocketed. T-745 fixed which date governs when export and receipt differ; T-746 fixes whether the receipt stamp is the keeper's at all. A stamp can be receipt-dated and still unproved, and keeper-proved and still late — date and genuineness are separate questions, and either failure alone leaves the notation self-dated-only.

The first rule is the keeper's book. A receipt counts as the keeper's when the keeper's own continuous record shows it: an intake log, a docket run, an accession register, in sequence with its neighbours. A stamp standing alone on the copy, with no entry in the keeper's books, is a mark without a keeping — it wears the keeper's face and has no keeper behind it, and it anchors nothing. The book need not name the notation's contents — T-742's sealed-envelope line still holds, existence-dating is not content-proof — but it must show the copy arriving, on the receipt's date, in the keeper's keeping. A book entry that names the copy by description only — "the Monday note" with no title, no paper named — carries T-742's identification problem with it, and is judged there; the book proves arrival, identification is a separate showing.

The second rule is the instrument's custody. The die, seal, signature plate, or server key that struck the receipt must be shown in the keeper's custody at the receipt date. A keeper's rubber stamp kept in the ratifier's pocket is the ratifier's mark whatever face it bears — the pocket defeats the stamp. And this needs no falsity showing: falsity under T-737 needs proof the stamp was forged, while custody failure needs only proof the instrument was in the wrong hands, and the receipt falls to unproved, not to false. An unproved receipt is not a false paper and carries no forfeiture; it simply anchors nothing, and the notation stays self-dated-only. The distinction matters because the remedies differ: a false paper is judged, quarantined, and may forfeit; an unproved receipt is merely set aside, and the amender may still prove the receipt another way — by the book, by a second paper — without ever answering a charge of forgery.

The third rule is the second paper. Where the keeper's books are silent and custody is unshown, a second independent paper can carry the receipt: a contemporaneous notice to a third party naming the filing, a publication record, a hash published at receipt. But a second paper from the ratifier's own hand, or from a hand that answers to him, carries nothing — it is the same hand twice, and two self-dated marks do not make an outside one. The second paper must itself pass T-743's control test: a keeping outside the ratifier's rewrite power, a hand that does not answer to him. A second paper that merely repeats the stamp's date — a copy of the receipt, a letter quoting the receipt — is the stamp echoing itself, and an echo is not corroboration.

The fourth rule is that a re-stamp does not re-date. A keeper's fresh stamp on an old copy, struck after the lump, proves the copy was in the keeper's hands on the re-stamp date, not on the original receipt date; the book's entry, if any, governs the original date, and without one the re-stamp is a new receipt at the new date — a late mirror under T-744, proving contents at receipt, not the notation's date at filing. A re-stamp offered as proof of the original receipt is a receipt offered for a date it does not bear, and it is judged as the new receipt it is. The amender who re-stamps after the lump has shown diligence, not contemporaneity, and diligence after the fact is not a keeping before it.

The fifth rule is the burden, and it stays on the amender throughout. A receipt whose genuineness the papers do not show is the amender's problem, not the checker's, and honest failure costs nothing but time: the receipt is set aside, the notation stays self-dated-only, and the amender may return with a book entry, a custody showing, or a second paper. The checker need not prove the stamp forged, the keeper compromised, or the book cooked; the amender must prove the receipt genuine, by one of the three showings above, or the receipt does no work. A rule that put the burden the other way — a stamp genuine until disproved — would let every pocketed die pass, because disproof of a stamp's genuineness is exactly the forgery showing T-737 already found hard, and T-746 exists so that hard showing is not the only gate.

**The named forms**, all to T-289: the Lone Stamp — a receipt stamp standing alone on the copy, with no entry in the keeper's books; a mark without a keeping, anchoring nothing. The Pocket Die — a keeper's instrument kept in the ratifier's pocket, or in any hands that answer to him; the stamp it strikes is the ratifier's mark whatever face it bears. The Keeper's Book — the keeper's own continuous record showing the copy arriving, in sequence with its neighbours; the showing that proves a receipt. The Second Paper — a contemporaneous independent paper naming the filing, carrying a receipt the books do not show; a paper from the ratifier's own hand is an echo, not a second paper. The Unproved Receipt — a receipt that fails all three showings: not false, not judged, merely set aside, anchoring nothing. The Re-Stamp — a keeper's fresh stamp on an old copy, a new receipt at the new date, never proof of the original receipt's date.

**The grades.** KEEPER-PROVED — a receipt shown in the keeper's own books, or by custody of the instrument, or carried by a second independent paper; the receipt does its work, and T-745 then fixes its date. UNPROVED-RECEIPT — a receipt failing all three showings; set aside, not false, carrying no forfeiture, and the notation it carries stays self-dated-only. CUSTODY-FAILED — a receipt struck by an instrument shown in the ratifier's keeping or in hands that answer to him; the pocket defeats the stamp without any forgery showing. SECOND-PAPER-CARRIED — a receipt the books do not show, carried by a contemporaneous independent paper that itself passes T-743's control test. RE-STAMPED — a fresh stamp on an old copy, a new receipt at the new date, late if after the lump.

**T-747 — the Book-Independence Rule — designed:** T-746 left its book-forgery problem named and open: whether a keeper's book the ratifier could write in — a shared register, a clerk who answers to him — counts as the keeper's books at all, or whether the book needs its own independence showing. T-747 answers: the book needs its own independence showing, and a book the ratifier could write in is not the keeper's books until that showing is made. A book entry proves a receipt only when the book itself is shown independent of the hand that needs it; otherwise the entry is the ratifier's paper wearing a keeper's cover, and T-746's first rule is not satisfied by it. T-746 fixed how a receipt is proved — by its keeping, not its face; T-747 fixes when a keeping counts as the keeper's at all.

The first rule is that access is judged at the entry's date, not at filing and not at challenge. A book counts as independent for an entry only if, on the date that entry was made, the ratifier had no write access to the book — no login that could edit, no clerk who would edit on his word, no shared page he could amend. Access later revoked does not retroactively purify an entry made while he could write; access later gained does not taint an entry made while he could not. The date that matters is the date the ink — or the row — landed.

The second rule is that a shared register is segregated entry by entry, never as a whole. An entry in the ratifier's own hand, under his login, or in a hand that answers to him is his paper, not the keeper's, however official the binding. An entry by another hand in the same book counts only when that hand's independence is shown — a keeper's clerk, a disinterested office, a hand with no direction from the ratifier. The book's cover proves nothing; each entry carries its own hand, and the hand carries the entry.

The third rule is that a clerk who answers to the ratifier is the ratifier's hand. Direction, employment, instruction, or a reporting line to the ratifier defeats the entry, even if the clerk's title sits in the keeper's office and even if the clerk acted without a specific order on that entry — a standing direction is direction enough. A clerk who answers to the keeper's office, and to no line running to the ratifier, counts as the keeper's hand. Dual reporting — a clerk answering to both offices — is carried below as an open problem, not presumed either way.

The fourth rule is that tamper-evidence rescues existence, never authorship. A gapless sequence, a hash chain, or a mirror predating the lump can show an entry existed on a date and was not inserted later — that is T-744's work, and it stands — but it does not show whose hand made it. A ratifier-written entry, perfectly sequenced and faithfully mirrored, is still the ratifier's paper, proved to have existed, not proved to be the keeper's. Sequence proves the book was not cooked after the fact; it does not prove the book was independent before it.

The fifth rule is the burden, and it stays on the amender throughout. A book whose independence the papers do not show is the amender's problem, not the checker's, and honest failure costs nothing but time: the entry is set aside, the receipt falls back to T-746's other two showings — custody of the instrument, or a second independent paper — and the amender may return with an access log, a clerk's reporting line, or a segregation showing. The checker need not prove the ratifier wrote the entry, directed the clerk, or cooked the book; the amender must prove the book independent, or the entry does no work.

**The named forms**, all to T-289: the Shared Register — a book both keeper and ratifier could write in, whose entries must be segregated hand by hand before any counts. The Borrowed Pen — a keeper's clerk who answers to the ratifier, whose entries are the ratifier's paper in a keeper's hand. The Mirror-Bound Book — a shared book whose sequence and mirror prove an entry existed, but not whose hand made it. The After-Hours Entry — an entry dated while the ratifier held write access, later defended by revoked access; access at challenge proves nothing about access at entry.

**The grades.** BOOK-PROVED — an entry in a book shown independent of the ratifier at the entry's date, by access separation, hand independence, or both; the entry does T-746's book work. BOOK-SHARED — an entry in a book the ratifier could write in, independence unshown; the entry is set aside, not voided, and may be carried by custody or a second paper. RATIFIER-HAND — an entry shown made by the ratifier's own hand or a hand answering to him; the entry is his paper, and it cannot do keeper's work however well sequenced.

**T-748 — the Effective-Write Rule — designed:** T-747 left its edit-by-request problem named and open: whether a ratifier with read access only, who could get a clerk to edit on his word, counts as having write access, or whether only direct write access defeats the book. T-748 answers: indirect write is write. The test is effective direction power, not the credential on the login. A ratifier who could cause an edit by asking held write access at the entry's date, whether or not his name appears on an account, a key, or a permissions list; a ratifier who genuinely could only read, and whose word moved no clerk, held read access only. T-747 fixed when a book counts as the keeper's at all — by access at the entry's date and by hand independence; T-748 fixes what counts as access, and closes the read-only loophole before it opens.

The first rule is that a channel is access. If, on the entry's date, the ratifier could get the book changed by asking — a standing direction to the clerk, a reporting line the clerk obeys, a custom of compliance, a request the clerk had no realistic refusal for — then he held write access, and the book fails T-747's first rule for that entry. The credential proves nothing by itself: a read-only login beside an obedient clerk is a write login with extra steps, and a write login never used is still write access. What matters is whether his word could move the ink, not which account moved it.

The second rule is that a single complied request proves a channel only with a standing direction behind it, and a single refused request proves nothing at all. One favour from a truly independent clerk — a correction the clerk judged on its own merits, freely adopted, freely refuseable — is not a channel; it is a clerk's own act, and the entry stands or falls on the clerk's hand under T-747. But a request made under a standing direction, a pattern of past compliance, or a clerk who answers to the ratifier is a channel even if that particular request was never made — the power, not the exercise, is the access. Conversely, a refused request does not purify the book: a channel that failed once, or a clerk who refused this time, leaves the standing power intact, and the next entry under that power is still ratifier-reachable. Refusal is evidence about one request, not a revocation of the channel.

The third rule is that the channel, like direct access, is judged at the entry's date. A channel opened after the entry does not taint it; a channel closed before the entry does not taint it either — but a channel closed after the entry, or a clerk's obedience that lapsed only once the papers were challenged, leaves the entry exactly where it was: made while the ratifier's word could move the book. The date that matters is still the date the ink landed, and the question is still who could have moved it then.

The fourth rule is that an edit made at the ratifier's request is a ratifier-hand entry under T-747, whatever the clerk's title. The clerk's hand on the page does not launder the ratifier's direction: the entry is his paper in a keeper's hand, and it cannot do keeper's work however well sequenced or mirrored. A clerk's own correction — suggested, even, by the ratifier, but adopted on the clerk's independent judgment where refusal carried no cost — stays the clerk's entry, judged on the clerk's hand. The line is direction, not contact: a suggestion the clerk could freely refuse is contact; a word the clerk could not freely refuse is direction.

The fifth rule is the burden, and it stays on the amender throughout, as in T-747. A read-only login alone is never a showing of read-only access; the amender must show no channel — no standing direction, no reporting line, no custom of compliance, no clerk answering to the ratifier — or show the entry was the clerk's own act under the fourth rule. Honest failure costs nothing but time: the entry is set aside, the receipt falls back to T-746's other two showings — custody of the instrument, or a second independent paper — and the amender may return with an access log, a clerk's reporting line, or a channel-negating paper. The checker need not prove the ratifier asked, directed, or obtained an edit; the amender must prove his word could not have moved the book, or the entry does no work.

**The named forms**, all to T-289: the Whispered Edit — an entry changed on the ratifier's word by a clerk whose login, not his, touched the book; the channel is the access. The Standing Order — a direction given once and obeyed ever after, a channel even for entries where no fresh request was made. The Refused Request — a single refusal offered as purification; it proves one request failed, not that the channel closed. The Free Correction — a clerk's own correction, freely adopted and freely refuseable, which stays the clerk's entry however the suggestion arrived. The Borrowed Login — a clerk who logs in and edits while the ratifier stands behind the chair; direct write wearing another name, judged here as channel and there as hand.

**The grades.** EFFECTIVE-WRITE — a ratifier shown able, at the entry's date, to move the book by asking, by standing direction, reporting line, or custom of compliance; the entry is set aside as ratifier-reachable. READ-ONLY — a ratifier shown genuinely unable to move the book at the entry's date, no channel and no credential; the book-proved path under T-747 stays open. REQUEST-CHANNEL — the middle finding, a channel shown but the entry's own hand unshown: the entry is set aside, not voided, and may be carried by custody or a second paper.

**Distinguished from the chain it answers.** From T-747's Book-Independence Rule (the book — there the question was whether a book the ratifier could write in counts as the keeper's at all, and direct write access was the assumed form; here the question is prior to the credential, what counts as write access when the hand on the login is not the hand that wanted the edit). From T-747's third rule, the clerk-answering-to-the-ratifier rule (the hand — there a clerk answering to the ratifier was the ratifier's hand for entries the clerk made; here the same direction power defeats the book even for entries another hand made, because the ratifier could have had them changed). From T-743's Controlled-System Mark Rule (the system — there rewrite power over a system mark was judged by anchoring outside that power; here direction power over a book's clerk is judged the same way, but a book's entries have hands, and a channel through a hand is still a hand).

**What this pairs with.** T-747's Book-Independence Rule (the gate this rule widens — a book proved independent there must now also survive the channel test here; a channel shown here sends the entry to custody or a second paper). T-746's Receipt-Authenticity Rule (the proof — a set-aside entry falls back to custody of the instrument or a second independent paper, never to the book alone). T-745's Mirror-Receipt Rule (the date — a channel judged at the entry's date, never at filing or challenge, dates with the receipt it gates).

*T-748 trick seeded 2026-10-28 ~06:2x PDT by the decoder-create-loop.*

**T-749 — the Free-Adoption Rule — designed:** T-748 left its suggestion-direction problem named and open: whether a suggestion the clerk freely adopted, on independent judgment, can ever be told apart on the papers from a direction the clerk could not refuse, or whether the distinction collapses whenever the papers show only that the ratifier spoke and the clerk acted. T-749 answers: the distinction survives, but never on the act alone. Spoke-and-acted, with nothing more, is direction for the purposes of T-748 — the papers must carry a clerk-side mark of independent judgment, or the entry is set aside as ratifier-reachable. T-748 drew the line between direction and contact; T-749 fixes how that line is proved when the only paper is the act itself.

The first rule is that the act proves nothing about freedom. That the ratifier spoke and the clerk then acted shows contact and sequence, and sequence is not adoption. A clerk who obeyed and a clerk who agreed look identical from the outside: same words from the ratifier, same ink from the clerk, same entry in the book. The checker is not required to find a paper proving compulsion, and the amender is not saved by the absence of one. Where the record holds only the suggestion and the act, the entry is graded as direction under T-748, set aside, and left to T-746's fallbacks — custody of the instrument, or a second independent paper. The collapse the problem feared is real, but it collapses against the amender, not for him.

The second rule is that only a clerk-side paper, contemporaneous with the act and independent of the ratifier's hand, rescues the entry as free adoption. The paper must come from the clerk's side of the desk and must predate challenge: a clerk's own notation giving reasons the ratifier never gave, a clerk's working paper showing a source the ratifier never named, a clerk's alteration of the substance — not the spelling — of what the ratifier proposed, or a clerk's partial adoption that kept one part and refused another on stated grounds. Each of these shows a mind at work between the suggestion and the ink, and that interval is the adoption. A notation in the ratifier's hand, a clerk's bare signature, a clerk's later affidavit recalling independence, or a clerk's routine initialling of a prepared entry shows no interval at all, and none of them rescues anything.

The third rule is that a pattern of refusal, shown on the papers, is itself a clerk-side paper. A clerk who refused the ratifier before — refused a like request, refused this request in part, refused on a stated ground the ratifier did not supply — has shown, on the record, that refusal was a live option for him. One refusal does not prove this entry was free, but a refusal history changes what spoke-and-acted means: the clerk is no longer a hand that always moves when spoken to, and the entry may be judged on its own clerk-side marks rather than presumed direction. A clerk with no refusal on the record, and no clerk-side paper for this entry, has shown neither freedom nor compulsion — and under the first rule, that silence is graded as direction, not as neutrality.

The fourth rule is that adoption is graded per entry, and partial adoption splits the entry, not the rule. Where the clerk adopted part of the suggestion and refused or altered the rest on stated grounds, the adopted part is the clerk's only if the clerk-side paper covers that part — a reasoned refusal of one clause does not free-adopt the clause the clerk copied whole. Where the clerk's paper covers the whole substance, the whole entry stands as the clerk's; where it covers only a passage, only that passage stands, and the rest falls to T-746's fallbacks. Adoption cannot be borrowed across passages, and a free mind on one line does not prove a free mind on the next.

The fifth rule is the burden, and it stays on the amender throughout, as in T-748. The amender must produce the clerk-side paper — the notation, the working paper, the alteration, the refusal history — or the entry is set aside. Honest failure costs nothing but time: the entry is not voided, the receipt is not lost, and the amender may return with a clerk-side paper, a custody showing, or a second paper. The checker need not prove the clerk felt compelled, was threatened, or could not refuse; the amender must prove the clerk's judgment stood between the suggestion and the ink, or the entry does no keeper's work.

**The named forms**, all to T-289: the Bare Sequence — ratifier spoke, clerk acted, nothing between; graded direction, set aside. The Reasoned Notation — a clerk's contemporaneous note giving reasons the ratifier never gave; the interval made visible, adoption proved. The Altered Substance — a clerk who changed what the ratifier proposed, not merely its spelling, and left the change on the paper; a mind, not a hand. The Partial Keeper — a clerk who kept one part and refused another on stated grounds; the kept part stands only where the grounds cover it. The Recalled Freedom — a clerk's later affidavit swearing he acted freely; memory after challenge, proving nothing the papers do not already show. The Silent Clerk — a clerk with no refusal history and no paper of his own; silence graded as direction, not as neutrality.

**The grades.** FREE-ADOPTION — an entry carried by a contemporaneous clerk-side paper showing independent judgment between suggestion and ink; the entry stands as the clerk's under T-748's fourth rule. DIRECTION-PRESUMED — spoke-and-acted with no clerk-side paper and no refusal history; the entry is set aside as ratifier-reachable, not voided, and may be carried by custody or a second paper. SPLIT-ADOPTION — partial adoption on stated grounds; each passage stands or falls on whether the clerk-side paper covers it.

**Distinguished from the chain it answers.** From T-748's Effective-Write Rule (the channel — there a ratifier who could move the book by asking held write access, and a freely adopted correction stayed the clerk's; here the question is evidentiary, how free adoption is proved when the papers show only that the ratifier spoke and the clerk acted, and the answer is that it is proved only by a clerk-side paper). From T-748's second rule, the single-complied-request rule (the favour — there one favour from an independent clerk was not a channel; here the favour's independence must itself be shown, and a single compliance with no clerk-side paper is not a shown favour but a presumed direction). From T-747's Book-Independence Rule (the hand — there a clerk answering to the ratifier was the ratifier's hand; here a clerk answering to no one, but leaving no paper of his own, is graded the same way for this entry, because an unshown freedom is no freedom the record can use).

**What this pairs with.** T-748's Effective-Write Rule (the line this rule proves — direction versus contact, now with an evidentiary test instead of a bare distinction). T-746's Receipt-Authenticity Rule (the fallback — a direction-presumed entry falls back to custody of the instrument or a second independent paper, never to the book alone). T-742's Self-Dated Paper Rule (the paper test — there a notation needed an outside mark to fix its date; here a clerk's notation needs a clerk-side mark to fix its freedom, and a ratifier's mark fixes neither).
