**T-750 — the Dictated-Notation Rule — designed:** T-749 left its dictated-notation problem named and open: whether a clerk-side notation in the clerk's hand but dictated by the ratifier — the ratifier's words in the clerk's ink — counts as a clerk-side paper at all, or whether dictation defeats the paper however it is written. T-750 answers: dictation defeats the paper as clerk-side proof, passage by passage, but the defeat is evidentiary, not moral. Ink proves a scribe, never a judge. A notation the ratifier dictated earns nothing under T-749, however clean the clerk's handwriting; what the clerk added on his own, where it can be separated from what was dictated, still earns what T-749 always let it earn.

The first rule is that hand is not mind. T-749 rescued an entry only where a clerk-side paper showed a mind at work between the suggestion and the ink — reasons the ratifier never gave, a source the ratifier never named, a substantive alteration, a partial adoption on stated grounds. Dictation supplies none of these: the interval between suggestion and ink collapses to zero, because the suggestion IS the ink, spoken first and written second. A clerk who took dictation faithfully did his job well and his judgment not at all; accuracy in transcription is a virtue of a scribe, not evidence of a judge. The notation therefore counts, for T-749's purposes, as the ratifier's paper wearing the clerk's ink — usable for anything a ratifier-side paper can carry, useless for the one thing only a clerk-side paper can carry, which is the clerk's independent judgment.

The second rule is that dictation must be shown, not presumed — but a matching draft shifts the burden hard. The mere possibility that the ratifier dictated a notation defeats nothing; clerks write in their own words every day, and a checker who cries dictation without a paper is asking the amender to prove a negative. Dictation is shown by a paper: the ratifier's draft matching the notation in substance, a contemporaneous mark on the notation itself ("as dictated," "per instructions," "taken down"), the clerk's own admission that he wrote to dictation, or the ratifier's own claim of dictation. Where such a paper exists and the notation matches the ratifier's draft in substance, the notation is presumed dictated in full, and the amender must show a clerk-side divergence — a passage the draft does not contain, a reason the draft never gave — or the whole notation falls. The presumption is rebuttable passage by passage, never by a general oath that the clerk "usually" wrote freely.

The third rule is severance: dictation defeats passage by passage, not notation by notation. Where a notation mixes dictated passages with clerk-added substance — the ratifier's words followed by the clerk's own reason, a dictated frame holding a clerk-chosen example, a dictated conclusion with a clerk-supplied ground — the dictated passages fall and the clerk passages stand, but only where the clerk passages are separable: a reader of the papers alone must be able to say which words are the clerk's without asking either man. Where the blend is inseparable — the ratifier's reasons restated in the clerk's words, the same ground in a different sentence, a paraphrase that adds synonyms but no substance — the whole passage falls, because there is no clerk passage to sever, only a clerk voice repeating a ratifier thought. Severance is judged on the papers, not on the clerk's later account of what he meant to add.

The fourth rule is that a dictated notation, once set aside, is set aside and not voided, and that a later free paper cures forward only. The entry falls back exactly as a direction-presumed entry falls back under T-749 — to T-746's custody of the instrument or a second independent paper — and the dictated notation itself remains in the record as a ratifier-side paper, proving what the ratifier said, which is sometimes worth proving. A clerk who later writes a free paper re-adopting the same substance on stated grounds of his own rescues the entry from that later paper's date, not from the dictated notation's date: the later paper is a new clerk-side showing, not a retroactive un-dictation of the old one. Backdating the rescue to the dictation would let the ratifier's words borrow the clerk's later freedom, which is the same fraud in reverse.

The fifth rule is the burden, and it stays on the amender throughout, as in T-748 and T-749. The amender must show either that the notation was not dictated — no matching draft, no dictation mark, no admission, and a clerk-side divergence the papers themselves display — or that a separable clerk passage survives inside it. Honest failure costs nothing but time: the notation is not struck, the entry is not voided, and the amender may return with a custody showing, a second paper, or a later free re-adoption. The checker need not prove the clerk felt dictated to, was ordered, or could not refuse; where a matching draft exists, the checker need prove only the match, and the amender must prove the mind.

**The named forms**, all to T-289: the Verbatim Copy — the ratifier's draft in the clerk's ink, word for word; dictation proved, nothing clerk-side survives. The Scribe's Hand — a clerk who took the words down willingly and accurately; willingness to transcribe is not freedom of judgment, and the notation earns nothing under T-749. The Separable Addition — a dictated frame holding a clerk-chosen reason the draft never gave; the frame falls, the reason stands. The Inseparable Blend — the ratifier's ground restated in the clerk's words with no new substance; no passage to sever, the whole falls. The Matched Draft — a ratifier draft matching the notation in substance, raising the presumption of dictation for the whole notation until a clerk divergence is shown. The Re-adopted Substance — a later free clerk paper restating the same substance on the clerk's own stated grounds; rescue from the later date only, never retroactive.

**The grades.** DICTATED — a notation shown dictated, in whole or in the passage judged; it earns nothing as a clerk-side paper under T-749, is set aside not voided, and falls back to custody or a second paper. SPLIT-DICTATION — a mixed notation; dictated passages fall, separable clerk passages stand as the clerk's. CLERK-FRAMED — a notation shown not dictated, by absence of any dictation paper plus a clerk-side divergence the papers display; it stands as a clerk-side paper under T-749.

**Distinguished from the chain it answers.** From T-749's Reasoned Notation (there reasons the ratifier never gave proved a mind at work; here reasons the ratifier gave first, repeated in the clerk's ink, prove only a hand at work, and the difference between the two forms is whether the ratifier's draft contains the reason). From T-747's Book-Independence Rule (there a clerk answering to the ratifier was the ratifier's hand by office; here the clerk answers to no one and the hand is genuinely his, but the words are the ratifier's — office does not matter, authorship does, and a free hand writing another man's words is still another man's paper). From T-749's Altered Substance (there a clerk who changed what was proposed showed a mind; here a clerk who first took dictation and then altered it rescues only the altered passage, and the alteration must itself be substantive and separable, not a rewording of the dictated ground). From T-736's reader-aid question (there a third reader reading aloud added no hand to the search; here the clerk's hand adds ink but no judgment, and ink without judgment is the same nullity as voice without judgment).

**What this pairs with.** T-749's Free-Adoption Rule (the test this rule sharpens — a clerk-side paper must be the clerk's in words as well as in ink, or it is no clerk-side paper). T-748's Effective-Write Rule (the channel — a dictated notation is also evidence that the ratifier could move the clerk's pen by speaking, but dictation of one notation alone does not prove a standing channel; it proves one act, and the channel still needs its own showing). *T-750 trick seeded 2026-10-28 ~07:0x PDT by the decoder-create-loop.*


**T-751 — the Verified-Facts Rule — designed:** T-750 left its dictated-facts problem named and open: whether dictation of bare facts the clerk himself verified defeats the notation the way dictation of reasons does, or whether a clerk who checked the facts supplies the judgment the dictation lacks. T-751 answers: verification rescues facts, never reasons. A dictated fact the clerk independently checked stands as the clerk's; a dictated reason built on that fact, however well checked the fact, still falls as dictated. Facts are checkable and checking is a mind at work; reasons are judgment and no amount of fact-checking supplies a judgment never made.

The first rule is the fact/reason line, drawn on the papers, not on the clerk's intent. A fact is a proposition the papers can settle by a source outside the ratifier's draft: a date, a sum, a name, a count, a location. A reason is a proposition that connects facts to a conclusion: why this entry follows, why that paper matters, why the finding holds. The clerk who verifies a dictated date against the ledger has done clerk-side work on that date; the clerk who then writes down the ratifier's dictated reason why the date matters has done no clerk-side work on the reason, however accurate the date. Verification travels with the proposition verified and no further. A checker who lets a verified fact carry an unverified reason has let the ratifier's judgment ride in on the clerk's diligence, which is dictation with a cleaner conscience.

The second rule is that verification must be shown, not sworn. A clerk's later oath that he "checked it" earns nothing, for the same reason T-749's general oath of usual freedom earned nothing: the papers must display the check. A shown check is a clerk-side mark naming the source the clerk consulted — a source the ratifier's draft never named — together with either a match or a correction: the ledger folio, the second register, the instrument itself, the witness the clerk sought out. Where the notation names no source outside the draft, or names only the draft, the fact is an unchecked copy however true it happens to be; truth is not judgment, and a fact can be true and still dictated. The source must be independent of the ratifier's paper: a source the ratifier supplied and the clerk merely re-read is the draft wearing a second cover, not a check.

The third rule is that correction proves verification outright, and match proves it only with the source shown. Where the clerk's notation corrects the dictated fact — a different date, a corrected sum, a name the draft misspelled and the notation sets right — the corrected passage stands as the clerk's without further showing, because no scribe taking dictation corrects his dictator by accident; the correction is itself the clerk-side divergence T-750 required, displayed on the papers. Where the clerk's notation matches the dictated fact exactly, the passage stands only if the checking paper shows the source and the match together: the notation, or a contemporaneous clerk-side paper, must say what was consulted and that it agreed. A bare "verified" scrawled beside a matching fact is not a shown check; it is an oath in the margin, and oaths are what the papers are for replacing.

The fourth rule is severance, passage by passage, exactly as in T-750, with one asymmetry the checker must hold. A mixed notation severs into verified facts that stand, unchecked dictated facts that fall, and dictated reasons that fall whether or not their underlying facts were verified. The asymmetry cuts both ways and both cuts matter: a verified fact inside a dictated reason does not rescue the reason, and a dictated reason sitting beside a verified fact does not taint the fact. The entry that survives is the entry the clerk's own checking built — the facts he sourced, the corrections he made — and nothing the ratifier dictated rides along on their strength. **T-752 — the Shared-Source Rule — designed:** T-751 left its shared-source problem named and open: whether a check against a source the clerk and the ratifier consulted together — a shared ledger both men read — counts as an independent check, or whether independence requires a source the ratifier never touched. T-752 answers: a shared source can verify, but only on a showing of the clerk's own consultation. Independence lives in the act of consulting, not in the shelf the source sits on. A ledger both men read is not a check both men made; it is one source and, unless the papers show two consultations, one check at most — and the check it shows may be the ratifier's, not the clerk's.

The first rule is the shelf/act distinction, and it is the whole rule in miniature. T-751 required a source independent of the ratifier's paper; it did not require a source the ratifier never saw, and T-752 refuses to add that requirement. A public register, a house ledger, a second book kept for all hands — these are shared by design, and a rule that disqualified every source the ratifier had touched would disqualify every source worth checking, since the ratifier's business is the book. What the clerk must show is not a virgin source but his own consultation of it: that he went to the source himself, by his own route, for his own check, and found the fact there. Where the papers show that act, the shared shelf is irrelevant; where they show only that the source exists and the ratifier knew it, the clerk has shown a shelf, not a check.

The second rule is that the clerk's own consultation must be displayed, and a display has a shape. A shown consultation is a clerk-side mark tying the clerk to the source by his own hand: his folio note, his tick against the entry, his marginal mark in his ink, a sequence placing his consultation apart from the ratifier's presentation — a note dated before the notation, a folio the draft never cited, a correction the draft never contained. The ratifier's note that "we both looked" earns nothing, because it is ratifier-side paper proving, at most, that the ratifier looked and the clerk was present; presence is not consultation, and assent in the ratifier's presence is the weakest form of spoke-and-acted under T-749. A joint reading in which the clerk merely watched the ratifier turn pages is a dictated check wearing a shared cover, and T-752 grades it as no check at all.

The third rule sorts the three forms of sharing, because "shared" names three different acts and only the first two can verify. (a) **Common repository, independent consultations** — the clerk and the ratifier each went to the ledger on their own business, at their own times, and the clerk's consultation is marked as his own. This verifies fully: the source is shared, the checks are separate, and T-751's Verified Fact stands. (b) **Joint consultation** — both men at the ledger together, the ratifier present, perhaps speaking. This verifies passage by passage only: passages the clerk himself located, compared, or corrected verify, because his hand on the source is shown; passages the ratifier pointed out and the clerk merely assented to do not, because pointing is dictation by finger, and a finger on the entry is no more the clerk's check than a voice in his ear was the clerk's reason under T-750. (c) **Ratifier-mediated access** — the ratifier supplied the extract, opened the page, copied the folio, or read the entry aloud, and the clerk checked the copy. This is not a shared-source check at all; it is T-751's Second-Cover Source, re-reading the draft in another binding, and the passage falls however accurate the copy.

The fourth rule is contamination, and it bounds the whole rule from the source side. A shared source the ratifier himself authored, altered, or controls is no source at all for T-751's purposes, however independently the clerk consulted it: a clerk who diligently checks a dictated fact against the ratifier's own register has checked the ratifier against the ratifier, and diligence does not launder authorship. The consultation must be of a source independent of the ratifier's paper — a book the ratifier did not write, a register he did not keep, an instrument he did not make — and where the source's independence fails, the consultation's independence is moot. Likewise a consultation made only after challenge — a trip to the ledger the clerk takes once the entry is questioned — proves the fact true now, not that the clerk checked before he wrote; it can support a later free re-adoption under T-750's fourth rule, from the later paper's date, but it cannot retroactively verify the dictated notation, for the same reason a later free paper cannot un-dictate an old one.

The fifth rule is the burden, and it stays on the amender throughout, as in T-748, T-749, T-750, and T-751. **T-753 — the Silent-Presence Rule — designed:** T-752 left its silent-presence problem named and open: whether a joint consultation in which the clerk located the entry himself, but the ratifier stood present and silent, still verifies, or whether mere presence, without pointing or speaking, taints the finding the way a pointed finger does. T-753 answers: silence is not pointing, and presence is not pressure — but neither is presence a substitute for the locating act. A clerk who found the entry with his own hand verifies, however silently the ratifier watched; a clerk who merely stood in the room with the ratifier proves presence, not a check. The question was never whether the ratifier was there. It was always whether the clerk did anything while he was there.

The first rule is that dictation requires a directing act, and silence is the absence of one. T-750's dictation was a voice in the clerk's ear; T-752's pointing was a finger on the folio; both are acts that steer a hand to an answer. A ratifier who stands silent steers nothing: he supplies no words to copy, no finger to follow, no extract to re-read. To grade silent presence as dictation would be to grade the room as a dictator, and a room dictates nothing. The checker who claims taint from silence alone must show an act, and where no act is shown the presence is neutral paper — it proves the ratifier was there, which nobody disputed, and nothing else. The burden of showing a directing act stays on the challenger, exactly as the burden of showing the clerk's consultation stayed on the amender under T-752; burdens do not migrate because a man was standing nearby.

The second rule is that silence lowers nothing on the clerk's side. T-752 required a clerk-side mark of the clerk's own consultation, and T-753 keeps that requirement whole: the clerk must still show that he located the entry himself — his folio note, his tick against the entry, his marginal mark in his ink, a sequence placing his consultation apart from anything the ratifier could have led. Silent presence does not excuse the showing; it only removes the suspicion that the showing was led. A clerk who located the entry himself but left no mark of locating it is in exactly the position of T-752's Silent Assent: presence proved, checking not, and the passage falls back to custody or a second paper. The rule is generous to silence and strict about marks, because the record can use a mark and cannot use a memory of a quiet room.

The third rule is the presumption and its rebuttal, and it is where the rule earns its keep. Where the clerk's own locating is shown, silent presence is presumed neutral, and the passage verifies. The presumption is rebuttable, but only by a pressure showing on the papers — not by the bare fact of presence, and not by the ratifier's later claim that his silence was meaningful. A pressure showing is a pattern on the papers: a run of entries in which the clerk's notations track the ratifier's drafts exactly whenever the ratifier was present and diverge whenever he was absent; a clerk-side note, contemporaneous, recording that he felt watched or hurried; a prior pointed session after which the clerk's independent locating stopped. A single silent session, with a locating mark and no pattern, rebuts nothing. And the ratifier's later claim that he pointed, gestured, or silently directed earns nothing by itself, for the same reason T-752's ratifier-side "we both looked" earned nothing: ratifier-side paper cannot supply the directing act the papers never showed, and a claim of pointing made after the fact is a claim, not a finger.

The fourth rule is the asymmetry of credit, and it cuts against the ratifier. Where the clerk located the entry himself in the ratifier's silent presence, the passage stands as the clerk's even if the ratifier later claims the credit — the locating mark is clerk-side paper, and clerk-side paper outranks ratifier-side recollection wherever the two conflict, as T-750's denial-versus-draft problem already taught in the draft's favor. Conversely, where the clerk's locating is shown but the ratifier was not merely silent but silently present after a history of pointing — the trained-silence case — the passage does not automatically fall; it goes to the pressure showing of the third rule, and the history counts as part of that showing but not as proof of it. A history of pointing proves the ratifier knows how to point; it does not prove he pointed this time, and the checker must still tie the history to this passage — the same passage, the same hand, the same pattern — before the presumption gives way.

The fifth rule is severance, passage by passage, exactly as in T-750, T-751, and T-752, with the presumption applied per passage rather than per session. A joint session severs into passages the clerk located himself, which verify under the neutral-presence presumption; passages where the only showing is joint presence and a matching entry, which fall as unmarked; and passages where a pressure showing ties the ratifier's presence to the clerk's assent, which fall as pressured and are set aside, not voided. One session can hold all three grades at once — the clerk's hand on one folio, his silence on the next, his hurry on the third — and the checker grades the hand, not the room. A session-level verdict would let one verified passage launder an unmarked neighbor, or one pressured passage condemn a located one, and T-753 refuses both launderings.

**The named forms**, all to T-289: the Silent Witness — the ratifier present and silent, the clerk locating the entry with his own hand and marking it; it verifies. The Standing Shadow — silent presence plus a pressure showing on the papers, a pattern tying the ratifier's attendance to the clerk's assent; it falls as pressured, set aside, not voided. The Claimed Point — the ratifier's later claim that his silence directed, pointed, or meant something; ratifier-side paper, earns nothing. The Trained Silence — a silent session following a history of pointing, graded on its own pressure showing, neither presumed tainted by the history nor presumed clean by the silence.

**T-755 — the Freshness-Threshold Rule — designed:** T-754 left its freshness-threshold problem touched but not settled: a rehearsed tick that carries one small freshness sign — a corrected letter, a reordered folio — does it count as a hand of its own, or must the freshness touch the passage's substance? T-755 answers: freshness is graded by provenance, not by size. A sign counts when the training cannot explain it, however small it is; a sign fails when the training can explain it, however large it looks. The question was never how much ink the clerk added. It was always whether the ink could only have come from his own locating.

The first rule is the provenance test. The checker lays the silent session's mark beside the pointed sessions' marks and asks one question: could the training have produced this mark? A corrected letter the ratifier's finger used to correct, a folio order the pointing used to follow, a marginal phrase in the ratifier's own wording — all fail, because the trained hand produces exactly those. A corrected letter the pointed sessions always got wrong, a folio order the pointing never used, a divergence on a point the pointing never reached — all pass, because no rehearsal explains them. Size is irrelevant to the test: a single letter corrected against the training is a hand; a whole paragraph reworded in the ratifier's phrasing is a rehearsal. The checker grades the mark's origin, not its volume.

The second rule is substance by effect, not by topic. A surface sign can be substantive when it changes what the passage says, and a topical sign can be empty when it changes nothing. A reordered folio that puts the clerk's own source first changes the passage's foundation, and counts, though reordering looks like surface. A corrected letter that fixes a name the entry turns on changes the passage's subject, and counts, though a letter looks small. A long marginal note that restates the ratifier's draft in the clerk's handwriting changes nothing the passage asserts, and fails, though the note looks large. The checker asks what the sign does to the passage, not what kind of mark it is: a sign that moves the passage's ground, its subject, or its conclusion is substantive in effect, and a sign that moves only its presentation is not.

The third rule is the kept divergence. An accidental freshness sign — a slip the clerk then corrects back to the trained reading, a smudge, a misreading abandoned before the entry was made — is noise, not a hand, and earns nothing. A divergence the clerk keeps and stands behind — the correction left standing in the final entry, the order kept in the filed copy, the note carried into the next session's work — is a hand, and verifies the passage it touches. The difference is not the clerk's later testimony about what he meant; a later affidavit claiming intent is an oath in the margin, graded as T-753's after-mark problem already taught. The difference is on the papers: the kept sign survives into the filed entry, and the slip does not. A hand is shown by what it leaves standing, not by what it once touched.

The fourth rule is accumulation within the passage, never across it. Three surface signs, none substantive alone — a reordered folio, a respelled name that changes nothing, a tick in a new place — together show a hand choosing its own order, and the passage verifies, because a rehearsal repeats one pattern and a choosing hand varies it in several places at once. But accumulation stops at the passage's edge: small signs in one passage do not verify its neighbor, and a session full of small signs, each in a different passage, verifies only the passages that carry their own signs. T-754's severance holds here as it held there — a session-level freshness would let one choosing hand launder a rehearsed neighbor, and T-755 refuses that laundering. The checker counts signs passage by passage, and a passage with one genuine divergence needs no accumulation at all.

The fifth rule is the taught-correction exception, and it is the provenance test's sharp edge. Where the training itself taught corrections — the ratifier used to correct that very letter, to reorder those very folios, to supply that very phrasing — the same correction in the silent session proves nothing, however fresh it looks to a checker who has not read the pointed sessions. The exception cuts only where the pointed papers show the teaching: a correction the pointed sessions never show is not a taught correction because the checker suspects it might have been taught. **The named forms**, all to T-289: the Kept Correction — a divergence from the trained pattern, left standing in the filed entry, that the training cannot explain; it verifies. The Surface Tick — a small sign that changes only presentation, a respelling that changes nothing, a tick moved without moving the ground; it falls as unmarked. The Accidental Slip — a divergence corrected back to the trained reading before filing, a smudge, an abandoned misreading; it is noise, and the passage grades as if the slip never happened. The Accumulated Hand — three or more surface divergences in one passage, none substantive alone, varying the pattern in several places at once; it verifies that passage only. The Taught Correction — a correction the pointed sessions show the training itself taught; it proves rehearsal, not locating, and the passage falls as unmarked.

**The grades.** FRESH-VERIFIED — a trained-silence passage whose mark carries a divergence the training cannot explain, kept standing in the filed entry, or a passage whose accumulated surface signs together show a choosing hand; it stands as a clerk-side passage under T-749. FRESH-INSUFFICIENT — a trained-silence passage whose only sign changes presentation without moving ground, subject, or conclusion, or whose correction the pointed papers show the training taught; it is set aside, not voided, and falls back to custody or a second paper. **T-756 — the Accumulation-Weight Rule — designed:** T-755 left its accumulation-count problem touched but not settled: it set three surface signs as the floor for an Accumulated Hand, but never said whether two far-straying signs could count, or whether three near-identical signs should. T-756 answers: accumulation is weighted, not counted. A cluster verifies not when it holds enough signs, but when its signs together stray far enough, independently enough, from the trained pattern. The question was never how many marks the clerk made. It was always how much choosing those marks, taken together, prove.

The first rule is distance before number. Each kept surface sign is graded by how far it strays from the pointed sessions' pattern, and the grade is a weight, not a vote. A NEAR sign — a tick moved a hair, a respelling that matches a variant the pointing itself used, a folio order the ratifier once followed — strays so little that rehearsal explains it, and weighs 0: it adds nothing to any cluster, however many near signs pile up. A MEDIUM sign — a reordered pair the pointing never ordered that way, a tick in a place the pointing never put one, a name spelled in a form no pointed session shows — strays within a dimension the training exercised, and weighs 1. A FAR sign — a choice in a dimension the training never exercised at all, a new ordering principle rather than a new order, an annotation placed where no pointed session annotates — strays outside the training's dimensions, and weighs 2. The checker grades distance from the pointed papers, not impressiveness: a dramatic-looking sign that repeats a trained dimension is medium at best, and a quiet sign in an unexercised dimension is far.

The second rule is independence before addition. Signs in the same dimension collapse to one sign, at the highest weight among them. Three respellings of the same name are one spelling choice, not three signs; two reorderings of the same folio pair are one ordering choice; a tick moved twice in the same margin is one placement choice. A cluster accumulates only across dimensions — order, spelling, placement, phrasing, annotation — because a rehearsal that slips in one dimension slips repeatedly there, while a choosing hand varies its choices in several places at once. T-755's intuition survives here in stricter form: its three-sign floor was really a demand for variety, and T-756 states the demand outright. A cluster of three signs in one dimension weighs exactly what its best sign weighs, and no piling inside a dimension ever reaches the threshold.

The third rule is the threshold, and it is three — but three of weight, not three of signs. A passage verifies by accumulation when its collapsed, kept, untaught signs sum to weight 3 or more within that passage: one far sign plus one medium sign, three medium signs, or two far signs. Two medium signs sum to 2 and fall short, however clean they look — T-755's floor holds for the medium-only case, and two is not enough. One far sign alone sums to 2 and also falls short as accumulation, though it may still verify on its own substance under T-755's single-divergence rule; accumulation is a second road to verification, not a shortcut around substance. The threshold is deliberately reachable by two signs when one of them is far, because a far sign already proves a choice outside the training, and one medium companion proves the choice was not a lone slip. A lone far sign proves a choice; a far sign with company proves a choosing hand.

The fourth rule is that only kept, untaught signs weigh. A slip corrected back to the trained reading before filing weighs 0 under T-755's noise rule, and it does not enter the sum at all — a cluster cannot be padded with accidents. A taught correction — one the pointed papers show the training itself taught — weighs 0 and, worse, breaks the cluster's independence claim for its dimension: a dimension whose only sign is taught contributes nothing, and the checker recomputes the sum without it. Where the pointed-session marks survive only in part, the distance grade for signs touching the missing part cannot be run, and those signs weigh 0 for accumulation while the passage falls back to T-746's custody or a second paper — a missing comparison is not a failed comparison, but it is also not weight. The sum is computed only from signs the papers can actually grade.

The fifth rule is recomputation on challenge, and it is what makes the accumulated grade honest. A passage verified by accumulation is recorded as FRESH-ACCUMULATED under T-755, and the record must list the cluster: each sign, its dimension, its distance grade, and the sum. A later challenge to any one sign does not void the passage outright; it recomputes the sum without that sign, and the passage stands only while the recomputed sum still reaches 3. This is why the record lists dimensions, not just a total: a challenge that collapses two signs into one dimension recomputes differently from a challenge that removes a sign outright, and the checker must show which happened. A passage whose verification rests on a cluster is only as strong as its weakest sign's grade, and T-756 makes that weakness visible instead of hiding it behind a count.

The Collapsed Pair — two or more signs in one dimension, counting once at the highest weight among them; piling inside a dimension is repetition, not variety. The Weighted Cluster — collapsed, kept, untaught signs across at least two dimensions summing to weight 3 or more within one passage; it verifies that passage only.

**T-757 — the Partial-Comparison Rule — designed:** T-756 left its distance-calibration problem touched but not settled: it said that where the pointed-session marks survive only in part, the distance grade for signs touching the missing part cannot be run, but it never said who grades a sign far rather than medium on a partial record, or whether a partial comparison caps every touched sign at medium or merely narrows the dimensions that can be graded. T-757 answers: it does both, and the two readings are one mechanism at two levels. A partial comparison narrows dimensions — far is removed from every touched dimension's scale — and caps signs — each touched sign is held at medium-or-zero by what survives. The cap is not uniform, because a gap is not a grade: far is unavailable in any touched dimension, medium survives where the surviving record affirmatively shows the dimension exercised, and where the surviving record shows nothing of the dimension the sign is ungraded, not medium by default. A missing record can never prove a negative, and it can never serve as a base.

The first rule is the declared split, and no grade exists without it. Before any distance grade is issued, the checker lists every dimension the pointed sessions touch and marks each SURVIVING or TOUCHED. A dimension is surviving only if every pointed session's marks bearing on it survive whole and legible; one missing, partial, or illegible mark on that dimension touches the whole dimension, not just the mark. A dimension touched in one session is touched for the comparison, even if other sessions' marks on it survive complete. No sign is graded until the split is on the record, and a grade issued without a declared split is void, not weak — the checker who grades first and declares later has graded nothing, because the scale itself was undecided when the grade was issued.

The second rule is that far requires a complete negative. FAR, under T-756, means a choice in a dimension the training never exercised at all — a new ordering principle rather than a new order. To prove a dimension never exercised, the checker needs the complete training record: the missing part might exercise exactly that dimension, in exactly that form, and a record with a hole in it cannot certify what the hole contains. So no sign in a touched dimension can grade far, whatever it looks like. A dramatic new ordering principle in a touched dimension is capped, not celebrated — the gap, not the sign, decides. A quiet sign in a surviving dimension can still grade far, because there the complete record genuinely shows the dimension unexercised. Far is the only grade that asserts a negative about the whole training, and it is the only grade a gap defeats outright.

The third rule is that medium requires a surviving base. MEDIUM, under T-756, means the dimension was exercised but never in this form — a positive comparison with two halves, and both halves must come from surviving paper. In a touched dimension, a sign grades medium only if the surviving part affirmatively shows the dimension exercised in some form, and shows it never exercised in this form. If the surviving part shows nothing of the dimension at all — the dimension lives wholly in the missing part — the sign is ungraded and weighs 0. Ignorance is not a base: medium is not the default for a gap, and a checker who calls a sign medium "because nothing surviving contradicts it" has graded from absence, and the grade is void. The difference between medium and ungraded in a touched dimension is exactly whether the surviving record speaks about the dimension or is silent about it; silence weighs nothing, and speech in another form weighs one.

The fourth rule is that the cap is per sign and the narrowing is per dimension, and neither is a substitute for the other. The partial comparison narrows dimensions: far leaves the scale of every touched dimension, so no cluster can draw weight 2 from a touched dimension. It caps signs: each touched sign is held at medium-or-zero according to its surviving base, so no cluster can smuggle a far grade past the gap by calling it medium. A dimension with a surviving base still contributes weight-1 signs, and a cluster of medium signs across surviving and capped dimensions can still reach T-756's threshold of 3 — the cap lowers the ceiling, it does not empty the room. A dimension without a surviving base contributes nothing until recovery, and nothing about a gap ever adds weight: no sign, in no dimension, gains weight because part of the record is missing.

The fifth rule is who grades, and what the record must show. The checker grades, from the papers, never from a presumption about what the missing part contains. The record must list the split, each touched sign's cap, and the surviving base for every medium grade in a touched dimension — the marks, not a summary of them. The clerk's own note describing what the missing part contained is not a surviving paper: it is a claim about a paper, graded as an oath, and it cannot serve as a base for a medium grade or as evidence that a dimension is surviving. A grade whose base is a missing paper, or a note about one, is void, and a cluster sum that relied on a void grade recomputes without it. The checker does not fill gaps with the clerk's account of the gaps; the papers grade the papers, and where the papers stop, the grading stops with them.

The sixth rule is recomputation on challenge and on recovery, and it is what keeps the cap honest rather than merely cautious. A challenge that shows a dimension was touched, not surviving, recomputes the cluster: far grades in that dimension fall to medium-or-zero under the third rule, the sum is recomputed under T-756, and the passage stands only while the recomputed sum still reaches 3 across at least two dimensions. A recovered record re-grades fresh: capped signs may rise to far where the recovered part confirms the dimension unexercised, and a passage previously ACCUM-SHORT may verify on the recomputed sum — but forward only. Custody steps already taken on the strength of the old grade stand; recovery reopens the grade, not the history, in the same forward-only spirit as T-750's later free re-adoption and T-752's post-challenge consultation. Burden throughout: the party claiming far bears the burden of completeness, and a gap defeats far, never the passage. The party claiming medium in a touched dimension bears the burden of the surviving base, and no base means no weight. The passage is never punished for a gap: ungraded signs weigh 0, ignored, not counted against the clerk — T-756's "a missing comparison is not a failed comparison" survives here, sharpened into a procedure.

**The named forms**, all to T-289: the Declared Split — the checker's on-record surviving/touched list for every dimension the pointed sessions touch, without which no distance grade stands. **T-758 — the Partial-Legibility Rule — designed:** T-757 left its partial-legibility problem touched but not settled: it said a dimension is surviving only if every pointed-session mark bearing on it survives whole and legible, and one missing, partial, or illegible mark touches the whole dimension — but it never said whether a partially legible mark counts as surviving, touched, or a third state with its own cap. T-758 answers: a third state, graded mark by mark, and split by grade level. A partially legible mark is neither surviving nor touched. It is PARTLY-LEGIBLE: its form-bearing portion survives, its form-neutral portion is lost, and it grades differently for far than for medium — because far and medium ask different questions of the same mark, and a mark can answer one while failing the other.

The first rule is that the form-bearing portion decides the state. Every mark has a portion that bears its form — the ordering key, the spelling, the placement — and a portion that does not: the date, the margin, the hand's flourish. A mark is PARTLY-LEGIBLE only when the form-bearing portion survives whole and legible and what is lost is form-neutral. If the form-bearing portion is what is lost, smudged, or illegible, the mark is TOUCHED, not partly-legible, whatever else survives: a date without a spelling proves the dimension was exercised on that day and nothing about the form, and a form is exactly what medium must compare. The checker must name, per mark, which portion bears form and which portion is lost; a mark whose form-bearing portion cannot be located is TOUCHED by default, because an unlocated form is a form the checker cannot certify survived.

The second rule is that legibility is graded mark by mark, not dimension by dimension. T-757's split declared a dimension SURVIVING or TOUCHED as a whole; T-758 refines the split into a per-mark ledger. A dimension's state for a given grade is the worst state among its marks at that grade's level. For far, every mark must be FULL — one partly-legible mark touches the dimension for far, because far asserts a negative about the whole training and a lost portion might exercise exactly the dimension claimed unexercised. For medium, a mark that is FULL or PARTLY-LEGIBLE counts as a surviving base, because medium asks only whether the dimension was exercised in some form and never in this form, and the form-bearing portion supplies both halves: it shows the form the dimension took, and the sign's form differs from it. A dimension can therefore be TOUCHED-for-far and SURVIVING-for-medium at once — the split is two-level, like T-757's mechanism, and a checker who reports a dimension as simply "touched" without saying for which grade has reported nothing usable.

The third rule is that the cap follows the level. A partly-legible mark never supports far, whatever it looks like — the lost portion defeats every complete negative, as T-757 ruled for touched dimensions, and a partly-legible mark is touched for far purposes. A partly-legible mark supports medium exactly as a full mark does, provided the sign's form differs from the form the surviving portion shows: the base is the surviving form, not the lost margin, and the comparison runs on what survives. Where the sign's form matches the surviving form, the mark grades the sign near or zero under T-756, not medium — a partly-legible base proves what the dimension did, and what it did cannot also prove what it never did. Nothing about a partly-legible mark ever adds weight beyond the medium it supports: no sign, in no dimension, gains weight because part of its base is missing.

The fourth rule is that the record lists the ledger. For each pointed mark: FULL, PARTLY-LEGIBLE (with the form-bearing portion named and the lost portion named), or TOUCHED. A grade issued from a partly-legible base without the ledger is void, like a grade without T-757's split. The clerk's own note describing what the lost portion contained is not a surviving portion: T-757's fifth rule stands — a note about a paper is an oath, not a paper, and it cannot promote a TOUCHED mark to PARTLY-LEGIBLE, supply a form-bearing portion, or serve as a base for any grade. The papers grade the papers, and where a paper is half gone, the grading runs on the half that remains and stops at the half that does not.

The fifth rule is recomputation on challenge and on recovery, forward only as in T-757. A challenge showing a form-bearing portion lost demotes the mark to TOUCHED and recomputes the cluster under T-756: far grades in that dimension fall, medium grades resting on that mark fall to ungraded, and the passage stands only while the recomputed sum still reaches 3 across at least two dimensions. A recovered portion promotes the mark and re-grades fresh: capped signs may rise to far where the recovered part confirms the dimension unexercised, and a passage previously ACCUM-SHORT may verify on the recomputed sum — but forward only. Custody steps already taken on the strength of the old grade stand; recovery reopens the grade, not the history, in the same forward-only spirit as T-757's recovery rule and T-750's later free re-adoption. **T-759 — the Distributed-Form Rule — designed:** T-758 left its distributed-form problem touched but not settled: it said a mark is PARTLY-LEGIBLE only when the form-bearing portion survives whole and legible, but it never said what survives when the form itself is spread across portions — a spelling split across the legible/illegible boundary, an ordering shown half by a key and half by a margin. T-759 answers: neither half surviving suffices on its own, and the whole form surviving is not required either. What survives is the determination. A distributed form counts as surviving exactly when the surviving portions jointly determine it uniquely, with no element of the form supplied from outside the paper.

The first rule is the determination test. A distributed form survives if and only if the surviving portions jointly fix it to exactly one form. Consistent with is not determined by: if the surviving portions fit two different forms, the form is not determined and the mark is TOUCHED, not PARTLY-LEGIBLE. A guess that happens to be right is still a guess; the papers must force the form, not merely allow it. Where the surviving portions force nothing, there is nothing to grade around — the smudge has taken the form, whatever letters or strokes remain.

The second rule is the form inventory first. Before grading, the checker lists the form's determining elements in the ledger — for a spelling, the letters that distinguish it from its neighbours; for an ordering, the positions that fix the sequence — and names which portion bears each element. An element not listed before grading cannot later be claimed as surviving; a form whose inventory is written after the grade is a grade without a ledger, void under T-758's fourth rule. The inventory is what stops determination from becoming retrofitting: the checker commits to what would count as forcing the form before seeing which half survived.

The third rule is that redundant halves are not distributed forms. Where the same form is borne twice over — the key and the margin each showing the full order, the spelling written once in the entry and once in the margin — either half surviving suffices, because each half alone determines the form. Redundancy is duplication, not distribution; the ledger records such a mark as REDUNDANT, and a redundant mark grades as its surviving half grades. T-759's determination test applies only where no single surviving portion determines the form alone.

The fourth rule is split spelling. Surviving letters fix the word only if no other form in the paper's own vocabulary fits them. The vocabulary is the paper's own: words the paper itself uses, not the checker's dictionary and not the language at large. If the paper's vocabulary offers two completions for the surviving letters, the spelling is undetermined and the mark is TOUCHED; the checker's knowledge of which word is likelier is not paper, and likelihood is not determination. A spelling whose surviving letters fit exactly one word the paper uses is determined, and grades as PARTLY-LEGIBLE.

The fifth rule is split ordering. A surviving half fixes the order only if it fixes the sequence: the first element plus a rule stated in the paper itself (the paper's own numbered key, its own stated sequence), or enough positions that only one sequence fits the surviving anchors. A half that shows order without fixing it — a margin arrow with no anchor, a key with its first entry lost — determines nothing, and the mark is TOUCHED. An ordering rule imported from outside the paper does not fix anything: the determination must come from the paper's own matter, or it is supply from outside, forbidden by the first rule.

The sixth rule is the level consequence. A determined distributed form grades as PARTLY-LEGIBLE, never FULL: matter is lost even though the form is forced, so far stays unavailable and medium stands on it as a surviving base under T-758's third rule. Determination rescues medium; it never restores far. An undetermined distributed form grades TOUCHED at every level, contributing nothing to any sum. T-758's two-level split now runs through determination: a dimension holding a determined distributed form is TOUCHED-for-far and SURVIVING-for-medium, exactly as a dimension holding an ordinary partly-legible mark.

The seventh rule is ledger and recomputation. The ledger records, per determining element: the element, the portion bearing it, and FULL or LOST. A challenge showing any determining element lost — or showing a second fitting form the inventory missed — demotes the mark to TOUCHED and recomputes forward only under T-758's fifth rule: far grades in that dimension fall, medium grades resting on that mark fall to ungraded, and the passage stands only while the recomputed sum still reaches 3 across at least two dimensions. A recovery that later restores a lost element re-grades forward only, as T-758 rules; it does not rewrite the grade the passage carried while the element was lost.

**T-760 — the Vocabulary Rule — designed:** T-759 left its vocabulary problem touched but not settled: it said a surviving spelling is determined only if no other form in the paper's own vocabulary fits the surviving letters, but it never said who fixes that vocabulary — whether a word the paper uses once counts as vocabulary, or whether vocabulary requires repeated use, and whether a word appearing only in the disputed passage itself can complete its own spelling. T-760 answers: vocabulary is attestation, not frequency. One clear use counts, the disputed passage cannot attest its own completion, and the vocabulary is fixed in the inventory before grading.

The first rule is that the vocabulary is fixed before grading. The checker lists, in the form inventory T-759's second rule requires, every candidate completion word together with the passage attesting it — the word, the attesting passage, and that passage's legibility state. A completion word not on the pre-grading inventory cannot be claimed later; a vocabulary written after the grade is a grade without a ledger, void under T-758's fourth rule. The inventory is what stops vocabulary from becoming retrofitting: the checker commits to which words the paper shows before seeing which completion the surviving letters favour.

The second rule is that one clear use counts. A word the paper uses once, in a legible and undisputed passage outside the disputed passage, is vocabulary. Frequency is not attestation: repeated use adds nothing, and a single use is not a weak attestation — the test is whether the paper shows the word, not how often it shows it. A word the paper never uses outside the disputed passage is not vocabulary, however common in the language at large; the checker's dictionary is not paper, and the language at large is not the paper's own vocabulary under T-759's fourth rule.

The third rule is that self-completion is forbidden. A word attested only inside the disputed passage cannot complete that passage's own spelling — not even from a fully legible line of the same passage. The passage under dispute cannot be its own witness: the surviving letters are the question, and a word drawn from the same passage answers the question with itself. The vocabulary is drawn from the paper outside the disputed passage; what the disputed passage contains, legible or not, is the matter being graded, never the vocabulary it is graded against.

The fourth rule is exact word-form attestation. Attestation is by word-form as written, not by stem or paradigm: the paper's use of "ordered" does not attest "ordering", and its use of "order" does not attest "ordered". A checker who completes a spelling with a form the paper never wrote has supplied from the checker's grammar, forbidden by T-759's first rule. The paper's morphology is the paper's matter only where the paper itself writes the form; a paradigm the checker infers is the checker's, not the paper's.

The fifth rule is that an attestation must be legible and undisputed. A word attested only in a smudged, partly-legible, or itself-disputed passage does not count: an attestation the checker cannot read whole is not a showing, and an attestation under challenge is not settled paper. But a word attested in a partly-legible passage whose form-bearing portion survives whole counts under T-758: the attesting word itself is legible even if its passage is smudged elsewhere, because attestation is about the word, not the passage around it. The ledger records the attestation's state alongside the word — FULL, or PARTLY-LEGIBLE with the form-bearing portion named — so a later challenge can see exactly what was shown.

The sixth rule is the level consequence. Vocabulary decides determination, and determination decides the grade under T-759's sixth rule: exactly one vocabulary completion fits the surviving letters, and the spelling is determined, grading PARTLY-LEGIBLE, never FULL; zero completions, or two or more, and the spelling is undetermined, grading TOUCHED at every level. A recovery — an attestation passage restored to legibility, or a boundary ruling placing the attestation outside the disputed passage — re-grades forward only, as T-758 rules; it does not rewrite the grade the passage carried while the attestation was missing.

**The named forms**, all to T-289: the Vocabulary — the set of word-forms the paper uses outside the disputed passage, fixed in the pre-grading inventory. Attestation — a legible, undisputed occurrence of a word-form outside the disputed passage, the only thing that puts a word in the vocabulary. **T-762 — the Overwriting Rule — designed:** T-761 left its overwriting problem touched but not settled: it said a word begun in one hand and finished in another attests for neither hand, but never said what an overwritten word attests — one hand written over another's, the upper hand legible and the lower hand partly visible — because overwriting is neither sequential alternation nor a divided word. T-762 answers: overwriting is layering, not writing. The upper layer and the lower layer are two separate inscriptions sharing one space, each graded on its own legibility and its own hand, and no word is ever assembled from pieces of both.

The first rule is that layers are separate inscriptions. An overwritten word is not one word with two hands; it is two words, one laid over the other, occupying the same ground. The checker inventories them as UPPER and LOWER, each with its own hand, its own legibility state, and its own vocabulary entry — never as a single DIVIDED word under T-761's sixth rule, because a divided word is one inscription split between hands in sequence, while overwriting is two complete inscriptions competing for the same space. The ledger records the layer for every candidate attestation, and a determination that fails to name the layer fails to name the attestation.

The second rule is that the upper layer attests for its own hand when it is legible whole. Where the upper hand's word survives whole and legible — every letterform readable despite the ground beneath it — it attests for the upper hand's vocabulary under T-761, exactly as an unoverwritten word would. The lower layer beneath it adds nothing to that attestation and subtracts nothing from it: the upper word's clarity is judged on its own strokes, not on the noise underneath. A checker who demotes a legible upper word because the ground is crowded has confused a crowded page with a damaged word.

The third rule is that the lower layer attests only when it, too, survives whole. A lower word partly visible through and between the upper strokes — a few letters showing, a stem here, a loop there — is not an attestation, however suggestive the fragments. It attests for the lower hand only where its whole form survives legibly despite the overwriting: every letterform readable in the gaps, in the margins of the upper strokes, or by whatever examination the inventory records as the reading method. Partial lower visibility is a trace, not a word, and a trace completes nothing. Where the lower form can be determined only by borrowing letters from the upper layer, it is not determined at all — the upper layer is another hand's word, not the lower word's missing letters.

The fourth rule is that layers are never merged. No completion may take letters from the upper layer and letters from the lower layer to assemble a word neither hand wrote. A disputed spelling cannot be completed by an upper "c" plus a lower "at" into a word found in either hand's vocabulary, because no hand wrote that combined form in that space. Merging is supply from the other layer, forbidden in the same sense as T-761's foreign form and T-760's self-completion: the checker would be writing the word the paper is supposed to attest. Each layer's fit is judged against its own surviving letters alone, and a word that fits only across layers fits nowhere.

The fifth rule is that a hand overwriting its own word withdraws the lower form. Where the same hand overwrites its own earlier word — a correction, a respelling, a second thought laid over the first — the upper form is that hand's current word and the lower form weighs 0 as an attestation for that hand's vocabulary. The hand has retracted the lower spelling by covering it, and a retracted spelling does not attest a vocabulary the hand no longer writes in that place. **T-763 — the Layer-Order Rule — designed:** T-762 left its overwriting-order problem touched but not settled: it said indistinguishable layers attest for no hand until a layer ruling separates them, but never said what counts as a layer ruling — what evidence orders two layers when the inks are identical and stroke order cannot be read, and whether an unordered pair is permanently indistinct or only indistinct until a better examination. T-763 answers: order is a ruling, not a reading, and indistinctness is provisional, never permanent — but a provisional pair stays indistinct until a recorded ruling separates it, and no order is ever inferred from the disputed passage's own content.

The first rule is that order is fixed before grading, from evidence recorded in the inventory, never from content fit. Which layer is upper and which is lower is settled before any vocabulary word is fitted to either layer, and the evidence for it is entered in the record like any other inventory item: the method, the examiner, the date, and the letters it orders. An order inferred from which word fits the vocabulary better, which reading is more plausible, or which hand is likelier to have written last is circular under T-761's fifth rule — it uses the disputed passage to order the disputed passage, then grades the passage on the order it just invented. A checker who orders layers because the upper reading "makes more sense" has graded the sense, not the layers.

The second rule is the order-evidence hierarchy, in descending strength. First, paper-internal sequence: matter elsewhere in the paper that fixes the sequence — a dated layer elsewhere in the same hand, a continuation that runs from one layer into an undisputed passage, a correction mark in a third hand naming the order, a dated copy of the instrument showing one layer alone. Paper-internal sequence is strongest because it is the paper's own matter, not an examiner's inference about it. Second, physical examination recorded as a method: stroke-crossing (an upper stroke rides visibly over a lower one), ink pooling where strokes cross, paper-fiber disturbance, bleed-through order, pressure displacement — each method named, each result recorded letter by letter, each letter's order resting on the method that ordered it. Third, custody sequence: the instrument's filing order, a dated receipt showing one layer's presence before the other's, a keeper's log recording the overwrite. Custody sequence bounds order — it can prove one layer predates a dated event — but it rarely proves the full order alone, and a custody claim that contradicts paper-internal sequence yields to the paper.

The third rule is that identical inks and unreadable stroke order do not make a pair permanently indistinct. A layer pair that cannot be ordered today is recorded as PROVISIONALLY INDISTINCT, not as finally indistinct: it weighs 0 for every vocabulary while it stays unordered, exactly as T-762's OVERWRITTEN-INDISTINCT weighs 0, but its indistinctness carries no expiry and no presumption. Age does not order layers — a pair unordered for years is still unordered, not presumed ordered by the passage of time — and a later examination method, a newly found dated copy, or a paper-internal sequence noticed on re-reading can separate it. A ruling that later separates the layers re-grades forward only under T-758's fifth rule: grades the passage carried while the pair was indistinct stand in the record, and only the forward grade changes. Provisional indistinctness is a waiting state, not a verdict on the layers.

The fourth rule is that order is per letter, not per word. Crossing evidence may order one letter cleanly and leave the rest of the word unordered — an upper "t" riding over a lower "t" at one crossing proves the order of those two strokes, not of the whole word. A word is ORDERED only where every letter relied on for its determination is ordered; where any relied letter is unordered, the word stays indistinct for that determination, however cleanly its other letters are ordered. A partly-ordered word does not attest on its ordered letters alone unless those ordered letters alone determine the word under T-759's distributed-form rule — order, like legibility, is judged on the letters the determination actually uses, not on the word's tidiest corner.

The fifth rule is burden and conflict. The party claiming an order bears the burden of showing it by recorded evidence; an order claimed but not shown weighs 0, and an order shown for one letter does not extend by presumption to the letters beside it. Where two examinations order the same pair in opposite directions, the pair returns to PROVISIONALLY INDISTINCT until a third examination — a method both sides accept, or a paper-internal sequence that settles the point — resolves the conflict. Conflicts are not settled by counting checkers, by preferring the likelier hand, or by splitting the difference between the two orders: there is no half-upper layer, and a pair ordered both ways is ordered neither way until the record says otherwise.

The sixth rule is repeatability: an examination counts only if it can be repeated. A physical method whose result a second examiner, using the same method on the same instrument, cannot reproduce weighs 0 as order evidence, however confident the first examiner. The inventory records the method in enough detail for repetition — the instrument, the magnification, the lighting, the crossings examined — and a method recorded too thinly to repeat is recorded as UNREPEATABLE and set aside. This is the examination half of T-762's examination problem answered in part: examination belongs in the inventory as a method, and a method that cannot be repeated is not a method at all, it is an opinion wearing a method's name. Who qualifies as an examiner remains open — repeatability guards the method, not the examiner.

The seventh rule is ledger and recomputation, forward only as in T-762. The layer ledger grows an order column: per candidate attestation, the word, the layer, the order state — ORDERED-UPPER, ORDERED-LOWER, or UNORDERED — the method that fixed it, the examiner, and the date. A challenge showing an order reversed — an upper word shown to be the lower after all — demotes the mark to TOUCHED where no surviving ordered-layer same-hand attestation remains, and recomputes forward only under T-758's fifth rule: far grades in that dimension fall, medium grades resting on that mark fall to ungraded, and the passage stands only while the recomputed sum still reaches 3 across at least two dimensions. A ruling that orders a provisionally indistinct pair re-grades forward only; it does not rewrite the grade the passage carried while the pair waited unordered.

**The named forms**, all to T-289: the Layer Ruling — the recorded evidence, fixed before grading, that orders a layer pair, never inferred from content fit. The Ordered Pair — a layer pair whose order is fixed by paper-internal sequence, repeatable examination, or custody sequence, inventoried with method, examiner, and date. The Provisionally Indistinct Pair — a layer pair that cannot be ordered today, weighing 0 for every vocabulary while it waits, with no expiry and no presumption from age. The Per-Letter Order — order fixed letter by letter, so that a word is ORDERED only where every relied letter is ordered. The Repeatable Examination — a physical method recorded in enough detail for a second examiner to reproduce its result, the only examination that counts as order evidence. The Unrepeatable Examination — a method recorded too thinly to repeat, set aside as opinion, weighing 0. The Order Ledger — the layer ledger's order column, without which no ordered-layer determination claim stands.

Comparisons keep T-757's COMPARISON-FULL, COMPARISON-NARROWED, and COMPARISON-GAPPED, computed on the ledger: a comparison is NARROWED, not GAPPED, where every mark is FULL, PARTLY-LEGIBLE, or determined-but-partial on an ordered-layer same-hand attestation, and GAPPED only where some mark is TOUCHED. **T-764 — the Examination-Reliability Rule — designed:** T-763 left its examination-reliability problem touched but not settled: it said only repeatable examinations count as order evidence, but never said which physical methods are reliable enough to order layers at all — whether ink pooling, fiber disturbance, or bleed-through order carry the same weight as a clean stroke-crossing, and who grades a method's reliability when the methods disagree with each other. T-764 answers: reliability is earned per method per letter, never assumed per method class — a method's weight comes from its control record and its blind repeat, not from its name; disagreement between methods is resolved by a shown failure mode, not by rank or vote; and the examiner who performed the examination never grades it.

The first rule is tiers by directness, not by prestige. DIRECT methods read superposition itself: stroke-crossing, where one stroke visibly rides over another. INDIRECT methods read a sign that superposition causes: ink pooling where strokes cross, pressure displacement, paper-fiber disturbance, bleed-through order. DIRECT outranks INDIRECT as a starting weight because indirect signs are confounded — pooling by ink load and pen pressure, fiber disturbance by handling and storage, bleed-through by sheet thinness and verso ink. But a tier is a starting weight, not a verdict: a clean DIRECT crossing on one letter does not bless a smudged DIRECT crossing on another, and a well-controlled INDIRECT sign can outweigh a poor DIRECT one on the same letter. Tier sets the burden; the record decides.

The second rule is control first. A method orders a disputed pair only after it has ordered a known-order pair — a pair whose order is fixed by paper-internal sequence — on the same paper, or on paper of the same stock and ink where the same paper offers no control. A method with no control record orders nothing, however plausible its physics. The control record is inventoried: the control pair, the paper-internal matter that fixes its order, the method's result on it, and the date. A method that has never been shown right on a pair whose order is known has not been shown right at all.

The third rule is that reliability is per letter. Each letter's order rests on the method that ordered that letter, with that method's control record under that letter's conditions. Reliability does not transfer across letters — a clean crossing at one letter says nothing about the smudged crossing at the next — nor across papers, nor across examiners. A method reliable on one sheet is unproven on the next until its control record covers the next sheet's conditions. A word is reliability-graded only where every relied letter carries a graded method; one ungraded letter leaves the word ungraded for that determination, under T-763's fourth rule.

The fourth rule tightens T-763's repeatability into the blind repeat. The second reading must be blind: the second examiner does not know the first result or the claimed order before reading. Two readings by the same examiner count as one however far apart in time, and a non-blind repeat is recorded as UNREPEATED, not as a repeat. A method whose only support is a non-blind repeat orders nothing. Blindness guards against the most ordinary failure mode of all: a second reader who reads the claimed order because the file told it to, then calls the agreement a repeat.

The fifth rule is disagreement by failure mode, not by rank or vote. When two methods order the same pair oppositely, the pair returns to PROVISIONALLY INDISTINCT unless the stronger result explains the weaker's failure mode and the explanation is shown in the record — bleed-through misread because the verso carries its own ink in the same place, visible on the verso; pooling misread because the pen was re-inked mid-stroke, visible as a load change elsewhere on the paper. A plausible story about a confound is not a shown failure mode. Where no failure mode is shown, conflict cancels: no counting of methods, no averaging, no hierarchy override by tier rank alone. A third examination may still resolve the pair under T-763's fifth rule, and a failure mode shown later re-opens it forward only.

The sixth rule is the independent grader. The examiner who performed the examination never grades its reliability. A second reader grades the method record — control record, blind-repeat record, confound check — and signs the reliability grade. A self-graded examination weighs 0. This grades the record, not the person: who qualifies as an examiner at all stays open under T-763's examiner-qualification problem. T-764 says only that the grader and the examiner are never the same reader, so no method's reliability rests on the word of the hand that used it.

The seventh rule is the reliability column and forward-only failure. The order ledger grows a reliability column: per relied letter, the method, its tier, its control-record reference, its repeatability state — BLIND-REPEATED, UNREPEATED, or UNREPEATABLE — its grader, and the date. An order claim without a reliability entry is incomplete and weighs 0. If a method's control record is later broken — the method fails on a new known-order control — every order resting on that method alone reverts to PROVISIONALLY INDISTINCT, forward only under T-758's fifth rule: grades the passage carried while the method stood remain in the record, and only the forward grade changes. A method that was reliable until it was caught wrong was reliable until it was caught wrong, and no earlier grade is rewritten for it.

**The named forms**, all to T-289: the Control Pair — a layer pair whose order is fixed by paper-internal sequence, on which a method proves itself before it may order a disputed pair. The Method Tier — DIRECT, reading superposition itself, or INDIRECT, reading a sign superposition causes, a starting weight and never a verdict. The Per-Letter Reliability — a method's grade applying letter by letter, never transferred across letters, papers, or examiners. The Blind Repeat — a second reading by a second examiner who does not know the first result or the claimed order, the only repeat that counts. The Shown Failure Mode — a confound visible in the record that explains a weaker method's error, the only disagreement-resolution that does not return the pair to indistinct. The Independent Reliability Grade — a second reader's signed grade of the method record, never the examiner's own. The Reliability Column — the order ledger's per-letter reliability entry, without which no order claim stands.

**The grades.** T-763's DETERMINED and UNDETERMINED stand, now gated on reliability: DETERMINED where exactly one same-hand, same-layer vocabulary word fits that layer's own surviving letters, every relied letter is ORDERED, and every ordering method carries a signed reliability grade with a control record and a blind repeat, grading PARTLY-LEGIBLE where the attesting layer is a surviving lower form or a legible upper form over a crowded ground; UNDETERMINED where zero or two or more same-hand, same-layer words fit, or where the only fit crosses layers, or where any relied letter is UNORDERED, or where any relied order rests on an ungraded, unrepeated, or self-graded method — grading TOUCHED.
