**T-765 — the Control Sufficiency Rule — designed:** T-764 left its control-pair-sufficiency problem open: it required a method to order a known-order pair before it may order a disputed pair, but never said how many controls earn a method, whether one control suffices, whether controls must span the paper's conditions, or whether a control on one sheet calibrates another sheet of the same stock. T-765 answers: one control never earns a method; a method is earned per condition class, by a control set that spans that class and includes a control near the disputed pair's conditions; a control the method fails voids the method for that condition class only, never globally; and a cross-sheet control is supplementary, never the sole basis for earning.

The first rule is three controls, not one. A single known-order pair proves only that the method could read that pair — it does not separate a method that reads order from a method that guessed right, and a single success carries no information about the method's confounds. A method earns ordering power for a condition class only after three known-order controls in that class, all read correctly, each fixed by paper-internal sequence. Three is a floor, not a guarantee: three correct controls earn the method a hearing for that class, and the blind repeat and independent grading of T-764 still gate whether any particular ordering stands. A method with two correct controls and one failure is not "two-thirds earned"; it is unearned for that class until the failure is explained by a shown failure mode and the set is rebuilt.

The second rule is span, not count alone. Three controls clustered in one corner of the paper, one ink load, one stroke density, earn the method only for that corner, that load, that density — because T-764's confounds (ink load, pen pressure, handling, sheet thinness, verso ink) vary across exactly those dimensions. A control set earns a condition class only if its controls span the class's known confound dimensions: at least two ink loads where load varies, at least two paper zones (edge and interior) where handling varies, and a control on each side of any verso-ink region the disputed pair touches. A set that spans nothing earns nothing beyond its own three pairs; counting controls without spanning conditions is how a method earned on clean crossings orders a smudged one.

The third rule is nearness. Among the three controls, at least one must sit near the disputed pair's conditions — same ink load class, same paper zone class, same verso state — not merely in the same condition class in name. A method earned on light-load crossings does not order a heavy-load pair because both are "crossings"; the nearness control is what ties the earned class to the disputed pair. Where no near control exists, the method is unearned for that pair however many distant controls it holds, and the pair falls back under T-762's fallback — custody of the instrument or a second independent paper, never the unearned method alone.

The fourth rule is condition-scoped failure. A control the method fails voids the method for that condition class only: a method that misreads a heavy-load control is unproven for heavy-load pairs, but its light-load controls still stand, and its earned status for light-load pairs is untouched. Failure does not propagate across classes, and success does not propagate either — earning is per class, failing is per class, and a method's ledger is a map of classes earned and classes void, not a single grade. A failed control is itself inventoried: the pair, the conditions, the method's wrong reading, and the date, so a later challenge can see exactly which class fell and why.

The fifth rule is cross-sheet controls as supplement only. A control on another sheet of the same stock, mill, and ink batch may join a control set, but it may never be the nearness control and never supply more than one of the three controls. Same-stock similarity is a claim about the paper, not a property of it, and T-764's cross-paper-calibration problem stays open in this narrower form: a cross-sheet control supports, it does not earn. A method whose entire control set sits on other sheets is unearned on this sheet, whatever the stock match. Where the same sheet offers no control at all, the method is unearned here, and the fallback is T-762's, not a borrowed sheet's.

The sixth rule is the control ledger entry. Each earned class carries an entry: the three controls, their paper-internal fixing matter, their conditions, the nearness control identified, any cross-sheet control flagged as supplementary, the grader's signature under T-764's sixth rule, and the date. An order claim that cites a method without a control-ledger entry for its class weighs 0, like T-764's reliability-column rule. If a new confound is discovered in a class — a handling mark, a verso bleed, a load change the set never spanned — the class's earning re-opens: the set must be rebuilt to span the new dimension before the method orders in that class again, forward only under T-758's fifth rule.

**The named forms**, all to T-289: the Control Set — three known-order pairs in one condition class, all read correctly, that earn a method for that class. The Condition Class — a bundle of confound dimensions (ink load, paper zone, verso state) within which earning holds and outside which it does not. The Nearness Control — the control in the set matching the disputed pair's conditions, the tie between the earned class and the pair. The Condition-Scoped Failure — a failed control voiding the method for its class only, leaving other classes earned. The Supplementary Control — a cross-sheet control that may join but never anchor a set. The Control Ledger Entry — the per-class record without which no order claim citing the method stands.

**The grades.** T-764's reliability column gains a sufficiency state per relied letter: SUFFICIENT where the ordering method carries a control-ledger entry for the disputed pair's condition class, with three correct controls, span across the class's confound dimensions, and an identified nearness control; INSUFFICIENT where the method has fewer than three controls in the class, no spanning set, or no nearness control — grading TOUCHED for that letter under T-764; CONDITION-FAILED where the method failed a control in that class and the failure stands unexplained — grading TOUCHED, and the pair returns to PROVISIONALLY INDISTINCT unless a second method orders it under T-764. T-764's DETERMINED now additionally requires SUFFICIENT on every relied letter; a determination resting on an INSUFFICIENT or CONDITION-FAILED method is UNDETERMINED, however clean the crossing looked.

**Distinguished from the chain it answers.** From T-764's control record (there a method needed a control record at all — one known-order pair proved before ordering a disputed pair; here the record must be sufficient — three controls, spanning, with nearness — because one correct reading does not separate a method from a guess). From T-763's repeatability (there a second examiner must reproduce the reading; here the method must first earn the right to be repeated, because a faithfully repeated unearned method is still unearned). From T-762's fallback (there custody or a second paper replaces a fallen passage; here the fallback is what an unearned method triggers, and the fallback is never the method itself wearing a borrowed sheet's controls).

**What this pairs with.** T-764's Examination-Reliability Rule (the test this rule completes — T-764 invoked a control record without saying what record suffices, and T-765 supplies the three-control floor, the span requirement, the nearness tie, the condition-scoped failure, and the supplementary-only cross-sheet rule that clause needed). Whether a failed control in one class taints adjacent classes — a heavy-load failure casting doubt on medium-load readings, or classes holding strictly separate (admitted here, new — T-765's adjacent-class-taint problem, still open). Whether a cross-sheet control on identical stock, mill, and ink batch may ever serve as the nearness control when the same sheet offers none, or whether same-sheet nearness is absolute (admitted here, new — T-765's cross-sheet-nearness problem, still open). Whether a control set must be rebuilt whole when a new confound dimension is discovered, or whether one added control spanning the new dimension repairs the set (admitted here, new — T-765's set-repair problem, still open). Whether a method that earns a class on one paper transfers that earning to another paper of the same stock at all, beyond the supplementary-control allowance (admitted here, inherited — T-764's cross-paper-calibration problem, still open). Who grades the second reader's reliability grade, and where the chain of graders stops (admitted here, inherited — T-764's grader-of-grader problem, still open). Whether a DIRECT method that fails repeatedly on controls demotes to INDIRECT, or whether tiers are fixed by directness regardless of record (admitted here, inherited — T-764's method-tier-revision problem, still open). Whether a second examiner can truly be blind when the dispute is famous or the file advertises the claimed order (admitted here, inherited — T-764's blind-repeat-feasibility problem, still open). **T-766 — the Class-Boundary Rule — designed:** T-765 left its class-boundary problem open: it earned a method per condition class, by a control set spanning that class's confound dimensions, but never said how a class is bounded — whether ink load, paper zone, and verso state exhaust the confound dimensions, or whether a class drawn too wide smuggles unearned pairs inside it and a class drawn too narrow makes every pair its own class. T-766 answers: a class is bounded by its declared dimensions, declared before any control in it is read; a dimension joins the declaration only by a shown confound, never by suspicion; a class splits when a shown confound divides it, merges only when two classes' control sets are interchangeable, and every boundary change re-grades forward only.

The first rule is declaration before reading. A condition class exists only as a written declaration: the confound dimensions it claims (ink load, paper zone, verso state, and any further dimension admitted under the second rule), the range each dimension covers, and the date of declaration. A method earns nothing in a class declared after its controls were read — retroactive class-drawing is how a lucky set becomes an earned class. The declaration is filed in the control ledger beside the class's first control, and any order claim citing the class must cite the declaration's date. A class with no declaration is not a narrow class; it is no class, and the method is unearned for every pair it would have covered.

The second rule is shown confounds only. A dimension joins a class declaration only when a confound is shown: a control the method misreads, or reads correctly only under a condition the declaration did not name, with the misreading or the condition tied to that dimension by the failure-mode showing T-764 requires. Suspicion never adds a dimension — "heavy ink might matter" is not a dimension, and a class padded with suspected dimensions is a class drawn too narrow by speculation, earning nothing it does not need. Conversely, a dimension once shown can never be dropped from the declaration while the class stands: a class that forgets its own confound is a class drawn too wide by amnesia.

The third rule is the too-wide test. A class is too wide when it contains a pair whose conditions differ from the control set's spanned conditions on a declared dimension — the span T-765 required was span across the class as declared, and a declaration wider than its span smuggles pairs in. A pair failing the test on any dimension falls outside the class, however the class is named, and the method is unearned for that pair until the set is extended or the class is split.

The fourth rule is the too-narrow test. A class is too narrow when it separates pairs that no shown confound distinguishes — two classes whose declarations differ only on a dimension with no shown confound, or whose ranges split a continuous dimension at a point no control straddles, are one class wearing two names. The test is the split challenge: a challenger names the dimension and the dividing point, and the class survives only if a shown confound sits on that point — a control misread across it, or a condition change recorded there. The fifth rule is split and merge as the only boundary moves. A class splits when a shown confound divides it: the new boundary is drawn at the confound, each side keeps only the controls that sit on its side, and each side must independently satisfy T-765's three-control floor and span before it earns anything — a split never carries earning across the cut. A class merges only when the too-narrow test fails for both sides and the merged set passes T-765 whole; a merge never rescues a failed control, which stays condition-scoped under T-765's fourth rule. No other boundary move exists: a class is never quietly widened to swallow a disputed pair, never quietly narrowed to shed a failed control, and never re-declared to erase a failure. The boundary ledger records every split and merge, with the confound or challenge that caused it, the controls on each side, and the grader's signature under T-764's sixth rule.

The sixth rule is forward-only re-grading. A boundary change re-grades forward only under T-758's fifth rule: orderings already graded on the old boundary stand as graded, with the boundary change noted against them; orderings not yet graded, and any re-opened passage, are graded on the new boundary. A split that strands a previously DETERMINED pair outside every earned class does not retroactively undetermine it — it bars the next ordering that would cite the old class, and the stranded pair's next challenge faces the new boundary. A merge never upgrades a past TOUCHED grading to DETERMINED; it only opens the door for a fresh grading.

**The named forms**, all to T-289: the Class Declaration — the written dimensions, ranges, and date without which a class does not exist. The Shown Confound — a misreading or condition-tied reading that earns a dimension its place in a declaration. The Too-Wide Test — the mechanical span check that keeps a declaration from smuggling pairs. The Too-Narrow Test — the split challenge that keeps speculation from multiplying classes. The Stranded Pair — a pair left outside every earned class by a split, barred from the old class's next ordering but not retroactively ungraded.

**T-767 — the Challenger-Standing Rule — designed:** T-766 left its challenger-standing problem open: it let a split challenge put a class's every ordering into UNBOUNDED until decided, but never said who may bring one — whether any reader may challenge any class, or only a reader with a stake in the grading, and what standing a challenger needs. T-767 answers: standing is earned by signing, never assumed by reading; a stranger may petition but cannot challenge; the challenger never decides their own challenge; a filing without the required contents is a note, not a challenge, and grades nothing; and a failed challenge costs standing for that class.

The first rule is who holds standing. Standing belongs to three parties only: either reader who has signed a reliability grading on the passage or the class under T-764 — first reader or second reader alike; the custodian of the sheet, for as long as custody holds; and the decider of a prior challenge on the same class, who earned standing by deciding it. No one else holds it. A reader who has read the control ledger but signed nothing, a reader who graded a different passage on the same sheet, and any stranger to the grading hold no standing, however strong their suspicion. Standing is earned per passage and per class by a signature, never by familiarity with the file.

The second rule is the stranger's route. A reader without standing who believes a class is too narrow or a confound divides it does not file a challenge; they file a petition to a standing holder — normally the second reader — naming the class, the dimension, and the dividing point exactly as a challenge would. The petition obliges nothing: the standing holder may adopt it as their own challenge, signing it and assuming the challenger's costs under the sixth rule, or decline it in writing. A declined petition is recorded in the boundary ledger as a petition, not a challenge, and the class's boundary state is untouched by it. A petition never grades a class UNBOUNDED, however detailed — the UNBOUNDED effect belongs to challenges alone, and only standing holders may trigger it.

The third rule is what a challenge must contain. A challenge is a written filing in the boundary ledger naming: the class challenged; the challenge kind — a merge-challenge, asserting the class is too narrow and should merge with its named twin, or a split-challenge, asserting a shown confound divides the class at a named point; the dimension and the dividing point; and the evidence — for a split-challenge, the shown confound sitting on the point, tied to the dimension by the failure-mode showing T-764 requires; for a merge-challenge, the absence claim, naming the twin class and stating that no shown confound sits on the point. A filing missing any element is not a defective challenge; it is not a challenge at all. It is entered as a note, the class stays BOUNDED, and the filer is told what element is missing. A note may be completed into a challenge only by a fresh filing, signed and dated as new.

The fourth rule is the disinterested decider. The challenge is decided by the second reader, unless the second reader is the challenger — then by the first reader, unless the first reader is also a party — then by a third reader brought in for the decision alone, who earns standing on the class by deciding it. The challenger never decides their own challenge, and no decider grades a class they themselves challenged. The decision is one of three: UPHELD, and the boundary moves under T-766's fifth rule; REJECTED, and the class stands as declared, with the rejection's reasoning entered in the ledger; or INSUFFICIENT, and the challenge returns to the filer for its missing element, the class grading UNBOUNDED in the meantime. A decider who cannot be found disinterested — every reader a party — leaves the challenge pending, and pending is itself a state, not a failure: the class grades UNBOUNDED until a decider is found.

The fifth rule is the pending effect, bounded. While a challenge is pending, the class grades UNBOUNDED under T-766, and every ordering citing it grades TOUCHED for the relied letter. But pending suspends nothing else: past gradings stand under T-766's forward-only rule, fresh control work on either side of the disputed boundary continues, and a second challenge on the same class from a different standing holder joins the first rather than replacing it — the decider decides them together, and the class stays UNBOUNDED until all pending challenges on it are decided. A pending challenge is not a verdict on the class; it is a hold on the next ordering, and nothing more.

The sixth rule is the cost of failing. A challenge REJECTED on its evidence — the confound shown not to sit on the point, or a shown confound produced against the absence claim — costs the challenger standing for that class until new evidence arrives: the challenger may not file again on the same class without a confound or absence showing not before the ledger. A second REJECTED challenge on the same class suspends the challenger's standing for the whole sheet until a fresh grading re-earns it. A challenge decided INSUFFICIENT costs nothing — incompleteness is not failure — and a challenge UPHELD costs nothing and confirms the challenger's standing. The cost rule is what keeps the UNBOUNDED hold from becoming a veto: a challenger who can stall every ordering for free will stall every ordering.

**The named forms**, all to T-289: the Standing Reader — a reader who earned challenge rights by signing a grading, holding custody, or deciding a prior challenge. The Petition — a stranger's detailed ask to a standing holder, recorded but grading nothing. The Challenge Filing — the written class, kind, dimension, point, and evidence without which there is no challenge. The Disinterested Decider — the reader who decides, never the challenger, never a party. The Failed Challenge — a rejection on the evidence, costing standing for the class, then the sheet. The Standing Ledger — the boundary ledger's record of who holds standing, who filed, who decided, and what each challenge cost.

**The grades.** T-766's boundary state gains a challenge state per relied letter: UNCHALLENGED where no challenge is pending; CHALLENGED where a standing holder's challenge is pending, grading UNBOUNDED for that letter under T-766 until decided; PETITIONED where only a stranger's petition exists, which changes nothing — the class's boundary state is exactly what it was before the petition. A filing by a reader without standing grades nothing, whatever it is called: a document titled "challenge" from a stranger is a petition by rule, and the ledger records it as one. **T-768 — the Custody-Transfer Rule — designed:** T-767 left its custody-transfer problem open: it gave standing to "the custodian of the sheet, for as long as custody holds," but never said what happens to that standing when custody changes hands mid-challenge — whether the incoming custodian inherits it whole, must re-earn it, or holds the sheet in a standing vacuum while a challenge pends. T-768 answers: standing travels with custody for challenges already pending, and with nothing else; the decider's seat never travels at all; and a transfer to a party suspends the inheritance for that challenge.

The first rule is what travels. Custodian standing attaches to the sheet, not to the person holding it — but only as far as the challenges already pending when the transfer is recorded. The incoming custodian inherits standing on every challenge pending on the sheet at the moment of transfer: they may answer it, supply the missing element on an INSUFFICIENT return, and defend the class's boundary as the outgoing custodian could. What does not travel is the right to open new business: inherited standing files no fresh challenge, signs no fresh grading, and decides no fresh dispute. For anything not already pending, the incoming custodian is a stranger until they re-earn standing under the fifth rule. The line is the ledger at transfer: pending then, inherited; arising after, earned.

The second rule is the transfer record. A transfer is effective for challenge purposes only when the outgoing custodian records it in the boundary ledger, naming the incoming custodian, the date, and every challenge pending on the sheet. Until that record exists, the outgoing custodian retains standing and the incoming custodian holds none — a sheet handed over in fact but not in the ledger is still the outgoing custodian's sheet for every challenge purpose. A transfer recorded after a challenge is decided binds nothing: the decision stands, and the incoming custodian inherits no standing on a closed matter. The record is what the next reader checks; an unrecorded transfer is a gap, not a handover.

The third rule is the seated decider. If the outgoing custodian is also the decider of a pending challenge — second reader, first reader, or third reader brought in for the decision alone — the decider's seat does not travel with custody. Decider standing is earned by deciding, and it is personal: the incoming custodian does not inherit the decider's seat, may not decide a challenge they inherited as custodian, and may not be appointed decider of a challenge on which they now hold inherited custodian standing, because the challenger-never-decides rule and the disinterested-decider rule would both break. The outgoing custodian finishes the decision they sit on, or steps down from the seat and a fresh disinterested decider is brought in; the class stays UNBOUNDED until that decision lands. Custody moves; the chair does not.

The fourth rule is the interregnum. If no custodian holds the sheet — the outgoing custodian gone, the incoming not yet recorded — the sheet is in interregnum. Pending challenges stay pending, and every class under one stays UNBOUNDED; the hold does not lapse for want of a custodian. But no new challenge may be filed during an interregnum, because there is no custodian to answer it and no standing holder to receive it; the stranger's petition route stays open, and petitions queue in the ledger until custody resumes. An interregnum suspends filings, never decisions: a seated decider still decides, and their decision still moves the boundary under T-766's fifth rule.

The fifth rule is re-earning. The incoming custodian earns full standing — the right to file fresh challenges, sign fresh gradings, and be appointed decider — exactly the way any reader earns it: by signing a reliability grading on the class under T-764, or by deciding a challenge on it. Until then, inherited standing is fenced: defend and answer pending challenges, nothing more. A custodian who inherits ten pending challenges and signs nothing holds ten fences and no keys. The fence is what keeps a transfer from minting a challenger: custody alone never creates the right to attack a boundary.

The sixth rule is the tainted transfer. If custody transfers to a party to a pending challenge — the challenger, a reader who graded the challenged class, or anyone whose own filing is at issue — the inherited standing on that challenge is suspended, not transferred. The incoming custodian may not answer, defend, or supply elements for that challenge; a disinterested reader answers in their place, or the challenge waits for a seated decider. The suspension lifts only when the incoming custodian re-earns standing on the class by a signed grading that is itself undisputed, or when the challenge is decided. A transfer that would put the challenged boundary in the challenger's own hands is a transfer that changes nothing about who may speak for it.

**The named forms**, all to T-289: the Travelling Standing — custodian standing inherited on pending challenges alone, never on fresh business. The Transfer Record — the ledger entry naming the incoming custodian and every pending challenge, without which no transfer is effective. The Seated Decider — the decider's chair, personal and non-travelling, finished or freshly filled, never inherited. The Interregnum — the custodianless sheet, where pending holds stand, filings suspend, and petitions queue. The Re-earned Standing — full standing regained by a signed grading or a decided challenge. The Tainted Transfer — custody to a party, suspending inherited standing on that challenge until re-earned or decided.

**The grades.** T-767's challenge state gains a custody state per relied letter: HELD where a recorded custodian holds the sheet; INHERITED where the current custodian holds only travelled standing on a pending challenge, fencing them to defence and answer; VACANT where the sheet is in interregnum, filings suspended and petitions queued; SUSPENDED where a tainted transfer bars the incoming custodian from speaking for that challenge. **T-769 — the Return Rule — designed:** T-768 left its return problem open: it said standing travels with custody for pending challenges and must otherwise be re-earned, but never said what happens when the outgoing custodian later resumes custody — whether the standing they held before departure revives automatically, or whether the returnee is treated like any incoming holder and must re-earn it. T-769 answers: a return is a fresh transfer under T-768, never a revival — except where the departure record marked the holding interim, in which case the standing was lent, not given, and returns with the sheet.

The first rule is the default. An outright return is an incoming transfer in full. The returnee records a transfer record under T-768's second rule, naming themselves, the date, and every challenge pending on the sheet; until that record exists they hold nothing, and the holder they replace retains standing. On the record, the returnee inherits standing on every challenge pending at the moment of return, fenced to defence and answer exactly as any incoming custodian's travelled standing is fenced, and holds nothing on fresh business. Gradings the returnee signed and decisions they made before departure still stand — a return neither revives decided challenges nor rewrites the record made in their absence — but those past acts confer no present standing. Past service is history, not a key. A custodian who held full standing, left outright, and comes back holds ten fences and no keys until they re-earn, same as a stranger who inherits ten.

The second rule is the interim exception. If the departure record, made at the time of departure, marked the successor's holding interim — naming the return as expected, and stating the condition or date on which it would occur — then the standing was lent, not transferred. The interim holder held only travelled standing on pending challenges, never full standing, and could not earn full standing on the sheet by grading or deciding while interim, because the lending record fenced them to defence and answer for the interim's duration. On the return record, the original custodian's standing restores exactly as it stood at departure: full standing returns as full standing, fenced standing as fenced standing, and standing suspended by a tainted transfer returns still suspended. Nothing was lost, because nothing was given — the interim holder was a keeper, not an heir. An interim marking made after departure, or added to the record once a dispute has arisen over the return, counts for nothing; the marking must predate the dispute, or the return is outright.

The third rule is the binding absence. Everything decided, bounded, or graded while the original custodian was away binds the returnee. A class bounded or split by a seated decider during the absence stays bounded or split; a challenge decided in the absence stays decided, and the returnee may not reopen it by virtue of returning. The returnee answers pending challenges from the ledger as it stands on return, not from the ledger as they left it. Where the absence changed a class's boundary, the returnee's inherited or restored standing attaches to the class as it now stands, and any fresh challenge they wish to bring must be earned under T-767 and filed against the new boundary. Return restores a speaker, never a state.

The fourth rule is the interim holder's exit. On the return record, the interim holder's travelled standing lapses. Their answers on pending challenges stand, and any grading they signed while interim stands as a grading — a signed grading is a record, not a standing — but they hold no standing on the sheet after return unless they held standing of their own before the interim began, in which case that prior standing restores as it stood. An interim holder who was a stranger before is a stranger after; an interim holder who was a standing reader before returns to being a standing reader, not to being custodian. The return record names both the lapsing and the restoring, so the next reader is never left guessing who may speak.

The fifth rule is the avoidance bar. Where the departure record, or a filing in the ledger, shows the departure was made to avoid deciding a challenge the custodian expected to lose, the interim exception does not apply even if the departure was marked interim. The returnee is treated as outright: pending challenges inherited fenced, fresh business unearned, and the avoided challenge is decided by a fresh disinterested decider before the returnee may speak for the class as anything but a fenced defender. This rule decides only that avoidance defeats restoration; whether avoidance further forfeits standing on return, and what counts as showing avoidance, are left to T-768's evasion problem, still open. A custodian may lend their standing, but not lend it to dodge a decision and collect it again on return.

**The named forms**, all to T-289: the Outright Return — a return treated as a fresh incoming transfer, pending challenges inherited fenced, fresh business unearned. The Interim Record — a departure record made at departure marking the successor's holding interim, without which no restoration is available. The Lent Standing — standing held by an interim keeper, fenced to defence and answer, lapsing on return. The Binding Absence — the record made while the custodian was away, which binds the returnee whole. The Avoidance Bar — the rule that a departure to dodge a decision defeats interim restoration.

**The grades.** T-767's challenge state gains a return state per relied letter: RESTORED where an interim return revived the custodian's standing as it stood at departure; RETURNED-INHERITED where an outright return left the custodian with fenced standing on pending challenges alone; LAPSED where an interim holder's travelled standing ended on the return record. A class under a pending challenge grades UNBOUNDED under T-766 whatever its return state; return states govern who may speak, never whether the hold stands.

**Distinguished from the chain it answers.** From T-768's travelling standing (there standing travelled forward to an incoming custodian on pending challenges; here the same standing is asked to travel backward to its former holder, and the answer is that it does so only when it was lent, never when it was given). From T-768's transfer record (there the record effected the handover; here a second record effects the return, and a departure record's interim marking is what separates a lending from a giving — a marking that must predate any dispute over the return). From T-768's forward-only transfer effects (there a transfer neither revived decided challenges nor rewrote signed gradings; here the absence binds likewise, and the returnee inherits the ledger as it stands, not as they left it). From T-767's earned standing (there standing was earned by signing, never assumed by reading; here past signing earns nothing present on an outright return, and only the interim exception lets prior standing revive — because it was never surrendered).

**T-770 — the Late Marking Rule — designed:** T-769 left its interim-marking-timing problem open: it said an interim marking made after departure, or added once a dispute has arisen over the return, counts for nothing, and the marking must predate the dispute — but it never distinguished a late marking made in good time, before any dispute and before anything relied on the absence of a marking, from one made to win a dispute already forming. T-770 answers: a late marking counts only as a correction, never as a new bargain; it must be proved by a contemporaneous trace, countersigned by both holders, and entered before any act relied on outright status — and even then it restores prospectively only, never backward to departure.

The first rule is correction only. A marking added after departure is effective only where it corrects an omission: the departure papers, or a writing made at departure, must already show interim intent — a letter naming the return as expected, an instruction stating the condition or date of return, a successor's acceptance marked interim in its own hand. The late entry then supplies the marking the record should have carried, and nothing more. Where no contemporaneous trace shows interim intent, a late marking creates intent that never existed at departure, and counts for nothing: the return is outright, however sincerely both holders now wish it interim. A correction repairs a record; it does not rewrite a bargain.

The second rule is countersignature. A late marking must be signed by both the original custodian and the interim holder, dated as late, and stating the reason for the omission — the clerk's error, the lost page, the marking made on a copy that never reached the ledger. A marking signed by one holder alone is not a defective marking; it is a note, in the same sense as T-767's incomplete filing, and grades nothing. The countersignature is what separates a shared correction from a unilateral claim: the interim holder, who stands to lose full standing if the return restores, must agree the holding was lent, and the original custodian must own the omission.

The third rule is pre-reliance. A late marking must be entered before any act made in reliance on outright status during the absence: a grading signed, a challenge filed or decided, a boundary moved, a control set built for a class as an outright holder's class. Once such an act exists, the late marking cannot retroactively convert it. The act stands exactly as an outright holder's act stands, and for every class that act touched, the return stays outright even if the marking cures the rest of the sheet. A sheet may therefore return split: corrected classes restore, reliance-touched classes do not, and the return record names which is which, class by class, so the next reader is never left guessing.

The fourth rule is prospective restoration. Even a valid late marking restores standing from the date of its entry, not from departure. The interim holder's acts in the gap — between departure and the late entry — stand as the acts of the holder the ledger then showed, and the decisions and gradings made in the gap bind the returnee under T-769's binding absence. The late marking does not reach back and re-characterise the gap as a lending; it converts the holding from its entry forward, and the return, when it comes, restores standing as it stood at departure only for classes untouched by reliance in the gap. Restoration looks forward from the correction, never backward to the omission.

The fifth rule is the dispute freeze. Once a dispute over the return has arisen — a challenge filed against a class the return would affect, a decider seated on such a challenge, or a petition adopted into a challenge by a standing holder — the record freezes, and no marking, however well-evidenced and countersigned, counts after the freeze. The freeze is the hard edge of T-769's "must predate the dispute": a marking entered the day before the dispute, with its trace and countersignature, is a correction; the same marking entered the day after is a move in the dispute, and the ledger records it as a note. A dispute withdrawn before decision does not thaw the freeze for a marking already barred; a fresh marking after withdrawal must still satisfy the first four rules, and the withdrawn dispute itself counts as a reliance act for the classes it touched.

**The named forms**, all to T-289: the Late Marking — a marking added to a departure record after departure, effective only as a correction. The Contemporaneous Trace — a writing made at departure showing interim intent, without which no late marking counts. The Countersigned Correction — a late marking signed by both holders, dated as late, stating the omission's reason. The Reliance Act — any grading, filing, decision, or boundary move made while the ledger showed the holding outright, which a late marking cannot convert. The Frozen Record — a ledger closed to markings once a return dispute has arisen.

**The grades.** T-767's challenge state gains a marking state per relied letter: MARKED-AT-DEPARTURE where the departure record carried the interim marking from the start; CORRECTED where a valid late marking, traced, countersigned, and pre-reliance, converted the holding; UNMARKED where no marking exists and the return is outright; FROZEN where a return dispute arose before any marking, barring every later marking for the classes it touched. A class under a pending challenge grades UNBOUNDED under T-766 whatever its marking state; marking states govern who may speak on return, never whether the hold stands.

**Distinguished from the chain it answers.** From T-769's interim exception (there a marking made at departure lent standing, and the return restored it exactly as it stood; here a marking made after departure only corrects, and restoration runs from the correction, never from departure). From T-768's transfer record (there the record effected the handover; here a late entry amends the record but does not rewrite the acts made while the record showed outright). From T-767's filing contents (there a filing missing an element was a note grading nothing; here a single-signed late marking is likewise a note, and a post-freeze marking is a note whatever its signatures). From T-766's forward-only re-grading (there a boundary change re-graded forward; here a corrected restoration is forward-only too — it neither revives decided challenges nor converts reliance acts in the gap).

**What this pairs with.** T-769's Return Rule (the timing this rule decides — T-769 required a marking predating the dispute without saying what a pre-dispute late marking must prove, and T-770 supplies the correction-only test, the countersignature, the pre-reliance bar, the prospective restoration, and the dispute freeze that timing needed). **T-771 — the Trace Form Rule — designed:** T-770 left its evidence-form problem open: it required a late marking to be proved by a contemporaneous trace, and defined that trace as a writing made at departure showing interim intent — but never said whether sworn oral testimony of interim intent at departure suffices where the papers are silent, or whether only a writing counts. T-771 answers: a writing counts, testimony alone never does; testimony may explain a writing that exists, or prove a writing that was lost when a second contemporaneous record corroborates it, but where the papers are silent in full, unanimous sworn testimony counts for nothing.

The first rule is writing controls. A trace is a writing made at or before departure that shows interim intent on its face: a letter naming the return as expected, an instruction stating the condition or date of return, a successor's acceptance marked interim in its own hand, or a clerk's docket entry recording the departure as interim. An original counts, and a true copy made at departure counts as the writing it copies. The writing's date is judged by its own face and by the ledger around it, not by the date anyone later swears to it: a writing dated after departure is a late marking's companion, not its trace, and a writing with no date counts only where a dated ledger entry places it at departure. The trace must exist in the record before the correction is sought; a writing produced for the first time with the late marking, however old it claims to be, is examined as a claim, not received as a trace.

The second rule is testimony explains, never creates. Sworn testimony may identify the author of an existing writing, fix its date where the ledger places it, or explain a term the writing uses — "lent" where the house word was "lent," a condition named in shorthand. What testimony may not do is supply the intent itself: it may not turn a silent paper into an interim lending, nor turn a paper that says outright into one that says interim. A witness who swears "we always meant it interim" where no writing says so has offered a bargain, not a trace, and the ledger records the testimony as a note in the same sense as T-767's incomplete filing and T-770's single-signed marking: a note grades nothing. Intent that lived only in spoken words at departure died with the departure, so far as the correction is concerned.

The third rule is corroborated loss. Where a writing existed at departure and was since lost — the lost page, the burned letter, the copy that never reached the ledger — testimony that it existed counts, but only with a second contemporaneous record corroborating it: a clerk's docket entry naming the writing, a ledger entry recording its receipt, a dated copy held by another hand, or another holder's letter referring to it before the loss. Testimony plus the second record together make a trace, and the late marking may then proceed under T-770's remaining rules. Testimony without the second record is a single voice asking the ledger to believe a paper it cannot see, and counts for nothing. The second record need not itself show interim intent in full; it must show that a writing of the kind claimed existed at departure, so the testimony is proving a loss rather than inventing a paper.

The fourth rule is the papers-silent bar. Where no writing, no copy, no docket entry, and no ledger entry exists at all — where the departure left no paper of any kind touching interim intent — sworn testimony, however unanimous and however disinterested, counts for nothing. Two holders agreeing, a clerk agreeing with them, and a witness agreeing with all three still leave the papers silent, and silence is the same state as T-770's no-trace case: the return is outright. This bar is what keeps a correction from becoming a new bargain by acclamation: if spoken agreement could supply a trace, every outright return both holders regretted would correct itself, and T-770's correction-only rule would be a formality. A correction repairs a record; a record must first exist to be repaired.

The fifth rule is the freeze and interest bars. Testimony taken after a return dispute has frozen the record under T-770 counts for nothing on the frozen classes, whatever it swears and whoever swears it: the freeze closes the record to markings, and it closes it to the evidence that would support them. Testimony from a beneficiary — a holder who gains standing if the correction succeeds — counts only where a disinterested record corroborates it, under the third rule; a beneficiary's uncorroborated word is a claim, not a trace, even before any freeze. Testimony from a disinterested witness still needs a writing to explain or a loss to corroborate: disinterest strengthens testimony, it does not promote it into a writing. These bars apply class by class, like T-770's pre-reliance bar: testimony barred on a reliance-touched class may still explain a writing on an untouched class, and the return record names which is which.

**The named forms**, all to T-289: the Departure Writing — a writing made at or before departure showing interim intent, the only unassisted trace. The Explaining Testimony — sworn words that identify, date, or gloss an existing writing, never supplying its intent. The Corroborated Loss — testimony of a lost writing joined to a second contemporaneous record, together a trace. The Silent Papers — a departure that left no writing, copy, docket, or ledger entry touching interim intent, where testimony counts for nothing. The Interested Witness — a holder who gains standing from the correction, whose word alone is a claim, not a trace.

**The grades.** T-770's marking state gains a trace state per relied letter: WRITTEN where a departure writing shows interim intent on its face; EXPLAINED where testimony only identifies, dates, or glosses such a writing; CORROBORATED-LOST where testimony of a lost writing joins a second contemporaneous record; UNTRACED where the papers are silent, or testimony stands alone, or the freeze or interest bar applies. Only WRITTEN, EXPLAINED, and CORROBORATED-LOST may support a CORRECTED marking under T-770; UNTRACED leaves the marking UNMARKED, whatever the testimony swore. A class under a pending challenge grades UNBOUNDED under T-766 whatever its trace state; trace states govern what evidence a correction may rest on, never whether the hold stands.

**Distinguished from the chain it answers.** From T-770's trace (there a trace was defined as a writing without deciding whether testimony could substitute; here the substitution is refused, and testimony is given its lesser offices of explaining and corroborating). **T-772 — the Corroboration Form Rule — designed:** T-771 left its corroboration-form problem open: its third rule let testimony of a lost writing count when a second contemporaneous record corroborated it, but never said whether that second record must itself be disinterested, or whether the beneficiary's own diary or ledger entry, made at departure, corroborates their own testimony. T-772 answers: authorship alone does not disqualify a second record, and disinterest alone does not qualify one — what qualifies it is independence from the claimant's later control, proved by lodging: a second record counts when it passed out of the beneficiary's sole keeping before the dispute arose, whether its author was the beneficiary or a stranger; a record that stayed in the beneficiary's sole keeping until the correction was sought counts for nothing, however contemporaneous it claims to be.

The first rule is lodging, not authorship. A second record corroborates a lost writing when, at or before departure, it was lodged somewhere the beneficiary could not afterwards rewrite it unseen: entered in a clerk's docket, filed in a shared ledger, delivered to another holder, posted to a custodian, or held by a third hand. A clerk's docket entry naming the lost writing counts, and so does the beneficiary's own letter delivered to the successor before departure, and so does the beneficiary's own ledger entry once that ledger was filed with the clerk — because in each case the record left the beneficiary's sole keeping while the dispute was still unborn, and any later alteration would have to defeat a keeper other than the claimant. Authorship is the wrong test: a stranger's record kept by the beneficiary alone is no better than the beneficiary's own, and the beneficiary's own record lodged with a stranger is no worse than a stranger's.

The second rule is the unlodged private record counts for nothing. A diary kept at home, a notebook never shown, a ledger page never filed, a draft never sent — each may be genuinely contemporaneous, and each proves nothing, because nothing stood between the claimant and its revision once the correction became worth winning. The ledger cannot distinguish a diary honestly kept from a diary honestly kept and quietly amended, and it does not try: a record that never left the claimant's sole keeping is testimony in paper form, not a second record. Two voices are required for a corroborated loss under T-771, and a voice plus its own echo is one voice. This bar holds even where the private record is detailed, even where its ink and paper test as old, and even where the claimant swears no hand touched it since departure — age proves the paper, not the entry, and the entry is the thing in dispute.

The third rule is the shared ledger and the filed copy. A ledger counts as lodged when it was a shared instrument at departure — kept by the house, read by the successor, or filed with the clerk — and not when it became shared afterwards. A beneficiary who files their private diary with the correction, or who shows it to the successor for the first time during the dispute, has lodged it too late: lodging after the dispute arose is presentation, not corroboration, and it proves only that the claimant possesses a paper now. A copy counts as lodged on the same test: a copy delivered to another hand at departure corroborates, while a copy kept beside the original until the original was lost corroborates nothing, because the same loss that took the original leaves the copy's provenance to the claimant's word alone. Where the ledger's filing date is itself disputed, the filing is proved the way T-771 proves a writing's date: by its own face and by the ledger around it, not by later swearing.

The fourth rule is the third hand need not be disinterested, only independent. A second record held by a holder who gains nothing from the correction counts, and so does one held by a holder who gains from it — provided that holder is not the claimant, and provided the record reached that holder before the dispute. Two beneficiaries corroborating each other's lost writings do not corroborate each other: where each stands to gain from the other's correction, their exchange is a bargain, not a lodging, and the pair counts as one interested voice, not two. But a successor who gains standing from the correction may still hold a corroborating record for the original custodian's lost writing, because the record's lodging predates the gain and the holder cannot rewrite a paper the claimant could not reach — interest in the outcome does not defeat a lodging made before the outcome was in play. Independence means the claimant could not alter the record unseen; it does not mean every keeper was indifferent.

The fifth rule is the corroboration bars follow T-771's bars. A second record produced only after a return dispute froze the record under T-770 counts for nothing on the frozen classes, whatever hand held it: the freeze closes the record to markings and to the evidence that would support them, and a lodged record first produced after the freeze is examined as a claim, not received as a trace. A corroborating record that touches only some classes corroborates only those classes, class by class like T-771's freeze and interest bars: a docket entry naming the lost letter on one passage does not corroborate a lost instruction on another. And a lodged second record that contradicts the testimony — a docket entry naming a different writing, a delivered letter saying outright where the testimony claims interim — defeats the corroboration outright rather than merely failing to support it: a trace contradicted by its own corroboration is no trace, and the marking grades UNTRACED, not merely unproven.

**The named forms**, all to T-289: the Lodged Record — a second contemporaneous record that passed out of the beneficiary's sole keeping before the dispute, the only qualifying corroboration. The Unlodged Private Record — a diary, notebook, or ledger page that stayed in the claimant's sole keeping until the correction was sought, testimony in paper form. The Shared Ledger — a ledger kept by the house, read by the successor, or filed with the clerk at departure, lodged by its sharing. The Interested Keeper — a holder who gains from the correction yet still holds a valid corroboration, because the lodging predates the gain and the claimant could not reach the paper. The Contradicted Trace — a corroboration whose own contents defeat the testimony it was offered to support, grading UNTRACED outright.

**The grades.** T-771's trace states gain a corroboration state per relied loss: LODGED where the second record passed out of the beneficiary's sole keeping before the dispute; UNLODGED where it stayed in the claimant's sole keeping until the correction was sought; LATE-LODGED where it was shared or filed only after the dispute arose; CONTRADICTED where its contents defeat the testimony. Only LODGED supports a CORROBORATED-LOST trace under T-771; UNLODGED, LATE-LODGED, and CONTRADICTED leave the trace UNTRACED, whatever the testimony swore and whatever hand held the paper. A class under a pending challenge grades UNBOUNDED under T-766 whatever its corroboration state; corroboration states govern what evidence a correction may rest on, never whether the hold stands.
